A really awesome interactive story. The story is presented to you as you read through message archives. More and more messages are unlocked as you progress, giving you more details and filling in holes in the story. Simple dialogue choices allow you to express your interpretations of the events, and are met with emotional responses. This game isn't for everybody, and I was even turned off at first; but as I played it, I became engaged with the story and couldn't stop. Completed the game in about 3 hours and only achieved a 70% completion. There are multiple endings available, and some additional dialogue if you like multiple play-throughs.

Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 throws you into one of Naruto lore's most titanic battles right from the start. Without any preamble you find yourself clashing with the 20-story-tall Nine-Tailed Demon Fox as he ravages Naruto's home village. Except it isn't Naruto's home village, because he hasn't been born yet. Because this is, at last, the series' cataclysmic battle from the past that's been teased for years, but never fully shown before. It's a great first impression, and it sets the pace for the best Ultimate Ninja Storm to date.
...And you're flung straight into it. First as Naruto's father, who must face off against the masked mastermind controlling the gigantic beast, and then as the Third Hokage in a breathtaking, intense battle that's fought leaping from rooftop to rooftop, circling around this monstrously large terror, coordinating with fellow ninja to hold the creature at bay. This series has pushed its visual spectacle to new heights with every installment, but it’s in moments like this that UNS3 proves to be the most epic and most fanservice-packed.
When you’ve finally managed to take down the Demon Fox, there’s no chance to catch your breath – because you’re then flung right back to Naruto's dad, still in the middle of his own fight. UNS3 bounces around like this dynamically. You can be halfway through a major clash, then the focus will shift to another battlefield or point in time and have you fight a second, simultaneous fight before circling you back around to your starting point. It's a brilliant break from tradition that constantly keeps your attention focused and your energy up. It could've gone wrong and been distracting, but since each instance is interwoven with the storyline and serves a plot-advancing purpose, I never felt like I was bounced around for no reason.
For the most part, this is the same Ninja Storm combat as before – just a bit faster. Ultimate Ninja Storm 3's feels as if the controls have gotten tighter and more responsive, which was appreciated as I ran, dodged, and teleported my way around each 3D battleground trying to gain a positional advantage over my opponent. Some mechanics introduced in earlier installments have been tweaked, too, like the fact that you can now enter your character's "Awakened" state without waiting until their health bar has been depleted to the edge of death.
Things are a bit easier, too. UNS3's difficulty settings seem muted, as few fights will offer a true challenge to anyone who's bested any of the earlier games. The most elite players will have to seek out high-level opponents online, because the AI won't keep up with you.
At some points during the story, UNS3 offers some confusing decisions about which of two paths you want to follow. They're presented as a choice between the "Legend" path or the "Hero" path, but aren't both of those good things? I suppose being a "Legend" is more epic than just being a plain old "Hero," but it's odd phrasing – and it's made even more perplexing because you earn either Legend Points or Hero Points for picking one over the other, and the distinction between those is never adequately explained.
Experimenting with picking different story paths does open up unique cutscenes and fights not previously seen on the cartoon, though, so the confusion is worth enduring. In the opening clash against the Nine-Tailed Fox, for instance, you get to witness Choza Akimichi grow to Godzilla-like proportions and bodyslam the 20-story beast. So it's worth experimenting with, at least.
Other than that, as with the earlier Ultimate Ninja Storm games, this one sticks pretty close to retelling the cartoon's plots point for point. Those decision moments are your opportunity to deviate a bit, which keeps things from being a total retread. You’re ultimately funneled back to the core timeline after having witnessed the extra, side content, so the decisions are never too earth-shattering – you can’t end up picking a path where Naruto dies or anything like that.
Some fans will no doubt take issue with the story's ending in this installment, as it's non-canonical and probably not a reflection of what will be seen in the show. Alternate story paths diverging from the events of older episodes are fun "what if?" scenarios worth taking a look at. But when UNS3 starts projecting out past the scope of currently aired TV episodes and currently published manga to invent its own vision of Naruto's future, the waters get a little choppy.
One area that disappointed was the limited exploration in story mode – we're teased with free-roaming areas every once in awhile, but they never amount to much and you're quickly shuffling back into watching the next sequence of cutscenes. Also: do we really need all Fuu the Insect Girl as a playable character? We have over 80 now – it's probably safe to stop scraping the bottom of that barrel.
Even if the difficulty skews toward the easy side, Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 speeds up combat with more responsive controls, and the visual spectacle of it all is more stunning than ever. Just as importantly, maintaining critical emotional connections to the story, even amidst all the chaos and explosions, overrides my concerns about non-canon story choices and lets us have fun with "what if" scenarios. Ultimate Ninja Storm's reputation as Naruto's most consistently enjoyable game series is safe.

The best word to describe this game:  Potential.
As of right now, there isn't a whole lot to do except wander around and grind wolves.  You don't "level," your skills increase as you use them (which is cool), except it isn't really followed up by anything.  You don't level up your gun skill, then go to the gun shop and get a badass gun.  You level up your gun skill, then look on the auction house for a gun mod that adds "+1 armor penetration."  Meh.
Furthermore, I played 11 hours early on, then didn't play for 8 months b/c killing mutated wolves got old.  When I logged back on months later, the only thing they had changed was the UI look.  That's it.
Basically, this game looks cool as hell, and the idea is cool as hell, but it's nothing drastically new for an early access game.

In Rimworld, the story is all that matters, and anything that makes the story more interesting is a good thing, no matter how much it sets your whole colony on fire.
So go ahead, try it. Settle a colony, have your only medic go on a drug binge just after a near-fatal raid, holler as your best shooter gets beaten to death by his bearded lover for being to ugly, get the plague, then experience your first nuclear winter and sit back and relax while the cannibalism kicks in.

If you enjoy idle or clicker games you will most likely like ClickRaid.
Game revolves around killing monsters with up to five party of cursors and heroes which you can level up.
There is class system, equipment, prestiges, competition, xp, tokens and so much more.
Game play is pretty simple, there is some strategy in pushing stages, where you need to find strong party to maximize your progress, or to farm efficiantly.
Real game starts after stage 650 when you can select your first class (I think it takes ~3-5 hours to get there, maybe less)
Game development is very active! (updates every day, sometimes multiple times a day as of 2017-11-23)
Developer himself is very active with the community, you can contact him through ingame chat, discord.
How ever it is not nearly perfect, so few cons:
- There is very little, to no guidance. Have to rely on community to help you get started (they are very friendly atleast).
- UI is attrocious (there is update for it planed)
- Can be boring if you don't enjoy idle/clicker type games

Mabinogi has a *lot* of things to do so many people tend to leave and eventually come back. The population of the game fluxuates constantly and in populated cities, such as Dunbarton there are many opportunities to make new friends and find help.
Some quick tips...
-Bless your gear with holy water. This halves durability loss, and reduces repair failure rate by 60%. Get more holy water by doing the church part time job.
-Rebirth often. AP is the bottle neck for progress until you get nearly every skill to rank 1. Getting more faster is going to help, even if you are weaker right after rebirthing. Starting out you're able to rebirth daily while receiving beginner benefits until you reach a total level of 1000. After that it is once per week.
-Don't AP train early on. That's reserved for people with vast pools of unused AP, and for skills that are an incredible resource drain.
-If you don't have a personal shop bag, get the 2x5 (8x6 on the inside) one from a general store. Storage is going to be a headache, and this bag helps relieve it a bit. You can only have one personal shop bag at a time, so if you have a better one (events ocasionally give a 2x2 (8x8, 9x9, or 10x10)) then you can skip this.
-Carry a stack of bandages. Until you get a bunch of clouds or clear G19, you will be greatly inconvenienced if you ever die in a dungeon after depleting your reserve of revive stones (nao or guardian). Bandages take up a very small amount of space, and can save your run.
-I cannot stress the importance and usefulness of the mabinogi wiki. It has most if not all of the information that you could ever look for. Such as step to step instructions for generation quests to upgrade pathways and stats for varieties of armor and weapons. There is never a day that l don't utilize the wiki while playing.
If you need any further assistance and tips, I'm on the Alexina server: IGN Tsukuomi.

If you're down with visual novels/things that focus way more on story over any sort of gameplay, this is rather good. And plenty of moral ambiguity and some fairly dark/gruesome subject matter depending on what you manage to dig up. It's not exactly the feel-good game of the year, but some stuff in it might make you think.
See also: "Digital: A Love Story" and "don't take it personally, babe, it's just not your story", Christine Love's previous games/VNs, which are both also pretty good and both free.

This game is a visual novel.  If you have no idea what a visual novel is, it is essentially a Japanese-style porn game without the porn.  What you have left is a heaping supply of writing, well-translated from Korean, and a mystery that you can uncover by reading it all.
There's some game elements to it in that what you read can be shown to your AI companion to unlock more things to read.  Plus a pseudo terminal in which you type in commands that will help you unlock more things to read.
There's not much game here and you're better off with the far more fascinating predecessor which is free on the Internet.  The predecessor is called Digital: A Love Story (and it will remind you why dialing into BBS systems was a ♥♥♥♥♥).
Ultimately, there's not much here, but it can be an interesting distraction for those who like art games like Dear Esther or Home.  This game is not like either of them.

Cool, fun, quirky, like a Saturday morning Disney cartoon version of Portal. So why the negative review? Because the ending is pretty lackluster. So much so that it ruins the game for me. That is to say, however, as soon as a sequel comes out for this game that perhaps will more adequately tie up the story - get this game. The physics puzzles are very fun and can go from pathetically easy to mindbendingly difficult. I noticed that different people got held up by different puzzles, and many puzzles had more than 1 solution (though only one solution would be the easiest to execute). The characters of your crazy uncle and his extradimensional friend IKE are engaging and interesting, though not really unique. The house itself also has a character, communicated via the paintings found hanging around the grounds. It was a nice touch by the studio to have the paintings change according to which dimension you're in. A fun game for kids and adults alike, as long as you don't mind the ending being a real let-down. Hopefully a sequel will let me change the recommendation in the future.

Alright, right of the bat I need to admit that I really love this game! I can't say it's perfect, or that I never got frustrated about the lack of actual controls in the story, but overall, the good points far outweigh the bad, and I know I will be playing this over multiple times to get different endings.
As a telltale games series, this plays more like a visual novel than a standard singleplayer game. There are a lot of cutscenes and areas where you do not control movement, and often the quick time events do not require any sort of quick reflexes or skill to complete easily. This can be frustrating for someone who wants more control or consequence on their games. However, the cutscenes are well framed, incredibly well voice acted and overall quite immersive.
For me, the best part of this game is without a doubt the incredible soundtrack, along with the art style I love in Borderlands games. You don't neccesarily have to be a Borderlands fan to love this game, and I would reccomend it to anyone, but it is nicely padded with nods to earlier games and charcters in the game's universe for fans to enjoy.

This game has a neat idea behind it with being class based and multiplayer, but the overall execution is abysmal.
First and foremost, the gameplay is incredibly shallow.  The core gameplay loop quickly devolves into just mousing over tokens every now and then, and then clicking the prestige button every few minutes, while occasionally entering a captcha.  It's a perfect balance of an incredibly low amount of interactivity that it grows dreadfully boring playing it as your sole focus, but requiring enough activity that playing it alongside of another game quickly becomes irritating as your progress immediately grinds to a halt the moment your autobuy falls off.
The primary draw of the game to me was the class system, however the classes do nothing but provide passive buffs to your group.  There are no gameplay differences between them whatsoever.  Ideally your group has a mix of one of every class, so it doesn't even matter what you pick, ultimately serving as a nuisance that bars you from who you can be grouping with and still progress optimally.  Sure you can level up everything, but that's less optimal, and seemingly renders the actual choice behind your class as moot anyway.
The overall systems in the game make little sense as a whole, and reek of the developer just putting in random things as he goes along without any real vision for the game:
* Early on you rapid-fire unlock every single artifact, which then quickly become irrelevant as the costs ramp up exponentially while your boss soul growth hardly increases after you cap the priest buff out.  The dev recently "rebalanced" it, but all he did was change the cost growth so you top out around 4x as high as previously before they become irrelevant.
* One of the artifacts, enemies respawn on death, literally makes you kill slower, so the dev just lets you toggle it off instead of actually making it worthwhile.
* There's a mechanic where you put in raid souls which reduce hero cost.  You completely max this out at 90% a few hours into the game and half of the raid soul screen is then completely irrelevant.
* There's a talent tree, with a low respec cost, so the optimal solution had everybody putting everything into resource gathering and then respeccing for damage once they wanted to push a higher stage to unlock more talent points.  So the dev added an ability to save two specs and toggle between them, re-enforcing this optimal one-way-to-play talent system.  Oh, and then later on you max all the points in the talent tree and just start dumping them into an infinite point additive +100% damage bonus anyway so it's not like there was any real depth to talents regardless.
* There's a competition that happens every other day that you enter where growth of enemies is doubled, meaning you just top out at half of your highest potential stage (with some variance due to wallbosses).  Everybody just enters competition and leaves once they stop instakilling so they get roughly 2x the boss soul gain, plus some bonus tokens at the end of the day based on how far they went in competition.  This entire system has literally NO POINT to it, and you could accomplish the same thing by just making every other day give you 2x boss souls and handing out bonus tokens based on the regular highest stage, and it would end up being less tedious as you could stop having to enter/leave competition repeatedly.
* The dev one day just randomly added a lotto minigame that pays out hundreds of thousands of tokens.  Ok then.
* The dev one day decided that he was going to remove seasons because people don't like them.  Probably because they're terrible and completely make the game around replaying the beginning over and over every month, despite the game having no replay value to justify this.  And then IMMEDIATELY 180'd and decided he was going to keep them because some people defended them.  It's a huge game-defining feature, yet removing/keeping it is decided on a whim.
Furthermore, the developer appears to have no idea how any of the math in the game works together whatsoever.  Or how math in general works, for that matter.  As I mentioned earlier, boss souls quickly become irrelevant due to exponentially increasing costs, while the reward for them is linear, and the gain of them pretty much flatlines.  The rebalance merely shifted the point in which they become irrelevant, instead of fixing the issue.
Gems are incredibly special.
* Spending them to start with heroes/xp accomplishes nothing.  The entire beginning of a run very quickly has you instakilling as fast as the game allows and even maxing out the buff does not speed it up.
* Wallboss class XP caps out super fast, and instead of something logical like later Wallbosses giving more class XP and the gem buff being a multiplier, they all give a flat amount that's just added to it, and it caps way too low to have any significant impact, making it where tavern quests provide far away the vast majority of your class XP.
* Token gain is a linear bonus which makes it fantastic to start with but then costs more and more for the same bonus making it progressively worth less, and its benefit is largely counteracted with the rising token cost required to increase it as well.  (The addition of the token cost was a change done on a whim as well, by the way.)
* Damage has the same issue, as the multiplier does not significantly increase it quickly becomes largely irrelevant as you'd need a weeks worth of gems just to double your damage from it.  And it just gets worse and worse.  Keep in mind like most incremental games, there's exponential growth in enemy health, and if you aren't at least doubling your damage, you aren't having an impact on your max stage whatsoever.
But the most amazing part of all is that the vast majority of gem gain is linear growth from +gems from a talent and the merchant class buff.  It's completely nonsensical and further reinforces that prestiging the moment you stop instakilling is the only sensible way to play the game.
Class levels largely become irrelevant as the buffs either cap out (raid soul/boss soul gain) or keep steadily increasing linearly while the class XP required outpaces class XP gain off tavern quests.  Leveling warrior from 100 to 200 will only double your damage despite taking forever.  And then 400.  Yeah...
After you effectively top out the rest of the progression mechanics, the only thing that matters is a mix of round table, RSE, and sticking raid souls into hero damage.  This is because both round table and RSE provide exponential growth while only having linearly increasing costs, while hero damage is just a flat cost while functioning as a multiplier.  But since your raid souls have a fixed gain rate, this just means you progress ever so slightly slower and slower, in an immensely unsatisfying way as your raid soul gain has nothing to do with how far of a max stage you can push.  The problem is compounded by seasons, as getting rewarded 2x of your raid souls at the end of a season really just means your progress is tied to redoing the beginning of the game over and over for eternity.  And your progress doesn't matter, so who cares!
I don't think the frequent updates are a good thing, either.  Updates are pushed out clearly untested and broken on a regular basis, with little thought behind the actual changes.  Awhile back the developer made bards scale to the number of people in the group, and bard ended up giving you a negative buff when solo.  And he wanted to prevent people from stacking merchants as adding a really high +gem bonus was obscenely overpowered compared to anything else (wow who could have seen that coming?!) so he made merchant buffs average out.  As in, 50+100=75.  Absolute genius.  And just a few days ago he pushed a build live that was screwed up and let people progress super high and needed rollbacks.
I do feel like there's potential for a good game here.  But this isn't it.

At first I was just looking for a game to itch the scratch I've had for any good clicker/idle games. This scratched it with a ruby encrusted scratcher dippied in the blood of christ and the golden blood of gods. The game starts out like any Clicker/Idle; play until you get enough Souls to buy your Artifacts, buy all of them and start upgrading them. Also unlike other clickers, you don't lose the damage boost from souls; once you get that % boost, you keep it.
The real game begins once you reach stage 650, which may sound heavy, but there are a good amount of players willing to assist (Join [EON] if you're new). At stage 650 you get to choose a class and level them up to unknown amounts. Some do however have hard caps, but those caps are there to prevent them from being too strong.
The classes may affect your attack speed, the amount of attacks you do in a given time frame, help skip waves (if you have enough power to defeat multiple waves at once, you will at a 5 wave limit. The Ninja class increases that limit), increase boss damage, Raid Soul increases, Boss Soul increases, and a lot more. And then once you reach stage 3,000, you can choose a sub class, which is half the level (if high enough, will be halved if higher) of your main, giving your party their effect too.
There are Gems that are gained from killing Wallbosses (every XX99 stage) that can be used to increase Token amounts, Wallboss class exp, damage, and make you start with more Heroes upon Prestige. That is a whole extra barrel of monkeys to get into.
Speaking of classes, they are MAJOR. As of right now a full party of 5 people can have one of every class, each one complementing one another. Berserker increases click speed and turns crit % to crit dmg and Archer increase Hero speed and gives crit %.
There is so much to the game, and the Developer, who is on every day testing out new test builds and talking with the community getting ideas (as of this moment he is developing a dragon raid a player suggested that is pretty sweet), that I honestly am not skilled enough to even describe. The player base is made of amazing people, most of my time playing this is just talking and fooling around, and they aren't shy to help. I'll add a few caveats: The developer is a nice guy, some of the people I've met playing are pretty decent people, and some of the features of the game can be fun at times. With that said:
There are interesting aspects to the game unique to the incremental/idle/clicker market, such as class-based party play, a useless-but-fun guild system, and mostly transparent foreground modifiers/numbers, but because of developmental inadequacies regarding general game development, early release compared to game polish/completeness, and the eventual increase in price from 2 dollars to 5 dollars (seriously, 150% price increase?), the community has pretty much disappeared. Active concurrent players are about 200 players on a good day, 1/3rd of overall peak owners have refunded the game, and most players who are playing sit AFK (while there is currently no viable AFK/Idle play to the game, unless you have other people doing the work for you). Worst part of all, the game has memory leak/caching issues that cause players who have made themselves available to host become penalized for being the backbone of the game's ability to be played.
As of now, 3/10, can't recommend for 5 dollars. Actually this is a really fine game for the price (purchased for 1.75 when it was on sale). It has oldschool graphics, classy music and the protagonist always knows a cool answer. By the way you always have multiple choices for your answer and they do affect the storyline a little bit. You can act tough, sarcastic or just funny, just what you are up for today.
The Gameplay is kind of interesting as well. The goal is always getting to a device and stealing/hacking it. The basic mechanics are climbing/jumping with your "Bullfrog" and getting around guards by redirecting electronic devices like cameras. But you always have the choice how stylish you want to infiltrate the building. Sometimes you can choose if you just jump through a window like "BOOM HERE I COME" or if you want to let a guard open you the door by passing a redirected motion sensor.
Facing or not facing the guards is often an option as well. There are three different types of guards which differ by their sight in the dark, their resistance to knockdowns or their guts while being held at gunpoint.
Therefore you should choose wisely when and where to sneak around a guard by switching off lights or creating decoys.
The manipulable tools for stealthy actions are:
- alarms
- cameras
- doors
- electroshocks
- elevators
- handscanners (you can bait guards to use them as well)
- lights
- motion sensors
- sound sensors
- trapdoors
and later even the guards' guns.
But take it from me: The guards shoot at sight, no questions. And they are precise marksmen, unless you got a special upgrade. So kicking down a door might knock out the first guy but the second one will send you a deadly bullet. If you bought the "Resolver" (guess what, a revolver) you can hold one at gunpoint, but only as long as you really aim at him. Coming too close makes him shoot as well. One type of guard opens fire in any case because they got the bigger balls.
The way you finish a level is rated in four categories: Violence, Witnesses, Noise and Time. In addition you get a rating for optional objectives.
So far for the game mechanics, you should find out the story yourself. I strongly recommend this game for a few hours of the old days' glory.

With over 5.8k hours in this game I believe that I have legitimate ups/down and critizisms that this game could do better or just do away with.
Pros: An infinite growth rate (Accumulative level can go as high as the player would like to go due to the rebirthing system)
In depth story line that gets you intertwined with a majority of the NPC's.
Combat in the game is different from other games, which has a slight learning curve but once learned its really nice to see that a good amount of thought was put into the game.
Freedom: You can do just about anything you want from the moment you get out of the tutorial, some restrictions aply to hardmode dungeons and such but thats fairly easy to avoid cause its entirely easy to get to an expert title in less than a day. Theres a set amount of classes that you can switch to throughout mabi, it allows you to combine talents like Ninja/Gunner to create you own combos. Some are better than others yes but the game doesn't punish you for trying out new talents/combos.
New Director: A very long standing critizism of the game is that the dev's haven't been keeping up with bugs/glitches etc, but with the new director, there have been some major bug fixes just within the past few months that make the game easier to play. (I'm very aware of how this sounds seeing the games been out 9 years but better late than never) Not to mention we (NA servers) are recieving updates much faster than previously, which means we get to have the same amount of content that KR, JP, OC have. (not quite everything but we'll get to there).
SO MUCH STUFF TO DO!: With the amount of hours I have in this game you'd expect me to have completed this game 10 times over. However this really isn't the case at all. I'm no where NEAR done with this game and I don't intend to stop playing anytime soon. Though I am very far through the game (18.2k accumulative atm) I still have a bunch of quests to do that help me progress with my character and community.
Now that we've discussed some Pros, lets look at some Cons
Graphics: This can be a HUGE turnoff for ppl who take graphics in thier games seriously. I have best friends who can't play this game cause the "graphics suck" in their own words. So i'm open to the critizism that its not exactly the BEST looking game on the market. But when you look at undertale, that doesn't have great graphics either, but that GAME is good.
Bugs: There still are a few bugs during the initial quests that happen 1/100 times and can be annoying to fix, but there are always the wiki to help you guide yourself though the game.
Portion of the community is toxic: Now me myself, am not toxic. I try my best not to be, even when someone might deserve it IMO. But there are people who like to get very cruel. As in any videogame you can blacklist/block them, but they can still hit some feels from time to time. However they can still note you (another form of messaging in game that you don't have to be friends with them in order to do) that should be patched in for absolutely no communication.)
Wiki Reliant: This game is HUGE! so the help from the community can be very limited from comparison to earlier years. Most of the people who have done the beginner quests did them 2+ years ago (myself included). So when a newer player asks for help, it can be difficult for us to not say (just look on the wiki) cause its going out of your way to play a game that you want to play. But for this game its very necessary. (Not to mention you learn an incredible amount from it) So if that turns you off, you may have to suck it up.
Can feel P2W: When it comes to spending money in this game, you can't help but feel all of the rich people are spending lots of money on Gachapon to get cool stuff. And this is true to an extent. 90% of gachapon is cosmetic and doens't really help you in game except to look fancy. Now there are exceptions from certain gahcapon (SAO, Haloween gachapon, Weapen Gachapon) But those are very far and few between, are actually LOWER the price of whatever it was previously before the gacha. (Not counting the exceedingly rare .05% drop rate of some enchants *COUGH COUGH CREEPY HAUNTED COUGH COUGH*) But again those are very fare and few between. And the players that have them are people who've spent a LOT of time in game gathering gold, materials etc to help them get what they wanted.
REFORGES: Reforges came out sometime after Generation 8 or 9 with the inclusion of Demigod. (yes you can become a demigod in this game) What a reforge is, is depending on how many lines/rank, it gives you bonus's to whatever it was you were reforging, it can be anything from combat power, to transmutation bonus to elemental damage. However all reforges are completely luck based and have no real rhyme or reason. You can spend over 200 reforges on 1 weapen and still be at the lowest rank, when in comparison the guy next to you can only use 10 and get it to rank 1 with a really good damage buff. THIS IN MY OPINION NEEDS TO BE CHANGED/REVAMPED. I wish that we had it like KR does, where their reforges are available IN GAME, (though not as good as ones in the cash shop admitedly but they're still free in real life money comparison) that way everything damage wise can be done in game and it doesn't feel pay to win. SO in that aspect of reforging sure, you can say its MAYBE pay to win cause you can get rekt by bad luck, or you can get really lucky and sell whatever it is for 40m gold and be rich. *Shrugs*
End thoughts: I honestly love this game, with its quirkyness, willingness to let the player do as they please without hounding them to do missions or dungeons. The freedom of this game is what really keeps me around. Not to mention involving yourself with a group or groups of friends to go do missions dungeons or just talk is always fun. Even in all its cons I still think that its fair to try this game out and see if you like it yourself.

The Good: Puzzle game play is still addictive, RPG elements add depth, lots of missions, mini-games are fun
The Bad: Stupid story, generic characters, unbalanced difficulty, the charm is just gone
The first Puzzle Quest was amazing and it just had a lot of charm, a great story, good characters, and there was just something magical about that game. Puzzle Quest 2 is a disappointment. The core game play is still intact, but it's repetitive, has a toss away story, and just lacks the charm of the first game.
You play as a generic character who is trying to free the town from the evil Orcs and Goblins and what not and it's not very interesting at all. The first game had a nice overhead map you moved around on, but you walk around with stiff two frame animations and it's not as appealing as the first game. Even the dialog is uninteresting and just feels like unnecessary filler.
The puzzle part is the best part of the game and it's still the same. You can use you weapon to attack but you must get the fist gems and reach the amount the attack requires. There are different colored gems and matching three adds to the amount the magic spell requires. Getting four-of-a-kind grants you another turn, and five-of-a-kind as well but lands a wild card. Skulls are used to attack the enemy, and there's great depth and strategy involved and it's highly addictive still. Trying to find the right combination of spells will make you unstoppable, but there isn't a huge selection and unlocking the spells can take forever.
You can level up (thus the RPG elements), but it never feels like it does much because of how unbalanced the game is. You'll have a regular foe with 184 HP then a boss with only 72. It's weird, but you keep coming back for the addictive puzzling. Another downfall is there's hardly any useful items in the game. Finding stronger armor, weapons, and shields should increase in quality as you progress, but half way through the game you're still finding stuff form the beginning. There isn't a large variety either and using mana potions and health potions is almost useless since just playing through the puzzle board is good enough.
There are some new ideas thrown in such as "mini-games" these vary from looting treasure, picking locks, breaking down doors etc. Looting is really fun since there are only four types of symbols. Getting treasure is fun since you can drop matches so many times and matching rare chests gives you "rare" items, but they don't seem rare at all. Not so much a game as a Visual novel, Analogue puts you in the shoes of an investigator that's been tasked to collect data entries from a colony ship once thought lost. The main plot throughout Analogue is a deconstruction of the pro-verbial "fish out of water" idea, with the female protaganist being awakened out of cyrostasis into an extremely misognistic culture. The tales told are very gripping, and based on cultural values and traditions upheld during the Joseon-era of Korean history. The novel is short (I completed it in 5 hours during my first playthrough), but there are multiple endings, and the overall quality of the narratives make Analogue: A Hate Story well worth its price.

1st Impressions review.
I love it so far. You can tell where the team's inspiration came from. It reminds me of the early days of SWG and seems to have the best parts of that game, Anarchy Online, UO, Vanguard, and others.
Even in alpha the game is playable and easily worth the $20. I've been waiting for a game like this since they butchered SWG. I even went so far as to try SWG emulators and others. I played Vanguard until it went offline as well.
The good: Solid base so far. Combat is pretty fun and you get a choice between RPG (tab target) and FPS style. The mission system is convienient and being refined. The skill trees are diverse and varied. The crafting system is complex (see below). There are numerous ways to progress your character (combat, crafting, harvesting, diplomacy, entertainer etc). These  are completley viable playstyles in and of themselves. And you can technically do them all on the same character (classless, lskill point based progression with no limit on skill points accrued). Pets, tamed, bought, built. Yes, you can go tame baby creatures and raise them, build bots, genetically engineer pets, etc.
The bad: I love crafting. I spent at least a solid year on SWG doing that almost exclusively (by hand, no macros). I love the fact they are trying hard to make the crafting (and other professions) viable. That being said, at first glance I think it's a bit too complicated and interdependent at the moment. There are very few (if any) low level recipes that are useful in an of themselves. Interdependence among crafters is forced. Even most low level recipes require components from multiple disciplines. You might as well include harvesting in this as well, as your skill at harvesting affects the quality of raw and refined mats. Unfortunatley it relies on the premise there will be crafters fulfilling all the parts required. A crafter just starting out, who has no money, cannot collect higher grade mats, and/or make high grade end products, will basically be forced to run missions and grind out sub-par items for xp.
Keep in mind this is a first impression and solely an opinion. I may very well change my mind after a bit more time.
That being said, I see HUGE potential. I think they can streamline it a bit, ease up a little on the interdependence, and tone down the recipe complexity a little. Honestly, even if it doesn't change much, I'd still play and most likely craft. I don't see it attracting many crafters in it's current iteration though.
I'll update as the game progresses. This is my first review after years of playing games on Steam. I'm not the guy that generally takes time to write reviews, but I really want this game to succeed. I'm tired of the trash that's being churned out.

I'm somewhere between neutral and dislike on this game. It has it's fun elements, but the devs don't appear to understand what a sandbox game actually represents. While the game nominally supports multiple play styles, in practice the devs design the systems to force players into a very limited set of choices. It's not really a sandbox, it's an open world game with a permanently broken crafting system and a lot of missions.
The more systems you have in a game, the more choices you should feel like you have. Instead, in Repop, so many of the systems they added are gated behind strict controls that it limits choice. The dev team has a few inflexible ideas on how the game "should" be played and they don't seem trust their future player base, so players end up with only a few inflexible options.
One of the biggest draws of the old-school sandbox games Repop is supposed to be emulating is that the players were allowed a lot of latitude in what they did. That latitude is not here.
A lot of fuss is made over the crafting system. Crafting has a lot of pieces and an obtuse interface, so it's easy to mistake it for a deep and interesting system. It's _confusing_, but it's not at all deep. After figuring it out, it becomes clear that it's messy and shallow and requires very little thought. Given the same pile of ingredients, a "smart" player and a "stupid" player will make exactly the same items. I would much prefer a system that allowed for intelligent decision-making on the part of the players.
The materials chain has been designed so that all but one-fifth to two-fifths of the in-game production is useless. Most resources are useless. Most items you can create are useless. Despite designing the harvesting and crafting this way there's no system to constructively absorb all the useless cruft.
The economy is only partially player-driven. Having figured out fairly early in the process that they were too ambitious with the crafting system, the devs integrated inexpensive vendors and common loot drops of key items that are too complex or too boring to be supplied entirely by players. Have fun slaving away clicking thousands of times to skill up making circuit boards or copper wires that can be looted off any NPC human opponent, just so you can be a provider of the high-quality versions.
Lore and back story is frankly...stupid. Even the most loyal players make fun of the lore on the forums. Not surprisingly, the lore is never discussed in interviews other than to say it's an original universe.
At the time I'm writing this combat is very uneven, but it has gone through a few balance passes and there's always hope they'll get something better. Right now it's almost as bad a joke as the lore.
The systems have been pulled from older popular MMO's with very little thought of how they fit together. Like Star Wars Galaxies? You'll find creature handlers, imagine designers, and entertainers. The skill system has been lifted from Ultima Online. The siege system was borrowed from somewhere else. Endless re-cloning and some of the market mechanics come from Eve Online. Because the dev team is trying to recreate so many different games at once but have skipped the planning stage where they consider how the different systems inform the world, nothing fits together. It's just like the crafting..a lot of overly complicated or broken systems shimmed together with vendors and patches.
If you're wiling to ride their rails, the game can be fun. If you want an old-school sandbox experience, I would look elsewhere.

This game has some serious potential.  It already has things I find as glaring deficits in most modern RPGs/MMORPGs: the basis for a robust economy,  a complex crafting system that requires specialization, cooperation, and market use (and abuse!). It has player housing, both instanced and open world. I thinik it will be interesting to see how these pan out in the long term.
All this game needs now is a driver for demand:  A population that has a reason to need or want the large myriad of items that can be crafted.  How to draw a population? This is a no brainer.  Incorporate some features that other games have already done well: A good combat system, good end-game content, and good aesthetics options, both in character and the characters' possesions.  Character development is key in keeping players. The Repopulation still seems to be (understandably, given its developmental stage) lacking in these areas.  However, it is definitely one to keep an eye on in the coming months!
For now, I don't recommend picking up this game.  While it is promising so far, it does have a long way to go in order to become viable.  If it ever gets to the point that I think it's worthwhile, I will update this review and change my recommendation!

Borderlands is a science fiction first-person shooter game with RPG elements created by Gearbox Software for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, and Mac OS X. The game was revealed in the September 2007 issue of Game Informer magazine and is the first of a planned series. It was released on October 20, 2009. Borderlands features four-player 'drop-in, drop-out' cooperative online play in addition to a single-player mode, and two-player split screen co-op modes for consoles. Much of the gameplay consists of traditional first person shooter elements, combining a selection of weapons to use and a selection of enemies to battle. Players also have access to color customizable vehicles for vehicular combat. Deceased enemies drop random equipment, which is available to pick up. Like traditional RPGs, much of the players' time will be taken up by missions. There are 127 missions of varying length and complexity, 47 of these being part of the story and the other 80 as side missions. Many of these missions can be completed together. Gearbox wants to encourage players to push themselves just a bit further to complete the next mission on their list. Each mission carries its own rewards, such as new weapons and items, or perhaps revealing a new piece of the story. The game also features a gun generator similar to Diablo's random item generation system. This new system generates over 17,000,000 weapons. The system randomized the guns by changing nearly everything about them, including barrel length, round type, round size, ironsights/scope, color, building material, and even elemental damage forms added onto the attack. At any time or place, a player can melee another player to issue a challenge. When the melee is returned, a 1 vs. 1 duel starts. Players can also travel to "arenas" located at  various locations in the game world. These arenas are specifically made for competitive play, where players can face off in both free-for-all games or team-based games
(winning duels does not win items but is solely for the purpose of fun). After completing the game, players are free to roam the world and wrap up any side missions left unfinished, drop the Vault key off at Tannis and collect their reward and wander around aimlessly. After returning to the title screen and choosing characters however, players can choose to begin Playthrough 2. On the second playthrough, characters have all of the gear, skills, levels, and money that they ended the game with. All of the enemies scale up, with bandits beginning at level 34, and ascending from there. The names of enemies also adjust to reflect the difficulty setting, i.e. from psycho-maniac-lunatic, midget-little-stunted and Bruiser-Brute-Bully. At the end of Playthrough 2, all of the enemies scale again, ranging from 48-52 and dropping even better loot than before. Players can revisit and battle most of the bosses, and fight for better gear, participate in cooperative play, and fight in the arenas. Colloquially referred to as Playthrough 2.5, marking the completion of Playthrough 2's storyline missions, all enemies and missions scale to either two levels below or above the character and adapts as characters level up (this carries over to the DLCs, and will significantly increase their difficulty when Playthrough 2 of Borderlands is complete). Borderlands includes four character classes, each with unique skills, abilities and back stories. As characters level up, they gain increases to basic stats, such as health totals and accuracy. Each class also has three unique focus skill trees to develop. There are also accessory items specific to each class. The four classes are:
Brick (Berserker) - Berserk
Lilith (Siren) - Phase walk
Mordecai (Hunter) - Bloodwing
Roland (Soldier) - Scorpio turret
In the distant future, in the year 2864, several colonization ships head to Pandora, a planet on the edge of the galaxy. The colonists are drawn there in search of a better life as well as vast mineral resources said to be on the planet, free for the taking, akin to a futuristic gold rush. Some time after settling, the colonists discover that there is little the planet offers aside from some decrepit alien ruins. When the companies mining the planet leave, they let loose the criminals they had employed as forced labor and left any other colonists there. Some of the settlers seek to get rich quick by discovering alien technology. Most others are just trying to survive. After seven Earth years, the planet's slow orbit brings a transition from winter to spring, and many horrifying creatures emerge from hibernation. A beacon of hope for the remaining colonists emerges in the form of a mysterious alien Vault carved in the side of a mountain. This Vault is said to contain vast stores of alien technology and secrets. The only problem is that the people who discovered the Vault were completely wiped out by some sort of protective force. The only evidence of their discovery is a scattered radio transmission, proclaiming the Vault's majesty, but not its location.

Now I've played the DBZ Budokai series and they too had fights followed by cutscenes along with various unlockables, however the game definetely was more challenging and fun due to customization of capsule skills, true you can customize your items for this particular game but at the same time I never found myself using them EVEN ONCE!

Bottom line is that you will most likely enjoy the game if you are a fan! But truth be told, there are better installments of the franchise and it's by far not a masterpiece by itself either. I think metacritic was very generous giving this game 80 or what they did.. I wouldn't give it more than 65 at the most!

Tennis Elbow 2013 is one of few games available on PC that actually covers tennis. From the screenshots it looks like a decent indie tennis title with aged graphics and a funny name. But is that all it is? Or are its looks deceiving? This is what I think of Tennis Elbow 2013.
This game surprised me in the best of ways. After taking a keen interest in the sport earlier this year and following the WTA, I wanted a good tennis game that I could play here on Steam. I didn't know of this title until I saw someone mention how great it was on reddit and I decided to take the plunge and purchase it. And boy was it worth it.
After struggling to get to grips with janky controls and being dismayed at the UI ripped straight from developmental hell in the 90's I was ready to write the game off as a bad purchase. But I persevered with it. I was losing matches and being humiliated but I was...enjoying it. I got used to the controls and began to appreciate the weight and depth to its mechanics. This isn't just an indie tennis game. It's a serious simulation.
The controls are not easy to learn and the help screens confuse you with strange key mapping but once you learn about the different shots you can use and bind them to more natural keys, you'll soon be bossing it on the courts. You'll have to learn to time your shots or you'll be hitting balls into the centre of the court leading to inevitably being picked off. During rallies, you'll have to carefully position for certain shots or you'll mis-hit them. I wouldn't exactly say it's easy to learn but it's definitely difficult to master. Luckily there are a number of difficulties, six of them, each with a subset of ten levels. You can switch difficulties on the fly, even during the match, so the game is as easy or hard as you want it.
The game really comes into its own in its main mode; the World Tour. You can pick an existing player or create one yourself and rise from a rookie to a Grand Slam champion. There is great customization for you to create the player you want and you can assign some starting skill points into different attributes for your player. This ranges from the power in your forehand and backhand strokes, whether you have a good serve or not, speed and stamina and specialization shots such as the drop shot and lob. Once your character is done it's time to play tennis.

Having only played Top Spin 4, I'm not an authority on tennis games but this World Tour is excellent. There are dozens of different tournaments to play in with each week on a variety of different surfaces. It's all a bit overwhelming but in a good way. As a rookie, you'll have to enter the lowest tier tournaments and work your way up, playing against a roster of 1000 players. You'll even have to play qualifier matches just to compete, just like in the real sport. You earn XP every tournament and the better you do, the faster you'll improve. It's excellent when you finally make a name for yourself, not to mention satisfying.
This is the best representation I've seen of tennis in a game, but apart from the mechanics on the court, it's incredibly bare-bones. In Top Spin 4 you had little random events that would require a little input, such as opening a local night club or attending events. This game would improve a lot with a similar approach but the great gameplay more than makes up for that. The graphics are very dated, even for an older game, and the aforementioned UI is truly terrible. Which brings us to the last thing I'd like to talk about. Mods.
This game is highly moddable and the number of high quality mods available for it enhance the experience. With mods that simulate both ATP and WTA tours with character likenesses, real names(different but recognizable names in the base game,) custom courts, scoreboards, stat sheets and new UI mods, the world is your oyster.
All in all, this game is the best tennis game available right now. While its hard to play at first, once you get into the game you'll be hooked. But if you aren't a tennis fan, this game probably won't be for you as it's all about what happens on court and nothing else. As a tennis fan, this is one of the best purchases I've made, I've had many epic matches and I'll be sure to enjoy many more. A wholehearted recommendation from me!

is a hack & slash game. That means the whole game is about slaying endless throngs of foes to get better equipment and to earn experience points to level up, which yields points to spend on stats and skills.
The first thing you notice when you start the game, is the lack of information
provides. You need to choose a class for your avatar but you get no information whatsoever about the classes: what are their strengths and weaknesses, what skills will they learn, what kind of equipment can they wear, and so on. So you either pick a class at random or you start googling for some basic information on each class and their respective skill tree.
If you only bought the base game, the second thing you notice is how DLC heavy this game is. There are 14 classes to choose from, but 6 of those are locked out. When you click on these classes, a pop-up tells you which DLC you need to buy to play that class.
You have an option to play the game on 'hardcore' mode, meaning if your avatar dies, it dies for good (aka 'perma-death').
When you have decided on a class, you begin the game in a town. Here you find one NPC who triggers a Steam Achievement and one NPC you can sell stuff to. There are no merchants to buy equipment from and no NPCs to give you quests. To get ahead of myself a bit:
has no quests and no story whatsoever. It's really all about the hacking & slashing & looting.
You see 7 portals in the town, labeled act 1 through 7. Each act has 5 areas. You have to start at area 1 of act 1 and unlock each next area and eventually each next act. Again, if you only bought the base game you notice how DLC heavy this game is: 3 of the 7 portals are inactive because act 5 through 7 is DLC content. So almost half of the game.
Before entering the portal to start your adventure, the last decision to make is the difficulty setting.
has 7 difficulties. Of course, you won't be able to tangle the most difficult modes until you have gained some levels and found some decent equipment.
I started playing the game using keyboard and mouse but almost immediately switched to a controller. You see, this game plays like a 'twin stick game': you need 4 keys (or 1 stick) to move your avatar in a certain direction and another 4 keys (or another stick) to have your avatar attack in a certain direction. Add to that another 4 keys (or 4 buttons) you'll need for skills and... suffice to say, a controller is optional but highly recommended for this game.
Once you get to it,
turns out to be a decent slayerfest. You find yourself in a small area. The opponents come in waves. You see a counter telling you how many opponents of the current wave are left. When you've killed them all, a new timer counts down to the arrival of the next wave. You can press a button (default: space) to skip the countdown and have the next wave spawn immediately.
But you may want to use the time between waves to explore the area a bit. You'll find chests to loot, crates and bushes to smash and see if they contain any loot, more foes to slay and most notably: sometimes you'll come across a dungeon. These dungeons provide more foes, more loot and sometimes a miniboss.
After about five waves of foes, a miniboss spawns. When you defeat this miniboss, you've cleared the map and can move on to the next area. The fifth and final area of each act doesn't spawn a miniboss but a full-fledged boss.
You can return to the town at any time. Also, when you die you get sent back to town, unless of course you decided to play the game on hardcore mode.
Like all hack & slash games,
is all about loot drops. There are 5 qualities of items: white, blue, yellow, orange and purple. A real flaw is the item labels do not show the colour to indicate the quality of the item. All labels have plain white text. If you don't want to pick up every useless item (and you won't want to do that because inventory space is limited and white quality items sell for almost no gold), you need to look for a very thin glow on the edge of the item which shows the colour that corresponds with the quality of the item. Depending on where the item drops, i.e. the colour of the background, it can be easy or hard to spot the colour.
There's a bug in the game that often causes loot to drop through dungeon floors and disappear. Sometimes, you see a purple quality item drop... through the floor and it's gone. In a game that revolves around loot drops, a bug like that is unforgivable.
The interesting part of
's loot drops are the relics. Relics are special items that boost your stats or give you an offensive or defensive bonus. You can gather and carry as many relics as you want and the total boost to your stats will grow... until you die. When you die, you lose all the relics you had on you. This an interesting mechanic because it motivates the player to be careful and try not to die when he has collected some useful relics. There are almost 200 relics in the game, so plenty of variety there, too.
Once you finished the game on normal mode, or sooner if you feel up to it or want to grind some more levels before continuing your campaign, you can change the game's difficulty and replay areas you finished before. In that case, you'll find harder opponents and better loot in those areas. What I couldn't figure out is how to choose a difficulty and an area to make sure the loot that'll drop will be about the same level as your avatar. I've seen level 20-25 loot drop in the same area where level 80-85 loot dropped, which makes no sense.
Another thing I couldn't figure out is what to do with gold. You build up a nice amount of gold but find nothing to spend it on. Sometimes, you'll come across a merchant NPC in a dungeon where you can buy a relic for a couple of thousand of gold coins but that's it.
The game has very nice pixel art graphics. They look detailed, vibrant and colourful but not overly cartoonish.
The music of
sounds great. On the other hand, the quality of the sound effects is just so-so. There also seems to be a lack of sound effects sometimes, or maybe they're just too subtle to be noticeable.
is a decent hack & slash game. It's not the same level as the great ones like Titan Quest and Diablo, and it does have some problems and rough edges, but it is an above average experience, especially considering its low price when it's on sale or in a bundle. If you can appreciate the genre, you'll get up to a dozen of hours of fun out of
. People who fall in love with the game and buy the DLC and/or play
multiplayer (co-op) will get a lot more hours of playtime out of it.
has 5 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 while running the game.
Although it's certainly possible, it's extremely difficult to unlock all 60 Steam Achievements for
. The main reason for that is RNG. For example, there is an achievement for slaying each of the 'alternate versions' of every boss. The chance of one of those bosses spawning is very rare.
Also, there are quite a few achievements for DLC content and for online play.
Lastly, there are some achievements that only people who play
for many, many hours will attain, for example 'slay 50,000 monsters', 'collect 1,000,000 gold' and 'demolish 5000 bushes'. To give you an idea: having finished the base game (no DLC), I had about 70,000 gold. And after dabbling in the other difficulties for a couple more hours, I still haven't triggered the 'slay 6400 monsters' achievement.
Although there are a lot of achievements that revolve around numbers like that,
does not have achievement counters to show your progress (you know: '412/500' for example), which is a shame.

From the moment that I picked up a copy of Interstellar Marines about a year ago, I have enjoyed it non-stop. Despite being low budget and with a failed kickstarter campaign, the small team of developers have used every last drop of gaming knowledge to create a beautiful, well rounded, tactical shooter that will give you hours of fun, while still using your brain and previous FPS experience to come out on top of the leaderboards
I must say that I was skeptical of IM (Interstellar Marines) at first. For an extremely low price tag of fifteen dollars (now nineteen dollars), the game looked too good to be true. I saw groundbreaking graphics on what is usually a lower-end engine, Unity, alongside tactical elements similar to those of Arma. On top of that there was a ‘dynamic weather’ system that was advertised, which most games, even really expensive ones, don’t have. But I decided to buy it, and let me tell you; My breath was taken away at how perfect all of the aforementioned aspects were.
Combat in IM resembles that of Arma, just with less aimless wandering around trying to figure out what to do. Each team is well balanced, with equal weapons and accessories. Since each player has the exact same supplies as all of the others, the best players will be those who have the most skill, not those with the best guns, so if you are new, you are not going to be killed immediately by some noob who has just been there for a long time and got a bunch of overpowered guns COUGH’callofduty’COUGH. The weapon mechanics are very well made and seem quite realistic, despite being in a game about space marines.
Most games today have a cluttered hud that is splattered with different icons and maps and chat boxes, but not IM. The hud in Interstellar Marines is well implemented and is fixed onto your helmet, which can be taken off. There are only a few icons such as ammunition and comms, but other than that it is clean and pretty. When someone, or something, shoots you enough, your hud vanishes and the audio muffles itself, as if your suit is shutting off, adding to the realism.
Every map in IM is well designed, from the foggy forests to the indoor complexes. Each one is different and has it’s own little specialties. Every map changes its layout after a certain amount of time, so you never know what to expect when the buzzer sounds. On top of that, the weather and environment changes every now and then, so it can go from being pitch black to a hurricane to dense fog, which keeps you on your toes and ready for anything. I personally enjoy the darkness, which allows me to use my sweet surround sound headphones to hear where the enemies are. Why? BECAUSE I’M BATMAN! IN SPACE! WITH SEVERAL GUNS! WHO WORKS FOR THE US MILITARY!
And the best part is, it’s constantly updating. If you somehow get bored, just wait a few days and an update will come out that is jam-packed with all sorts cool new stuff. The game is constantly evolving from a bare-bones shooter to a survival-horror to a ‘day-z’-like survival game. The various campaigns are tough to beat, but that is good compared to most run and gun, shoot ‘em up games that seem to be constantly crammed down our throats by big companies like EA and Ubisoft. They are scary in some parts and epic in others and stealthy all the rest of the time. I don’t care what type of game you like, because this is all of them mashed into one big, nonlinear game.
All in all, no matter what your style is, Interstellar marines is the game for you. You can sneak around, not killing anything, or you can use your experience in games like arma to dominate the enemy team. If you like horror games, buy it! If you like action games, buy it! If you like sharks with legs, buy it! What more can I say besides stop whatever you are doing, even if you are skydiving, and buy it now.

Mabinogi, the house that looks amazing on the outside but is rotting and needs fixing on the inside. Before you even get into the game you must realize that this game was originally built for windows XP and it was amazing then but now in the era of windows 10 it needs to be rebuilt from scratch. If your machine doesn't meet the recommended requirements expect to have an unstable experience filled with random crashes and lots of lag.
Assuming you make it past the login screen the game in its current state is an "exponential curve". It's really easy for new players and you'll experence this rapid growth with daily rebriths and beginner bonuses. However after you reach atotal level of 1000 you'll significantly slow down and find that you need to invest in your gear before you take on higher level content. However to do that you will have to pay with time or money.
Many other player reviews have stated Mabinogi is essentally "pay to win". While this is infact true at the same time it is not.. A player can spend money to get OP pets and use the gatchapon to essentally get himself end game gear (if they're lucky). However at the same time a player can do the Saga missions and get himself a Pegeasis at the end(six free pets if you do it on every character) and viewing coupons which can be traded for capsels that can give rewards like black dye). So effort can be used in place of money (HOWEVER DO NOTE THAT THE USE OF MONEY WILL SPEED THINGS UP A LOT FASTER). Also Nexon sells pet adoption medals so you can essentally buy other peoples pets with gold.
Overall this game has many quirks and issues however with an amazing soundtrack and nearly infinite customization options on your clothing and looks this game has essentally captivated me. However you should only play this if you have a bunch of time to waste.

I just recently finished Tales from the Borderlands and I'm at something of a loss for words when it comes to describing this game. When I first heard that Telltale, the people behind the excellent Walking Dead Games were going to be making a Borderlands game I had a lot of misgivings. Truth be told after they made the Walking Dead I started noticing that the games they were putting out were just not as good as the Walking Dead was. They were not bad by any stretch of the imagination, but I didn't feel that they were on an equal level as the Walking Dead. Boy did this game buck that trend.
If you've played any of Telltale's recent games before than you already know what to expect. The game itself doesn't really deviate from the Telltale formula. There's lots of dialogue, some world interaction, and choices to be made along the way that can alter they way the game plays out (although I don't know by how much). As with their previous titles, the story itself is the game.
Tales from the Borderlands follows two characters. The first is a guy named Rhys who is a Hyperion company man that gets involved in a scheme to get back at another company guy. The second is a conwoman named Fiona, just trying to make it by day to day on the unforgiving world of Pandora. Both of them get wrapped up into the same story and they are retelling it to a mysterious stranger. Oftentimes, they come across as unreliable narrators as they embelish what they did or straight up lie.
Honestly, besides the Walking Dead, this is my favorite Telltale game ever. The game seems to be made with the Borderlands fan in mind when it was made, as there are lots of events that unfold throughout the game that have their beginnings in previous games. This game ends story arcs from previous games that were left unanswered while opening some new doors for the Borderlands franchise.
If you are a Borderlands fan, then there is no question, this game is a must buy. It may not be a "shoot and loot" like the other games but it is most definitely a Borderlands game. If you have never played Borderlands before, or you didn't like the other games, I still implore you to give this game a shot, it's one of the best story driven games out there.

A pure shoot-and-loot game. Even though this review is mostly for Borderlands 1, it applies to all three, so I copied it to all three. Since the games have been out for quite a while, there are convenient bundles with two or all three of them etc., make sure you check them out before purchasing.
At first, I didn't get "it" and thought that the game sucks. I thought it was just a generic shooter (and once again with failed FOV - *sigh*) with gimmicky cartoon shader, very generic loot containers, guns with somewhat randomized values, and the super obvious fetch quest cliché.
But then, a year later, I tried again - and I got "it". It's a well done generic shooter (whose FOV can be edited in a file) with an interesting fun-depressing otherworldly feel, cartoon shader, reliably balanced generic loot containers, a surprisingly powerful procedural weapons system, and simple quests that make you deal with all these things in various places and that give you some story background. What makes all this work is the whole that emerges from it. It's like acid music of the 1990s. The Roland TB-303 alone sounds boring, but if you use it right and let it play together with other stuff, it's a very powerful driver, and music history might remember you for
.
I ended up buying and playing through BL1, BL2, BL The Pre-Sequel (which came out after 1&2 but whose story plays between 1&2), and almost all DLC. No regrets. It was not a perfect experience, but there's a reason I bought and played
games, and the story didn't contribute much to this reason. It's just the mix of all the gameplay ingredients and - excuse me - the mindlessness of it. A simple but sufficiently deep shoot&loot trip that goes on for tens of hours. (According to
, roughly: BL1 20-60, BL2 30-80, BLps: 20-40)
The quests become available over time, and you can choose freely which of the ones you soaked up into your quest management screen you tackle at which time. There's an indicator expressing how hard they will be for your current character level.
I thought the procedural weapons approach would probably be stupid, that it would be e.g. just a bit more power or range. But no! There are many changing variables, even the weapon designs (and visual effects) change, fitting the weapon's character. Hunting / comparing for the best weapon and learning about where you'll probably find those and where rather not turns into a passion.
Too bad the inventory interface is not half as good as it should be. Well, at least you can mark weapons as garbage so that you can bulk-sell them once back at a vendor or machine, and you can even do a buyback for the identical price. But what
thought it would be a good idea to have the inventory interface move around incessantly? And you need to realize: You'll spend
with this interface, because comparing your guns is a core element of the game.
Then there's the fact that the game will just forget where you have already killed people - they'll just be back on your next visit and loot containers will be refilled, you don't even have to die or reload/restart the game for this. This has upsides, of course, which would be why they decided for this, e.g. now you can keep grinding, and you can enjoy your new toys and your leveled-up character against old foes. It's rather important for balancing that you can't just wipe the world clean. But even though hypothetically, people would repopulate fortresses in reality, you will have to make yourself blind to the feeling that all you're doing is in vain, your actions leave almost no lasting consequence in the world. Just like in real life, right? Except in real life, you don't constantly whip the lands with powerful guns.
What also sucks (but again makes sense, of course) is that you lose a lot of money whenever you die. There will be deaths, though, that are just unnecessary or unfair, or you might even get caught in a loop of dying, which maximizes frustration. This happened to me when I fought Wilhelm and didn't realize that I could just travel away via the obvious terminal. Why didn't I realize? I was mostly blinded by the fact that the arena is a place you can only reach by dropping in from a height that you can't jump, so you can't get out again. This clear message and the fact that I was still relatively new to Borderlands made me blind to the fact that there was an electronic exit right there.
You can't save your game. At least it's not a classic campaign shooter quicksave that bakes every relevant world state detail into a nice file. Instead, you have your character profile which will change as you progress (e.g. incl. money loss from deaths; hint: If you Alt+F4 while you're still dying, nothing is lost.), and it's rather one of those "general player state" and "checkpoint" saves. On the one hand, this very character of savegame is a good thing: Checkpoints have the clear upside of getting you more involved and making the reality more real because you can't beat it into obedience by saving/loading at your leisure. The downside is: The game completely forgets everything but you. While fortresses have been repopulated when you revisit them even without loading, there are a few aspects of the world that stick - until you exit to main menu or out of the game and then continue playing, that is. It all couldn't revolve
just around you.
And there are the quite hard boss fights. Personally, I don't like boss fights, so ignore this paragraph as an actual negative, but I just find them stressful, and what others might misinterpret to be a sense of achievement in me is really just the relief that I managed to overcome this obstacle between me and more of the satisfying gameplay I want to enjoy. You know, like 1990s Eurobeat "music" (That I never liked.) where the painful hectic rap was the desert you had to endure before reaching the next fountain, making the refrain ever so slightly better than it actually was. The game does not have a whole lot of boss fights, but I had to throw everything into them and was often very frustrated when I didn't manage, because dying cost me a bunch of cash, and I had to start the fight completely from scratch.
But Borderlands is fun. A well done shoot&loot world to forget yourself in.

The game is a purely sandbox adventure in every sense of the world. The mission system tailors itself to your playstyle, so you can do things that are purely crafting, purely combat, delivery missions, etc, or a blend of them. You can further tailor missions for specific factions. The game does not really lead you from one place to another. You move from one place to another and the missions presented to you will reflect that change.
You raise your skills by doing, not by level, as there aren't any levels. You want to raise your pistol skills, then equip a pistol and use it. A specific armor? Equip it and use it. It goes on and on. It also has viable entertainment and cooking skills, so it is conceivable to just be an entertainer.
The crafting system is fairly complex. If you want to craft, prepare to have a second job. It's an exaggeration, of course, but not by much.
Player cities. Rogue nations. PvP, either on the hardcore server, or if you go beyond the starting areas. You can concievably play the game without PvP, such as a crafter character, or by staying around the core areas.
It's an entertaining game with a lot of depth and complexity and will hopefully do well. Release looks to be later this year and it will be F2P.
