I really fell in love with the unique style of storytelling and character growth. The game has you gradually exploring and expanding on the experiences of those long past to uncover a startling mystery. The characters in the game each have a unique and very distinctive personality. Once I picked it up, I couldnt put it down- luckily a full playthrough is only about 2-3 hours.

First off, yes, the graphics aren't very good. Sometimes the players move a bit awkwardly and the overall look of the game (UI in particular) is quite dated. Seeing this initially turned me off from the game, but it seemed like people really enjoyed its accurate gameplay. I had previously played Virtua Tennis 3 on the PS3 and later purchased and enjoyed Top Spin 4 because it was less arcade-y. But Tennis Elbow 13 blows both out of the water in terms of precise gameplay that really simulates tennis.
There are a number of things about it that I really like, but the most notable is the realism when it comes to unforced errors. In most other tennis games, it's either impossible to make an unforced error (other than double faulting) or it's ridiculously difficult and will only happen after your player is extremely tired. This means that you can paint the lines on basically every shot without any risk involved. In this game, you have to precisely aim your shot and if you aim too close to the line, you may miss. If you're in an awkward position when you do it, there's a much bigger circle of uncertainty around your aimed shot, so you can easily miss if you go for too much.
Some people might have issues with the lack of licensed players, but I personally find the obvious knock-offs absolutely hilarious. Riccardo Fidirir, Nenad Djakavec, and Ruben Nodol will never fail to make me laugh. (Plus, I think there may be mods that you can download to make these accurate)
There's also a ton of granularity when it comes to skill customization and opponent level (4 levels, 10 sublevels per level). Overall, I would really recommend this game to people who want a true tennis sim. The graphics don't really bother you after a bit because the gameplay is so good and immersive (the satisfaction of struggling to beat an opponent, but then succeeding 4-6 7-6(4) 7-6(5) is fantastic). However, if you want a more arcade-y game with great graphics, Virtua Tennis is probably the way to go.
For anyone who is planning on getting this game, I really recommend using a gamepad. I personally use a PS3 controller connected to my Macbook via Bluetooth and have mapped the D-pad for movement, the X button for topspin, the square button for slice, the circle button for an accelerated shot, and the triangle button for a defensive lob. I find that it works very well. (Normally, I prefer to use the analog stick for movement, but you also use the movement input for shot aiming, which requires a lot of precision. Thus, I use the D-pad, which I got used to pretty quickly)

In my opinion (yes, all mine), this is the best Telltale game to date.
TL;DR
Good story, well written characters, great sense of humour, sentimental stuff, Borderlands "myth", development and twists over the five episodes. A full recommendation. If there's one Telltale game I'd recommend, buy this one!
Story, characters:
The story is well established, is exposed over the full five episodes and makes extremely sensible but also nice narrative twists. The two main characters are well written and flesh out through the five episode. The side characters are sufficiently crafted to not just be cardboard set pieces.
Borderlands "mythology":
All the Borderlands backstory is there including the graphics/artstyle of the game. Of course it's on Pandora involving vault hunters and Handsome Jack. Other familiar Borderlands names, brands, monsters, locations are here Scooter, Atlas, Hyperion, Dahl. Skags, Old Haven.
Configuration:
The game can be played with with mouse and keyboard or with a controller. I found the controller a bit annoying because of the QTE but that's my general annoyance with QTE and the quick reaction of navigating to certain points on a screen with a stick. Other than that the screen resolution can be set to at least 4k, so no issues from my side.

I like this game, I really do. Why won't I recommend it then? Let me explain.
Currently, the game is in decent shape, with nice gameplay, nice graphics, a reasonable amount of content for the price. The problem is, the developers say it will have so much more. The "vision" of IM is quite grand, and it would be great if it actually happened. I just doubt it will happen...
I mean, the progress is waaay too slow. Updates are few and far between (once every two-three monts), and when an update does comes out, new features are almost non-existant. Even many of the bug fixes that are stated as fixed on the changelog, are actually not fixed. It's like "This update, we are going to release the sprinting and fatigue system! In three months we will fix the broken sprinting and fatigue system! Three months after that, we will impliment our super advanced crouching system! AND, don't forget that after six more months we will add a flash light! Our game is uber-tactical with ultra advanced and realistic (unimplimented) skin system! Land sharks are just around the corner (and have been for the last year or so)! And of course, stay tuned, because we are going to take this game (advertised as a mainly SP/COOP game) and add a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ MP survival mode that no one wants, instead of focusing on the campaign or on adding more guns!"
They advertise their crouching and sprinting systems as "realistic", "advanced" and "revolutionary", and yet I do not see how they are different from any other FPS... And this is what gets to me. This dishonesty on the part of the developers.

I don't really write reviews much any more unless a game is extremely bad or extremely good since Repop falls under one of these categories here I go
Rating 15/10
Yes that's right you see it 15/10 is the rating I give Repop and I'll you'll find out why
Repop is a Sci-fi sandbox mmo that in my eye's is more of an amazing futuristic VR world feel perfectly combined with all the RPG elements we love and on top of that they expand and made every system their own.
Repop gets a 10 out of 10 just for being amazing and allowing you complete freedom and systems that are not only unique but perfectly set up.  The extra 5 points is for the fact that with all it's greatness it's still in early access beta which is impressive.  Most alpha's I enter always end up with the game being unplayable whereas Repop is not.  Keep in mind there is bugs, and stuff going haywire from time to time but the bug reporting system in game and on the forums are constantly watched, there's even GM's in game pretty much 24hours a day for in game help and most of the time the GM's have your problem fixed without you even needing to leave the game.
I definately suggest you drop all the games your playing and get this game but before you do I have a few tips for starting out.
REPOP is not your traditional "handholding" rpg, you are not guided to your next step.  it's more of a here's what you need to survive , and ya get kicked out the door.   Some people find this frustrating others love it the best way to look at it I think is to think of it this way, say you get your memory wiped and get dropped off in a different country where nobody knows you what do you do? Well ya don't just sit there and whine about it you get off your but and do what you can to survive, make money, and work your way up the ladder, well that's Repop.
When you first get into the game after you created your character and everything you will be put into the tutorial area.  This area is where you will learn the basics of playing this game.  In most MMO's gamers generally just click through the chatting and use the mission tracker and map to do the quests this technique might work well in other games but DO NOT click through,  read everything you can , absorb all the information given to you in the tutorial zone because if you don't you'll spend hours out in the real world going "How the hell" and spend more time figuring it out that it would've taken you to listen to the trainer.
Along with the fact that this game is decades ahead of any other game I've played (which is a lot) in terms of systems, features and game mechanics it's definately a must buy and the community of players repop has drawn in are an amazing bunch, they are helpful, active, dedicated , and understand the importance of community and ultimately it's that aspect that makes or breaks a game.
Repopulation is amazing definately worth every penny the Devs, Community , support and GM's are the best their is and really dedicated to bringing the best experience to all of us

As of this writing, on the startup screen this game is identified as "early access".   The single player gameplay is kinid of old school with very limited story and repetitive fairly plain levels and graphics. On the upside the game seems to run smoothly and the engine is ver responsive and seems well suited to a twitch and shoot.
I should mention that I generally don't do multiplayer, or co-op, so can't comment on those modes.  This review is only about the single player mode.  Something that is kind of surprising is that so far in the first two levels, the only enemies are these dumb robots that seem like they are modeled after the "droid" soldiers in Star Wars.  The have a similar metalic voice and the AI is kind of predictable, and a little clutzy and, well, dumb-- just like in Star Wars.  From the title, "Interstallar Marines" I was expecting some aliens or maybe a race of militant humanoids like in Kill Zone.  But, no joy-- all lyou get are these dumb robots.
As dissppointing as the robots are, a larger weakness is that there currently seems to be no way to save progress.  What this means is that if you are killed on a level you have  to start over from the beginning.  This is especially painful when almost at the end of a level.  After playing the first level  for about a half hour, and almost "exfiltrating" the compound, I was killed at the last moment (by a dumb robot who didn't die even after I emptied a full clip in hsi stupid face).  The thought of having to start from the beginning was too unpleasant to contemplate, so I quit and played a different game --one with a way to save progress.
So far this game has single player potential,  and I like to support Indie developers.  If you wnat to support development then spend a couple of bucks on this early access, but don't expect too much from the single player mode at this  point-- my guess is that the single player mode is more of an after thought with little focus or effort from the developers.  Hopefully there will be an improved single player update soon.

Eh. It was a good game. But honestly, I don't know how good. Worth the 5$ I spent? Absolutely. Worth more? Maybe. You decide.
The one issue it really faced was the lack of puzzle variety. Launch this here. Jump there. But now do it with lighter objects! And then with objects that fall up! If there were more dimensions that really felt different, interacted more often, and allowed more freedom of puzzling, the game would have hit me much harder.
Other issues being that there's little room to just futz with the dimensions, and that there aren't really enough of them. Sure they could've limited you to 4 at a time still, but they could've put in more than 4. As is, heavy and light honestly felt like two sides to the same coin, so it was really just 3 dimensions.
On top of that, if the dimensions weren't prescribed to levels, or if the developers didn't try to shoot down any varying solutions to the problems (either by making dimensions unavailable or by silly placements of walls) then the game would have felt more like a puzzle game instead of an execution game. I don't mean a game kills you, but you usually instantly know what you need to do with what you have, and you just have to do it to beat the level. It was like how Portal 2 felt after playing Portal 1. The game was enjoyable, but the exploration was gone. All the white walls were replaced by shiny paneled walls with a white panels obviously sticking out in one area.
And to add to the Portal analogy, the story didn't carry me through as strongly as the Portal 2 story did. And the game's aesthetic wasn't as pretty either. Not to bash on a small company, but the same idea has been done better by other people for cheaper cost to the consumer.
The Uncle was a fun character, but the puns can get sigh worthy, the "surprise" in the story is foreseen by the end of the first chapter, and basically the game's feel relied more on quick chuckles than anything else.
I think to sum it up, this game felt like it was made for 8 year olds. Fantastic for them, but sadly not advertised to them. Worth a look if you want a casual puzzle experience and find it on sale, but don't expect too much out of it.

EVE Online is, in my honest opinion, the only MMO truly worthy of consideration.
The problem with other MMOs is, players have no real, long-lasting impact on the game world. That boss you just killed? He's going to respawn in 2 minutes to allow for the next group of players to complete that quest. And so most MMOs are a tedious grindfest of fetch quests and uninspired raids in which every player is but a puppet in a world devoid of life, just running around on endless errands that go nowhere.
EVE is not like that.
EVE isn't a game: it's a sandbox. A hypercapitalist simulator. The players make the rules, they enforce them, and they break them. The consequences are real. Mistakes are costly, and death is permanent. The learning curve is steep. Very, very steep: more than 300 hours in, I still feel like a noob. But whether I'm mining on my own in a low-security area of space, or exploring a wormhole in search of a quick buck, or speculating on the commodity market, or trying to gain some notoriety in a remote outpost along with a rabble of scoundrels, I know that danger is lurking around the corner, and that I can't afford to let my guard down.
The friends you make in EVE are real friends. The ships and cargo you lose are worth real money.
But like a wasp in a hive, you feel like you contribute to the collective. And while a single wasp sting is only a warning,  the swarm is a sight to behold.

Tons of areas to level your character, you'll never reach the end.
I could go on but I'll put it bluntly: This is a complex game that requires some time but if you invest. it becomes extremely rewarding.  It may be comforting to know the community is very friendly and helpful and GMs are active in General and Newbie chat to help you figure out the game.

As of right now, April 2016, there is a big conflict in Null Security space. Alliances on both sides of this conflict are currently recruiting a lot of new players into their ranks, so if you ever wanted to try EVE Online out; Now might be the best time to do so.
The game is now free to play, but I would still suggest using my buddie invite link found in my profile description here on steam. It will give you 250.000 skillpoints upon account creation, which is a good few days worth of skill training and can be pretty useful for anyone who wants to get into the game :)
EVE Online is a very time consuming game but it can be very rewarding as well, depending on what you do with your time in-game. It has been said many times before but still rings true: The game is only as boring as you make it. It's a sandbox game and therefore very open-ended, it doesn't hold your hand after you're done with the tutorial.
I'd recommend you head over and do the career agents after the tutorial. It'll give you free ships, skillbooks and items to get you started. It also provides you with a small taste of the things you can do in-game like; Mining, industry, Missions and exploration.
For a new player I'd recommend doing exploration to get ISK. It is very profitable in low sec. and null sec. and definetly better than mining. I would also recommend you to find a corporation (Guild) that is 'newbro' friendly. Playing EVE solo is possible, but more likely to burn you out before you get into the game, joining a corp. that has a like-minded playstyle will increase your enjoyment and let you learn from more experienced players at the same time.
One last thing: You are never truly safe in this game unless you are docked. You can be killed at any time, anywhere. I'm not trying to scare you away from the game, chances are you won't be ganked until you are several months into the game. I just want you to understand that you should NEVER fly anything you can not afford to lose. It should be obvious, but some people still do and then complain about it, don't be that guy.
If you didn't know it already, you lose your ship and everything on it once you get killed. That includes cargo as well, so don't move anything extremely expensive.
EVE Online is a game that requires time to learn and patience to master, hope to see you in-game! o7

Rimworld, on its surface, is a sci-fi colony building sim with influences from Dwarf Fortress and Prison Architect. There is soooo much more to it though. First, the game was designed as a story generator, not a game, and this comes out in the gameplay; you grow attached to your colonists, and the comedy and tragedy that inevitably unfolds is sometimes moving, sometime frustrating, but ALWAYS entertaining.
Rimworld offers easy to understand gameplay and just jumping in is fairly easy. Surviving, however, isn’t. There is a learning curve here. You will die. Probably a lot. Don’t sweat it, either just reload that save  or start a new colony, learning from your mistakes. It’s even possible to continue a base that fails drastically, if you are attached to it; just wait long enough after everyone dies and someone will eventually come by to join and start anew.
Rimworld also offers nearly unlimited replayability, offering many options for worlds, terrain, and scenarios. When you’ve exhausted all that, the modding community is, hands down, amazing. From quality of life mods that just tweak the experience to new content that completely alters the game, its all there. Even when I take a break from playing I am  keeping up with the new mods.
I have also rarely seen a developer so involved with the community. He listens to what people say and the game greatly benefits from it.
Don’t wait for it to go on sale; it likely won’t. Rest assured, if you are at all intrigued, you WILL get your money’s worth.

Whether in short bursts or long durations, this a tennis sim with depth that will keep you engaged and challenged.
+Depth
+Realism
+Longevity
+High skill ceiling
-Graphics: Probably the game's worst but most insignificant fault.
-Controls: A bit clumsy, hard to learn, but intuitive once grasped or mastered.
+/- Sound: Works, minimal, true to life, but low quality.
Welcome to Tennis Elbow 2013, a tennis simulation featuring painstakingly realistic physics at the expense of graphical fidelity. It supports warmup, practice, campaign, and multiplayer modes, via double or single matches.
The gameplay in Tennis Elbow 2013 is fast and fluid, but the controls may leave you scratching your head at first. I spent a long time trying to figure out how to not hit the ball straight to the center of the court before figuring out there's a default shot that is performed even if you don't take one. So not only did the default kb+m controls not seem to allow me to take actual shots, but when using a controller, I was under the impression the shoulder buttons would, but they did not. Then I tried using the face buttons, and everything changed.
So in TE13, in order to get the ball where you want it, you have to move to get to it, move correctly to take the correct type of shot, and also move to aim the shot once you start to take it. If that sounds like a lot to deal with in a split second, then you are correct, but it is so much fun getting it right and the amount of precision with which you can crush your enemies with once you lock it down.
As stated earlier, there are a variety of gamemodes. The AI is quite competent, featuring various levels of difficulty as you ascend the ranks. If it does particularly well or poorly against you, you can opt for higher or lower difficulties. The scoring is...well, like tennis, and the hitboxes for the racket are good. There is an RPG factor here with the extensive character customization present, where you can even select your character's preferred playstyle.
I should also briefly mention that the animations are actually pretty nice, and there are quite a few. I don't care for the backpedaling animation, though. At any rate, it is a game that isn't especially fun to learn, is fun to play, and is very fun to learn to do well and play well with.
So you're not going to see the shadows and leaves falling off of trees. There will be no sunshafts or lens flares. You won't see much lighting at all, actually. You won't see everything fluttering slightly in the breeze. The character models even, are pretty poor. The physical build isn't too awfully bad, but the lack of lighting and shading and quality textures especially stands out on them, and the UI...the UI is straight out of the 80s.
The graphics aren't bad exactly (excluding the UI,) everything is functional and represents what it is supposed to. They just aren't good. In any way. They would be bad if you consider anything not having good or amazing graphics bad, but in the end, this is a game about playing tennis. Even more, it's a simulation focused on tennis. You don't need flashy effects when you hit the ball, or cinematic angles distracting you. You just need to see yourself, your opponent, and the ball going between you two.
The audio quality in Tennis Elbow 2013 is a bit low. There won't be any unrealistic uproar of a crowd 10 times bigger than any crowd ever present, nor any exaggerated effects involving fire and lazers when you hurl your ball 10 meters into the ground creating a crater amidst an explosion. What you get is simple sounds that are there when they are supposed to be. They are realistic in that sense. Hit a ball with a racket, you hear a ball being hit with a racket. On the other hand, the recording quality and the sounds themselves could be much better, but again I must stress that this is a sports sim and not a walking simulator meant to immerse you in deep story and compelling visuals and audio.
So, it gets one component majorly right, and two others, sometimes very important ones, very wrong. "What gives?" you might say, "since when is getting just one thing right good enough?" Well, I will tell you. It's enough when it is this damn fun to experience, however, I should also point out that the game is very capable of being modded, and many people have created packs featuring better/different sounds, player models, animations, courts, etc.

This is my first review ever written. I felt that after 800 total hours in this game, and that the final version of Rimworld will be released soon it deserved one. I will put it like this, this game is the best game I have ever played. My friend convinced me to buy this game last year, and while at first I was extremely skeptical that it was just a Prison Architect wannabe (considering the graphics), I was immediately convinced otherwise by the amount of depth this game can produce out of just three pawns, a world, and some factions. Not only is the game itself amazing, Tynan Sylvester (Rimworld's Original Developer) has been adding loads of new content to the game, souping up the AI of enemy raiders, constantly fixing bugs, and even adding entirely new, gamechanging systems. When you eventually have the game down to a science and you are feeling the fun trickle away, turn the the Workshop, where so many mods for what seems to be every conceivable topic are lying in wait, ready to be downloaded. This final portion of the review will serve as a warning for all those looking to buy Rimworld and my eventual final rating.
*Now, this segment are some warnings for peple who haven't bought Rimworld yet.*
This game will not be a constant firefight, and the majority of the game is actually spent gathering resources, constructing, and farming.(depending on your playstyle, of course)
You will lose in this game, and you will lose a whole lot more if you do not take the time to think about your actions.
This game will push you to the brink of insanity, as raid after raid leave your colony a smoldering ruin, barely capable of sustaining one human, let alone three. (I do feel the need to tell you that this pain could be alleviated by PLANNING, which, as I have said before, is necessary for the survival of a successful colony)
*Rating and Review*
All things considered, I give this game a 10/10. From the moment your colonists land on the rimworld to the time that they are all either dead or in space, this game will have you captivated. The developers care about their game, and have been extremely faithful in updating it, and the workshop is an (almost) limitless supplty of new material th keep Rimworld fresh and exciting, no matter how long you play it.

The primary developer, SlikeyTre, provides quality updates consistently. Furthermore, he's quite active in the community and dedicates a tremendous amount of time-effort to help individuals with any issues that may occur. In my personal opinion, I believe SlikeyTre is an amazing developer that deserves far more recognition for his contributions.
Although the mechanics are simplistic, it becomes outrageous frustrating when they don't provide adequate instructions regarding necessary information that's essential for the gameplay. Luckily, the community is very welcoming and will assist you with any questions you may have.
Overall, ClickRaid is an enjoyable game that will appeal to any fan of the Clicker genre. While multiple glitches still exist, in addition to the disappointing instructions, the incredibly inexpensive price of 1.99$ makes this a highly recommended game of my list.

The thing that bums me out about Tales From The Borderlands is that is starts out so, so, so promising and ends fairly dull and forgettable.
The game starts you out as this scummy duo of a con-artist and a corporate schmuck, it's a beautiful contrast to the authority figures and respected characters that Telltale's games have become so accustomed to. It actively encourages you to make ♥♥♥♥♥♥ decisions and be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, something I loved! It was a game with a gray decision area, letting you have attitude and take the easy way out because that's exactly how your character would act! It's great! The first 3 acts even follow this formula to a T and it feels just wonderful.
But then the fourth episode rears its ugly mug and things start getting cliched and choices become very black and white. It immediately starts with some horrendously forced attempt at a tear-jerker by killing off a character none of the cast knows much about and tries to act choked up about some guy they kind of knew dying. It's also at this point Telltale starts trying to sell a romance between Sasha and Rhys which I find equally dumb. There's no need for it here.
Episode 5 turns the plot for a u-turn by completely forgetting about the initial plot and making some crappy power-rangers fight the climax of the series. It's horrendously out of place and it doesn't satisfy the curiosity I had at the beginning of the series.
It's not all bad, but man it really hurts the overall product. I can't say I wouldn't recommend it (at least the first 3 episodes that is), but it is so very, very disappointing. I guess I'd recommend it, but it's not without problems.

I think the easiest method of telling whether or not you will like this game is this: do you like Dragon Ball Z? If so, you're probably going to like this game. If not, well, while the game won't set your world on fire, it does a lot of pretty cool things.
One of those cool things is the fact that, while there are heavy liberties taken, it DOES tell the basic story of the Dragon Ball universe. This is nice for newcomers, but the heavy liberties are more for the benefit of old fans, as these liberties make sitting through the same story we've been watching, reading, and playing for the last 30 years a somewhat fresh experience.
One of said liberties (that was advertised heavily leading up to the game's release) is the use of custom avatars. That's right, you can create your own character using any one of five universal races, those being Earthling, Saiyan, Namekian, Frieza Race, and Majin, and take said character throughout the Dragon Ball Z timeline, participating in iconic battles against the backdrop of an almost shameless excuse plot of time travel and interventions in the timestream. While I say "shameless", that does not mean "bad", as the game's story does what it should by giving you a reason to do what you are doing and context for why some random humansaiyannamekenmajinfriezaguy is helping out in these iconic fights.
But story isn't what brings you here, hopefully. Instead, you're probably wanting to hear about gameplay. Well, it's great. I mean it's far from the deepest of fighting games, but that being said I tend to agree with ProJared's opinion, which is that this game isn't really a fighting game, but more of an RPG, as you take your previously mentioned hero into battles, learn new techniques, level up, and mess around in the surprisingly large amount of customization offered.
That being said, there are a few gripes I have with the game that I would like to see addressed, possibly in a sequel? I mean as well as this game has done I wouldn't be surprised, and I'm willing to bet some people have the same gripes as me, but here goes.
Said customization is a bit of a crapshoot. While it is cool that you're capable of attaching pretty much any move you want from a vast pool of techniques throughout the series, it does kind of require a decent prior knowledge base in Dragon Ball moves, who uses them, how powerful they are, et cetera. In addition, while I REALLY like the clothing system (that is, clothing changes stats as well as your character's costume), because there is no way to preview how the costume will look on your character, you kind of have to blindly spend your money and hope you like what you get, the exceptions being the staggering amount of costumes from different characters throughout the series. You pretty much know what you're getting there, if you tap into said prior knowledge of the DB universe.
Another personal thing I would like to see changed is the option of accessing different places in the game's hub through the use of a menu. Don't get me wrong, I like the ability to walk around the hub and see other players who are online in real time, but there are times when I feel like a fast-travel menu would be nice.
One final gripe is the fact that the game is a LITTLE grind-heavy, which is both good and bad. Good in the sense that side-quests (called Parallel Quests in game) have a TON of loot to get and a nice grading system just in case your Completionist OCD wasn't bothering you enough, but bad in the sense that, if you want to continue with the story and NOT have your face rearranged, you need to put in some time with redoing main-story missions and Parallel Quests.
But as I said before, these gripes aren't game-breaking. I'm 10 hours in, and I foresee much more time spent here, and I will be keeping my eye out for a sequel. Recommended for DBZ fans, especially if it goes on sale. The uninitiated who are looking to get into the series, however, I recommend watching some gameplay videos to see if you'll like it, and, putting this as politely as I can, watch the show immediately. Heck, even watch Dragon Ball Z Kai. It has a better translation, much of the fat that bogged down the show is cut, and it's about half the length of the original show.
That or watched the abridged series. I mean....I liked it.

TL:DR at the end!
I do like this game but there are some things you should definitely be aware of if you consider buying it. But let's start from the beginning.
Character Customization:
Do not rush it! Check out builds and guides to choose which race and gender fits your playstyle. Your first character is the most important because it takes a really long time to unlock the other slots. You can delete the character and all skills and items you got so far will be saved but it would still be a waste of time.
The cosmetic customisation has some variety. You can definitely create something more or less unique...or werid.
The part where the customization truly shines is the skill-system. There is a massive amount of skills and equitment that will make you character unique. Sadly the skills aren't well balanced.
Most gear isn't dyeable. Only the starting gear and some high-end Sets.
Tutorials:
I personally found the tutorials to be bad. I had to figure out most of the controls myselfe wich brings us to the next point.
Controls:
They have their flaws especially in close-combat but you should get used to minor issues. Controller is strongly recommended! But overall it's easy to learn unless you want to memorize some insane combos.
Online:
Connecting takes way too long. Some people like to call it an mmo-something. It is not! Between Battles you are walking around in an interactive Lobby called Toki Toki City. If you have an internet connection and chose Multi-Lobby you will see other people running around as well. (but not blocking your path) You can recruit them to fight with you as NPCs. If their level is above yours you have to pay for it. This also works in offline mode but only with NPCs integrated by the developers.
You can battle with or versus other people. Beware of lags! I mean serious lags! Most people you will encounter will have lvl 80+ characters so make pvp with friends at the beginning or just wait for your character to become strong enough.
Port:
Yes, it's not the best port but not the worst either. Toki Toki city is seperated in 3 areas. 4 if you count the time-thing. These areas should be one for pc-users in my opinion. Every pc that can run this game should be able to run the whole city at once without loading screens.
The inventory isn't really sortet. There are ways for mouse and keyboard to make it way better but i guess the developers really wanted us to play with a controller anyway.
Story:
I don't like it! For me it feels like the developers were looking for a way so you can have a custom character AND replay battles from the series. Well it worked but the story around it feels forced. The battles are still fun even if some of them feel unfair and maybe 1 out of 30 jokes was funny!
The Storymode has no co-op!
Paralell Quests:
These are sort of sidemissions you can complete with 2 NPCs or 1-2 players online. As rewards you can get skills, outfits, playable characters, items, dragonballs,... Well nearly everything in the game comes from Paralell Quests!
Paralell Quests are usually fun but if you're going for a specific skill or item you may throw your PC out of the nearest window. Some things just have an insane, luck based droprate. Wanna farm that item? Do that Quest 40 times!
Dragon Balls also take a lot of farming but if you're trying to grind your way to level 100 you will have more than enough.
Leveling:
Every time you level up you'll get 3 Skillpoint. That means you'll have a total of 300 Skillpoints to invest IF you rech level 100. With 300 points you can max out 3 stats. If? It takes FOREVER! As soon as you hit level 85 you will curse the developers for how asian the amount of exp you need to level up becomes!
Gameplay:
So far i pointed out a lot of not-that-great-stuff but now it's time to praise the game!
The gameplay is really fun! Making your own character in the DB-Universe to fight with or against well knows characters from the series is a unique Experience. The combat is fast and you will often rely on muscle memory for making combos. Each build is it's own experience more or less. Each fight has little, unskippable cinematics (without lip-sync) that might be a little annoying if you repeat the stage for the 10th time. But those are usually about 3 seconds long so not a big downside. Usually they are like *character appears* "I will totally defeat you even if you killed me x times before!".
Mentor/Master System:
Very early in the game you can get a Mentor. Those are original Characters from the DB Series who will teach you skills and sometimes give (and sometimes demand) items. You fight them first. Then you make a lot of story/paralell quests to get to the next stage and fight again. Repeat this three times and you've completet a Mentor.
There are two downsides. First Mentors spawn randomly in Toki Toki city. If you look for Cell for instance that means you might have to restart a game a few times before he appears. The other downside is the time it takes to get from one stage to another. It's not too bad if you grind for stuff anyway but it still gets annoying.
DLC:
O-V-E-R-P-R-I-C-E-D-! Yes, they add content to the game. Short content that does in no way justify the price.
If you really like the game and finished the story you may buy the Season Pass but that's your decision.
TL:DR:
Dragon Ball Xenoverse is a well made fighting game that requires a lot of time to put into repetitive things.
The Story isn't well written but fun to play and if you always wanted to make yourselfe a fat, tiny, black boo with SSJ-hair this game is for you! (Note: Small Majins are not part of the meta)

After what seems like eons, Clicker Heroes' supremacy in the clicker arena seems to finally have a worthy challenger.
While ClickRaid isn't free like Clicker Heroes, it also doesn't have tons of micro-transactions. Granted, Clicker Heroes was never greedy about their micro transactions, but they were always there.
ClickRaid offers two things to pay for, the base game and a DLC that makes your cursor shiny, as well as supports the dev. I think it also increases the odds of encountering Raid Bosses, which is a good thing.
Personally, I hope the dev offers more DLC for the game, not micro transactions. More little knick-knacks to support the dev as well as pimp my cursor even further. Who knows.
So what's the biggest difference between this one and all the other clickers?
Many clicker games are single player. Some of them do a little extra, Clicker Heroes has what is basically a message board that your guild can use, though it's extremely limited. Worse yet, messages are limited to one per 30 seconds or something like that. It makes having a conversation with the guildmates quite frustrating.
ClickRaid has guilds AND a live chat, which is a core focus of the game itself. You can chat to the whole world, or you can chat to the party you're in.
The party system is really a server system. One person hosts, 4 others can join their game. Each time you encounter a Raid Boss, other players all receive Raid Souls, which are one of the games' upgrade points. Additionally, in later levels, there are classes which provide speed and damage bonuses, increased experience, increased souls, faster hero damage, etc. If you have 5 different classes in the same room, you'll find your bonuses get buffed to high heaven.
This is awesome.
If you're a clicker fan, as I am, then yes... yes you should. You should stop reading this and buy the game immediately. It's worth the very modest price of it and its "Supporters" DLC. You'll get thousands of hours out of it currently, and the dev is updating the game like
.

As of right now, April 2016, there is a big conflict in Null Security space. Alliances on both sides of this conflict are currently recruiting a lot of new players into their ranks, so if you ever wanted to try EVE Online out; Now might be the best time to do so.
The game is now free to play, but I would still suggest using my buddie invite link found in my profile description here on steam. It will give you 250.000 skillpoints upon account creation, which is a good few days worth of skill training and can be pretty useful for anyone who wants to get into the game :)
EVE Online is a very time consuming game but it can be very rewarding as well, depending on what you do with your time in-game. It has been said many times before but still rings true: The game is only as boring as you make it. It's a sandbox game and therefore very open-ended, it doesn't hold your hand after you're done with the tutorial.
I'd recommend you head over and do the career agents after the tutorial. It'll give you free ships, skillbooks and items to get you started. It also provides you with a small taste of the things you can do in-game like; Mining, industry, Missions and exploration.
For a new player I'd recommend doing exploration to get ISK. It is very profitable in low sec. and null sec. and definetly better than mining. I would also recommend you to find a corporation (Guild) that is 'newbro' friendly. Playing EVE solo is possible, but more likely to burn you out before you get into the game, joining a corp. that has a like-minded playstyle will increase your enjoyment and let you learn from more experienced players at the same time.
One last thing: You are never truly safe in this game unless you are docked. You can be killed at any time, anywhere. I'm not trying to scare you away from the game, chances are you won't be ganked until you are several months into the game. I just want you to understand that you should NEVER fly anything you can not afford to lose. It should be obvious, but some people still do and then complain about it, don't be that guy.
If you didn't know it already, you lose your ship and everything on it once you get killed. That includes cargo as well, so don't move anything extremely expensive.
EVE Online is a game that requires time to learn and patience to master, hope to see you in-game! o7

However, if you actually care about the PC as a gaming platform, and how it is treated by some publishers, then you might want to sit this one out.
Look at the screenshots in the gallery above. You see the texture quality, the lighting and visual effects such as ambient occlusion? Not there. The nice fire and ice effects on characters? Not there. You see the rain in two of the screenshots? Not even
to that weird effect that's actually in the game.
The reason for this? It's a straight PS3 port. A port of a version that was made for a console

When you look at this comparison

, you may think that the game actually looks decent enough to enjoy it. And I totally agree with this! But I do wonder why the PC has to get the inferior PS3 port? I mean, it's almost 2016, and one might think that we've actually moved away from this practice. Especially since many PS4/XboxOne games don't even get PS3/360 versions anymore.
What's even worse, is that Bandai Namco had several months to actually communicate that PC is getting the PS3 version, but instead they chose to not say anything and advertise with PS4 footage.
Amongst others, I initially gave Bandai the benefit of the doubt, and believed that the graphic settings are bugged and locked at the lowest settings, since changing them does absolutely nothing
, but it seems that they're supposed to not do anything, since the game is locked at PS3 graphics...
The game is also missing the online
that's included in the console versions. When asked on twitter for a reason, or if they would consider including it in an update, Bandai simply responded with:
Make of that what you will. The port also doesn't have cloud saves, so you better copy your savefile manually when uninstalling...
Now this is the problem with Steam's rating system. I have to decide between two options. If it were for the game itself, as it is across all platforms, I'd totally give a thumbs up, just like other people who are glad that the game is on PC. But the false advertising on the store page, the missing communication from Bandai, and general quality of the port
, simply keep me from doing so. I have to make a choice between fan and consumer here, and the consumer wins. I missed my chance to refund it, but you might wanna think twice about supporting this port, and Koei Tecmo's practices.

At first glance this game really doesn't look great - sub part graphics, sound and all around presentation. Yet it absolutely nails it as far as gameplay is concerned. I've been playing tennis games since the C64 and can confidently say that Tennis Elbow 2013 is the best one I've ever played. Games are realistic. Players frequently hit the ball out, double fault, hit the net and miss easy shots. It just feels right. It's not perfect but it is a huge step forward from the arcade style tennis games that've appeared in the last few years.
I struggled for the first 2 or 3 hours and lost every match. At first I could hardly even win a point, never mind a game or set. Stick with it for a few hours and the controls will start to feel comfortable. Download the demo from the dev's web site, stick with it for a few hours and that should tell you if you want to buy the game.
What else...I'd recommend that you download one of the mods if you want to offline play a fairly realistic pro career. They contain real tournaments, players and venues. You can start off as a 17 year old and progress through the ranks as the years pass. Right now I'm ranked number 992 of the world and have just won my second qualifying match in a tournament. If I win the next match then I'll actually get to play in an actual first round of a tournament. So yeah, starting off at the bottom isn't glamorous but it is immersive and satisfying.
Recommended!
edit: I've put a lot more hours into the game now and am really happy with it. Once you install one of the mods the visuals get a decent boost and the offline career mode is fantastic fun. A top class tennis game, even if it doesn't look like it at first glance.

This is easily the best tennis game I have played (console or PC). Some might find that odd, considering the UI and game visuals seem a bit dated. I didn't say it was the prettiest. It isn't, but it's also not terrible, either. The core gameplay is what makes this the best tennis game I have played.
The controls are excellent. They take a little getting used to and become second nature after a bit of practice. The available strikes in the game can be mapped to your preference. They are as follows:
o Normal Strike
o Short Strike
o Top Spin
o Slice
o Drop Shot
o Defensive Lob
o Acceleration
o Short Acceleration
o Aggressive Lob
o Safe Strike
The game also supports modding and has a strong community that have been modding the various iterations of the game over the years. Several mods add all the real players, statistics, animations, sounds, courts, etc. They also update the UI visuals, which is a nice touch. At this time, there are two major mod packages which seem to have most of the 'best of the best' mods from the community in a nice tidy package:
o Sam's Patch - solo World Tour play with all the real pro players (visuals, stats, animations, courts, scoreboards, etc).
o ITST - online play with all the real pro players (visuals, stats, animations, courts, scoreboards, etc).
This is strictly tennis. You won't be knocking down bowling pins in mini games for example (not that there's anything wrong with that). You will either be playing quick matches, trying your hand at an extensive career mode, or playing against others online.
If you really like tennis, this game is a no-brainer. If you are very casual, I would suggest that you download the 14-day demo that is provided on the developer's website. It even lets you play online. This should be more than enough time to see if it suits you.

TL:DR at the end!
I do like this game but there are some things you should definitely be aware of if you consider buying it. But let's start from the beginning.
Character Customization:
Do not rush it! Check out builds and guides to choose which race and gender fits your playstyle. Your first character is the most important because it takes a really long time to unlock the other slots. You can delete the character and all skills and items you got so far will be saved but it would still be a waste of time.
The cosmetic customisation has some variety. You can definitely create something more or less unique...or werid.
The part where the customization truly shines is the skill-system. There is a massive amount of skills and equitment that will make you character unique. Sadly the skills aren't well balanced.
Most gear isn't dyeable. Only the starting gear and some high-end Sets.
Tutorials:
I personally found the tutorials to be bad. I had to figure out most of the controls myselfe wich brings us to the next point.
Controls:
They have their flaws especially in close-combat but you should get used to minor issues. Controller is strongly recommended! But overall it's easy to learn unless you want to memorize some insane combos.
Online:
Connecting takes way too long. Some people like to call it an mmo-something. It is not! Between Battles you are walking around in an interactive Lobby called Toki Toki City. If you have an internet connection and chose Multi-Lobby you will see other people running around as well. (but not blocking your path) You can recruit them to fight with you as NPCs. If their level is above yours you have to pay for it. This also works in offline mode but only with NPCs integrated by the developers.
You can battle with or versus other people. Beware of lags! I mean serious lags! Most people you will encounter will have lvl 80+ characters so make pvp with friends at the beginning or just wait for your character to become strong enough.
Port:
Yes, it's not the best port but not the worst either. Toki Toki city is seperated in 3 areas. 4 if you count the time-thing. These areas should be one for pc-users in my opinion. Every pc that can run this game should be able to run the whole city at once without loading screens.
The inventory isn't really sortet. There are ways for mouse and keyboard to make it way better but i guess the developers really wanted us to play with a controller anyway.
Story:
I don't like it! For me it feels like the developers were looking for a way so you can have a custom character AND replay battles from the series. Well it worked but the story around it feels forced. The battles are still fun even if some of them feel unfair and maybe 1 out of 30 jokes was funny!
The Storymode has no co-op!
Paralell Quests:
These are sort of sidemissions you can complete with 2 NPCs or 1-2 players online. As rewards you can get skills, outfits, playable characters, items, dragonballs,... Well nearly everything in the game comes from Paralell Quests!
Paralell Quests are usually fun but if you're going for a specific skill or item you may throw your PC out of the nearest window. Some things just have an insane, luck based droprate. Wanna farm that item? Do that Quest 40 times!
Dragon Balls also take a lot of farming but if you're trying to grind your way to level 100 you will have more than enough.
Leveling:
Every time you level up you'll get 3 Skillpoint. That means you'll have a total of 300 Skillpoints to invest IF you rech level 100. With 300 points you can max out 3 stats. If? It takes FOREVER! As soon as you hit level 85 you will curse the developers for how asian the amount of exp you need to level up becomes!
Gameplay:
So far i pointed out a lot of not-that-great-stuff but now it's time to praise the game!
The gameplay is really fun! Making your own character in the DB-Universe to fight with or against well knows characters from the series is a unique Experience. The combat is fast and you will often rely on muscle memory for making combos. Each build is it's own experience more or less. Each fight has little, unskippable cinematics (without lip-sync) that might be a little annoying if you repeat the stage for the 10th time. But those are usually about 3 seconds long so not a big downside. Usually they are like *character appears* "I will totally defeat you even if you killed me x times before!".
Mentor/Master System:
Very early in the game you can get a Mentor. Those are original Characters from the DB Series who will teach you skills and sometimes give (and sometimes demand) items. You fight them first. Then you make a lot of story/paralell quests to get to the next stage and fight again. Repeat this three times and you've completet a Mentor.
There are two downsides. First Mentors spawn randomly in Toki Toki city. If you look for Cell for instance that means you might have to restart a game a few times before he appears. The other downside is the time it takes to get from one stage to another. It's not too bad if you grind for stuff anyway but it still gets annoying.
DLC:
O-V-E-R-P-R-I-C-E-D-! Yes, they add content to the game. Short content that does in no way justify the price.
If you really like the game and finished the story you may buy the Season Pass but that's your decision.
TL:DR:
Dragon Ball Xenoverse is a well made fighting game that requires a lot of time to put into repetitive things.
The Story isn't well written but fun to play and if you always wanted to make yourselfe a fat, tiny, black boo with SSJ-hair this game is for you! (Note: Small Majins are not part of the meta)

I wouldn't necessarily recommend the game at this stage, but I am interested in the game and I'd like to see where the game goes in the future.

Xenoverse is the game many of us Dragon Ball fans have been waiting for years. While it is a fairly good game, it tends to fall flat on its execution on many parts of the game.
The game revolves around your "Create a Character" and you play out the events within the Dragon Ball universe. Mira and Towa (the two main villains of this game but not featured in the shows) are disrupting previous events in history that begin to cause changes in the current timeline. You, the Future Warrior, along with Trunks and Supreme Kai of Time create the Time Patrol, a squad aimed at traveling to different timelines and restoring the timeline to how it was supposed to go originally (like in the television shows).
The main city, Toki Toki City acts as a central hub for players. It's divided into three parts (that seem some what unnecessary to split apart unless it's to help reduce lag and overcrowded maps). One section of the maps allows you take part in Parallel Quests (repeatable quests that recreate some fights and ‘What If?’ scenarios from the show) by speaking with a counter attendant, and on the other side is online battles where you can spectate, duel other players, and participate in endless battle. The second section of the maps contain the stores, while the third leads you to the Time Nest (where you can progress the main story), tournament mode setups and an altar for you to summon the Dragon Balls you can collect. Because there's only one main central hub the music in the game tends to get annoying very quickly after hearing the same song start over for the 100th time.
The chat options are limited, where you can only speak from selecting from a list of pre made sentences, phrases, questions and answers. While you can see many players moving about the city it still feels somewhat lifeless and players seem robotic. No one is really interacting with each other and most people seem to be just standing still.
The main and best feature of this game is the customization of your Create a Character. You can become mentors of the shows favorite heroes like Goku and friends where over time they'll teach you new skills related to that character. Created characters can be equipped with almost all types of apparel that the characters in the show wear; from the Red Ribbon Army uniform to Trunks GT outfit. All of these items are stat based making PVP turn into who has better gear/min-maxed their character better metagame ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Most of these items and skills are dropped from defeating enemies in Parallel Quests, but you'll often find yourself repeating them often because of the some-what low drop rates and prerequisites for some of them. Luckily there are tons and tons of skills to choose from that customizing your character never gets old. It feels like there's endless combinations and different types of 'builds' to mess around with.
The battle system is fairly simple and plays out very similar to the Tenkaichi games released on the PlayStation 2. You have a basic and heavy attack, ki-blast attacks, and dodges/blocks. There's a ki bar that allows you to use a Special Attack when one ki bar is filled and your Ultimate Attack when you reach 3 full ki bars. There's also a stamina bar that determines how many times you can teleport dodge, block and charge. The keyboard controls are decent enough to get by but you'll have a much easier time using a controller, as with most fighting games.
While the overall game is extremely fun but I think that people who aren't fans of the Dragon Ball series sadly won't find too much of interest here as the game really isn't suited for those with little interest or knowledge of the series. Anyone looking for a serious/balanced fighting game should look elsewhere.

If I could downvote this game on Steam I would.  Figuring out the puzzles is easy.  Pulling off the complex timing and repetitive reflex manuvers needed to solve them is maddening.  Being forced to restart from the beginning of a puzzle because of one mistake is the work of the devil.
The art assests and level design are the very definition off cookie-cutter layouts, and the music is as bland as it is forgettable.  John De Lancie phones this one in, but he can't take all the blame as the writing is as witless and dry as he portrays it to be.
I've actualy encountered game halting bugs while playing, where the game fails to keep track of objects being destroyed through the various dimensional shifts causing me to have to reload certain sections of the game in order to retry them.
I can't even recommend this game for kids as death is a constant factor in the game, which is handled poorly with one-liner throw-aways telling you of how bland and stale life is.  Add to the fact that some zones that appear to be safe are infact instant death only makes this situation worse.  In one area you can walk on metal plating and in another area it will kill you without rhyme nor reason.
If there was one word to describe this game, it would be "Bland."  What made this game so annoying was that I was actually trying to enjoy it, but at almost every turn the crappy gameplay would just get in the way and punish me with death for a mis-step or force me to start an entire room over for a single mis-click.
I will attest to being a masocist for challenging games, but there was no hint of a reward that would make me want to pursue playing this game further.  I can easily forgive bad gameplay if there was good writing, music or art to back it up  But this game has none of those things going for it.
One afterword:  This game was designed for consoles in mind and it shows.  If that bothers you, well that's even more of a reason NOT to play it.

In all honesty, it's a good game. It's simple, it has a lot of variety, and it's genuinly a fun game.
But, here's the thing... Aeria Games.
Aeria Games want, you guessed it, money. So most of the features in the in-game store require you to, A: Level up high enough and spend your Euro's (cash you don't pay for) or B: Pay money (Usually ranging from 15-30$...) (I'm english, there's no pound sign on my keyboard) to get the item insantly.
It gets worse, if you want your character to, let's say, wear a beret, it costs even MORE money than the weapons. I haven't spent any money on this game, but I don't want to, it seems like a waste of money to wear a hat for 7 days.
But let's talk about gameplay.
I don't have a great graphics card. But this game runs at 30-50 which is very suprising for me, atleast. On a good PC I'd say it runs at more than 120fps.
Gamemodes: Oh the variety.
You got Scenario, a 4 player co-op game mode which either has you fighting off hordes of rogue prisoners, or fight rogue robots to lead up to a big mega robot, which is really tense and fun.
Infection, a multiplayer game having players spawn in a big map, the run to camping spots. Then after 10 seconds I think 3 players will be chosen to be zombies. They gotta go kill the humans, making more infected, which leads to a giant slug-fest.
Annhialation is a tdm like gamemode. It has you killing a certain amout of players before the game ends. Simple.
Demolition, a SnD of AVA. 2 bomb sites, 1 team takes the bomb to a site to blow it up. Other team stops them.
Escort. Players must escort a tank to the end of a set course. The other team must use RPG's to stun the tank, making the escorter's repair the tank.
And that's about it for the gamemodes, I think they're is more, but these are the main ones for now.
Now, a common problem in FPS games: Hackers.
They're pretty common here. I don't encounter them in PvP modes but in the co-op modes they're is a lot of them. Just saying.
And that's about it for my review. Personally I'd rate this a 7/10 for the great gameplay mechanics but the conds being bad voice acting and p2w features, it's still pretty good.
TL;DR, Good game, p2w.

On balance, I think this game will be incredible when finished. Even now in late Alpha it's amazing, but it has some issues. First, it needs some stability fixes, still a lot of crashes while zoning. But don't get me wrong, there are NO loading screens in the open world, the "zoning" is almost totally seamless and will be more so once the new Hero Engine update is added. The graphics are sufficient now but will include HD textures with the new engine and should look fabulous
The crafting system is at the heart of the game and it is breathtaking in its depth and functionality. This is a game that keeps me up all night for just "one more turn" just like the old days, it's utterly compelling if you like to craft. Combat works well but will be more fun when more encounters are added. Right now, there are just lots of roaming mobs who will threaten your gathering.
Speeder bikes, woot!  Harvesters, complex crafting, local player merchants, faction fighting, this is so reminiscent of the original SWG that the inspiration is inescapable. Usage based skillups, endless choice of skillls and abilities, every character is guaranteed to be utterly unique. The interdependence of the crafting system along with the incredible depth and complexity assures that the best path to success will be focused specialization in a relatively small area of expertise that will give you the ability to feed the demand for sub components that no one will be able to master on their own. Everyone will be dependent on specialists. Great system that favors crafters and supplies combatants.
Siege warfare, non-instanced player housing on plots with the most unbelievable assortment of customizable furnishings ever seen in any game. The interior decorating some players have created is just phenomenal, from stylized research facilities to armed encampments.
This is a wonderful game that is young and promising, but fun to play right now. And the dev team is a dream, the owner answers questions on the forum, listens to his playerbase and is a hardcore kickass player himself. If you liked SWG, you may love this game. Gets my highest recommendation for new MMO's to watch and play.

Negative Comments are not 100% factual.
MY RATING:

Yes the company went bankrupt, yes their are only two weapons however what people are saying just isn't factual.
1) Multiplayer IS TONS fun, their is deathmatch, team dm, a mode where you respawn a friend by getting a kill and another mode that I can't remember. Their are also 1 or 2 COOP missions and a game mode where you fight against bots.
Think CSGO but with better maps, the maps are very good and have bushes and grass to hide in, the maps change as the game goes on (day, night, snow, rain, mist etc.). Even from South Africa and a ping of 200+ I had a lot of fun (ping doesn't mean much if you can hide in a bush and shoot a guy from behind, hope the make a small RSA server... please? please!).
2) Excellent community, none toxic people that report bugs and make jokes, 2nd to none.
3) Okay Graphics (COD level I would say, not BF level but acceptable), yes the graphics still overuse resources but my old GTX 660 OC does fine on highest @ 1080 and a 750ti will also. No need for a $300+ GPU.
4) Best sounds ever, even BF3 falls behind on sound.
5) Cheap, <$20 for a game that gives a lot of value and fun.
If you Like the good old shooters (like Rainbow 6 and Ghost Recon originals) this is for you, you do regain health as far as I remember but it is basically 1 shot 1 kill. Tactics like not capping a point and shooting guys as they try and cap it are a must, teams of two also help (usually I get shot and my friendly then cleans up the enemy, as I say my ping is bad).
HOWEVER SOME OF THE CRITICAL POINTS ARE TRUE:
1) Original backers will be sour that they have had to wait years, I don't blame them or the devs as the game simply didn't get enough support from the FPS crowd.
2) 2 Guns only, this is fine as the gameplay is basically 2 body or 1 head shot however more weapons are about to be released soon from what I have heard.
3) The game is early access and their are a few bugs (far less then some post releases) and A LOT of content is coming (not a bad thing is it?).

Oy vey. If the developers play their cards right, The Repopulation will cause an earthquake in the MMO market of epic proportions. A word of warning -- this game, and many others like it, will not appeal to a certain faction of MMO gamers. I would argue that this is largely due to many MMO players wanting to have everything spoon fed to them, whereas in TR you'll have to do a lot of brainstorming and theory crafting if you want to succeed. However, once you "GET IT", it'll be one of the most realistic and enjoyable gaming experiences that you'll ever partake in.  The Repopulation is in every sense of the phrase -- the ultimate successor to Star Wars Galaxies, and perhaps even has the potential to be greater. The game is overall very steady, the bugs aren't bad at all for alpha (at least on my end), the community is a breath of fresh air, the nation/city system is incredible, and the crafting is highly in-depth and fun (no, I'm seriuos, you really get the feeling that you're a genetic engineer in real life without the complex mathematics). The PvP is somewhat minimalistic at this time, but the developers have big plans including but not limited to guilds being able to siege other guilds cities (and you can fight them off with laser towers and the like). In conclusion, if anyone is even remotely interested in being apart of the next big thing, then I highly recommend that you get involved in the mix NOW and purchase early access -- you WILL NOT regret it!

Downloaded this not expecting much, but it's probably one of my favorite games right now. It's only a couple hours long, but those hours have been great.
[minor spoilers below:]
Basically, Estranged is a well-written love-letter to Half-Life 2: there's a shady corporation, hints that something went wrong, zombie-like creations, and a military-is-hunting-you deal. But where it really, really feels like Half-Life in a way I haven't seen done outside of Valve is the atmosphere. The music is amazing, especially for a free  game like this (minimalist orchestral parts, eerie electronic swells, pulsing bass), and the quiet exploration through Pacific-Northwest-style scenery was excellent. There is noise when there should be noise, but unlike most games, it isn't overly-cinematic. Walking around, solving basic puzzles felt incredibly quiet and natural. The actual game-mechanics still feel a bit blocky, and some sound-effects could use some work (your gun makes that early-90's video-game "pop" sound), but overall, I'm already looking forward to seeing Act II.

Ok lets start from the beginning. The game has a lot of features which are not so common like in other clicker games.
1) Talent System
2) A Class System
3) Multiplayer features
4) Incredible active Dev
5) This is not an idle game!!!
Ok now the long explanation:
1) Every 50 Stages u beat u gain 1 talent point which can be spend for various bonuses like more crit chance, more damage etc. When u spend 5 points you can spend those points to unlock the second row of talents and the third row will be unlocked after 10 points spend.
2) There are 6 classes so far which each on their own give unique group bonuses. Those can either stack with other party members who own the same class or the different classes build a supreme combination. ( Now there are 8 clases )
3) Ok u can party up with 4 other players and build a farm group. In this group everyone kills their own raid bosses and each killed raid boss grants the party 1 raid soul. (Those are spent to increase ur stats and also let’s you buy an arrow which multiplies your damage)
4) Well lets just say i have seen more content updates in the last 4 days than in other games ever....... Whenever someone encounters a bug it will be fixed within 10- 15mins since he is in chat or Discord almost all the time.
He accepts suggestions for new features from players and asks his community for future plans. A rare thing these days!!!
5) What do i mean when i say that this is not an idle game? Well u could basically play it as an idle game but from a scale from 1 -100 ur effectivity would be around 1% and active players will be so much stronger and faster. U have to manually collect tokens which can be spend for new classes , u have to prestige a lot ( rebirth in other games) and u have to prestige a lot to gain more power.
Ok last but not least the game is still an early access title and there are a few bugs here and there. Which is not a real problem which i stated above. The content comes fast and the improvements in the last 5 days were incredible. So give the game a chance. Oh and there is no pay to win or pay to anything. The only time u will have to pay is to buy the game and enjoy ur time! The DLC is only there to support the dev. ( Which will provide you with a small bonus to start, nothing which couldn’t be gained really fast )

This is a game I would not recommend to everyone simply because, to some, it may or may not come across as one of those "pay to win" games. While some of the items and pets in the premium shop do have some rather powerful capabilities, the absolute strongest equipment and skills are only accessible by actual gameplay. For example, that Thunder Dragon I use for my combat pet/mount starts off with a skill fittingly called Thunder Breath which when you first get this pet deals 200-300 damage per use. However, to make the best of it, you need to level this pet or any other pet like it through actual training, which for this particular pet requires you to level it up to Level 60, in which Thunder Breath then does 1,600-2,400 damage per use. For context, when you first get a pet, they all start at Level 1; you can either bring them with you while fighting mobs OR you can actually play as them to fight mobs to gain experience with.
Like I said, even if some of the stuff like what I mentioned above appears pay to win, you still need to put actual effort into even the stuff you pay for in order for it to become a killing machine if you intend to use some of your pets in battles with you and such. Now then, that aside, let me get into another example; the racial transformations, demigod skills, and the brionac. All three of these are stuff that you can absolutely NOT simply buy your way to victory with unlocking these, among other skills I'm not fully aware of that were introduced after these ones. My point is, do not let the cash shop get to you and make your judgment of the game too early before you actually get into the game and play it for yourself to see what it is actually like. It is true, though; some of the pets and other items in the cash shop can be overpowered, but to be perfectly honest, you're more than likely to get mad with the purely cosmetic purchases than the ones that affect actual gameplay.
In terms of how you play the game, the game itself is very open ended for how you ultimately want to play. Once per week, you're able to rebirth to reset things like your character's age and level, but your skills and training for them will be intact. When you rebirth, you'll be able to select a talent which for the most part all it does in the long run is give you a 2x training bonus for skills within that talent, but for some skills, you need to have the talent active to learn a certain set of skills related to it. It's not a big annoyance, but I can understand if it does annoy some when you're just getting started. Combat talents give you access to various combat related skills as you'd expect, but life talents give you special perks such as +50% in part-time job gold rewards.
As I mentioned, Mabinogi is not a game I'd recommend to everyone, but it is a good game if you're willing to actually give it a chance. I'd say sink about a week into the game to experiment with the gameplay, quests, and skills, and then come up with a decision of your own regarding the game. As somebody who has been with the game since 2009, I've had many ups and downs with the game before, but most of the negatives I've had with the game originally had long since been patched out of the game and things are generally a lot easier nowadays for anything you're desiring to accomplish. Not only that, but the new tutorial questline nowadays also flat up gives you access to free pets that'll make your early playing experience much easier to begin with.
The actual game proper has what are the generation quests which for the most part are optional, and primarily for bragging rights because these are by no means easy quests no matter how you choose to approach these quests when you start. When you start off, you're probably not going to be strong enough to even take on the enemies in specific dungeons or missions that are generally weaker than what you'll be facing towards the very end of a given generation. If you want to clear the generation quests at all, it is advised to group up or simply get good at soloing specific quests that won't let you bring a party. As of 2017, activity is pretty low in general for the game's servers, but it's still possible to find a decent party if you go to the party board for help.
Perhaps the one thing that might annoy some early players who want to get access to certain items will be the shopkeepers and their general pricing for the items in question; typically it is much easier to obtain certain items through mob hunting or crafting than it is to simply buy something outright. Not only that, but even the manuals for crafting stuff like armor, weapons, or shields, even with their limited uses per manual, can fetch you quite a bit of profit if you know your craft. Not only that, but while learning how to make stuff via crafting does take a while, it's only natural considering crafting in many games does not get you the best stuff as soon as you start the game. Not only that, but key advise when it comes to fishing; some minigames that certain skills have don't need to be interacted with in-order to get a reward from it.
For my final verdict, I'd recommend the game from my personal experience; I would advise anybody else who has played for as long as I have to make up their own judgments before they recommend to anybody else this very game. Also, as a word of advice for those starting off who need to level quickly; Rath Royal Castle's first floor hosts a banquet every week on Saturday at 7 PM PST to 8 PM PST. You'll find this place in the city of Tara, which is not very hard to get to once you have the special mount(s) from the tutorial quests. Log in with any character or pet you want to level and keep them logged in for the duration of the event. In terms of how much experience you'll get, if you're at Level 1 with no experience and you attend this event, you'll be Level 40 by the end with approximately 20%-30% experience remaining until Level 41. This may be subject to change if they adjust the experience tables in the future, but it is still useful information to know ahead of time.
Also to anybody wondering why my hours recorded for the game isn't high on Steam, it's exactly that; I don't use the Steam version of the game because of the fact, while it could be just a problem on my end, that the Steam version crashes when loading specific maps in Mabinogi, primarily the homestead in which I see this the most. As a result I simply use the Nexon Launcher and play Mabinogi through that. The Steam launcher isn't exactly bad but it does have its share of problems compared to the Nexon Launcher available on Mabinogi's website.

Ok, to all those who said I'd hate this....you're right,25 hours in and I officially don't give a sh*t. It's a pointless waste of time and can best be summarised as 'Waiting for days to elapse in space'
Yes, there is clearly a 'real world economy' and my God is it....probably detailed. Oh and the ships! Everything is generated in game, if there is something you see....a player built it! Isn't that amazing?!
These are the things that drew me to EVE, however after spending 25 hours, over a solid day of my actual life on this garbage I am about as close and involved to the EVE economy as a 25 hour old baby would be to the human one.
It's spreadsheets and being a dickh*ad in space. There really is very little nuance beyond this. The whole thing plays like a space stock trader game....ok not the end of the world, right? I still think I could get into that, hopefully there is some action and excitement to make it 'feel' like a game whilst you are actually gathering resources to trade, right? Nope, for all this 'It's a griefing paradise' that I was promised, I barely saw another ship.
25 hours in, few other ships, few missions - lots of clicking around and waiting for actual time to elapse to build my skills up. That's another thing worth considering - this game charges a monthly fee. You can only 'level up' by waiting. Not even waiting 'in game' time, waiting real life, human hours that you could spend walking your dog, shouting at your wife or playing anything that isn't this drab attempt at making Excel fascinating. You get better exclusively by paying them money, and waiting.
I wanted the sweet economy thing to be true so badly. I even talked down other MMOs because 'EVE has this amazing online economy' and it does, it's clearly going on. I have never come across a game less accessible than this. EVE fans tout this as though it's some great selling point, however I think what's actually going on is people who have invested thousands of hours into this dross now need to convince themselves that it wasn't time wasted.
If you haven't already invested a thousand hours, and if you're in any way normal, just don't bother. Jesus Christ this is tedious.
If you've got a thousand hours, £120 and a strong desire to be part of the biggest game of spreadsheets in the world, then yeah you can probably watch your summer vanish whilst living your life in fake space.
