Most people write pretty short or narrow reviews, so let me just burn some time by making a big one that covers many parts of the game! Scroll around to find the parts you are interested so that you don't have to read the whole thing!
Progression: [Obligatory]
I was only in the tier system for a few days and thought it was "okay" but I preffered when it was gone. The way I saw it was that people still abused newer players by bringing in higher level parts, but if you had a high enough skill level you could fix that without too much trouble. Same with the update afterwords, people would bring in bugger guns but be very fragile because of it. I preffered that stage of Robocraft of all the stages I played, the progression was somewhat slow, but that encouraged me to experiment and make more bots to pass the time without leaving me stuck for too long if I couldn't put many hours into Robocraft a day. The new system had an interesting idea to add lootboxes which would cause new players to try and patch together random parts onto robots, which was interesting, but not a good experience as they were promptly steam rolled by boring cubes or older players who were no longer sorted out in any way. All I remember of the early days of the update was endless seal clubbing that I didn't even plan to engage in and not getting the parts I wanted to build new robots, which kind of ruined the game for me because I was bored of only having mechs [which were the only thing I knew how to build well until I felt the urge to experiment] but now I couldn't afford to make a new bot for a new, fresh play style unless I kept grinding. This is something that I always end up coming back to, as I did not have enough time to amass parts so that I didn't have to use the... *shudders* forge. Winning protonium crates that dropped me nothing but tier 3 [out of the 5, not counting legendaries] or below items meant I got next to nothing to buy new overpriced parts with.
Progression Suggestions:
Adding robit drops to crates was a step in the right direction, I started to be happier to find a rare robits pile than I was opening 5 protonium crates that contained [again] only tier 3 or below items. I would suggest adding a robit reward based on the players performance in addition to the crates, just giving protonium winners say, 2000 robits, and reducing the ammount by 300 every position? That way even rusted crates will give 500 robits, and then just increase the price of forge items a little bit, maybe 30%? Saving up for a single tier 4 mech leg would go from 10+ games while winning protonium crates with bad luck, to 10 games even getting silver crates. After all, it's a single leg, you need two of the things at least! If the game is about building and players can't even build something usable, there is a problem!
[P.S. Please PLEASE, make cubes cheaper, several times I had to spend everything I saved up just to get cubes even after I stocked up on them before the update, it's insane what buying cubes will do to a new players budget based on my experience]
Weapons:
Simply put, everything that is not tier 3 lasers or an epic/legendary weapon is completely useless. I've watched someone with 40 laser wasps on a cube do only 20% damage to another, smaller robor that was standing still, with just 4 tier 5 plasmas before dieing. Useless. Don't treat all weapons as equals if almost half of them exist only to be recycled for enough robits to make less than a dozen cubes.
Plasma: Almost only useful on bombers or drones unless you have a mega/legendary plasma. Tier 4 plasma is bordeline on useless, but I've made it work on a shoestring budget enough to say it's useable. Tiers 4 ans 5 are used almost exclusively by bombers due to high damage, compatablility with hit and run that favors planes, and biggest yet most subtle point: When fired horizontally a missed shot is more likely to fly outside of the blast radius of an exploding plamsa, while vertical blast almost always explode on the ground around targets, close enough to deal consistent damage.
Lasers: Tier 3 is sometimes useful, but generally does so little damage and is so inaccurate that it [and all tiers below it] are generally useless. The redundancy and higher fire rate don't help much when you can't hit the broad side of a mega-barn from 60 blocks away, they also fail in close quarters [and I mean about to scratch paint close] because they still cannot aim reliably enough to break off specific weapons without being burst fired, and whn burst fired they do less DPS than a larger laser defeating the point. Tier 4 and 5 lasers seem to be [very arguably] the best weapons in the game, with the same range as rails, high damage, fairly high fire rate, ability to hit glass cannon bots, and general ease of use. Mega lasers are also amazing, but sadly not very practical unless your robot is small to gain a damage boost, making it a glass cannon easily able to eviscerate bots at any range with high reliability.
Rails:
Generally don't see these aside from the mega/legendary version. Rails suffer most from the newer maps, of which only one gives them enough open sightlines to be an actual threat, rather than a minor annoyance. Unable to cripple most targets before they reach cover and no longer able to inflict long lasting damage due to auto-regeneration they have lost their favor in the majority of players. After weapons could no longer reload when not in use, rails died off, even as secondary weapons leaving only to rail impaler to be commonly used. The rail impaler offers a high risk/reward by dealing crippling damage in one or two shots if the player can finish of their targets [as long range support is generally impossible due to a lack of sight lines] with secondary weapons. This does cause a minor problem that smaller glass cannon robots can be shut down by a single shot from an impaler, which when combined with the commonly used lasers makes glass cannons a rare sight, especially in league.
Shotguns:
One of the current meta weapons, massive damage and massive health, only weak against flying targets, and those fast enough to run away. The problem is that you can often move faster than your target can, or at least faster than they are when they bump into things trying to backpedal away from you while trying to shoot your gun off. This generally means that people who turn and run are not fast enough due to the current movement type system to outrun shotguns, and die from extensive damage to the back that they cannot outrun. Those that stay often suffer severe damage before being able to remove the shotgun and can be finished off with secondary weapons in most cases. This is, of course, assuming that you aren't a literal cube with 2 legendary shotguns on the side. In this case, you simply drive towards your target and click until they are dead.
Miniguns:
Diamond League is made out of these. Same general effect as shotguns.
Mortar:
Why? It's just a mega plasma. Buff Widow Maker for team play and increase range.
Movement:
Too Floaty. Spend hours making a robot that is cannot be controlled easily, which is why mechs and plasma bombers are everywhere, good luck making a tesla bot. [Please fix this]

This mod is fairly interesting. The backstory isn't presented other than how you ended up where you are, but I'm hoping that they'll reveal the origins sometime within the 1st episode.

The puzzles are fairly simplistic if you've played one of the Half Life games before, but the adventure if quite enjoyable. You have this sense of fear that there'll be an enemy right around you.
However, one of the main problems with this linear story with the Half Life engine means that you can just zip by everything and there's nothing to stop you.
Many times have I just ran past an entire bit to save time and myself, and it was somewhat disappointing that the game lets you do that.
Overall though, the game is fairly interesting and I would definetly enjoy playing the 2nd act.

It's hard to describe EVE properly in a review as the game is completely different for everyone, you are given a framework (should you do the tutorial missions) of what you can do to give you an idea of roles that you can take on but you are not forced into anything, EVE is what you make of it.
You can sit in hi-sec relativley safe and run missions, mine ore, play the market, craft things to sell, run cargo for players, defend people, explore and more. That's pretty much more than most games like this offer, and that is just hi-sec.
Should you want to be a bit more daring, earn more money, blow up some people then enter low-sec and null-sec...
This is for me where the fun is, you get all of the above and more, join a corporation, defend your systems, enter faction warfare, mine ore that sells for millions, scan down combat / data / relic sites to earn a fortune or hell monopolise the corner of a market.
Like I said it's hard to describe because everyone has their own way of playing the game and enjoys different things.
I've tried a lot of things in EVE, some that I thought would be boring as hell that turned out to actually be really fun - This sentence has never rung more true for the actual game, I thought it would be boring but god damn I love it and every person I have introduced to it has thought the same and stayed!
Give EVE a shot, try and play with a friend or ask the amazing community in rookie help should you need any help, plenty of corps take in new players and are very helpful.

Each turn you get a random item to place in your city, when three or more items connect they fuze into a new thing. You go from planting lowly grass to making houses and even castles which improve your score and provide a visual asthetic of people running around and talking gibberish. You also have bears and ninja bears that will block your progress and make things difficult for you. Managing all this is the key to victory, you will eventually fill your city and the game will end, but how you do will give you more things to improve your island which is a hub world you visit in between games. The game is cute and challanging and before you know it you will rack up a bunch of hours after thinking "just one more game".

As someone who isn't in deep into the Naruto lore here, I'll try and give a brief summary of what you'll be getting with your purchase:
You'll get a fighting game that, compared to the 6 button combo-fighters you'll find out there, is relatively simple. Its easy to learn (although the in-game tutorials are not exactly helpful), and I can imagine it gets pretty deep the more time you invest.
To the best of my knowledge, the story is interesting and carries itself based on how much you like the franchise. Not to say there isn't anything here for new comers, but you'll definitely get your moneys worth if you know the story.
However, the characters from a superficial samepoint all feel samey, and a lot of characters need to be unlocked in the story mode (which combines the one on one fighting with horde fighting), and that gives some incentive to playing the game in full. Theres a sort of morality system too: you choose between legend scenarios (ones that are generally shows of strength and power in the story) and hero scenarios (think mass effect paragon.) that give the story minor replayability, and allow you to level up these respective attributes. (For the most part, if you're looking for a challenge, you'll find yourself picking legend as unscrupulous as is despite your personal feelings on the matter.)
Well, what else can I say? Good art direction, plenty of things for fans, online play, fun, pick-up-and-play action, you could do worse. I would wait for a sale, though, if you aren't in the fanbase already.

The more you harvest Plants the more your Flora skill goes up, The more you craft weaponry, ect. This makes the game more time consuming yes, but at the same time you do not have to put a full 12 hours of gameplay to progress, For instance if you only have 2 hours a day to game you can still get to do things others do, Granted it will take you longer than someone who spends 12-18 hours a-day but still you can do it too with no restrictions other than your time.
Gameplay: This element of the game can be played majority in two ways, RPG mode; Simple understanding, Movement keys work and you use your mouse and keyboard to play like you would in World of Warcraft.[ Not comparing just saying that you use number keys to use skills and what not]
So basicly your standard MMO controls almost with key differnces that are easily seen when you play.
Action Mode: This mode is my personal fav when it comes to combat. This mode turns the game into a Fake shooter, You aim with the mouse you get a crosshair and you attack with your left and right mouse buttons. There are ALOT of bonuses to this, If using guns you can AIM and hit Certain areas dealing more or less damage. making combat more fast pace you can still use # keys for skills, The only thing that changes ins the control scheme.
So i use RPG mode for everything else but combat mostly. If i feel lazy i will use RPG to attack. In RPG mode damage is mostly chest as spread is wider in RPG mode with guns. (This as if firing a gun from the hip its more inaccurate yeah?)
Sandbox Features: These features plays a major role later on, I have yet to buy one i am working on my offical character now but with these features you can do several things, so far what i can tell there are going to be Three memberships which are all going to be a ONETIME PAYMENT, Silver, Gold, Plat. Gold and Plat can both make towns/cities while plat will get access to Nation. Not sure as this is Early Access so i do not know the Release prices. Nations are part of the Sandbox features as this makes you a Rouge faction, This is a playermade faction. (Sorta like guilds) Now i know what everyone is thinking. "OH GREAT I HAVE TO PAY REAL CASH TO HAVE A GUILD" You may have to MAKE ONE, but joining a nation that exist is going to be the better option early on, as a Nation your going to have alot more problems. Such as the old faction likly to start hating you more. (You deserted what'cha expect Cake and cookies? This aint no girl scout army) You will be able to make houses with out needing to pay at all. housing will let you do several things, Craft, Party, Live. housing lets you place Crafting devices, Decorate, Invite your friends over and entertain them and ect. so this is one of the fun features. No info on towns/cities yet.
No combat needed: This is added to the game where you do not ever need to swing a sword, Fist,shoot a gun ever. You can do all the crafting and everything not involing combat if thats what you want with out ever equiping weapons.
Now onto the Cons i see of this game.
Grindy!: This game is grindy beyond grindy. Skills require you to use that skill stuff to advance it.
Lengthy: This game needs people who are Dedicated to playing when they can, Otherwise you wasted your time even looking at the game, But if you think you would like it give it a try but make sure your willing to try to put time and effort into the game.
Slow: This game is not going to let you max your skills in a week, a month, or likely in a year, If you were to focus on one skill it would likely take you six months to max it out and from what ive heard, the skills max out at 60,000 points, and you gain your skill one point at a time.
Alpha: This game being in alpha is a Con unto its self, its a great game so, if your not willing to support and report bugs and such, Dont even bother with the game IT IS NOT COMPLETE!
Huge amount of skills: Over 75 different skills to use, and you can use em all. But to master EVERY skill would take even the most constant gamer  years to do so. Its like Eve online They do not go easy on you.
The pros of the game are a smaller list but more impactful.
Nice Community: The community is nice and helpful, there is always someone there to help you.
Great gameplay: the gameplay is amazing and the Random gen quests dont stop, Always something to do.
Amazing stability: There are so few game breaking bugs as far as i can tell, Ive ran into the minor/annoying bugs and a few Quest stoppers. But for this game being in alpha its great. Never crashed once.

If somebody told me last year that I would not only play this game, but own it; I would have laughed in their face. You see, I'm not an avid Naruto fan. In fact, I find the idea idiotic. Ninjas that run around screaming their attacks while wearing bright and revealing clothing? Not very appealing to me (Most anime isn't). However, I was introduced to this game on the PS3 by a roommate of mine. He knew I liked games like Soul Calibur and Super Smash Bros, so he told me I HAD to try this. Well, here I am, six months later, owning it on the PC.
The gameplay is probably one of the best systems for a fighting game and the controls are superb when using an Xbox controller. The graphics are beautiful and clear. However, because of the impressive visuals, you're going to need a pretty good PC to run this well. The gameplay works like an extremely fast paced and more strategic yet simplified version of Soul Calibur. There is no confusing button combonations to destroy your opponent, but instead all attacks are keyed to one button while pressing a different button a different amount of times changes what kind of attack you do. The story is alright (Like I said, not a fan of the series), and the voice acting is not anything to be impressed by (Rather painful in places). However, the one terrible and good thing about the game is the cutscenes. It plays like a movie when you aren't interacting. Sometimes it is enjoyable to watch; other times it drags out way too long. Another negative is the online multiplayer. From my understanding, it used to be worse than it is already. The only thing that gets in the way is the connection signals. The rounds lag from beginning to end and it is very difficult to actually find a person to fight. Once you do find someone who doesn't lag and is willing to fight, you tend to stay with that guy and keep fighting him rather than try finding another person.
The only bug I have encountered in this game is one that could be considered a major annoyance. It tends to crash during local multiplayer battles. At the menu, choosing characters, sometimes even in the battle itself, the game crashes and shuts down. There is a fix however: play it in windowed mode. It does not really detract from game play and keeps it from crashing.
All in all, I give a positive review of a game I thought I would never play. The gods of video games and anime must have conspired to create a video game of an anime I despise and make it as amazing as possible so I would get it. Get this game when it goes on sale (because it definitely will). I got it a few months after being ported to the PC and got it for $5 instead of $55; total steal!

Now, I am by no means an expert on this game. However, to all the people who say it's "dead," I'd have to say I disagree with you.
In the starting village alone I saw several high-level players just hanging out and chatting while a bunch of noobs like myself were running around doing the tutorial missions.
Later on, in the first major town you visit (Dunbarton) I met a decently large group of people standing aroung playing music. I blew all of my money on a lute and a ukelele and joined them. In the process, I met a couple of friendly players who ended up teaching me the art of combat later on. After they logged off, I went back to Dunbarton and spent an hour jamming with this guy who had a lot of custom music. I made a total of 3 friends.
Conclusion
While Mabinogi may not have as large a population as, say, WoW or Tera, it is by no means dead. The community, as a whole, is friendly and helpful. If you're a skeptic like me, you should check out this game. I'd give this a solid 9/10.

If you don't like crafting constantly don't play it. If you don't like unnecessarily complicated crafting, don't play it. If you don't like spending the majority of your in-game time harvesting resources of unnecessarily largley varying "quality", don't play it.
Let's also dispel the myth that this is SWG reborn. Nonsense. I played SWG for years and this game does not even come close. In some ways it is similar, but so are other games. Yet still it seems that nobody has learned the positive lessons SWG put out there about sandbox games.
Crafting is an absolute joke. To make one simple T1 component (one of several needed to make a basic item) is a real exercise in patience and/or frustration. The game relies on you being able to by certain parts or resources from other players, and you can't. Not with the current player base at least. All crafting is also carried out at a generic crafting station that seems capable of such diverse tasks from bio engineering to simple woodwork. Ridiculous.
Combat is dull and uninteresting. It has 2 modes, classic rpg and "action" (direct aim etc). Neither of them work particularly well. And watching the trajectory of your high powered sniper rifle bullet as it bends and twists it's flight path (slow one at that) to follow your target like some sort of mini homing missile, gets rather annoying after a while.
Lots of missions to do, all the same thing though. They repeat over and over and over.
The world is large, looks ok, and is well populated by some imaginative denizens. Most of which will tear you to pieces early on when you get sick and tired of running around the same city for ages and attempt to go somewhere else.
The stats system? Stupid. Its all down to whatever "fittings" you slot in your armor and weapons. I think this is a pre-cursor to a free2play model in the future where fittings will be available in some kind of ingame store etc. I don't know.
All in all, a bad game with great potential. It is boring and repetitive when starting out, you cant craft anything worth while and will spend most of your time chopping logs just to make some money to repair gear or buy fittings. It will not hold the interest of anyone of average intelligence for long. Watch this space though, it could get better. For now though, save your money. This game is not worth anywhere near the asking price. Its still in early access of course, but nevertheless, not worth the same cost as a full release game

Let's talk about my 4h experience.
First of all I've never played an One Piece game before, so my review is going to be centered only on this game.
Let's start with the settings, I've a PC that can run almost every game in ultra (CPU: i7 4790; GPU: GTX 970; RAM: 8GB).
So far the graphs in game look fine and the gameplay doesn't stutter or anything.
Secondly Controls. I play with my XBOX One controller, and had no problems setting it up cause everything was set up by default for the controller. But the down side of it is that the controls are written for general controllers, so the X button was the button no. 1 and the A button the no. 2 (I don't really recall the numbers), but in the end it was pretty easy to understand which button did what.
To finish let's talk about gameplay.
The game is pretty straight to you, every thing is explained to you, the missions, what you're supposed to do, when and where. The combo moves are quite funny and easy to do.
There are 3 game modes:
- Legend Log, where you play the main story with the crew characters, when Zoro enters the crew you can use it instead of Luffy, and when Usopp does you can switch it too.
- Free Log, where you can play the chapters from the main story but with whoever you feel like playing. For instance you can play Buggy in the Prologue to save Zoro.
- Dream Log, this is where it gets funny. You choose a character, for instance I chose Robin, and you navigate the grand line from island to island. In each island you are given two random allies (in my first I had Law & Chopper, in my 2nd I had Jabra and a Lapahn) and you have two Bosses to defeat in that island. In the end you can advance trough the islands and you get epic encounter (for example in my 3rd island I've to fight Ace).
From what I've played, I can say the game it's pretty good, awesome gameplay, great combos, but a little bit repetitive.
Awesome game for the fans of the series (anime/manga) and even for those who never thought about watching it. If you have friends and they never felt like watching One Piece, this game is awesome to start them up.

I was somewhat disappointed after playing through this. From what i read from the other reviews, i expected it to be excellent and top of my "pay attention to" list. Sadly, after playing it, it just felt like any other mod. Then again, I might of been spoiled from Underhell.
First off, the first thing i noticed was that the voice acting was pretty good, and excellent if you consider this is a free mod. It can't compare to Underhell's voice acting, but then again, Underhell has voice acting better than most comerical games.
Secondly, I have to admit the map design is pretty damned great, resembling some of the orginal half life 2 levels. I consantly explored everywhere I could, hoping not to miss any of the beautiful landscapes. Some of the tiny touches too, like a newspaper you can read and a guard's humorous note, really add to the feeling this is a real place. Combined with the Voice acting, this is some of the best immersion i have ever experienced in a mod, on par with half life 2.
The story is a bit... meh. Ignoring the plotholes of your guy being a fisherman that somehow seems to have military level training with firearms, it feels like the standard Zombie Movie/Zombie Game plot. Evil Organization unleashes zombies on island and stops anyone from rescuing for help, and you, crash landing on the island, need to go and stop them. Its horribly cliched.
Where the mod TRUELY falls flat, however, is in the gameplay. You can only hold one weapon at a time(yes, you can't even carry the one melee weapon in the game with you along with a gun), and they don't really... feel very interesting. The Smg is the same as the half life 2 one, and the hammer reskin of the crowbar has some wonky animations(doesn't feel like I should be doing any sort of damage with the swings). The pistol on the other hand, looks and feels great. Onto actual gameplay, the zombies(and thats what im assuming they are) aren't much of a threat. They are slow, do low damage even when they hit you, can you can 1 shot them with the pistol. The whole first part of the game is super easy. Even when you lose you lose your gun and you are stuck with the hammer, they don't feel like much of a threat, as you can hit them 3 times before they can even finish a swinging animation. By the time the company soliders show up, its very close to the end of the game, and they where also pretty meh. Except for one case with one moving in a patrol pattern, they simply stood still and shot full auto at you, with almost aimbot level aim. Fighting them turned into a case of who hit who first.
Now, you might be wondering how I can recomend this game even with my 'hate'. I recomend it, because it is free, and the mapping is amazing. Plus, i know this is not finished. Im hoping ill find this again one day and it will be a lot better than it is right now. This has a good future ahead of it, as long as the creators work on the story and gameplay. Ill give this a 7/10.
On a side note, it is rather short, but that is to be expected from it being Act 1 out of a planned three Acts. So don't expect this to fill up more than a single day.

Gunpoint will bend your mind!
Gunpoint is one of those games where you can go back to it and play it all over again, there are so many different routes to take! You can be stealthy, sneak past the guards, acquire the objective then leave without a trace. Or you can be the opposite and go in guns blazing, still keeping your wits about you however because you only have so many bullets and the missions get more challenging with harder puzzles to bend your mind and beefier troops to go up against.
The music in Gunpoint is absolutely amazing, it just sets the mood for this crime infested world you are traversing and it makes you feel like a freelance spy with the dark and mysterious tones that they have created to accompany this beautiful game.
The graphics are pleasing, now I know not many people like going back to the pixelated games but the incredible gameplay makes up for this, even if you don't like playing in the blocky 2D worlds, this puts a different spin on things and it immerses you in this awesome game with the other features like the story, music and even the comical humour like the funny one-liners and the achievement names by doing something utterly ridiculous.
This game is beautiful, I would recommend it to anyone who likes a good mind-bending puzzle to solve and for anyone who likes a good crime story.
It's no Portal 2, but it's still an enjoyable puzzle experience while it lasts.

Quantum Conundrum is, well, a conundrum. While I was at first drawn in by its Portal-esque humor and gameplay, this game can become quite infuriating It relies heavily on physics puzzles and first-person platforming. The former is difficult to do well, and Quantum Conundrum makes a valiant effort, but certain puzzles are simply broken and rely much on repeated tries before the game deems you worthy to work properly. First-person platforming, however, is impossible to do well. QC is no exception; oftentimes you will know exactly how to finish a puzzle but keep falling off the platform you're on. That's not difficulty - that's just infuriating. All in all, if you like Portal and etc., you may indeed like Quantum Conundrum. And I do like it, but it is a flawed game.

As someone who played some of the previous Ninja STORM titles, "Full Burst" takes two steps forward and one step backward... all the while having a deadweight called "online mode" clamped down on its ankle.
Gameplay is broken into three parts - story mode, versus mode and online mode. Here are some highlights and lowlights for each mode.
Story Mode Highlights
- Multiple battles with new characters
- Boss battles with quicktime events continue to be visually stunning
- Has a little bit of a "choose your adventure" vibe to the story
Story Mode Lowlights
- Story telling continues to be weak in distribution - subtitles are boring and most of the cinematics involve scrolling stillshots
- Fights can get tedious - there's only so much variation you can do in this game
- Final few boss modes are incredibly frustrating as poor camera angles ruin the fun
---
Versus Mode Highlights
- The real star of the game, more playable characters than ever
- Action continues to be fast-paced, great art direction
- Adding cinematics on ultimate skill takedowns adds a bit of flair to fights
- Challenge mode is pretty fun in a mindless sort of way
Versus Mode Lowlights
- Several characters are carry overs from the previous title, making their skills outdated in comparison to story mode progression
- Some characters missing from story mode for no reason
- Balancing issues, certain characters standard attacks can hit you even if you spam log
--
Online Mode Highlights
- It allows you to play with people online
Online Mode Lowlights
- Net code is absolutely terrible. Ridiculous input delay makes the game nearly unplayable.
- Very low online population. The people who do play are veterans with hundreds of hours - you will get wiped.
- Items are not standardized and reflect larger balancing issues.
--
Overall, I can't recommend buying this game with the next one coming out next month. Unless you REALLY want to play some Naruto goodness right away, hold off for the next iteration which will have three times more characters and some real development on the versus mode side. But don't hold your breath for better online - this is clearly not a priority.

I never had the pleasure of playing Ultima Online.  But I was fortunate enough to play SWG (both pre and post Combat Update and NGE).  Much of The Repopulation is very reminicant of my days as a TKM (Teras Kasi Master) trying to get to blue glowy (Jedi), with some notable exceptions.  Therefore, the comparrison that the company makes is a very fair one as far as SWG is concerned.
The game is highly skill based.  There are your main skills (of which there's around 75) and then there are skills within the skills.  I will use the character I have played with the most (I've tinkered with three) to try to illustrate the point.
My main character is primarily a hunter type with some gathering side abilities.  There are several but the ones he specializes in are, mining (minerals and ore extraction from nodes), wood cutting (cutting down trees), and survival (skinning animals and scavenging for water).  There's others but those are the ones I use.  For every mob type there is a set skill pertaining to them.  A common early mob is a Setlang, they are reptilian dog-like creatures.  As you hunt/skin more and more of these creatures you begin to become more and more familiar with them.  So there's your overall skill (say survival) and specific species skill (in this case setlang) the higher they both are the better you do, obviously.  This holds true across the board.   Are you a miner?  What kind of miner are you?  There's a skill for each ore too.  Woods man?  What trees/plants are you good with?
On the flipside.  Lets say you go into crafting.  The same thing applies you have your base crafting schools, lets say chemistry, and then you have all of your chemistry recipes.  They have separate skills associated with each one of them (i'm quite the badass water distiller but i can't do acid extraction for crap).
Harvesting is interesting in that you have several options.  There's auto harvesting (you can put down extractors over some nodes) and there's manual extraction.  Many nodes under manual extraction come with 2 other options enhancement of the node you're on, and enrichment of the area.  As an area is harvested it looses quality and it shows in the nodes.  The immediate and personal fix is by enhancing the node you're working on but it only works for you.  Enriching the area restores the area's quality not just for you but everyone.
The game is in alpha so please expect crashes, bugs and issues. They aren't abundant but they exist, most can be fixed with a soft log.
Pros
Massive skill system
Great in game community
Very ambitious
Rewarding if you're willing to work for it (those who seek immediate gratification go elsewhere)
Decent early teaching methods (nooby training instance)
Cons
Steep price tag for alpha *redacted con, see edit*
Alpha lots of bugs, they're being worked on but it's alpha
Future possibility of microtransactions
Steep learning curve, with many skills "hidden" for you to discover on your own, and little direction given beyond the original training instance
All in all, if they add a twitch based flight aspect I will be at their door screaming "Shut up and take my money".  As it sits, for me, it is worth the early investment.  These guys are clearly serious and want the game to work.  That being said I enjoy alphas and betas, and realize many don't.  So if you're one who wants a clean and polished game don't buy in yet.  The game is clean and has some polish, but isn't finished yet.  They are making progress (think an update comes out today or tomorrow actually) but they've still got work to do.  The price tag of 40 bucks for an alpha is a bit steep in my opinion but being that it harkens back to my days in SWG as much as it did I took the plunge, and am glad I did.
There's many things that you can do in game that I've not mentioned this is strictly the path of one of my characters, the character is truly yours when you get in.
Enjoy
-Rk
Edit: Thanks to WubZero for bringing this to my attention.  There's been a price reduction removing that con.  Game is now 20 bucks as opposed to 40 now makes it a very viable competetor in the current market.
They do plan on having twitch based flight once they've smoothed out the majority of the ground game.  So we are at "Shut up and take my money" status.

Lets get this over with, this is a Koei Tecmo game. Meaning the port is awful, right? Well, for once, no.
First, this game is designed around a controller. Expect to use one, or suffer greatly. The control prompts are locked to PC keys, and the control types are a bit weird, but a controller is still highly reccomended, simply due to the ease-of-access that the right analog camera controls bring, among other things.
Secondly, this game's framerate is variable between 30 and 60, but for the most part stays at 60 for me. Considering my cpu and gpu are quite high end (stronger than the PS4) if not old (i5 3570k and GTX 670), the game runs very well, and appears to use low cpu and gpu usage, making it suitable for weaker rigs. The options menu, while sparse, is fine, and for the most part the port seems pretty good. Graphically, the game is not a stunner, but none of Koei's games are so dont expect anything above the PS4 port of the game.
Thirdly, this is a  Dynasty Warriors game with a One Piece Skin., meaning youre going to bash and whack and cut and smack and burn and otherwise kill thousands of enemies over the course of a single stage. Tecmo Koei's main strength is their fanservice and from what I've played, it's top of the line. Of course, you should be a fan of One Piece in General if you plan to get this game, and if not, I can't advise getting it, but if youre trying to get into the series (which is very long), then this game is a great place to start. It covers up to almost the most recent arc, and does a great job so-far of condensing over 700 chapters and 600 episodes into one video game.
Fourth and finally, This game can be repetitive, but its great fun with its large cast of One Piece characters and amazing fanservice. Oda's legacy is well-represented in a better-than expected PC port.
TL;DR
Use a controller
Great Port
Looks serviceable
One Piece Fanservice is off the charts
Would reccomend.

The nostalgia is real.
The game, overall, is great, but does severely suffer from some serious drawbacks in its design.
The Good:
-Making your own Avatar, and choosing from the games selection of races to do it.
-Leveling up, and experiencing that feeling of growing strength that is at the core of Dragon Ball.
-Unlocking Skills, Items, Equipment, characters and more. The content is very rich.
-Great sound design. Voice acting and music are both on point.
-Multiplayer. Good for when you need help, and fun when you want to see how other people play.
-Polish. Overall the game has a ton of content, rich features, and a lot of seamless play.
The Bad:
-The grinding. Unlocking certain items seems to mean repeating quests for an unknown amount of times. The formula seems truly random.
-Unlocks. Though there are certain hidden conditions in some levels that must be done in order to unlock certain things, completing those conditions doesn't mean there is a 100% chance at success. Which means, more grinding.
-Pacing and Leveling. If you complete the story quests, you'll quickly become overwhelmed and be subjected to more Paralell quest grinding to level your character.  While this does simulate "training" in a way, it can become frustrating if you are interested in moving the story.
-Lack of clan support.  Would be awesome to have a more organized way to group friends and expand the community. This was a big missed opportunity here.
-Not many people doing PQ's.  You will spend lots of time waiting for 1-2 people to join you, even though you'll see hundreds of players idle'ing the lobby.
-Lack of customization.  No way to change your characters auras, basic fighting moves, and there is a very limited amount of choices when you create your character as far as physical looks go.
-No skill required in PVE.  You can simply grind your way up to power, unlock SSJ, and spam your ultimate attacks to victory. On the other end, the AI can gang up on you, if your quest has you alone, and there will be no amount of skill to get you through.
-Lack of transformations. The game embraces storylines up to GT.  But, for your avatar, if you're a Saiyan, you can only unlock up to SSJ2. There are also no real transformations for other races like the Freiza race.
-Transformations don't seem accurate. SSJ, for example, only boosts your character by a little bit, and causes a huge drain to your characters KI.  Making it only last a few seconds, when we all know, SSJ transformations in the story last much longer. They could have done these differently, and more accurately.
-Rewards could be done differently.  I feel, instead of grinding, you should be rewarded for your success (like the D through Z rating on quests) on missions to unlock items. Instead of grinding in hopes to unlock SSJ or that piece of clothing you want, should you achieve Z, you should earn rewards proportional to the rating. This would cut down grinding, and reward players accordingly for their hard work and skill.
-More RPG and MMO elements.  For the game to puts its toes in the water of these genres, it doesn't really take advantage of these elements. It lacks exploration, social elements, and end game content that other MMO's and RPG's have.  But its obvious DBXV was sampling these elements, without fully committing. It took the safe route, when it could have done a lot more.
Summary:
While I might have more bad to say than good, it doesn't mean I don't like the game. I enjoy it quite a bit, but the grind is causing me to run out of motivation to play it. Its a well polished game that is rich with content.  But design choices have hampered it from being truly great.  Its worth buying on sale, and enjoying for many hours, with friends. But it does have a shelf life, and it's not going to be something that will be played for months on end.

Estranged: Act 1 is the first installment of what is to be a continued series built on Valve's Source engine, and for a free mod built on an outdated engine it was quite impressive.
Don't read too much into "impressive". What I mean is that the world and atmosphere of Estranged are wonderful and you feel like something terrifying can happen at any moment, which sadly doesn't happen. I found the build-up for confrontations to be a bit of a let-down, you're exploring an abandoned island that shows signs of recent struggle after being shipwrecked when you encounter the cause...
Zombies.
Yes, it is another Source zombie mod, which I found to be quite the letdown when I first encountered the enemy of the first half of the mod. Since this is the first installment of Estranged I overlooked the fact that there was no exposition to the background of the "outbreak" (which I'm reluctant to refer to as, since the zombies were few in number and were generally underwhelming in combat) and soldiered on through its three chapters. About halfway through you encounter the second enemy, which are gun-toting Half-Life 2 citizens that, also like the zombies, left a bit to be admired.
With such a well-built atmosphere it was all the more disappointing to observe the lack of effort in the character models, even going as far to recycle Dr. Kliener's model. If you're a veteren of the Source engine then this method of re-using content will deal a large chunk of damage to any immersion, which for a mod that aims for atmosphere is not a good thing at all.
The level design was very restrictive with almost no potential for exploration or discovery. The pacing was just messy inconsistently jumping from long winded and empty hallways to short and cramped office spaces. The puzzles are just horribly easy and the only way to fail them is if you suffered head trauma as a child. Overall the gameplay in both combat and level design was rubbish in laymans terms.
The story is lacking and failed to grab my interest, but since this was only Act 1 I'm willing to overlook that and give the developers the benefit of the doubt and assume that more exposition will be given in the future installments.
Now I may be giving Estranged a bit of a harsh lashing, and my expectations may have been a bit high for a free mod, but I just felt underwhelmed by the whole experience and I left Estranged very disappointed because of the apparant lack of effort in the character models and the combat.
If Estranged cost any money then I would be much more harsh, but since it is a free mod with low memory and hardware requirements there really isn't any legitimate reason to not play through it for yourself and develop your own opinion about it. Who knows? You may just like what you see.
The music was pretty good though.

3) Slow Time - All items and lasers fall and zap at a snail's pace.  If you jump on an item travelling through the air, it will be solid to jump on.

Quantum Conundrum is a first person platforming puzzle game by ex-Valve employee and Portal lead designer Kim Swift.
You have control over 4 different dimensions (fluffy, heavy, slow, reverse gravity) where each dimension manipulates your surroundings and objects in different ways.
The puzzles aren't exactly hard, but often require good timing and reflexes. QC has a rather funny and cartoon-y art style, which definitely fits the overall theme of the game.
On the downside, the level design is kinda repetitive and the devs seemed to use the copypaste function more than they should.
Unfortunately, the game doesn't seem to offer that much replay value, so unless you're a completionist, you're probably done in about 6-7 hours. For a fun and polished game like QC, that's still a pretty good deal, though. And with the DLCs already being announced, there's enough reason to boot up the game again and try the new puzzles.
So, if you're into first person puzzling, make sure to check QC out!

What is with our predisposition for match 3? What purpose does it serve our primordial lizard brains to delight us when we put three of something together and watch it disappear? Whatever the reason may be, the game industry has seized upon this weakness with terrible force, compelling us to crush candies and swap orbs and do all sorts of ridiculous things to rack up points. Triple Town would be no different, save for one additional level of complexity that adds a unique hint of progression to the formula.
Rounds in Triple Town take place on small islands, gridded off for you to set your plants and buildings on. You're given something to place, anything from a tuft of grass to a sturdy oak to an entire house, which you can put on any open square. If three of the same thing end up adjacent to each other, such as three bushes, they combine on the spot of the last one placed into the next level of thing, such as a tree. In this way you can work your way up from grass to bush to tree to house to mansion to castle and on. Most of the time you'll be placing grass but you occasionally get higher-level objects straightaway, which you can use to your advantage or store in your single storage spot for later.
There are other factors at play, such as bears you must place that move about and block your construction, or crystals that act as wildcards, combining with any two other things to complete the set. Your goal is to amass points and reach certain milestones like Settlement and City, and the simple challenge of trying to finagle everything into place is honestly enough to keep you going. You'll slowly start puzzling out how to plan your grasses ahead to get the bushes in the right places to get trees where you want, and then realize you need to plan even further for the houses that the trees become. There's a remarkable amount of planning and strategizing involved, as well as the challenges of unexpected bear or crystal appearances.
All this would make for a fine coffee-break puzzle game, at least for awhile, but there's thankfully more to it than that. As you play, you obtain special items like farms and ores that cannot be used in normal maps. In between rounds, you travel to your capital city where you can place these to grant you additional resources periodically. These resources come in the form of items that can be used during rounds to place certain clutch objects when you need them most. The capital follows the same match-3 rules as well, meaning placing your special items intelligently can yield much greater returns. Triple Town basically gives you a hub city to develop which provides resources that makes the individual puzzles easier, allowing you to earn more items to develop your hub. It's a brilliant little gameplay loop that can keep you hooked for want of one more upgrade to your city.
It's almost a perfect package, but I must admit the presentation drags it down a little. The actual feel of Triple Town is like that of a Flash game, trapped in a static windowed mode with simple vector graphics and animation. There's almost no polish to the menus or buttons, either, which makes them feel more like developer placeholders than finished products. The sound is adequate for what it is but does nothing to alleviate the otherwise cheap feel of the game. Coming off of titles like Mini Metro that manage to be simple AND stylish, Triple Town can feel a bit disappointing. Still, the core mechanics are plenty solid and the progression systems are very addictive, so if you can look past the presentation you'll have a lovely little timesink to enjoy here.

Lets get this over with, this is a Koei Tecmo game. Meaning the port is awful, right? Well, for once, no.
First, this game is designed around a controller. Expect to use one, or suffer greatly. The control prompts are locked to PC keys, and the control types are a bit weird, but a controller is still highly reccomended, simply due to the ease-of-access that the right analog camera controls bring, among other things.
Secondly, this game's framerate is variable between 30 and 60, but for the most part stays at 60 for me. Considering my cpu and gpu are quite high end (stronger than the PS4) if not old (i5 3570k and GTX 670), the game runs very well, and appears to use low cpu and gpu usage, making it suitable for weaker rigs. The options menu, while sparse, is fine, and for the most part the port seems pretty good. Graphically, the game is not a stunner, but none of Koei's games are so dont expect anything above the PS4 port of the game.
Thirdly, this is a  Dynasty Warriors game with a One Piece Skin., meaning youre going to bash and whack and cut and smack and burn and otherwise kill thousands of enemies over the course of a single stage. Tecmo Koei's main strength is their fanservice and from what I've played, it's top of the line. Of course, you should be a fan of One Piece in General if you plan to get this game, and if not, I can't advise getting it, but if youre trying to get into the series (which is very long), then this game is a great place to start. It covers up to almost the most recent arc, and does a great job so-far of condensing over 700 chapters and 600 episodes into one video game.
Fourth and finally, This game can be repetitive, but its great fun with its large cast of One Piece characters and amazing fanservice. Oda's legacy is well-represented in a better-than expected PC port.
TL;DR
Use a controller
Great Port
Looks serviceable
One Piece Fanservice is off the charts
Would reccomend.

Here's my review from the PS4 version. Having compared the two versions gameplay wise there's no difference aside from the lack of Online MP on PC. Graphically, they both have their own strengths and weaknesses. So my review remains pretty much the same.  Cool game regardless of platform.
EDIT: There seems to be issue with the current PC version not saving controller options when using a gamepad and there's also apparent issue with the graphics settings not updating when changing them in the options. If these things matter to you then perhaps wait for a fix before purchase.
Text Version:
Today we’re taking a look at Omega Force’s One Piece Pirate Warriors 3 which for the first time sees the outlandish cast of character appear on the PS4 and PC. It has been almost two years since the last game on PS3 and so the question one has to ask is, aside from the visual upgrade, is it worth jumping in for more of the same hack and slash gameplay.
In a nutshell yes, if you’re making the transition from PS3 to PS4 or jumping in on the PC, that’s a given, for PS3 gamers there’s perhaps less of an incentive unless you’re a sucker for the extra story elements. The core gameplay remains pretty much the same, with Omega Force’s trademark actions making themselves well known here.
For the uninitiated, players can tackle Luffy’s story across 22 stages where the onus is on fighting in open environments against a slew of regular forces and more powerful captains with some boss characters thrown in for good measure. There’s a few combos players can utilize and as the story progresses more moves become available. There’s no block button per se but an evasive move which also doubles up as a means of closing the gap between your character and any locked on target. It’s all straight forward and with the option to team up with secondary characters for devastating attack moves or Kizuna attacks and the choice to build up powerful specials there’s enough options to keep the game from being too repetitive and allowing for a bit of individual flair. That said, players who simply wish to button mash can do so with ease and still come out on top due to the forgiving nature of each stage. The only real spanner in the works is the slight tactical elements where players need to stay focused on events that happen during the skirmishes which require being in a certain location for special sequences or aiding an ally before they get taken out. This aspect is a mainstay of Omega Force’s games and certainly makes each stage much more challenging although failure does mean restarting the entire level from the beginning.
One Piece Pirate Warriors 3 offers a wide range of characters to play with (37 to be precise), across its two main modes of play which are the story based Legend Log and Dream Log. The former also allows for free play where any unlocked character can take on completed stages. Essentially though each mode plays out the same with the core gameplay and unlockables being consistent across each mode which is neat. Players can earn cash to upgrade characters, or purchase extras such as additional costumes, music and movie sequences. The coins also make a return which are essentially the game’s skill levelling feature.
In terms of visuals, the game ups the ante quite a bit over the last game with an overall level of sharpness bringing the characters and on-screen enemies to life with much more clarity than before. The 60 frames per second smoothness is also well apparent on the PS4 with very little to slow it down even when the screen is filled with masses of enemies and regardless of whether they are just standing around doing very little. That said, it’s pretty satisfying to unleash powerful attacks which send large groups of enemies flying across the screen which for some reason doesn’t get old.
The One Piece characters are well animated where players are treated to numerous scenes before and during the stages which adds a bit more personality to the gameplay. Expect lots of crying, snotty noses and shouting here as there’s some excellent use of visual effects and manga style still images interspersed with animated sections making for amusing and entertaining moments throughout. For some, the constant interruption might begin to grate – although for the less patient the option to skip is offered which is handy especially if replaying a level.
The audio is a love or hate it area which has to be said is drenched in Japanese with English only making itself known via subtitles and in the menus. However, the voice overs regardless of their origin are excellent and performed with an intense variety. So even if the native tongue isn’t understood, it’s obvious some great talent has been used to bring the diverse set of characters to life. Sure, a complete localization in English as an option would have been nice, but then again, there’s a certain charm listening to the original Japanese voices. Aside from the voice overs, there’s a usual assortment of sound effects and background music which is pretty much standard fare.
In terms of length, there’s quite a bit on offer here, the Legend Log alone will take up to 15 hours to beat (or more) with some stages lasting 40 minutes and longer. Players then have the choice of upgrading unused characters with earnings, which again takes time, alongside just replaying the game with a different character if desired – especially as each one has their own style to mess around with. The Dream Log mode extends the same flavours as the Legend Log but with specific challenges and bosses to overcome across a set of islands. The core fighting gameplay remains, but the mission structure is slightly more condensed here and makes for a neat extra to play with.
Players can also team up locally for split screen play for up to two players and if the wider online community is your thing then there’s the option to tackle the Legend Log stages with others via creating or searching for games. Players can also request assistance from others at any time in a persistent rescue request option.
One Piece Pirate Warriors 3 certainly makes its mark on the PS4 as a worthy entry for the series. PS3 gamers might feel a bit short changed in terms of there being little new here. However, with an abundance of entertaining characters and amusing new scenes following much of Luffy’s story fused with compelling simplified gameplay makes it an accessible game despite following Omega Force’s usual formula which they have used for years now. There’s obviously quite a bit of gameplay repetition here, but a healthy cast of characters and progression makes up for it in many ways. Whilst hack and slash games of this ilk aren’t everyone’s cup of tea, fans of One Piece will love the transition to PS4/PC here despite the lack of English voices and probably need no encouragement to buy the game. Anyone else on the fence will find a neat game filled to the brim with content that’s worth picking up if you’re in need to let off some steam and just attack masses of enemies over and over again.

I've played since 2008, so I have way more hours logged than what I've played on Steam. As such, I can say that I whole-heartedly recommend this game... if you have friends to play with. It's a hard solo experience, with a very rewarding dungeon system that gives better loot at higher difficulties (but you're not able to outright solo them). The questing is a tad sparce, but it makes up for that with a chapter based story system with fleshed out cutscenes that tell the story of Erinn very well.
Now, as it's a Korean MMO, it's very grindy. Very, very grindy. The game softens this, however, with its unique rebirth system; every 7 days, you're able to start over from level 1 and ages 10 through 17. Your character ages up every Saturday, and as they do, they gain stats and ability points (AP). There is a diminishing returns factor when it comes to stat gain.
The pet system is a lot of fun, giving you the ability to play as your pet and level them up in dungeons. They do have a time limit, however, which replenishes every real morning. They are a real boon to your gameplay, giving you a large inventory to compliment your own, and opening up a plethora of combat tactics. Unfortunately, they cost real money in Nexon's very aggressively marketed NX shop.
The combat is a lot of fun albeit clunky. Although, the game is from 2003, so it gets a pass. It doesn't help much that Nexon's servers are some of the laggiest pieces of garbage known to mankind (the dungeons are on a seperate server, and that SoB crashes so much and if you're inside a dungeon when that happens, the monsters will not spawn and loot will not drop). Nexon support is janky at best; they do respond, but most of the time give copy-paste responses. However, this doesn't affect my opinion on Mabinogi on a whole.
The community used to be one of the best. Helpful, friendly, always willing to play with you and hang out. Of course it did have its bad eggs and drama queens, but it was amazing. It changed for the worse over the years, where everyone sticks to themselves, are unwilling to help those in need (unless you're their friend or popular), and play the game only for the fashion (which isn't a bad thing, but is similar to RuneScape's atrocious bankstanding culture). I've met some of my best friends on this game, some whome I still keep in constant contact with.
Overall, the game is a lot of fun. You will most definitely have a vastly different experience than what I've had. It will be a great experience where you will meet friends, form relationships, and embark on an amazing journey.

As one of the few people still playing Mabinogi, I've noticed that the game has been on a rapid decline since when I first began playing. This, of course, can be attributed to many things, but I feel like what stands out the most is how little attention has been payed towards bettering the game. Within the past year, the changes have been minimal and largely focused on adding new gimicks and events. Customization is only an option when you have Pon, the premium currency, and opportunities to get this are far and few in between. The community is slowly dying out, and nowadays you'll only find 5-6 players in one area.
With this in mind, I continue to hold out hope that Mabinogi will make a comeback, as I really liked the rebirth feature and have yet to experience all that they have to offer. If only attempts were made to smooth out the edges of the game and perhaps introduce new features that actually matter to the gamer, it wouldn't be too far a stretch for Mabinogi to gain back what its lost as time has passed.
However, as Mabinogi is now, I just don't feel like this game is really worth playing. I'll still keep waiting for that game-changing update, though, if it ever arrives.

After the first awkward 5 hours, Risen 3 has far exceeded my expectations in the remainining 40 hours or so. The game has beautiful scenery, huge worlds to explore, lots of quests and interesting characters, nice voice acting--essentially almost everything I could ask for in an open-world action RPG. It gave me a sense of freedom, of unlimited choices, and that's very important for me in a game.
Combat is uncomfortable. In melee mode, a chicken or rat can jump on me and kick me away by 5 metres--are they made of titanium? What's the body weight or logic in this? The combat frustration stopped after learning magic, but combat also became repetitive and not challenging. If you are looking for combat experience, this is not for you.
The companions are a little crazy and they constantly whine. Patty is the only joy to be around, and the only character who has retained funny dialogue.
In comparison with risen 2, the main character is coarse-mouthed, shallow-minded, and far less funny than before. But by the time I finished the game, he has become endearing, as if his actions define him more than the shallow dialogues. While playing Risen 3, it's nice to revisit the same island locations, the same characters, but because your character has changed since Risen 2, they don't maintain the same connections with you.
Expansion packs:
- Highly recommend the "Uprising of the Little Guys". Gnomes and their woes and worries are most entertaining and their island is huge. It is one of the highlights of the entire game.
- "Fog Island" is okay, it adds several additional quests but did not overly impress me.
- "Adventure Garb" is like medium-level wardrobe, it's only useful for a few hours while you are a newbie, not essential.
Oh and kudos to the voodoo tribe and the theme music, both have touched my heart :)

Dragon Ball Xenoverse is one of the best Dragon Ball games to come out in a long time. The battles feel nice, the character customization does it's job well, and the story adds a new interesting spin on the DBZ story we all know. They did a good mix of fighting, and rpg mechanics. You are able to equip up to 7 skills, and put skill points into 6 different stats. The skills are easy to use, but it is when to use them that takes skills. The hand-to-hand combat feels nice, and you can string together nice combos, that can string into more combos.
The story is nice, but really short. There are few missions in the main campaign, and they don't cover most of the story. They hit all the main points of the DBZ story, but they leave out things like cooler, and most of the movies besides broly, and bardok. They are costumes from other movies, but no missions/characters.
The multiplayer is fun, and works farly well. The servers are haing problems right now, but that will be fixed soon. There are some cheap tactics that people can use, and are annoying to deal with. Most of the time though you will have a far fight.
The game is not perfect though. Some missions have you fighting a 3-5 on 1, and the computers will stagger you, and basically make it impossible to move. It is possible to deal with it, and win but it can be very annoying to the player.

For me this game, though it can be challenging, always helps to relax me. You can play the map for just a few moments or a few hours, it's up to you how seriously you want to play the game. That is a virtue I love since I don't want to invest myself in a game all the time yet I can challenge myself if I want to.
✘ It can be frustrating.
This game relies heavily on random items that you get and have to put on the map/level. If you get a bad combo, it can potentially end the round. You can buy items in the store however they can be expensive (with in-game coins, not real currency) and there's a limit to how many of each item you can buy per round.
✘  There isn't diversity in level design.
The game is still cute however the maps are all pretty much the same. Though some have lakes while others have none, they can all look alike, and thus appear fairly bland.
✘ I do wish there were maps of different sizes.
All the maps/levels are the same size, though some have less space with lakes and rivers in the way. If this game were ever updated or a sequel made, I would appreciate if there were more diversity in the size of the towns. It would be fun to have some huge, some small, etc.
Overall this is a wonderful game and all flaws aside, I think it would make a lovely game for any gamer.

The word for this game would be 'underwhelming'.

The idea of the 'match3 kawai settlers' sounds cool. And the design is decent, and the very first impression is rather good, but.... there's nothing going on. Like literally. No sense of progression whatsoever, no story, no new levels, zones and themes\settings to aim for. The mobile version had themes, by the way. But here it's just the same old tiles to combine on the same few tiny zones in order to grind coins. And then grind for more coins. Oh, and have I mentioned grind for coins? The only reward for that grinding are the extra tiles for the 'permanent city', grind for 3 woods - get a tile of fence, or go for 'aesthetics' and put yourself a giant(=tile-sized) bear statue or a 'F'-shaped bush.
Don't get me wrong, I was not expecting  miracles from a match3 mobile port. I don't have anything against raw and pure timekillers. Hell, my playtime for Bejeweled or Zuma are actually significantly higher than I would care to admit.  But this game? It just...pretended to be something more, that's it. It was never meant to be a stand-alone PC game.

It's a fun strategy game, a different take on the Match 3 genre. You match up 3 patches a grass to make a bush(it appears where the last patch of grass was placed), 3 bushes make a tree, 3 trees make a house, 3 houses make a large house, etc. There are many other mechanics that  I don't want to spoil, and there's in-game store to buy items with in-game currency.
There's also a home island, called your Capital, where you can place industries like farms and mines like you would in the normal game, but as you score points these industries give you items. A nice little meta game. I definitely recommend Triple Town.

Okay, so with Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm Revolution coming out in about a month, I guess I figured "Why not make a review on the last Storm game?"
Only, I don't want to go lengthy on this, because most Storm games will play like most Storm games.
With a few new mechanics thrown in here, and there, and boom, you got your Storm game that's somewhat different than previous Storm game.
For this one, I guess that would be the fact that this is the first Storm game that pushed pass the Shippuden Story line, and gave us a ton of DLC later on during the game's launch.
So, what will I be rating this game on?
Delivery.
Did it deliver?
Yes.
Did it deliver MUCH?
Not that much, but enough to hold you off until the next Storm game.
With all of the characters, online mode, and DLC they packed in, I'd say Storm 3 would hold anybody off until Revolution came, and the DLC was fairly decent, amped graphics, more costumes, a new part of the Shippuden story added in, along with Sage Mode Kabuto added in.
And now, WITH the DLC, this game is about $30.
So, with Revolution coming out in about a month, would I say this game is worth buying?
I'd say if you don't have this game, and you're really itching for some Storm to play, but have some extra money on hand, then buy it.
It is fun, and will keep you busy, and if you're a fan of Naruto, or any fighting game for that matter, you'll enjoy it.
If I were to rate the game itself?
Mechanics: 9/10. (Some nicer
Story: 5/10 (Rating how well it did in adapting from the Anime/Manga.)
Replayability: 8.5/10 (Online mode, and story mode have some stuff going for it.)
Music? 10/10 I thought it was done very well throughout each stage. I might be giving it too much credit, but it's definitely doing Naruto music justice.
Variety? 8/10. Despite how much is put into the game, a story mode, an online mode, and a vs mode is really all it has. It wasn't jam packed with much, so the online mode, and even vs mode is really all you'll be coming back to the game for. Unless you're that psyched for the story mode in the game (Which, I'm sure not AS many were.)
Overall rating for the game:
8.5/10.
I'd recommend picking it up if you had some extra cash at the moment.
And definitely if you're a Naruto fan.

When I see Early Access Games I see games with potential, it is how the developers use this to make it bad or good in the long term. Interstellar Marines is set in our world's future, where you are a Special Forces soldier and you are getting trained for the interstellar Marine Program (IM). You get sent on various missions throughout the campaign.
The first thing I'm going to say is this game has the best AI I have ever seen in a shooter. If they hear gunshots they will keep looking and patrolling for you. If they hear you they will look for you, if you’re in the dark they will not see you but if you stand in light they will. Another thing on that in the game you can shoot the lights and they will get destroyed and it is amazing how immersive it is. For example when you sprint you get tiered and it affects your accuracy but there is one problem with that when you get tired you don't recover with in a reasonable speed and the sound affect needs to be polished more.  The lightly is amazing and it feels like I’m really there. It is the best I've ever seen in a game before; the ability to destroy lights at will is a rare thing in games. The lights affect how you play as well as how the AI act when you’re in darkness. I personality loved going through building and destroying lights and having fun hiding from the enemy. The graphics are awesome and it has ambient partials. The multiplayer is good but could improve with more multiplayer game modes but I still enjoyed it and the game mode already in it is a great thing and you will still enjoy it. The difficulty setting is great because the lower ones are good for beginners and realistic is good for the advanced. The campaign needs to be polished more and the story needs work so that you can follow it as you go. In future they could add more than 2 guns, to add more of an experience. There is a cliping bug with objects but I'm sure this will be fixed in a later update

Right I didn't play this for an extended period of time so I won't speak as if I have. In truth I couldn't bring myself to. The game forces you to drift at about 50 KM/H the moment you lightly touch the analog stick (I used a controller, keyboard was impossible to me) which I understand, it's a drifting game, but my god I want to feel as if I have some control. Thing is, there is actually a handbrake which allows you to somewhat initiate a drift which perplexes me because why should I be forced to drift when I can choose to?
Another thing that bugged me, this game has no automatic controller support. I had to go into the settings and set up keybindings on my controller manually, which annoyed me because I don't play racing games, how am I supposed to know the best layout? The reason I find this an annoyance is because so many other games just automatically switch to controller mode when one is plugged in, like NSUNS4, Happy Wars and Rocket League, why can't this? While not a flaw with the gameplay mechanics itself, it is annoying to have to deal with.
Car customization is awful. There's too much just thrown at you. As a non car expert I didn't understand about 70% of what I was upgrading my car with, plus you're eased into NONE of it. The tutorial takes you through the process of upgrading your engine I believe and that's it. So, after the tutorial I thought "Great, can't be too hard then." Oh but it is. See while the process isn't difficult it's extremely confusing, every single car part has a sub series of parts that have no specification on what they do to help your car other than a little stat gui at the bottom right, which provides little to no help as I know NOTHING about cars. It's a drifting game, not a simulator, though it definitely feels like one.
Overall, while in Early Access, this game isn't great, though I will happily give it another look at a later development stage.

Mabinogi is a rock-paper-scissors type alternate-life MMO. Essentially this means the main core aspect of the combat, is based off of a rock-paper-scissors system in which each skill has an added advantage, and disadvantage. There is no real class system in Mabinogi, for mostly every character can fully master every available talent that is provided in the game, save for race specific talents. This means that you as a player start off very weak, and can rise to the ranks of the most formidable opponent through time, patience, and effort. It is plenty fun to slowly accumulate new skills, new weapons, and develop your own combos. This game is great in the fact that there are no class barriers, you can master every talent, from which, are a few such titles such as Warrior, Martial Arts, Knight, Mage, Archer, Bard, Gunner, Ninja, etc. All of these talents can be used together in synergy to create a stronger, hybrid-type talent through practice. This game has its own storyline, PVP system, and three continent world.
Although Mabinogi does not offer too much in terms of raw character creation capabilities, it makes up for this loss by providing a multitude of clothing, armor, and such to buy, find, or create as you start your journey in Mabinogi.
As a veteran player who has essentially everything mastered, and has done everything available to be done, I can say without a doubt - Mabinogi certainly is fun. However, depending on what kind of person you are, you may not like the community of Mabinogi - which is heavily saturated with lovers of anime culture and the like (whom of which it is technically marketed towards) - and you will most definitely not like the Pay to Win aspects this game creates with its cash shop. Mabinogi is completely conscious of just how much earnings they can reap in by giving players the upper hand in the game, and what some may say an "unfair advantage". While others work hard for their items and damage, can be attained with a couple of paychecks in a fraction of the time by people who are so inclined. Disregard these unfortunately major problems, and Mabinogi is quite a fun and satisfying game, however these issues certainly must be taken into consideration.
Overall, this game has some really nice core aspects, but a fair amount of internal, problems such as community and pay 2 win really deduct from this games potential. I would tell you to check it out, and see if you like it. It's much better to play with friends, or make friends who can help you along in the game as it can be rather difficult and over cumbersome at first. I thought it was terrible the first time I played it, picked it back up, and now I have more than ten thousand levels under my belt.

I know this game is in Alpha, and they have many disclaimers posted all over the game and on Steam stating the game is in Alpha. We are told to expect bugs and an overall unfinished product. This game will be a free to play business model whenever it finally 'releases'. As such, I don't know what possessed me to plop $40 of my hard earned money on this game, and I sincerely wish I could get a refund.
First, before the Fanboys start the flaming, let me say I am a hardcore SWG fan and played the game from initial release until the end, and let me say this game does a good job at recreating the general feel of SWG right down to the UI. But something is lacking.
I find it ireprehensible that this game is in such a horrid state of development after the amount of money people have pourd into it and the amount of time the game has been in development. The development of this game began in 2008...yes, almost seven years ago. It's 2015 now and we are no closer to release then we were in 2010 when they switched engines for this game.
The problems of this game start in character creation. with the general premise of the game, I understand there is only one race, humans. Thats fine. The issue is in the general lack of options. The control scheme in creation isnt very intuitive, and your face always looks the same. The only real way to change the general look is to make your character fat or skinny and slap facial hair on them. Even after that they still look like shiny claymation characters.
Then you get in the gameworld and get to stumble through the shoddy tutorial. SWG honestly had better graphics and ran jus as choppy. and how old is SWG. Also, when you get in game you realize the terrain is horrendous, the rocks and stones look like cardboard and the grass looks like pipecleaners. The town's feel vacant. Most NPC's don't serve a purpose or show any signs of AI. When you get into combat, the laser effects are downright cheap and goofy.
The premise for this game is great, the vision is epic and the spirit of SWG is there, but after close to seven years of development and a lot of consumer investment, I expect better than this rough shod heap. If you are thinking about paying $40 for an Alpha, remember it's an alpha...seriously. And there are no signs after playing it there will be a release any time soon.
