I first played Gearbox's Borderlands on an Xbox 360 with my older brother. I was somewhat young, and much of the game's finer details escaped me, especially the humor. Now that I can comprehend  the game, I've decided to leave a review.
Borderlands is the first entry in an FPS series by Gearbox Software. It's pretty typical as far as gameplay mechanics, but it mixes in some RPG-style elements and is a really hilarious experience.
Let's talk gameplay mechanics first. The game is full of guns. Gearbox marketed the game as having "bazillions" of guns. While that's not even a real figure, there are still a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of weapons to use. Something around a few billion, in fact. The system works by generating guns in parts. A sniper rifle, for example, might have different parts for the stock, scope, handle, barrel, and body. Each in-game manufacturer probably has a few dozen parts for each component of each gun. So, with all of the game's different gun classes (pistol, SMG, sniper, rocket launcher, assault rifle, and Eridian), manufacturers, and parts per manufacturer, you have a pretty ridiculous amount of guns.
The second gameplay mechanic I'll talk about is the vehicles. The first Borderlands is a bit more limited on stock vehicles than later entries, only allowing two variations of the basic "Runner" vehicle, the variations being machine-gun or rocket turrets. You can spawn them out of thin air at stations throughout the game world.
Third are the characters. There are four characters to choose from:
Each character has a different skill tree and certain weapon proficiencies.
Fourth is the leveling. As you kill enemies and complete missions, your character will gain levels, up to level 61 with all the necessary DLC. When you hit level 5, you get to unlock your action skill, which is a character-based usable skill that can turn the tides of battle. Roland can deploy his Scorpio Turret, a sentry turret that has shields and can even heal players within its radius. Lilith can phasewalk, which allows her to move quickly without taking damage and get close to enemies to release an explosion at the end of the skill's duration or to move somewhere with better cover, for example. Brick goes berserk, where he trades his guns for his fists. Yes, he literally punches people to death. Mordecai releases his pet Bloodwing, which will fly at enemies and do ridiculous damage, and will often one-hit enemies once the player reaches higher levels and purchases the correct skills along the way.
Now that you have an idea of Borderlands' gameplay mechanics, let me inform you about two of the series' trademarks.
Borderlands has an iconic graphical style. The developers employed "celshading," a technique which outlines all of the objects in the game world with thick black lines, sort of like tracing around everything with a black Sharpie marker. It's a very noticeable effect, but it still looks really good.
Borderlands is known for its humor as well as its graphics. One of the first main characters you meet is this funny, idiotic robot named CL4P-TP, but goes by his "locally-designated name," Claptrap. He's kind of hilarious, and the reactions of other characters to him are just as funny.
Borderlands was and still is a fresh take on the FPS genre. It beats games like Call of Duty on multiple grounds, and is overall an extremely unique experience. Unlike other games, Borderlands' DLC is worth buying because all of the DLC is major, rather than being $3 packs that let you reskin your character, or something like that. I highly recommend the game, and really encourage you to buy it if you haven't already considered it.

After a few good hours dedicated to this game, I have grown to love it.
Admittedly, the tutorial is quite crap but once you get past it with some help from some more experienced players as well as teaming up with other fellow newbies, I have become absolutely addicted to the game.
For my pro's: The game has a unique look. The gameplay mechanics are also very different from any other MMO I've ever played but I like them. I love the rebirth system. I love how I have the option to play as a pet. Customizing your character to make them totally unique from any other player is so easy. There are so many little hidden features and abilities. It's very easy to level up and glide through most quests and dungeons. I think the marriage and family system is adorable. The NPC's seem very fleshed out. The artwork for the game is just awesome. The choice in variety of pets is immense and I love it to pieces. The world seems very open and very immersive. Most enemies are pretty easy. You don't lose all of your items when you die. The aging system is pretty neat. The weight system is nifty as well.
For my con's: The combat system is crap as is the tutorial. When you meet a difficult enemy, it literally takes you ages to beat them and you end up using all of your "Ask Nao for Help"'s and Lorna Balloons on one boss battle. Dungeons can become extremely painstakingly repetitive. Getting to the Another World is hell and being able to sustain yourself within the world is even harder. The enemies in Another World are ridiculously OP no matter what level you are. Losing important quest items happens all the time to me and makes it that much more frustrating when trying to further quests. Some quests are beyond impossible to complete, especially when you can't even join a party for other players to come help you out. I've ditched three quests so far because my level 55 gunslinger can't even make it past the first few enemies.
8/10. Just because the game is so much more fun with friends, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who loves MMO's.

You into full out, detailed as crap stories of adventure and/or romance? There's, again, a ton of different storylines and they add event stories to the game for even more adventure. This game honestly just never really ends.

Alright, now back to the music. In this game, you can take REAL music and create it in the game. Not only can you play/sing it with friends, you can also use it as a weapon. Harps, pianos, flutes, lutes, even electric guitars.

there's alot of potential here for the long pined for and in recent years much touted and vocalized demand for sandboxy mmo play that earmarked the early years of the mmo genre but has long since been forelorn in favour of an extreme dichotomy between hardcore corpse loot ffa pvp games like eve and DFO and others, and the increasingly on rails and narrow avenues of gameplay of themepark games ranging from wow to gw2.
instead here we have a a middle ground answer to the ever widening gap that takes another look at the mmo as a virtual world. while there will be a hardcore corpse loot server option eventually, currently the game's economy and avenues rely on swg like decay system rather than corpse loot or bind on equip durability systems of the two polar extremes that inundate the genre over the past 10 years.
there's a wide degree of freedom and options on both avenues of progression and gameplay roles. want to be a dedicated crafter? you can do that, and rely on combat oriented players or trade to feed your manufactury efforts. want to be a non combat entertainer? you can progress dancing and story telling and help road weary combat players both at clubs and in the field at campsites. want to be a combat player? there's a wide variety of weapon and combat styles to choose from, ranging from mobile ranged options to longer range but less mobile options. to a wide variety of setting appropriate melee options each with their own tasty nuances.
the freedom to dedicate yourself to one of these avenues, or mix as you please, is also refreshing. want to be a dancer who also farms wildlife with an automatic? well hell that's what i do in game already right now.
and pvp vs pve? on the normal mode servers, pvp is always an option, but not a required one. each faction gets a full third of the game world to themselves each. while the final third is open pvp for the less faint of heart. and factions themselves are not set in stone - if you wish to break away and make your own decisions as to whom you ally with and fight against, you can do so via the rogue nation systems.
i have watched in and out of game the amazing pace of progress by these developers over the past year, while engaging with them on their forums and getting personal and well reasoned replies from them. maybe i have an idea to suggest for the game that doesn't work or has been tried already? the devs have let me know that, or why that thing i suggest doesn't work or they might like it but plan not to use it. and at other times for feedback that they do plan to take, they ask for more information to get a better picture of what i'm asking for or suggesting.
the downsides of the game currently are, however, quite obvious: character creation is very light with not a lot of options beyond tethered together sliders that change the shapes of body parts. the UI in general needs a lot of work, as it's heavilyinundated by drop down menu paradigms. this affects everything from AH shopping and selling to crafting to character creation - they have told me they are aware of this though and asked for examples for inspiration of what we desire and expect in these places. and ofc the art assets quality is also lacking at this time.
i also want to note, that if you like mmoRPG combat, ie tab/click targetting stuff, the combat is solid, responsive and punchy. this game feels just plain nice to farm mobs in so far, and i can't wait to get the opportunity to try the combat in pvp in the future.
my verdict is that if you're looking for something that scratches that pre wow/eve dichotomy sandy mmo itch, then repop is the game to watch. if you aren't ready for wipes and bugs and all around roughness, keep this game on the backburner for now, but keep an on it and this is the middle ground sandbox mmo to watch in the coming year above all other big studio hype machine offerings being bandied about.

Note: As I play this game I will update this Review. As of now I am a noob with very little play time, however, as of right now, the review is a great "first glimpse" of what it's like, and a non biased look at the game.
Note 2: Also remember.. This is Alpha, things are subject to change.
-----------------------------------------------
When I first stepped into the The Repopulation, I won't lie. It didn't excite me. I was thinking "Oh great, another 40$ wasted on a well made video on steam that has nothing to do with how the game actually is"... I was wrong.. This game, honestly is a true RPG.
The graphics themselves are nothing amazing by any means, for those of you need decent and or awesome graphics.. this game isn't for you most likely. However, if you're a player who can look past that, and see the depth of game mechanics and the treasure trove under the surface. This is definetly a game to really look into it more closely if what you saw on the Steam page peaked your interest.

The Character Creator or TCC for short isn't anything special. You get the usual choices, height, weight, customizing the face, etc. Atm It's pretty bulky as moving 1 slider will move another, and you end up having to move 4-5 sliders in little notches to really fine tune your characters look.
However, as a plus you get to choose and customize its starting armor, which actually is alot more important than a  beginner may think ( They don't actually explain this too well in the tool tip when choosing, except vague things). As a tip.. When choosing your starting armor look and color, think of how you're going to play.
If you're gonna be a sniper, choose lighter equipment, if you're going to go head deep, choose heavier stuff. If you're ont going to fight, or be as passive as possible, choose nothing, or as light as possible. (A cook doesn't need heavy armor after all).
---------------------------------------------
Since my over all game time atm is very little, what I will say right now before I start breaking up my Review in a day or so, is simply this. So far the game already has proven to be quite deep in mechanics.
For Instance.
As Stealth, leveling it up will unlock your ability to use Camoflauge, Disguises, disarm traps, and multitude of other things you'd think would be helpful for playing that style of character, (whether you want to be a sniper, spec ops, thief, assassin, or a window peeker). Yes, you can get disguises to change your look. Be that Spy... <3
There are even deep mechanics for socializing, such as dancing. Already in my short time of playing I met a player who, all they do.. is dance..
By dancing and raising a specific skill you unlock other dances, which both buff nearby players and NPCs, and can be linked and interlinked with other dances by other player, buffing the buffs even more. This can only be done in social area's; however, this player dances in their player made town, at the pub they created. Where other players can come in, socialize, and watch the dancers.. (who are real people). It's more of a fun social have fun, as the dancing is nothing more than clicking a few buttons, but.. MMO's are about socializing anyway right? It's a great way to kick back after roghing it out in the woods and fighting off other players from the other faction.
You can also setup camp, which opens a small temporary socializing area, allowing players to dance and have a good time out in the wilderness.
The NPCs themselves are very in depth. Most NPC's have an "Inquiry" button, when you click this you can type in another NPC's name you may be looking for, and if they are in a good mood, and they like you, they will tell you roughly where they are, or even mark them on your map, -IF- that NPC knows. Some may, some may not. Inquiring one NPC 30 ft away may result in a much better result in what you're looking for.
It doesn't stop there by any means however, you can also Inquire NPCs about new events in the area, or possible situations going on that you may be interested in.
As you complete MIssions, engangements, talk to NPCs in general, and raise your diplomacy skill(If you're going that way), read books, or inquire about various topics you will gain new bits of knowledge. These will open up additional questions with NPCs that you can ask about, which may result in learning backstory, or even opening a Mission or Assignment, or Oppertunities you'd otherwise not have gotten.
-------------------------------------

Unlike most games out there, NPCs in this game have a schedule. They will close up shop at night, go home, sleep, and do things normal humans would. This even includes Quests. If you recieve a Quest from an NPC at their shop, and you return late at night, they'll probably be gone, and you'll need to wait until morning to hand it in.
Some shady thief NPCs, or underworld characters only come out at night as well, so if you're one of those players who really wants to go in and be that dark alleyway skulking thief or killer, you'll definetly find some fun in this game, as the Underworld only comes out at night (Since you know, that makes sense, don't you just hate other games that put them out on the street in broad daylight??)
------------------------------------------------------
From what I've seen in the tutorial, and the time I've played, the quests really are tailored to how you play. Though there are NPCs who may give you their usual quest to anyone regardles of who they are, you will recieve quests via your PDF. These you can tailor to how you want to play. Whether that be Combat, Military, Crafting, Politics, Underworld, etc. You can choose which type Quests are randomly generated for you.

Dragonball: Xenoverse is a solid game. Honestly, I like to call it "Dragonball: Fan Fiction" because hey, oh if only some strong, unique snowfloke hero could come save us. Enter DBZ OC (don't steal). You even get personally complimented by the characters many times... and honestly, it's a little awkward. But that's OK, because you get to make your rockin' human, saiyan, buu, frieze clan or namek person and beat the heck out of most of Dragon Ball Z's heroes and villains. So points there!
That said, there are two things the game does that really get in the way of an otherwise addictive game. The first is the difficulty spikes. There are a few places where you basically have to grind 10+ levels to have a chance in beating it. I realize this is a feature in many genres of game, and some people might resent being able to more-or-less coast through the story mode unhindered. But dang it, I want to unlock my multiple characters and spend hours playing that way, not grinding.
The second sin is the worse one, in my opinion. There is no chat beyond pre-canned chat options. very restrictive, likes lots of kid-oriented free-to-play games (and not-so-free ones, like the LEGO MMO was). Ironically, however, once you enter a party with someone the voice chat is enabled and unfiltired. So you get to hear the feedback from your teammate's monitor, or their profanity, or whatever the pre-canned chat was supposed to eliminate.
Positives! You get to make your own character. A lot of pieces can be used to make easily-recognizeable people from the show, (I don't think they have unique models), but can also be combined in ways that give you the Toriyama look without being Gohan With Green Hair (although some do this anyway). Slight downside is that costume pieces that explictly belong to a character cannot have their colors altered, but other more generic ones can. Fashion Souls, eat your heart out.
Fighting is simple, with stamina used to fly at mach speed and ki used to power energy attacks and special moves. Combos are frankly a little boring (x,x,y or x,x,x,x,y) type of deal, but show characters often have unique variations on moves and some supers and whatnot can be put into the chain, so it's not 100% bland... just don't expect Street Fighter or Mortal Kombat here.
Visuals are great, it's really like the cartoon in 3D. Iconic areas like rocky windswept wastlands, the windy rockstrewn wasteland, the towering windy rocks. ;) Some are very similar, but others are the middle of town or outer space or a huge water-filled cave much like where that Red Ribbon base was in Dragon Ball. You can move up and down as well as all around, and terrain is destructable but serves no real other purpose.
"Parallel Quests" are side-quests that, while optional, provide the real meat of the cooperative experience. You and up to two CPU or online players spend time wrecking the timeline you've been fighting so hard to protect. Go figure, but it's where the real challenges are (do you keep Krillin alive, or let him die when he is supposed to?), and more importantly, the real loot.
Overall, this is a 7/10, with solid gameplay and replay value somewhat hampred by draconic chat restrictions and sudden but inevitable difficulty spikes. Worth playing if you're a Dragon ball fan, or a fan of quasi-online fighting games in general.

If you are familiar with the Tenkaichi series then you might think you know what is in store. You are wrong. You make your own character at the start of the story who at lvl 50, after hours of grinding, is still weaker stat wise then Hercule then go up against altered fights from the main series (which is actually very well done).
The first thing you will notice is the input lag, especially when going from dashing to guard or ki balst to anything.Players familar with fighters like MK or SF will feel very out of place especailly without any form of guard cancelling.
The AI is abyssmal when it fights other AI, and only shows any level of competence when facing you. To counteract this, the game gives them more of every stat and will often see you outnumbered, where the lack of defensive options really shows. Simply put it is impossible to guard against 2 AI if they are agressive enough, though often one will be randomly floating around in the distance somewhere.
Another strength that a lot of the high end opponents have is super armour. This means that the opponent will not flinch until you do a certain amount of damage first which can get really tedious and in certain fights that have multiple parts (that you do not restore your already low health by default) can be game changing. Imagine a fight where you beat you're opponent, then they come back with a friend, then by themselves again with a power increase when they have 6x your health AND super armour. It gets very old very quickly.
In terms of performance the game is smooth, sitting easily at 60fps with an acceptable (not great) graphics range.
This game could have been amazing but between the absurd grind, clunky controls for a fighter, woeful AI (especially friendly), this game will quickly outstay its welcome unless you are a diehard DBZ fan.

To be honest, I didn’t have high expectations for this game. I got it with a Humble deal, which I only bought because of Sonic Generations. Also, I don’t find the 2d Bionic Commando games to be very fun. They are enjoyable, but only for a short period of time. That’s why I was really surprised over how good this game actually is!
Probably the weakest part of the game. The story is not very good. Something I didn’t know before going into this, was that the game is a sequel. So why did they call it Bionic Commando? When using the original name for a game in a long running series, it usually means it’s a reboot. But not this one! Well, it doesn’t matter, since the story isn’t good anyways. The dialogue is really bad at times. There’s a lot of notes you can read, but I didn’t even bother reading a single one of them. There's also a plot twist near the end about the arm. I think it was supposed to be emotional, but it ended up just being weird. While the story isn’t good, it’s better than nothing I guess.
The game looks surprisingly good for an almost ten year old game. Compared to modern games it doesn’t hold up, but I would be impressed if I played it when it was released. There’s a lot of advertising in this game. I didn’t mind it, but I can see how it could be annoying for some. There’s something about swinging from a huge Nvidia sign that doesn’t feel right.
The music in this game is actually pretty good! It isn’t very memorable, but it made me excited to play more. Something I don’t like is the sound that plays when picking up a collectable. It doesn’t match the rest of the game, and the music will stop for a second to let it finish! Other than that, I don’t really have a problem with the music.
First of all, who is responsible for making the tutorial show you the xbox controls, regardless if you’re using a controller or not? I was gonna use my keyboard for this game, but after the confusing tutorial I ended up switching to a controller.
The best part of the game by far is the bionic arm. It is a grappling hook! At first I thought you could only attach yourself to a few objects, but no! You can do it to almost everything! This game is the best Spiderman simulator I’ve played! The levels have tall buildings and signs you can swing around, and navigating the area is fun as hell. You can also use it as a weapon. One of my favorite ways to kill enemies, is to throw one enemy at another. A problem I have is the “radiation”. Since the game gives you this amazing tool to explore the levels with, it is quite easy to get out of bounds. Instead of having an invisible wall to stop you, the places that are out of bounds are radiated. If you stay at a radiated spot for too long, you’ll die. The problem comes when you're swinging around and having fun, until you suddenly die, since you moved into a radiated place. It killed me quite a number of times, and is really annoying.
Even though the bionic arm mechanic is really fun, the gunplay is not. You have your standard gun, which you get from the start of the game. this one you’ll have through the entire game. There’s also special guns. You can only have one special gun with you at a time, and the ammo for them are really rare. You also have grenades, which got really useful. I don’t know why, but the guns just doesn’t feel right to me. They can be really hard to aim at times. If you’re not using a sniper, good luck hitting anything from a long range. The death animations for the enemies are also really weird. When killing an enemy, they will often be sent flying, which can lead to some hilarious deaths. While to gunplay feels really weird, it does what it has to do.There were only a couple of times I got mad at it. What I really want to do, is to shoot the enemies while swinging from building to building, but that’s almost Impossible.
You can’t save in this game. Saving is done when doing something plot related. This is horrible, and I ended up losing at least half an hour of gameplay throughout the game. While it isn’t a big deal for most of the game, there is a part near the end where there’s hundreds of enemies coming at you in waves that you have to kill before continuing. If you die, you’ll have to start from the beginning again. I spent a long time at this section, because I continued to die!
I was surprised that I liked the game so much. I think the only reason why I’ll give it the score I’m gonna give it is because of the bionic arm. It’s awesome! Swinging around the levels made me forget about the bad parts of this game, like the story and gunplay. Since the bionic arm was so fun to use, I’ll give this game a:
This was my first big surprise with this project. All the other games I’ve reviewed, I had already played, or at least knew what they were about. This was the first game I went in completely blind, and I loved it. If you find the grappling hook to sound cool, I recommend checking it out. Now I’m even more excited for the new Spiderman game!

First of all, the art and music alone are reasons enough to buy and play the game in my opinion. I really dig the 8 bit art and music. I’d compare Alwa’s Awakenings art and music to Shovel Knights. But gameplay wise it’s rather a metroidvania kind of game (So no overworld with many levels, instead, one big map with several areas and unlocking items which can be used in previous areas to obtain certain items and discover new areas).
The world of Alwa, once a beautiful and peaceful land, is now under control of a dark being called Vicar. With the help of the four protectors (strong henchmen of his) he gathered the four ornaments, which are said to make the owner very powerful. If nobody stops Vicar, the land of Alwa might never be the same.
This is when you come into the play. You are Zoe, a heroine from another world, who has to claim the four ornaments in order to be able to defeat Vicar at the end.
You begin with barely anything in your inventory. The only actions you are capable of are walking jumping and ducking. A few screens further you get a magic staff though. The staff is not only for hitting, you can earn 3 different spells (two of them are upgradable once) which are used to get around obstacles or fighting enemies. For example with the first spell you can get a little bit higher, block enemy bullets, (more a glitch/trick which is not needed to beat the game) jump a second time and after an upgrade float on water.
There are other things to gather as well:
There are 99 orbs hidden all around the world. Some are very easy to get but some are hidden/tricky and may require items you don’t have yet (metroidvania!).
Every few orbs you become stronger against the protectors and Vicar. Meaning you inflict damage depending on the amount of orbs you have.
Other than the orbs you can also collect keys, an item which increases your melee power or other more passively stuff.
When you die you recover at the last checkpoint you activated (special rooms with a torch). The checkpoints are rather generously distributed so you’re only thrown back a few rooms.
There are also a handful teleporter rooms on the map, so if you found a new item you don’t have to walk all the way back to use the new item in order to get some orbs or unlock new areas.
What I really liked was the fact that I could sometimes reach an orb/area with my current items by using certain tricks like the previously mentioned second jump. So you don’t have to wait till you have the proper item/spell and it was very satisfying after getting the jumps or whatever done. BUT that doesn’t work in every situation. More than often you may need another spell/item to get the job done. ”Oh THAT’S how it’s done properly.”
If I convinced you, go get the game! I genuinely enjoyed playing Alwa’s awakening and would like to play much much more games like it.

Alwa's Awakening is a retro metroidvania platformer with pixel graphics.
You play as Zoe, the purple caped heroine on a quest to free the world of Alwa from the 4 Guardians (bosses)... or something like that. I wasn't paying much attention to the storyline, it's the usual thing.
The idea is to explore the world, jumping gaps, climbing ladders, killing enemies, collecting keys to open doors to new (named) areas, and collecting the 3 gemstones to gain new powers: create a block to allow you to jump a bit higher; bubble to raise you a little higher than the block; fireball to shoot enemies and open lightning-bolt doorways. As you gain these new powers it allows you to reach previously inaccessible areas, so you have to revisit previous areas with your new powers to open up more map. There are the usual puzzling elements in as much as "how to I get up/over there".
You manually set your own waypoints by lighting torches along the way, so you have a choice of where you want to respawn which is quite useful if you want to focus on an earlier area. You have 3 lives before death/respawn - sometimes you find an extra life along the way to delay your demise and some hazards mean insta-death. In any case, there is a lot of death, and each time you die you're given a reminder of the overall number of deaths you've suffered. It does mount up. There are also warp gates dotted around the world which can transport you to any previously-opened area so you don't have to navigate huge distances.
You can access the inventory/minimap to see how many keys/orbs/items you're holding and keep tabs on where you are in the world. It's a well thought out map, showing the locations of bosses (even in the yet-unmapped areas), waypoints, warp gates etc. Everything you need to know.
In general, there is no confusion or frustration as you're kept well informed about objectives and what's required to meet them by the strategically placed characters who give you information and progress the (bare bones) storyline.
The pixel graphics are fine, interesting enough characters, nothing spectacular. Chiptunes (different one for each area) are pleasant and original.
The enemies you meet along the way are very easy. Some move from side to side, others shoot at you. Standard stuff. The bosses have traditional attack patterns that are easy to defeat once you work out the method. How-do-I-reach-that puzzling is also as expected. Overall this will not tax your brain too much, it's a casual game.
In Windows, Xbox and Steam controllers both work without any tweaking. In Linux, neither is recognised at all. I used Steam Big Picture mode to map my Steam controller to keyboard keys and it worked well, but if you have Xbox + Linux you'll have to resort to keyboard controls. Movement is crisp, responsive and satisfying. It feels 'fair' at all times.
There are only 3 resolution options in windowed mode but they are good enough. Sliders for volume control and the default sound level is good.
No bugs or glitches found; rock solid performance; intuitive/complete menu system; no complaints.
15 achievements - interesting ones; 6 trading cards. I would like to see cloud support.

This is just one of those fun little games where you can sit down during an evening, open it up and relax while playing. It isn't intense gameplay. It's very simple. Match three of one object to make another one. Match three of those. And so on.  Yet, the simplicity doesn't take anything away from the game. However, if you want a high enough score, you have to be strategic in your placements of every object. But if you just want to put things in random places and see what happens, it is possible to get through the game that way too. So if you really don't want to put any effort in, you don't have to.
Triple Town is designed in a way that makes it look a lot like many Facebook games that people get addicted to (or annoyed by). Yet, it separates itself from them because you are not compelled to fork out your hard earned cash to keep playing... because there are no in-game transactions, which makes it aces in my book.
What I really like most about the game in addition to the simplicity factor is the soundtrack. The sound of birds. It's like you're sitting out in the middle of a garden on a summer afternoon.
In short, if you want a game that requires minimal brain power (but rewards you if you put more in) that you can wind down while playing, give Triple Town a go. Just be careful. It's addictive.

It's Dark...It's quiet...I can only hear the sounds of my breath and lights flickering on and off from the malfunctioning power. I turn to my right and open the ship's hatch to let myself out. I cringe as it loudly hisses and pushes open to leave a ramp for me to walk down. I turn left, then right and make my way to a staircase and activate a fuse box at the bottom as lights come to life and the vents unlock for me to open them. I crouch and crawl through the narrow maze to find myself an opening leading into a very large room, the darkness making it seem like an endless void beyond my field of view. I drop down and hear some mechanical being whir to life...my heart sinks...that sinking feeling as if things are about to go very wrong. I pick up the audio log under some shelves as it emits a bright yellow light. I listen and hear the robots sounds coming increasingly louder...and faster. I equip my silencer and turn to the door way behind me. Knealing down as I wait, I hear some sort of intense sound come from this robot with it's footsteps growing heavier as it bursts through the doorway. I unload my mag on the damned thing as it drops to the floor, my HUD revealing a skull above it's head with multiple indicators of where I damaged it. I waited for my heart rate to slow down as I gathered myself. Once calmed, I made my way into the ventilation system again and found myself in a room with shelves lining the walls and fences sectioning the different areas off from each other. I heard the footsteps of multiple entities and assumed that they were to be like the last synthetic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I ran into. I crouched down and made my way into a room, walking backwards to check if anything were following me...this was a mistake. I backed into another robot and heard it's mechanical yell as I whipped around and unloaded my SMG's whole clip into him as I panicked. The other's respond to this cry and I heard them all scream to life as heavy footsteps grew louder...faster...stronger. I reloaded quickly and hauled it into the next room only to alert more of these beasts. I had awoken the hive and wasn't ready to go down without a fight. I steadied my aim and fired bursts at the machines' heads. Left...right...left...right...they were dropping like flies. My mag ran out and I quickly switched to my assault rifle and activated it's laser due to the fact that it's scope was too long range for this situation. I aimed carefully and fired more shots through their metallic brains one by one. Thus I had been victorious against the horde of synthetic zombies.
Sci-Fi Horror is back ladies and gents and others.

Heed my warning though: the platformer part is just brutal and unforgiving. Probably 3rd person perspective would work better.
If you try to limit the number of dimension shifts, you need smarts and sometimes patience, so it's good, but I sadly don't see myself getting the time constraints achievement.
Also, seems like if you want real closure, you'll have to buy the upcoming DLCs. Looks like there are even achievements for them already in the game!
Despite the mentioned caveats, you are bound to have some fun quality time with this gem.

The bears are come to remind us that all is chaos. All will be left to the bears, and to the shrubs, as empires fall, each in its time.
It is a somnambulant and disquieting reality, this Triple Town. Unknowable Lovecraftian horrors await at every turn. Quake at your smallness! Madness slathers with hunger and claws at your door. Yes, in the gaping maw of madness lies your perdition.
Your perdition is Triple Town.
This seems impossible, you say. Impossible! But all things are possible through Triple Town. All that becomes impossible beneath the great and terrible gaze of Triple Town, all that shall not linger—cannot linger!—in this dismal, eternal city...
...is you.
You say that you have come to conquer and dismantle Triple Town. I tell you that your heroism is the buzzing of a gnat amid a tempest. I tell you that your endeavor is doomed before it has begun. I tell you, for I pity you, that your eternity is but the blink of an eye to Triple Town. Therefore tremble, and depart.
Depart, while there still is life in you, though your retreat, like your bravery, means nothing. Triple Town will find you, wherever you may run. And should you live a thousand thousand lifetimes, your happiness will turn to ash as you hear the bears approaching, their growls crisp and icy and immutable.
And then, darkness.

I've never played SWG or UO before, so I was kindda curious what the game like, as I was looking for games that put more emphasis on crafting system and economy like Wurm Online and Haven and Hearth does, and I've been dissapointed time and time again with the current ecosystem of MMORPG. All the other MMO that I've played put crafting and economy as a side mini game of grinding that the only main objective is to drain your gold coffers (so you would microtranscation more gold from them). I wanted to find a game that making something is meaningful, not grinding harvesting and crafting by making worthless items just so you can make the end-game items, and any items you made before that is pointless and garbage after you level up a few times. And this game is EFFING it!!
This game will be a complicated game to review, since it does have a huge pros, and also a few deblilating cons.
- Crafting is meaningful. Each of the item you crafted is useful. Each items made is used in alot other recipes. You can make almost every single item in the game. And you can actually do, without too much of a grinding like in other MMO, you can make alot of things using the lowest quality items and its not a hassle to do it at all. But to make a really high quality items, you need to depend on other and this is where the grind is. How cool is it to be a master crafter of making single core processor motherboard :3
And I must say, when you make something, the satisfaction is astounding. <3
- Fitting system. Fitting system is great since you're not tied to a armor or weapon, and you don't need to change your armor/weapon/accessory every 5 levels. If you found a set that you love you can just stick with it and customize your armor to be what you want. Slashing defense maxed out armor? Full armor penetration defense armor? Hell yeah.
- I haven't experience the player housing, town and shops, but any game with that is a huge plus.
- Living world. Day and Night cycle. NPC have their own schedule like what Ultima 7 had. Alot of MMO keep yapping on and on about how their game is alive and how the city is bustling, yet when you're the only one in the area, its feels like you are in a town fulls of puppet, every NPC just stand there doing nothing. This game means it and NPC will close shop at night, Guard stop patrolling the town outskirts at night, Guard will change their guard post every day. Shopkeeper will go to the disco at night.
- Quest is randomly generated based on a template. Each area have their own quest type and story. Not one player will have the same quest like the other one (kindda). While the quest is not that great and buggy, but its a huge step on the right direction. Each quest is different (somewhat) unlike the old system where the same NPC keep forcing everyone to collect the same bloody 10 animal hide over and over again. This game is on the right path, imperfect but on the right path. While you have to send the cupcake to the guard, your friend might be sending some rose to a girl. <3 and another guy is sending a cupcake to the guy in the pub.
- Away from the stupid classic leveling system. Mega plus. The more you do on certain area the more it will progress, and you will get skill point bonuses also. This is what all MMO should aspire to be.
- Huge world and multiple passanger vehicle and mech!!!
- Dance routine (that give buff to everyone depending on the type of dance and the dance step) and story telling (that also give buff to everyone depending on the type of story, plot-twist and ending, oh and anyone can jump in can contiue to story tell the story started by another.). Make a camp in the wild, and start playing the guitar, dance and storytell, and then go lay teh smackdown on the bandit camp nearby.
- Early Access : God the game is buggy as hell. I know its early access, and people need to be reminded that the game is buggy and it does takes off the enjoyment sometimes (ok maybe more then sometimes). Wait till the game enter a more stable stage if this is your main concerns.
- Combat is very unpolish, laggy and not particularly fun. Well I've seen worst (aka Fallen Earth) but I hope they can polish it more down the road.
- UI is nasty. just plain nasty and unfriendly. The ingame Map is probably the worst I've seen in any game, hard to read just filled with freaking orange colored dot that can mean anything, even worst when compared to Fallen Earth in-game map (and Fallen Earth UI is first on my Top 10 list of most nasty UI in an MMO). UI is unresponsive, the map (M and Shift-M) is impossible to use. Mini-map should just be deleted for how useless it is.
Crafting UI is bearable, Quest UI is pretty bad. And omg, the talking to NPC UI and speech bubble is horrible nasty piece of buggy crap.
Please dev, fix this at the utmost priority. UI is the most important gateway for user experience in MMO. User spend more time using the UI then combat, then gameplay and all the other thing combined.
- Character Creation is pretty bad too and buggy on top of that :( which is really making me sad.
- Player economy is yet to sprout because of the lack of player. Hopefully this will change once the game goes Free2Play.
- Graphics is way behind, but if you want to play an MMO with beautiful gals with perfect bewbies and booties physics, then the Korean Dev is working hard to make those. I prefer the dev to spend their time making the game mechanics more unique and fun rather then asking them to spend most of thier time making the bewbies bounce prefectly and copy-paste the old, tired and grindy MMO recipe to offset the time wasted. Rather you should just google "Porn" watch it then come play this game.
Back to the point I wanted to make, the graphics is not great, but it is playable. While I would love this game to have the graphic of TERA and gameplay of Repop (wet dreams) I know thats not possible, and I would choose gameplay with a playable graphics any time of the day.
- Very steep learning curve (like 90 degrees steep, also known as a brick wall), but once you get the hang of it, its like magic, everything will seems to make sense and you will love the complication of the system. Will probably turn alot of poeple off tho.
- The community is filled with smarta$$. Not quite sure to either to put it as pro or cons. The community is matured, no tarding chat because most of those type probably quit in the tutorial. Unfortunately this make the community very stiff, and  asking a noobie question in chat will usually get you ignored or answered in a non-helpful way since everyone thinks everyone should already knew the obvious things already, and shouldn't be asking about it, and any points/suggestion made in chat that the game should be more easier to understand will be shot down pretty fast. So beware.
I find this refreshing though, no more global chat spam about virtual sex and all that crap, god, Tera chat is nasty.
I recommend this game wholeheartedly if you :
- Can handle a buggy early access.
- Can handle a huge learning curve.
- Likes making shiny things.
- Dont mind the laser from your gun shooting from your bottom at times.
- Likes to support a dev who is making what a MMO should've been all this time, not like all the garbage that is out there.

Games can be many things.
Games can challenge us, can be an outlet for our stresses and our boredom, and they are absolutely wonderful for that ability. They can be exciting, gripping, and engaging, certainly. They can demand your full attention, and hold you, breathless with anticipation, spellbound by the compulsion to uncover more of their world, to play the next match, the next level, the next moment. They are magical, in the way they can draw the player in and keep them engaged despite the challenges they may present and the stress they can occasionally cause.
But games can also draw stress out of us, too. They can soothe, they can relax, and they can even heal. Certainly, they can provide a distraction, and often... that's enough.
And Proteus makes a wonderful distraction in that regard. It isn't much in the way of mechanics -- you generate a new world and wake up there, free to wander around and explore it. That's all there really is to it -- seeing what comes next, seeing what the world has to offer as it changes and evolves over the days and the seasons is its own reward, and some people may find that off-putting. Certainly, those people are entitled to their preferences, as well.
But others may find in Proteus the exact break they need from whatever they've been playing recently, a quiet escape away from everything else nagging them in worlds both real and fictional. There is beauty in simplicity, and sparse mechanics executed well can be better than feature-rich experiences with less polish, to the right person. I happened to really enjoy this game personally (and do pardon my playtime, I tend to be an offline player in most things.)
As to whether or not you might enjoy this -- if you want to interact and get into the nitty-gritty of things, you may wind up diappointed here. Walking around and sightseeing is the brunt of what you will find in Proteus' gameplay offerings. Those who already enjoy walking simulators will feel right at home so long as the art style appeals to you! For anyone left undecided, all I can advise is that if you think you will enjoy it, with the knowledge of how the game operates fresh in memory -- if you need a break from your traditional fare or you feel drawn to this game -- give it a chance, grab it on sale if you can, and see how you feel about things.
I hope you find what you're looking for in it. I certainly have found an appreciated sojourn, here, and for that reason I recommend this game.

This game is ugly, clunky, confusing, repetitive, bug riddled, and boring. I'm generally willing to overlook issues that others are not. But man, this game gives me a headache. Not because it's hard, because it isn't - but the graphics, UI, map, and minimap are just all so poorly implemented that it literally makes my head throb in pain.
The Audio is awful. I work in the audio industry and i'd be embarrassed if this were my sound design work. The quality of the sound effects are bad. The music flutters in the game and needs to be muted.
The graphics in this game are mixed. The 3D player art is really nice. Beyond that it's between bad and laughable. People argue that it's early access or alpha so graphics shouldn't be considered. I think those people are wrong as i've been a part of a ton of alpha's and early access games where the grahpics showed promise. What i'm looking at is certainly not representative of the final product but it is representative of the art teams talent. In this case i'd say the art team is not talented.
The UI consists of a ton of menu diving. Little boxes with tabs that extend out of site. I'm forced to open little windows and click a little arrow key to get to the tab I need which consumes quite a bit of
time. These information menu's are things that you need to access constantly. It becomes annoying and adds to the tediousness of this game. Keep in mind that i'm a 10 year Eve vet. People jokingly refer to Eve as "world of spreadsheets"... so I can deal with data. I imagine that these things will be refined over time.
The minimap is a tiny little circle that shows little detail in the terrain. NPC's, monsters, players, quest items are little tiny dots. They are everywhere and it needs a lot of improving. In all honesty it should be scrapped. Around the minimap you have little yellow arrows that tell you which directions to go for quests you have. Only problem is that they blend in with the terrain or with some of the icons around
the minimap so you can't even see them. Literally they disappear. I expect this is something that will be changed shortly cause right now it's just a clusterf**k of dots.
The map itself is a little more useful. By pressing M you get a little map window, that's notexpandable, that shows you your immediate surroundings. I had complained that the map was terrible because it
didn't scroll. Someone from the development team commented on my review that by pressing "Shift-M" you get a scrolling map. He was correct but the map is still bad. It's a tinly little box, that doesn't appear to expand, that's about 1/8th the size of your screen. Even if it did expand it shows very little detail, is ugly, and causes my framerate to drop very low.
The combat is clunky and the way it's implemented I basically can't use any of my skills. You have to right click your target to shoot and left click items on your bar to activate them. Maybe i'm missing something but that's not my fault. This games just so clunky and confusing, including the tutorial, that it's not obvious in any way. I have found that by assigning some of my abilites to extra mouse buttons is really the only way to go. For people who don't have a fancy mouse with extra buttons then i'd say that you'll be at a distinct disadvantage compared to those that do. Also the combat is not fun or challenging. Combat consists of right clicking on your target.
The gameplay is very repetitive. Questing is like WoW. Though you receive quests through an email system the meat of the quests are the same. Go to location X, gather resource Y, deliver to NPC Z. Or Kill 8 of these and return to NPC X. Or pick up package at NPC X and deliver to NPC Z. That's fine because that's not really what this game is about. However, it adds to the repetitive feeling of this game.
Resource gathering thus far has consisted of running out of the town, finding nodes which are clustered by the dozens in specific areas, and harvesting one after another after another after another. There is no real danger, there is no real challenge, and it's very repetitive. From what i've experienced thus far it's completely a solo activity.
Crafting has been much of the same experience. You can only craft at a "crafting station". These are situated inside cities and you generally find a number of people all huddled around it. You find the item you want to craft in your recipe book, place items in window, and you get your crafted item. There is a fairly deep crafting system that is somewhat rewarding. I think this is where a lot of the potential in this game lies. I've been following the advice of the tutorial and sticking with one profession. Generally that's the right thing to do in all MMO's but I find the process of gathering resources in the game extremely boring. I find that crafting in this game is extremely boring. This does not appeal to me though in other games I enjoy carebear acitivities.
Hopefully more people read the negative reviews and think twice. I bought this game because of the positive reviews and the pretty pictures. BIG MISTAKE. I understand that hardcore SWG fans have been waiting for this game for a while. I'm glad that they have a new home. I am not one of the SWG refugees.
Yes, it's alpha and yes the developers have intentions of improving this game. Well they better because as it sits now it's a bad game. So many good games out there and in my library. This game isn't one of them.

That being said, when you fork over your 35 bucks you're doing it in good faith that the developer is going to do something positive with it. Let me start off by saying that if you're looking for a game to replace the hole left after SWG went down, then this may not be the game you expect it to be.
The general lay out of the game and the overlays are effectively a carbon copy of SWG so you may start to feel like you're back in that world... until you begin to explore and play the game. I got this game because people get referring to it as a spiritual successor to SWG and I haven't played a really GREAT MMO since SWG (I don't think there are any MMO's out there that can match SWG for being a true MMORPG Sandbox game)
However I found myself comparing every tiny detail to how SWG did things, and The Repopulation came up short on absolutely everything. Ofcourse this game is still being made, and you can really see what they are trying to achieve with it. I'm probably jumping the gun with my judgements and I should come back in 6months to a year to see the progress.
Having said that I don't think it can compare to SWG, i'd still recommend picking up this game, or atleast watching it's progress. It has the potential to be the only true Sandbox MMO out there that doesn't send you on linear quests from level 1-90 killing boars and running from point a-b until you max your characters level out. You can see that they want this game to be for the players and run by the players, in game economy driven by player crafting, player cities, completely explorable landscapes etc...
Just be warned if you're missing SWG then this isn't the game for you (currently)

I loved this game.
You might be confused as to why I'm not recommending it, but I'll talk about all the positives and you can decide if you are up for playing the game.
First off: Alwa's Awakening is a "Metroidvania", with a stronger emphasis on the Metroid, in particular, Super Metroid/Metroid Fusion/Zero Mission. Sequence breaks are very easy to pull off, however it makes you feel amazing when you do them.
The combat is adequate, mostly melee based with the ability to use a slow charge ranged attack towards the end of the game.
The controls are beautifully precise, I never once felt that the controls were causing me to miss jumps and even if I did stuff up, it was quick back into the action. The map system, while sometimes a bit vague when showing you what was on each screen, at least showed you the basic gist of where warp rooms and save rooms were.
Now the not so great points: The story is practically non-existant, you are given a goal and that's it. And that's where the problems come in. If the game sounds great, buy it. You might enjoy it, however the next point is where everything fell down.
The story is the major problem of this game. Once you have beaten the game, you get a glimpse of your character in a 16 bit art style, back at the start and the game ends with the girl saying to do the same thing again. Then you go back to the title screen. Nothing after. This is why I cannot recommend the game in terms of a review, simply because it felt like the developers ran out of time and just rushed it out to make money. It's sad, however I do not recommend this game simply because of that fact.

I honestly wasn't expecting to like this game.

The movement is very weird. Using WASD is fine but when you're trying to strafe, you're gonna end up dodging. The game tells you that if you want to dodge, just double press one of the WASD keys. But if you're holding one key and then press another key you're gonna end up dodging anyway.
The quest markers don't work. When I marked one of my quest so that I can track it, I couldn't find out where I was going because the quest is on a different island, and you don't get to see the full map unless your sailing, but if you're sailing it doesn't show the quest markers. As far as I played, there are 4 different main islands. That's all I got out of the world of this game.
The gameplay is simple. You got your attack buttons and you got your hotbar that holds your spells and healing items.  One strange thing I found personally was the fact you have to press the middle mouse button to  bring your weapons out. But you also need to sheath your weapons every now and then to  pick up loot or to interact with characters and other things.
Luckly, this game doesn't bombard you with hordes of enemies. Instead, it throws in very few enemies but they're hard to take down.
Combat in this game takes a while, you have the option to parry your opponents by holding down right mouse button. Trust me, you're gonna be holding that button down a lot in this game. Enemies will attack you with a barraige of quick but powerful attacks, so you'll be parrying most of the time, waiting for a good opening. You gotta learn the enemies attack patterns before you go in for an attack, if you don't, you'll most likely be taking a good chunck of damage.
Personally, this seems like a 6.5/10. It's a good game, just wouldn't recommend it to my friends.

How to start. I'm honestly not sure what I expected to get when I bought this game. I was expecting it to be good, but more in the same way that Escape Goat is good. It's not flashy and it's not spectacular, but certainly it's functional and does what it does very well. What I wasn't expecting was fun dialogue, an interesting story and some really fabulous music. The team/person/supercomputer that put this game together is simply genius.
The gameplay, while really simple at its surface, is also very compelling and very intricate. While there's typically the one real solution to a presented puzzle, there also exist the options to do things that are just totally out there and whacky. This is not in the sense of what Goat Simulator gives you, that is to say a barebones game that gives you only the option to ♥♥♥♥ around for the sake of ♥♥♥♥ing around. Really, what I mean is that I have a certain set of tools to use on enemies and other such obstacles that make it fun and interesting.
Now, the actual scope of what you can do means that the fun you can have given the circumstances is fairly limited. There are only so many times I can punch a man 1000 times after he's long since bled to death below me, but the novelty of that moment is such that once I'm done with doing that, I can go do something else (like literally knock a door off its hinges and send the man on the far end flying out a window). And more importantly, I can go play the remainder of the game that exists. Even though you can finish the game in abbout 5 hours, I'd say that it's cheap and entertaining enough that that's all you should really ought to expect.
For $10, I can't really think of any other games that do something similar and are still fun to play. If you'ree interested in the concept presented, go ahead and get a copy.

My complaints are as follows -
It's very short.

I recommend picking it up on sale if you're interested.

Wow. After reading all the hate and negative reviews, I thought
(which I'd been looking for) and downloaded it without expecting much. Boy was I wrong...
I honestly don't know what people are complaing about. This game has been on steam (in early access)
, it's not gonna be the equivalent of the latest big budget racing game! However, that does
mean it wont be fun. High Octane Drift really surprised me; it's actually quite well made. The menu looks clean and smart, the driving is fun and the customisation is better than some AAA games. There are plenty of options for tuning, visual customisation and performance parts as well as a vinyl editor! :D The car you drive in the tutorial seemed unbalanced to me, but once you're left to play around with your own car, learning to drift is pretty easy. Online has worked perfectly for me and I've thouroughly enjoyed the online free-roam mode that lets you drift with other players without any time restrictions or elements of competition.
Of course, being an early access game, there are bugs. The descriptions are missing and finding your way around the garage menus can be difficult at first (btw, if you want to check your car's condition or maintain it move your mouse to the bottom of the screen!). The game could be improved by adding menu music and garage sound effects etc, and I've had an issue where my car has lost all power while changing between 2nd and 3rd and i've come to a complete standstill. Over time, I know these bugs will be ironed out and improvements will be made. Also, I understand that this game is free and the dev(s) can't survive on praise alone, but I am a little unhappy that there are features of this game that can only be unlocked with premium currency (paid for with real money, though 1 is awarded easch time you level up) and i'd like to be able to unlock everything simply by playing the game. I have seen people complan that they earn Rupees (the earnable in-game currency) too slowly but in my opinion, that aspect is fine. I'm happy to grind for a whole evening just to get that air filter or raise the cash to paint my rims.
As someone who is learning to use Unity (the package this game is made in), I have immense respect for the developer(s). You've made a really great start and I can't wait to see where you take this game! It has massive potential.
Overall, I highly recommend High Octane Drift. Play it! Go on... now! Stop reading and download it. You won't regret it.

Through the last few years, there has been a lot of good Telltale games, it all started with The Walking Dead and then there has been games such as The Wolf Among Us, a second season of The Walking Dead ... and this, the Telltale-Gearbox marriage. I think I wasn't alone who thought this was going to pan out when they first announced "Tales from the Borderlands".
To start off with, the engine is the "same old", the gameplay is the "same old". What is different is the story, the environments and the characters. Nothing too surprising there, is it? The game takes place on Pandora and Helios, you play as two different characters (Rhys and Fiona), going back and forth between the two in your quest for revenge against Hyperion - the evil corporation of the Borderlands universe. Since this game is HEAVILY story driven, I don't want to write anymore about the story, it should be experienced first hand.
In the end, the characters are likeable (some more than others), the game looks decent and the audio is great (especially the voice acting). A fun game to be played for somewhere between eight to twelve hours, depending on if you explore everything or not. But not the best Telltale has done, at times I felt bored when playing it, but the end made it all worth it.

I really wanted to like this game, I have been following its progress for a few years, I like Sci-Fi, MMO's and sandbox games so this really should be a hit with me.
Game: The graphics, animations and game play are bad. I understand this is early access and the final Alpha testing phase but that does not account for how bad the core game looks and feels. There are bugs, which is understandable, these can be ironed out and fixed through the Alpha and beta. The mob AI and pathing is very weak but I believe I did see a post from the dev's saying this is one thing to be updated later. The graphics and game play however, I think the game needs to go back to square one with a new engine and artists (Trying not to be rude to the artists, but they really should look into something called colour! Large portions of  grass, mountains, buildings are black, which is also the primary colour for players and most mobs. Seriously it hurts my eyes at times.) The performance seems rather poor, given there are very few NPC's and players. I expect spikes, crashes and disconnects but being stood still with players/mobs jerking past in the open is not what I would expect, nothing seems to flow smoothly.
Crafting: Very complicated, too complicated for an average gamer I imagine. Personally I don't mind this, I think it can help the community stronger, force players and nations to work more closely.  It is very confusing and I would hope to see more detailed tutorials played out in the beta's. Where crafting falls down is that you obviously need to gather materials before you can craft; Gathering is boring, looting the same flower three or four times, killing mobs in mind numbing combat, running around an ugly world. I struggle to find a reason to explore when everything looks so bad right now.
Sandbox: My “sandbox” experience was rather disappointing. The first training zone seemed a small instanced area and then loaded into a new city area. A quest in this city sends you to visit an apartment/tower block, which was also instanced! A building in the main city is instanced, even though it seemed to lead to one room with one NPC? Then there were quests to go to another zone and housing area which are also seemed to be separate instances/areas.
Conclusion:
For modern day gamers and MMO fans, I would advise avoid this game, certainly for this phase. I think the game requires a large investment of resources to make the graphics and game play enjoyable.  I believe The Re-population, as things stand, will have a small niche market of retro ex Star Wars galaxies fans who really don't mind playing something without the graphics and game play we have come to expect from games in the last 10 to 15 years.
Personally I will check back in a few months to see how the artists have changed the textures, colours, animations and how smooth the game runs; hopefully I will come back and find the game has ported over to the CryEngine – then I’m sure I will be happy.

Reinstating my original review with minor tweaks in preparation of the games re-launch. Previous edits to this review touched on the developers and the controversy around the dev cycle, but I've decided to just review the game itself in its current playable state. Some points on here may be considered dated and will change as the new developer's intentions and design goals become more clear in how they differ from the original, if at all. Any paragraphs that mention design philosophy where I only knew the original developers stance will be marked with an asterisk.
In its current alpha state you should be aware that the game is not finished, but it is feature-complete enough to play and that access to an alpha makes you a tester as much as a player. You cannot expect a bug or crash free experience, and you will be asked for your input throughout the game on how well features or quests are implemented. The Repopulation will be releasing as a free to play game. By purchasing the game on early access, you are recieving access to the alpha and also a player package (see below).
I want to reiterate that The Repopulation has been planned and designed as a free to play game from its inception. This means eventually there will be a cash shop, *but the developers have said over and over that it will be for cosmetic and Quality of Life items, and nothing so broken that it will make the game feel Pay2Win*. Member packages, which I mentioned before, will be one-time payments that give you perks like extra bank space and cosmetic pre-order items.
Now that I've got all of that out of the way, I'll move on to the game itself.
I've decided to add a section to the review here that gives an idea of the basics of how the game plays, since I realize my pros and cons list (below) isn't super in depth on the different aspects of gameplay.
When you start the game you will be in a tutorial zone with NPCs related to every skill available (over 75 skills in all). I won't go extremely in depth into what every area of the tutorial teaches you, but I will urge that you visit every area and at least read learn the overall skill themes (ie you don't have to read all the different weapons, but at least take the time to familiarize yourself with combat. Same with the trade skills and the idea of crafting). That said, there is no cap on how many skills you can learn, and Alpha is a good time to get a taste for what you like and what you don't. Each skill individually caps at level 6000, so while it is theoretically possible to become a grandmaster at everything, you're looking at a huge, huge dedication of time and resources. For this reason it is recommended that you specialize and outsource for the best use of your time.
"Questing" in Repopulation comes mainly in the form of missions. These can be found in multiple ways, like talking to NPCs directly, or having one mailed to you. They can also be filtered to your skillset. For example, someone who focuses on combat might choose to only recieve military-related missions, like clearing out hostile creatures in an area. A crafter might be asked to create an item and deliver it to someone, or gather a resource. There is no overarching "main quest line" in Repop, so expect to have to come up with your own goals and motivations.
Crafting is a very deep system divided across many skills, including Armor/Weapon Crafting, Cooking, Genetic Engineering, Robotics, Farming, Architecture and more. Materials have Grades, so not all refined metal will be of the same quality, and this will reflect itself in the quality of the items you produce. If you want to go into one of the advanced crafting disciplines you will need the help of the player economy as no one person can easily collect and refine all the materials needed. I would go more in depth on this but I wouldn't be able to fit everything in this review's character limit; that is how complex you can expect the crafting to be.
Combat can be done in the usual RPG 1-9 hotbar mode, or in "Action" mode using LMB+RMB and aiming with the mouse. There is a % based cover system, stances, and resource management in the form of Momentum and Weapon/Shield Energy. There is melee, short range, and long range weaponry available, as well as a stealth mechanic. Every weapon and combat skill has it's own ability set based on how practiced you are with them.
This is just a very barebones look at how the game plays to help you make a decision, and the world itself has much more depth than I have room to write. So, with that in mind, let's move on to Pros and Cons.
-A true sandbox experience. This game feels like a living world, with tons of options. You are not the themepark "savior of the world" (along with every other player that you have to pretend to ignore during the story), but rather a person living within the universe.
-"Living within the universe" meaning that your choice of skills, jobs, and things to do is huge. Crafting isn't secondary to combat, it can be its own focus. There are no set classes, you "level" by practicing skills (i.e. using a rifle makes you better with rifles, etc.) You create who you want to be.
-Player cities, factions, housing, shops... an economy and world based on players.
-NPCs have their own likes, dislikes, lives and schedules. They will talk amongst themselves and how you handle quests will have an effect on how people treat you.
-Combat, while not extremely ground breaking, is fun. Crouching, going prone, and the cover system add an immersive layer to engagements.
-Because the game is a true sandbox, it can feel very overwhelming. This is especially true if you're not used to this type of MMO. The feature-complexity of the game also translates to complexity overall, and people who aren't intuitive or experimental may have trouble with learning to navigate the menus, crafting, etc.
-The UI in its current state is cumbersome, however that is something that has been receiving tweaks and will hopefully improve.
-I'll reiterate that the game is alpha and you will encounter bugs and crashes. This is a testing environment, and this con won't apply as much later.
-Some people fear that the reliance on player-made content (as a player economy, player factions, and the social experience are a majority of the content as opposed to quest lines, etc.) will be a downfall if the population dwindles. I think it's too early to do anything but speculate on that, but it is something to keep in mind.
-Combat, while it has its positive attributes, can also be frustrating. It can be maddening to lose fights and not really know why. For example, since you don't have an overall character level it's easy to fall into the trap of thinking that because you've been playing your character for a substantial amount of time that trying a new weapon out will just take your power down a little. Because every weapon has it's own skill level, weapon swapping, for all intents and purposes, means starting over at killing level 1 creatures. (There is a little leeway here as you will retain your defensive and generic combat skills, but it really brings home that you should specialize and commit if you're not testing new things for testing's sake.)
-Combat can also feel like a means to an end sometimes. As crafting has such a deep and diverse attention paid to it, you wonder if you're just fighting for the sake of collecting materials, which can be disheartening for combat-centric characters. However I have not experienced PvP or non-starter-zone PvE content, soyour mileage may vary.
As the game stands, it will be heavily dependant on whether it can bounce back from the PR nightmare it has incurred over the last year. As far as actual gameplay goes, it's worth following if you previously enjoyed or always wanted to try games like Star Wars Galaxies or Ultima Online.
It's a good game if you need to blow off steam or just want to take a short break. Simple, yet efficient.

Pros:
- Great universe and unique graphics
- Good soundtrack and sound design, especially when played on headphones
- Fun and fast-paced gameplay
- Borderlands' unique kind of wacky humour
- Vast map and good variety of monsters and bosses
- Many sidequests and collectibles
- Multiple DLC's with many additional biomes, enemies, storylines and weapons
Cons:
- Relatively bland storyline. Thankfully the universe makes up for this.
- May seem repetitive over longer periods of time
- Poorly designed map and navigation system, leading to frustration at times
- Several organisation issues when trying to play co-op with friends on Steam
- Snipers have 2.0 optical zoom at best, and glitches occur when shooting very distant enemies anyway
- Good but scarce voice acting, forcing the player to read (or ignore) short texts for all quests in order to understand the storyline
