I almost rated this a game as "Not Recommended." That's because some questionable design decisions marred the experience. However, at the end of the day the actual game part of the game is interesting enough to warrant a purchase, especially if you're a fan of Naruto.
So, I'll start with what's bad.  Basically, any part of the single player that isn't fighting (with the exception of the final boss battle. ) Full disclosure: I've been reading Naruto for over 10 years, but I stopped watching the anime at episode 60. It was at that point that I noticed the anime's tendency to draw things out unnecessarily. A manga can be read in a couple minutes, and the anime has the habit of stretching that couple of minutes to half an hour. It makes the experience feel bloated, and that unfortunately is how the single player feels as well.   Through at least 80% of the single player you are, essentially, watching the anime. Yes, it plays out with the game's models, and has a fidelity that arguably surpasses the anime, but it still takes too long to get to anything interesting.
The second problem this game has is when the game gives you control outside of fighting. Too often, you are put in a small area, go forward a couple of steps, and a cut scene starts. Even Hideo Kojima would call this♥♥♥♥♥♥excessive. Any part where you were "exploring" was entirely uncessary and could have been removed from the game.
Thirdly, the final boss fight is a poorly designed piece of schlock that prioritizes spectacle over playability. Without spoiling too much, the final fight happens over a large area where you can barely see your character and are fighting multiple enemies at once. The fight is grandiose, and fun to look at, but it's still not worth the frustration. You'll get through it, realizing that this was so poorly designed the designers put in multiple checkpoints during the fight, and allow you to refill your health completely and try again if you die. Nowhere else in the game does this happen. It's if they are admitting "we made this to look cool, and for no other reason."
Finally, and here's the real kicker. You HAVE to play through this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to unlock characters. If Capcom can figure out that forcing players to unlock characters in fighting games is stupid. Other studios don't have any excuse.
Ultimately (heh) what makes this game good is its fighting mechanics. They do a good job interpretting the fiction and are basically a continuation of the mechanics introduced in the arguably superior Ultimate Ninja. However the twist is that this takes place on a 3D plane and looks way way better.
The fighting isn't mechanically complex, but it is strategically satisfying. Fighting games are based entirely around the idea of "what I can do vs what the opponent can do." and playing a technical fighting game at a higher level involves a lot of mind games.  This game allows casual players, who don't have the time or the wherewithal to learn 1 frame links and juggles, a chance to play in this manner. You will be thinking "is it better to use substitution, or to block" , "should I attack or throw" , "should I use a jutsu" , etc. It is this fact alone that saves the game. It makes multiplayer* battles so much fun.
If this game is between 0 - 15 dollars, it's worth the purchase for an average gamer who wants a fighting game that doesn't require a significant time investment. If it's 15 - 30 dollars it's worth the purchase for a fan of Naruto who is a fan of fighting games.
* I have  not tried the online multiplayer, my connection is generally too poor for online fighting games. However, I did test it with a local 2nd player, and was surprised at how this improved my opinion of the game.

I can recommend this game for one reason: it offers a type of fun that you can find almost literally nowhere else. And it looks really good sometimes.
That being said, there is much wasted potential in this game, and a few things that are periphal-smashingly frustrating. But at the times when everything just clicks together, this game gave me enough pure, stupid fun that I literally laughed out loud with joy. I don't remember any other game doing that, at least not more than once.
You should get this game, but you need to understand a couple of things first.
- You will have to get used to the swinging mechanics, but when you do, it's amazing. Your bionic arm manipulates your momentum, and you will need that control, so don't expect it to feel natural at first.
- The story is stupid. The story is impactless. The characters are stupid, and flit in and out of the story with stupid whimsy. Some levels and events feel like they were designed by different teams and hastily jumbled into order by a commitee.
- The game uses deadly irradiated areas to fence off the play area. The problem is, they aren't clearly marked and the warning only activates about 2m from the radiation. And so, waaaay too many times, I swung into the radiation, unable to reverse my momentum before it killed me in LITERALLY 1.5 SECONDS. For gameplay that's all about forward momentum, that is unacceptable.
Another problem for me was the introductory city levels. Much of the time they felt unconvincing, bland and devoid of any kind of intrigue. (EDIT: I'm replaying the game at the moment, and the 2nd time around is much, much better, now that I got good at swinging. Also, don't try to get all the collectibles on your first try, it just adds frustration to an already difficult swinging mechanic.) I just wanted to rush through them to get to what I had hoped was the good part. Thankfully, the good parts do come, and they're absolutely worth the wait.
The first time I started swinging around the skillfully crafted canyon and jungle areas, I felt a physical release of tension. It's as if a different team entirely made these levels, and it's an absolute blast swooping around a tree, dropping down, flinging a couple of fascists at a boulder, punching the boulder into a mech, then swooping up, around and away as their hopeless bullets fly behind you. I repeat, you can't find this type of fun anywhere else.

I like to think of this review as a compare-and-contrast of my review for Hydrophobia: Prophecy. The two games have a few things in common, being sci-fi titles that came out a year apart from each other and bankrupted their developers. I gave Hydrophobia a negative review because, above all, it left me unsatisfied. I'm pretty easy to please. I can forgive bad-looking graphics, hammy dialog or wonky controls if the game still yields some enjoyment for me. Hydrophobia: Prophecy failed to live up to my already quite low standards, and therefore I felt it was deserving of a thumbs down.
On the other hand, I like Bionic Commando a lot. I had quite a lot to say about this game and I had to trim down my word count a LOT before Steam would accept it. It's not a perfect game, and I can see a lot of people giving it a negative review out of spite for the usual pitfalls of remake, such as taking the story in as dark and edgy a direction as possible. You can't expect to mess around with people's nostalgia and not face some criticism, but I enjoy the game for what it is. Let it be known, fans of the original Bionic Commando, that this is nothing like the game you remember.
The main feature of the gameplay is Spencer's bionic arm, which has a grapple hook and can be used to swing through the ruins of Ascension City like Spider-Man. And let me say: that is fun as hell. You can hook to just about anything in the game and there are lots of places to build up a good rhythm swinging between lampposts, buildings and debris. Some have said that the swinging lacks a sense of momentum, but I found it very satisfying. And yes, you can use the grapple gun on enemies! Unfortunately, Spencer is a little squishy and it can be dangerous to expose yourself to enemies to grapple them. However, the gunplay isn't much better. You can't pick up guns from downed enemies and there's a two-gun limit, which is especially bizarre when the main character is a guy with a bionic arm the size of a plow. Don't tell me he can't stash an extra gun or two in there.
I don't like how the game shows you all the grapple gun powers in the tutorial and then withholds those powers until later in the game. Why bother? Also, the controls can't be changed without 3rd-party software. They are shown as controller inputs on the screen even when playing with a keyboard, forcing the player to check the system settings to see which button corresponds to which key. I'd suggest making it a little easier on yourself and playing with a controller.
The game never gives you too much room to swing around and have fun, which is disappointing, but it's not the worst example of railroading I've ever seen. Be mindful that the areas filled with  blue fog are radiation zones and they will kill you if you swing into them. The tutorial covers this, but the radiation zones can take you by surprise sometimes, usually just as soon as you've built up a good rhythm swinging, and you're not given enough time to swing out before you die. Also, YOU CAN'T SWIM! At least this time, there's a pretty good reason for it: Spencer's bionic arm weighs a f*ckton and he sinks like a stone.
The enemy design is a little uninspired. The enemies come in two varieties: the usual "bad guys with guns" and mechs/aircraft, and of the two, the machines are more diverse and easier to tell apart, but also less satisfying to kill. The game teases us with the idea that perhaps we were once meant to melee with the more unique "Vulture" robots, but sadly this never came to be. I think it's fairly obvious that the game faced budget cuts during development. There's one moment when the game sets you up for a boss battle in a fully-modeled arena and then disappointingly jumps to cutscene. The final boss "battle" is nothing more than a series of quick-time events. the fights with the Mohole (mole? mole-hole?) and Groeder make up for it somewhat for having some of the funniest moments in the game.
The story's not quite A-material and the infamous "plot twist" is baffling for its lack of explanation, but it had enough good ideas to be enjoyable. Any story involving an army of Nazi stereotypes is bound to be a little campy. On the other hand, the mood shift from the earlier Bionic Commando titles is to say, the least, JARRING. The original Bionic Commando was a fun action game with the plot of a Van Damme movie. In the remake, terrorists blow up America and Spencer is a bitter a**hole on with dreadlocks and a problem with authority. This is writing penned by an angry teenager off his meds. But it still has its moments, like the laughable Groeder, voiced by a guy doing his best drunken impression of a German accent.
TLDR: Is Bionic Commando good? I would say it's "better than average". The PC port sucks and the writing treads water, but it's a better Spider-Man game than the actual Spider-Man games. Personally, I think it's a lot of fun. I wouldn't quite call it a hidden gem, but there are worse ways to spend ten bucks. Thumbs up.

This is the best incarnation of everyone's favorite childhood fighting show. It does still have its flaws, and these can be glaring at times and non-existent at others.
Story: 9.5/10. Does not interfere with DBZ canon, only minor errors with story details here and there.
Gameplay: Overall: 9/10
Customization: 10/10. You make your own Z-fighter. What else do you want.
Skill variety: 8/10. Dissappointed by lack of transformations for Frieza race, meaning only Saiyans have transformations beyond Kaiokens.
Battle system: ...
Hoo boy. The targetting system....wow. You'll be punching air a lot.
The AI is not a joy. Its favorite strat with one opponent is to circle you and fire little ki blasts. This doesn't actually give it a better chance at beating you, just makes it take longer to kill. Not a problem in story, but a big one in PQ's as they have time constraints. Its strat with multiples is that whichever one you're targetting will do the above while the other will likely be behind you punching you. Or killing Future Trunks. Because he dies a lot as an ally, and spams ults as an opponent.
PvP is good all things considered.
Sidequests: 10/10. Highly annoying parallel quests, and the frustration of waiting for your master to want to spar! But it's all fun for a DBZ fan.
Grind factor: 9/10. Do the PQ's and build yourself well and you should rarely have to grind. Currently defeated Beerus and Whis, only had to grind for one mission (Androids, again because they kept killing Trunks so I needed more damage).
Player-player interactions: 9/10
Teaming up is actually a big help to you. Battles are entertaining, though getting challenged by someone 30 levels above you one day and then someone 40 below you the next is concerning.
DLC'ness: 8.5/10. There is currently three DLC's; a few new skills and equips, some new stories and PQ's, and a couple new masters. But nothing that says you *have* to get them to succeed.
Overall: 9/10 Worth getting while still at peak activity.

Alwa's Awakening is a game that succeeds at what it tries to do: To feel like a legit NES classic, with all the features a NES title needs but also missing those features that a legit NES title wouldn't have.
The graphics are simple but well done and feel like they could be from a real NES classic. The soundtracks are long and varied enough to not get too repetitive and add a nice atmosphere to each area. Controls are really easy to understand and moving and jumping are responsive and precise. Be warned though that you currently
change keys. They are set to be on B, N, M and Space (along with the arrow keys as direction keys) which in my opinion is a bit weird, but it worked out for me at least.
Apart from the NES graphics and NES soundtrack you also get NES insta-deaths and NES difficulty. Nothing too bad, but some save points are far enough apart to make it frustrating to die inbetween them a few times, re-doing many rooms over and over again, so be warned if you're rather clumsy at platformers and/or hate re-doing easy rooms to get to "that" room again.
Like with most NES titles there's not a whole lot of items or similiar to find. Yes, there are collectibles, 99 blue orbs and some other stuff. For many people that's all they need, but if you expect to find new weapons, armor and magic jewelry all the time like in one of the newer Castlevania games or the like then you'd be quite disappointed by the amount of actually meaningful upgrades, that said each item and upgrade you do find is immensely helpful though.
Replayability isn't very high. Doing a sequence skip (which is both possible as well as an intended possibility) is fun and it's also a game that can be speedrun really well if one feels like it but since there's no customisation like different characters or skills to use or random events to happen it will ultimately be the same dungeons again, although maybe in a different order and therefore with different items and upgrades available. There's also no New Game+, Boss Rush Modes or similiar after the game has been completed. Just like with the collectibles though all these features would feel off in a NES title so one can't really complain.
All in all Alwa's Awakening nails the NES feeling in every way, and while I wouldn't mind if it had some totally non-NES features added, it's already well worth its price  in my opinion. Depending on if you want to just complete it or collect everything there is you'll probably have about 8-12 enjoyable hours in a game that looks nice, sounds nice and feels nice.  Considering my biggest complaint is "There's not enough of it" I certainly did enjoy it.

The land of Alwa needs a hero. It's power is fading and its towns are broken and disjointed. Our hooded protagonist awakens with not much memory of herself, and an elder resident of Alwa informs you of the lands' impending doom. With no power, no abilities, and no recollection of your whereabouts, it's up to you to scour the wide and open map for sources of power and the terrifying guardians who protect them.
A metroidvania with a huge, beautiful world holding many secrets and shortcuts. There's the exploration, the tight combat, and the challenging platforming you would expect from an 8-bit action adventure of this nature in the same vein as an one of the first
titles.
sets itself apart from the 8-bit platforming of old by mixing it up with the addition of block-pushing puzzles that feel akin to a sidescrolling
. The obstacles are difficult and eventually require the usage of combined abilities, and the platforming ranges from relaxing to rage-inducing. Luckily Alwa's Awakening's controls are responsive and smooth allowing for pitch perfect mid-air control during jumps that make the rather difficult platforming fun and engaging, as opposed to stiff and repetitive.
Just like any good metroidvania or more recently, the 'SoulsBorne' games, the game takes place in one large interconnected world. Exploring is mandatory, and lots of backtracking will be done of the satisfying variety. With each earned ability your exploration into previously conquered areas is rewarded through the discovery of newly accessible secrets and more of the power-granting blue orbs. New shortcuts from desolate areas are discovered giving that awe-inspiring and rewarding metroidvania or
-y feel of grand discovery, and making long and complicated treks much easier in the future.
For anyone with a keen ear for 8-bit chiptunes and sounds Alwa is a nostalgic ear-gasm. Not just from the crisp and upbeat Famicom-era soundtrack, but the warm and crunchy retro-game sound effects that evoke total nostalgia. The tunes might not be
levels of energetic, but their hyper and bright retro mood comes very close. Everything about
is authentic, the visuals and the sounds giving flashbacks of everything from
to
.
As incredibly rewarding and addictive as it is to explore the depths of ruins and the crumbling towers of Alwa's world, the payoff for your adventuring here are the bosses and the power-bearing gems they hold. With each defeated guardian of an area comes the epiphany that areas previously unreachable are now reachable. Discovered shortcuts now have an exciting purpose, and beckon the player back to what was once out of reach to discover new secrets and routes.
is an excellent addition to the metroidvania genre. It stays authentic to its roots while mixing things up with a variety of puzzle elements through the usage of clever abilities.The pixel artwork is beautiful and some of the most detailed of its kind, and the music is infectious enough to have to humming along for the entirety of your journey. A must have for retro enthusiasts and an easily accessible treat for non-enthusiasts to enjoy, as well.

血肉横飞的战场、完美的物理引擎、真实的 HDR特效，能使玩家身临其境，彻底体会游戏的乐趣并感悟战争对人类的摧残，让人们为了全人类的和平，时刻不能忘记二战的历史。
DoD和CS的区别在于，游戏脱离了目前火爆的反恐题材，取而代之是第二次世界大战背景。玩家将扮演盟军和德军中的一名士兵，使用自己独有的技能与武器，在争夺区域、守卫海滩等多种玩法模式中，从各个角度去感受战场的残酷和生命的宝贵。每个地图都力求给玩家带来真实感，宏大的室内战场，飞机震耳欲聋的轰炸，满目的残墙断壁，敌人临死前的叫喊，仿佛我们真正置身于60年前的世界大战中。在作战方面，DoD和CS有着截然不同的规则，DoD注重的不只是团队配合精神，更重要的是地形的选择以及勇敢的牺牲精神。这样的设计使得双方进攻和防守都是平等的，不会再出现CS中因地形而导致双方不齐。任何违背DoD规则的玩家，只能用鲜血来证明自己的错误。放眼望去，DoD的出现对于《半条命》发展有着深远的影响，也再次为MOD树下了一块坚实的里程碑，它让我们学会了勇敢、果断、机智与团队合作。如果你想挑战自己，就请戴上钢盔，拿起步枪，随我一起上战场吧！
DoD的地图普遍要比CS所带的地图要大很多。场景力求真实，每一个窗户后面都可能隐藏着敌人的狙击手，在某个拐角处你都可能和敌人遭遇。总的来说大部分地图对德军比较有利（最明显的是诺曼底登陆地图），其实大家都很认可这种设计，二战中的每一场战役对盟军来说都是艰苦卓绝的战斗，胜利之日本身就是来之不易的。
DoD现在在很多城市大有流行的趋势，很多CS玩家纷纷转业投入了DoD的阵营，并且涌现出了很多战队，像国内最早的一支DoD战队[RED'CHINA]*战队、台湾省的GFF战队和STW战队等，大家为了一个共同的爱好走到了一起交流切磋。如果你已厌烦了警匪枪战的小场景，想体验战争的真正感受，就和我们一起拿起汤姆逊去迎接胜利之日的到来吧！

This is one of those games that I wished I could give a mixed review, like a 6/10. I'm saying recommended because if you can get it really cheap it's pretty neat, and I don't think it's "bad" especially if you are extremely non-competitive (I'm not even that competitive, but this game is enough to make me rage from bad mechanics).
On one hand the overall design concepts of the game are great, modes are creative, stylistically it's really creative, everything about it sounds great on paper. But the way some aspects of this game were executed is ABYSMAL. I think the two most infuriating for me are the movement and the networking.
The movement feels clunky. I honestly can't put my finger on it, I usually love platformers, but this games movement just does not feel good at all.
Far worse than that though, the netcode design of this game is SO BAD. I can give it a pass on being p2p, it's an indie game and servers are expensive, so I don't blame them there. But some decisions for what is client-side and what is host-side are just some of the dumbest things I've ever seen. Most infuriating to me is the "red blocks". Essentially these are blocks in the game that kill you from touching them, very common in platformers, totally fine from a conceptual standpoint. Except WHETHER OR NOT YOU STEP ON THEM IS RENDERED SERVER-SIDE! This is quite possibly the worst way to implement this feature that I can think of, in extreme cases when the hosts connection is really poor you will find yourself exploding to these blocks while standing 10 blocks away from them. This is amplified heavily in modes like falling blocks, where these blocks rain from the sky in a random pattern and you have to dodge them (usually with very near misses). You will very often find yourself exploding on this mode and not knowing why. Even on modes where the blocks are stationary though like the "speed run" mode where you try to traverse a specially designed course faster than anyone else, you can die while being nowhere near them because you were in a different location on the host's end. There are several other little things, like locations of certain objects being completely different on your screen than others, but this is by far the worst. Given how common these blocks are, it will get very frustrating very quickly.
It's a good game, turned into just a decent game by incredibly stupid and lazy design decisions. It's such an easy fix from what I can tell, but this game has been out a long time and is still the same.
Be wary when buying it, I would never recommend this for the 15 dollars it asks for on a non-sale price. I find it "worth" what I paid for it though since it was in a 10 dollar humble bundle with plenty of other good games.

As you probably already know, Quantum Conundrum is a new game from Kim Swift, the creator of Portal. And while it does share a few similarities with Portal (1st person puzzle solving, an omnipresent narrator), QC is a distinctly unique experience. Instead of Portals, the tools at your disposal are 4 "dimensions" (fluffy, heavy, slow-mo and reverse-grav), which you can swap between at will. Just like in Portal, each dimension, and the various techniques needed to solve puzzles using them, are introduced gradually. Each of the 3 main levels start out easy, but end up requiring ever-more mind-bending uses of the various dimension shifts to solve. I never found the game to be particularly hard, but you will definitely have to think hard about some of the solutions. All in all, it's very satisfying as a puzzle game. One other note - in addition to puzzles, a significant degree of platforming skill is required throughout (just something to be aware of). Great game... highly recommended!

This probably would be my favorite Risen game if they just did a few things better. I'm going to be extra critical in this review as a fan of both the Gothic and Risen series' from Piranha Bytes.
PROs:
1. Great level design in the wilderness areas. Lots of hand-placed treasures and little nooks and crannies to explore. Classic PB stuff here. However, some of the areas feel smaller than they should. I'll get back to this in a minute.
2. Really fun combat. Button mashing will get you a quick death on Ultra difficulty, and surprisingly the game is remaining challenging more than 30 hours in on Ultra. It's very satisfying to shoot things, use magic and generally time a perfect attack. The companion system is actually good in that the fights are designed around a person helping you, so while an enemy is distracted you can get in a nice shot or two. However, don't think you can just exploit the system and let them do all the work as there is an aggro system in the game, meaning the more you damage the enemy the more they are going to want to eat you. Multiple enemies can surround you and pick you apart and your companion will only hold the attention of an enemy for a limited time. Your teammate can also get KO'd during the fight, but that seems a bit too rare even on Ultra difficulty.
Regarding combat, some things are a bit strange. Being able to fire so many shots so quickly could perhaps be exploited, and I would have preferred if they added a longer cooldown on some pistol and ranged weapons. But overall the combat is very satisfying, fun and exciting. I also would have preferred even higher difficulty levels. That said, I die all the time in the game, especially if an enemy gets two or three quick, unguarded shots in. Also, why did PB remove the Kick function? That was a great move in Risen 2. Timing a good Kick would help a lot in Risen 3 as well.
3. Lowkey loot. There's just tons of stuff to pinch, pilfer and plunder. The inventory is unlimited capacity so you will be hoarding essentially entire islands worth of goods in your inventory, and a lot of it will be useful at some point or another. By lowkey loot I mean a lot of it is "low fantasy" or "low excitement" (lol) like PB is known for. This is not Diablo-style loot by any means, far from it actually. A single Long Sword can be rare and a great upgrade, and even better when you craft it to improve it. So armor, weapons and accessories are still pretty scarce, although not as much as the Gothic games. The gold for 30 hours has been kind of scarce, so decisions get made on which important upgrades to make. You could sell stuff but then you may need it for something later on, so it's your choice.
The crafting is sweet, too. There's tons of different professions you can take on, from Blacksmithing to Distilling, and it's typical PB style where you have to find recipes, ingredients, and learning the skill itself is expensive and can also be an adventure to figure out where to train it. There are lots of different ways you can approach the game to make your character stronger. Become a Distiller and start making Rum and Grog much cheaper, saving your precious gold for other stuff. Or learn to Create Talismans to craft some great trinkets and upgrades on what you'd normally find in the wilds. Lots of possibilities here, and while PB always makes it challenging to get the rewards, they do reward you quite nicely and also give you a lot of freedom to come up with interesting and unique playstyles.
4. Graphics. The wilderness areas and textures are really quite beautiful. I'm not normally a graphics guy but I enjoy looking at the prettiness of this game. The armor and loot looks cool and the overall vibe of the islands is pretty atmospheric. Good stuff here.
Now for the CONs:
1. Most areas have too few NPCs and are too small. While the Guardian camp on Taranis has a decent amount of NPCs, the overall feel of the place is that it's just tiny. If you look back on the Gothic games, the 3 main camps there felt much, much larger with more NPCs. IMO, to take their games to the next level (again, back to what they had with the Gothic series), Piranha Bytes needs to increase the size of settlements, towns and areas, as well as add more NPCs. Maybe a handful of NPCs can be trimmed back in the dialogue and quest-related stuff they offer, or just other tricks can be used, but they need to increase the scale again. The size of some of the islands like Taranis is pretty nice, but they would do well to increase the scale of them as well. There are certain areas like Calador where it feels so crammed at the start, yet the island itself is a decent size, if still a bit small. An NPC has you follow them to a village which is about 10 feet away from where you docked and met them. That's an exaggeration, but they should really increase the size and scale of things if they can to give more of a feeling of getting lost in the world like you do in other open-world RPGs, and a feeling of being in a really huge world.
2. The writing. Sadly, it's just not that great. I'm not sure why, but the lowkey writing just doesn't work too well here like it did in Gothic. The main character isn't that interesting, a far cry from The Nameless Hero, and you aren't going to meet a ton of interesting characters along the way, either. They really need to overhaul this aspect for future games. The overall dialogue really needs to be improved. I think this also plays into the fact that some areas are so small, so when an NPC tells you all about this dangerous, crazy war their faction is in, but you see about 4 people in the area, it doesn't work too well, IMO. And overall the writing just feels uninspired most of the time, unfortunately.
3. Very important, but the world is too consistently challenging. What I mean is, unlike previous PB games, there are no *real* dangerous areas as everything is, for the most part, equally dangerous. So, you will never stumble into an area you shouldn't be, get wrecked and have to retreat, get stronger and come back much later to progress there. This is a big omission, IMO, because this is a huge reason why PB's worlds are so interesting to explore. I really hope they bring this feature back in ELEX and future games. So while it's cool to have a constant challenge, there still needs to be very deadly areas that you can't venture just yet.
4. I don't see any more big cons for the game, so I'll just mention the writing again. Please make the dialogue and writing interesting, quirky and well-written like it was in the Gothic games. Lots of text is great, but it should be intriguing. The hero from Gothic was a witty, hilarious guy, and a lot of the quests and characters made me smile or laugh, and the overall premise, story and presentation was more interesting. This is not nostalgia talking as I played the Gothic games for the first time a few years ago, so they are quite fresh in my mind. I think better dialogue will help a lot here, and better quest writing in general.
Overall I really like the game. I'm also a fan of Risen 2, the original Risen and the first 2 Gothic games, and Risen 3 holds its own, if falling a bit short of the greatness of Gothic 1 & 2. I definitely recommend it but be prepared for some of the underwhelming things as well. If they improved the writing, story and quests to Gothic levels, tweak a few balance things and increase the scale of the areas with more NPCs, this would be a God-tier RPG, IMO. It's got tons of content, great exploration and interesting ways to build your character, if not offering as much of the classic PB dialogue stuff as its predecessors.
TLDR; If you can get past some dull writing the game will hook you in with the overall world and gameplay systems it offers. It's not perfect or as good as the first 2 Gothic games but it is still a quality PB RPG.

There's a system which lets you "Recycle" parts that you're not using for more bits, BUT it utterly destroys the value of the parts, so you don't get nearly as many bits as you should. If you get Premium, you get 3x the amount of bits out of parts.
- The game is MASSIVELY pay-to-win. Worse than it was before. Since I played in Alpha, I had ~25 chests to open, and got enough bits to buy a tank build off of the factory. This is pretty much where players can upload their builds and other players can buy them with bits. Well, I bought the tank, went into a game, and literally no one could kill me. I went 14-0 and 9-0 in both games that I played. I felt really bad because it's very unfair to other players, I didn't expect it to be that busted.
- The graphics in the menu itself seem to have gone in reverse as far as progress goes. The ship that displays your builds was replaced with a grey texture everywhere, even on Fantastic graphic settings. If you go into build mode, the room goes back to its original texture, but it's very choppy sometimes? I know it isn't my computer causing the lag, I get great framerates everywhere else, but sometimes in build mode, it jumps around a TON for awhile.
Honestly, the game went from being something decent with its tier unlock system and general theme it had going on, to seeming very greedy while also cutting back the quality of the graphics nearly everywhere. Even the cut scene when you launch the game looks like it's a 240p video.
RIP Robocraft.

I've only played for 60+ hours, but I think I have a good idea of what this game is all about.
Here is a list of everything subjectively good or bad about the game:
-Buggy and glitchy. I've only tried the Steam client, but it's almost impossible to start up and impossible to quit. It crashes all the time, and lots of things ingame don't work. It usually takes me 3 tries to get the game running.
-Visuals. The game does a good job at being very cutesy and anime, the style is not the problem. I'm sympathetic for a 2004 game, but the graphics are very outdated. And even then, the game is very poorly optimized and your performance is usually impaired by flashy abilities. Many of the dungeon maps are reused often resulting in confusing awkward rooms and hallways that have nothing in them. And the game's dungeons are always the same thing: Hit the orbs. Kill the mobs. Get the key. Go to the next room. Repeat until boss room.
-Soundtrack. The music in this game is usually really bad, and sometimes ok. It's also very repetitive, with the same tracks used over and over again. Many characters have their own unique theme, however, which is a plus. Here's an example... make sure to turn your volume down for this one:
-Clunky Combat. The combat system in Mabinogi is unique, with a rock paper scissors type of system going on. Mabinogi is not a button smasher, and if you go in and press random buttons you will die. You have to actually go through the tutorial, and it's pretty frustrating and complicated to figure out at first. It's not even worth it in the end; yes, it makes the game harder as it forces you to pay attention, but the horrendous LAG that Mabinogi innately has makes the combat system which relies on reflexes impossible. Generally you just DC, everything stands still, and when you reconnect you're already dead.
-You can play the game without paying money, with an exception of the social life aspects of the game. You have a homestead, which you can put things on for free overtime. However, you can't go inside your house (unless you pay for a different kind of home in a seperate place), and it's purely for looks or for a place to put work stations in. Even the houses you can buy and go into in the game cannot be decorated, and are used as stores where merchandise literally just lies on the ground. The game is very bland and has minimal scenery decoration indoors. You have to pay for pretty clothing and pets, making roleplaying even more difficult without spending money, especially for "fashionistas".
Most everything combat wise however, is given to you for free as you go through the main questlines. You can get decent armor and weapons, and you can get a land mount and a flying mount. Most of the "talents" or classes are unlocked for free. Rarely, especially during certain "events" that happen over and over again annually (no new content), you can get the ingame shop items for free. Overall though, I'd say the game does a good job at not being P2W.
-The game is essentially dead. You do most things alone, with the exception of some dedicated groups of players left. Definitely play on the most popular servers.
-Bards. The game has bards, which is an usual sight in an MMORPG. The bards are a perfect example of something that can be both combat capable and something that can roleplay well. The music system in the game is really awesome too, since you can compose your own songs. There is a variety of instruments, though most are very expensive and difficult to get besides the standard lute.
-No endgame content. There's very little to do eventually, especially if you power through it and try to progress quickly. I took my time slowly, which is where most of my playtime comes from.
I wish I could give an unbiased recommendation, but I'm going to recommend it. I've heard that in the past it was much better. But as of right now, it's at that threshold where if you're really bored and looking for something to do, it's worth a try, especially for being a mostly free game. I had a fun time personally.
Turn back now if you're looking for a good game.

This game feels like... a solid concept for a game. But one that the game doesn't seem to know what to do with. There's very little challenge to the game; only the last level has any remotely hard platforming, and the biggest challenge there is getting the blocks to line up right. Which shouldn't really ever be an issue, but, well, it is. The puzzles aren't very well thought-out or challenging and there's never really any penalty for failure, you just respawn a few seconds back. Except in the two cases of more vertical level design, which, even then, aren't that hard or punishing.
And the collection aspect... the game won't tell you this, but you do have to buy keys from shops. I collected every key in the game and had no keys at the end of the game, and bought a handful of keys from the shop in the meantime, which means that outright you do need to get some keys from the shop, which is... silly to me. There's also the stomp power, which is behind like three locked doors, and servers very little purpose other than unlocking a few small secret areas, not required for the main game.
The levels all try to have an explory collectathon feel to them, but they're all too small to really scratch that itch well, and there are very few collectibles really hidden away anyways. And, well, according to my experience as well as forum posts, it's literally impossible to find everything, some of the collectibles outright don't exist, despite what the devs are saying. So yeah, that's great...
It just feels like a game that lacks polish. The graphics are pretty and the music is solid, and the idea is there, but not really well developed, and the game's a bit buggy as well. And the missing collectibles really make it feel like a mess. On top of that, the game is very short, only 9 levels, and one of them is barely a level at all. And the ending is a big textdump followed by an ambiguous moral choice that holds no weight because there's barely any story and no characters to get attached to.
I don't mean to sound too hard on this game because it's not "bad", but for its asking price (originally $15, now only $10, which is still a bit much for the length/lack of polish) I'd really expect better. It's a shame, really. It's still kind of charming in a way, even with its flaws, but I can't really recommend it.

Mabinogi is probably the most diverse anime-themed game I know. With a fantastic gigantic fashion clothing & armor system where you can express yourself in anyway you imagined yourself. The talent, combat, exploration, and life activity skill system is always adjustable to whatever you want & anytime you want. Regardless of whatever you choose to begin as in Mabinogi, you can change anytime during the game and begin working on something else while retaining any experience and skills from the previous class/talents you used. This game is also unique due to the fact that you can use Music Markup Language to write songs in-game and play them in-game on a variety of instruments from the lute to the mandoline to the piano to the electric guitar.
It's a fun ride when you're playing it together with friends you know on there. Having a huge friendly community makes the experience inside this game ever better! And it's a shame the community suffered many declines in the past years, but it's being revived in 2016. I've met a lot of friendly people and seen a lot of new beginners finally flowing through the northern towns in the Uladh continent as well as explorers flying throughout Iria again. And I'm glad. This game needs some attention.

Gameplay:
In Poncho the player moves in three layers, lets call them front, back and middle. With two buttons the player jumps between them but can only jump one layer at the time. Most navigation of the levels and even most of the puzzles of the levels are pretty fun and relaxing. You are not limited in lives and if you fail a jump Poncho respawns at the last solid piece of ground he had jumped off from. That was a good decision as it takes the edge of some  of the games problems.
None the less the game becomes a play in frustration when it starts to introduce platforms/blocks that change between these levels as well platforms/that move between the layers when the player does.
Many of these are a problem because the front layer can often barely be seen wich makes knowing the rythm of movement a guesswork. Often i mastered these more by brutforcing it. This makes apparent that the mechanics and some of these puzzles are clearly not well enough designed. Three times i managed to more or less break the game and maneuver into a situation that i only could get out off via leaving the level.
Content:
Poncho has not enough content whatsoever. In only 3.5 hours i am pretty sure i have seen everything. After finishing the game it mostly felt as if they had stopped developing in the middle of the process.
For example around the third level Poncho gains the abbillity to stonp down and open up secret areas. The whole thing is barely even used, a handfull of times at most. And that counts for every part of the game.
The biggest insult though is the claim that Poncho is a game of exploration. But i talk about that in the last point.
Story:
The game claims that the player explores the world to discover the secret behind the faith of the world in ruins as well as the origins of Poncho.
That is simply false. The levels, while beautifull to look at, are there to be traversed, that is it. There are no secrets or artefacts to discover that may tell you what happened. The same counts for the robts you encounter. Even the most prominent of these add NOTHING to your understanding of the world and Ponchos place therein.
But it gets worse. Bercause all there is to discover is a few words at the beginning and a big text dump at the end.
And lets talk about that ending. In NO WAY has the gamne earned it's attempt at a heavy ending. Because the world has nothing to discover it ends up feeling like we have the very beginning and the very end of the story, no built up, no hints we could have guessed what was or is going on and most of all not enough infos to make the binary decision at the end.
I mean NONE of it makes sense anyway.
SPOILER! (although there really isn't anything worthwhile)
Tuns out Poncho is the son of the person that caused the end of humanity (the game shows us that by giving that person also a poncho to wear over a labcoar wich is ridiculous). To prevent Poncho from disappearing he changed him into a robot and then gave him his heart.
He then went into the Red Tower and built himself a machine so he could stay alive (we see him connected to that machine via a breathingmask) to try and change the fate of humanity and bring them back (the games makes clear that since then a loooong time has pased).
To be able to bring back humanity Poncho needs to give him his heart back so the Father can move freely. That means that Poncho would die.
The player can then decide to give him his heart back so he can restore humanity and die or keep the heart and with the last human (we never get to learn his name btw.) humanity dies forever.
If the player chooses to die, we witness how poncho gets bared up and then in a scene that suggest that all the robots had been humans changes the robiots we have seen into humans.
If the player choolses to live we see the Proffessor/Father/Guy bared up and the robots besids Poncho standing last guard next to him.
In both scenes the world afterwards makes a undeserved "everything end eventually" ending that it didn't deserve to make and that also makes no sense the way it shows.
NONE OF THIS MAKES SENSE!
What kind of machine is that, that could make the world a better place, but also can kill ALL OF HUMANITY if "something goes wrong". We never get ANY idea of that!
Why did he give Poncho his heart?
When Ponchos memory got wiped in the process, doesn't that mean he died anyway?
Great job killing your son (and humanity), dad! Twice!
So he can't move from that machine without his heart?
How did he even reach the tower if he would have died without a heart?
Has he ever heard of the concept of EXTENSION CABLES?
Or for that matter, humanity was clearly technologically advanced. How about  an artificial heart? We have those TODAY!
Or how about using that massive restless ARMY OF ROBOTS THAT WANT TO SERVE SOMEONE?
And why not give that artificial heart to Poncho in the first place?
Why leave Poncho back somewhere in a massive ruined city and not take him with him?
How the hell did you get your hearth out by yourself anyways?
Or a transportable version of that machine.
I mean you clearly must have had several decadees if not even hundreds of years for making something like that seeing how overgrown the world has become!
---------------------------------------------------------
There are more things that make no sense but the end of the song is that Poncho neither has earned such a heavy ending nor did it do it any form of real worldbuilding to support it.
Would i recommend this game?
Not at the full price because beyound the pretty optic it can't keep any of it's premisses. And what is there isn't that good.
I recommend though to buy the SOUNDTRACK!

I thought the negative reviews were basing the game off of very popular publishers like Turn10's Forza series...
I was wrong, this game is almost unplayable...
Pro's : It's a drifting game.
Decent amount of car selection
Nice realistic upgrading capabilities, like Valves, Pistons, Camshafts, Crankshafts, Turbos, etc.
Free to install
They tried to incorporate real factors like engine wear, tire wear, oil life, etc.
Con's : This game is not modeled around any realistic drifting principals...
The engine sounds are very annoying.
There is no player base.
You can't earn enough cash to get a better vehicle without spending real money.
Everything basically costs real money.
The cars don't even feel arcady, they feel like you took a 64bit game and translated it into a modern dress...
Again, the driving characteristics stink...
This game is a grind, you get almost nothing per race: 3-4000 credits... This sounds nice until you realize just a set of pistons will cost you around 50,000...
When you finally get enough to upgrade your internals you find out you have to be a higher level...
All of you money ends up going back to repairing your car 24/7... You tires last about 5-6 races, and cost about 10 grand, so there goes half your money... Then you need an oilchange, another 5 grand, and to service your engine, another 5 grand... You get the point...
The game has been set up as a pay to play, for instance it costs you 120 greens to get a new license plate... Which greens can only be bought with your real life cash....
This could all be over looked if it was a great game, but I added a tuning kit which added 100hp 100 torque to my engine... And I still get the same characteristics... The drifting feels very unrealistic... You can't use body roll...
In real life, I use body roll to get my subaru to lean into a drift and I use my cars weight to continue the drift... In this game, if you use body roll your stuck taking the corner normally but with your tires smoking... Then when you use and E-brake your car drifts for 1 second and loses all of its speed...
I thought upgrading my car would fix these issues and make the game playable... I thought that with my torque and hp I could engage a drift by knocking my rear end loose through sheer power... However, the car acts just like before except I can now hold a drift for 2 seconds...
I would say, save your time and hardware space and skip on this game... I was honestly hoping for a very nice game to play with but I got a crappy game....

A well-built game hampered by a terrible story and restrictive environment that still manages to be fun if not live up to its own full potential.
The good:
- The swining mechanics, once you get used to it, transitioned into 3D well. Towards the end of the game I was swinigng around like crazy, truly using it to overcome increasingly powerful opponents that were satisfying to take down. And it comes naturally while being fun.
- Bosses, enemies and the environment combine well and are challening.
- The game does vary its environments, changing gameplay and your focus. It is clear that some competent game designers were at work in making the actual gameplay.
The bad:
- A truly terrible story. It is as if they took some clueless marketing excutive with a loundry list from the 90's on "how to turn a franchise more mature by making it darker and edgier": that is, the approach is that everything is smeared and drained in♥♥♥♥♥♥ It is very clear that this hyphothetical marketing executive confused himself for a writer and had an overriding effort of any actual, possibly-competent writing staff. Everything is terrible, everyone is an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, everyone has done terrible things or is about to. Everyone is either working for their own, secret selfish agenda trough psychotic ruthlesness or is a fool working for someone who is. Everyone is mean and swears on general princible. Any sense of idealism or selflesness are lies. The actual aspect of what would make a story more mature, dealing with serious topics in a meaningful way, creating depth of motivations, creating genuine gray areas, dealing with uncomfortable questions, most of all creating constrast, is of course not done or done incredibly clumsily as to be accident. Someone wanted to make the original game's cheerful fantasy more "grown up" but all it succeeded is making the good guys ugly (and spoiler alert: the villains) while the villains remain cartoonishly evil. They don't even manage to create sympathy for the protagonist for pete's sake.
- Did I mention that the story is stupid? The worst offense of it all is that the story is stupid. The story comulations and sub-plots end in stupid or are largely forgotten. The ending is head-bashingly stupid. There is some pretencion of it being a military story but of course it fails at that spectacularly because it doesn't seem to really understand how a military works and what it means to be in one. The only vaguely intelligent thing about it is that it goes out of its way to justify its setting and why sending one man with a bionic arm makes any kind of remote sense.
- The game display large, open environments but the actual playable space is much smaller and without having a careful eye, it is too easy to wonder in a no-go zone that you are punished by deadly radiation.
- If anything, the game does not take enough advantage of its own physics and combining attacks and swings. For example, there is no way to take down enemies without stopping your momentum and stopping your momentum is the most dangerous thing you can do while surrounded by better-armed, more numerous enemies. You can throw and use adrelaline attacks, but not say, land on someone with high speed.
Overall, if you want a third-person shooter with spider-man-like swinging game without it being the burder of playing spider-man and have no care for the story, this is a worthwhile game to play.

This game is pretty infamous, so I won't bother with a recap. Plus, that doesn't have much to do with its quality.
It's one of the very few games I've gone back and replayed and will definitely replay more in the future. It's legitimately fun. It's cheesy, quirky, idiosyncratic, sure, and it's FUN. And that's what matters. No game is perfect. Plenty of games are crap. This is anything but crap. Special consideration goes to the environment and music - stunning.
It looks like most of the negative reviews are from people who didn't bother playing it. Yes, it could have been ported better, but I've played it both with mouse and keyboard and with a controller. It's fine either way. It IS possible to look the controls up yourself, you know.
That said, this game takes a bit of work to become proficient at it - between the porting and the swinging mechanics and difficult enemies, etc, there's a clear line between knowing what you're doing and not. But that's what makes it fun, rewarding, and even exhilarating. Things that are rewarding are very seldom easy. If you want that, I guess, you can play Call of Duty or Mass Effect. And yes, there's some artifactual difficulty - mostly from the porting, but you can get over that. And once you do, there's a fantastic game waiting for you.

Recommended, but only for die-hard fans or if it is on sale.
No individual bit of gameplay stands out as poor, but nothing stands out as great, either.  The music and graphics are passable, the voice work isn't bad, and the control is sufficient to meet your needs. A lot of reviewers praise Mike Patton for the voice work, but I don't see where it is any better or worse than any other game.  The dialog is bad enough that good delivery doesn't save it.
Some serious negatives: Collectibles and challenge achievements do not "save" on death, meaning they must be collected/achieved again if you die before the next save point. This brings up the biggest annoyance- the checkpoint and save system can't make up its mind.  Sometimes the save points are close together with no real "difficult" challenge in between, and other times they are spread out through multiple fight sequences mixed between grappling sections.  Considering the number of things that can cause death (drowning, mostly invisible radiation, etc) the save and checkpoint system feels like a way to pad the average length of time to complete more than a good design choice.
Positives: Combat with your bionic arm is great fun. Lauching yourself in the air to then perform a downward smash before attaching to an enemy and planting your feet in their chest just feels good.  The grappling movement feels great when you can get a rhythm going, but that seems to happen too rarely.

DoD和CS的区别在于，游戏脱离了目前火爆的反恐题材，取而代之是第二次世界大战背景。玩家将扮演盟军和德军中的一名士兵，使用自己独有的技能与武器，在争夺区域、守卫海滩等多种玩法模式中，从各个角度去感受战场的残酷和生命的宝贵。每个地图都力求给玩家带来真实感，宏大的室内战场，飞机震耳欲聋的轰炸，满目的残墙断壁，敌人临死前的叫喊，仿佛我们真正置身于60年前的世界大战中。在作战方面，DoD和CS有着截然不同的规则，DoD注重的不只是团队配合精神，更重要的是地形的选择以及勇敢的牺牲精神。这样的设计使得双方进攻和防守都是平等的，不会再出现CS中因地形而导致双方不齐。任何违背DoD规则的玩家，只能用鲜血来证明自己的错误。放眼望去，DoD的出现对于《半条命》发展有着深远的影响，也再次为MOD树下了一块坚实的里程碑，它让我们学会了勇敢、果断、机智与团队合作。如果你想挑战自己，就请戴上钢盔，拿起步枪，随我一起上战场吧！
DoD的地图普遍要比CS所带的地图要大很多。场景力求真实，每一个窗户后面都可能隐藏着敌人的狙击手，在某个拐角处你都可能和敌人遭遇。总的来说大部分地图对德军比较有利（最明显的是诺曼底登陆地图），其实大家都很认可这种设计，二战中的每一场战役对盟军来说都是艰苦卓绝的战斗，胜利之日本身就是来之不易的。
DoD现在在很多城市大有流行的趋势，很多CS玩家纷纷转业投入了DoD的阵营，并且涌现出了很多战队，像国内最早的一支DoD战队[RED'CHINA]*战队、台湾省的GFF战队和STW战队等，大家为了一个共同的爱好走到了一起交流切磋。如果你已厌烦了警匪枪战的小场景，想体验战争的真正感受，就和我们一起拿起汤姆逊去迎接胜利之日的到来吧！
为了胜利的那一天奋勇前进！！！！

Alwa’s Awakaneing is gaming comfort food.
Proverbially speaking, it doesn’t deviate from the recipe, it measures each ingredient carefully and everything is cooked exactly as it should be. Now aside from the fact that I am obviously hungry, the metaphor fits perfectly. Alwa is a game that you have played before but never ceases to be fun, enjoyable, and addictive as hell. While Alwa doesn’t re-invent the wheel, and some may question its innovation; what it does bring to the table is exactly what you want from these types of games.
Alwa’s Awakening is a side-scrolling, 8bit, Action/Adventure, Metroidvania. That sentence is gaming yum. The story of Alwa is rather simple, four mystical gems that kept everything harmonious and all around good were stolen and now its up to you to make it right again. To be honest, the story is super light with some dialogue interspersed enough to keep you moving forward through the game. The real highlight is the gameplay, retro-atmosphere and its enough to make the story not really matter.
Now I hate to compare games but Shovel Knight came to mind quite frequently when playing Alwa’s Awakaneing. I mean that in all good ways too. The game has very few buttons and controls are simple and precise. One thing that I definitely felt was that Alwa is a game far more about platforming and defense than attacking and boss fights. There is an attack button and one offensive spell but you spend a great majority of time playing defensively and chipping away at your enemies or avoiding death traps. Enemy AI is rather predictable and easy to overcome.
Speaking of death, you have three hitpoints at start with the ability to get a potion later for more. As you traverse the game, you quickly find yourself in situations where you’re constantly hoping for the next save point, which also function as healing/spawning nodes. Reason being, Alwa is an unforgiving game and dying is easy. Three hit points don’t go very far and there are SO MANY instant death spikes/water that it made me rage quit a few times. Matter of fact, instant death scenarios are the bread and butter of this game, if you don’t like that kinda of thing, think twice.
Standard Metroidvania conventions apply, you gather upgrades, fight bosses, and are building yourself up more and more to the end of the game. There is a large map for you to explore with so many nooks and crannies its boggling. Parts of that map are dungeon areas, that usually involve a theme to a particular spell/upgrade you acquire from that dungeon. Each dungeon usually has a boss. These are all a joy to play and I never got tired of seeing what was next.
Bosses feel very overwhelming at first, but all have that one weakness that nullifies them. That’s one thing I found slightly unbalanced, you will find the bosses either stupidly easy or die fifteen times in a row. There doesn’t seem to be a middle ground. I think that plays back to the game being more about defense. Once you have that boss strategy down, you are going to win every time. One thing that I absolutely loved was that collectibles in the game served a purpose beyond buying upgrades or what not. As you collect blue gems they help you lower the bosses health down, making bosses easier to fight and looking for them gives you a reason to explore. It felt very rewarding beyond the same old health upgrades or standard collectibles.
I love the 8bit graphics of Alwa’s Awakening. There are some palette swaps when it comes to brick work but every area is given a distinct feeling, color, and enemy design.  Certain areas have some bright colors that really make the game just pop. I also appreciated the way the camera would flow from area to area. There are no load screens except when you die. This is all enhanced even more by the OST which is underlined on the Steam page for good reason. It’s very well done and while I don’t consider myself a music savant, I enjoyed the soundtrack quite a bit.
Mixing the sound effects, seamless gameplay, and great aesthetic you will have a tough time finding fault with Alwa in the visuals department, if you love retro games. I had a hard time putting down this game from the moment I started it up. I wanted to keep going and see what new spell I might get or what challenge awaited me. Alwa is an extremely addictive game and has a great pace. The only problem I ran into, is that the game hides a pivotal item behind a hidden door two thirds of the way through the game. I spent a good three hours searching for this item and no hint in the game is ever given to its location.
While future players and guides will alleviate this frustration, my first initial run of the game was soured slightly by this damn door. Despite that hiccup, you are looking at a initial run of four to six hours of gameplay or less depending on your skill/lust for collectibles.
Alwa’s Awakaneing does have some replay value to it, as certain challenges are more likely to be completed in a second playthrough than in the first. Such as dying less then five times, and beating the game in less than two hours. This sounds freaking impossible given how many instant death scenarios there are. I had a personal gripe with the game over screen telling me I’ve died for the 188th time. The screen is easy to skip, but does twist the dagger a bit. Best of luck to you achievement hunters out there! Steam Achievements/Cards are also available for you collectors out there.
Thankfully Alwa’s controls are very tight and the game does feature full controller support with rebindable controllers. Always an appreciated feature no matter what game. Given the fact I died stupidly many times, I never felt cheated in the game and knew that it was my mistake. There is no delay from the controls or any bugs to speak of. Depending on which save node used, retreading of areas is something that is going to happen often and will become frustrating. Retreading of rooms is something that becomes less a hassle as your powers become enhanced. Besides the game is packed full of little secrets everywhere so it always isn’t a bad thing.
If you are looking for a game that is a good solid challenge then Alwa is very well balanced, it ups the ante at a good pace. Just expect by the time you reach the last dungeon everything is going to kill you in one shot.
To wrap this up, I loved Alwa’s Awakening, I raged, I laughed, I won battles, I died, a lot. This is a great comfortable game that will feel familiar from the beginning all the way to the end. You can tell this game was a labor of love and it shows. I highly recommend Alwa’s Awakening to any lover of retro games or Metroidvanias as I guarantee you won’t be disappointed.

I've been with this game since it's inception from the outside as a follower and a fan while also making Trailers for the game. Before I begin it's worth mentioning for me that I usually don't play these kinds of games. I've played through the final build twice before release and I have to say that the game is absolutely stellar.
It might be hard for me to not be bias since I know the team so well, but for me it was something that made the game even better. With only four people this team was able to extract amazing talent from one incredable musician, one great pixel artist, one extremely smart programmer and one man to lead and design the game from start to finish, which mind you is his first game project ever. There was no sleazy Kickstarters or Patreons, just hard work for several years with a goal and a dream to create their own game.
You could expect the game to be easier than let's say Shovel Knight because of it's slower speed, but the distance between the checkpoints and flow of the game is super challenging and is something I really recommend to people who loved those kind of hardcore games from the NES/SNES era. Although the game looks, sounds and feels professional, it still maintains the "home-brew" charm that it was looking it to create with it's silly story and and characters which puts it on another level than most homemade indie games.

A Metroidvania style game where you play a young girl who's been sent into another world to help defeat the evil Vicar and his Protectors. You have to find a weapon and a few spells to make it through.
It sounds like a decent story for a NES throwback game. And it plays decently well too. But... well, let's just say that after the first 1.5-2h I had done the first three dungeons/areas and bosses, they sort of came and went.
Then I spent about 1.5h getting things I needed to get to the next dungeon/area.
Then it was time for the final dungeon/area and all kind of decent level design and difficulty curve went out the window.
But there were some pros:
- the graphics are stunning
- the music is great
- the level design up until the last few areas were good.
The cons were:
- the pacing (1.5h for 3 areas, then 1.5h to get to the next area and then about 1.5h for the rest of the game.)
- the level design towards the end (insta-death water, insta-death spikes, things that shoot at you inside save rooms)
- this ties in with the above points, but the difficulty curve is... weird: Most of the game is easy, sure there are some kinda sorta mean jumps here and there, but nothing too bad. Then you get to the final area and BAM, super-hard, with no inbetween. And boss fights are a joke. The boss that took me the longest was the fourth one and that was only because I kept screwing up my jumps due to the point below.
- and the thing that makes me most annoyed is that for a game released in 2017... you can't change the keyboard controls. You can only change the gamepad controls and the keyboard controls were far from optimal, my hands felt cramped trying to play with them. So I had to dig out a 15 year old gamepad that works most of the time to play the game.
When it comes to Alwa's Awakening you can tell that they put in a lot of effort in making it a NES throwback title, but it feels like they wanted to make 2 or 3 different games and sort of mashed it all together. At first it's a more Castlevania style game, but with some minor exploration, generally short areas with a nice little boss fight at the end. Then it turns into a Metroid game with lots of exploration and just one or two bosses after a lot of stuff has been done. And finally It Wants To Be The Game (I Wanna Be The Guy) with death-pits, insta-death spikes, jumps where you barely have enough time to cast the correct spell.
I really wish I could recommend this game, but I just can't. My recommendation, if you really want to get the game, would be to get the game, beat the first three bosses and then just listen to the amazing soundtrack while you do other stuff.

Przyjemna gra, ale coś w niej nie zagrało. Twórcy w trzeciej części powracają do takich elementów świata jak magia, gildie, może też trochę mniej tych pirackich klimatów, ale ta gra ma strasznie dużo bolączek, które najpierw chyba omówię.
Pierwszym rzeczą jest chyba sam świat który składa się w dużej mierze z tych samych lokacji, lekko tylko pomniejszonych, i o ile na początku mimo lekiego uczucia wtórności, jeszcze ma się chęć do explorowania tych wysp to z czasem robi się już to zwykła formalność z której już ciężko czerpać dużo przyjemności. Podobnie jest zresztą z fabułą i zadaniami pobocznymi, jeszcze do połowy gry były to questy jak dla mnie dość przyjemne, ale później jest to dla nas tylko idź z punktu A do B, nie wiem jakim cudem, ale jakoś zrobiłem wszystkie możliwe questy, oraz inne aktywności w tej grze. No i jak na zakończenie trylogi dostajemy chyba najsłabsze zakończenie jakie się tylko da, a sam główny boss jest chyba najgorszym w całej trylogi.
No, ale gra się nazywa Risen 3- Titan Lord, więć co z tymi władcami? Niestety, ale spodziewałem się czegoś trochę lepszego, jest ich dość nie wielu, i nie stanowią większego problemu w walce, a odnośnie samej walki to jest ona moim trochę lepsza względem dwójki(nie sprawdzałem broni dystansowych), ale nadal jest jedną z najbardziej kulejących rzeczy w tej seri, i o ile na początku gry z tymi przeciwnikami trzeba się jednak trochę pomęczyć, to później nie stanowią oni rzadnego wyzwania, powiedziałbym, że gra nie ma żadnego stopniowania poziomu trudności wraz z rozwojem rozgrywki.
Dodałbym jeszcze do takich pomniejszych minusów sporo błędów,beznadziejne bitwy morskie, dość ubogi inwentarz w jaki morzemy się zaopatrzeć, oraz cały interfejs, ciężko powiedzieć według mnie czy już nie lepszy był ten z pierwszych gothiców w porównaniu do tego.
No dobra, ale jak wynika z tego co napisałem, że jest tak słaba, to dlaczego ją ograłem, i poleciłem?
A ponieważ dla każdego fana Piranha Bytes jest to sentymentalny powrót, gra miewa swoje momenty oraz sporo smaczków dla fanów Gothica. Fabuła mimo wszystko potrafi czasem wciągnąć gracza, są dość ciekawi towarzysze pokroju Kostucha czy Jaffara, których chyba najczęściej z wszystkich postaci brałem do podróży. Gra ma też swój specyficzny klimat, oraz mimo nie porywającej grafiki jest czasem na czym zawiesić oko, i nie chodzi mi o Patty!!!
Dla większości graczy podejrzewam, że ta gra to może być kompletny gniot, ale jeżeli ktoś chciałby pograć we wpółczesnych czasach w gre robiąną w oldscholowych klimatach odnajdzie się tu od razu.

While I recommended this game at first, I have to change my review due to its lack of improvement over the last year.
Let me begin by saying that this game has so much potential to be a great sci-fi shooter. It has all the pieces of the puzzle to make it awesome. That being said, the puzzle is a complete mess. The controls are very awkward and the gameplay is confusing. For example, when you pick up a gun, you have to immediately reload and/or find ammo for it. This is contrary to nearly every other shooter which typically has plenty of ammo and automatically reloads. It gets very frustrating, very quickly. Next, the FPS is horrendous. My computer has beyond the recommended requirements, and I can barely scrape up 20 FPS while playing single player. Finally, the game has been in early access for several years, and no improvement has been made to it since I bought it back in March of last year. It is a shame that a game with so much potential has yet to get the care that it deserves from its developers.
Here's my suggestion. Skip the game for now. Wait until it gets out of early access, or at the very least until they fix the main issues.

Mind bending first person puzzle platforming, ridicilous environments and funny main characters providing quirky commentary on your progress.
Sounds familiar? Exactly, we have our first Portal clone, with a cartoony twist!
Altough to be fair, the developer behind this game is one of the main designers on the original Portal game, and the game mechanics here are completely different (but as much fun as shooting portals).
I'm enjoying this game very much. Jumping around on flying objects in the slow motion dimension will surely put a big grin on your face, not to mention the fun commentaries of the crazy professor.
Only issues: could've used some more polish (early tutorial levels can be frustrating), sometimes the prof gives the solutions away too quickly (spoiling them), and the art direction is a little bit flat. But this is a smaller budget game, and as such, these can be forgotten.
All in all: fun time, highly recommended!

Okay, so here's the thing, this game isn't BAD persay, it just doesn't seem to be able to do anything that stands out as partiuclarly GOOD. I just found myself incredibly annoyed or bored while playing this and daydreaming about Witcher 3, Skyrim, or Black Flag and I would seriously recommend playing those games instead of this one. Sure, I picked it up for a couple bucks on sale, but just because something is cheap, doesn't make it more worth your time.
I legitimately don't think I can really list a single thing that stood out to me as being great and that I enjoyed in this game, which is weird because there's usually some redeeming quality of a game for me. Let me just break down the issues I had with this game real quick:
Graphics: Just to be upfront, I installed a Nexus complete overhaul mod for this game before playing more than an hour. Full texture overhaul and some UI stuff and it looks great...well, it would if textures didn't constantly pop in and out and the animations during cutscenes weren't just painful, and just to be clear there was no difference between unmodded and modded with these issues except actually the mod helped a bit with the texture popping since I could tweak the load distances to be greater than 2 feet. I found myself skipping all the dialogue after the first 10 minutes or just looking away because it hurt my soul too much to watch the aliens that had possessed the corpse of the humans of this world try and fake it. All the cutscenes had serious tearing and just felt super clunky too.
Pirating: Okay so let's be real, the main draw you all probably came for is the pirate aspect of this game because there aren't a lot of good pirate sims out there. I would say it kind of does a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job in this regard. Remember I didn't get super far in this game, so certain elements might come later, but there were no sea battles or even any sailing. There was very little plundering to be done, no sea shanties to sing even. It's basically just a standard RPG where you character goes around telling people they're a pirate, but you really aren't, you're just Standard RPG Hero #7. There's pickpocketing and lockpicking in this game...barely...like about 1000x less than in Skyrim. You literally have to talk to someone in order to pickpocket them, which means to steal from them, you have to wake them up if they are sleeping. Because logic. Overall, I wouldn't even call this a pirate game really, so moving on...
RPG: Okay so to me there's a few core aspects of an RPG. There's the looting, the exploring/questing, the combat, the skill tree and the talking with your group. So lets break this down:
--Looting:
Basically the worst I've seen in a long time. Kill some goblins? Have a spoon! Kill a viscious Croc? Have a single tooth! Maybe! Kill a big boss man? Have some rocks! The drops are basically insignificant, but at least there's lots of stuff lying around to pick up, right? Yes and no. Sure, you can horde items like Skyrim to your heart's content, as long as you enjoy carrying around 700 spoons, forks, knives, and dinner plates...because that's basically the only thing to pick up around here. It takes FOREVER to find ways to improve your starting garbage gear and its not a simple task. This is probably the most disappointed I've ever been with an RPG's loot and item system. There's very limited items, sometimes no way to get essential ammo, and everything sold or lying around does the damage of a wet noodle.
--Exploring/Questing:
Every friggin conversation option in this game gives you a quest. At first I thought that was cool, but then it just got stupidly obnoxious. The rest of the quest come from books you read, which is actually kind of a nice twist. You read a story about the legend of whatshisface the brave and how he had this cool weapon and then you go looking for it. Every quest is boring and extremely clunky though as there's very little useful direction given and I genuinely don't know if quests go away or they stay there forever in the Logbook. They don't update your map all the time or gives progess updates and just list the initial quest, so if you get 3 or 4 subquests in and then go do something else and come back and forget what you were doing, TOO BAD. Every quest I did I found obnoxious and difficult to understand and made me feel stupid. I don't like feeling stupid.
--Combat:
Hate it. Hate it. Good lord make it stop. It reminded me of Witcher 2, but where every enemy is a bullet sponge right from the start and dodges every stupid attack you make, making every battle take FOREVER as you both dodge around in circles whiffing at each other. Magic and ranged are extremely unhelpful due to their consumables early on, leaving you with melee, which is just a cruel joke if you have anything other than some magical unicorn imbued weapon. Every sword I used was hot garbage and I only finally began to stop hating my life once I grabbed a sickle I found stuck in a tree because I finally swung fast enough to hit something before it ran away.
--Skill Tree:
Ugh so basic and yet so obnoxious. Takes way too long to level up and nothing ever feels rewarding. Hey did you just spend an hour doing quests and getting a ton of Glory? Your reward is a 5% increase to your sword damage...yay. You can't level up pickpocketing/lockpicking without using Glory either since that's somehow a skill you have to choose between and health or damage. To be fair, you can dump gold on the problem and get training, but its not like gold is easy to come by unless you're collecting every spork on the islands. Skills take an absurd amount of money to level and you have to find a specific trainer for that skill and then remember where they are because the map is no help.
--Party:
I hate everyone, I hope they all get scurvy and die. Their animations are what actually stole the soul of my character and they never shut up. Also, Patty's outfit is just absurd and it's one of the first things you see in the game and instantly broke my immersion. It's like someone went to a halloween party as "sexy cosplay pirate" or something.
Overall I kept playing this game hoping it would get better and I know it probably does since it seems to be leaning that direction, but then I thought to myself...self...why aren't you playing something you enjoy NOW rather than later? So then I uninstalled this game and played something else...ANYTHING ELSE I knew i liked. I have hundreds of games in my Steam library, most of which I haven't played yet and you probably do too. Skip this game, even if its on sale. It will just bum you out and sit on the digital shelf forever.

I bought this game when it first came to the steam greenlight program. It was the first and only game I ever felt like backing on Greenlight. I watched the video, and was instantly enthralled with what the Dev team wanted Interstellar Marines to become. So I took out my wallet. Got my card, and proceeded to give them 15 dollars.....or was it 30....w/e. I rushed to my computer whenever a new update was announced on twitter. Testing out each new function. (dat crouch) Playing the multiplayer and talking about the game with the community was a great experience. Then my computer took a dump and I was computerless for about 7 months. When I bought a new computer Intersteller Marines was the first game I re-downloaded from my library. I couldn't wait to see the new changes, as they are on udate 17 (my computer died around update 6).I was not very impressed. I was expecting the game to be more complete. Instead it feels hollow, even after 11 more updates.
I Don't know how much the greenlight program has earned them and I know they are doing all they can to make the game they not only want to make, but prommised. I just feel like whatever money they are puting toward Interstellar Marines is bound to dry up soon. They are a small team with families and bills. A lot of games end up not being finished, and I feel like this game even after all the work and struggle the dev team has commited to this IP will end up being one of them. If you want to take a chance on this studio then by all means go for it. However given that there is no obligation to actually finish a game once it's on greenlight, I would highly advise caution. For that I cannot recommend Interstellar Marines. </3
