As a standalone game Xenoverse would be mediocre at best. If you're not already in love with Dragonball this game should be a solid pass. That said, if you love Dragonball then you'll most likely enjoy this game. As much as I want to love this game being the DB fan I am it only gets a 6/10 from me.
Story: 5/10
The entire story revolves around you being summoned by shenron after a strong warrior is wished for to help defend time. You then go into all different parts of time helping the usual Z warriors beat the bad guys. It's a decent plotline but leaves much to be desired as you face stronger and stronger opponents without the difficulty scaling much. It gets to a point were you face Beerus and he's just as easily defeated as Raditz is in the first fight. Non of the bosses and anything special about them other than a larger health bar.
Subquests:6/10
Subquests, or PQ's as they're called in Xenoverse are basically add on missions were you go back and revisit missions or areas to fight different enemies who have or will be possessed by evil during the fight. These tend to be very similar to each other and don't really bring much to the table. The AI is the same and they use the exact same techniques without any variation.
Graphics: 7/10
Dragonball has always had cartoon style graphics because, well, it's a cartoon or anime as most would prefer. Though even on the maxed out settings you get some really weird looking stuff happening in the hub-world. Up close everything looks quite nice but as you look farther out you see the textures extremely blurred as they only load fully load as you get near them. This is a huge eyesore and it has no reason to it especially considering the low-res look of the game. Other than the hub world this seldom happens and looks quite nice, but the sheer fact you spend an large part of the game in the hub it really takes a toll on you.
Combat:6/10
The combat system is mediocre at best and extremely annoying the rest of the time. It's basically repeated left and right mouse button spam with the occasional super / ultra as they load. The biggest flaw is that the enemy AI gets a massive amount of KI (your chargeable ability you only get via combat) to begin with. Meaning you can literally come out of a portal or just at the start of the mission and you're already getting smashed with an ultra. It's one of the most frustrating things in the game made even worse when you're fighting multiple AI. While we're speaking of AI lets address how poor friendly AI is. The only use or AI in this game it to keep you from getting double, triple, or even quadruple teamed. It's so useless that almost every time I fail a "main story" quest is because a friendly died. It's pathetic. Then while they are alive all they seem to do is jump right in the way as you use your spec and they absorb all the damage.
Audio:7/10
Xeonverse has a decent audio track with some nice combat music and generally nice combat sound effects. Though they can get a bit repetitive at times.
- Voice acting: 3/10
The voices for this game are atrocious. The worst and most noticeable example of this is the supreme kai of time. Every line she speaks sounds extremely forced and it sounds like the voice actor was near gargling the mic as she spoke. It got to a point where I muted the character chatter and just read the text bubbles or subtitles.
Overall:6/10
If you're not in love with Dragonball you should pass on this. Even if you are a fan I'd strongly suggest only getting this on sale. It's quite short for a $50 game taking me only 22 hours to complete the main story and sidequests.

Putrefaction is a first person shooter in an post-apocalyptic world setting, similar to Doom or Quake. It contains a lot of zombie shooting, gore and some sci-fii weapons.
The story: you are a soldier in a post-apocalyptic world set out to find a source of a disease. I think we heard that one before in some other games. The gameplay - shoot everything that moves at you. No other buttons to press of any kind of red line across the levels.
I played this game through in an hour on hardest difficulty possible. That should tell you how hard to is to shoot monsters in this game. Weapons are just the standard FPS ones - assault rifle, shotgun, minigun, electro-gun, rocket-launcher. The limbs shot off enemies are fun to watch for first 5 minutes but gets boring and repetative.
Almost no detail through all levels. Only some final levels contain some marking on the walls worth looking at, besides that its either grey space ship areas, brown undergrownd or red gore area.
The progress is based only on shooting and running almost completely linear hallways. No other mini-games or anything else to do.
Both the music and the shot sounds are really cheap and thankfully this game does not take long to complete. There is almost no immersion in this game, especially because when monsters start coming - you get battle music. Once the music stops you know you killed the last one. Cheap.
I can not recommend this game even when its on sale. The most important resource in life is not money, but time and I want to save you from wasting your time on this game. Its short, has no innovative features, bad graphics and sound and is simply not fun to play through.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying and installing this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

I would definitely recommend this game.
The graphics are good, particularly the environment.  There's quite a bit of fun dialog with NPCs and your companions which had me laughing at times, it was entertaining.  There are a lot of side quests which I didn't get to finish all of because I got so focused on completing the main story line.  That's actually a compliment though because I was so focused on the main story because I'd really gotten caught up in it.  Towards the end of the story line I was REALLY wanting to kick the butt of the main bad guy.  In my first play through I focused mainly on melee weapons (swords) and enjoyed the combat.  It wasn't too complicated but at the same time had a nice level of challenge to it that gave you a sense your own skill matttered.  The kill moves were also pretty good (with the possible exception of one where you slit the throat of a skeleton which just seemed silly, but I can live with that when the rest was pretty cool).  There are also a LOT of cut scenes, the developers devoted a lot of time to this and they're generally pretty good.  It gives the game a more cinematic feel which was fun.
Okay so that's the good, now for the bad.
Not everything is explained very well, so I found myself sometimes just saving, trying things and reloading until I had a sense of what I should do or what was the best decision because the game didn't give me enough info about various skills and so forth to make anything other than a random guess.  Couple of examples.  Spending glory on skills and attributes, I was never entirely sure how important different ones, what the effect of raising one attribute vs another really was or how useful some skills were.  Another example, whether to keep or sell some things I'd gathered.  I gathered a LOT of iron ore, gold ore, etc. but by the end of the game all the gold ore was still sitting in my inventory.  Should I have sold it, was there some crafting I could have done with it but missed, or was it just another form of "wealth", I don't know and the game never explained this.  This was my first Risen game experience so perhaps previous games had explained this but, again I don't know.  But for someone coming to the game franchise for the first time some parts of the game were a bit too puzzling.  Overall though these problems didn't stop me from enjoying the game.  Also the game doesn't prevent you from saving at any time you like and you can have as many saves as you wish so you can always just save, experiment with choices and then reload as necessary.
There's a lot of weapon choices but your armor / clothing choices were limited so being able customize your character's appearance was likewise limited more than that I would have liked.  (I guess Skyrim has me really spoiled with all the options I got used to there.)   If you have the Adventurer's Garb, which I did, I wore it for much of the game.
One other criticism I would have is that once you finish the main story line the game ends, there's no option to continue in a sandbox mode as you can with other games such as Skyrim.  There is a lot to explore and with such an engaging main story line its easy to miss stuff.  But I don't necessarily want to start a new game or go back to one of my many older save points just to finish exploring a richly detailed game world.  So the lack of a sandbox mode after finishing the main story line would have been a plus in my book.
Lastly, if the game developers happen to read this I have a small criticism about the game ending.  I don't want to give away any spoilers here so I'm going to be a bit vague.  But, the end cut scene was abrupt and short.  Your hero emerges you briefly see your friends and then it cuts to you sailing away and rolls credits.  As it cuts from seeing your friends to sailing away, that was very abrupt and for a game that had so many well done cut scenes the ending felt a bit anti-climatic and short.  So just wanted to point that out, it could have done with more of a celebration and renunion with your friends and crew at the end after such a big final battle.
Overall though I'd very much recommend the game.  All the important aspects of the game worked, nothing felt broken to me or unfinished.  I had a lot of fun exploring the world the game presents, getting to know the NPCs, forming alliances and making enemies.  Some of the sarcastic dialog was just FUN, it was nice to play a game where you really could tell an NPC, "Hey, you know you're a moron, right?"  LOL

is a procedurally generated walking simulator. There is only one aim to this game and that is to explore the pixelated environments. The soundtrack is also procedurally generated, meaning it changes as you move through your surroundings. Each playthrough is distinct as the terrain and topography is different. This is a very minimalistic game.
There is no story or any achievements. I played the game for about 1.5 hours and the following are the positives and negatives of what I experienced.
- The game has a very relaxing melodic soundtrack which is also procedurally generated. Basically whatever you look at produces a distinct sound and together a tune is made.
- The graphics are pixelated and colorful. I personally thought they were pretty but they might not be for everyone.
- The weather and seasons change and have smooth transitions. The environment looks really good in the spring season.
- There are many small creatures in the game which appear depending on your location or time of day such as owls at night and frogs near water. You can also chase them :D
- I did not experience crashes or any bugs.
- The game is relaxing and very causal and something someone would like after a stressful day at work.
- There is no saving system which adds to it's casual "in and out" experience.
- The game is the most minimalistic game (genere defining almost) I have ever played and tbh there is not much to do. I was immersed in the game for the first 30 minutes, wandering here and there but it got repititive soon.
- Having some lore or interactions would make this game so much more interesting but unfortunately there is none.
- The pricetag is too high for what it offers.

This game is surprisingly good for a free FPS game!
I originally downloaded it a few months ago to get the black rose spy knife thing from getting the first achievement, but the game was broken for me, so I couldn't play it until they finally fixed the installer.  I played this all morning and had a blast!  The combat feels more like a watered-down Call of Duty game, but it's not like you paid anything to play it!  I didn't really notice any lag, even though I had 220+ ms ping since I was playing at 4 AM my time, which meant I was automatically connected to European servers.  Sniping was really fun, and I'd say it ranks up to stomping 1.6 pubbers, since people panic when there's an actual sniper that can aim!
There's basically 3 classes - Point, Rifle, and Sniper.  The point character gets the heavier weaponry, and is meant to be the squad leader-type (heading the front).  Rifle guy is the 'CS' archetype since he has the M4A1 and AK47 weapons.  The Sniper is basically a Scout-user with AWP-sounds.  It takes 2-3 hits to kill anyone (depending on if they bought armor), although a headshot is a one-hit kill.  There's a cash shop thing inside the game, but I don't think anyone spends actual money on a game like this, so there really isn't a downside if you only spend in-game credits over actual cash.  You can buy new grenades (like flashbangs!) in the shop, but everything has a durability price so that you keep playing forever.  None of the items for me expired in the several hours I spent testing this game out.
There are about 7 game types, I think, ranging from Deathmatch style to L4D-types.  Obviously there's also CT vs Terrorists bomb defusal game-type as well as a horde mode game-type.  The robot horde mode was the first thing I played, and it actually impressed me when you actually got to the boss LOL.  I thought it was easy as heck, until my party of 4 reached the boss, and it was a gigantic mech straight out of something like Vanquish.
The regular DM maps are pretty bland, but it's still fun to play in!  It's a free game, so I can't really complain because it was actually really fun to play even though I had no idea what I was doing.  It's a pretty easy game, but if you and your friends have nothing better to do and want to play an FPS game, you might as well give this thing a shot since it's free.
TL;DR
This is a fun Call of Duty/Counter-Strike/Left4Dead clone, but free2play and has a non-intrusive cash shop to actual gameplay.  Play it if you're bored and feel like dicking around in another FPS game~

RimWorld?
Pros:
+The amount of content to experience is only limited by your own in-game decisions.
+Run your colony however you see fit. (Will you seek peace or will you raid the neighboring factions ? Will you take prisoners in hopes that they will join your cause or will you keep your prisoners, only to be harvested for organs later?)
+The game has a ton of options pertaining to difficulty. (You pick between three A.I. storytellers each with their own difficulties & playstyles)
+The modding community is one of the best I have seen. (Some mods change the game entirely, some are quality-of-life tweeks & others will challenge your leadership/strategy prowess)
+The replay value for RimWorld is great. (Starting a new colony is all part of the fun)
Cons:
-The $30 price tag may be a turn-off initially, but that's for you to decide. (Maybe watch some livestreams to see if it's worth it to you)
This game is amazing, especially if the colony-sim/survival genre is something you love dearly. The choices you make when tragedy hits is what you live for in RimWorld & mods just make it that much better. As of writing this review, the game has just hit it's beta stages & I can't wait to see where it goes from here.

After Spending around 900 hours in this game, I do believe it's time I make a review for Mabinogi.
In short, mabinogi is a Open World, Fantasy Life MMO, You're free to do literally anything you want too, you can run around and explore dungeons or you can take up smithing and make weaponry, or you could take up tailoring or carpentry instead, you can even play music to help buff your team mates in what they're doing.
Honestly, I've put a lot of time into Mabinogi because I fell in love with it's charm and how it plays, it's not super fancy, it doesn't have the top notch graphics that most MMOs have nowadays but it has so much more to offer outside of it's looks that it just blows other MMOs out of the water.
With that said, there are quite a few Cons for Mabinogi too, forinstance the lack of support for people who are on newer system and the extreme amount of stuff to wrap your head around, it's very overwhelming, it's not really as popular as a lot of other MMOs either, which to me is honestly a good thing because that means most people on there are just as deticated on there as you and are usually willing to help a friend out, it's also just not built as well as most other games either.

Triple Town has been around for a while. I first stumbled upon this game via Android, during a more basic age for Triple Town. Now, in the desktop version, you're faced with additional modes inclluding city management and new "arenas." The idea is simple, connect three of the same type of object to upgrade them into one new one. Connect three of the new objects to upgrade those into yet another upgraded object. And.. Continue. In the meantime, terrible bears and ninja bears appear to block your open tiles, as they move between each of your object placements. To remove them? Trip them inside your objects to them into gravestones. Guess what- Connect three gravestones and you get a church, and upgrade those, too! No Triple Town experience is ever the same, and if you're a fan of puzzle games, this game definitely screams for your attention.

Blatantly an iOS game with little done to remodel the UI, but despite feeling like I should be playing this on a phone the game is surprisingly addictive. Gameplay consists of dropping down items on a playing field to build up match-3 combos and get bigger and bigger chunks of points. Good combos can be rewarded with items to use in the overworld, where you again match things to get combos and build more and more...for no reason other than to do it, really. Like I said, blatantly an iOS game designed to addict you into doing things and dropping money to make doing that easier, though the PC port features no microtransactions.
The game also features a few presets of modifiers like field size, lakes, and the presence of types of bears (which try to block you from placing blocks but can be trapped and combined to make large amounts of points) to mix things up, though I feel it would be much more fun to have control over each individual modifier as well and build your own custom game types. Overall I enjoyed it, though I think it'd be a stretch to call it a good game. Pick it up for 75% off sometime and you can probably get your money's worth out of it.

The one thing I would say is that while it's a very fun fighting game and easy to pick up, it's not good as a hardcore one. All characters work offline against bots, but online you're going to have a rough time if you just go with your favourite dudes. So, y'know, don't take it too seriously.
Oh, and one more thing: Look at that title! LOOK AT IT! How can you not stare in awe at such a magnificent title! I give this game a 10 out of 10 for that behemoth alone!

To start with, I finished "Risen 3" 5 days ago. So with its completion, I have done with the series, at least for now. I think I can say without hesitation that Piranha Bytes did a marvelous job there with Risen series.
In regards to Risen 3, I have read a lot of reviews and comments that says the game is just more of the same of its predecessors and I kinda agree on that. However, I think it is a good thing that R3 got the best of these two worlds.
As an RPG gamer, what impressed me in R1, is the faction system which utterly failed in R2 because your faction was shaping your play style and it was limiting the player to a certain role. Now these factions in R2 plays a role in R3 but for instance, if you want to be an inquisitor, now you can't but there is a whole bunch of quest for them, too and even if you are submitted to another faction which also can heavily consists of magic usage, you can develop you character in both magic skills and/or other gun/musket skills.  Also faction system makes replayability of the game skyrocket, just like it did in R1 and R2; you can revisit the game and play a different storyline with a different faction.
Story-wise, it is on par with 2 previous games; although, for me, first one is still the best. It goes without saying, it was also heart-warming to see the characters from previous games; heck, you can even meet with the antagonist of the second game(playerchar) and clink some booze with him; even though it plays a small role it is very nice addition and I really appreciate the developers for giving us, players, tangible lines to merge previous games to the newest and latest title.
As for the map, it shares the same location with 2nd game's. I am not sure but maybe, 1 or 2 island were added. So if you played the 2nd game, it's not a big surprise to say  yourself "I think I know this place but from where?". One can say it is a disadvantage or a proof that developers didn't work as hard as they worked for the 2nd game but I found it really satisfying. Because instead of spending time on recreating a new world, they spend the time on enriching the story and quests, giving us a better game in terms of story content from the other previous titles. The story length is quite satisfying in comparison to today's standard; just to give an example, my play-through took around 45 hours.
So what I don't like about R3 is, still the same since the beginning of these series. Item-wise, you are still searching for the strongest weapon in regards to your level, not really thinking of any other option because there is no real option there. Second, Lockpicking and Persuasion skills are all needed but for one tenth of whole cases, really. In nine tenth of cases treasure loots or things we steal are totally garbage.
So there is not much negativity for me in this game; even they integrate a teleporter system. In the previous titles, it was becoming tiresome to walk over all the island just for 1 quest item.
So I think I can safely recommend Risen 3 to rpg lovers and also, with its friendly UI, even to the newcomers from other genres.

I loved Risen and Risen 2.  What I mostly enjoy in games is the plot and characters and the interactions between them.   In the first two, I loved the "Hero" and Patty, and the way it danced around them having a romantic relationship but never really went that far.  When I heard that a Risen 3 was in the works, I was so excited about the possibility of the Hero and Patty officially getting together.  Thus, though I thought the game OK, I was thoroughly disappointed that the Hero wasn't even the main character, and that he and Patty seemed to have come across a rough patch.  I am still hopeful for a Risen 4 that brings the Hero back, along with Patty, and finally a deeper relationship.
So overall, yeah, the game was OK, I just couldn't get past that I wasn't the "Hero" from the previous games, and I did not enjoy it near as well.  I didn't find this hero, who was Patty's brother, as interesting and likeable.  Though I still enjoy playing Risen and Risen 2 over and over again, I have no desire to play Risen 3 again.  I also thought the foul language was excessive and unnecessary, and I did not like that.  It seems each game the language got worse.
Still holding out hope for a Risen 4 with the original Hero and Patty, and the foul language toned down.

As a huge fan of Gothic 1 and 2: After Risen 2 I didn't have any expectations for Risen 3 and I only picked it up after it was dirt cheap. And boy, was I surprised! Ok, start is rough, but let's be honest - which PB game's start isn't. After that the game does pick up and if you go for the crystal magic path, you can perform some pretty fun magic moves. Beats those dull Skyrim spells by a mile!
I would suggest playing the game with German audio if possible. PB was never renowned for their English versions and after first 10 minutes, I switched from eng to deu and never looked back.
If you're a PB games fan, I can only recommend giving this game a try. Especially if you can get your hands on it during a sale. It's no masterpiece, but quests are fun, most characters are just enough cheezy to still be enjoyable and you get used to combat eventually. Just use your companions until then. And if you like weird remarks, I suggest Bones.
Overall, an enjoyable, decent RPG. Worth the money, just don't expect the next Gothic masterpiece. Let's just accept the fact that we'll never get one and move on.

"Speaking on the base game, it's gripping."
Borderlands immerses you in the alien world of Pandora, where intergalactic legends that tell of a "Vault" have spurred colonization efforts with the promise of fame, power, and riches to whoever finds and opens it. A time of grand exploration, expansion, and civility...
... This is not that time.
Welcome to Pandora! A dilapidated, dangerous, criminal-infested outcropping of the galaxy, and you decided to go there in search of a Vault that even the best minds of the known universe haven't been able to find in the entire time of this forsaken planet's colonization. Congratulations, you just earned yourself the madman's title "Vault Hunter".
I love the universe of this game, it explores what would happen to a world with superficial promise that is ultimately deemed a failure. Withdrawing any solid policing force and left to the ruin of the inhabitants, Pandora goes from, as originally advertised, shimmering haven to, now more accurate, broken dystopia. The lore is firm and is one of my favorite things about Borderlands.
In gameplay, the game works. To sum it up, it's a FPS with RPG elements and an award-winning formula embodied in the loot mechanic. You can easily pick up the game with sprinting, crouching, meleeing, grenade throwing and gun handling near-identical to most modern shooters, and does a good job at all of it. RPG elements are taken into account as you level up, granting you access to different character-specific powers and allowing you to wield more potent weaponry. Areas are typically level-centered so if you are sufficiently leveled previous areas will be a lot easier, but the opposite is true in that if you are not sufficiently leveled future areas are tons more difficult. You can offset the difficulty of future areas by grinding in current areas, largely around being a completionist of quests in your area, I found that this made the game less stressful (and less costly on your ingame currency).
One of the biggest selling points of the game is its loot system, basically enemies have a chance of dropping weapons, energy shields, and grenade mods that you can equip onto your character so long as you meet the equipment's level requirement. Equipment chests are also scattered throughout Borderlands and can host not only the previously listed items, but also class mods which give unique bonuses to your character. It is fun going around questing and finding a chest and having the giddy anticipation of what might be in the box, hoping for some rare OP item that can help you mow down the hordes of bandits and psychos care-free... with your hopes quickly crushed under the abysmal quality of the things you find. When you do find that one awesome weapon though, it can be hard to contain your glee. I have found from my experience that the game is fair and will give you something you're looking for at intervals.
Now for the things I don't really like about the game, all you ever fight are bandits, psychos, skags, bugs, whatever Rakk are, the occasional freak of nature, and varients of them all and that's it. Their AI is simple, predictable, and occasionally bugged. There are fetch quests but they are a necessary evil to help with the pacing of the game. There are inconsistencies on what you will and will not survive. Finally, map design that can be too big and confusing and can get curious adventurers stuck or even killed.
In conclusion, the story and gameplay are good, the pacing is well done and really feels that you are gradually building and building up to something big and making something of youself in the barren wastelands. I like how you eventually are recognized as a planetary threat and there's a lot of crap that happens with that. Overall, I would recommend this game for people wanting the feel of a rugged space frontier complete with guns and energy shields, and even a little magic to boot!

I played about half of this game back on the Xbox 360 with a friend, but never finished it, so I decided to re-do everything on the PC instead.  Let me start off by saying, the game is not new, so the controls are a bit stiff sometimes, and the driving mechanics are ATROCIOUS, and there are plenty of bugs or problems you might encounter in the game.
In-between all that, there's the story and the fun.  The actual story, by itself, of this game is really not that good.  It's pretty standard alien race invaders kind of thing.  What actually makes this game unique is the amount of uncensored humor in the story and characters, as well as the graphics style the developers chose.  The art style is reminiscent of comic books or something along those lines, and it does it very well.
Though the story itself doesn't have much value, the humor, graphics, weapon system, and how much fun it is when playing with other people really bring the game to life.  I cannot recommend this game if you do not plan to play it with someone else, as solo play in this game is really pretty boring, but with another person or more, it can be a blast.

Mabinogi is a game based off of the Celtic myths called Mabinogions. I don't know much about celtic mythology, but the game's icon is based off the celtic knot. The game is made by Koreans who are well-versed in the art of coding crack cocaine into video game form.  You look like an anime character from the PS2 era, doing mundane tasks to rank up how well you can sheer a sheep, or mix strawberry milk.
Onto the gameplay,
This game has no excuse to run at 15 fps at some places, being from the 2000s. If you can get past the horrible engine this game forces you to play on, you're in for some not very exciting gameplay. The game is based off of a rock-paper-scissor type combat (at least for the basic combat skills, this starts to matter less once you get more specialized skills) which would work well if the game didn't lag to ♥♥♥♥ing oblivion.
I forgot to mention the lag. Depending on the day you play, time of day, position of the sun and moon, and if your oven's clock is synced to your microwave's clock, the game can lag terribly to unplayable.
After 6 days (everyday if you are under a total level of 1000), you can rebirth and reset to level 1, but keep the progress you have made on any skills you were ranking up. This is a core aspect of the game. Optionally, you can use rebirth potions that you can buy with real life money (NX) to rebirth anytime. Eventually, you'll be level 80 after one day and have a whole 5 days to wait, wondering what the hell to do now. The game tries to keep you playing everyday with events, and opportunities to give you more ability points (what you use to rank up skills, these run out very fast).
The community is absolutely awful, since it mainly attracts weeaboos, middle schoolers, weeaboo middle schoolers, edgy middle schoolers, edgy high schoolers, people from Gaia online, and actual adults who spend way too much money on a Japanese anime life simulator. All of the above will try to prove how much better than you they are by using the classic "my damage is higher than yours" reason. Although this doesn't really change the fact that you are both playing a Chinese timesink.
One thing I do like about this game is it's NPC art. Not the graphics themselves, but the little portraits that appear when you talk to NPCs. Also there's cute waifus which is VERY nice. The music is ok, some pieces are actually pretty good. But one of the things that attracted me to this game originally was the fact that there are musical instruments in the game, and you can compose songs using MML (Music Macro Language). Eventually, everyone just ends up playing Naruto openings, Bleach openings, Mario, Pirates of the Caribbean, Zelda, Skyrim, Carameldansen, Power Rangers, and other songs you've heard to death.
The skill ranking system goes from rank F - A, then from 9 - 1. Getting some skills to from rank F to rank 1 can take either a day, or a few months. You spend AP, or ability points, to rank up these skills. Some skills will take about 60 AP to get from rank 2 to rank 1, and that's not including all the other ranks before that. The main reason for rebirths is to get more AP for your skills, which to why you keep coming back to this Taiwanese basketweaving tutorial.
The quests are ok, I guess.
This game is ok, I guess. Play it if you have a few hundred-thousand hours to waste. It's easier with friends.
Fun, funny and exciting game. Would recommend for anyone with a spare $5. Or just anyone who wants some fun with friends and players online. :)

Estranged: Act I
A free first person adventure game powered by the HalfLife 2 Engine. Correction, a Free First person Survival Horror game. The reason I corrected myself is, before I downloaded Estranged, I was under the impression it was going be one of those first person interactive stories.
Well, I was wrong.
Basic story is, you receive a distress call on your boat. Something about they" have taken over the island. NExt thing you know you are floating in the water looking at your boat on fire right next to shore. From then you travel inland learning the jump, sprint, push, throw and other commands. The story progresses as you met a man who seemingly just murdered three people. He gives you his gun and away you go again.
The atmosphere is eery and the sound a little jumpy. I unlocked my first achievement (yes this has achievements.. doesn't everything now?) when I found the lightswitch for a lamp in one of the cabins I came across. A moment later is where I came across my first Zombie. Equipped with glowing eyes and running full speed at me.
This game requires a little bit of thinking to get past each area. There is a barrier and you have to examine the scene and determine what is missing. Once you figure it, usually by interacting with the environment or placing an object in a certain place or pattern you can move on.
I eventually got stuck. About eight Zombies at once attacked me. I killed all but one when I ran out of ammo. I was able to evade him but couldn't find out where to go so eventually gave up.
The AI isn't too bright. One of the Zombies ran straight into a train and died. It wasn't as cool as it sounds though. The train wasn't moving.
The game is free so I do recommend giving it a try just don't have high expectations.

The dungeon's difficulty increases exponentially. The first maybe two dungeons you could do on your own, but anything after is nearly impossible without a party. Also the inventory idea in this game is terrible. You have like 100 inventory space in your bag. Tht doesn't sound too bad right? Think again. The Items aren't limited to one inventory space, so I often have to throw things away just to get my reward for my quest. This feature does make the game more realistic, but it makes the game feel less and less fun. The storyline is pretty good, but it is hard to follow, because you have to complete a dungeon to get to the next storypoint. And as I mentioned earlier, you just can't solo it. This game does have many problems, but I would definitely recommend playing it.

Like most of the reviews here. I am one of those who played before Mabinogi entered steam, and just as what others mention, this game really is one of a kind. I'd be tragic if Mabinogi ever died.
I don't remember the exact year when I started playing, but there only used to be three or four classes you could pick, being the typical around MMOs, Mage, Melee, and the Archer classes.
The community, I also found to be as good as family. Like most others, I also wish we could still be in contact, because of how such an amazing time we had merely just socializing. The best part is, that you can actually start a family by getting married and adopt others. "Living the fantasy life" just as they say.
Being unique is also a very major thing they worked well on. Having the exact same clothes, with the exact same colour, is even more rear to find than in real life. But I happen to be lucky enough to get the majority of my clothes that I buy at the time to be themed Yellow and White, giving my own signiture no matter how much time passes.
The major parts in customization would be the absurd amount of clothes they have available to sell. While some are very high price, nice clothes can still be bought at a decent or rather generous price for their beautiful, impressive, or complex design.
While I can understand the complexity it takes to upgrade the graphics and having to almost completely rebuild the game to impove the travel and combat system, as well as the general animations for the envioment interaction. I find the lacking of these improvements really bothered me, even when I continued to play frequently, or when I return every couple of times. It really annoyed me when I get stuck in complex or tight spaces, like in small stores, or between trees, when chopping for some wood, and having to click a lot to get out. I like how the designs are improving, but because of the old age of the game with it's unimproved flaws, it really sets me back on how much more I can actually enjoy it. But I guess that makes it classic.
Still to this day, the combat system is a bit lacking, but it's very unique, being able to approach combat with different tactics and styles. Especially over time when they began to implement much more unique ways for combat that are not found in many other MMOs.
The thing I love the most about the combat system, is that you don't have to stick to your class all the time and could use a mix of skills, hybridizing any skills you decide to build on your character, beaing able to master all classes and obtaining hybrid titles to prove your skills.
There are times when people mention how bad I am at building my skills, especially when contributing to melee even though I'm an elf. At first combat was really hard for me, being an elf was really being like a glass cannon, having impressive magical and archery power, but heavily lacks on the armour and defence department.
Until you manage to get stronger, then even an elf, with just light armour on, could withstand just as much as humans and giants can.
But as a hybrid, I looked for more ways to withstand damage, the exciting part, is that I can actually do that. My most happiest momment is when I obtained the Mana Shield skill. Able to withstand all sorts of attacks, but the weaker the skill, the heavier burden it is to your mana pool.
Later on, with the release of a dedicated music skill set, with the already ability to write your own songs, they included skills you could use to support your team directly by improving their abilities in combat and non-combat situations, much more instruments and the ability to fight with them. Being a big musical fan at the time, I loved the update and used my instument for every close combat situation, expressing how much I love music.
At first I got into alchemey and tried to master the golem, but as it was high maintence and quite costly for long term adventuring, I dropped it for more simpler skills, but I still figured ways to reduce direct combat for my elf. Such as obtaining and training a pet. They helped me a lot in a varity of situations, such as holding my things, saving me from a group of monsters, or healing me and my party. But even when they are strong, they were not as efficent as fighting directly.
Then after a while more classes arrived in Mabinogi. The most unique and game changing for me, was the marionettes. As an elf with a weak body and the massive difference in the marionette combat style, I absolutely loved this update more than anything else and I still look back in all my adventures with my pierrot marionette when ever I think of Mabinogi.
The biggest difference in this combat style was when you equip the control rods, you could still use them like regular weapons and includes three skills you could use to bind and pull your enemies with, but the main role is to control your marionette, which you had to summon with no cost, other than actually taking care of it, had a ridiculous amount of health and defence conpairable to some or most boss grade enemies, and the combat, had their own unique damage, which mean't any enemy with any resistances will not be able to mitigate a marionette's attacks. They are also one of the few classes which has skills that can directly break through the defence skill and able to combat multiple opponents with a very large attack range. Also the stats required for marionettes are majored for Strength and Dexterity, which gave versitility for both melee, archery, and life skill majors, letting any race to be reletivly equal in terms of mastering the marionette. Using the marionette skills require stamina, but quite little compaired to most other stamina required classes, allowing for much longer combat with little worry of overspending your stamina and having to carry extra potions.
There is little negitives I have for the marionette, other than being quite slow, which gives long range enemies opprotinities to attack it, but can be overcome by walking up to them yourself and using act 1 or attacking directly. Also it has incomplete skills, or "acts" having little combat varity but it does have a very high flexability for all sorts of enemies, dispite only having six marionette skills.
All in all, I would like Mabinogi to be improved even if they have to rebuild Mabinogi, but I really would like them to keep all their content, and unique apporach to the MMO world. All the've built, really attracted and kept many people loyal to the game for a longer life span than most other MMOs.
Back then when I saw them advertise with "Live a fantasy life." I thought "What a joke!" but when I look back, it was a life totally worth living. But now that many people I know are gone, it feels really lonely. To me, making new friends got a lot harder than before. But there still are some really good people out there.

As an Early Access game, it has managed to keep my attention ever since its initial release.
The game has come a long way since its initial release, and the updates are starting to come in faster and faster. If one wants to know how far this game has come, check out videos of the original release vs the current game version (Update 18 for the time this review was written).
In terms of gameplay, here is what players can expect to see (As of Update 18):
Solid gunplay mechanics. the weapon's sights aren't "glued" to your screen, and will move around as you walk, fire, etc. (Think kind of like Red Orchestra). The weapon does reset at the centre of your screen however.
A stamina system that affects your character's accuracy as he gets tired. Stamina is drained when jogging, sprinting, and jumping. You can hear your character's breathing and when your HUD is offline, his breath will fog up the inside of the helmet.
An intuitive crouching system that allows you to change stance between a low crouch or a higher stance to shoot over low walls. Aiming down sights will also make your character peek over cover, and if you change stance while aiming, he will only bend at the knees for faster movement.
Sprint, Jog, and walk. Three movement speeds that are very useful and easy to cycle through.
Two weapons. An Assault Rifle for long range combat and an SMG for close range combat.
The ability to attach a sound suppressor to your weapon. It actually works really well in both multiplayer and co-op/single player
You can shoot out lights to create darkness in order to sneak around (Think Metro 2033/ Last Light)
Multiplayer maps will change time of day, weather, and sometimes layout as you play. Matches have a sense of unpredictability for newcomers because of this.
Three game modes to chose from: Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, and Domination.
3 campaign missions, and a few other side-missions. Currently, all missions are training excercises for your character (A new recruit to the Interstellar Marines).
HUD deactivates when you take 50% damage. This makes it hard to identify between friend and foe because IFF markers and objective markers all vanish.
I hope that this review has convinced at least one person to try out the game. Despite all the praise I'm throwing at it, note that there are many missing features in the game. The updates have been coming in more quickly recently, and a big one is apparently going to be coming in soon. So if you feel like taking a risk and betting on this extremely promising title, I highly suggest that you buy it. If you can, go for the spearhead edition to get a few extra goodies.

Gunpoint is a stealth-based puzzle-platform game.
You play as Richard Conway, a freelance spy in a noir themed world. You were in the wrong place at the wrong time, and have been framed for murder. You must go through numerous levels to find out who framed you, and clear your name.
The gameplay is great. You have a gadget called the "crosslink". It is used to rewire circuits in any way you wish. From basic changes such as making a light switch open a door, to causing an elevator to switch off the lights, making a guard walk through a booby trapped door, and having it slam in his face. The combinations are endless.
The game is very much stealth focused. Confrontation with a guard will quickly result in your death. But this does not mean you cannot sneak up on everyone and beat them to death. You can get through levels silently, with no witnesses. Or you could rush through and make sure no one is left breathing to be a witness.
You have multiple other gadgets to utilize too. Conway wears no ordinary trousers. They are spring loaded allowing him to jump great distances. His trenchcoat allows him to survive a fall from high distances. There is also an upgrade system which allows you to buy new gadgets, and improve already purchased ones.
The story is great. The dialogue is incredibly funny, and the characters brilliantly wrote. The game also has an absolutely superb soundtrack. One of my favourite in any video game. You can check it out for free
.
The average time for completion is about 2-3 hours. So if you are looking for a short game to pass time, this is definitely one to consider. With multiple dialogue options, and plenty of achievements to earn, the replayability is great too.
Gunpoint is easily my 2013 Game of the Year. I absolutely recommend this to anyone and everyone.
Edit: As of some date a few days ago, workshop has now been integrated into the game. You can now browse from hundreds of user-created levels, adding hours more fun to the game.

I'm so on the fence about whether to recommend this.  Because for those who enjoy "walking simulators," there's quite a lot to like.  Pretty scenery, nice music, interesting conversations dancing around Buddhist and Daoist ideas, locations to explore with logbooks.  Not to mention the highly unique premise of the entire game.
But the issue is in the execution.  As obviously a bit of a low budget game, it doesn't have a huge amount of landscape or texture variety.  This is a problem, because the individual areas to explore are often quite large - particularly the first area.  So after awhile, exploration starts getting to be something of a drag.  There's no map, and waypoints are nearly useless until close to the very end of the game.  So you'll do a LOT of aimless wandering in search of content through areas that can look pretty samey.  In particular, you could be looking for a LONG time to find the entrance to the final area.  The game basically gives no clues whatsoever as to its location.
Plus, the final area is just dull to explore, and it's capped off with - as others have mentioned - an utter anticlimax of an ending.  And to be clear:  I knew from the tone of the game this was not going to have some spectacular shebang for the finale.  But even *expecting* this to be a "it's not about the destination" game, it still really let me down.  Like, it's not even an ending, per se.  It doesn't end; it just *stops*.
Was that the point?  Were they going even further down the "expectation-subverting finale" rabbit hole that Gone Home and Firewatch dug, by having an outright anti-ending with no resolution whatsoever to go along with the general detached Zen-ness of it all?  I just don't know.
Since I have to click a button, I'll go ahead and give it a thumb's up since I like supporting smaller devs doing artsy games.  But I'm still not sure if I actually recommend it.

I remember finding out about this game a few months ago when the developers made a thread on reddit to show it off. I instantly fell in love with the setting, art style and exploration in the trailer, but I couldn't spare the money at the time to get it (bills and stuff). Anyways, I picked this up during the Summer Sale and was excited to finally get a crack at it. It was actually hard to decide whether to recommend this or not, because there were things I did enjoy about the game (and it kinda makes me dislike the binary rating system Steam has). Overall, though, I found myself frustrated too many times and ultimately let down at the end. If none of what I'm about to say applies to you, then go ahead and buy the game. I'm not at all saying it's a bad game (although this review will probably focus on the negatives), but I feel like it could have been much better, and for $15 I just felt four hours of sometimes-good-sometimes-bad play time wasn't worth it.
Pros:
-Colorful art style
-Relaxing soundtrack
-Thoughtful dialog (although sometimes it can drag on)
-Intriguing premise
-Unique setting (incorporites some Indian culture, which is rare in gaming)
Cons:
-The game can feel sooooo sloooow at times when you want to run and your stamina is empty
-While the premise is interesting, the ending is a huge letdown
-The world can feel empty at times
-The blessing system feels tacked on and adds no real value, making exploration feel forced just to get upgrades
When I started playing the game, I was drawn in immediately by the premise and the interesting and kind of funny fox that talks to you (I love his "voice acting", btw). You trudge along as a tired, weak old woman who can't see very well and has no idea where to go. Once the world opened up a bit more, though, the tired, weak old woman started to get a bit annoying because it could take forever to get somewhere. You have limited stamina, and while you can eat fruit to help it regenerate faster, much of the game just felt like a stamina-management simulator. And when you run out of stamina, be prepared for the slowest walk ever. Now, this wouldn't be a problem if you were walking down a corridor in a linear game and the whole point was to take in the surroundings, but a huge part of this game is traversing the world and finding what you can, whether it's items, NPC's, books, or wayshrines. You can even upgrade your stamina bar later in the game, but that just means it takes even longer for it to refill. I honestly would have enjoyed the game a lot more if could just run from the start and play at your own pace.
That leads me to another problem--the game also would have been better if you just had all blessings available at the start. There's no real feeling of accomplishment or value by upgrading them, it just feels "gamey." If you compare it to a Zelda game, for example, most of the upgrades have a real purpose. They make you feel stronger, they help progress the story, and they ultimately power you up enough to beat the final boss. Getting a new item/ability in Zelda feels amazing, like you truly achieved something. Almost all of the blessings in this game felt like a way to ease some of the annoyances I had. Good, now I can run longer without having to stop and trudge along or search for fruit. Good, now I can walk on water so I won't drown. Good, now I won't die from sliding down a mountain. Only maybe 1 or 2 are necessary, the rest are just like, "why couldn't I do that in the first place?"
Another (minor) problem I had was that the world felt kind of empty at times. The fox (I can't remember how to spell his name, something like Dhiyonisis) was an interesting and colorful character, but he was really the only one. You can unlock blessings to read books and wayshrines, and to talk to random spirits, but they don't fill out the world enough. If there were more fleshed out characters like the fox, it would have given the game much more character and made the journey feel less empty. This wasn't a huge problem, but I did notice it more than a couple times.
Before I get to the ending, I do want to touch on the things I enjoyed about the game. As I said, it's not a bad game at all, and it did do some things well. The art style is colorful and pretty, and the relaxing soundtrack fits it perfectly. I also liked the design of the areas; even though they were empty, they had a "somebody once lived here" feeling to them which was cool. I especially liked the dialog between the old woman and the fox, with his vague but wise comments and her reactions to him. Another thing I liked was the squint mechanic, especially at the start. In the first area (before I found a compass), I was feeling lost and directionless. Then I remembered I could squint, so I found a high place, looked off into the distance and saw a couple important looking places that rose up above the fog. After that, I was able to figure out where to go next without any trouble. It felt rewarding because I was able to overcome the old woman's weak vision by using a natural mechanic to my advantage.
OK, so now on to the ending (minor spoilers ahead). Honestly, I feel like I would have recommended this game, even with the complaints I had above, if it had a decent ending. Sadly, it didn't. In fact, it didn't really have much of an ending at all. It just...ended. The game (mostly through the fox) unravels an interesting premise, and I was excited to see how it would turn out. Would the old woman get her wish? Would the fox turn into something (or someone)? What would the Avatar of Death (who looked really cool) end up doing to you? But nothing really happens. Game over, credits roll. Look, I'm one of those "the journey is more important than the destination" people when it comes to storytelling, so I can usually shrug off endings that other people have problems with (like the endings of Lost or The Dark Tower series). But this ending was basically "all that stuff you learned about along the way? Not gonna happen, now close your eyes so we can roll the credits." I don't know what happened with the writing, but man, that was a letdown. Anything would have been better than that.
With all that said, I will still gladly check out the next game this team makes. There were some stumbles in The Wild Eternal, but I think they have their heads in the right places, and they did give a unique experience that was occasionally beautiful and occasionally thought-provoking. I just wish they wouldn't have added in "gamey" collectables/upgrades that really only helped ease frustration, had a good ending, and filled out the world a bit more with unique characters. But if none of the complaints I had with this game apply to you, then feel free to check it out.

I’ve always had a bit of a soft spot for cute story worlds with dark, mysterious undertones - and Poncho here is no exception! It’s a pixelated post-apocalyptic perspective-based puzzle-platformer (try and say that without spitting everywhere) set in the overgrown ruins of a futuristic dystopia. All assemblance of animal life is missing. Even the tiny snails lurching along the stalks of pixelated grass are entirely robotic. The machines have taken over and formed a society of their own. But, much like an allegory for the current decline of the mobile games industry, a society cannot function on shameless cloning and metric data alone. The machines lack the human quality to innovate and evolve and subsequently digress into small tribes of nomads. Now they wander the earth, falling apart, cursed by their own immortality as the last computerized image of a human face slowly decays from their rusting harddrives. Into this bleak arena steps Poncho, a small blue mini-fridge with a tablecloth stuck in his door, on a quest to find the illusive creator and restore humanity to its former glory.
Poncho plays like a condensed version of Fez, another pixelated perspective-based puzzle-platformer (spit spit), but unlike Fez, the developer of Poncho hasn’t been ostracized from the internet for declaring war on his critics, playerbase and youtube lets-players; so pre-emptive brownie points for you, Delve Interactive! To contrast the mechanics of Fez, instead of spinning the entire world around on axis, Poncho exists within 3 or 4 two-dimensional ‘layers’ in the background and foreground, allowing the player to platform jump between them in order to collect keys and shiny red floating sweeties. This makes for some mind-bending exploration puzzles when the platforms are static, but it becomes downright infuriating when the platforms start to move a few levels in. Not the standard left-to-right floating platforms most gamers have become accustomed to. The floating platforms in Poncho shift through every dimensional layer within the Z-axis of the gamespace.
This led to multiple situations where I would mistime a jump, land on a platform, only to have the existential rug ripped out from under my feet, or worse - get blindsided in mid-air by a shifting platform as it suddenly occupied the same space as Poncho, smashing the last hope for humanity into quantum glitch soup. The constant shifts between orthographic and perspective views can give the player a rather sketchy view of where they reside spatially. Luckily, Poncho has opted for the Super Meat Boy school of design in that the time between ‘death’ and respawn is almost instantaneous. It's difficult without being punishing.
However, Poncho isn’t all about the platform dimension jumping. There is also quite a strong focus on exploring the open world and being able to come back to any level during the game to collect any keys, sweeties or powerups that you may have missed. Boasting an ‘open world exploration’ element in a game like this is usually shorthand for back-tracking. Fortunately, the level design is fairly tight and succinct, meaning that the player doesn’t have to retread too much ground in order to reach new heights -unlike Fez, where the landscape was so vast and complex that my desire to explore it would evaporate almost immediately. Poncho does its best to keep the next little shiny red breadcrumb always in sight of the player, giving them a firm idea of areas they haven’t explored yet. There are also a couple of fun secrets and easter eggs to keep the completionists checking under every rock!
As a whole, I found Poncho surfing the knife-edge between challenge and controller-smashing frustration. If you fudge a jump, it’s your fault for not thinking ahead X amounts of steps. Perhaps this will amalgamate to that wonderful ‘good’ kind of frustrating which will keep more determined players slogging away until they get it right. But what really sold me on Poncho is the charm of the characters within. It’s show-don’t-tell for the most part, which intrigues me to improve my platforming skill if only to reveal a little bit more of the world!
So if you have a high tolerance for MeatBoy-esque difficulty and enough spare controllers and keyboards to justify hurling a few against the wall, love cute colourful storyworlds and little robot folk, Poncho is for you. For this is the way the world ends. Not with a bang, but a whimper ... as the player misses a platform jump for the umpteen-billionth time.

I hesitate to thumbs-up this game because not everyone will experience the same catharsis as I, and others who've reviewed this game have. Before I go further, I'll say I'm a sucker for interesting art styles and good music. The reviews on Proteus and the Summer Steam Sale convinced me it was time to give it a go. I smoked, fired up Steam, and embarked on my journey into Proteus.
I was delighted with every little creature I came across. Some animals were recognizable, others were alien to me. Each creature emanated its own ethereal melody; not a single bit of negativity to be seen. The pixelated art encouraged me to use my imagination to fill in the blanks--
, if you will. Before long, I began to feel the anxiety of having no objectives, or even a button to interact with my surroundings, creep into my psyche. But when I found a group of singing pink mushrooms that popped down into the earth at my approach, only to pop back up nearby, I was satisfied to just experience the land. It became refreshing to not have to put forth effort to have a lovely experience, like receiving a massage. As for the circle of mysterious stone statues, the gravestones littering the land, the cabin in the woods, or the mother tree at the foot of the mountain...the lore behind them was whatever I want it to be. I learned to be
in the moment.
This game reminded me a bit of Flower, the game that many folks insisted was not a game, but more of a toy. But the message behind Flower is the same I received from Proteus; sit back, relax, experience, and do or don't do whatever you like.
My only frustration with this game is the mouse sensitivity. Even turned all the way up, I would have to lift my mouse up off the mousepad at least 10-20 times to turn around and go back the way I came. It definitely fudged with the flow of the game and introduced frustration where there had previously been calm delight. At times, I was so annoyed that I wanted to put the game down, but wanted to see it through to the end--and there IS an end.
I can see many traditional hardcore gamers getting frustrated with this game. Many might perceive it as empty, devoid of any sense of accomplishment or productivity, with the beautiful art and lilting music being small compensation for the cost. Unfortunately, I think a large majority of gamers simply won't want to find the headspace to enjoy this game to its fullest, hence my hesitation to recommend it. If you can read the reviews and know Proteus is your cup of tea, buy it, mate! If you're still cautious, wait for it to go on sale and buy it for a few bucks.

I recommend Wild Eternal to anyone looking for an exploration and story driven game with a little bit of “leveling up” (as in you can trade tributes for skills like better jump in order to reach new areas).

A hard one to really call here, as the base gameplay that's present and the unique gameplay mechanic of going into the foreground/background does make a game that's appealing on the surface. It's got the presentation down: despite it being another pixel platformer, the use of that aforementioned background/foreground goes a long way, and helps create an experience that many may not have seen before. It definitely provides good puzzle based elements to the game to complement it's mechanics, and it can be great for those liking exploration elements and “collectathons” with having to find elements. What drags the game down however is what causes the negative elements in the game: The checkpoint system, and vertical level designs. This game has a high frustration factor, which is compounded by several little problems that forces you to re-do large sections over and over again in the worst way. Checkpoints are based on time on platforms, and it shows lots of flaws as opposed to a generic checkpoint system because of it. In addition, the gameplay causes inconsistencies with times where you have no idea how to get through a section, and having to wait for platforms to get into place for large amounts of time. The negatives are what's going to make/break the game for you: it broke it for me as it caused too many problems for me as a whole. But if you can tolerate it, you've got an experience that is worth your time.

This game is... Something else.
I don't know how many hours I have in it, nearing or past 100, but oh Lord do I have stories to tell, just to make sure you get it.
Let's just do one, and it involves the wonderful, wondeful plague.
I started with 3 colonists in a mountainous area, and I dug into a nearby hill. Standard opening for a mountain base. Made a barracks outside for the first month, and had them grow food, again, standard.
And it continued standard through the first 2 or 3 raids, my colony grew from 3 to 7, and it was named Karimi, under the Treaty of Wakarmath. Then, 3 of my colonists got infected with the Plauge. My construction master, Slag, my negotiator, Kelley, and one of the newer colonists, the Animal master Pyromaniac, Madcat. I had my healer, Crane, ready to treat them in the old barracks-turned-hospital, since 8 or so bedrooms were made in the mountainside.
What the colony didn't account for, however, was the Chemically Interested, Pyromaniacal Madcat to go on a series of binges and fire starting sprees that had to have our main fighter, Ryknyk at the time, arrest him 4 times. Then 5. Then, after he was being treated by Crane, Ryknyk got the plague. Sent to the hospital, Crane treated her, and she died within the hour due to a heart attack at the age of 40. Slag and Kelley also died, though no one except Kelley's husband took notice. Madcat was the only survivor. But he was still showing symptoms of the plauge, and at one point, he was fed up. He got up from his hospital bed, and set fire to the Barracks. The only ones who had a chance at stopping this were the animals, but they burned in his flames.
Madcat himself ran to the beds again, and died from the Plague. His damage, however, was done. The Barracks, housing the prison, hospital, and leisure room, was gone, and the fire was spreading into the wood-panneled mountainside.
2 colonists were left, Crane, a healer who could fight fires with  a crew, and Anderson, another Pyromaniac.
Crane died, and Anderson "fell" into the flames.
Game Over.
However, looking back, there are about 15 things I could have done better to not have it be game over, which is what I love about this game. You can tell these dark, horrible tales, sometimes halarious, and there will be always something for the teller to learn about in the future.

Well, I'm about 64 hours past the 1,100 hour intro, and I'm really starting to enjoy the game when they go and change everything! Now it's much more newbie-friendly and accessable, so I can't enjoy endless weeks of slaving over a 24-hour max skill queue...
On a more serious note, it's not a first-person cockpit experience like Elite: Dangerous. This is a great game if you want a true social MMO experience with beautiful effects and systems. You can get into mining for profit if you are naturally gifted at staring at rocks for hours on end (or employ chemical help). You can troll the everliving hell out of other players, for profit, and not be at risk of being banned (as long as it's all in-game and not real life stuff).
The true strength comes from the game's PVP and Industry structures, imo. These are the aspects that this game does well and does unlike any other MMO. The sheer options of PVP available (fleet combat, sov combat, gate camping, interdiction, seige fleets, small roam fleets, cloaked bomber fleets...) will give you no end to how to mix it up.
One last thing: If you want to give this game a solid shot, plan on taking at least 2 months to really feel it all out. There are tons of new player corps around that are willing to guide you along!

Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 Full Burst is the update release of Ninja Storm 3 and it's a fighting game with some RPG elements that follows closely the story of the second part of the Naruto Shippuden manga series till its most recent chapters.
The main beef of the game is its story mode: you can do some free roaming in the world of Naruto while taking part in the most important battles from the series, collect items and clear some side quests too. In story mode there are either normal battles or boss battles, with unusually strong opponents who need advanced strategies and some QTEs to be defeated. The RPG elements of Ninja Storm 3 comes into play regarding some "ultimate decisions" you can make in certain battles (which can change the way some encounters are played) and the items you can equip and use in battle (some of them being able to heal you, others to boast your stats, others to depower your opponent, ...). The game follows the series' main plot very closely, sometimes even expanding upon some specific events (and always for the better). The only downside of the story mode is the enemies AI, which leaves them wide open to exploits, making several battles rather easy (with the exception of later bosses).
Ninja Storm 3 is a solid fighting game with some unique and interesting features: you can use a substitution technique in battle to escape an opponent's attack and get him easily (althought the technique works only with a set of charges that aren't always ready); you can summon a maximum of two supporting characters to either protect you, attack your enemy or pull of powerful combination moves; you can use ultimate awakening modes if low on health to gain the upper hand.
Ninja Storm 3 features also a multiplayer battle mode and a free battle mode, which are made very entertaining by the high number of playable characters and combinations of them you can make.
The Full Burst expansion comes with updated graphics, a challenge mode that requires you to beat a series of battles with specific conditions and a short new bonus story chapter, "Brothers reunited", which pits you against a new bonus boss, Sage Kabuto.
Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 Full Burst is both a great game for Naruto fans (who will surely appreciate its many details coming from the series proper) and an entertaining title for who is just looking for a fun fighting game

I like that the blue on friendly armor  is all that differentiates your teammates from your enemies when you are lacking a HUD. Gunpoint: A game of stealth, sneaking, tricking people, and intriguing, yet still humorous dialog!
Gunpoint is a stealth puzzle game that lets you rewire its levels to trick people. You play a freelance spy who takes jobs from his clients to break into high security buildings and steal sensitive data. It's 9:99$ on steam, and is about 0.5GB if you care about those types of things.
As you continue on through the game, the levels get progressively harder and harder, it's not a bad thing at all. It gives a nice little easy time for the first bit of the game, but the more and more you continue on, it starts to become challenging, making you use your brain to solve puzzles, rewire different contraptions around the buildings, and finding different ways to knock the cops and their agents out through various different solutions
Pro's to the game:
It's EXTREMELY easy to run on your computer, (My old computer ran it on high settings.) the graphic style is cartoony, and is appealing to the eyes
The Gameplay is very smooth, controls are simple yet still efficient. As the old saying goes "If it ain't broke, don't fix it."
As I said earlier, the Dialog is witty, sarcastic, but still tells a story in the artform of gaming, even if it is just finding out random things about random people.
Con's to the game:
The game is short, like, REALLY short. If you have a good 2 hours of time to yourself, and you know what you're doing, boom. Good going, you can complete the game in that long.
The replay-ability all relies on if you enjoy seeing how fast you can beat a short game (I've beaten one of my favorite games in less than 2 hours.) So if you're like me in that sense, or you wanna make sure you've gotten 100% on the game, like I did.
The is in-between too pricey, and too little. It all depends on what you think of it. They do have a demo though, if you wanna try it.

Things I wish Telltale would improve in future releases:
Graphic Engine:  I think it’s about time they did a total overhaul for their graphic engine. While they argue it’s being constantly worked on I keep seeing the same issues on every game, random flickering, texture pop ins and out… that kind of stuff totally breaks your immersion.
Less QTEs, more puzzles: I’m sad to see how they keep replacing puzzles with more and more QTEs. They are not bad but they do get pretty annoying after a while.
Illusion of Choice: Telltale has become pretty good at giving you the illusion of choice, I think most people agree that they would like their choices to have more impact on the story.
Now, on to the actual game: Tales from the Borderlands is my favorite Telltale Game so far. They took the borderlands universe and told a pretty compelling story that actually made me care for things the main game didn’t before, so heads up and prepare for a fun ride, cowboy *points finger guns at you*

Cosas que Telltale debería mejorar en un futuro:
Motor Gráfico: Me encanta el estilo artístico de Telltale, pero si algo claro esta es que necesita un cambio radical en su motor gráfico. En cada uno de sus juego se puede ver como hay parpadeos aleatorios, texturas que aparecen y desaparecen y otros bugs gráficos que en ocasiones destruyen por completo la inmersión en la historia.
Menos QTEs, más acertijos: Es triste ver que con cada juego nuevo los acertijos disminuyen para incluir a cambio más QTEs, ¡no más por favor!
Ilusión de Elección: La queja principal, Telltale es bastante bueno haciéndote creer que tus elecciones tienen peso pero al final del día suelen ser bastante efímeras.
Ahora, hablando del juego en sí, Tales from the Borderlands es fácilmente mi juego favorito de esta compañía, tomaron el universo de Borderlands y con el crearon una historia más interesante que la de los juegos principales.
