I really, REALLY wanted to like this game. Hell, it was a new Piranha Bytes release, and I LOVE these devs. However, I'm not sure what's going on with them after seeing this. Sadly, I would have taken more consideration into pre-ordering it had I known what Risen 2 ended up being, as PB in my opinion has had a relatively solid track record with their games, with titles that were at least good enough for me to pitch in and support them, and that's saying something in most cases.
I've been a Piranha Bytes fan to the core when it comes to their RPGs since I had the manual dexterity to use a keyboard, and Gothic was actually my first RPG experience. Even to this day, I have a hard time finding games in the RPG sector that manage to captivate me as much as G1 and G2 did.
However, this isn't a Gothic 1 or Gothic 2 review. This is a Risen 3 review, so let's get on with it.
What really ruined it for me:
The Combat
-   -   -   -   -   -
This was the first thing I noticed when I began playing the game, and I have to say PB fell flat on their face with this one. First and foremost, the main character has about as much ability in using a sword as a dead cat, and he's about as stalwart as one, too. His attacks have an atrocious wind up that make even the simplest combat situations into an ordeal of timing and hoping the enemies don't hit you first, which brings me to my next subject: Enemies have NO WIND UP to balance this out. Just about everything you encounter and fight in the game will attack you relentlessly and without any kind of delay, meaning that if you go in and swing at the enemy, they can just attack and interrupt you, doing damage and bringing you back to square one. Oh, and that's another thing. EVERYTHING, and I mean EVERYTHING stuns your character. Tiny♥♥♥♥♥beach insect thing? (I still have yet to understand those creatures.) Yeah, their tiny attack will stagger your character the same way you'd expect him to if he got clocked upside the head by Chuck Liddell.
As a whole, this results in an absolutely infuriating combat experience that was one of the main reasons I had to put the game down for good. It's completely unbearable, and frankly I've come to expect far more from these developers.
Now, I know, I've seen it everywhere. People could say that Gothic's combat was just as awful, if not worse, but there's a key difference there: Gothic's combat is anything but horrible, for one. If anything, it's about all you should expect from an RPG from around the year 2000; on the other hand, this game from 2015 manages to have combat that, unlike Gothic, doesn't just take a bit of time to get a hang of, but instead is completely impossible to work with and that, in my opinion, makes the experience null and void. I even used cheats to increase my combat skill in hopes of making my character's attacks worthwhile, and even THIS did absolutely nothing whatsoever.
In terms of major flaws, this really is the only one, and it manages to be so outstandingly, so GLORIOUSLY bad that the game is completely ruined by it.
Now, the game has some things that I like about it, namely the fact that it really does feel like a Piranha Bytes game still. The dialogue, characters, world, and music all still make me feel like I'm playing a good old PB game, but once I get into a fight I simply can't force myself to get through the whole thing.
Now, for an open recommendation for the developers and a closing statement:
You clever ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s have given me gaming experiences throughout my entire life, and I absolutely adore you all for it. I've often burst out in laughter from the Hero's dialogue options and an NPC's response, as well as the numerous easter eggs and goodies you leave lying around. This, just as often as I've have slammed my fist down on my desk in frustration from the challenging and punishing, yet rewarding combat experience, but this game hardly managed to do any of that for me, as the whole thing was sadly cut short by its one fatal flaw.
When I say this next bit, I want you guys to know (and this goes to other readers as well) that I'm not just putting on the nostalgia blinders; I just know a working formula when I see it.
Hypothetically, if you lot made another RPG, regardless of if it's Risen or something new entirely, and you used the same formula for G1 and G2 (here's where you could call me out on nostalgia blindness, if it weren't for the fact that an overwhelming number of your fans will show agreement) and adapted it for a modern market, using a newer engine with better graphics and the like, it would probably end up being another great installment; and, when I say 'formula' I'm talking about everything that made the first two Gothic games what they were, from the controls to the stats. Hell, you could make it on the old G2 engine and it'd probably still be great, but if there's one thing I'll admit, it's that the controls, while not inherently bad and not in need of outright change, could definitely use a tune up to make it feel a bit more fluid and responsive.
At this point, I doubt anything in the paragraph above will happen, but I do sincerely believe it'd do the team a lot better than what they're going with as of now. Some things don't need to change, and it really does seem like the games started going downhill once the controls went through the big overhaul they did starting with Gothic 3, which changed the other two games' main control drawback of being somewhat stiff at times and generally feeling rather old-school to making the whole thing just feel outright clumsy. Risen 3 seems to have marked the apex of this clumsiness, and it's so atrocious that I couldn't even recommend this to my worst enemy.
Hopefully this review shed some light for players on the fence about getting it and why I sincerely believe they should just go to GOG and buy one of the Gothic games instead. (It's probably obvious which two I recommend.) If you can be a proper human and adapt to the controls that are most definitely different from what most are accustomend to, you'll find what is an experience that is worlds better than what this title provides, and possibly one that you may find unforgettable.

Putrefaction is a first person shooter game. It's not too bad; somewhat reminiscent of a 1990s game of Doom. It's not fantastic, but it's quite ok to play.
You are deep in a laboratory facility, with the intent of investigating the outbreak of a disease, but you end up fighting off hordes of horrible mutants instead (my initial investigation of the facility lasted about a minute, the rest of the time was spent being attacked by mutants, or walking around being scared of being attacked by mutants).
As someone who doesn't like horror movies (and therefore never watches horror movies), I think that this game had a bigger impact upon me than it would upon someone who loves horror films and is therefore inured to the genre (of course, it could be that someone who loves horror movies has something a bit psychologically wrong with them in the first place).
The ambience of Putrefaction is quite good; the confined darkened corridors, the spooky music, and the monsters all add up to a "perfect storm" of heart-pumping action (although, bear in mind that it looks like a 1990s-style game).
I must admit that, when I was attacked for the first time by one of the second type of mutants, who was skittering along the ground towards me (and therefore I didn't see him straight away, until he was almost in my face), his initial attack elicited an involuntary "F**k me!" from my lips (this is coming from someone who doesn't like to swear, and who tries to avoid doing so).
Each time I walked through a doorway into a new area of the underground complex and a "Game saved" message appeared upon the screen, I though "Oh no!", because I knew I was going to be attacked by yet another horde of mutants.
My only real gripes about the game were:
1) It doesn't tell you what the controls are; you have to figure them out for yourself. However, they are the standard FPS WASD type of controls, so it should only take an experienced gamer a few seconds to work them out.
2) You can't change the controls.
3) You can't save the game. However, it does auto-save when you enter into new areas.
As an aside, I thought that the music was very well done, and possibly outshined all of the other elements of the game.
It's only $5 on Steam, so it's not a bad price (and if you buy it when it's on special, then even better).
It might not exactly be my cup of tea, but it is well-made (albeit, 1990s style).
If you like horror games or fighting mutants, then this game would be worth getting.

If you enjoyed the Gothic franchise, you're going to love this game.
I won't lie to you and say it has the best graphics for its time, because it doesn't. They're mediocre at best.
The voice acting is some of the worst I've seen since Daikatana.
The combat is a bit clunky, but once you understand the subtle nuances of timed combat, and learn the patterns of the different enemies, it's actually quite enjoyable.
The story is alright; with better voice acting it might even be pretty good.
Here's the thing, though... This is basically Gothic 3 (without the awful frames / freezing bug), except you're a pirate. There aren't a lot of games like that out there. Additionally, the sea combat is wonderful. If you don't really enjoy the genre, this game isn't going to be for you. However, if you love this sort of game - your elder scrolls, your gothics (before 4), or earlier Risen titles - this game is going to be a blast. It's very open in that it doesn't force you to visit places in a set order. You can go just about anywhere right from the start, and the different gameplay styles and factions give it a fair amount of replayability. Overall, I'd give this game a 3/5. For me personally, though, it's a 5/5. It just comes down to what you're into and what you're willing to put up with.

Great game with some flaws, still these don't prevent it from being second to Budokai Tenkaichi 3 in terms of the best Dragon Ball game.
If you want an arcade mode only where you just collect hundreds of characters (dozens, just repeated versions of the same), and all you do is fight, then this might not be the Dragon Ball game you are looking for.
Xenoverse expands the fighting genre conventions, adding many features that would make any fighting game a better game. From the freedom it allows you when creating you character's fighting style, to the many activities and types of missions you can play on your own, with friends, against them, or even with total strangers. Playing with friends is a literal Blast.
At first seems simple and botton mashy, but there is a deep combat system to master, and the fighting feels just as good as it did in Budokai Tenkaichi 3, but way more varied and thoughtful. Also there are tons of unlockables, and when you create a new character all skills and gear is shared, so you dont have to grind back again for "that rare skill" you really need. In terms of lasting appeal, you really do get your money's worth.
In other parts the game feels a bit rushed sadly, small details, like Saiyan hairs don't spike up when transforming, to bigger ones like the block being a total unresponsive joke for the most part. To solve that, just play crazy offensive, and you won't need to block anyways.
I say is the second best Dragon Ball ever, and the first Dragon Ball game in history to run at 60fps.

Quick Summary: Third Person shooter/platformer with somewhat clunky controls (if you use keyboard + mouse) and not too much depth. It’s still fun and challenging though, so it’s worth playing through. If you have a mediocre computer like me, you might want to artificially cap the frame rate (using your video card settings) since the game will try to run at as high an fps as possible and heat up your video card.
You play Spencer, a “bionic commando” pulled out of prison many years after the events of the original Nintendo game from the 1980’s (imprisoned for murdering all the bad guys). In this version of the future, many soldiers who have lost limbs in combat have been outfitted with cybernetic “upgrades” turning them into super soldiers, kind of like the Deus Ex games. Due to the threat of super soldiers running around, bionic upgrades have been banned, and a lot of soldiers have been forced to give up their arms and legs, leading to bad blood between the government and some very dangerous people. In this sequel, a terrorist group called BioReign has attacked a city and it’s your job to go in and discover what they want while killing everyone in your way.
You control Spencer in third person perspective and with the aid of your bionic arm, you can swing around like Spider-man. Seriously you can swing from pole to pole or wall to wall just like the recent Spider-man games (Shattered Dimensions, Ultimate Spider-man, and Web of Shadows). This makes it a lot easier to get from place to place once you master the timing and aiming required to swing across the battlefield without ever touching the floor. Unlike Spider-man, you actually need to aim where to grapple. That arm of yours is also your best weapon since it can snag enemies and throw them around, or just punch them in the face.  You can kill any basic enemy in the game with 2 punches.
As for gunplay, you have a basic pew pew gun with lots of ammo, but the secondary guns (shotgun, sniper rifle, rocket launcher, etc.) are all extremely limited in ammo. You cannot pick up guns dropped by your enemies and they rarely drop any useful ammo. You can only get more ammo by picking up a new gun from drop pods that land near you (especially in boss fights). Because of this gun scarcity, you need to get used to using your melee punch and grapple slam.  I didn’t realize until about 75% through the game how easy it is to pull in enemies and throw them at other guys. You’ll barely need your guns after that unless you get swarmed or need to fight heavy cyber gorilla dudes.
Pros:
+Decent graphics and an okay story. The visuals for the characters faces aren’t that good, but the gameplay visuals are well done in the ruined city, as you would expect from a modern console port.
+A few challenging boss fights to test your reflexes.
Cons:
-This is a console port, and even if you use keyboard + mouse, the on screen directions are for an xbox controller. This can be a problem during the quick time events if you’re not used to playing with a controller. It can also take some time to get used to the swinging mechanic. The arm’s grapple range is a little difficult to estimate at times, so you’ll be falling to your doom a few times.
-The game uses a checkpoint system, and the checkpoints are farther apart than I’m used to. There are a number of action sequences where you’ll die and think “wtf, I have to do the whole thing over?” Fortunately, I realized about halfway through the game that you don’t actually have to fight most of the enemies. The game doesn’t have “experience” or money so there’s no real reason that you need to kill everyone. Some places have doors that won’t unlock unless everyone’s dead though.
Overall the game is not bad, but it could have been a lot better. It’s not that good as a shooter, and the swinging portions can be annoying where you’ll swear you should have grappled but still fall to your death.

There I am, bored on a Friday night, browsing through my product queue on a whim. Suddenly, I stumble across The Wild Eternal, a game that seems to be exactly up my alley - it appears to be all about exploring an interesting world, and it instantly catches my eye. One impulse buy and half an hour or so of extremely-slow-internet download time later, and I'm ready to start the game. I make myself a cup of tea, grab a quick snack, and get ready to dive in.
The tea remained practically untouched for the rest of the night.
Within the first fifteen minutes of getting into the game, and being somewhat coldly greeted by my new guide, the Avatar of Dreams, I was transported into a far-away world - a world of vibrantly-colored, beautifully stylized, and strangely ethereal landscapes, with the slightest sense of danger lingering behind every hill and around every tree hiding within the fog. I found myself searching for many things: Aum's Tears, which would allow me to open portals to new locales; magical Shrines, which could offer me blessings to make me more powerful over the course of the game, and the Tributes I needed to offer in exchange; and even just new, cryptic conversations with the strange fox-shaped demigod that the Avatar of Death coerced me into helping.
The visual style of the game is absolutely superb, and it creates the perfect atmosphere. It's stylized enough to not appear all that dangerous initially, but then one discovers the hidden threats lurking within the fog - everything ranging from falling to your death to drowning in deep rivers to being stalked, chased and devoured by any number of dangerous beasts. The music perfectly complements the sense of mystery, which at first seems mostly innocent, but grows increasingly suspenseful and mysterious the further you descend into the depths of the fog-covered wildernesses.
If even
of what I've so far described in this review sounds appealing, or gives you the slightest shiver down your spine as you think about it, this is
the game for you. I went into this game barely knowing what to expect beyond "explore the foggy wilderness with your talking fox-buddy", and came out
to explore more of this surreal world and learn more about its inhabitants and history.
if you'll excuse me, I have to get back to my third consecutive playthrough in the last three days.
What isn't there to love? DLC is a must of course, but other tha`n that, replayability and hours of fun are definitely yours to have.

I'd be lying if I said I don't enjoy this game, but I'd also be lying if I said I love this game.
Bionic Commando is a sequel to the original NES game (or Rearmed which was made to bring the younger generation up to speed and you totally play that one) that starts Nathan Spencer being called to do a mission after being imprison for years and Bionics are shunned. The story is pretty samey to a lot of other story: There's a macguffin you need to get, your characters a bitter hardass while mission control snarks at you and you need to complete your mission against an army of Not-Nazis and save the world. Of course that's not EXACTLY the story but that's what I felt as a good summary. Spencer comes off as an♥♥♥♥♥compared to his radical self in the original and Rearmed (with good reason but still) and Super Joe shows up but he's an♥♥♥♥♥as well. The entire universe of Bionic Commando got a lot grittier in this one, and while it's not a huge deal for me, when I keep hearing swearing during gameplay I get the feeling it's trying too hard to be mature rather than just letting it come out on its own.
The gameplay it rather abstract but nice. Swinging around feels pretty good (though it says ♥♥♥♥ you physics) and you can grab onto almost anything you can think of on the environment and using your arm to pull off throws and impressive feats makes you feel like a badass while Spencer hoops and hollers like a madman. Gunplay is pretty meh, you have your pistol which you will be using most of the time, it's somewhat reliable but it god it eats through ammo, you also get a special weapon that can be swapped out and grenades, but good luck keeping a special weapon you like, because special weapon pick-ups are rare as hell. Also using the throwing technique is a bit add because after kiting, throwing leads to items being flung in a very odd and nonsensical angle before being throw which leads to odd situations (like a mook flying off to the right before stopping for a split second and zipping the other way to hit the thing you wanted to hit). Combat in general is kinda nice but I've come to realize 3 things about it
1.Your Bionic arm is your best friend. Seriously by late game I only used my weapons to take care of Biomechs quickly or when I had to shoot someone on the double. Throwing OP
2. Spencer cannot take a hit worth a damn in this game, but nothing's stopping from swinging to safety and healing up like a ♥♥♥♥♥, which kind of takes away from the momentum of gameplay if you ask me.
3. Biomechs can go to hell, because they're annoying as hell and they WILL swarm you by lategame. Also aiming at their weakspot can easily lead to Spencer shooting his arm at a barrel right beside them as much as their back which leads to much frustration
Also another major issue I have with the game is that it railroads you hard. What I mean by that is that you'd expect to be able to swing around and enjoy yourself and your mobility taking out bad guys however you see fit. However, you can't as radiation has covered the city and the very second you hit an area with radioactivity, you only have a few seconds before you're dead. This gets ridiculous as you're swinging around avoiding gunfire or looking for collectibles (which do very little from what I've seen) and then all of a sudden you hear a blaring warning signal before Spencer flops over dead taking you back to a checkpoint. Speaking of which when you die, you go back and all your progress (objectives, ammo, and collectibles) are gone and you have to get them all bad.
The ending is screwy and while I won't spoil it, I feel like it was just a waste of potential of what could have been an amazing final boss.
Overall, give it a shot if you find this on sale, but it is a hit and miss game. It's not horrid but you can easily hate it as much as you like it. Just be warned that this PC port is lackluster compared to other ports and is rather lazy, it's crashed twice over the course of the game for me, has no windowed options or even any graphics settings so if you have a low-end computer you probably won't be able to play this.

Mabinogi is a game deep to me on so many levels, having played it off and on for roughly 6 years. To this day, it provides an experience no other game can quite capture, though saying that also gives me personal grief. The updates the game has seen in the last few years have not played well to the game's strengths, and have soiled what I once considered a "historically inspired" MMO.
Up through the first major expansions, the title held true to its Celtic and Irish mythos and assets-- which is bizzare because the art style doesn't inherently lend to that type of setting. True with any MMO, the developers sought to appeal to the playerbase en masse, and tossed aside their creative direction in favor of something more widely appealing (being anime, japanese culture, and straight up crossovers with anime titles).
The hay-day of this title persisted up through the 4th generation, just before the expansion involving Iria and additional playable races. The playerbase was not centered in any one area due to convenience, and the content available in-game gave every location significance.
I would reccommend this title if you enjoy anime, slow-paced (strategic) combat, and want to take things day-by-day, or if you are looking for an unique MMO experience. That being said, the age of the game is very evident, and the developer has not updated old content. It's very obvious, playing through quests and observing different items in-game what assets are newer and which are older.
Pros
- dynamic weather
- wide variety of in-game activities
- thoughtful combat (Mashing buttons WILL kill you.)
- aging system/ no level cap/ not pay-to-win
Cons
- infrequent updates/ developer is bad
- clashing art directions
- graphics have not aged well
- combat is buggy
- user support is almost nonexistant (I've had tickets sit for months without being reviewed.)

I ***ing love space-ships, and this is the most player-influenced MMO you'll find.The "EVE Dream" of being some sort of god and owning some massive alliance in nullsec attracted me and many others to this game. Don't expect a constant fun time once you start playing though; EVE takes a hell of a lot of work and time to get anywhere, and you'll only get somewhere if you're lucky. Unless you're willing to devote months of your life to this game (which mostly will end up being used for skill training and monotonous isk farming), find friends and blow up ships. That is the best way to legitimately enjoy the game.
Two pieces of advice:
-Don't mine, it requires so much time to make money, and after a month or so, you'll realize that training for an Exhumer was a waste of time.
-Get into null/lowsec as soon as possible. Fit up a nooby frig, watch a few PvP vids, and get going. It's really beneficial to overcome the "nullsec jitters" early on, and it's worth losing a cheap frig or two to accomplish that.

Let me say quite Clearly that I love EVE to death, and while I'm recommending it to practially anyone that will give me the time of day, it is not a game for the faint-hearted or the easily bored. EVE is game about finding what you want to do and then doing it, but you have to be aware that what you're going to do has been done before and you aren't that special snowflake that will do something completely innovative. At least for the first 2-3 months you can expect to be bouncing around from one thing to another trying to find what you wanna do.
The very first thing I recommend doing after you get through the super quick tutorial they give you is to do the "Career" missions, which are quest lines related to the most basic things you can do, you wanna fly around and shoot stuff? do the Military missions. You wanna mine rocks and build things? Do industry. Do you wanna explore space and find interesting and often valueable salvage? do Exploration. In fact, do them all, because if you stick with EVE for any length of time you're probably gonna end up doing them all anyway.
After you complete the "Career" missions or even while you're doing them, find a corporation (a Guild for those of you familiar with other MMOs) because EVE is not a game for playing by yourself. Yeah you can go and be the lone pirate in the lawless zones of space, but you aren't gonna last long and you definitely aren't gonna be making money that way. Corporations are groups of people that can literally be thousands of people at a time that can form or join an alliance with multiple corporations to work towards a common goal, usually to hold territory in the most outer areas of normal space, or to head into a wormhole and establish a base, or multiple bases where other people can't get to the them as easily. Corps are essential not only because EVE isn't a solo friendly game, but because you are a new player and corporations will hold at least 1 moderatly experienced player that can give you a more accurate account of what EVE actually is.
Now, while I don't have the most amount of hours played on this game in steam, I have played this game off and on since about the Empyrean Age release, which came out in 2008. So i can say with at least some certainty that I know the basics of what I'm doing. So knowing that, I will tell you that I honestly still have only scratched the surface of what EVE has to offer. I've been part of a Wormhole Corporation that was kicked out of one wormhole and had to move (which was hilarious honestly), but i've never done too much large scale PVP, nor have I really delved into industry. So look to the other reviews to see what they have to say about those things.
Don't go into EVE after looking at some videos online and seeing that bigs ships and saying to yourself "I'm gonna fly a capital ship" or something along those lines. It takes a LONG time to even be able to sit in a capital ship. And i stress this, to SIT in one, not fly it, but sit in it. Because you could train straight to Dreadnoughts and be able to fly around all you want but you will not have the necessary skills to be able to use anything else other than the pilot seat. My current character was made in 2011, so about 4 years ago, and i came into the game saying i wanted to fly a carrier, using my fighters to blap people out of existence, but when i got into the game and did some research, i found out that capital ships take billions of ISK (in game money) so i needed to make some. I went into mining as a newbro and tried to make money that way, i got bored of that very fast, so i teched into battlecruisers, hoping to get on some kills and get some awesome loot and joined RedvsBlue (which is a good corp if you wanna get into fights constantly but with honorable people so you don't have to worry about losing anything but your ship) and now, finally after almost 4 years of training skills (with some breaks because I play EVE and then drop it sometimes so i lost some time to train skills there) i'm finally only 11 days of straight training to be able to sit in a carrier. THAT I STILL CAN'T AFFORD! So do your research, find what level of ship you would like to fly. then train in frigates. Doesn't matter what you want to do at the begining, frigates are what you are gonna be flying for a long time unless your corp can hand out the bigger stuff. Now this all applies if you want to be a PVPer or a PVEer, doesn't make too much difference there, but for people that want to explore or mine, totally different conversation that I don't know too much about, but if you wanna do that, you can ignore this for the most part.
There are literally tons of guides and wikis on pretty much everything that can be done in EVE. So my biggest recommendation would be to look at some videos (like the wonderful trailer on the steam page), look at some different videos, because this is a very cinematic trailer and then look at wiki pages about what interests you. Because while a lot of the stuff you'll find on YouTube will be tutorials or even videos big fights people go into, you won't find everything looking only at one section of the giant resource we call the internet. look at everything you can stand to watch. and then do a 30 day trial. if you don't understand something look it up or ask someone for help. You could probably figure it out yourself but it's much easier and less frustration to go to someone more experienced that could explain it to you.

A while back, Yahtzee, the dude who does Zero Punctuation, made a game called The Art of Theft, a 2D stealth platformer that felt very similar to old platform adventure games like Flashback and Out of This World, but had a focus on Trilby as a catburglar. It was a very fun and highly unforgiving title that focused on stealth at its very fundamental core.  Gunpoint reminds me of this game for two reasons. One, it looks and feels very similar.
Two, there is a heavy emphasis on stealth, but it allows for a lot of creativity and experimentation, plus it’s not nearly as tough (you can rewind time to seconds ago before mistakes you’ve made). You don’t really have a weapon in this one (at least not initially), so you have to rely on stealth, rewiring circuitry, tackling enemies, and the best tool of all: a ridiculous leg spring thingy that allows you to vault several feet in the air and never die from fall damage.
Honestly, the title has nothing to do with this game, but then I guess calling a game “Springy Spy” wouldn’t have sold too well either. The game is funny, clever, involves a lot of great puzzles, and has great stealth elements. It can be frustrating at times, but not nearly as frustrating as certain other titles with actual or near insta-death scenarios like Hotline Miami and Dark Souls, so if you enjoy stealth action, then you’re in for a good time.
Was not expecting it to be this fun, or to drop such a nostalgia bomb.

(I rewrote this review, as my last one isn't really helpful.)
This game is a VERY acquired taste, and, by looking at my game hours on it, it's clearly mine.
The game is fast-paced, quick game that isn't ment to be taken seriously. The basic game mechanic of constant movement works well for the gamemodes included. The game is very fun, even in public lobbies (Even though I can't find a lot with good ping, but whatever).
I wouldn't say it's perfect, but it's definitely still good. It gives off a sorta BattleBlock Theater vibe, which is nice. My only true fault with this game is the phrase "Modding Friendly." The game should run fine. (Unless your computer was built in 2005) but once you start install game modifications on a "Just Good Enough" PC, (Meeting only the minimum requirements) the game's FPS will drop significantly.
Edit: As unfortunate as it is, having an AMD Processor and playing will lower FPS, but it shouldn't be too bad.
Second issue: Items. Items are a fun unlock after leveling up, they are your rewards, but the problem comes in how RARE some items are. Chainsaw Backstab, a VERY fun mode, is so incredibly rare you will never see it in an online game. It's price on the market is about 5 USD, And I think lowering the rarity on Gamemodes specifically, would be MUCH more beneficial. I can understand the rarity on Characters, as they provide no benefit other than cosmetics, but a gamemode being that rare is effectively locking players away from experiencing the full game.
The gamemodes you do get to play in the big climb of trying to find Chainsaw Backstab are very fun. Fizzle Floor, the floor disappears, standing on one tile may seem easy, but remember that moving mechanic? Spike Ball, avoid a rapidly bouncing ball that increases as the match goes on. Heavy Bullets, (Which is also a nice game on Steam, and what it's based on) Shoot one bullet, just make sure it actually hits the person.
The visuals in the game are very aesthetically pleasing, along with the big burst of color on death, and smooth graphics.
Also, Props to the developers for adding in Color Blind Modes, it's a nice touch.
I know this seems like a bunch of scrambled nonsense at this point, so I'll leave it there.

This is what would be a textbook example of how you make a Dragon Ball game properly, and make it fun.
Pros:
- Gameplay's solid, not deviating too much from the formula set in Budokai Tenkaichi 3, but keeps it varied enough to make it fun.

- The story is great, and shows how far the developers are willing to deviate from just telling the tale of the anime/manga.

Summary:
If you like Dragon Ball, get this game. If you like 3D fighters, get this game.

Putrefaction claims to be a shooter akin to those of yesteryear. And at first glance, it seems like a viable option among the ranks of DOOM, Quake, etc. However, upon playing the performance didn't quite live up to the expectation.
CONS:
*Slow movement speed.
- When someone thinks of a 90's era FPS, they generally think of fast paced action, gore, and heavy metal. This however.. moved more like a snail on a hot summer day. Now, that might be a bit of an overexaggeration, but when I'm dreading having to encounter enemies due to the sheer fact that if I get cornered I can't quickly circle strafe out of the situation, then I'm a bit peeved.
*Poor lighting and tiny flashlight radius.
- The lighting in the game is for the most part, okay. I understand the intent was for a dark decrepit building and dank musty caves, but the execution was not well thought out. When you're in the building, often times it's difficult to see where enemies are due to the fact they can spawn in dark cut-outs in the walls. This led to me running around trying to find the last enemy only to realize it was in a hole in the wall you're unable to see into, and he never moved. The flashlight option, when you finally managed to press every key on the keyboard or look at the control menu because it's never mentioned anywhere, emits a very tiny radius of light, that doesn't help when navigating through the enormous cave sections. The flashlight allows one to see only what is directly in front of oneself, and if there are multiple enemies bouncing from one end of an expansive cave to the next, this is of no use.
*Level design.
- This one is a bit nitpicky, but I found the level design way too linear. Every path either ended up at a dead end or at a "spawn site" where waves of enemies spawn in and the only way to progress is through killing every last enemy.
*"Spawn Sites", random enemy spawning, and you have to kill every enemy?...
- 90's era FPS games didn't force you to kill every last enemy to progress and in fact, some of them even encouraged finding ways around killing every enemy in the game. Putrefaction however, forces players into "spawn sites" where enemies can quickly spawn in and surround you, forcing you to kill every enemy in order to progress. The spawning of the enemies also seems very random, and not well thought out, with some enemies spawning behind doors, some behind the player, and some on the other side of the map. It didn't help the game feel cohesive or drive me to keep playing.
PROS:
* It's a simple boredom killer.
- If you can find the game on sale for a low price, it might be worth it to pick it up if for nothing else than to kill some time every now and then. I can't really force myself to play through the game for long periods of time, but a quick level here and there doesn't bother me .... as much.
*Decent variation of weapons and enemies.
- The weapon and enemy variety is, like most other aspects of the game, okay. There are plenty of enemies to add some variety, and the weapon assortment was on par with most other games of the genre. However, this did not stop the action from becoming repetitive, it did allow for a change in scenery for a bit.
This game gave me extremely mixed feelings and while I can't reccommend the game at it's full retail price, I can say that at a sale price the game isn't terrible. Sure the lighting is bad in some areas and it moves a bit slow, but overall its just an okay FPS. The story.. or lackthereof.. is extremely simple, and who even plays a DOOM-esque FPS for the story anyway? So, if you're looking for something cheap to kill a few minutes, and you have some leftover change in your steam wallet, go ahead and pick this game up. Just, don't expect it to be the next big thing since sliced bread.

**Update 12/09/17**
Back when I first wrote this review, Putrefaction was priced at $5. The price is now $1.
While the game is a better value at this price, the cons I mention below still prevent me from wholeheartedly recommending Putrefaction to anyone but FPS fans with lowered expectations who are desperate for something to burn a few hours on. Most others will likely be disappointed.
Putrefaction gets a C for effort and a D for execution. It isn't a completely awful game, it just never comes close to scratching the old-school shooter itch it claims to scratch. Aside from that, I honestly found it to be unremarkable and somewhat lacking in almost every other important element as well. Despite its $1 pricetag, the minuses outnumber the plusses here so it's a difficult game for me to recommend.
- Decent enemy variety rather than a small selection repeatedly reskinned.
- Customizable keybind and mouse y-axis invert options.
- An almost complete lack of story. While the classic shooters of yesteryear typically skimped on plot, they had compelling gameplay to propel the player forward and keep them interested. Putrefaction unfortunately doesn't provide solid or enjoyable enough gameplay to justify its own lack of narrative.
- The environments, level design and progression just don't flow very well, aesthetically or logically. The maps didn't always seem to have any overall theme connecting them, leaving me feeling I was being funneled through linear and seemingly random facility hallways/interiors/caves (This isn't helped one bit by the aforementioned lack of a story).
- I both clipped through the map and got stuck in the environment several times.
- Combat is the most important area for a FPS to nail (especially one that counts the classics as inspiration), but sadly the combat in Putrefaction is generic, brainless and repetitive, requiring very little actual skill to overcome the oddly-grouped waves of enemies with fairly poor AI. The game's arsenal is just as uninspired as the combat, offering up crudely modeled/skinned weapons that lack punch. Even the rocket launcher felt underpowered.
Putrefaction is described by the developer as being heavily inspired by old-school shooters from 3D Realms and Id Software. While it's true that it is in fact a FPS that has no regenerating health, cover mechanics or other modern contrivances, any similarities between Putrefaction and its inspirations end there. If you can get it at a good discount and don't expect much from your shooters, you might find it worth the gamble.

I loved Gothic 2, but never really ventured out to play any other games by PB.
I picked this up on a whim, and I'm completely blown away - in a good way.
Yes, the dialogue is cheesy. The script can be bad and jump around. The bugs can be awful, and laughable. You may rage the first time you accidentally back up a palm tree during combat only to fall out and die. You'll get headaches from the twitching textures, and the jittery lighting during cutscenes. You'll think the voice actors are sometimes intentionally trying to be do a bad job. The quality of the character design varies greatly from on to another.
But, I still love this game, and for a good many reasons.
Combat is excellent. It won't be everyones cup of tea, but its a better twist on difficult than some other games. I hate combat and levelling in Skyrim. I love combat and levelling in this game. It just feels better, and I feel like I'm accomplishing something. Enemy placement is also excellent. The world is dangerous. For example, after returning to the tutorial area after finishing the tutorial. I had killed all the monsters, and was grabbing a shroom from near a pool of water and waterfall. I almost jumped out of my seat when a massive crocodile charged at me. Almost died, but surviving a far stronger enemy after being surprised felt great.
I really love the level design. Risen 3 takes relatively small maps, and makes the most of them. I love exploring and trying to find every nook and cranny, because you actually benefit from doing it. Think that ledge over there looks like you can land on it? There's probably some dead dude in a weird position, with some coins and a bottle of rum. Maybe some flowers for some extra stat points. Looks like there is an out of the way beach around a jutting out rock? I bet you'll find some useful loot, and some lore. Found a way onto that roof that makes it seem like you were glitching the game? Nope, devs figured players would do that and planted a few potions/spells.
The devs understand me as a player. They know I like to mess with things, and they took it in stride and made their game great.
This game won't be everyone's cup of tea, but for me it's up there. I give it an 8/10. Well worth the cost, especially on sale.

This game has some prettyminor issues; but they became glaring problems when you need them to work perfectly to survive in Hardmode. I was already inundated with knowledge of how to play the game when I played the demo way back when this was first set to launch. I had a lot of fun; but I ultimately was not financially set enough to just buy the games I wanted at the time. Fast-forward to 2016, and I find myself buying the Humble Bundle containing this game as a bonus. Naturally I picked to play the game on Hardmode, since I already know how to play the game pretty well. I was hoping the game would give a decent challenge, and I feel much of that expectation has been met.
To refresh myself with the games controls, I took care to pay close attention to the Tutorial. Swinging, Throwing, Ripping, Heavy Uppercut Launching, and Shooting were the main subjects covered in it. To my dismay, I would find out during the actual game that I wouldn't be able to use these skills until I reached a point in the game where it would be important to progression. This of course made enemies more difficult than they should of been when I didn't have the tools I had learned to use in the Tutorial. It's one of the few negative about this game; but it's not really gamebreaking. Not being able to throw items at the first biomechs was just annoying, I was forced to use Handgrenades or rely on luck in hitting their back hatch with the pistol(as there was not enough ammo in the bonus weapon they drop for you to use).
This game makes good use of Bonuses, Challenges, and Hidden Retro Icons. You're never really left that often with an empty area; although the Retro Icons are never hidden that well. They're more or less sprawled out to challenge your swinging ability. This isn't really handled well since dying means you have to get everything you got before the next Checkpoint. I don't really have an issue with this; but It was annoying to have to rewatch certain cutscenes or grab collectibles all over again. I found myself skipping things I had already done upon dying, to save myself the sanity of fighting that extra mobs of enemies again.
After fumbling a bit with the controls, I managed to learn of a very unique way in taking down the Biomechs. There is some deep meta with this game in regards to enemy ventilating; but sadly there isn't much variety in enemies to explore. The trimming of this unrefined depth to gameplay; was most likely for thesake of the tacked on multiplayer. This game came out right around the time Multiplayer games were being churned out left and right, so single player experiences were routinely hampered by the need to substantiate XBL subscription costs. Too bad they couldn't just work on the Single Player more, a great deal of time had obviously gone into making the swinging feel so good; but the limitations in regards to invisible walls(Death Radiators), Sparse selection in weapons, and overall underwhelming-swiftness to the plot, brings down the rest of the lasting appeal.
To tie it all together, it's not a bad game; but its way too quickly snapped together with lots of underwhelming bits, creating a very desultory feel to the game. Swinging, Fighting Enemies, and stealthly navigating the scenary, make the experience all the more fun. Perhaps multiplayer could be fun as well; but I'm not really interested in multiplayer games. Had this game poured it's heart into the Single player, it would be much better than it is. In the current day, this is probably the last we'll ever see of another Bionic Commando game; but I really hope there comes a time where the idea is explored again.

In terms of pure game mechanics, Bionice Commando 2K9 is an absolute hidden gem.
Very few games handle 3-D swinging properly, and it can be quite a difficult mechanic to implement, yet it's done so with aplomb here. On top of that, the game combines this swinging with a militaristicly styled 3rd person shooter to create a very unique experience of highly mobile tactical shooter (thanks to your generally small health bar and generally limited amount of ammunition and weapon carrying capacity).
When this game is firing on all of its cylinders, you'll have truly amazing moments where you'll Spider-Man around large maps taking out squads of enemy soldiers, their air support, and mechs bit by bit fighting against larger numbers and gravity all at once. And it can be glorious.
However, there are a host of very real problems too:
> The radiation walled death zones can be very, very annoying
> There isn't enough enemy variation in either the number of types of opponents, nor the AI for the more advanced ones present in the game
> There DEFINITELY aren't enough bosses, and only one boss battle takes full advantage of all of the player's mechanics
> The weapons are functional, but not terribly imaginative
> The linear progression of levels is not the best choice considering the player's abilities - one big sandbox or multiple smaller sandboxes would have made much more sense considering the nature of your moveset
> The world's tone is trying to ape Gears of War bleakness far too much, but doesn't have either that game's Bromancing or gallows humor to add necessary levity to the experience, and just becomes the king of Edgelord Grim-Dark apathy
> The plot gets mind-bogglingly stupid two-thirds in while leaving off on a horrible note that includes a bunch of QTE's in a game without any of them up to that point (with a terrible cliff-hanger tease on top of it all), and finally . . .
> they seriously spit on the character of Super Joe, who is ostensibly the original Capcom mascot (you'd think they'd have treated him better, considering).
(Oh, and the Multi-player, which is just as amazing as the absolute best the SP has to offer - think UT/Quake 3 style tournament shooting DM with grapple swinging all over the pretty big, very vertical maps - has never found even a small audience, and so is very dead)
But all of that said - this is still a great experience every once in a while to load up and play through a run on a weekend. A fine little adventure that showed off some great mechanics that could have been very well served in a sequel that would have more time to be developed (and which understood the proper level and enemy design for a swinging super-soldier character type).
In a way, it's painful to play as a result. Because you can TASTE the missed potential with this series. But if nothing else, this might be the best possible game to teach game design: it shows you so many "Do not do this" lessons, while still retaining a core of solid gameplay that you can tell it wasn't incompetence of craftmanship that was the problem here.

The Zombie Island of Dr. Ned features irritating undead enemies, including birds (so grab your shotgun), but I did like the ambience.

I'll start by saying I've re-written this review to be a little more coherent and sensible.  Bionic Commando has gotten a lot of flack, and caused an unfortunate closing of GRIN studios, whom which had a decent amount of fame due to their hit remaster Bionic Commando:Rearmed.
Bionic Commando, with dreadlock Spencer, is by no means a perfect game but definitely holds ground for some praise.  The combat becomes a little repetitive and tedious at points.  However, satisfaction is the real treat of the game once you've beaten a tough segment.  This player, finding himself a little frustrated at times for playing on Hard mode first playthrough, was still happy with the presentation and overall experience.
The visuals are nothing special, but do their job.  You have your standard fare of cityscapes, and certain jungle segments that looked pretty cool, but nothing out of the ordinary.  Having a toaster with a mere Intel i7 processor, and an extremely old nVidia GT520 (yes not GTX or anything beefy), the game runs pretty darn smooth, even with hoards of enemies on screen.  Never being one to bicker about framerate drops to a certain degree, I've never noticed anything game breaking.
The soundtrack is somewhat memorable, but pretty typical military pep affair -- it's what you'd expect to hear from a game like this.  The voice acting was definitely believable.  Mike Patton did a good job as Spencer.  But their choice of famous Steve Blum as Super Joe was kind of off.  Steve's voice just doesn't fit how Super Joe's character looks in this game.  Steve could've probably done Spencer's voice, it'd have fit the look of Spencer far better, I think.
The meat of the game for me was the swinging and grapple combat as is a lot of players who've favored this game.  You're given various guns and grenades throughout the game to use to dispose your enemies.  However, there's ample opportunity to grapple, throw, and zip kick your enemies just the same, and is probably better suited for it usually eliminates enemies quicker...and it looks cooler.  You can even throw boxes, crates, and other soldiers into each other for kicks.  My only beef with the swinging mechanics, was there were a LOT of deaths in my playthrough because of the questionable range of the grapple arm.  Sometimes it felt like I had to be two feet from a surface in order to grapple at times.  There are points where you have to swing across "mine fields", where the air mines are the only things you can swing from, and sometimes if you're not used to the swinging mechanics, you may die if you're not careful.
A big gripe I have with this game kinda goes hand-in-hand with each other.  I'd have loved a big sandbox world, or many different trial courses seperate from the main game --without combat -- just to swing around and have fun in.  The game offers "breaks" in between combat so you can have fun, but they're always pretty short lived.  I'd have loved a bigger playground and not be limited to blue radiation clouds that can kill you instantly, and sometimes are unable to get out of due to the somewhat finnicky range on the grapple arm.  There will be times where you'll swing where you THINK you can go to shortcut your way to an objective point, but there are a stray cloud or two that will just kill you instantly.
All in all, this game isn't absolute trash, and despite certain struggles and frustrations, I did have a blast in the end.  This game is definitely meant to be played with mouse and keyboard, and it was really fun in retrospect.  After certain tough segments, I couldn't imagine people even thinking of playing this on pad.  In fact, I think that was partly why a lot of people hated this game...
I can see one playing it again to try to find the collectibles, but they don't really unlock anything.  It's a damn shame there isn't more to the game other than the story, and the multiplayer servers are completely trashed.  But first time through?  I'd recommend this game on PC.  7/10

First of all I must stay I am a Naruto addicted so my recommendation may be biased xD
This will be a long analyses, but I am hoping useful for people interested in the game.
Naruto is a 3D fighting game developed thinking mostly of the fans of the anime. A proof of this the extent of the cutscenes in the story mode (some of them go as long as half an hour - you are basically watching a tv show), which means that if you are not a fan you will probably not enjoy this game very much. It is also advisable to have a
to play, since fighting style games are not really developed for keyboard and this one is no exception.
You have 3 game modes available: Ultimate Adventure, Free battle and Online.
Starting by the Ultimate Adventure, the story picks up after Pain destroyed Konohagakure and goes until the end of the Fourth ninja war (giving it an alternative ending to the manga). The main story takes about 10-12 hours to complete, of which probably 6-8 are cutscenes. After you finish the main story there is a load of side missions to do, and if you want to complete everything to 100% (S-rank every fight with bonus) it can take close to 30 hours. The art is fantastic, with little to no bugs in the free world map, and with very interesting side quests in my opinion. In here was where I learned the game mechanics which are pretty simple but still manage to make the game enjoyable.
After you finish the Ultimate Adventure more than 100 characters will be at your disposable to use in Free Battles. In this section you can also do the 100 misssion battles with different challenges each, which should take you 10 more hours if you go for the 100% again.
Lastly the Online. It is terrible in my short experience. Games crash a lot (I wasn't able to finish a single combat in 5 tries and have a 100mb connection), and there is also a significant delay between when you press a button and the action takes place. This could be a turn off for you if you are buying the game for the online, but for fans like me, the offline mode will keep you very happy.
I saved the best for last: YOU CAN USE MODS IN THIS GAME!! It is awesome, you can add characters like Goku Naruto, change characters movesets and even add new stages, all developed by a fantastic community and just ready for you to download xD
TL; DR:
Pros:
+Simple but addictive gameplay
+Lenght (40 hours offline only)
+Ammount of characters
+MODS
Cons:
-Extensive cutscenes
-Online

Hmm... how do I begin to review a game. I guess we should start off with the plot.
The Story:
*SPOILERS!!*
You start the game in the shoes of Richard Conway, a sometimes incompetent freelance spy with a flexible morality. We watch as he unintentially launches himself out of his apartment window and through the glass ceiling of the lobby of the gun company across the street using his newly purchased Bullfrog Hyper Trousers (Yes, that's what they're actually called.) As he lies there on the floor, he recieves a phone call from one of the guards on duty, who introduces herself as Selena Delgado. After Conway refuses to tell how he landed in the lobby so as to avoid hurting his ego, Selena Delgado tells him he has a job for him, and Conway accepts and heads for the top floor to discuss the terms of the contract. On his way up the stairs a gunshot rings out, with two more following. When he gets to the top floor and looks out the window, he finds Delgado's corpse on the street below. Thanks to his trench coat that allows him to survive falling from heights, he promptly exits the crime scene. He then gets a message from someone named Melanie Rooke, who owns the gun company Rooke Firearms, which is in a financial crisis due to the recent gun ban on the city. She knows that Conway didn't kill Selena because he walked right in front of the camera leading up to her office right after the shots were fired. The Eastpoint Police department will take it as an easy conviction, so Rooke hires Conway to erase the backups she has at several locations so that the police will have to look for the real murderer. After the job is done, Conway recieves another message from a woman named Katie Collins, who has been arrested for being the only one with access to the camera footage that was erased and for being the only one who had access to the building last. She pleads with Conway saying she's innocent and wasn't there at the crime scene, but she can't prove it because she lives alone and no one can vouch for her. She eventually runs out of leads for Conway to follow, with the only information obtained was the suspicion that Mark Jackson, Rooke's husband and CEO of Lucena Logistics, might have setup the hit and framed Collins. At the same time this is happening, Conway is recieving messages from Fritz Gesseler, who owns Intex Firearms, the rival gun company in town. He is determined to find out about Rooke's secret project that will get her around the gun ban. Rooke than contacts Conway saying that she has no secret project and wanted conway to steal an automotive part with a bug on it, so that Conway could steal it from her to give to Gesseler. So Conway does so, and the bug leads to one of intex's labs. Now if you didn't tell Gesseler that the part was a bug, then what you steal from the lab benefits Rooke, and Gesseler promptly flips you off in a "interesting" message. If you did tell Gesseler about the bug, what you steal from his labs will turn out to be a bomb that explodes when it reaches one of Rooke's facilities. Gameplay wise, the only thing this affects is whether Gesseler pays you more money or not. Whichever event you choose, this ends your relationship with Gesseler. As for the Katie Collins case, and anonymous figure who turns out to be the chief of police is working on it secretly so as to make sure he dosen't "dissapear mysteriously" if it turns out his police force is corrupt. You learn that he was simply testing you to see if you were the murderer, and depending on whether you were honest with him or not will influence his decision. Afterwards, he has no bearing on the plot whatsoever. Rooke then calls up Conway telling him that if he helps frame her husband for the murder, who she had a falling out with, she will give him the real killer. Mark Jackson also calls you saying he didn't kill Selena and that his wife is trying to frame him, so he needs you to gather this piece of evidence in order to prove his innocence. No matter which mission you choose, it will take place in the same level, and it only determines whether the killer, Hightower, we'll be in the final level. After wards, you learn that Gesseler was behind the hit, and Conway goes to settle the score. After you reach the seventh floor of the building Gesseler is held up in, Hightower will tackle you out of the window (provided he's there in the first place), which he will then start punching you until you blackout. After you take care of Hightower, it's time to face Gesseler, and you are given seven delightful ways to do it as follows:
-shooting him
-jamming his gun
-punching him
-punching him to death
-slam a door in his face
-kick a door into his face
-tackle him out the window
After it's over and done with the game ends, and you get to write a custom blog describing your take on the events that happened.
Gunpoint's story is very convoleted, and so it's understandable if you get lost. The creator of the game, Tom Francis, even acknowledged this by putting in a dialogue choice that shows your not listening to the story.
The Gameplay:
Each level in gunpoint consists of an objective (usually a computer terminal) before you can exit the level via the subway entrance. Thanks to a gadget known as the Crosslink, this can be done in many (and often hilarious) ways. The Crosslink can be used to rewire electronics, for example and I can get a light switch to open a door. This leads to many possibilities to solving a level, from turning the lights so guards don't see you, opening doors in their faces, or even shocking them by using an electrical socket. As you complete each mission, you will obtain a certain amount of money based on your performance in a certain area. For example, if a client required you to use minimal violence, then they will add or take away money based on how well you met that criteria. You can use money you obtain to buy new gadgets from the shop. This includes the Crosslink, the Wirejack, which allows you to hack electronic that are on a different circuit, Dropshot, which allows you to fall silently from great heights, Deathfluke, which increases your chances of dodging incoming shots if you leap towards a guard, Hushcracker, which lets you break glass silently, Prankspasm, which allows you to booby trap electronics such as switches, Longshot, which allows you to rewire enemy guns, Resolver, a hand gun, and Gatecrashers, which allows you to kick down doors and anything in the way of it. The levels our well designed and our meant to be approached in different ways, increasing replayability. The only problem is the game is short. As I right this article I have played the game for 6.7 hours, and in that time I have beaten it twice and made my own level in the level editor. The level editor is fine, but I wish there were more options to choose from, and that it was designed a little beter.
The Score:
I was addicted to this OST way before I got the game. It's a great jazz track that fits well with the noir-like atmosphere. The most popular piece it seems is the "Five-Floor Goodbye," and I particulary like "Dig" and the variation of it that was done for the last level, "Leviathon." Those two pieces made me feel like a badass super spy, especially the latter.
The Verdict:
Gunpoint is a fine game, but you may find it lacking a bit if you prefer quantity over quality. In that case, wait till it goes on sale, or wait until steam steamworkshop integration which is coming soon
score: 8/10
replayability: moderate

Let's be honest. I love DBZ. A lot.
But this game took a moment of my childhood and crushed it slowly over the course of two hours.
When I saw this title go on sale during the sales I thought it was a golden opportunity to jump in and grab a title I had been waiting to play for some time.
I have nothing but regrets.
The game does what DBZ should do: large environments with plenty of ground and aerial combat, fast fighting and flashes of sound and fury as players jump from place to place. But was that enough?
Dragonball Xenoverse sets you on a story as a new hero, a saviour pulled from the reaches of time and space by Shenron, the Earth dragon, to intervene in the villainry that is besieging the DBZ universe's timeways.
That's when it started to fall apart for me. Like when you look at a magnificent piece of architecture and start to notice the small imperfections that ruin the larger image for you.
The poor storyline butchered an already well established volume of canon through a time traveling story that was so convoluted that you wonder how anyone at Funimation could endorse it. Oh, that's right. Money...
The voice acting was lousy, and the greatest moments in DBZ history were watered down to rough cuts of dialogue during the fight that had just begun.
In all honesty I thought it would be like Burst Limit, but with a unique story arc and would retain the great moments in their entirety.
I was wrong.
If you have a fondness for DBZ and want to maintain that don't play this game.

Hmm... how do I begin to review a game. I guess we should start off with the plot.
The Story:
*SPOILERS!!*
You start the game in the shoes of Richard Conway, a sometimes incompetent freelance spy with a flexible morality. We watch as he unintentially launches himself out of his apartment window and through the glass ceiling of the lobby of the gun company across the street using his newly purchased Bullfrog Hyper Trousers (Yes, that's what they're actually called.) As he lies there on the floor, he recieves a phone call from one of the guards on duty, who introduces herself as Selena Delgado. After Conway refuses to tell how he landed in the lobby so as to avoid hurting his ego, Selena Delgado tells him he has a job for him, and Conway accepts and heads for the top floor to discuss the terms of the contract. On his way up the stairs a gunshot rings out, with two more following. When he gets to the top floor and looks out the window, he finds Delgado's corpse on the street below. Thanks to his trench coat that allows him to survive falling from heights, he promptly exits the crime scene. He then gets a message from someone named Melanie Rooke, who owns the gun company Rooke Firearms, which is in a financial crisis due to the recent gun ban on the city. She knows that Conway didn't kill Selena because he walked right in front of the camera leading up to her office right after the shots were fired. The Eastpoint Police department will take it as an easy conviction, so Rooke hires Conway to erase the backups she has at several locations so that the police will have to look for the real murderer. After the job is done, Conway recieves another message from a woman named Katie Collins, who has been arrested for being the only one with access to the camera footage that was erased and for being the only one who had access to the building last. She pleads with Conway saying she's innocent and wasn't there at the crime scene, but she can't prove it because she lives alone and no one can vouch for her. She eventually runs out of leads for Conway to follow, with the only information obtained was the suspicion that Mark Jackson, Rooke's husband and CEO of Lucena Logistics, might have setup the hit and framed Collins. At the same time this is happening, Conway is recieving messages from Fritz Gesseler, who owns Intex Firearms, the rival gun company in town. He is determined to find out about Rooke's secret project that will get her around the gun ban. Rooke than contacts Conway saying that she has no secret project and wanted conway to steal an automotive part with a bug on it, so that Conway could steal it from her to give to Gesseler. So Conway does so, and the bug leads to one of intex's labs. Now if you didn't tell Gesseler that the part was a bug, then what you steal from the lab benefits Rooke, and Gesseler promptly flips you off in a "interesting" message. If you did tell Gesseler about the bug, what you steal from his labs will turn out to be a bomb that explodes when it reaches one of Rooke's facilities. Gameplay wise, the only thing this affects is whether Gesseler pays you more money or not. Whichever event you choose, this ends your relationship with Gesseler. As for the Katie Collins case, and anonymous figure who turns out to be the chief of police is working on it secretly so as to make sure he dosen't "dissapear mysteriously" if it turns out his police force is corrupt. You learn that he was simply testing you to see if you were the murderer, and depending on whether you were honest with him or not will influence his decision. Afterwards, he has no bearing on the plot whatsoever. Rooke then calls up Conway telling him that if he helps frame her husband for the murder, who she had a falling out with, she will give him the real killer. Mark Jackson also calls you saying he didn't kill Selena and that his wife is trying to frame him, so he needs you to gather this piece of evidence in order to prove his innocence. No matter which mission you choose, it will take place in the same level, and it only determines whether the killer, Hightower, we'll be in the final level. After wards, you learn that Gesseler was behind the hit, and Conway goes to settle the score. After you reach the seventh floor of the building Gesseler is held up in, Hightower will tackle you out of the window (provided he's there in the first place), which he will then start punching you until you blackout. SINGLE PLAYER REVIEW ONLY - I understand there are some multiplayer issues, but I don't care.
This is a cross between Diablo II and a twin stick shooter.  Send your hero into four acts of five levels each (if you have the base game, seven acts with expansions) on various levels of difficulty.  Waves at mobs come at you from the sides. At the end of each act is a boss. Move with the left stick, kill with the right stick. Collect loot, level up, upgrade, crush your enemies - see them driven before you - hear the lamentations of their satanic lords.
As with Diablo, the loot drops are a lot of the pull of the game.  The other bit are the relics - as you beat each level boss or in dungeons and crypts you will collect relics. There are hundreds of these things and they add power-ups and can seriously change the way you play.  When you die nothing happens to your character or inventory but you lose all your relics. At first this is 'noooo' but then it becomes fun and adds to the longevity - every play is a bit different.
The characters play different too. Nomad (barbarian) is very different from Necromancer is very different from Marksman (hunter).  Not you can up the difficulty at any time at the act selection screen (in the middle), so if things are dying too easily, ramp it up for better loot and more xp!
Short, but bloody brilliant in writing, visuals, audio, and design all together.

Playing somewhat like a Match-3 game in reverse, TripleTown has a lot more depth and strategy than many would expect from a casual game. Wrapped in a super cute art style, it is one of the most clever and surprising games I've played in a long time.
Easy to learn, hard to master is the best way to describe the gameplay. Instead of the traditional removal of gems, stones, or Chuzzles, TripleTown has you placing various tiles in order to advance up the food chain so to speak. Though this sounds simple on paper, once the board starts filling it becomes an incredible challenge to keep the game going, and really makes you have to think with every move you make.
It only took one round for the uncomplicated, but all the same engadging mechanics to have me completely addicted to building my towns, beating my hi-score, and getting rid of those horrid Ninja Bears! Don't let the casual label turn you off, TripleTown is much more than at first meets the eye, and any puzzle fan should absolutely check it out.

Miss the good old online flash games? Were you a fan of stickdeath (green vs blue)? Did you miss the simple, but well done effects that flash used to provide? Stick Fight : The Game will bring you back to the late 90's or early 00's where everything was a party.
Stick Fight's
is quite simple and effective in its delivery. What you see is literally what you will get, an action packed game in which will force you to move. The objective of Stick Fight is to be the last survivor on the map. To eliminate enemy players, opposing players must push enemies to the edge of the map or deplete their HP. HP can be depleted by recieving melee blows or "bullets" from weapons. Options regarding weapon drops, map selection and HP amount can all be modified easily, quickly and efficiently through the in-game menu. The movement of the characters are quite fluid and it seems their body position can play a big role in delivering damage (especially if you have no gun)! The body physics do move accordingly and hands and feet will get caught on edges if you move carelessly. The guns are quite diverse and come in all shapes and sizes. The regular weapons are all there from swords, pistols, machine guns to rocket launchers, but the devs added a bit of spice to the mix. Imagine a rocket launcher or a shotgun that shoots out snakes that chase you down. Now imagine a giant flame thrower burning up parts of the map. The variety of guns with the option to jump/dodge/melee adds some more depth to the gameplay. The maps were creatively and well done. I definitely like how some maps will give you open space to work with, while other maps will force you to use whatever land you have left to stay alive! Some maps will include explosive materials, land deformation capabilities and explosive materials containing snakes.
The
are simplistic. They do not, however, not take away from the game. If anything, it allows the players to focus in on the gameplay and enjoy the diversity of the maps. The maps do follow a theme, but are very different stage to stage. Maps can also be randomized or specifically picked by theme (just incase you get tired of barrels with snakes blowing up). I really like how they did the body physics movement as players can try to raise an arm/gun over cover to fire. The
are okay. I feel this domain could have been done a little bit better. I feel when players got hit or collided with objects, there should have been a little bit more emphasis and immersion with the sounds/effects. They did do a good job for the halloween themed levels. They mixed up not only the gameplay, but the music and sounds when one player turns into a pumpkin. Don't worry, just because you turn into a pumpkin doesn't mean your game is over... it just means you can fly and use a variety of attacks regular players can't use!
Overall, a pretty good game if you have some good friends to play with. You should know that SINGLE PLAYER IS NOT AN OPTION! Either play local or go online... no soup for you if you want to play by yourself. This is where adding AI's into the game would have been great, but no such feature exists (yet hopefully). Game is definitely worth it on sale.
RATING : 7.3/10

The more you explore the Proteus world the more you realise that there's more to this world than pretty graphics and nice music.
The world responds to you. Not just to your simple actions, but to the emotions you're feeling in a particular part of the world because of what's going on, what's already happened and even what you already know. It's amazing that no matter what path I choose, the game always has something for me; a new experience that surprises me, even when I think I know what's coming.
If you don't like games without tick-box goals then maybe this one isn't for you. But if you're willing to put aside your search for objectives for a few minutes and just explore instead, you may find that you come across them anyway.

A good Dwarf-Fortress-like game is designed with the recognition that complexity makes the game interesting, but only if that specific complexity both makes sense as a simulation and leads to interesting stories. This game is built around that concept, paring out complexity for its own sake while taking care to make sure that the systems that are in palce are intuitive and easy to use while also being deep enough to be interesting. You don't need a wiki to play this game well, although there's subtlety that you can choose to make use of- but you don't need to worry about details deeper than what you see in-game unless you enjoy it.
The real emphasis is story. As opposed to the Dwarf Fortress approach of leaving your fate up to the RNG and a larger world simulation, Rimworld is focused on making an interesting narrative. Sometimes it's a meeting with long-lost relatives (maybe on the other side of the field of battle), sometimes it's your best doctor suffering a mental break and wandering around naked when your colony's best shot is bleeding out, sometimes it's trouble in the power grid during a heat wave, and sometimes it's a colonist's pet monkey getting into the beer stash.
There's also a more gentle storyteller mode for when you want to just build a prosperous colony, and a more random one if you want a more chaotic experience. Each storyteller has a difficulty setting as well, allowing you to fine-tune the game to the experience you want.
The excellent mod support and mod community are worth mentioning as well- there are mods allowing you to fine-tune the experience any number of ways, from new storytellers or widespread rebalance to minor modifcations and cosmetic additions.
