TRIGGER WARNING - This review has spoilers
The whole revival of the Bionic Commando IP happened at an unfortunate time in history. It was when nearly every company was looking to have their games be more darker, serious and brooding.
It happened as Inafune was outsourcing most of Capcom's IPs to Western devs. And to be fair maybe that's the only reason this series ever made a comeback. Because of Grin's interest in the series. Or atleast that's my take from it. Even having tried to work on Strider and Streets of Rage as we know now. But back to this series. Grin made two pretty decent Ghost Recon games (and the racing game Ballistics) before making Bionic Commando Rearmed. I had no idea what the series was at the time but the remake received pretty unanimous praise back then and after playing it later I must say it's an amazing game. It's a frolicking Indiana Jones -esque action platformer where you gun down nazis and eventually explode Hitler's head in graphic, satisfying detail. It's a colorful adventure with funny writing and with gore in appropriate places. It plays, sounds, looks and reads great and it had it's own distinct vibe.
Now how does this relate to the Bionic Commando Reboot and to what I said earlier about bad timing? That vibe is gone. See when Grin could reimagine the series for the reboot, they took all the story elements and made them super super serious. Basically gave it the ol' 'Man of Steel' treatment. Nathan "Rad" Spencer is now an angry vet with cornrows and a gravely voice. He's been left to rot in jail for years after saving his country but having been sentenced for "war crimes". Nathan is called to action one last time by his old friend Super Joe who also talks all broody and is voiced by Steve Blum doing his Jack Cayman voice. Joe tells Spencer that unknown terrorist group has nuked one of their cities, killing millions and it's up to Spencer to traverse the city and find out who's behind the attacks. Spencer also looks to find his lost wife.
Also worth mentioning briefly is that Nathan Spencer is voiced by Mike Patton whose music I love but I think he's terribly casted in this game and his delivery doesn't come across believable in the slightest. He's better at voicing characters like the Darkness.
(Spoiler) Super Joe later turns out be evil and it's revealed that Joe killed Spencers wife so that her mind could be put into Spencer's trusty Bionic Arm for it to have worked in the first place. Joe and Spencer later have their final battle in the sky. Joe ends up dieing with Spencer falling down out of the sky. It's uncertain if Spencer actually dies and the game ends with cliffhanger with no sequel in sight ever. (End Spoiler)
It's these kinds of changes to the story and mood that affect other areas of the game and by extension my enjoyment. You see form follows function. So with a darker mood in the story comes a darker color palette and environments in the art direction. That said the game is too grey. Like way too gray compared to the vibrant palettes of the previous games. The environments also consist mostly of different parts of a destroyed city. It's a sad contrast to the caves, factories, jungles, mountains and forts of the previous games. I shouldn't feel depressed when playing a game about a guy punching evil in the face. Unless it was done well like in Rambo or First Blood, but that's beside the point. I don't think that's what the series should be.
Tonally the game is a mess. Imagine if in the Raiders of the Lost Ark, Marion just died a horrible, bloody, murder porn death in the hands of the nazis because Lucas and Spielberg were feeling edgy that day. Also Marcus Brody wishes Indy dead throughout the whole adventure. Sallah sells Indy out to the nazis and him and Indy have their final battle on top of the ark where Sallah melts into nothing but you don't see if Indy died or not because maybe he was able to avert his eyes at the end, who knows. Indy collapses behind the ark and as you think the camera will pan around to show him alive the screen goes black and the credits roll. Also the movie is in black and white and instead of the Raiders score, it's the Schindler's List score.
The gameplay however is great and that's where the problem lies. Even with the depressing tonal shift it's a joy to just play. Especially just swinging around in the environment is a lot of fun. It's hard to give this game a clear yes or no recommendation. Just this muddled maybe. It's a game that you maybe should try but it's also one that you don't lose much by not doing so. And I am honestly surprised how well they turned this series into 3D and would love to see someone else implement these grappling mechanics into another game. However one flaw with the gameplay itself is that mechanics encourage exploration. You want to see just where you can get to with the bionic arm, but the game is sadly overly linear. The areas may look open but there are invisible barriers everywhere to block you. Some kill you instantly and others simply don't let you progress. This ties into the bad timing. Triple Town is a match-three game paired with simplistic city building elements that requires more strategic thinking than games in this genre usually do.
The game is easy to learn and pretty hard to put away. The premise is simple: You start with a somewhat empty board, the "city", and then receive one component per turn, which you need to place on the board. Three of the same kind result in one piece of the next higher tier. For example, three bunches of grass give you a bush, and three (or more) bushes connected horizontally or vertically give you a tree.
The tricky part is that the resulting item appears in the spot where you put the previous item, and this is where the strategy originates from. Not only do you need to create matches on a small board, you also need to plan ahead so that future pieces fit together and you can upgrade to, say, a castle. Matching the highest tiers will grant you a treasure chest. with random loot.
Depending on the mode you play in (the game offers several with individual rulesets), there will also be bears. Bears wander around the board and turn into tombstones when you trap them. Three tombstones can be matched for a church (which does give you points) and three churches give you a cathedral. Building those is extra hard because the bears move around  and trapping them may require you to clutter the board.
To make it easier, you are given a storage spot where you can swap and keep one item, and there are special components such as the bot (that removes any item from the board) and the gem (which works like a joker). There is also a shop where you can purchase items and components with gold that you get by making larger matches. This is strictly in the game, there are no in-app purchases or DLC.
The other element of the game is your permanent capital city where you can place grain fields, military buildings, etc. which yield resources. These, too, can be matched and thus upgraded. If you play well, the game gives you rewards that can be put down in your capital.
Overall, Triple Town is a deeper-than-it-looks match-3 game that gets quite addictive (further made "worse" by there being achievements!). It's a friendly game that does not get stressful (it's all turn-based). Sadly, while the iOS version got ratings in the 80s and 90s, the identical PC version scored much lower. Different audiences, I guess.
I enjoy it, but I do like match-3 ganes, turn-based strategy and puzzlers. :)

I just wanted to note before I go on that the hours on above are innacurate. I have actually played this game much, much more than four hours, I just linked the wrong account to my Steam, so I play it through the Nexon launcher.
Mabinogi is a very fun game, but it's very hit and miss depending on the person. You either enjoy it or hate it, and it just depends on who you are. Because it's free to play, I would reccomend at least trying it out for a little bit and see if you get a feel for it. No risk involved!
It doooes have some pay to win elements to it, but not so drastically that it's absolutely required. In the beggining of the game, it's not so bad. It's actually better now then it used to be, as they have made the game a lot easier, and give you a free mount to begin with. As you go on, there starts to become a little pressure to buy some things. It doesn't make quests easier or anything, you're not ridiculously weak without it, it simply makes the game more enjoyable. It makes for more character customization, the pets are amazing (probably the best investment in the game, I would say), and the gachapons are usually fun to play and very addicting. I have spent QUITE a bit of money on the game myself, and so have many many of the players, not so much because you have to, more because they manage to make it so appealing.
As weird as it is to say, I actually don't think the battle mechanics or general game play are the best part of the game. Battle can be fun, but it can also get tedious and annoying. It gets pretty repetative, but as you get farther there are more and more fun skills. However, battle doesn't even have to be all that prevalent. There are a lot of different classes to play, some for different kinds of combat, others for different life styles entirely. Don't feel like fighting? Be a chef, be a cleric, be a bard! Most of them are very interesting and fun to try out, but most people tend to find their niche and stick with it.
The world is huge, and there's a lot of different places to see and things to do. Despite the sort of lack luster graphics, some of the scenery can be very beautiful! There's a lot of different activities, mobs, and dungeons around and most of them are very fun!
The game is okay to play solo at first, but the further you get into it, the more it becomes a multiplayer kinda game. I've actually kind of fallen out of the game a bit because I don't have a lot of friends to play the game with. My advice is to just be social. The game is WAY MORE FUN with friends!
There's a lot of short quest lines in the game with little mini stories to them, and also a lot of lone quests to play. But I would say the best quests are the story line quests. Not because they have better objectives and things to do, as far as I've noticed it's a lot of playing messanger. But! I think the stories are very fun to follow. They're pretty interesting, and it's fun to learn the lore! As far as the npcs go, it's a large spectrum between awesome and annoying as hell. Most characters aren't so bad, but everybody has some they hate.
All in all I would reccomend giving it a shot. If you don't like it, it's just a little time spent, not really any other risks. If you do end up liking it, though, there's a lot of game to have fun with, and you can make some pretty good friends!

It is the most immersive of the MMOs still in existence, and honestly the best.  Be aware that it is different from WoW or other traditional MMOs where you get a small group of people and run quests against NPCS with the random meaningless PvP.  In EvE, everything minus a few basic missions are player run; everything you buy is from players, all of the space is divided up with players, and it is a brutal experience solo.  Once you experience the big fleets and complex missions, particularly PvP, it is hard to match just how intense the game is.
There are a few hiccups though; solo playing, as mentioned earlier, is not easy or gratifying.  You will be limited to hi-sec and maybe low sec, and opporitunities will be few.  You will also feel powerless in PvP.  My advice would be to get out of hi-sec, and check on Reddit; the community in game will troll you to death, but if you are new and ask questions in game or on support community sites, people will shower you with isk and teach you everything.  I have often heard that many people quit because of the community, but that only really occurs when people try to talk tough and out of their league.
In short, try it, join a (null-sec) corp or a hi-sec ganking corp and you will learn to love EvE in no time!

Decided to give EXIT a try after watching a few videos and previews of the game.  I enjoyed playing through the various levels this game offers.  At first glance, it's a tiny bit pricey at $8.99, but given the amount of content and the future updates that will include many more levels to play through, you'll be getting more than enough value for the price.
Music is solid.  Controls are responsive, with only one ball being allowed to move at a time.  You can use the keyboard or mouse to move the balls around.
Gameplay is simple to pick up on with easy levels at first to show you the basics.  Simple objective to get all the balls into their matching color slots.  All levels are pure logic, with no guessing needed.  It's more learning the mechanics and obstacles in later levels and seeing how they play into solutions.
You can play in Casual, Normal, or Pro.  Only difference is the tighter time limits as you go up on difficulty.  So in Pro, you'll want to have solid routes planned already.  Achievements are not that hard to get after a little practice.  Once you beat a group of levels, you can practice the individual levels to learn new strategies, which can help in getting achievements and getting through Pro if you want to go that way.
Overall, a very solid puzzle game.  Good amount of replay value if you're trying to improve chapter stats.  With the future updates, this will get more value.

"Triple Town" is a unique Match 3 game where you build as big a colony town as possible by matching three or more objects. These objects can evolve into others by making appropriate matches (e.g. three Grasses make a Bush, three Bushes make a Tree...three Trees make a Hut...and there's more after that! ;-D). Matching more than three items, or mathcing certain high-end items will gift you different goodies that improve your score or other parts of the game! What you're given to place each time is random, but you can place these objects in any free space you want (with the objects melding where you place the last item in the cluster), so there's more strategy involved than the average Match 3.
Besides building materials, there are helpful items, like the Crystal, which is a wild card that completes matches (often important for much easier matching of high-end items!), but placing them without a Match makes a Boulder. Match three Boulders with the Crystals, however, and you'll get a Mountain that contains a Treasure Chest that contains a random prize. To get the Chest you need the Imperial Robot, which also lets you get rid of an unwanted item (most items penalize your score when destroyed, though...keep that in mind).
But watch out, there are Bears and Ninja Bears who'll try to impede your building! If you can trap a Bear or use an Imperial Robot on him, he turns into a Tombstone, and if you can trap three or more bears, the resulting Tombstones turn into a Church, and three of those make a Cathedral, and three of those make a Treasure Chest. Ninja Bears jump around and mostly can only be stopped by the Imperial Robot.
There are more items such as Fortune Cookies (which tell you the next five items that you'll be given to use), and Crates (which let you temporarily stash an item on the map), but these are gotten through the Shop and the Captiol City (more on those later!).
If you can't place something in a good spot right away, there's a little space set aside on each level where you can save an item, hopefully for a better use later in your game.
When you do run out of space (hopefully later rather than sooner!), your score is finalized, and you win some Coins and Capitol City materials (more on those in a bit!). If you need to stop playing a level, you can pick up where you left off later. There is no limit to how many times you can play a level; if you start a new level after finishing one, a new one is rolled for you!
There are six different kinds of levels: "Standard colony" (self-explainitory), "City on a lake" (actually, it's a "Standard colony" with a small lake in the center), "Peaceful Valley" (island with no Bears!), "A dangerous forest" (island with lots of Bears!), "City on an island" (small island). You can also revisit the Tutorials that you play the first time you launch the game, if you wish. You visit these from the Capitol City hub, which you build and improve mainly by making matches, too! You'll mainly get the materials from playing the game. The highest level buildings in your town will gift you materials and items everytime you earn so many points at a time in levels!
There is also a shop system that lets you buy building objects and helpful items with coins that you win in-game, mainly by completing levels. There are two different shops; one for the colonies, and one for the Capitol City. The colony shop lets you buy materials and items, but they're limited in supply, and replenish after so many turns. But if you've got the money, they can help you keep building for longer! The Capitol Shop lets you buy materials, Decorations, Expansion Tiles, and a Crane that lets you pick up and move an item to a better spot. These will cost you, though, so build some colonies!
There are personal High Score lists for each level, and 10 Achievements to earn. Recently, support for Steam's new Trading Card program has been added, too.
Overall, this is a great and different Match 3 game! Definitely check it out! :-D

EXIT is an appealing game that works on multiple levels.  While the objective is simple, as befits a puzzle game, the difficulty levels allow for very different experiences.  At the Easy level, it's a more casual game, allowing for trial and error, but at the higher difficulties, the levels are timed, with the timer starting as soon as you make the first move, so you have to visualize the entire sequence beforehand.  Even experienced puzzlers should enjoy that challenge.
The graphics are nice and crisp, the sound of the marbles rolling around is satisfyingly solid, the techno soundtrack is punchy but unobtrusive - the presentational elements are very well done for an Indie puzzler.
For a single run-through, the game probably offers about 4-5 hours of game-play, but the different game modes offered, along with the promise of more levels, could expand that substantially.  Since it's only been a week from release though, none of the additional levels have appeared yet.
That brings up the only downside to this title in my mind:  the price.  While I don't think it's unreasonable, there's no doubt that compared with the price of other puzzle games, this one stands out.  However, I think that most puzzle afficianados who try this out won't regret adding it to their libraries, so I recommend that if you have an interest in puzzle games, check this out.

- if you own naruto 3 and have yet to play it, just cry now and regret that you didnt buy DBX instead
- if you own neither naruto or DBX, get DBX

EXIT:
~~~~
Sometimes, in order to escape a situation, you might need a bit a luck or a bit of je ne sais quoi! Well, in “EXIT” you will need to use your marbles.  It is all about connecting them to their appropriate squares! Beware, your brain might get its hat on, pick up its luggage and run for the exit!
EXIT is a puzzle/casual game where you have to successfully place coloured marbles into their respective coloured squares to complete a stage.
After launching the game, you will arrive on the main screen where you can choose which difficulty and mode you want to play the game. They are two modes of play - campaign and survival. You must complete the campaign mode to unlock the survival. The easy difficulty will give you unlimited time to clear each stage but if you decide to play on the normal or pro, you will have a limited time to complete a stage, which can be quite tricky.
Essentially, what you have to do is to place the red, blue and green colour marbles into the same colour squares as fast as possible and using a limited number of movements. In some of the stages, you might be able to roll over a couple of icons. The 45 icons will give you 45 extra seconds to complete the stage; the green cross will give you an extra life; the coin icon will give extra points.
The difficulty will increase with each stage, which and be both fun and frustrating.
In terms of the gameplay, each stage is like a mini maze where marbles and square colours are located in different places within the maze. A countdown will start as soon as you touch or move one of the marbles. One trick you can use is to analyse the maze and study how to move the marbles before actually touching one of them.
Good 3D graphics and the soundtrack is really fun. I really like the progressive difficulty as you work your way up the stages. Control-wise, it’s ok but I occasionally have difficulty selecting a marble. The great news is that additional content will be available soon and will free of charge to everyone who purchases the game.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	60 levels to complete + more to come
-	Fun and addictive
-	Good soundtrack
-	Achievements & trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Can be a bit frustrating at time
Exit is a good workout for your marbles!
7/10

Having done 16 complete playthroughs on console of the first Borderlands, I bought the retail GOTY version. Was able to convert it to a Steam copy.
I have only done 3 playthroughs of Borderlands 2 and there's a reason I stopped at 3. Many poor design choices were made in Borderlands 2. It's still a great game, but there were too many issues.
The first Borderlands is by quite a large margin the superior installment of the Borderlands in my opinion. The game hasn't aged too badly, yet it is far less buggy than Borderlands 2.
A lot of Borderlands 2 felt too ambitious and got a lot wrong. Borderlands 1 is far more simple and gets everything pretty much on point first try. There are a few bugs that crop up every so often, but they are all fixed by doing a simple Melee attack.
Biggest issue with Borderlands 2 is the damage scaling is awful. Your weapons get out-dated every 4 or 5 levels. You know that gun that was amazing at Level 13? When you hit Level 18 it's now an absolutely garbage weapon.
Borderlands 1's damage scaling is a lot flatter. Your weapons can be usable for 15-20 levels above their "Level Requirement". I had a Level 13 shotgun that was still useable and effective at Level 35.
Weapon proficiency and the In-Game Challenge system in Borderlands 1 were a superior system compared to the "Badass Rank" system in Borderlands 2.
Borderlands 1 >>>>>>>>>>>> Borderlands 2

This is one of the most fun action games I have ever played.
It's actually fun to just move around in this game.  How many other games can make that claim?  Swinging around through the levels to get to places is actually fun and enjoyable.  On top of that, the combat is kept engaging with a wide variety of ways you can dispatch your opposition.  The bionic arm is not merely some gimick, the game is built around the unique additions it brings to the table.  The game is amazingly fun and appropriately challenging.
The only downsides to this game are things that aren't related to the actual game itself.  The story is terrible and so predictable you can set your watch by it.  For being a AAA game, you might expect there to be more variety in the environments, objects, character models, etc.  There's also some obvious in-game advertising, but none of it is anywhere that you wouldn't expect to see a bilboard; it's just that the bilboards are a little unrealistically geared toward a gaming audience.  And personally, I wish the game had levels you could back-track to instead of being arranged in a linear fashion.
But none of these flaws detract from what you really play the game for.  The gameplay is still solid, fun, and amazing.

When looking to buy this game, you should take note of the fact that it is in Early Access. This means that the playable content is very limited. However, there are 2 large co-op missions, 5 smaller co-op missions, 8 player versus player maps (I think), 2 weapons (customization is going to be added in later on for weaponry), five movement speeds (crouching, walking, crouch-running, jogging, sprinting)... it is already incredibly advanced for a game in Early Access, and the developers play the game as well, to communicate with the community and see what they want, and have excellent presence on the forums.
There are some glitches in the game. Naturally; it's Early Access. However, there are so few compared to most Early Access games, or even FPS games in general, that it's almost mind-boggling. Each update is extensively tested and prepared before it becomes available to a small segment of the community - Spearhead testers - and are then further scanned for glitches and bugs before being made available to the entire community.
Many people had a bad experience during the Free Week, and gave this game bad reviews. Unfortunately, this is mostly because of people playing it on the Free Week only to annoy other players, and the limited customization available at this point. However, what many people don't seem to understand is that it is in Early Access, even though it entered Free Week; it's nowhere near complete, and rating it as if it were the full game is unfair to the developers and potential buyers.
Now on to gameplay.
When I first began playing the game, I went into multiplayer. DO NOT DO THIS. The game is so extraordinarily fast-paced that unless you play co-op and single player first, the people in PvP will be killing you so fast you'll suspect they're hacking - quick hint, they're not; they've generally played the game for literally days straight, and have become fifty times as good as any beginner. Don't think you can compete just because you've played other FPS games.
The robots in single player and co-op are still a tremendous challenge. Start off Easy and find that, without other people to revive you, you're dead in minutes. Two to five shots will kill you in Easy, and it only gets harder.
One thing I've found is that many people complain that Realistic isn't any harder than the other modes. Here's the thing: It is, but not for the reasons most people think. Yes, the robots one-shot you on Realistic. Yes, they have a shorter delay to begin attacking once they see you. Yes, they see you better in good lighting and notice you more quickly in bad lighting. However, the real thing that got me was that the closer you are, the faster they react; open a door and there's a robot immediately on the other side? You're dead.
In spite of this game being in Early Access, the amount of content already implemented is amazing, and the gameplay and realism of the game is incredible. So there are a few glitches and fewer weapons than you'd want in an FPS game. So what? It's still remarkably complete for something in this stage.
I would definitely recommend buying this game, and if you don't feel like it's right for you, check back in a month or two; the content increases with updates constantly. The results might surprise you.

Exit is a wonderful puzzle game. It is simple, but I find it very relaxing to play and solve each level. The coins are a nice little bonus challenge as well, though not required to beat the level… technically. Over 60 levels make this a pretty good buy, even if it is $11.99 not to mention that the developer mentioned that there will be more levels coming out and will be available for FREE to anyone who buys the base game. You can play by clicking each ball with the mouse and then clicking again for the direction, or use the keyboard to choose directions and toggle between balls.
The three game modes are Easy, Normal, and Pro. Basically it just means that you have a tighter time limit the harder the difficulty you choose, and believe me when I say that it will pressure you on some levels. My advice to people playing this game is to analyze each level before starting to move the balls. The timer will not start counting down until you select a ball. Also, be patient with each move. I have screwed up a few times already by moving the wrong ball because I did not properly select the one I actually wanted to move.
As for what can improve the game, I can only think of two things. The first, and most important, would be an option to turn off the motion of the board. Although it does make it a bit disorienting (or who knows, it may be my current sleep deficiency) and therefore slightly more challenging, I think that some people may find it hard to look at if they get motion sick easily. The second thing would be more background music tracks. But to be honest that is asking for a bit much. It is a good game regardless of what music is playing in the background.
At the time that I am writing this review, I have only made it through 24 levels (not counting the demo)… mostly because it is 2:45 AM. All of them have been a blast and I look forward to playing more of this game.

Do not come here expectng a game. Do not come here expecting a story. Come here for a calm, immersive, beautiful world. You literally just walk. And look. And listen. And Everything comes to life around you. You don't have to be one of those hippy-dippy "peace love and happiness" ♥♥♥♥♥ to understand. Because there's nothing to understand. This is a game about relaxing. And walking. And wondering.

To be honest, I started this game with high expectations. Loads of people I know were talking about Telltale games, which they were told were amazing. The same resonance seems to be in the professional reviewer community. And then you play the game. If you can call it that. You don't really play at all. Telltale games are (essentially) glorified movies. You move the story along by choosing dialogue lines. While your choices matter in the short run, the grand scheme of the story stays unchanged, so it quickly begins to feel rather futile. You might as well program a bot that always clicks the first option and enjoy the movie. "But wait", you ask, "isn't there any actual gameplay?". Well, I'm glad you asked. There is one form of "gameplay": Quicktime events. That's right. The worst kind of gameplay.
So overall, while the storyline is quite funny and at times original, I would hesitate calling this a game. It is desperately trying to be a movie. But then, I'm quite sure, this wouldn't make for a good movie either. It is, in one word, disappointing.
TL,DR: Quicktime events are the only gameplay. The majority of the "game" is spent staring at the screen and making dialogue choices without meaningful impact. If you were hoping for another fun Borderlands adventure, you will be sorely disappointed.
Judging by the "Overwhelmingly Positive" reviews, it seems that people around here are more and more looking for the one-way kind of entertainment that TV used to offer and streams offer these days. If that is for you, this game might be for you. But honestly, you're probably cheaper off and even happier watching someone play through it on a stream. It will cost you even less effort than playing the game and it allows you to shut of your brain entirely.

A short game, with lightweight mechanics, although both of these things are in keeping with the original (and awesome) Bionic Commando games. Be aware if you are a fan of the series like me, this is not the remake, the remake is "Bionic Commando: Rearmed" (which is actually not bad), and I happened to pick this up with it as a bonus.
It's a simple 3D shooter/platformer. The central character Nathan Spencer (if you aren't familiar with him) has an extending bionic arm that enables him to swing around a bit like spiderman with guns, and this is his first - and probably only - departure from the world of 2D side-scrollers.
The all-important grabbing/swinging mechanic is done nicely, enabling the player to smoothly chain swings and feeling "fun", gunplay is ok (always zoom in for max damage) and the bionic arm can be put to effect in combat - making it fun to clear a mob of enemy soldiers without firing a shot. There is some throwing around of objects which can get a little janky at times but is mostly just fun.
Difficulty is not (in my opinion) punishing, and the game itself is playable enough to be fun to the end - although in traditional Bionic Commando style you will be facing lots of the same enemies, so be prepared for that. Some of the bosses are a bit easier than you'd expect, although not to the point where it spoils the game, and there is one boss (no spoilers) that makes for quite a long battle.
I completed it in a shade under 12 hours, and I tend to take my time completing games. The game is generally polished, except for the fact that button presses are generally listed as control pad buttons which sucks if you are playing with a KB/M.
It's not earth-shatteringly great, but I enjoyed it from start to finish and will probably be playing it again.
PS: This "review" is for the single player experience. I didn't try out multi-player - the online play doesn't seem to work. The LAN play actually looks like it will be a blast, I will try when I can cajole a friend into it.
PPS: There's a little bit of gratuitous swearing in this, including for one boss fight where it happens at random. I don't mind but my kids love the Bionic Commando games so I'm glad I played through it first - you might not want to play this while granny is in the room.

I feel like this is overall one of the most underrated and unappreciated games on Steam. Despite a slow start and some small annoyances like a lacklustre story and some weird technical choices, Bionic Commando is very fully featured and comes with its own achievements, collectible/upgrade memories, area notes, a great variety of enemies, excellent boss fights and most importantly a plain old fashioned fun central gameplay mechanic.
There were plenty of highlights in Bionic Commando for me and none of them stood head and shoulders above the rest because most components were fully rounded. Large open maps were very rare in gaming until Croteam came on the scene years later, and the textures, changing environments, well designed levels and artifacts all create a compelling and fairly memorable world.
The weapons are also rounded, and in most modern shooters you'll find yourself sticking with just one or two weapons, whereas in Bionic Commando, while the firing animations are occasionally mildly annoying, everything is well designed and different enemies and situations warrant different weapons. The variety of enemies is also worth mentioning, even if I thought the standard grunts were frivolous and redundant by the end, the different types of enemies with different variations added a depth to combat, and the boss fights all have a small setup, good intro animations and a genuine need to remember arm moves and combat techniques to progress which harks back to the good oldschool learn-and-apply method.
* Consiquential achievements are far too rare and they're used here to give you upgrades and extras when you experiment with your abilities. They actively reward varied play. Bulletstorm is the only other game I can think of off-hand that does anything similar and it's very welcome.
There was nothing game-ruining here, but there were a few annoyances worth mentioning. Right off the bat the tutorial segment is a frustration because the controls are mapped for console rather than PC, which stand out because the mechanics take some time to get used to. Small things like the unskippable cutscenes which made for waiting several seconds to load the same boss fight each time you died, collectibles having a strange audio flag that pulled you out of any immersion, and the God awful menu system which makes you go through 3 menu progressions, then reload back to the title screen, then access another two menu points to quit just boggle the mind. Together these small annoyances made this feel like a slightly weaker title.
The other thing that actively takes away from the game though is the marriage between great voice acting and poor dialogue. The dialogue is really subjective, and personally I found the crude humour and occasional bad one-liner fitting for what is essentially a fun mindless action game, but after hiring such great voice actors it's a shame they haven't spent more time and effort on the story and writing, which could've easily made a good game great.
At just £6.49/9.99€/$9.99 at the time of review, Bionic Commando clocks in at an average play-time of 8 hours and the collectibles add at least another 6 or 7 hours for completionists. This is also a fantastic game to come back to and I can see anyone interested in speedrunning having a blast trying for a faster completion with this game.
My conclusion then, is that this is good value for money and a good buy for anyone who doesn't mind a mildly dated and fairly mindless but strong platforming shooter with a hidden depth of ability.

TripleTown is a fun strategy/puzzle game in which you get random tiles to place that, when grouped in 3's, turn into the next rank of tile. Put 3 weeds together, you get a bush. Put 3 bushes together, you get a tree. Put 3 trees together, you get a house. Simple concept, yet there is a struggle to manage space on the board as well as the addition of bears that you place, but are mobile afterwards. These guys get in your way, invariably screwing up your best laid plans.. and not to mention the ninja bears, who blink around the board each turn. After the game finishes, you are rewarded with bonus tiles that you can play on your home island map (which plays with similar rules, but sans bears). I will probably not be explaining how fun this title is. There is a free version of this online on facebook if you want to get a taste of it. This version just eliminates the need to wait for turns to refresh or for the user to have to buy extra turns (which is annoying as the game is addictive). Well worth the $10 I spent on it.

Checked this game out during a free weekend on the Beta. Beautiful graphics, interesting adjustments to the normal fps character style, esp in the respirations, etc. Beautiful environments with nicely done environmental effects and some really nice 'world' touches oustide the normal gameplay environment; additional areas to wander at base, overhead mechanisms for environmental control in simulation rooms. Nice interactivity with the environment - such as the ability to shoot lights and the way that the lighting effects detection.
A few things that could use improvement while still in beta:
Some environments can be a bit overly dark at times even at the highest brightness settings.
Objectives, Use Buttons, Tools/Object, etc. need different symbols. The letter in a diamond doesn't work for everything and begins to get confusing as these things overlap.
Missions need save points. It's one thing to have to restart a section/level, kill the 10 guys and reach the next point... it's another to have to restart, have to walk/run a while to get to the area where the gameplay actually begins, creep over terrain to the side of the building, snipe the 4 guards, get the key, snipe the 4 guards, creep to next area, creep around the light, look through the crack and be killed by a guard. Repeat entire level, kill that guard, creep around everything for another 20 minutes and be randomly killed by another unseen guard and have to restart the level again. I appreciate the stealh aspect and the unexpected... but when you have to creep everywhere with litle action and start over completely each time, gameplay drags and interest wanes.
Enjoyable and definitely worth some play even while still in beta and without the above improvements.

Triple Town is an excellent match-3+ game with a small twist. Combine three bushes and they'll turn into a tree. Create and match three trees and it'll become a house and so on and so forth. It's all about the points and the coins. It's quite addictive, trust me.
The coins can be used to upgrade your hub, a place where you can pick a gameplay mode (sort of) before playing/ Or it can be used to buy items, like extra houses or bushes. Unfortunately, items are limited so you have to choose wisely. The items are also quite expensive, so buying an item isn't always a good choice.
The hub is all about creating farms, mines and other buildings. See it as some sort of mini-game. Except you can't really mess things up here. You'll be able to collect rewards from your buildings every couple of hours. Rewards that'll help you when playing the 'real' game. The developers haven't thought things through with the time limit though, because earning coins is kind of slow and tedious and waiting for several hours before being able to collect a reward could make people lose interest (more quickly than intended).
But I heard it might be changed in the near future, so let's just hope for the best.
Anyway, Triple Town is easily one of the my favorite casual games.

I feel like my issues with this game have less to do with this game in particular, and more to do with the style of Telltale "games" as a whole. The experience felt less like playing a game and more like watching a movie or TV series, except that the periodic interactions required to keep the story going prevented me from enjoying it in the same way I would a movie. Some might argue that's the price for a custom story, but very few choices seemed to matter 30 seconds after being made, and even then I suspect no choice affects the overall story much.
As a fan of the Borderlands series I did find some enjoyment in the story, but I could have gotten that from reading a synopsis or watching someone else's screen recording. If you are also a Borderland's fan and want the story told in Tales I would recommend finding an alternate way of getting it.

Risen 3 is the type of game that will appeal to those who enjoy the solo parts of certain MMOs.
The nameless hero is ultra cool and seriously♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off that he has lost his soul. The language that spews forth from his mouth is foul but it is also smart and full of confidence and no nonsense attitude. In my opinion the voice acting altogether is  very clear and consise for a pirate themed game. It is sometimes exhausting to listen to the amount of voice work in RIsen 3 though and I found myself skipping it to get to the point of meandering conversations or more prominently when the fixed camera gets stuck behind an object.
The orchestral score adds to the cinematic quality of the game, more on that later. Classically epic for a swashbuckling adventure to the pit of a man's soul while slaying undead monsters and feral beasts. Music quality seems muffled underneath the sound effects but reappears at the right moments to genuinely solidify the moments of sentimentality and heroics. The sentimentality that exists between the gamer and this adventure, the game supplies the avenue for the heroics.
Sound in general is good. Your going to hear the seagulls high pitched squwack on the beach and  they are there to accidentally interrupt those moments of sentimentality that this experience provides. The sound of the waves and ocean could encapsulate the vivid scenery when the 3d sound would like to work. Chatter from npc's is repetitive.
The views displayed during gameplay are heavy hitters for sure. If you like the bloom, then keep it on, but by default it is a bit too much. I am not sure if the landscape design and environmental effects are purposely directed to the player's best field of view but you can rotate the camera enough to see the brilliance. Which is nice, the game is not over trying to establish itself as an over-achiever with AAA graphics, but what is there is decidedly cool looking. Player models do their justice and close inspection of monsters shows surprisingly deep design. I feel the land design, including craggy landscapes and beautiful beach vistas are only eclipsed by the feeling of traversing over them and losing your poor AI companions in the process.
If you can see it, then you can go to it - most of the time, that is a good thing because with the amount of exploration here - not being able to go somewhere is a clue that there is absolutely nothing to gain by going there. okay, the game is deep on many levels. The islands are charachters in themselves and hold many secrets and surprises. You will explore shallow and deep caves, old ruins, mystical rock formations and many more fantasy cliches. This game is different, firstly it is a pirate adventure so things are just a bit off kilter than the standard fantasy fare, the lore holds it's own steadfast and doesn't apply the pressure to the player to like it. Secondly the level design is in my opinion, the entire game and it surely amounts to being something to experience in it's entirety. Quests are abound and only those who play CRPGs all the time will get sick and tired of the hubs and fast travel openings that games like these emit. There is a large portion of learning the game here, then a middle part that is exhausting but refreshing up until the final chapter which plays out kind of like a thriller. That is how this game is like a cinemaic experience. Seemingly so in the perspective given to the player and his choices during gameplay such as dialogue or it's open worldness.
This ancient world made up of islands did feel a bit like it was showing the player the motions to run through it, but there is so much charachter depth to sink your role playing teeth in here. Lots of weapons and skills, crafting. It should be stated that there is not much armor to choose from but there is cosmetic diversity thats fundamental to the storyline. The companions you accumulate over the entirety of the quest definetely makes it feel like family and the comedy shines through more than a handful of times.
It could be said that this game is a loot grind or simply quest after quest after quest but that is not necassarily an insult as I have meticulously attempted to be a completionist and loot everything. I have enjoyed the game as a whole and really liked going on treasure hunts and living like a pirate in this fantasy role playing game.
As far as combat is concerened, I felt this - there is alot of it! The amount of enemies to fight is comparitive to an all out action game, minus the bosses, but the combat system here is extremely banal compared to a spectacle fighter. Although the combat engine is adequate and it is up to the player to find their own style of magic, melee and missile, the wish for a quicker resolution to encounters may occur due to the engine's simplicity of hit or be hit and remembering enemy patterns. All in all this method is rightly better than all out button mashing or turn based applicatons. There are the occassional stuttering animations not just in the combat, but this can be overlooked, but add in, at the same time a grossly boggled camera in unleveled jungle floors mired in bush, then you may be reloading a previous save.
This is a game that knows it is a long ordeal, and epic it may be when realizing the credibility of the game design and excellent mechanics overshadowing the many minor bugs that fail to sink this ship.
Advice: Try the shapeshifting skills and admire the animation.

The Wolf Among Us has long held the title of my favourite 'choice based game', staying well ahead of the competition posed by Life is Strange or Telltale's Walking Dead.  This game has taken that title by miles.   Tales from the Borderlands is both one of the most heartfelt and the funniest story to come out of Telltale, and manages to maintain the style of the main Borderlands games while having a far better story and much more realistic dialogue.  The characters in this game are far more relatable than any of the previous protagonists, and you will probably care far more about them because of it, especially in the moments when Telltale pulls their signature 'everything went wrong' moments out.  But through all the drama it maintains a generally lighthearted tone, with lots of laughs from both physical humour and great writing.  It also has the two best action scenes in any game of this genre.  I won't go into details for fear of ruining the surprises, but believe me that you'll know them when you see them.
This is a must play whether you care about the main series of Borderlands or not.  If you've never played the originals, they're good games in their own right, but a wiki summary of the series will be enough for you to get a great experience out of this one.  A full recommendation from me.  CATCH A RIIIIIIIIDE!

Okay, I did not expect something this good from TFTB. I've played a couple other Telltale games before, and have this kind of love-hate relationship with them. The narrataive always feels extremely strong, but leaves something missing, in the case of TWD, it's the lightness of a game. The Wolf Among Us, it's the explanations of what is happening.
It was absolutely not the case with this one. Telltale gave a fresh brand new story that Gearbox will be able to use in the future. Familiar and new faces came and were loved once more, or hated entirely to their core. A humour known to the series stays, but an additional element of drama is put, plus we get to see more than just the vault hunter lifestyle on Pandora : you get to see the bandit lifestyle, Helios and Hyperion, and the colonist one.
But if you never played any Borderlands and are telling yourself ''hey, I'll try this Telltale game.'' First off: HOW DID YOU NEVER PLAY BORDERLANDS BEFORE?! Second, you're probably going to miss a lot of references in the game, and you'll be lost as to what the goal of the game actually is.
If you HAVE played Borderlands before, pick it up. I guarantee you, if you liked the story and setting of the others, you will love the story TFTB brings on the table. And you might want to pick it up soon, Gearbox will probably use this story to start the events of Borderlands 3. Too much happened here and it will start a new age.
Personnally, I want to say to Telltale : Bravo. I doubted you for a while on this one. I should never have. Personal all-time favorite in the narrative aspect and I'm sorry I didn't give you enough credit. Now please, bring season 2.

The dialogue in this game is so absolutely, hilariously, cheesy. The voicing of our "Hero" was probably supposed to be along the lines of Captain Jack Sparrow, but actually sounds more like Jason Stratham (Transporter) doing an impression of Mel Gibson playing Jack Sparrow. ;o) And the general character animations during dialogues were usually restricted to swaying back and forth and a few complimentary waves of the hand. Oh, and Patty, looks like a strip-a-gram in a naughty pirate costume, which MAY be very distracting for some players.
But, you know what? None of that's, by any means, a deal-breaker. I did groan a few times during the first hour or two, but once I got used to it, I actually started to accept it as "just the style of the game" and began to find it quite funny.
As for questing, well it takes a little while to get yourself up and running to a level where you can at least deal with stuff. Spending a good few hours on the same island at the start (your chosen faction) will serve you well. After that, it's off to explore the map, and do all the usual "Questy" stuff...which was really quite fun, and only minimally "back & forth, back & forth".
The graphics/environment were pretty good, and the free-to-roam aspect was fun. Especially once you've figure out how to get to the seemingly impossible to reach places.
If you like this type of game, it's pretty good fun, and does not take itself seriously AT ALL! It does for RPG-questing games, what Spinal Tap did for Rockumentaries.
70 hrs of fun, no regrets...8/10

I'm not new to Gothic/Risen series. It's reception was fairly mixed with a small dedicated fanbase. Most criticism came from  lack of polish, overal clunkines and no clear gameplay guidelines. Risen 3 is no different. Although it's far from original Gothic's awkwardness, the core of the game mechanics is the same. Much of the blame was put on difficulty scaling. You're free to go anywhere you like, be it danger seeping cave that's to be tackled by powerful character or trivial fights with monsters as challanging as shooting shotgun at chickens with nunchucks. Risen 3 hints what needs to be done but it doesn't hold your hand throghuout the game.
Risen's 3 contuinues it's precedessor carribean setting which is quite unusual, yet eye-catching. Piratey theme is dominant in this RPG. Being so colorful as Risen 3 is, some RPG gamers may be a bit of put off. What needs to be said, is that plot and characters are less than exciting and unique but not subpar - just the usual fantasy RPG mambo-jumbo plus ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ish protagonist.
What shines in third Risen installment are numerous quests, items and skills. The latter, though not balanced perfectly, provide variety in gameplay. Many assignments are clones of each other but somehow it manages to be satysfing. At least for a bit more than half of the playthrough it's challenging and gaining experience either by killing monsters or completing quests is satisfying. By the end I was far too powerful to have any kind of challange but getting there was a pleasure and that's the strong point of this title.
In conclusion, Risen 3 is surprisingly a somewhat solid RPG. Lurking in shadows of AAA titles, it's mostly overlooked. That's a shame because even with it's shortcomings I honestly enjoyed Risen 3. If it's on a sale, just try it. Just don't expect much in story compartment.
Final score : 7/10
The good :
- Attractive graphics
- Lots of quests, items and skills
- Freedom to choose your own path and game style
The bad :
- Pirate setting may be not appealing for many RPG fans
- Some of the Gothic's clunkiness is still there
- Story and characters are ok. Just ok.

I grew up playing Bionic Commando in the 90s. It was a side scrolling masterpiece: innovative gameplay, epic level design and an actual storyline.The kid in me was trembling with expectation when I started playing this 3D sequel.
Although I was annoyed by the many modern gaming sins: no health bar, mandatory/not always well placed checkpoints (now that just added 5h of replaying through parts of levels thank you), invisible level barriers (radiation and water) and etc...Still, I was literally hooked, in part because I was curious to see what's next: the environments are lush even if the level design is either repetitive or slightly inconsistent (often too hard or too easy). By adding more realistic FPS gunplay Grin took away some of the fun of shooting bullets and chasing them while swinging with your arm, in fact shooting and swinging simultaneously is never really required so you're either playing 'Prince of Persia' jumping and flying around or 'Splinter Cell' shooting guards in buildings over the shoulder. The only two cool gameplay mechanics are the dive bomb (death from above) and the abilities to throw objects (even cars and billboards) but Spencer's a total wimp as a couple strong shots will take him down most of the time and even near the end of the game he has limited abilities and a small arsenal (only 4 classic guns). And as the controls are far from perfect (specially for precision swinging) you will die abundantly.
There are some epic moments like the boss fights, but all in all this feels for fans only, the amount of pleasure to be derived from this mechanical arm is somewhat inferior to the pain. But if you wanna find out why the hell Spencer has dreadlocks this is the game for you!

The world of Bionic Commando is a blast to traverse and it is oddly satisfying to play around with Spencer's bionic arm. While I recommend Bionic Commando, there are a few things that detracted from my experience that I feel are worth discussing.
The story is a zany military conspiracy satire of sorts that isn't and shouldn't be taken too seriously. Characters are rather flat and predictable. The protagonist in particular is almost impossible to empathize with due to his violent and cliche behavior. That being said, I would like to stress that Bionic Commando is all about the power trip you receive from the gameplay, not the story so Spencer's lackluster tragedy is acceptable.
While enemy soldiers pose an appropriate threat most of the time, the sheer volume of enemies in the later sections is more annoying than fun. Mech enemies in particular are a chore to face in the higher difficulty settings because the amount of time it takes to set up an attack leaves the player open to sniper fire. The unforgiving enemy placement rewards cowardly tactics that goes against the power trip philosophy of the game.
Finally, without spoiling too much of the game, the later boss fights are poorly executed. Instead of making interesting use of the bionic arm mechanics, these fights boil down to waiting for your turn to attack then entering a prompt to deliver the final blow.
Overall these are nitpicky complaints. The game is great and consider giving it a shot if you're on the fence of a purchase.

On the surface, this game appears to be a clicker fused with the idle benefits of
...and you're right.  You click on the house, get screams (currency), and spend those screams on upgrades to your haunted house to produce more screams for you.
For most of the game, you'll probably be using an autoclicker, but after a while, this game becomes more of an idle game than a clicker game as your click screams will be quickly outclassed by your idle screams.  But fret not, the dev thought of a benefit for when you reach this point.  You can click various areas on the house to activate some minigames (or...Microgames, really) that will lead towards achievements.
The graphics don't seem to be fantastic, but for a free casual game, they're somewhat charming.  You'll find various aspects to be inspired by various Halloween stories and movies.  Can you spot all the references?
Of course, when you complete one "map"/"world", you'll be granted a new world (so long as you pay some gems on the access key to the new area).  Plan well, and you can 100% this game for free.  Keep in mind, however, that it will require a little dedication.  You may find yourself bored while sitting and waiting for the next milestones...and you might find yourself irritated from the repetition of the soundtrack and sound effects.
That said, yes, I do recommend
to those who enjoy Halloween stuff and want some easy achievements.   However, you may be opting to use your own autoclicker shortly after picking this game up.

Gunpoint is a stealth-based puzzle-platform game from indie developer Tom Francis. It was released earlier this month and in it, players will take on the role of secret agent Conway in his task to be a great spy. Players will be able to infiltrate buildings and retrieve data from mission objects by avoiding guards and other security features using gadgets and Bullfrog pants. The trick with the game is thinking completely outside the box because you get a Crosswire device fairly early in the game and this allows you to make some fun and very interesting things happen.
If you see a light switch on the bottom floor and want it linked to the gun of an agent, then that’s something that you can go ahead and do with the Crosswire. The end result would be that as you turn the light on or off, the agent’s gun starts firing uncontrollably. This is one of the funnier aspects of the game because you can actually do a lot of useful things with the Crosswire. For example, you could wire it so that a light in this room, opens the door in another room and when a guard walks past a certain trigger, it would open the floor beneath him, making him fall to his death. This is the nature of Gunpoint and as you progress through the game, more and more things will crop up for you to do. Thankfully though, a lot of thought has been put into it and you can only Crosswire with the same colour and you will need to progress through stages that way.
What’s awesome about Gunpoint though is not just the way in which the pixelated game plays, it’s the ability to tell jokes and create a story out of almost thin air. The game is funny and has a dark sense of humour about it which appeals to me in a great way. It starts off with you flying out of a window and landing on a floor by complete and utter mistake. A few seconds worth of flashback earlier, you see Conway testing out his new Bullfrog pants which allow him to leap high and walk up and down walls. From there, you can tell that the game is going to be something special and thankfully, it really is.
In and amongst the humour and silly things that go on, Gunpoint is able to tell a story to gamers, one that is engrossing nevertheless. I found myself first skimming through a lot of the conversation but as things progressed, I found it really difficult to formulate a reply in the multiple choices that are given to you.
All in all, Gunpoint is a short, little game and will probably only get you about two or three hours of gameplay.

Character customization has alot to offer, although sometimes you do see alot of clones walking around, you be the judge. The character needs more specialization than just putting points into particular attributes. I remember being able to unlock special abilities in BT3 (for example immune to charge attacks etc..) and build characters with them as you would imagine them to be. Argueably this made those characters pretty OP which could be a problem for online, but we'll get to that.
The controls are absolutely diabolical. The whole ctrl/alt thing to do supers and ultimates is frustraing. I ended up rebinding them to my naga mouse, so at least I use my thumb and can keep up with the game instead of having to stretch my fingers into some wierd position to be able to sit on WASD, Q, R, shift, ctrl, alt and space. This "fast paced" type of game is not designed for those types of keybinds.
Graphics:
Camera angles become a pain when you get put in a corner, or your enemy is directly above or below you, or you're in a small arena (eg. Frieza's ship). Basically the camera angles suck, except for when you are far away from your enemy in the middle of a field. Other than that the graphics are the same as I'd expect from any other Dragonball Game. It's interesting that they have some scenes where there is actual cartoon animation. Wish they'd have done that alot more instead of using the in-game animation.
Gameplay:
Plays like BT/RB series games, over the shoulder view. They've changed the way transformations work now. Super Saiyan is now more of a buff than a character change. Before if you transformed you'd have an entirely new moveset, whereas now you have the same moves, just more power.
Has a fair bit of "end game" style content in the form of having to repeat missions in specific ways to unlock items. That I do like. The story missions seem pretty short, but it makes up for it by offering a diverse amount of "parallel missions" for you to do. You can do these parallel missions offline, or online co-op.
Which brings me to online play:
Hardly existent. Sure you can see players in the lobby, most of which are AFK. Now I'm not even going to sugar coat this one - the server this game is hosted on, is absolute dog♥♥♥♥♥♥ It is constantly lagging out, or just unavailable. When you go to do an online parallel mission, it takes way too long to search for a "quick join" match, and by the time you have actually found a match and you go to join, the lobby is full, kicking you out of the entire thing only to have to search again. Alternatively, people seem to not understand what "private slots" are, and you find a lobby only to be kicked out by the person that is hosting is and saving a place for his friend...
Now lets talk about chat. There is none. Well there is.. but there isn't. Users can use some wierd "auto text" messages, which can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥when there is a 10 year old spamming the same auto text over and over again in the lobby, and all you can hear is the annoying sound that plays every time someone puts a message in chat.... and guess what?? It can't be turned off. Massive fail on that one.
Don't ask about online battles, because I pretty much refuse to go near them. After playing online on BT2, BT3 and Raging Blast, I learned that online battle is not a test of someone's skill, it is a test of who can spam the most OP super and ultimate attacks. I will not be going anywhere near that♥♥♥♥♥♥..

Pros:
Beautiful scenery. Literal galactic vistas that can be more beautiful than your own night sky. Highly detailed ships. (So detailed you can identify what the armament is by looking at them.) Cons:
This game is one of the most unforgiving MMOs out there. If you blow up your big fancy ship that you worked months to save up for and trained to fly.. Too bad. It's gone now. Have to buy a new one. And if you had implants, they're gone now too.  No magical respawn where you appear in a "safe zone" complete with your newly rebuilt ship. Nope, you regain consciousness in your home station.. Another con.. players can be giant jerks sometimes and scamming is rampant in the trade hubs. The devs take a very hands-off approach to this. So be wary about deals that seem to good and read every detail of contracts.

Much better than expected. I did not watch anything Dragon Ball for something close 15 years back in the days of Toonami. Not a super-fan, yes I liked it as a kid and grew out of it. I know some kids from school never grew out of it, ever. Not a problem to me. I'm not coming into this game as a fan of the series, I'm looking at it purely from gameplay perspective.
Honestly? Wish they did the bits where you wander around town better. Shorten the walking distances or at least let your character fly faster in town instead of just running at a (comparitively) slow pace. Going between shops and other places takes way too long. Story I am indifferent to but the writers came up with a neat way to re-do a lot of fights from the shows without breaking the canon, you have to go back in time to fix alterations made to the past like Goku getting beaten when the Saiyans initially invaded etc. and with your help things are set back straight while you are hunting down whoever is trying to alter the timelines. There is lots of customization. Like a crazy huge amount. Tons of moves though at least half of the ones I unlocked so far are just not useful or extremely circumstantial. You can make a wider taller stronger character or a thin and smaller fast character, there are a few races and each gender of each race has statistical differences even. Everything seems well done for the most part, lots of tiny details.
Gameplay itself is great. Not sure why, this is the first time I really got into a fighting game for years. This one is fun. The controls can take a quite a bit to learn since there is more to this game than simply punching like light strikes, heavy strikes, charged heavy strike to break a block, grappling, blocking, teleporting behind someone or quickly teleporting short distance to the sides, just so much it can be overwhelming for the first few hours. I would hate to play with with a keyboard and mouse and suggest a Windows 360 controller since that has native support. The only gameplay nag I have is how you must repeat missions to get some random drops like certain moves or pieces of cothing you want, and since it's random you might have to play a mission several times over and still not get what you want. Lots of people suggest save editors for this exact reason, no need to waste your life doing the same thing over and over. I did not go down that route yet, the game is still fresh to me and I don't mind a little bit of grind for exp and stuff. But once I get to the point where I don't want to repeat missions I will do that.
As for online the co-op is awesome. PvP is not. Firstly don't even try PvP unless level 99. Period. Otherwise you are going to be beaten on the basis of stats alone. And from what I heard even if you get to level 99 then you will still lose several fights due to lots of people who have played this game and a prior one similar to it for a very long time. Not to mention lots of the top fighting builds are the same thing, there are a few specific stats like basic attack and stamina that matter much much more than the rest and builds that do not max those two stats out are at a distinct disadvantage. So the game isn't balanced for PvP. I did not buy it for PvP. I was honestly happy to learn there was a form of co-op anyhow. I'm playing singleplayer to get better at the controls mostly and will hit the co-op a bit after that. I'm surprised I'm having a lot of fun playing this game but it is what it is. Still expensive though, buy on sale like I did. I don't think this qualifies as a game worth $40 or more. $30 seems like a more than acceptable deal, less is best.

I was really hoping to enjoy this game despite what the negative reviews had to say about it. Unfortunately they were quite right.
The AI is basically complete rubbish, even on the highest difficulty level. If you find a higher spot you can jump up to, or some boxes to jump behind, the melee guys got nothing on you (save for the first boss which has an impressive reach on his swing). Ranged units feel cheap. I've had them not even try to find me at times, then shoot me the instant they can see me, including through walls at times. And many of the baddies can run faster than you. Considerably faster. And when it comes to the exploding baddies, that really sucks.
The level design is both nice and leaves a lot to be desired. In my short time playing through the game, I fell through the map at least five different times. One of the times it wasn't even an instant death, I just saw the game world float out of existance and needed to manually reload the save. I also saw the baddies fall through the world a number of times. The levels themselves felt reasonably well built in terms of layout and lighting, though they also felt fairly empty too. And a others said, it's a very linear game. You go into a room, some silly looking energy field goes up (though not always), and swarms of baddies come at out. The spawning sucks. I went into a room to have some cover from one of the waves and found that it was one of their spawning locations for that wave. On the plus side, you always know when a new wave is about to start because the game always saves just before go far enough into a room to trigger it. And after a wave it over you generally can find enough medpacks to get you back up or close to full health.
Oh, and don't even bother trying to rebind your keys, cause you can't. I ended up going into my keyboards settings to set the keys to what I wanted. And there is no point to the reload bind, as there is no reload for any of the guns...
I can't recommend this game. It just wasn't fun for me. If the AI wasn't so lame/cheap and if the levels didn't have so many holes for me to fall through so often, I probably would have had a lot more fun. If you must get it, do so on sale.

Another amazing pixelated adventure!  There are so many different settings and scenes to explore, with such variety.

I have truly never seen people use pixel graphics is such a touching and beautiful way!  I found myself screen shooting a number of images that were so very expressive.

Bionic Commando is a seriously underrated game. It is a sequel to Bionic Commando Rearmed and the story continues off from there, placing the player in charge of Nathan Spencer.
Story: The game has a cliched story about a soldier seeking revenge after some people do him wrong. The characters aren't all that interesting and the voice acting in general is pretty mediocre, especially in Nathan Spencer's case. My god does he have an annoying and unlikable voice.
Graphics: The graphics for Bionic Commando are passable, just good enough to justify being in the PS3/Xbox 360 era. The game is in HD and the character models and environments are crisp, but don't expecting breathtaking graphics like Uncharted 2.
Gameplay: This is where Bionic Commando shines. It is a lot of fun to zip around obstacles and the environments using Spencer's bionic arm. It is also very tricky at times to get around, as the control system can be a bit finicky and you might lose track of where you are (using the bionic arm can be very tricking when swinging and grappling onto balloons).
Overall, Bionic Commando is an enjoyable game that may not win any awards but is worth your time and money. It is definitely too harshly criticized and is by no means a bad game.
I'd give it a 7/10.

I bought and played this game the day it was released for Xbox 360, and thoroughly enjoyed it.  Recently bought it on sale, and decided I would try it again, years later, to see if my opinion still holds. It does. (In depth below, skip to the end for final opinion).
At its core, the game is an excellent 3D translation of the classic Bionic Commando and remake Rearmed gameplay.  The swing mechanics, while it can take some getting used to, feel precise, even when you screw up using them (getting wrapped around a light pole you have attached the arm trying to swing at an odd angle).  The arm mechanics are adapted well to combat, giving the player many options beyond a gun to kill enemies. Many of these arm combat mechanics were adapted to Rearmed 2, released a year or 2 later. Throwing things with the arm, for me on the PC, did leave something to desire, as it seemed perfectly open throws would fly backwards instead of forward. The weapons part of the combat is pretty typical for a third-person shooter, with the addition of being able to shoot while swinging.
Beyond that, however, is where the game becomes a matter of taste.
The level design is similar to previous installments; mostly-linear levels confining the player to the beaten path (not unlike other modern 3D shooters).  Unlike many 3D linear games, the area boundaries aren't solid.  They consist of radiation which the player only has a few seconds to leave before it kills them, or water in which the player has a few seconds to use the bionic arm to escape before drowning (lenient considering most games, and previous installments, killed the player instantly for entering water).  I thought the level design is fine, conveying the developers' intent to have the player roam through the city completing missions for the government.
Game progression is slow relative to the length of the game itself, and the pacing of the game is terrible.  By the time the player unlocks all arm abilities earned through game progression, the game is over halfway finished.  And the game itself is too short, probably a good 2-4 hour experience from start to finish depending.  The game needed at least another major section.
The story, while quirky and excessively profane, left a lot of things to be desired. And the soundtrack, while I quite enjoy it, doesn't have much variety.  I would say about half of the soundtrack is either a loose remix, or uses several parts, of the first level theme from the original Bionic Commando/Rearmed.
In the end though, the game is worth the current price ($10), and definitely any sale price.  Ignoring the story, the slow start to the gameplay picks up greatly about a third of the way through the game and you'll be flying around full speed about halfway through.  Combat is simple, and the arm and swinging opens up a variety of ways to destroy the enemy, which doesn't get old.
Pick it up, don't take it too seriously, and it should be a good time.

tl;dr, Mix Diablo RNG with a Mad-Max wasteland and a healthy dose of dry humor.
Borderlands has long been one of my favorite video game series, as it features a number of qualities that make it different from other shooters on the market. While it does feature all the hallmarks of shooters and Role Playing Games, Borderlands mixes the ideas together. Borderlands uses RNG ala Diablo to produce many variants on each of the weapons used.
The RPG elements also expand to action based leveling and skill points. Action based leveling increases your proficiency based weapon usage. If you use revolvers for example, each kill will increase your pistol exp until your weapon level increases. You also choose a class (a balanced soldier, melee focused brute, long ranged focused sniper, and an elemental based siren) and level up to put skill points into your skills.
