The hall is silent, and cold. I stand there in the doorway, taking a moment to observe the emptiness. The hall had been a bustle of activity and life (or perhaps "unlife") just a moment before; now, all that remained after the reset was a swarm of spirits, black as shadows and shimmering in the pale light. They gather to me, swirling at my feet and trailing up and down my spine. Instinctively, I put my hands in my pockets to warm them up, only to brush up against the jewels and scratch cards that threaten to burst out of the fabric. I sigh as I stare at the sole corporeal object in the room: an old, tattered rug, barely larger than the door I just walked through. I knew what I needed to do, for I had done it many times before.
With silent resolve I nudge the rug with my foot, kicking up dust and remains of previous owners. The chills crawl down my back immediately afterwards, stronger now than it was a moment ago. When the chill reaches a certain point, I bring it forth in various forms. I set about building up stairs and landings, setting up a fireplace and eventually lighting it. I hang a chandelier from the ceiling and carefully adorn it with candles, lighting each one with the precison of a surgeon operating on a patient. I hang paintings of spiders and ghosts on the walls, and build bookshelves lined with ancient magical tomes. The spiders come and build their webs, the rats burrow through the walls as they emerge, and ghouls drift through the walls and floor. I bring in clocks, then pianos, and then I wait. I wait, and watch as my handiwork plays out before me.
Perhaps it was the lack of activity on my part, or maybe it was the faint glow of the books on the shelves. But in that moment, I came to a realization.
"Why am I still here?" I ask loudly, more to myself than to anyone else. "Halloween was a long time ago! It's not even autumn anymore! Christmas and colder winds are on their way, so why should I care whether this haunted house is completed or not?"
Desperate for fresh air, I make a mad dash out the door, stumbling down the steps into the cold, dark night. There is a shadow on the moon above, which turns into bats when I look at it. Witches cackle as they stir their foul-smelling cauldron, which has produced rotten apples and eyeballs that bob gently among the green ooze. Ghosts of every color rise up from the tombstones, handing me intangible bags of the screams that were produced in my absence. The deranged laughter of the mad scientists in the basement carry through the night, as lighting strikes the top of the house and sparks fly across the signs and decorations. In the distance zombies shuffle mindlessly through the darkened forest, while at my feet a pack of black cats brush against my legs purring and meowing for attention. A spider drops down by my face, but I do not try to swat it away. All I can do is stand there, and stare, at what my life has become.
I gave up my life, my dreams, my very soul for this damnable house, but that is not what scares me.
What scares me is that, if given the chance, I may do so again.

I really want to like this game, but it's very difficult too. I would recommend it on an extreme sale, but overall (even for $10), I cannot.
A slow start to a game, and certainly a slow start to a story. They did a decent job trying to keep the old Commando perks in the game (from sounds, clothes, and music), but for what they have, they could have upped the intensity of the situation. The story doesn't feel like it impacts the game what so ever.
The game overall is decent. The premise of it feels somewhat correct, and the bionic arm isn't as limiting as some reviewers say. Although be it so, the arm's momentum feels very stiff (maybe that's the way a machine arm is supposed to be) and the swing mechanic feels limiting. One would imagine themselves swinging all over the level, but in reality one can only go in the direction that is blatantly laid out in front of them. The distance the arm can be used is also a factor, as it is not very far. There is the capability of using melee, in which the coolest part is knocking an enemy near a ledge and watching their animation struggle not to fall. Problem is, it's quite bland and doesn't give the player any impression of an impact. The shooting is bland and literally feels like it was put together in seconds. You can zoom in for a better view, and yes there are different weapons (not really to choose from, rather wait for the proper drops throughout the levels), but shooting and fighting enemies feels like a grind. Enemies aim is quite well, and snipers will take you out if you stay motionless for at tops, three seconds. Spencer can use his bionic arm against enemies, but only to jump in the air once (press A), then zip towards the enemy (pressing A again). They could have done so much more with the arm but it seems they chose not to. They could have given it abilities, or a capability to throw an opponent. Nope, none of that is present here.
A game that could have been that much more, just simply lacks. The multiplayer is alright at best, and probably won't keep you busy for too too long. The choppy-ness of the jumps and the difficulty of grabbing opponents with the arm just all feel flawed. It is nice however, that they did decide to include multiplayer. If you are going to make a game with guns and a bionic arm, maybe try to incorporate the two a little better, or at least try to combine the two. The graphics are alright, and the sounds are basic.
Due to the reasons stated above, I simply cannot recommend it. Unless you are a complete die hard fan of Bionic Commando, is the only way I can say buy it... and even then on sale. It hurts me to rate this game instead of calling it acclaimed.

There are plenty of games out there that aren't bad per se, but don't give a particularly compelling reason to play them. Loot-based games can run afoul of this issue if the loot is no good, and combat-heavy ones have the same issue if the combat is boring or repetitive. I'm bringing this up because Hero Siege isn't really a bad game, but it fails to do anything that isn't done better elsewhere. It's built out of a potent combination of systems, and just never achieves anything of note with them.
The story is... okay I honestly have no idea what the story is, or if there even really is one. You play one of a dozen or so heroes sent to some town to slay infinite monsters that are aggressively milling around the area. These fights take place in randomly-generated arenas where waves of foes approach from the cardinal directions to menace you. Beating five waves of monsters summons a boss, and every five levels ends with a face-off against a world boss. You'll score piles of gold, gear, potions, and artifacts for your trouble, as well as experience to level up with.
What you end up with is a funky mix of Diablo, Binding of Isaac, and Robotron. Defeating enemy waves is your primary concern; there are usually additional monsters and hazards around the map but you only have to kill the wave-spawned critters to progress. The map elements are all randomly generated and include optional mini-dungeons that contain potent artifacts which can boost your stats or skills. Equipping gear is important but the artifacts provide the most benefit, and are also what you lose when you die. Experience and gear stays with you but dying means starting over from the village with no artifacts.
This all sounds like a good way to kill an evening or two, but the trouble lies in the execution. Unlike the games I alluded to earlier, Hero Siege is sloooooooooow. You're slow, your attacks are slow, enemies are slow, abilities are slow, everything happens at a glacial, uninteresting pace. In fact, you can manually trigger new waves whenever you want and there's almost no reason not to pop them all at once, because the enemies take so long to reach you and attack that you can whittle them down in relative safety. I say "almost" because you need decent gear to make this work but the balance of levels and equipment is so out of whack that it's entirely possible to become functionally immortal not halfway through a full run.
There's 20 or so arenas to battle through (with more to unlock) and some ridiculous number of difficulties for when one gets too easy, but the flawed formula never changes. You're ALWAYS going to be hacking or blasting away at snail-crawling enemies with weapons that either one-shot them or take ages to wear them down. There might be ways to spice things up in the town but I wouldn't know how, because all the residents there offer goods or services I've never heard of in exchange for things I don't have. I suppose it's all endgame stuff which does me no good in the boring stretch I'm at, and renders the town essentially pointless.
The graphics are decent enough 2D with some meaty effects and dense monster packs, but there's nothing particularly memorable about any of it. The voiceovers for the different classes stand out for being super cheesy and over-the-top at least, and the rest of the sound design does what it needs to without much impact. Really the whole game is a very safe, unambitious loot grind that fails to offer anything to keep you invested. Even if you're a fan of endlessly growing numbers the mindless, boring combat is bound to turn you off. Hero Siege isn't bad, but I can't find anything really GOOD to say about it and that wouldn't make much of a recommendation.

This game could have been far greater than it actually is. I recommend to DBZ fans (as any hardcore fan can make it through any kind of related game), but as for players looking for a new detailed ground-breaking fighter, this simply isn't it. Get ready for a grind ladies and gents and get ready to break your X and Y buttons from repetitive mashing. In short, I like the game but it's hard to recommend for this price range.
It's well done, but if feels like it could have been done so much better. The general Toki Toki City area you get to "freeroam" is slow paced at most, and for some reviewers, a shot in the dark and grind to do the next mission. I find simply moving about the level is a nuisance at most. Why not allow for flying? You have great characters and such a rich ability range to incorporate into the game, in and out of fighting! For something that could be so good, it's simply decent. Not only that, half the stations you go to are oddly "closed" or unable to process your request. When they do work though, online parrallel universe fights with other players add some replayability to the game.
There are two basic modes to the game : freemode and fight mode. In free roaming mode, you essentially get to run around and either shop (for new skills, items, or clothing), talk, upgrade and change your personal stats, or choose between different game modes from either the story line or the online/offline parrallel universe modes (which are comparable to single matches). In fight mode, you get to do the juicy stuff like fly around and throw wild energy balls everywhere.
The story character creator is satisfactory, while the story itself is well integrated into the series. Maybe it's because I chose Namekian that I'm limited in options, it doesn't seem otherwise there is much to choose from in variety. Either way, the story line is a good addition to re-visiting old DB episodes. Gameplay itself isn't too shabby, but can sometimes seem all over the place. Flying is slightly choppy and isn't as smooth as it could be. The fighting seems nominal once you get how the teleportation and fighting system work, as well as the stamina. There is a lot of tutorials that slowly creep up on you, rush through them and it can be a rough play through. To me personally it seems at times random combo's and teleportation from side to side happen. In all honesty, I'd like to be in full control if I can dodge VIA teleporting or teleport to bounce the opponent to the other side of the map. The fighting has it's ups and downs, but when buttons start matching up to what your character is doing, there is a nice flow to what your watching in addition to being in control of. What was disappointing to me was there was no real feel of impact when you sent an opponent flying into the ground (there is an animation for it). Granted, there is some landscape that can be broken but it feels like crumping cardboard paper toghether, then it quickly unraveling back into perfect shape. The damage animations (not effects) are nice as breaking a tree with your opponents back but that permanent damage isn't there.
Visuals are nice and the custom character looks really good in cut-scenes. The fighting sounds seem on par, but addition of a few more sounds (especially collisions) would have enriched the auditory experience. What really drives me nuts is the music in the free roam. If being on repeat isn't bad enough, get ready to go nuts hearing the same song over and over. They have also incorporated built in phrases and actions the player can perform (such as waving or sitting). Credit definitely has to be given to the level creators as the places you can fight are all in the DB saga. Some locations you get to fight in are Kami's lookout, planet Namek, different places on Earth and even a stage outside of the Earth.
This game is good, but no where near worth it's stated price. I'm a huge DBZ fan and for what it's worth, I wish they gave a little more into the game. I like it because it's something I can relate to. Will you like it based on it's gaming aspect, or it's content? I have to give the game credit though for trying to give the player more than a story to play with. WIthin TokiToki city, you may run into a Ginyu force member or even Gohan asking you for help (with a sidequest). You can also ask different characters within game (like Vegeta or Piccolo in TokiToki city) to be your trainer. That voice will follow you to every debrief after every quest.
For future DBZ's give some freedom for the player to use the specials whenever, or at least have the choice to fly or walk in free roam. The incorporation of actions such as waving or squatting added a bit of depth to the open world. That I definitely liked and would like to see that again. Also, the attacks were well done (minus button mashing X and Y at times) but I feel there needs to be improvement for the vanishing system. Dodging consist of jumping in the air while doing a front flip, which is fine, but the actual trait of disappearing and ending up behind an enemy is the whole fun of the Dragon Ball universe! I'd like to be able to vanish half the map for half or more of my stamina, but the closer I am, let me jump around my enemy for a bit!
If this game was $15-20 I would recommend it, as of now though, no. To true Dragon Ball fans : I think you will enjoy the game and play a decent chunk of it. You may find the money's worth.

Alright, so first off, lets just start with what you'll be introduced to first upon entering the game's world. These will be seperated into pros/cons respectively afterwards, but first I'm going to give you an explanation of how the game felt to me (and me alone. Obviously, this first bit will be biased.)
You get your 5 minute download complete and you start the game up. The companys are shown before you're presented with the main menu. If you've played the 2nd Diablo game, you may feel some small vibes from the game, because I did personally. You're presented with Single Player and Multiplayer, along with options and the option to exit the game, along with the "Hero Siege" title presented above the selections. Most likely, you're going to hit Single Player.
There are literally more character slots then there are characters. So go wild.
Once you enter the character selection, you'll see hardcore mode and go "Well there's the Diablo vibes he was talking about." where if you die you're perma dead and have to make a new character. You select your character and enter. Again, you're going to feel very light Diablo II vibes. You check the shop and see you can only sell, but not buy. You go up and find a blue rift, so you enter it, then you go to the left and step on the roman numeral for 1 and enter the rift that pops up.
Now, the combat.
Also take note that the music cues and the announcer is just....PERFECT. Lol.
Enemies at first seem a bit tanky. I'm gonna tell you this, with how OP items can get at only 15 (and yes, they are by definition Over Powered) enemies being tanky will be a mere memory and you'll be slaying everything with one shot and straight up rushing. Your character is level 35, and enemies are slightly becoming tanky again. You will most likely disregard it and still rush in thinking you're still the OP beast you once were, and you'll die from getting bashed from literally every angle from allowing yourself to get boxed in, along with enemies glitching via teleporting or simply making your screen freeze for a few seconds simply from spawning in.
You then go to the main menu and almost click quit game, but then you notice the Multiplayer selection. You suddenly go "Well....maybe it's more fun to play with others." And then almost as soon as you login after a long loading screen, you eat your words as you enter the most laggiest lobbies even if you enter the region that you're in with just the best wifi around. Your teammates most likely rush a lot just because they know they aren't alone, and will die a lot. You spend 10 seconds to revive them and will average a total of one minute and 30 seconds out of every 15 minutes (if you even manage to stay connected that long.) Have fun being the opposite of the reaper for the entire multiplayer experience, or you can just make the person think you're a♥♥♥♥♥♥and go off somewhere else ignoring his revival circle.
You get disconnected after spiking heavily, then say "Eh, what the heck. It's just a minor d/c." You then realise that the game doesn't auto save frequently, because before the d/c you were 45 and had a tonne of gear, now you're 35 and all of your gear is suddenly gone due to an irreversal loading error that cannot be fixed apparentally because I had this game for a good year and they haven't fixed it. The servers also seem like they got worse. You rage quit harder, and consider uninstalling, but you most likely enjoyed the singleplayer so you held onto it and waited for the next time you had literally nothing to do.
SO! You got my biased part of the review out of the way. Here's the "General" review. I will take each piece of the puzzle and put it together next to a # rating. 1 = Bad | 10 = Good
Gameplay - 4: It's fun! It's entertaining and is a nice grindy beat-em-up dungeon crawler/treasure hunter. It's like a discount Binding of Isaac if it had sex with discount Diablo. *Now, that's if you disregard the glitches. But with the glitches, the game just SUCKS. No way around it...*
Multiplayer - (Official Server Hosting:2 Peer-To-Peer Hosting:4) The official servers suck so badly. That's all I can really say for that. Peer-To-Peer is pretty much hosting your own server, which for the most part fixes the lag issue to an extent. It at least makes it easier to play without disconnecting so frequently. I know this because I've played the majority with my girlfriend (all the way in Japan and we both still had good connectivity compared to the official server(s).) and we had plenty of fun playing together on there, however we both encountered the bug that makes our gear disappear and our levels drop due to rare auto-saves.
Bug Free/Playability - (BF:1 Playability:*3*) Oh damn. It's bugged alright. *It is playable but....the glitches really ruin the mood as they're so frequent.* Nothing more to really add, just saying if you can ignore the mere gear/relic/level deletion, it really isn't that bad.
Intruiging - 3.5: Honestly, I can't say it's boring at face value but it's definetally not attractive. I'll probably play it for 30 minutes then get off and do something else. But it's something I'll always come back to once in awhile, and maybe with my friends.
Story - There isn't any. Unless you count slashing through mobs and randomly killing bosses as "story".
DLC - (*) I haven't bought any DLC however some accessories and characters are locked behind them. I can't make even a biased review on them because I honestly don't really want to buy them. Technically, I'd rate the DLC at 1 from face value as I'm not really intruiged by any of the other characters. *The fact that they are being so rude to their customers and deciding to not fix bugs, in essence making the game a mere cash grab. Seriously. Just don't waste your money or time.*
Community - 2: They are either silent or illiterate kids being angry in the lobby chat. If you're going to play, just go P-T-P with a friend.
Overall - *1*: *This game is a nightmare. It's a wreck. It's a ruin. It's a cash grab. It's so. Very. Bad. I'm so sad that I can't get a refund so I don't have to fund the creators deciding to make such terrible broken games that are mere cash grabs, scams. I'm going to refund the gift I gave to my girlfriend so I can buy something else that's better and put heart into, even if the game is only 5$. Don't support the company until they learn to actually fix their coding.*

Putrefaction is one of those games that makes me wish the Steam reviews section had a rating that was right in the middle.  I've played through Putrefaction on "normal" once, dabbled in survival and have a game on the "hard" setting started.  The game is enjoyable enough but not wholly recommendable either.  On the other hand, it was pretty fun while it lasted.  Unlike a game I really, really enjoy and am encouraged to come back and play all of the difficulties, Putrefaction feels like a chore already to start over.
In the game you play as an unnamed operative who is sent in to clean up a monster-creating infection in some underground stronghold beneath a mountain.  That is as much story as you're going to get.  This game probably has less story/atmosphere than Doom I, Quake I and the first Serious Sam.  In this game you get equipped with a fun selection of various guns and blast your way through levels crammed with ugly baddies.  There's no voice-acting or other distractions to keep you from the task at hand.  This game makes even Doom and Quake seem complicated as there are no secrets to be found, keycards or otherwise.  As much as I love a back to basics game, this one feels like a totally dry piece of toast with no jam or butter added for flavor.
The shooting is fine for the most part.  Sometimes things will hiccup graphically but overall I had very little trouble there.  The guns are cool, satisfying to use and do some Soldier of Fortune-esque gore damage to the monsters.  Monster A.I. on the other hand is dumber than dirt for the most part.  You can jump on top of a box if you're having any trouble (and it wasn't very difficult on normal overall), and just pick off ranged enemies while the landlubbers dumbly run up against it...trying to nail you yet being too stupid to figure out how.  At least those classic games had beasties that each had their own way of making their demise a pain in the butt.  Thankfully some small enemies, ones with guns, a type that rolls, a self-destructor, etc. shake things up slightly from all of the goons that run straight at you (and they are plentiful).   There's a pair of boss fights to further spice things up and they were fun enough to fight if rather unoriginal.
Sound is unremarkable, the shooting is alright although the monster sounds are rather laughable and shouldn't scare anyone under the age of 10.  Control is a little loose, not enough to cause alot of cheap deaths, but don't be surprised if one or two occur.  When you need to dodge out of the way of anything, you'll find that you have to plan your movements because Mr. Unnamed Operative skipped the space marine diet/exercise regimen.  Jumping is wonky which really isn't a problem as there isn't really any pesky platforming segments.  You just shoot, blast, shoot, blast, rinse, repeat.  I would say I got more enjoyment out of Dead Effect in recent times than this.  Simplicity in gaming is a beautiful thing and I"m always down try these new school takes on old school gaming.  The problem here is that it's so very linear.  With no secrets to find, no overly challenging or memorable battles, respsawning monsters that block your progression and such point A to B gameplay, it becomes very mundane very quickly.  Throwback games are fun, but there has to be some salt, pepper or touch of seasoning to make sure you don't end up "boring" instead of "old school."  That's the biggest problem here.
I'll break it down into some pros and cons...
Pros
-Simple, mostly fun old school shooting
-Plenty of monsters to fight
-Solid selection of guns and most are fun to use
-The way guns gore the monsters is entertaining
-Boss fights were decent
Cons
-No secrets, little variety, very plain, bland levels, etc.
-Ho-hum graphics (but good enough for what it is)
-Unremarkable sound
-Controls slightly wonky
-Pretty short
-Doesn't encourage much replay even with a survival mode and different difficulties
-Almost zero of its own personality as a game
Overall, depending on how much you are into first person shooters or not will determine if you need to play this.  I'm glad I did but I'm not sure I'll get much past my 6/10 achievements and a normal completion.  Most every game I own I play through more than once.  For whatever reason, it's a struggle to want to progress on hard with absolutely nothing to find because the game is so bare bones.  I'm impressed what a single person was able to develop here and Oleg shows lots of potential for future gaming projects but I don't think he's quite found his whole groove yet.  I'm going to have to say this one is a pass unless it pops up for less than $5.
Rating:  5.0/10
UPDATE:  I did find some glitches on hard.  I fell through the first level no less than 2 times near the end right when I was about to finish.  I dropped the score and uninstalled the game.  Yeah, this one is a definite pass unless you got extra cash sitting around.

I enjoyed it a lot more than the first season. I might have just got used to its conventions, but I prefer to believe there were actual improvements on the development team's side. For one thing, Season 2 contains some actual well-thought-out puzzles (especially in the riddletastic Episode 2). I also found the mystery storyline (however commonplace and cliché-ridden) much more engaging, with some genuinely tense moments.
I still hold that the extra-blocky pixel art aesthetic works against the aims this game otherwise sets out to achieve. The characters come off as cute retro gamey people rather than tragic Victorian heroes facing unspeakable horrors. Point-and-clicking is little fun when you cannot discern what it is you're pointing and clicking at. That being said, I appreciated the skilfully done cutscenes, well-composed and animated despite the limitations of low resolution.
I had to consult the walkthrough a couple of times to find solutions I would never come up with on my own (which of course I'm going to ascribe to their unintuitiveness rather than my own intellectual limitations). A few puzzles felt wonky and badly designed; the maze was a particularly unfun throwback to the adventure genre's beginnings. I'm willing to forgive these flaws, however, considering the amount of times everything went just smoothly.
Since I have a soft spot for dreamlike or nightmarish imagery and logic, I enjoyed the last episode immensely. I would say it was worth playing through both seasons just to get to that experience.
Make no mistake, The Last Door: Season 2 is neither a stunningly great adventure game nor a particularly good example of a cosmic horror tale (I was quite surprised to learn that the series seems to have an actual fan following, with people talking enthusiastically about its "lore" and supposedly-intriguing storyline). I do recommend it, however, since it sits just above the average and did manage to provide a pleasant distraction for a couple of hours.

I wanted to like this. Risen 3 is clearly a bigger, more ambitious, and more polished product than its predecessors, which always felt like they wanted to be bigger than they were. The combat is slightly less clunky than before, but still recognizably the traditional Piranha Bytes plodding, stunlock-loving style that I would inevitably toggle God Mode to avoid eventually.
The fact that I can't actually do that this time without 3rd party programs is a factor in my negative review.
Honestly, the killer problem with this game, the one bad enough to make it the first of these games since Gothic for me to abandon outright a few hours in, is that it's just horribly balanced. I don't mean "unfair" - Piranha Bytes games are always unfair. But normally they're a consistant level of unfair that simply presents a steep learning curve, like a poor man's Dark Souls.
Risen 3, meanwhile, is just plain inconsistent. You can be playing along, managing to more-or-less stay on top and not meeting the traditional fate of being stunlocked to death by a passing ostrich, when you'll wander into an unremarkable-sounding quest and be killed in three shots by some complete nobody that the game in no way warns you is fully capable of handing you your♥♥♥♥♥on a platter. And with no way to cheat my way around it this time around so I can enjoy the parts of the game that aren't awful, I simply don't have the patience to roll the dice every single time I fight a new enemy and hope that they just haven't arbitrarily decided to make this nondescript monster deal five times as much damage as everyone around him.
I suppose it's worth noting that this inconsistency is foreshadowed somewhat by the story, which is by far the least concrete of the series. After a kind of rushed-feeling tutorial level, you're thrown into the wide open world with what the previous games would've called late first-act gear and a vague mission to do something about your missing spirit. I didn't like the way Risen 2 bottlenecked you for the first third/half of the game by locking you onto a single story path, but at least it gave me time to understand what the hell I was doing and what the stakes were. Risen 3 by comparison legitimately feels like the entire first act is just missing, and I frequently find myself feeling like I'm showing up to certain areas prematurely as random plot points are discussed as if I should have been told about them beforehand somewhere else.
Between that and the random difficulty curve, I'm not sure the game was designed to be as open-ended as it is, and ultimately it just winds up feeling like a mess. I know it's not Piranha Bytes' style, but this is probably one game that could have benefitted from the traditional RPG approach of having character and quest levels to guide the player along. The intent was to make a game that doesn't hold the player's hand, and I can applaud that, but I don't have the patience with a game that not only doesn't tell me what to do, but then kicks me in the gut whenever I fail to read its mind about what it expects me to do. "Open-ended challenge" isn't the same thing as "be psychic or die."

Mabinogi, by definition, is the closest MMORPG to Sword Art Online ever created. Wether you acctuly like the anime or not, there is no doubt that Mabinogi closely resembles some of its elements. However, I whole heartedly say this, Mabinogi is not for everryone. Why you may ask? Well, simply but, Mabinogi is very, very, VERY grindy. If you want to have a half decent character, you need to grind. See, there are 2 ways to play Mabinogi. 1. You can play just to dork around and talk to some friends you convinced to play with you. 2. You can feel like a toatol badass when your character is so combatically stacked, that plowing through hoards of enemies with one quick swoop becomes incredibly entertaining. That' right folks, you want some fun out of this game? You gotta learn to fight, and fight like a pro. This is where Mabinoig is the most grindy. See there are multible classes (or talents). And each talent has its own weapons, and stats, and blah blah blah. But here's where the game is intresting, some talents work off the same stat, thus making it that if you did both classses, both would become stronger due to you training that stat. Here's an example for you: If you do Close Combat, which get's its power off of your strength stat, and you alos did Ninja, which also get's its power from the strength stat. Now both of these talents become stronger because they both work off the training of the strength stat. Some people will take this to the extream by taking many different talents that rely on strength, or intelligence, and train them up so that they can be powerful in a whole arsenal of classes. Now how do these classes work? Well remember how I said this game is kinda like Sword Art Online? Well basically each class has X amount of skills, and each skill can be trained and ranked up by using AP. Every skill can go from rank F to rank 9, and then rank 9 to rank 1. This obviously is where the game becomes very grindy. In order for your skillset to be half decent, your going to have to train that skillset a lot and earn lots of AP. However, that makes becomming a respectable warrior all the more rewarding. Mabinogi is honestly very addictive, it plays off its own grindiness, pulling you in and making you beg to bring your skill up just one more rank before bed. Basically if you give Mabinogi time, and take the time to learn the ropes, and find your way around (I would suggest using the Mabinogi wiki page) then you will find that Mabinogi is a really great game.

If you use revolvers for example, each kill will increase your pistol exp until your weapon level increases. Bionic Commando is clearly a game that was developed and produced with a clear target market.  I was very much shocked to find that this game apparently reviewed very poorly upon release, and am even more shocked to find that others would still regret playing this game, as it is, truly, "an underrated gem".
The most fascinating piece, is that i was actually skeptical about this game upon purchase.  It was on sale, however, and also came packaged with the Bionic Commando Re-armed game.  I've never been a fan of Bionic Commando on the NES.  I thought the game was ambitious for its time, and the controls a tad confusing.  This game came across at me as another generic third-person-shooter with another gimmick in gameplay, but it is actually so much more.  Despite my lack of interest in the original Bionic Commando, i am a huge fan of Capcom games, and this game carries with it the same love and care that most Capcom games have traditionally carried.  This game is one of the best games I have played in a long time, and it hasn't been since i played Mega Man X4 as a teenager that i felt this badass playing a video game.
The clear breadwinner of this game is the gameplay.  As i mentioned, i was worried this game would be another generic third-person-shooter, with the bionic arm being another gimmick in gameplay.  However, i am proud to say that this game took a bionic fistful of my words, and shoved them right back down my throat.  The bionic arm is clearly amazing, with the range of actions you cam accomplish with it.  Swing through the leaves like a crazed bionic Spider-Man, ready to eliminate anything that moves in the most spectacular fashions.  Grab your enemies and smash them with your iron boots!  Fling your dead enemies at your enemies!  Throw cars at your enemies!  The way this game mixes classic shooting elements and a new, bionic arm is absolutely amazing.  The way you must master your swinging through the apocalyptic ruins of the city is breathtaking, and the way you can mix traditional elements with the versatility of the bionic arm is some of the most refreshing gameplay i've seen in a while.  Bionic commando is a game that is clearly designed with the gameplay at heart, and that simply touches my heart.  The game does give you a variety of paths to follow, although the game is for all intents and purposes linear.  It's a game that requires progression in story and location, much like Halo(but no one complained about Halo being linear, did they?).  Waypoints are a way of life.  love them.  In fact, the linear gameplay may be something to be desired of Bionic Commando, as too many times i have found games leaving me wondering where i'm supposed to go, or what to do.  Bionic commando is an action game, and it makes certain to keep you in the action, as well as making certain you are the absolute center of action.
The next great thing for this game is the controls.  This typically isn't mentioned in a review as far as i've seen, but i believe it deserves note.  The controls for this game are some of the simplest i've seen in a while, yet still some of the most versatile.  The controls for Bionic commando, from the tips of your fingers to the moving image on the screen, are fluid and intuitive.  The game lets you grapple on to almost any surface, which was a shock to me, as I was expecting the bionic arm to be a gimmick to use in only certain locations.  The bionic arm changes everything, though.  You can literally make your own path, and when you get good enough, you'll be one crazy flying death monkey.  it's simply amazing.  You can do about five or six different moves along with swinging and shooting like a crazed ape, and that perfect mixture of bionic awesomeness with shooting like a normal person makes the game feel so versatile.  Also of note, the jump button works finally.  ALso of special note, this game apparently features keyboard and mouse support, but i couldn't be bothered to figure it out.  The game DOES, however, work 100% fine with wired 360 controllers, and the simple way the controls are laid out is absolutely beautiful, as well.
Second clear winner on this game experience is the sound.  The soundtrack is well balanced and masterfully crafted.  The music can be serene at times, when you're exploring the ruins of the city, but is intense and fast as you progress into more enemies and bosses.  The sound effects are amazing, and if you play the game enough, your characters WILL break the 4th wall and/or go off script.  For the sake of it's short-lived life-span, i will also mention the story here, as it basically reduces to sound.  The story isn't a bad story, but with the way it's delivered(both in simple dialogue and in the voice acting), it is a bit lacking.  The best bits of your story actually come from within the actual gameplay, and for whoever voices the mad german scientist guy, well done.  You nailed the classic video game villain with your shrill voice, and the angry german accent gave the words such strength that it filled my heart with glee every time you spoke.  It was your voice alone that made the citadel level with all of your minions at once bearable, as i had to repeat that level about a million times.  I wish, however, that i could say the same for the rest of the voice cast.  While the lines do feel very silly at times, however, the easter eggs you can come across simply make this game evenmore endearing.
Of final note is the visuals for this game, which are simply astounding.  I was actually pretty surprised to find such low system requirements for this game, and had a few concerns, but thankfully i was not disappointed.  Character animations are very fluid, and feel good to watch and make.  Moving around the game feels natural, the swaying of the trees in the breeze is very pleasing, and lighting is actually very well done(even in the underground caverns).  Water for this game looks AMAZING, debris flying around the city looks fantastic, ragdoll corpses always feel nice, and nothing is left to be desired, i must say.  Close-ups on characters do look a bit odd sometimes, mostly when speaking, but luckily the game doesn't take you in that close most of the time.
Overall, Bionic Commando is clearly a game made by people who love Bionic commando, for people who also love Bionic Commando.  It's a refreshing piece of gameplay with some very unique pieces, and it serves a heck of a lot of fan-service.  The game even ups in replay value, as there are certain unlockables you can only access by playing(and progressing) in the classic remake, Bionic Commando Re-armed.  this may actually tend to annoy others, believing it a scheme to grind more hours into the game, but it really isn't.  for those that love the game, this isn't even an issue, and for those who are just getting into it just have more incentive to play.  I didn't enter this game with high hopes, but it proved itself to be a game that remembers what it's like to be a video game, and that itself is something very special.  Would i recommend this game?  every day of the week.  My co-workers already think i'm crazy because i just can't shut up about this game.  whatever you might play, there's something in this game for everyone.

This is a stealth game about rewiring things and punching people.  And it's a great game.
Each mission, you're asked to break into a building and reach a computer terminal.  To do this, you need to figure out how to rewire circuits to open the correct doors, while avoiding being shot in the face.  This gives the game a pseudo-puzzle-game feel.  However, if you don't feel like solving puzzles, or are just a generally violent person, you also have the option of pushing the guards out the windows or beating them with your fists.
The best part of this game though is the dialog.  Dear lord that dialog.  Whereas I usually skim over dialog for most games, in this game I found myself genuinely looking forward to the between-mission cutscenes, because the choices you're given are so funny.  I laughed every time.  Every time.
My only complaint is that the game was so short.  It took me 3 hours to beat the first time, and 2 hours to beat a second and get all the achievements.  I don't normally recommend such short games, but I enjoyed the gameplay and humor so much I feel it was worth the cost, even at full-price.
9/10

Ok, first off, you die WAY too fast. Second off, people are idiots and never revive you. Third off, the tutorial is literally worthless.
Movement seems incredibly clunky and stealth is a worthless mechanic in this game. Don't use it.
Yeah, I've only played about an hour of the game, but if I can't move past one hour because of these glaring issues, we're going to need to have a heart to heart, you know?
So, there's literally no explination to how the mechanics work. In every other FPS it's either so simple only an idiot wouldn't understand it, or there is an extentive, scaling campain which teaches you how to play the game.
No no, in this game I have no idea how to do half the crap in it, and the missions are worthless wastes of time.
Did I mention the control layout?
Press shift to switch between 'jog' and 'walk' and hold shift to run. F is for flash light, which is understandable. G is for the laser, which is OK because there are no grenades.
Did I mention there's also no mele? Yep, you have to spray n' pray at close range. Oh yeah, there's no reticle to help in that regard, either.
Oh yeah, and there's no surround sound. Someone can be on the right of you, but the noise is coming out of both speakers. So have fun trying to pinpoint where people are based on sound.
I understand this is a small dev team, but there needs to be some serious work put into this game before it's even worthy to be mentioned anywhere but here. On steam.
I'll try to mention anything gamebreaking that I come across, but that seems to be the high point of this game....There are no bugs. For an early access game, this is practically bugless.
My advice to the dev team? Bring this game over to Bethesda and have them produce the bulk content. Then you guys can make it bugless. It would literally be a perfect game with no issues that everyone would love no matter why they play the game.
So, here's the TL;DR: It will need a lot of work in the gameplay, audio, and content department. This is a given for an early access game, and I'm not telling you to forget this game forever. I'm telling you to wait a while to see what happens.

INVEST WITH CARE.

I can only recommend this with a caveat: DO NOT PAY FULL PRICE.
For some reason, there are a lot of developers out there with much hate in their heart for headphone-wearing gamers.  Gunpoint doubles the hate quotient by neglecting to include options for remapping the controls, as well as the sound volume.  You do get the option to change your (windowed) screen resolution, but it requires restarting the game.  For the $10-$15 price that Gunpoint is asking, I expect a game written in a proper framework that supports all the conventional options that have been the norm for PC gaming for decades now.  Instead, we get a game that feels like it was made using the same kind of software people use for creating training videos or websites.  It's great that there's authorware out there that enables people with creative vision to make games without requiring any technical know-how, but I don't want to see the resulting products proffered up at the same price as purpose-built software.  There are a quite a few other games in this price range that have the polish of AAA titles, but everything about Gunpoint feels amateurish.  With that out of the way, please let me say that this is a pretty fun puzzle game.  The rewiring mechanic is well executed, and sets this game apart from other 2D puzzlers and platformers.

An extremely addictive twin-stick hack'n'slash. There are six "acts" divided into five or six maps. Each map contains a series of "waves", in which you are dropped into the middle of a randomized arena and have to fight for you life, looting and leveling along the way, until you reach the boss. Occasionally a secret dungeon, shop, or buff-enchanting statue will appear for the duration of a wave; enemies drop gold and potions, which lack description until you use them at least once. They can either raise or lower your stats, so it's a gamble. There are dozens of characters with their own unique skill-trees and abilities, and more than a few difficulty levels that can be raised or lowered at will from the main town hub. The art design is reminiscent of old-school Zelda, but with way more gore.
Unfortunately, there is much-maligned "pay to play" cost structure to the game. The whole second half is DLC, as are most of the characters. However, I logged at least a hundred hours in the first three acts before I even realized this, and was more than happy to shell out a few extra bucks for another hundred hours of fun. Technically, Hero Siego is 99% sound. The only time the game crashes is when I exit, oddly enough. It freezes for one or two seconds every time a boss is defeated, which is jarring, but not a deal-breaker. Another frequnt complaint in the forums, which I can attest to, is the imbalance of the higher difficulty levels; one or two shots from even basic enemies can kill you, costing valuable progress, which, considering the often hectic, chaotic nature of swarm battles, is extremely frustrating.
There is a multiplayer community, and even a heavily-populated Discord channel just for this game, unfortunately it seems to consist only of people idling in the chat lobby or the main town hub for no apparent reason other than to show off their loot or leave the game running while they cook dinner. On the off chance that you manage to join a stranger's public match, more often than not they are high-level a-holes with glitched loadouts spamming around the map with no sense of challenge or skill. Considering the baddies level to match the host, you have no chance. Avoid.
Highly recommended, but be warned: it's a time-sink. Say goodbye to weeks of your life.

The second season of The Last Door relies less on keeping the player shrouded in mystery and more on revealing some of its secrets through a more traditional adventure game setting. This small shift in focus still cannot harm its excellent atmosphere and storytelling mechanics.
Lovecraftian style suspense horror that relies on the primordial fear of the unknown is a dangerously complex subject, yet a small Spanish development team managed to tackle it with The Last Door, a game that invited us on an eerie, surreal journey beyond the world of reason.
This kind of atmosphere is difficult to keep up; this is probably why Season 2 chose a different approach. It is more of a straight-line point ‘n’ click adventure game now with all the associated staples, like collecting all movable everyday items to involve them in some needlessly overcomplicated task. As a result, the dread-inducing atmosphere only pops up during cut-scenes, chiefly at the beginning and at the end of each episode—except for the last one, that is dreary from start to finish.
Just like in Season 1, the pixel graphics provide only a vague representation of the game world, so our own imagination has to fill in the blanks, creating an even more powerful effect. The plot itself chooses a similar approach: we get many answers to our questions through the eyes of our new protagonist and the story has a definite ending, but there are enough questions left to leave the door slightly open for any potential new entries in the series. And this is exactly how a suspense horror story should be.

Proteus has consistently created meaningful and deceptively unique journeys for me. This is rare for a repeatable activity, since I am part of a fickle species with fickle minds where the nice things get less nice each time it's revisited.
Aided by the procedurally generated visual and aural elements, each time I wake up on the island I am treated to something new across the four seasons. On a whim, usually during stressful times such as winter's months, I'll launch Proteus with a skeletal memory of what I saw last - honestly, it
dream-like in that it just feels so personally true and authentic moment-to-moment until the very end, on an inverted awakening, you don't feel ready to climb out of sleep just yet, until you are, until you aren't, until you see the (spoilers)
. Its affinity for synthesizing such majestic, natural sights with paradoxically quiet melodrama hits me hard. There are some genuinely frightening set-pieces/events/moments, too, to mirror the genuinely heartwarming set-pieces/events/moments. Throughout it all, it takes me to another place for a set of time and helps with the sometimes-stress of life.
There are some bonuses. It runs well, has a fantastic options menu, and has a "postcard" system that allows you to snapshot moments you want to and are able to revisit. Perfect.

You can also snag melee weapons to dish out devastating damage to the daunting demonic nightmares and put them back in their place! Even with mediocre graphics and (relatively) poor controls, this game will have you constantly on edge due to the massive hords filled with different kinds of enemies-- all with their own methods of menacing you.

Make your way through hallways, buildings, and other such locations, fending off deadly zombie-esque critters while finding health packs to patch yourself up and some ammo for your guns. I didn't like this game much at first, but, after I got to a higher level and found more guns, I started to survive longer, and the intensity started to, well, intensify! The hordes are relentless and get exponentially stronger, which forced me to be constantly aware of my surroundings, scanning for health pickups and ammo drops to ensure my survival.

The main rules of A Druid's Duel are pretty simple to learn, but hard to master. There are no random elements involved so it all comes down to strategy, tactics and your wits.
You start off with a grid type playing field with different types of druid's on both sides. There are 4 types of druids. Each druid has their own abilities which you use to move around or attack enemies with. Every turn you move the pieces around on the board and the opponent does the same. And every turn you spend your mana, by either transforming into animals, placing new pieces on the board or build bridges. Mana is the big component in this game. The more lands you own the more mana you will get.
When you move around you can grab lands which will give you more mana. You can lose the mana if the enemy gets the land back in return. You can attack and kill your opponents with one hit making this game feel a bit like chess. However with the mana you can buy new pieces and place them on the board again. The game ends when either side has no lands left.
The Good:
- Nice graphics
- No luck or randomness involved
- Challenging AI
- Balanced
- Multiplayer option
The Bad:
- Good music, but can become repetitive
- Can become boring after playing for a long time

This game has blown me away by how much popularity it has gotten over the span of just a year. Trust me on this: You can go into the game at any time (even at midnight) and there will be at least ten or eleven servers waiting for you to join. Honestly, this just boggles my mind, and this is one of the few games I've seen that can sell more than a million copies in under a year.
Let's adress a problem you might be thinking about: Updates. When you first see the game's thumbnail, it has whatever update is the newest next to the "Move Or Die" logo. You might be thinking, "That update must've happened four months ago or something." Actually, this game has the most responding developers I have ever seen. They update their game whenever the Winter Holiday season starts, as well as Christmas. They have always asked their players what they want to see sometime before the update, as well. Plus, if you were to ask the developer if he could fix a bug, chances are that it will be fixed sometime within the next one or two months, maybe even a shorter amount of time.
The game does have a major problem, though: Internet connection. If you have poor Interenet connection, the game will almost always lag. This problem is fixed if the person you're playing with is in the same country as you, or if you're in the same room playing a couch game. This problem might even fix itself soon in the PS4 version. Yes, you heard me: It's coming to Playstation 4. (GET HYPED!!)

is a turn-based strategy game that plays like a board game. You can play
single-player and multiplayer but I have only played the single-player campaign.
Each turn, you move your pieces around the board and then the opponent does the same. The pieces are druids that come in four varieties. Each type of druid has a different set of rules for moving across the board and for attacking opponents. Also, each type of druid can change into an animal. In animal form, the druid can perform powerful abilities. Changing into an animal and performing abilities costs mana. Your mana pool refreshes each turn. The amount of mana you get depends on the amount of tiles of the board you own at the beginning of that turn.
The various rule sets for the druids and their animal form are well thought out. The game really is strategic and requires a tactical playstyle. On the first attempt I usually failed miserably but when I tried again and took a completely different approach, I won the map. This had nothing to do with luck as the AI's strategy is pretty consistent, so I think this shows that the game's basic premise is solid.
However, I ran into two mental obstacles that made me think I'm done with this game after only a few hours:
Like I said, I didn't mind restarting a level a couple of times to try a different approach. But the only increase in difficulty results from the opponent getting more and better units than you at the beginning of each map, which gets old quickly. In the level after the first boss I thought the opponent got too nice a head start, and I couldn't be bothered anymore, really. What I can't wrap my head around is that I hit this difficulty wall even though I chose the easiest of the four difficulties at the start of the campaign! Something seems off here...
So at the start of each level, it's a matter of taking the correct actions in the first few turns to undo the opponent's advantage and then finish the map using the same tactics that proved to work before. This gets very repetitive as only the first few moves really matter. When you find a correct approach, you just need to clear the remaining 80% of the map the same way you did the previous levels.
Also, nothing new gets added after the first level. You know all the units and tactics, and that's all there is to the game. What this game lacks is some feeling of progress. Some sort of mechanic to upgrade your units, for example. Or gradually introducing new tactical elements to the game.
The graphics are very simple and basic but vibrant enough to be easy on the eye.
The music fits the game. With games like this, any music will get repetitive after a while but the tune you keep hearing while playing
manages to not be annoying and merely 'neutral'. So that's okay.
doesn't have a lot of sound effects but they do sound clear and sharp.
All in all, there certainly is a base for fun to be had in
, but I found the game too difficult and too repetitive to play for a long time, so I can't recommend it. But if you do a bit of research and still think
may be your cup of tea, and if you can pick it up cheap, by all means give it a try. I'm not saying it's complete rubbish, after all.
Or maybe you want to buy the game to play it online with a friend. Like I said, I didn't play online so I can't render a verdict there. One thing's for sure, online you won't encounter the artificial increase in difficulty because the opponent just gets increasingly more and better units than you at the start of each level.

If you take your time mastering the games tactics and unit combinations you might have found a real treasure here. If you can grab it for 5 to 10 euro you should be fine. , thus I can't represent what the game is now, however I can give my thoughts on what it was like a few years ago. The only reference used here is my own memory; this will mostly likely have bias, as a person who did enjoy the game. I bolded the important bits for tl;dr.
, or at least the first three generations were. I can't remember what the rest of them were about, though I do remember that they continued the story line in one of the later generations (17~18 I believe). I don't think I've ever seen characterization of this extent in any MMORPG; to this day I still occasionally wonder what ever happened to Triona and Ruari. The NPCs are recurring, meaning that they still are relevant through out the game relative to the story. There's even a relationship system with the NPCs, though I do think it could be fleshed out some more. Perhaps they've already fleshed it out by now, who knows? I remember giving lots of bread to the nun that's always outside the Church in Tir, I'd finally got her to warm up to me after ~50 loaves of bread and occasionally she'd give me a boiled egg. It was ... heart warming, and it's probably the only thing remotely similar to human affection I'm ever going to get from a girl.
Each NPC has their own special song. The nun outside the Church had a particularly wonderful tune. Here it's better to show you, listen for a bit:
It almost seems like each song was composed to maximize nostalgic value, even more so once I heard the lyrics to the theme song sung by Tanaka Rie; it was as if it was speaking directly to former players. Not to say that new players can't enjoy the music as well, it's just that listening to these pieces right now, it has more impact than one would think.
There is no level cap, how it works is that every so often you'd reset yourself to level 1 again keeping your skill progression. You can literally play for as long as you want with out it getting too slow to level. And when I speak about leveling it doesn't nessesarily mean grinding.
The game doesn't follow the point, click, and wait system that was common during that time, it was a little more dynamic than that; in fact back in the day getting hit twice usually meant death. Goblins, being one of the lower forms of enemies, would still deal out high amounts of damage both in raw damage and in numbers (multi-aggro). The good thing is that you don't have to kill monsters if you don't want to, with the release of non-combat leveling, you can be a farmer that levels up by touching chickens, milking cows, etc, or you could just blacksmith things all day. I found it particularly fun to simply search for gems to feed to the loli living in my knife.
If I had one good thing to say about Nexon's cash grabbing, it's the customization options. They do a pretty good job of offering a bunch of choices. That's all on top of the innate customization in the game, I can't even count the amount of clothing articles this game has. Even in the case that you see someone wearing the same thing you are, there's dye. mathmatically there are millions of possibilities, for God's sake you can dye your weapons. You write your own music, you design your own plot of land, etc. Combat wise some of the key choices the game shoves at you is Paladin vs. Dark Knight, Elf vs. Giant, I think you have to choose the Demi-god thing too; I can't say for sure, I never got that far in the game (those quests were too dificult for me).
The graphics may be a bit blocky for this generation, especially with these fancier games coming out. My defence to this is that the magnitude of customization offered here would not be realistically possible with "next gen" graphics, though keep in mind this game is aged, for if we look at Elder Scrolls, Black Desert, etc we can obviously see model level character customization. Even those games however lose to Mabi in the amount of apparel there is.
From what I understand with recent updates the player character gets incredibly stronger, putting less emphasis on the need for tactics. (Who needs tactics when enemies that used to 2-hit you now only deal 1 damage). Perhaps this is to accomodate for this new age, refer to Pokemon ORAS and it's justification for not having a Battle Frontier.
I remember the movement system being a little quirky, though they did mention they were working on improving it, adding features like auto-pathing and anti-clipping.
There's actually so much more wrong with the game, but to me it's just part of what makes it special. In fact, given this age, I predict that you probably won't like the game; the AI was all over the place, it was really laggy sometimes, and there were many glitches. In the end, they all just grew on me after so long.

Putrefaction lets you play as an unnamed operative of a team whose objective is to stop the spread of a disease that turns humans into monsters. The game intro states you found a secret entrance to a base that seems full of the diseased monsters and, in true hero fashion, you assault it alone after calling in its location.
What follows is a very simple game where you face hordes of infected one after the other while trying to find the exit of each level: dull gameplay, a few perplexing design decisions and a couple of bugs make this a forgettable experience at best.
-the graphics are modest but work well enough
-good amount of weapons
-decent gore and dismembering
-the monsters you'll be facing have enough variety to not become too boring
-dull level design made worse by rooms and corridors that all look the same
-basic, unimpressive gameplay
-horrible enemy spawn system
-bad AI, melee enemies can't jump or climb so if you can reach, say, a tall box you'll be safe from them
-weapon sounds are tinny and weak
-some enemy animations, like jumps and dodge rolls, are clearly missing some frames
-basically no story or objectives whatsoever
-a few lingering bugs, one also makes the last boss almost unbeatable unless you read about it in the forums
-has a reload button but weapons have bottomless clips, in fact you can't reload at all
-very short, 1 hour and a half at most
Putrefaction claims to be inspired by the FPS games of old like Doom, well I'm sad to say they have little in common qualitywise: those old games were simple, sure, but had good levels with places to explore and secrets to uncover, nice enemies, challenging boss fights and at least some item hunting to switch things around a bit.
Let's start with the story, I'm not expecting much since it's a shooter after all but there's nothing after the intro text,nothing at all apart from a small text note at the end...why are people mutating so much that they resemble full blown aliens? Why is there an huge boss? What's up with the base itself? Why can infected spawn out of thin air like ghosts? And why do the infected disappear and their place is taken by some sort of glowing spirits in the last levels? No idea whatsoever.
But story isn't an important part of a simple shooter after all, sadly the gameplay is just as uninspired and boils down to moving towards the exit slaughtering waves of infected/spirits whenever a locked door/light barrier stops you, rinse and repeat. There are no objectives, no keys to find, no computers or switches to activate, nothing. It gets dull fast to be honest as you walk yet another nondescript corridor/room waiting for the next ambush.
All this is made worse by the nonsensical spawn system, infected can spawn anywhere, even right behind you or out of thin air one foot in front of you: this not only looks surreal and silly but also makes the game hard in an unfair way. You have no dodge or sprint moves and having a melee enemy spawning right behind you can be a disaster: it actually gets even sillier when such spawning tactics are employed by suicidal exploding enemies that will take 1/3 of your health each...when faced with them my only tactic was to put myself into a corner to make sure none'd spawn too close, but having to cheat the game this way to make it playable shows how bad this design choice is. There's also a few instances where enemies will spawn a bit far from the area you're in or refuse to leave a certain room forcing you to look for them to be able to progress.
Last but not least even a month after release there's still a few bugs the worse being one making the final boss not being affected by your weapons for about 20/30 seconds after each time you destroy its shield. I had to look it up on the forums after trying twice and wasting all my ammo only to die in return.
To sum things up no story, bland levels, simple gameplay, horrible and unfair spawning system, some nasty bugs and generally low production values make this a game I simply can't recommend: if you're looking for an old school FPS fix please look elsewhere.

This game is currently in a bundle in indiegala (as of 08/29/15) and caught my eyes enough to go pinch in and purchase a bundle having few games that I already owned.
The game is advertised as a Doom-like and unfortunately it is not... It is a Serious Sam like.  In other term, don't expect moving freely in an entire level being pursued by hordes of monsters while trying to solve some puzzles to make it to the next level... In this game (like in Serious Sam), you are trapped in a subsection of a level, have to kill every monsters that appear and then will be granted right to go to the next level subsection.  This is quite a difference of gameplay and it is probably why I never like Serious Sam and still believe that Doom 1 and 2 are the best FPS ever made (with L4D).
The control are poor or not implemented in the usual FPS way.  The left shift key does nothing which is extremely frustrating because you will expect to be able to run for your life with it.  The interaction with the surrounding is null... simply opening door and picking up ammo and life, nothing else.  The sound is average especially for detecting monsters on your back which appears out of thin air.
All of these make the game strongly outdated and still fall short from the comparison with Doom and other major old-school shooters.  I might sound a little harsh especially since Putrefaction seems to be  a one man project but the price tag of $5  is quite high for a game I would probably never play again.

Comparing this game to old-school FPS such as Doom, Quake, Serious Sam, Painkiller or even the more recent Killing Floor is kinda insulting for longtime pc gamers like me!
The player's movements are kinda slow. The enemies are poorly animated and always spawn in dead angles. The weapons lack punches and are badly designed. The level design is very linear unlike Doom, Quake and Serious Sam where levels were built like mazes that feature sometimes open spaces. If only it had good background music during exploration and combat.
The only enjoyable thing about the game is the gore effect which is not bad for an indie game. (+1) Also, it features lots of different enemy types and some boss fights. (+1) And at least, it's not a broken game which means I never had any crashing (+1) or clipping issues (+1).
Overall, the game feels tedious and very generic. Another typical indie FPS powered by the (unoptimized) Unity engine. In fact, the game has more in common with Slaughtering Grounds, Devils Share, Into the Dark, Prisoners of Power, Country Justice Revenge of the Redneck, Liquidator, Dark Vampires and Dracula The Days of Gore.
The title "Putrefaction" says everything about the game. You can smell it from your computer screen.
Before the indie dev and its fanboys dislike or delete my review avoid the game at all cost! I wish the actual reviews on the store page could have more common sense.

Without a doubt. I would recommend this game to anyone who wants more in an MMO.
Pros:
- Player created...'everything'. --From your story, to the crap you buy. There's very little that did come from the players
- Stunning graphics.
- Built for PVP from the ground up.
- Massive PvP combat. --It may be a "blob" but where else are you going to fight some 300 other players at the same time.
- Consequences for everything you do. --Because of the nature of this game. You can do pretty much anything to other players short of hacking their account. You can scam them, aide them, kill them. But, depending on your actions be prepared to either be praised or hunted.
- No "safe zone". --Well, unless you count sitting in the space station.
Cons:
- Poor ship controls. --Ships do not handle like they do in Star Trek Online
- No "fast lane" for character progression. --Skills are trained at a set rate that can't be hastened by actively playing the game. You could literally sit in the station for 4 years and be just as 'progressed' as someone who spent 4 years running around in the 'verse doing missions, mining, PVP, PVE combat. While many will see this as a plus. If you're looking to have your play time rewarded (ie you gained levels/direct character progression). You'll quickly be bored with this game; left with a feeling that you didn't really accomplish anything.
All in all, a very fun game to play every once in a while. And those hours of playing definitely warrant a continous subscription. I can't wait to see how this game continues to evolve.

Are games art?
That's a pretty loaded question. It's hard to call Proteus a game, and it's also hard to call a game "art".
Typically, games consist of objectives, things to accomplish. Proteus does not. Proteus is a procedurally generated experience, the music and visual style changing rapidly throughout.
Is Proteus a game? That's up to you.
Is Proteus art? That's up to you.
But it's something worth your time.

I bet if you told someone last year that a Borderlands adventure game would be one of the best games of the year, I’m sure most people would think you’re full of♥♥♥♥♥♥ I know I would. But now that I’ve finally played through TftB, I have to say that it’s in my Top 3 GOTY 2015 alongside Witcher 3 and Undertale. (That was originally Life is Strange’s spot for most of the year until the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ last episode, didn’t think Borderlands would be taking that spot either) I think Tales is far and away Telltale’s second best game, only being beat out by Walking Dead Season 1. It’s a strongly written roller coaster ride that feels longer than it is in a good way. (And it’s around nine hours or so give or take so its decently long to begin with for an adventure game.)
I think one of the major strengths that Tales shares with TWD Season 1 is that both were free to be their own stories. Borderlands has more of the characters from the original source material appear, but because they’re just a bunch of treasure-hunting mercs from an FPS where they just shoot♥♥♥♥♥♥and aren’t tied into any real plots Telltale could do what they wanted with them. Funny thing is Tales is actually a direct sequel to Borderlands 2 as its events feature heavily in the plot, but you don’t have to play or even like 1 and 2 to enjoy Tales. Borderlands as a series doesn’t deserve a game as great as Tales really.
Tales is genuinely funny on its own merits. The main series is rather infamous for its Internet meme laden writing, but Tales takes the high road and instead has the cast be likeable and have the comedy come from their interactions and other silly situations. If there is any references they tend to actually be good. (Like one real good in Episode 4) And as I said the writing is real strong, the characters are all likable and they develop over the course of the game.
Gameplaywise it’s more on the linear side like Telltale’s recent fare, it tends to just shuttle you along through interactive cut scenes, but there’s enough there to keep you engaged. (It sure as ♥♥♥♥ is leagues better than Game of Thrones) You play as both Rhys and Fiona depending on the section of the game, though you play them separately and can’t switch between them or anything like that. Choices are in the TWD Season 1 vein, where you can change the characters' personalities and their relationships.  This is illustrated best with the ending which allows you to recruit characters you’ve befriended throughout the game. The ending itself is great and ties together everything real well and can bring some great conclusions to the characters’ arcs. (One of which most people missed out on, but I didn’t.)
Tales from the Borderlands is overall just one of those pageturner type games where you don’t want to put it down until you’re done. Its charming and entertaining as ♥♥♥♥ and if this ends up being the last quality game Telltale ever makes, at least they ended on a hell of a high note.

This is one of those games that I got in a Humble Bundle and knew absolutely nothing about, but, it’s one that I would’ve happily bought on it’s own. A Druid’s Duel is a turn-based strategy game from Thoughtshelter Games and Surprise Attack. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
Take a moment to imagine the game of chess. Now, imagine that it was cool. The result you’ve come up with my very well look similar to A Druid’s Duel. In a way, it’s like blending chess with Risk: you have several types of units at your command and your goal is to destroy all the enemy units and control as much land as possible. Simple, yeah?
The color palette in this game is pleasing; it’s easy on the eyes. It complements the scenery nicely.
There’s a surprising amount of depth to the strategy in ADD. Every unit has a special ability (some have more than one). Every unit dies in one hit. Every time you step onto a tile of land, you take control of it and earn more mana on your next turn as long as it remains under your control. You use mana to summon units. Bearing all of this in mind, you can work out a strategy for your grand victory.
The Bad
I got nothing here. I got this game on the cheap and I think it is really fun for what it is.
The Meh
There is one unit that can shift it’s shape into a bear. The bear is a bit goofy looking.
Verdict: Yea
If you can get it on sale, good; get it and get a copy for a friend. If you like games of this nature, I’m sure you’ll enjoy playing A Druid’s Duel.

Working title: The Last Door: Season 2: The Awakening: The Resurrection: The Rebirth - Collector's Edition - Complete Edition - srorriM: Game of the Year Edition: The game.
Warning: This review contains spoilers for The Last Door: Season 1. If you haven't played the the first game... Well, why the heck are you reading the reviews for the second one?
The Last Door: Season 2 is a point and click horror game which follows doctor Wakefield as he investigates the disappearance of his patient, Jeremiah Devitt, who entered the veil with his childhood friend Alexandre. Wakefield must travel through England with his friend Kaufmann, as they find out more about the four witnesses and strange experiments with the intent of going beyond the veil.
The gameplay is very similiar to the first game - it's still walking around, picking up objects and solving puzzles, but this time, you have the option to travel around to different locations, making this game longer and more complicated than the first one. In my opinion, the puzzles are still very good, but it's easier to get stuck in this one and it's very likely that you will end up using a guide.
The story of this game is, in my opinion, even better than that of the first game. You play as Devitt's psychiatrist, doctor Wakefield, who teams up with his friend Johan Kaufmann to investigate Devitt's mysterious disappearance. Soon enough, you're haunted both by the mysterious force that haunted Devitt in the first game - the eye of the bird, and a mysterious organization called the Playwright. The game answers all the questions you had left after the first game and ties it all into a very satisfying ending.
The horror aspect of the game was still very strong, with very original scares, psychological horror, great suspense and many interesting characters with chillingly disturbing stories. I thought that the first game was creepier, with scares sometimes being very unpredictable, but I didn't feel disappointed in this one, as it manages to deliver the spooks pretty well.
The pixel art has noticeably improved - even though I thought that the first one was gorgeous already, this game is even better at setting the right atmosphere using colour palettes and there's plenty of very beautiful sceneries and designs in this game. The music was also very good at reinforcing the atmosphere. The intro music was the same (but the intro art was more beautiful) and the music was the same genre as in the first one, so, if you enjoyed creepy classical music in the first game, you're gonna like it again. Just as in the first game, the sound design is very good, with many sounds used to create suspense, the jumpscares were handled well and there's interesting use of audio channels.
For a completionist, this game gives you achievements for finding secrets. This is nearly impossible without a guide, but, with one, it should take you less than 10 hours. It's pretty short, but a good choice if you only want to get a higher percentage.
Overall, this game lives up to the first one quite well. You can play it for free online, so, if you're stingy, you might want to play this one for free or on sale, but I thought it was a very good purchase and I recommend it to everyone who liked the first game.
