The game itself is a very fun and simple strategy concept with quick rounds and decent amounts of depth considering the easy rules. I'd recommend it if you intend on playing it single player.
The online multiplayer, however, is an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥how. I bought the 2 pack to play with a friend, and in the duration of one ~half hour session, we experienced the following:
- Whether we were able to join each other seemed like a complete dice roll; we just had to keep making new games until one finally became visible in the games list. There's no invitation system.
- Upon joining me one time, friend's game did not load the board or characters and they had to quit.
- Said game then became invisible forever, despite both of us attempting restarts/rejoins.
- Seemingly random server disconnects that cause your turn to be reset to the beginning.
- Friend's "end turn" button completely broke; when pressed, nothing happened on my end, it only affected fairies on their end.
In addition, you also have to sign up for an account JUST for this game and use their friends list system on their website if you want to play online. The online interface in general is terrible as well; there's not even any way to see who you're playing against while you're ingame, and there's no local chat (only global).
Note that this was with cross-platform Windows/Linux play. I don't know if that makes it more likely to break, but broken is broken.
Again, the core game is fine. This review takes into account that I bought this entirely for the online component.

Interstellar Marines is an ambitious take on the old school tactical FPS genre. It presents this concept through its focus on immersion. As a soldier chosen to participate in a secret military program (Project IM), you are sent to protect mankind from threats outside the solar system. While this narrative is barely developed during the campaign, it provides an opportunity for the game to include more futuristic environments and less generic enemies.
The game features three modes: single-player, multi-player and co-op. The single-player and co-op modes both include exactly the same missions, while the multi-player puts a competitive twist on each map. However, since there are few people playing the multi-player, my ping was high when reviewing the game and I'm not very good at it, I’ll only be reviewing the single-player and co-op experiences.
Should you choose to play the campaign, you will be greeted with a decent-sized, open area to explore as you please. This area is probably either a stronghold or an eerily quiet spaceship. Although these differ in numerous ways, they both contain the same enemy: robots specifically designed to train soldiers. It is best to dispose of them through stealth, but you also have the option to just run wild with an SMG and shoot everything you see. This is the true appeal of Interstellar Marines. The option to use tactics to get to each objective is refreshing in an age of often linear, overly simplified shooters with tacked-on narratives about Russian people attempting to blow up the world.
Additionally, many of the areas in the game require you to navigate tight, claustrophobia-inducing corridors. Pairing this with the unnerving sound of nearby enemies and a day-night cycle that is inclined to leave you in the dark with just the torch at the end of your gun, there is an undeniable sense of tension. However, you must compose yourself and make sure you are not found. If you are, you will have to react quickly. Robots deal a large amount of damage, but are susceptible to head-shots. It is wise to keep your distance and take them out with your assault rifle if possible. Despite this, there isn't much opportunity to do so. Often, you are forced into close-range combat.
Alongside the campaign, there are escape, elimination and survival missions. Of the three, elimination is the one I spent the most time with. It provides the tension that makes the campaign worthwhile, but it contains no objectives other than to kill all the enemies on the map.
I would recommend having a friend to play with, as it allows for co-operative tactics and adds to the enjoyment of the game. There are dedicated servers for every mission that can be used to set up both public and private games.
In conclusion, Interstellar Marines has potential to be a great game. The concept is nice and the execution is good, but it is still in development. There isn't a huge amount of content at the moment; particularly in the campaign. Occasionally, your gun disappears and you run around holding nothing. If little problems like this bug you, avoid Interstellar Marines until it is released as a fully complete game. If they don’t bug you, buy it on sale and you will have a decent experience playing the game at its current stage.

This game is extremely different from Counter-Strike. Day of Defeat has Respawns, within a time-limit. It is Map Objective Based. Though skill is required for this FPS, the Objective is the most important. This means that your K/D Ratio is not as important as your Objective Points. Having a score similar to... 5 Flag Captures, 7 Kills, and 20 Deaths, is not exactly unnatural. The more Objectives completed, the higher ranking you get on your team. The team to complete the Objectives, wins. When I was an Honorable Skilled Player, I took on a Side Project for a Community, as I was asked to run their Day of Defeat section. This game is considerably more fun and less serious than Counter-Strike, due to the Auto Respawn, Weapon Function, Objectives, Team Work Required, World War Style Layout Story.

I wanted to love this game, and in many ways I did.
The controls are tight and satisfying, the games are typically and appropriately frustrating, but balanced, and the mutators add a great twist to gameplay. Now, the marketing for this game is a bit questionable. While there is an element of chaos to the gameplay, it's an organized chaos that lends itself more toward fierce competition than wacky party antics, since most of your deaths will be your own fault even amidst the layers of changing rules. Make no mistake: this is a game about gitting gud. What's more, in the time I've owned it I've watched the developers steadily iron out nearly every bug or issue I had upon buying this game, and it's flourished into a strong couch game - that is, if your couch friends have the stamina for it.
Unfortunately, its potential as a couch game is stifled by its hardcore influences, and your average couch guest will be overwhelmed by the pressure. This is no Ultimate Chicken Horse or Duck Game, people will be frustrated by the immediate and obvious skill differentials. Even more hardcore guests will have trouble simply by virtue of your familiarity with the game, leading to an unfun situation of curbstomping your friends or trying to avoid doing so while they figure out how the rules work.
All of this brings me to the online. At the surface, this game seems built for the online environment. With such intense competition and plenty of competitors, the game should be at its finest where you can play against other people who get a chance to play and practice. The developers have made improvements even here: they've added in-game chat, and the matchfinding button has been drastically improved to actually be a viable alternative to the Server Browser. That said, Move or Die's proverbial nail in the coffin is the player-hosted servers. Stable connections are more common than reviews would have you believe, but every millisecond of latency tilts the game in favor of the host, the only player playing in realtime. Games like Bomb Tag are utterly ruined by poor connections, which will leave joining players wondering why they ran on top of a player for 3 seconds or more without passing the bomb, yet the host seems to magically be able to pass the bomb to them from half a screen away. There's no joy in winning a game you can't lose, and Hosting a game in Move or Die sets up exactly that. When I do play, I no longer Host in order to avoid this inescapable advantage.
Move or Die desperately needs a better online system. I'm not going to pretend I know everything about PvP network infrastructure, but even equally-poor dedicated servers would be more satisfying distributing the lag to everyone instead of being explicitly in the Host's favor. An imbalance like this is unacceptable in a competitive game, and it ruins the thrill of the experience knowing its effects. No one wants to finish a match and question whether they only won because it was their own game. Until this game has a fair online system that either advantages or disadvantages every player based on lag instead of all but one, I cannot recommend it in good conscience.

A turn-based strategy game about using units with differing areas on control and capturing/expanding/securing tiles until you get them all. Has the feeling of a few elements of chess/checkers/risk. Graphics and sound are fine, story is mediocre but it at least gives the levels a little flavor/something to tie the campaign of miscellaneous levels together. Every once in a while there are 'boss' levels where the enemy starts with a superpowered unit that is a nice break from the regular levels.
You capture tiles by walking over them and each turn you gain mana from those tiles to summon more units. There are 4 types of units: the basic and inexpensive spear druid that can be used as fodder or to capture many tiles, the archer druid that can attack from range or transform to pick off a key/undefended unit, the knight melee druid that can transform to kill multiple foes in a row, and the mage druid that can manipulate tiles to either kill multiple units from range or shape the landscape to direct/block unit access.
In general, you want to expand as quickly as possible to gain the mana advantage (which becomes unit advantage) but without being punished for overextending (somewhat like how I think risk is played). You'll have to reinforce your border areas and chokepoints, make sure any incursions into your territory can be repelled, and try to make unit trades in your favor.
Worth a look if you like turn-based territory-control games like risk.

At first I was really sceptical when I entered the game and it looked just like Risen 2 but after the first few quests I realized the numerous improvements the devs have made to the game. Some major complaints I had with Risen 2 have been resolved.
Gameplay & Story:
The standard melee combat system is still not at a level that i can truly say I liked it. Muskets felt really underpowered in this title. But magic is straight up powerful and feels (and looks) pretty nice. I really like that they don't use a mana system in this title but rather cooldowns only. It helps to remove those annoying downtimes
I really liked the idea of the parrot spell, where you can just fly around the world for a limited time. A stronger version you can learn would have been great though
Like in the previous title there are some minigames you can play in most major cities, which is a nice idea although not a time dump like in some other games.
The very numerous quests played out nice. The map system has a solid design. The fast travel points are well placed enough to be helpful and still in "believable" locations.
As in all RPG titles the story plays a major role. The story telling is pretty solid in this title. The story is interesting to the end although nothing too new.
For fans of the series there are a lot old acquaintances to meet.
The voice acting was pretty solid, although some npcs obviously shared voices. Calling spiders insects all the time drove me nuts though (Yes, I know that in olden times people probably didn't know, but still).
In total it took me a good 40-45 hours to play through on a high difficulty and complete all quests I could find, which were quite many as stated before.
Looks & Performance:
The game looks really pretty for a huge world story driven RPG. There are very few bugs and glitches. The world design is well composed and feels for the most part realistic
Finally I really want to praise the optimization levels the devs have gone through. With all options on max my old third gen i5 used all it's cores equally and rarely went above 50% total load. Most of the work was done by my GPU (as it should be)
This game is actually really fun for a pass time game! :)

Being one of the older gamers and growing up in the NES era of harder then fsck games, this game resonated in me, thinking of the NES Bionic Commando (and having to beat it in shifts with my brother, since we were allotted a 30 minute timeframe to play games in as a kid).  I didn't know there was an arcade version before, just the NES version. But here we go!
Pros:  It's Spiderman with guns.  You start out with gunplay (and what you think is a weak pistol, until you start aiming for the head), but the game eventually becomes swinging, shoot and dodge and throw things action.  To me the swinging action felt natural and easy, without the "optimal swing" suggestions from the UI. There were many panic'd moments of swinging under buildings and all while dodging enemy fire, hoping for that moment when I could pop up and do massive damage.  The plot takes so many twists and turns, that you can't (until the end) guess where you are going.  It can be forgiving.  Enemies respond  appropriately to being approached in melee range (often snapping out some sort of electic stunning/killing baton, or taking advantage of your zipline).  It's gorgeous for the time, and even now.  And the humor makes me laugh (see the easter egg regarding the mechanical worm, your character breaks the 4th wall talking about it's health bar, and on playthroughs Joe suggests you fsck it which your character gives a VERY APPROPRIATE RESPONSE of uhhhhh).
Cons:  This is NOT the glorious open world game that it should have been. It falls into a "We'll keep the player confined due to a crappy mechanic" catagory, which makes it much more linear then it begged for.  Yes, I realized that the whole area is full of radiation, but the moment I hint about getting on the edge of where the designers ment me to be, I don't want to immediately die to radiation.  The same applies to water, yes I realize a giant metal arm would drag me down, but I didn't expect to drown in 3 feet of water before the game EXPLAINS it to me.  And while I praise the plot twists, I also lament in them... there's times where the plot makes zero sense (mysterious congression member that is only there to be Joe's foil, I'm looking at you).  Or is easily guessed.  Especially at the end where...  Well, I don't want to do any spoilers but the jump from when you fight Groder, who has final boss material written all over him especially considering the NES game, until you fight the actual final boss... makes no sense. It's like the writers and designers went "Ok we have to finish this up". The final boss battle is a simon says mashup that is painful on the keyboard (if you've gone with the origional keybinds, which INITALLY MAKE SENSE).  It's probably better on the XBox controller that the onscreen commands referense, without notating keybinds.  I felt like I was playing the old Track and Field games, letting go of the mouse to twitch/mash the F button.  Even the menus and all leave me with thise sense, losing a ton of interesting reading to the "ok, do I press the down arrow, or the actual down button (bound to S) to read all of it?" syndrome. The ending left me feeling... unsatisfied.  That's all I want to go into without spoilers.  It wasn't even worth waiting for the epilogue, especially since the last part isn't even translated (thank you wikipedia).
Final Verdict:  If you can get it on a grand sale, it's worth it. Like a $3 or less kinda thing. You'll have 5ish hours of gametime, feel mostly satisfied (until the end) that you are the speedy, dodgy, spiderman killing machine you are, only occassionally hampered by game mechanics, random deaths, and a final fight that is stupidly annoying on the keyboard with the default binds.  And you'll get that rush of being spiderman. With guns.

For me, this game had a big focus on what you should follow in life. You start off with a large unexplored island full of life, and you end off with just the moon being the only thing to guide you. Everyone need something to guide us, and this game has alot of examples of it.
I found myself aimlessly wandering around, looking at the beautifull landmarks, only to get lost after a while, but when the night came, a large vortex of light swarmed away into a direction.
I followed, and when i got to the end, i found a large stone circle that changed the seasons. When it was done changing, it went all dark. The trees were dead. The life was gone, and the island was full of gravestones. The music changed into a dull string of nothingness. The things i used to guide me around the island were gone. With nothing to guide me, i wandered away from the island,
With nothing happening, i went back again, but this time, it seemed that the island was a bit small, but to my surprise, i was flying. Higher and higher, until i saw the only landmark to guide me; The moon. The screen went dark.

Stick Fight is a comical, multiplayer fighting game. Its was developed by Landfall West and published by Landfall who have developed Clustertruck and published TABS. It was first released on the 29 of September, 2017 and costs $5 USD.

Stick Fight has great gameplay bringing you hours of fun the fighting feels great and responsive. The controls are also easy but also requires a bit of learning and getting used to. The melee combat is well done with it feeling responsive, it is also well balanced making the melee weapons a viable option against projectile weapons. Even if you are stuck you are able to through your melee weapon, and gun, which can be quite useful.
The projectile weapons are really well made adn are a ton of fun to use. There are a range of different types of weapons from snake guns which shoot snakes which stick to and attack the closest play (including the person who fired the gun), there are also normal projectile weapons like assault rifles, snipers, shotguns and miniguns which produce lots of recoil. There are lava guns and also so many more variants of guns in these 3 types. All these guns are well balanced and fit into how this game is meant to be played.
The maps are also great fun. They provide different obstacles on maps like breaking floors, falling boxes or a full movement of the map making even more fun while also requiring you to think on what to do to not dye from the maps changes and to still be a to kill the other players.
All this gameplay is even better with friends

The artists did a great job keeping it simple, it also keeps the game running at a great frame rate.
The sound design of this game is great giving crisp sound effects and really well designed up beat music adding to the fast paced, fun, gameplay of Stick Fight.

Simplistic, and yet deeply satisfying and immersive, RimWorld is a great game.  I have been playing since about Alpha 16, and it has felt like a complete game since then. You can play around on your planet forever, or finish your ship and write your own scenario and add some mods to continue your story.  There really is no excuse not to buy this if you are a fan of survival and base building games, and if the developer content is not enough, the mod content will surely fill in the gaps.
At this point, I'm just waiting for some polishing up before I revisit it, though I am always satisfied with my play time in this great RPG/Survival/Base-Building Sandbox.

I'm not the biggest Telltale fan. I didn't like the Walking Dead, it bored me and I found all the characters to be mopey and kinda devoid of any personality besides what terrible thing happened to them. I know it was a zombie apocalypse and stuff but there was just nothing I found enjoyable about listening to any of the dialogue. The Wolf Among Us was a definite improvement, but I still didn't love it.
Tales From the Borderlands is so much better I don't even know how to express it. If you like Borderlands then even better, I think this does more with the world than any of the main franchise has done so far, every line is brilliant, every character is full of personality and quirks and I found myself already attached to them partway through the first episode.  The story is completely wild, and while occassionally predictable, never in a way that bores you, it's always more of a, "YES THIS IS HAPPENING," as opposed to, "pfft called that."
But even when the storyline gets predictable, the action sequences save it. That's something that Telltale has never had before, and it adds a lot. Telltale games are basically interactive movies, and that's fine but when 90% of it is dialogue, it gets a bit tiresome. Tales spices that up with some ridiculous setpieces, set to aways fantastic music, making it an absolute joy to watch. For once, I didn't care that I couldn't participate in a certain sequence, just because it was so much fun watching the insanity on screen happen. There's more action packed into the first episode of this, than the entirety of their other series'.
100% recommended, if you don't mind the default Telltale style, this is a must own. The best thing they've put out yet by a country mile.

The Last Door: Season 1 was described as a "journey to the brink of madness" and "a love letter to H.P. Lovecraft".  I agreed with this and Season 2 is no different.  The themes are clearly Lovecraftian and even as a story driven point and click game, it offers enough of a challenge and some great secrets to make it more than just a "click here to progress" adventure game.
Like Season 1, Season 2 is not "terrifying", but it has that feeling of dread and the score really adds to the tension.  Over the course of the episodes you can feel it all building up.  The graphics are the definition of pixel art, but it''s actually a beautiful game with some amazing locations and cutscenes on offer.  Though this means that some objects are still difficult to locate as they blend in with the background a little too well.  Fortunately these moments didn't become frustrating.
So it's a fantastic entry in the series, with a really interesting story that warrants more than one playthrough.  Like Season One, you should at least pick this up on sale if you want a great horror atmosphere, a few interesting puzzles and a brilliant soundtrack.

For some reason, Piranha Bytes games tend to be underrated. I love the art in this game, the tropical scenery is fantastic to look at. Lots and lots of quests, hidden objects, places to explore. A rather unusual concept - think of it less like a traditional tactical RPG, i.e. Final Fantasy Tactics et al, and more like.. half that and half chess/checkers. Units don't really have spells/abilities/attack/def/HP/etc., they each are a 'type' and each type has a movement/attack range and an animal transformation that lets them move/attack in an unusual fashion (movement/attacks are usually one space/one attack per turn, at a glance.)
If you're looking for a turn-based grid-based tactical RPG with character classes/levels/etc., then look elsewhere. If the appeal of something of a light dusting of that plus some puzzle/logic/forward thinking used in chess, then this game may be for you.

Surprisingly unique 3rd Person Action Adventure
BC is kinda interesting to rate, because for a AAA title, the contrast between the bright spots and the shoddy stuff is pretty pronounced.
Let's look at the major copouts first- because they stand out like buckteeth on a souped up Miss World:
This game yearns for exploration- but you're not allowed!
There's semi invisible "radiation" everywhere that will cokkblokk your curiousity, sometimes in a very surprising and unfair way.
Alternative routes - nopenope.
That's insane given how predestined the core mechanics would be for exploring different aerial paths .
Further more, the game will dangle it's secret collectibles right on the edge of these hard to gauge radiant deathtraps, so you'll probably die a few times before you'll find out how to snatch them.
Additionally, cheap easy-to-spot critique include the game's inability to clearly teach and differentiate the hero'ss different abilities.
And finally, BC loses a bit of steam at the end. They can't come up with fresh challenges or ideas.
(And -nagnagnag- some core combat stuff could be better polished but which ambitious game started out perfect?)
That's rather regrettable, since the game's main feature is kickazz:
If you stuck with me till this line, you might just be the hardcore gamer who would enjoy that unique thing which is sooo great about Bionic Commando:
It is...the frikkin Bionic arm!
Climb, attack or simply frolic like a tripped-out berserker gibbon!
No game offers the joy of cybernetic brachiation, the moments where a deft but well-timed tarzanic swing lets you pounce between foes, grab one of them and hurl him into another group of baddies.
Superb!
The rest is at least solidly done:
Artistic designs and animations are tight.
Most of the action, weaponry and enemy encounters are nicely done.
Music and sounds are great.
All in all, it's a shame that sales tanked and we probably won't see a BC 2.

Borderlands, developed by Gearbox is an action/adventure/ballsy/Diablo loot gun/fps/co-op/RPG/ and probably some more genres included. At it’s core Borderlands thrives with co-op and endless fun. I played a good chunk of the first half of the game solo, embracing it’s mechanics, what to do, what not to do, and just plain o’l satisfying my urge to shoot an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥/s(hint: there’s a ton of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bags in this game). Yet, I still found myself enjoying the experience. Finishing side quests and leveling up in order to upgrade my equipment to a better standard than before. I mean why wouldn’t you go hunt for a better weapon than your current pea shooter?
Let me break down the other aspects of Borderlands, mainly it’s questing and landmass. There are over 120+ quests in this game and a partial amount contains the main missions intertwined with the side quests you can undertake separately. I like a lot of quests personally, in order to grind. However, I found myself constantly going on side quests and couldn’t figure out the main quests mission from the side-quests(And let’s not forget the dlc’s of which there are more quests to finish!) I found myself frustrated, after endless hours grinding only to realize the main quest wasn’t in sight. Due to my lost track of time and playing co-op with some buddies of mine (of which I attribute as my fault, for not paying attention to the game-play(Doh!)
Nevertheless, once I found my bearings I was able to complete the main quests in the aftermath of my frustration. What really bugs me in this game is the lack or any quest tracking. You are only designated to track only one quest. Not 1 or 5 or 10. Just bloody 1. While I would’ve liked multiple tracking of the quests in order to finish multiple quests I realize it didn’t detract from my whole experience of enjoying the game in it’s entirety I’m only saying it out there for folks wondering what could be some negatives for them.
With that said, let’s go to land in Borderlands. Hell, it’s enormous, there are multiple zones you can travel to and with the help of fast travel and vehicles (that can shoot guns + can load a buddy with you) I found myself quickly traversing the areas with haste and glee mowing down my enemies like a lawn mower vs. grass. It was only tedious because the target tracking for my quests on their exact position in an area was not made clear. For ex. I track a quest, then look to my fast travel to the location to go to, but there’s no indicator for it. Some quests don’t even tell you the location in their quest summary, but some do. This was somewhat frustrating for me so used to automated tracking with the location in areas. Nevertheless, I put the thought away and continued and realized if the developers intended it this way in order to make you take in the surroundings of each area more. I found such a revelation striking and thus, found myself looking at my surroundings with more awe than before.
Until I realized I died, by gawking at structures and not paying attention to my surroundings...
There are 4 classes you can choose from, Hunter, Soldier, Berserker, and Siren. Each has their own specialties unique to their respective classes offering different benefits and each differs from the other by having their own special ability and different sub trees. Of the trees you can input your points into there are only 3, yet differ from each class accordingly. I only played on the Soldier class which is basically a support class with a special ability of deploying a turret and three sub trees to pour my points into. The skill trees offered varieties that can suit a play style. Want to support your allies. No problem! Dump them here. Want to support your special abilities? No problem! Dump the points here. Want to support another tree for your guns? No problem! Dump them here too! While it’s not as rigid as that, merely summarized generalizations of the 3 sub-trees you can allot your points into. Each class is different and therefore offers different sub trees to spend your points on. With 1 level up = 1 point you can spend. Offering different play styles to emerge if you want to focus heavily on one tree or mix and match to suit your play style. For my soldier class I ended the game with level 35, but don’t be alarmed! You can over level up to 50 without dlc and up to 69 with dlc.
In short Borderlands, begins on the planet Pandora where you a vault hunter are stringed along by some weird chick with static on the H.U.D.’s display ordering your clueless body around the planet in search of the vault. Vaults which contain secrets and mysteries unknown to some residents on Pandora, it’s kind of like a treasure hunt? In a super condensed generalized state of the game, but it’s more than that. You have to pay attention to a colorful cast of interestingly, crude, sarcastic, humorous individuals with their own set of goals. And while you can scratch they’re back for a favor to you. In Borderlands it’s not as simple as 1 to 1. You will find in its entirety the game boasts a large landmass to explore, guns to sink your teeth into big or small and quests near endless everywhere. I found no problems with the music and often would spend some time of mine roaming the lands shooting my guns at annoying pests in my vision.

Ah Gunpoint.
Let's start out with the negatives of this game: It's too damned short.
Roughly 20 missions, most of which can be beaten in less than 5 minutes, can result in a very short game. I only wish that there was a workshop for this game so that the level editors that MAKE levels can be more easily seen, subscribed, and then played.
As for the game itself let's get down to the bare bones.
I don't think I've ever played a game like this. In Gunpoint you are able to cross wires remotely and as a result- different things cause different things. E.x: A switch turns off a door- you rewire it to open a door- and that door can be rewired to open another door and so on, and so on.
That is an amazing system than can be easily abused in a fun way.
Now for the enemies. There are 2 forms of enemies encountered in Gunpoint- normal guards, and enforcers.
Normal guards are easy to deal with; pouncing on them being the most common way of dealing with them.
Enforcers are more deadly forms of guard that cannot be pounced, so you have to use more stealth and wit to either take these guys down, or avoid them entirely.
The fun part about taking down each enemy has it's own special feel.
When you take down a normal guard and bash his face in for the second...third... fourth.... 300th time in a row, it kinda gives a sense of brutal joy out of it.
When you take down an enforcer; either by electrocuting them, or knocking them out of a window- you gain a certain sense of accomplishment of taking down a non-pouncable enemy.
The upgrades in Gunpoint are nice and very useful, especially after the story is well and done- so you can see how far you've come along ever since the start of the game.
Now for the more artsy fartsy aspect of the game.
The game itself is a pixleated, and for this game, I don't there there would be a better way to portray this game.
It's simplistic, and get's the job done. A lot of dark tones of the surrounding city, bright insides to show contrast. The environment of the game is well done.
The music- oh the music! It's  from cool jazz to an electronic feel, and that's a beautiful mixture in this game.
You may or may not notice it when playing, but it's there- and it sets the tone for the game.
The story itself is very short, and I am not going to give anyone any spoilers.
Story is thought out, and executed as the basis of why you are in the levels you are.
If it had a lot more levels, I would like it much much more.
Overall 9/10 for the price, try the demo if you are uncertain if you want to buy this game or not.
I'm looking forward to what other games Suspicious Developments makes in the future.

TellTale's Game of Thrones showed that they can tell a story just as good as the source material.
TellTale's The Walking Dead showed that they can tell a story that surpasses the source material.
TellTale's Tales from the Borderlands showed that these guys can forsake every major aspect of the source material, but still make a compelling, heartfelt, and surprisingly faithful adaptation.

I'm not the biggest Telltale fan. I didn't like the Walking Dead, it bored me and I found all the characters to be mopey and kinda devoid of any personality besides what terrible thing happened to them. I know it was a zombie apocalypse and stuff but there was just nothing I found enjoyable about listening to any of the dialogue. The Wolf Among Us was a definite improvement, but I still didn't love it.
Tales From the Borderlands is so much better I don't even know how to express it. If you like Borderlands then even better, I think this does more with the world than any of the main franchise has done so far, every line is brilliant, every character is full of personality and quirks and I found myself already attached to them partway through the first episode.  The story is completely wild, and while occassionally predictable, never in a way that bores you, it's always more of a, "YES THIS IS HAPPENING," as opposed to, "pfft called that."
But even when the storyline gets predictable, the action sequences save it. That's something that Telltale has never had before, and it adds a lot. Telltale games are basically interactive movies, and that's fine but when 90% of it is dialogue, it gets a bit tiresome. Tales spices that up with some ridiculous setpieces, set to aways fantastic music, making it an absolute joy to watch. For once, I didn't care that I couldn't participate in a certain sequence, just because it was so much fun watching the insanity on screen happen. There's more action packed into the first episode of this, than the entirety of their other series'.
100% recommended, if you don't mind the default Telltale style, this is a must own. The best thing they've put out yet by a country mile.

The combos don't always chain, and when they do, they tend to knock the opponent out of the chain. This is especially true with the most simple "hold down the ki attack button to rapid fire" combo.
I wish that instead of such a big hub world (which you have to walk around, no running or flying) they had spent more time on the fighting aspect. The game would have been far better and well worth the money then.

Scream Collector is just not a fun game for veterans of the idle game series. I've been trying to give it an entire playthrough, but it's just not captivating, fun, or pretty. Here's why:
The GUI is clunky, and annoying to look at in general. The low-resolution, old-school graphics don't hit close to home unless you were a fan of playing really bad knockoffs of old PC games. It looks unironically, purposefully poor and half-finished. It's initially confusing, and even when you figure it out, it's still annoying to remember which tab does what.
You don't get any sense of progression in this game. The still image changes only slightly when you purchase something, but there are really no animations, no true feeling that the item or upgrade you just idle-grinded 10 hours for is actually doing anything for you. It makes sense on AdVenture Capitalist, but on this game it just feels poor. Top that off with the grindy progression being one of the lengthiest endeavors in comparison to the other, more popular idle clickers I've played, and this just doesn't come close to what else is out there.
It's hard enough to get immersed into an idle clicker, but the developer of Scream Collector didn't even attempt to capture players interest. It's even harder to find a reason to play this one when there are tons of other good, free clickers to play. Unless you ran out of other clickers and are desperate for something new, give this one a pass until some massive upgrades come in.

Let me preface this by saying that I really enjoyed Season 1 of this creepy suspense macabre point-and-click adventure game. I was mad about it ending a cliffhanger, but what can you do. This season brings the finale of the story, and...well, it's an ending at least. Season 1 was about unraveling a mystery through the main character of Devitt, and this season you play as his doctor, Wakefield, trying to track him down. There should have been a lot more explanations as we drew closer to the ending, but it was one big "Mystery Box", with more and more mysteries and very little answers. They kept introducing new lore even in the final chapter and gave only the briefest few lines to explain what had actually happened over eight full chapters of the game. The result was that, when I watched the recaps from previous episodes, they were mentioning plot points that were never outright revealed, but that the devs had assumed they had made clear, but I had just played that chapter and my conclusions about what had happened during the very abstract, surreal or just not obvious actions in the story were VERY different from the recap. "What? That was all a dream? Where did it say that?" or "Wait, the townsfolk were doing what?" There was so much cool stuff going on, but so much of it just got shoved into too late in the story.
Pros:
+ The music is FANTASTIC. Also good sound design despite it not having any voice acting. Creepy singing, screams, squeaks...great atmosphere.
+ Great art. It's pixel graphics, but it's well done. The lack of detail makes your mind fill in the blanks. Can be either beautiful or downright creepy, or both.
Neutral:
~ Some episodes had great puzzles. Others had very abstract ones, where you had to do things that made no sense just to trigger the next area/event.
Cons:
- Story was meh (see above). Too much buildup without enough satisfying explanation.
Overall: If you liked the first season, it's probably worth it to buy it, if only to finish off the story. Or if you like semi-unresolved mysteries, this one also fits the bill. Or if you just like macabre point-and-click adventure games. 7/10

I understand that this is an early access title and that with any title in this status there are things that are not going to either be incomplete or necessarily function correctly.  However this game needs so much more development than I think it should even go into early access. After playing this game for a bit over an hour here are my thoughts:
* You are restricted to only using the keyboard and you can't even customize it so that if you don't like using the arrow keys you're out of luck
* The car models and track models in this game are beyond bland.
* The car models (appearance only) are straight rips of real life vehicles. The e190 is a straight rip of a 190 Evo, the Mustang is a straight rip of a Ford Mustang, the Camaro a Chevrolet Camaro, so on and so forth. There is no way the developer paid to license these names or the vehicles themselves. I'll be very surprised if they don't get sued by the various auto makers that hold trademarks on these vehicle likenesses and names.
* The only way I could slightly differentiate between each track was what was in the background. The tracks (limited as they were) were not distinguishable or special in any way
* There is only one playable race mode and who finishes first has zero affect on the winner. It  simply looks at who had the highest scoring drifts. That makes sense since it is a drifting game but it would be much more of a challenge if placement affected the total score
* You can only race one friend at a time. This is beyond silly in the day and age where it's not unusual to have a lobby full of 16 people playing a game, even a racing game
* It is far too easy to drift in this game, it takes absolutely zero skill. The slightest tap sends you careening around a corner. I was hoping that this game would actually take some effort and timing to get the best drifts possible but that is not the case
I could go on and on about this game but it is going to need a lot more development before it is even remotely close to something that I would even vaguely consider playing again.

Bionic Commando was a game that almost showed enough self awareness to be awesome. As fan of the original, I am happy to see it get a modern mock up. Although it was clear they changed some things (like, the ending), I was happy that the developer brought the classic back in an updated fashion and then used it for the basis of their full on modern sequel. And in this sequel, the game play is tremendously fun. The grappling hook arm left nothing to be desired. Unfortunately that is the extent of the awesome. The story is predictable, passe, and all around dumb. Simply put, it makes little sense (even with having played the original and the reloaded version of it), and, where the voice actors do a decent job with their lines, those lines are frequently so bad that they could only save it if they lampooned it.
If you ignore the story, which you should since it is that bad, and take the game to simply be a long ride with a grappling hook and a variety of challenges, then this game is great. If you care anything about story, look elsewhere.

An rpg in the classic style, Last Heroes finds three brothers at odds over who should really have been named king after the passing of their father. One brother is the game's hero (Viktor) and king of the land, another (Viper) has nefarious plans to unseat the hero by finding 4 relics that will give him the power he needs, and the third is reluctantly in the middle of the conflict.
There are other characters rounding out Viktor's group as they set out to find the relics first so the land will be safe. A simple enough beginning to a story that expands as you go. And you do go to many places to hunt down the relics ---- all with their treasures to find, secrets to discover, and enemies to battle.
Enemies do not reappear, so you can't level up by repeatedly fighting ---- instead, you have to carefully manage the money, items, weapons, spells, etc. that you gather along the way.
And, as you let the story unfold, it draws you in bit by bit.
Originally released some time ago, the graphics and music hold up nicely, and you will soon enough find yourself absorbed in the task of seeing what happens next, who is allied with who and why, and finding out about the different characters' individual backstories. I'm happy to see this one arrive on Steam, and believe it to be an excellent addition to my rpg game library.

Last Heroes is your typical, run-of-the-mill RPGMaker game. The king's brother is angry he wasn't crowned king and now wants to take control of four powerful relics so that he can rule the world. Your "unlikely" group of peope - the king, a magician, a thief, and a knight - will journey through dungeons trying to retrieve said relics before the angry brother can.
The title is fairly short (3-5 hours), and the dungeons all feel the same (perhaps because the majority of the dungeons in the game you go through twice). Enemies don't respawn, meaning you can't grind. Some enemies drop orbs so that you can buff stats, but since enemies don't respawn, you can't grind them. Not all of the chests refill when you make your return visits either.
I have a hard time finding a reason to recommend Last Heroes. The game is plagued with spelling and grammar errors, and there are some really cheap strategies you can use to beat all of the bosses (including the final boss). There are better RPGMaker titles out there, so unless you really want something that is short and basic, then give this game a pass.

!SPOILERS AHEAD!
Please note, this review is written in bullet-point form, as that's all it deserves.
What Bionic Commando did right:
Large, open areas idea for free-roaming with the grapple
Good use of grapple/momentum technology
Large, glowing hidden objects, requires skill  as well as finding them
Satisfying use of the grapple system to throw or throw at enemies
Interesting use of challenges to reward upgrades
Nice use of enemy dialogue
Played on Hard first time – difficult, but not impossible
What it did wrong:
Last-gen use of checkpoint system with very few checkpoints
Instant death pitfalls, invisible walls, fire and water
Limited incentive to collect hidden objects
Hidden items requiring very risky jumps that will easily kill you and require you to start again
Clunky aiming system
Some long, vulnerable animations (Kiteing)
Very basic gun system
Limited use for the melee system
Clunky in-game menu
Generic hide-to-heal health system
Enemies see you from far too far away, no stealth element
Badly voiced, unlikeable main character
Tenuous plot, badly written script
Gigantic plot holes: What is the 'item'; What did they plan to do with it; Who is the 'Sniper; What is the purpose of Mag's character (dies); Main character's unclear death at the end; Giant army of angel robots out of nowhere; Absurd betrayal for no clear reason; Main character's wife died so he could have a robotic arm, doesn't seem to bother him; Who are any of these characters (supposedly from previous games)
Terrible quick-time-esque final boss
Unskippable credits
What it should have done:
Melee system like Batman: Arkham Asylum
Use of time-slow while aiming
Heal back only the last full chuck of health on a bar of parts
Decoy weapon/item to lure large groups away/together
CONCLUSION:
This game is clunky, flawed, and written like a bad fan-fiction... but there is some fun to be had here. You may get frustrated, you may find it unfulfilling, but if you get this cheap on sale... why the hell not? And let's make this very clear: I'm recommending this because "why not". It's not good, you won't love it, but there isn't a "meh" button for me to choose.

I first played this game back in 2009, soon after its release on the Xbox 360. From what I can remember, I spent a lot of hours and had a lot of fun playing this game. The game was addictive, trying to farm for the best loot felt rewarding, co-op was pretty fun, too (especially with friends).
Unfortunately, this time around, I've spent most of my time on this game configuring the engine files, and trying to optomise performance without making the game look♥♥♥♥♥♥poor. To put it bluntly: the PC port of this game sucks. There's no FOV slider, instead you need to edit the input files and create your own bindings (which, to be fair, wasn't difficult, it was just an inconvenience.) The video settings are pretty basic, closing the doors for graphical variety. And for some reason, enabling dynamic shadows really puts a hinder on my FPS (ranging from around 25 FPS to 40 FPS). Without it, my laptop can achieve up to 62 FPS (as that is the framecap, for whatever reason) on maximum settings relatively easily. But, the game looks shoddy, unpolished and brighter than heaven's gate.
However, the gameplay is still there, the loot is still rewarding and co-op has been restored. If you've never experienced Borderlands, I would definitely recommend it, as it's certainly a unique and unforgettable experience. The performance of the game is bearable, but it can be really distracting at times and therefore tempt you into configuring files or searching on forums for any miracle tweaks for the game. If you're like me who bought the game for a trip down memory lane, I would still recommend, but be cautious. Nonetheless, if you do buy this game, I hope you have better luck with it than I did.

Proteus is ugly, and beautiful; empty, and full; depressing, and joyful.
Proteus is a game about discovery. After waking up to find yourself in (shallow?) waters, you wade toward an island and discover. The procedurally generated world hosts animals, landmarks, and oddities for you to find -- perhaps not all during your first playthrough -- and the music is shaped by your path and location. In other words, each time you visit Proteus, it truly is a new experience.
This game isn't for everyone. It's an extremely slow boil, and there are no objective markers, quest givers, or prompts popping up all over the place. Dialogue and terminals aren't drowning you in exposition. There is a narrative, but it's slight and so completely shrouded in mystery, that the actual point could simply be a projection of the player. There are things to do, but the question is: Are they important? Are they part of the island's mystery? Are they merely moments allowing you to catch your breath before seeking your true purpose, or are they diversions keeping you from your end goal?
This isn't meant as an insult, but rather a caution: If your entire Steam library consists of shooters and survival horror titles (likely containing zombies), you will likely hate Proteus. If your Steam library contains thoughtful adventure games, puzzlers, and ambient experiences, give Proteus a spin. It's been priced as low as $1.99 so even if it's not really your thing, you'll probably get your money's worth.

If you are purchasing this game to sit in an asteroid belt and shoot rocks with lasers to generate enough ISK to purchase a PLEX each month to continue shooting rocks, you aren't doing it right.
We get sold on this game from seeing the exciting trailiers depicting intense space battles involving dozens of ships and we imagined flying in those conflicts. This isn't a pipe dream. Newbies can start fighting PvP conflicts immediately, no matter what part of space you are in.
Don't let so called "newbie corporations" lie to you and tell you that the focus of the game is running missions or mining rocks. Instead get involved with a group like Red vs. Blue, or CODEdot and start fighting right from the start. EVE Online is full of players interested in assisting newcomers and getting them up on their feet. Red vs. Blue is a group consisting of two separate corporations with a permament war declaration (wardec) between them. You can join sides and immediately engage in the PvP. CODEdot (CODE.) is an organization dedicated to changing the way high securty space functions in the game and engages in near constant PvP against large targets, like mining barges and transport ships. They take newcomers and have a blog with information on how to prepare to fly with them
.
This game has a learning curve like no other MMO out there, so getting help and reading the content on the wiki is pretty important. Do some research and make sure this is really a game for you. Watch some people on youtube playing the game, especially the PvP elements of the game they participate in. Don't expect a theme park like world of warcraft, instead, recognize that the game allows for PvP in any part of space, and you are always at risk of getting destroyed. You can come prepared and learn how to outfit your ship correctly and play strategically to improve your chances of not only surviving, but blowing up other people's ships.
Play the game and have a lot of fun. Sign up for the two week free trial and really give the game a spin. Go out, get blown up, learn, and try again. Get involved in the community, talk with others, and definitely investigate some PvP corporations.

I'd like to preface this with the notion of respect.  I see something promising under all of it, I really do, but after completing all of the songs and bosses on normal, I'm just left feeling very unsatisfied.
First and perhaps foremost, I think the soundtrack is awful.  Not the songs themselves, many of them are decent and they're certainly popular tracks in their genre (which consist mostly of dubstep, some feelings of house, things like that) but holding my control stick in a direction to a grinding bass tone is just not exciting.  Rarely did I ever feel like I was interacting with the music.  I could mute the sound and probably play the game just as well as I did with the music.
Along with that, the core gameplay is just not fun to me.  That may be in part to the whole "glowing blue to a bass tone" bit, but again the interactions with the music consisted solely of firing on like... the 16th note before the beat of the measure, which was honestly just really kind of annoying, especially since they explained it very, very poorly in the tutorial.  The shooting itself revolved around scrolling a large circle around to lock-on to enemies and pulling the trigger.  It's as shallow as it sounds, really.
The environments and aesthetics are just... dull.  There's this vaguely low-poly sci-fi universe with plenty of glowing lights, and 90% of what you see is just brown and gray dodecahedrons?  Is it to help the large, bright blue glowing line to stick out?  I just feel there's a lot of missed potential here, especially considering the change in pace with one level that has these crushing traps timed to the music.  They're pretty similar in color but they hold a different look.
As a music and rhythm game enthusiast, I'm just left bored at the end of the day.  Not insulted, nor do I feel like I wasted my time, but I find it hard to suggest to others.

It's a must have. It has obvious elements of Rez with the lock and shoot, though this calls for some conscious timing to maximise returns on it. Others might try the ribbon mechanic and feel nostalgia for Gitaroo Man, or dodge obstacles in the tunnels and think of Star Fox - but it's not just an homage, this game makes these mechanics its own and maybe even surpasses all three... When I got into stage 7 I was dancing in my seat with tears of joy while playing because I couldn't believe someone nailed the fun, look, sound, etc all at once like that, and I wasn't even through the game yet!
Soundtrack is heavy on the dubstep and glitchhop end of the spectrum - some would want to avoid that, but I think it fits great and makes a lot of sense for the mechanics. The sound of each song varies a fair bit within that broad umbrella and they're not only well curated but surprisingly well known.
I have some issues at times with the incoming missiles - they're very visible, but if there are other things in the area, I can sweep and shoot and sweep and shoot and still never get the lock to lock onto them, so losing a ship is inevitable. I've saved replays and watched myself track over the same missile 3 times to no effect. This gets worse at higher difficulties where the screen will very soon start filling with them, and to compound it, you can't shoot anything down while you're blown up, so you can come back just in time to blow up again. It can all be solved with the right approach, but it can be tricky.
Still, this is the kind of game you won't even find every several years, if even in a decade. The fans of this type of thing are probably already interested, so all I can suggest is don't sit on the fence or pass it up - if you're wondering about it, go for it! There are good reasons to be skeptical, but this one nails it, I promise.

Out of all the MMO's i have played over the years, EVE tops them all, i have played WOW, PWI, DCUO,RS, D&D:NW, FFXIV:ARR etc etc
EVE is not a game that holds your hand, nor is it a game where evything is handed to you on a silver plate.
EVE is an MMO sandbox where you can be involved with battles of up to thousands of players
Example:
B-R5RB BY THE NUMBERS
·         Around 21 hours of total fighting
·         7,548 unique characters belonging to those two coalitions participated in the overall battle (i.e. landed on at least one killmail).  6,058 participated directly in the B-R5RB system with 2,670 in system at max
·         717 unique player Corporations
·         55 unique player Alliances
Just from that battle.
To survive in EVE you need income, to buy upgrades, ships, modules, anything really, so you need a proffession. Now as i write this, Mosiac expansion was released not two days ago, introducing the Opportunites system (revamped tutorials) so whe you start EVE they will show you the basics of the basics, nothing hardcore. After this you can choose a path to proceed on, be it:-
- Exploration , wandering the EVE universe scanning down abandoned relic or data sites, or protected sleeper sites, and even wormholes, and making money off what you find in these sites.
- Industrial , from mining to building ships and components, to manipulating the markets for yoru benefits, you make money ehre by being patient and clever.
- PvE , in EVE there are still missions to do that go up in levels, if you would prefer not to PvP, and there is also Pirate (Ratting) sites where with the right friends and in the right areas, you can make a LOT of ISK.
- PvP , obvious, blow the enemy up and loot their wreck, but on the side there is also bounty hunting, while not the most productive way of making money, and usually over-looked by players, by finding the right people and putting them down you can roll in some nice amount of cash.
EVE is unlike any other MMO, as you are not told what to do or where to go, it's open, you do what you want, and one thing EVE has been applauded for is that, what you are punished for in most games, youa ren't here, it is encouraged.
You want to manipulate a CEO for months, become "best friends" fight side-by-side, only then. once they open up a weak spot, you take everything from them, everything from the Corporation and run with it. That is fine.
You want to get a few friends, and set up a camp on a stargate, killing anyone that comes through, it's fine.
Want to manipulate the prices of items in certain regions for your benefit, yup, it's fine.
Obviously the specific rules still apply, like any exploits, hacks or RMT is against the rules (With some exceptions with RMT, like with selling characters, so long as it is done through the right proccess.)
But, honestly, this game is fantastic, you will make many friends and enemies, some of these may even come into your Real life. One of the best things about this game is it is a mostly mature adult community, no annoying 10 year olds or whining emo-teens. (some exceptions, but they never last long)
Why take my word for it anyway, play the game now! But don't play alone, join a corp, get contacts, make allies/enemies, play the game to it's true potential, and you will never love another game more.
TL;DR:  Addictive, demanding, socialising...download now. You won't regret it.

Let me start with the goods:
-Great music (if you're into wub wubs)
-Aesthetically pleasing
-Chilled out game that you can use to wind down and just relax for a night VERY easily
-Challenging if you decide to go for top scores or GREAT acc, but not impossible for people who don't care too much about the competitive aspect!
-Completing bosses is VERY pleasing, as well as getting great pass accs and so on.
Now for some of the bads, but with being in contact with Madfellows, I can say I know they will change and do what they can to improve on these:
-Somewhat short song list
-Replayability is kinda small, as theres only the harder diffs but no new  songs in addition to the harder difficulties
-Not KB+M compatible but it makes sense as to why it isnt, it'd be hard to nail with that.
-Music can get monotonous if you don't appreciate the flow or genre~
-Kinda a suggestion, but maybe something like a proper rank leaderboard as opposed to JUST song leaderboards that we can see in UI?  Idk, and community mapping if possible!-
Now for one that I think should be brought  to attention to anyone who achievement hunts this game like I did.
To get all secrets, you must have your top play be the one that unlocks all in a level, so if you get ALL secrets but lower score, you have too retry it. I find this VERY inconvienient because if you don't go for secrets WITH top scores to begin with, it takes HEAPS of time to get a new top score with them (if you get high ac % on your non-secret run, that is)
A work around for this is doing the song on a lower diff, but you MUST know where they are if you intend on doing it this way as the leniency for acc is alot lower and you can easily top yourself without realizing.
All in all, I'd recommend this game ANY day of the week to rhythm gamers, it's fun, it's challenging, and it's a nice change of pace in rhythm gaming compared to the bigs like Osu!, Guitar Hero (or Clone Hero), and Step Mania, and the Pros REALLY outweigh the negatives, most of mine are just nit-picky but they should be known. If you enjoy trying out all types of rhythm games, it's worth the buy, and especially for the price you pay for this.

A Druid's Duel is a very simple Strategy game on the surface: but that's only on the surface. What's underneath is a chess match that is pretty excellent: with the ebb and flow of the mana pool being the resource you need to take control of the match, and the different use of tactics with each of the 4 units strengths helping to really bring out your A game in terms of luring your enemy, and tactically taking regions. It's not a game where you're going to make an epic comeback on, as at a certain point the game goes down hill for the team with the mana deficiency, but overall if you're looking for a cheap and interesting strategy game, this is it. Easy to learn: hard to master.
+:
Simple 4 Units and skill design make for a lot of tactics despite the lack of overall variety.
Emphasis on land control and mana collection and how mana is collected makes a great pull-push nature to gameplay.
Art design and sound design make for a relaxing experience but does the job.
Building land and those mechanics help add to defensive play and does open the board as a whole.
Quantity versus Quality of units makes a huge difference in strategies and attack plans: reacting to opponents layout is key.
-:
Lack of options to view range/enemy unit range, which could have helped in strategy elements.
Learning mechanics could be better for medium/high level tactics.
Archers seem a tiny bit overpowered in some senses.

I am constantly impressed by the game and the development team.  In my opinion, if you enjoy tactical grid-based strategy games, you should definitely give this a try!
Gameplay: In this game, you grab land to generate mana, which can be used to summon four different classes of druids or transform the druids into animals to gain special power.  The game plays a bit like chess in a sense that you always kill your opponent in one hit.
Campaign and Multiplayer: In my opinion, the campaign is worth the full price of the game, but the multi player is probably the bigger selling point!  The lengthy single player mode takes 6+ hours to finish.  It doesn't really have a story, and can get a bit repetitive towards the end.  Nevertheless, I still find it really fun and enjoyable.  The multiplayer is where the game really shines.  It has two different modes: a play-by-email mode, and a live mode, which was added after a patch (v1.05).  The action can get really crazy considering that you may have a 4-player free-for-all games!
Excellent Development: I find the dev team to be one of the very best that I have seen on Steam.  Despite the game being bug-free, they are still constantly on the forum answering questions and rolling out patches to improve the game!

Did you like playing of the previous Ninja Storm games or perhaps the DBZ Budokai games?
If your answer is yes then I have little doubt in my mind that you will love this game as it is all that you would come to expect from the Bandai family.
To keep things to the point and spoiler free I will cover some of the Pros and Cons of the game on PC:
+ The game is beautiful, the cell shaded graphics and stunning animation have been put together beautifully to make all that crazy-epic anime action come to life.
+ For those of us who watch the anime or read the manga you will be happy to know that the game covers most of the story line with good accuracy [Please play it in Japanese, this is just my preference but the Japanese voice actors are the best!]. For obvious reasons the game deviates from the anime slightly towards the end to create a suitable conclusion to the in game story.
+The combat system is easy to master and very fluid; this makes it relatively easy to play on a keyboard [xbox gamepad is better] and still have a lot of fun.
+The main story mode allows you to explore the ninja world on foot which for naruto fans is an amazing experience; you get to see parts of the villages that you don't really get to in the anime.
-A large portion of the game revolves around secondary events and requests that you get from all sorts of NPCs which is not bad as it adds a lot of extra hours to the game but running back and forth through the same areas can get tiresome. One of my biggest issues is the lack of effort put into the way you move through the world; you can run, jump and break stuff. It would have been amazing if you could actually jump on/off of trees or buildings, or at least dash.
- The combat system is a little limited due to the simplicity in my oppinion and I personally would have liked to see a few mor button combinations to allow for more jitsus [special moves] than just Y+B or Y+Y+B.
- Multiplayer is an option for PC but in my opinion nothing beats a console at this sort of multiplayer; not having the person in the room as you smash him/her into a mountain with a giant Rasengan is just not the same as seeing that person slumping in defeat right next to you :D
To conclude I would have to recommend this game especially right now as it is on special, it is a great addition to the Bandai fighting game family.

If you're looking for a fun little game, this isn't bad. If you're looking for a strategy game, it still needs quite a bit of improvement. Every multiplayer map suffers from severe First Move Advantage, and One on One is the way I wanted to play a strategy game like this (since I found it reminiscent of chess), but this game is currently not designed for that.
Single Player is just an excercise in manipulating the enemy AI to fight each other and not you. Not too much different than most other single player strategy game ecperiences, but it includes "False Path" maps that are really frustrating and can add hours onto your play time by forcing you to replay levels you already beat.
Levels are small and there's no expandability or map maker.
For $10 I can't really recommend it at this point in time. Wait for it to go on sale and it's a cool little diversion, or wait for the next version and we'll see if it fixes some of these problems.

I'll try to keep this short. I didn't really enjoy the 5 hours I've played, so I probably won't play it more, even though I've heard it gets better. I was so frustrated from the combat that it wasn't fun. I didn't want to play the game, I wanted to STOP playing the game. Judging from what I saw, I was expecting the game to be more like a Medieval fantasy RPG, not about pirates, and I saw absolutely nothing about Titans. Not that that's a bad thing, it just didn't meet my expectations.
The combat consists of little more than clicking, followed by slow animations, and lots of rolling. Risen 3 requires more rolling than Dark Souls. Blocking is worthless, as you can only block the first hit and then take the rest of the enemy's combos, and almost everything is faster than you. This means they can also break your combos. The only useful tactic I found was to roll after nearly every hit, unless I was lucky enough to fight an enemy that was slow and stuck in a corner I could combo attack. Don't expect to hit anything with your pistol at a low level, especially short enemies like goblins.
The combat system is also based on auto-targetting, so you can't choose which enemy to attack. Sometimes when you're just about to kill an enemy, another one walks up and then you have to deal with that for the next couple minutes before finishing the other. I found that it was really easy to accidentally hit NPCs because of not being able to target well, and had to reload my game because I don't know if they ever stop trying to kill you.
My main issue with the voice acting is the protagonist. He sounds like he's always in a bad mood, and he talks incredibly slowly. I didn't have the patience to listen through all the dialogue.
The opening tutorial battle was awful on my computer because of all the water FX and animations. My computer isn't the best setup, but I can play games like Skyrim decently. The only thing I can say is the game just isn't optimized well.
I'm somewhat disappointed now I bought the complete edition and I can't get a refund, but at least I bought it on sale. If you really want to buy the game, don't buy it at full price. I wouldn't even pay half price for it.

Bionic Commando. Those of us who were there on it's orignal release on the Nintendo... great memories when games were simple on the simple fact there wasn't much to work with those limited systems.
This game killed us with it's killer gameplay and story and then almost killed us with it's god aweful sound track. How could a game that plays this great make my ears bleed!?! But the formula worked and the game was simple and fun enough to bring us back multiple times to beat it.
Now the next generation release... Systems are not push-overs anymore and how sharp this game looked was limited to the developers. Man they didn't disappoint and the sound track got upgraded to actually enjoyable. My ears aren't bleeding hearing it this time yet the track stayed true enough that you hear the orignal music from the first sneaking through but sounding 10 times better.
But one failing lead to another just as critical failing. First game's sound made me winch despite everything going for it. This next generation made a simular mistake which is much less obvious until you beat the game. STORY... How could they craft this masterpiece and botch the story enough to make half of us hard-core players throw our hands up in dismay?! Gameplay... nailed. Sound... awesome! Graphics... totally killer!!! Story??? Really???!??? Story is a quarter of what makes a great game... great and they failed so hard as to throw and E (or F) depending on the school you go to. A's and B's get knocked down hard with just a single F.
So this game does have a failing point but the other three are it's saving grace. Forget about it!!!. Are you having fun? YES! Does the game look sweat? YES! Does it sound awesome? YES, YES, YES... So this game will sucker punch you in the end but until then, enjoy! Never seen a game get sucker punched so badly on the last chapter... the very last minute of the game? A story that ran well until they throw in a twist nobody could swallow, me included... HOW FREAKIN LAME! But I was enjoying myself extremely until that literally KILLER ending. Man that ending really killed the game. Killed it enough that I can't forward to it's sequal, and dispite the story I'm really gunning for the sequal, that's just how powerful this game was dispite it's failing grace of a story.
Should you get this game... to put it mildly... HELL YEA!!! Killer Graphics, Killer Gameplay! Killer soundtracks!!! Forget the lame story and you'll really enjoy this game proper on that note! Was I dissapointed? No... I've suffered through the orignal Bionic Commando with it's horrable sound track and loved it just the same. Now I got another awesome game that simply suffered a tragic and horrible story but everything else was an A+ effort!!! This game is almost all gold with a distastful lump of coal thrown in. Ignore it and it's all GOLD on that note. This is a strong thumbs up with a side note. Story aside... a game you wont lose on.

Risen 3 is a third person open world action roleplaying game made by Piranha Bytes, the team that gave us the Gothic games and of course the first two Risen games. It's hard to talk about Risen 3 without referring to the previous games, which I'll call 'PB games' for short.
Risen 3 is definitely a step up from Risen 2 but all in all, it is probably still a game that only fans of PB games will love and a game that only fans of the genre may learn to like.
To talk about this game more in-depth, I'll take the list I used for my reviews of 'Risen' and 'Risen 2'.
The melee combat in Risen 2 was bad, very bad. The melee combat in Risen 3 is a lot better. It would certainly not win any prizes for the most exciting combat in a RPG ever, but after the fiasco of Risen 2 it feels like a huge improvement. The melee combat in Risen 3 is a lot like it was in the first Witcher game. Your character can perform a combo of moves and all you need to do is click the mouse at the right time to make sure the combo is performed correctly. If you click at the wrong time, the combo will be interrupted by the opponent or you will at least notice a decrease in your effectiveness (lower attack speed and damage dealt).
The secondary weapons are back: you can use a pistol, a crossbow or throwing daggers. But since melee combat relies on performing a series of successive attacks (combo), you will hardly ever use a secondary weapon because that interrupts the combo flow.
The ranged combat in Risen 3 is about the same as it was in Risen 2. Muskets and shotguns are back, they work about the same as in Risen 2 and they are about as powerful as they were in Risen 2. But because of the improved melee combat and the return of magic, ranged combat isn't the only viable build anymore like it was in Risen 2.
Magic is back after being pretty much absent in Risen 2. Each of the three factions have their own type of magic (rune magic, crystal magic or voodoo magic). I can't really comment further on how a mage build would function in Risen 3 as I went with melee/ranged.
Like in all PB games, there isn't just a learning curve for the player but for the character, too. He needs to learn to fight better. As the game progresses and you improve your character's skills, you actually feel your character getting better. This curve is not very steep in Risen 3, making it by far the easiest PB game so far. For the sake of Steam Achievements, I only improved my stats and skills a bit and then started saving 'glory points' (what XP is called in this game) to be able to max out each stat one by one (there is an achievement for getting each stat to 100). This means that I went through the better part of the game with only minimal stats and skills, and the game still felt too easy. You can up the difficulty in the game settings, but that only makes the monsters hit harder, which isn't really an issue when the problem is that most monsters don't hit you at all. You could artificially increase the difficulty in two ways, though:
Factions are back, after being more or less absent in Risen 2. They aren't as different or game defining as they were in the Gothic games, but at least they feel like real factions and they come with their own armor sets, like in the good old days ;-)
The character development system is very close to the one Risen 2 had, with some minor but welcome changes. You still increase stats with 'glory' (XP) and you still learn or increase skills by finding and paying a trainer who can teach you. It would go too far to describe all the skills and all the stats and their impact on the skills in this review, but I must say that I found the overall character development system in Risen 3 a bit better than in Risen 2.
The settings, the NPCs, the towns, the music, the humour, ... everything adds to a distinct atmosphere that only PB can create. Although the 'slightly dumbing down' of Risen 2 & 3 compared to earlier PB games is still noticeable, there is a slight improvement compared to Risen 2. NPCs will react to your actions (e.g. stealing in plain sight) a bit more often and a bit more logically than they did in Risen 2, but it's still far from the first four PB games.
Something that reminds me of Gothic 2, is that a part of the world of Risen 3 is 'recycled content' from the previous game. Some people find this incredibly lazy. While I see their point, I personally like the vaguely familiar settings. Those islands look different enough from the previous game to be a largely new experience, but you have a feeling of “Hey, here used to be...” and a curiosity of “I wonder if ... is still there”.
