I've found that I can be really picky about MMO's to the point that I'll only play one or two. Character customization and freedom are key things for me and Mabinogi has those. It is not perfect, but I don't think any MMO will ever be. I'll list some of the good and the bad (and other key notes) and let you decide if it's for you.
--Cons--
Cash Shop: The cash shop does support the game, but with people spending hundreds, if not more, each time a Gachapon comes out it gets a bit excessive. There are some useful consumables, and some pets and outfits that change frequently.
Nexon NA: Nexon North America, sometimes it seems like they don't really care about the game. At the time of this edit, there's an issue with guilds that's been going on for a while now, and their only response was only a month ago to state: "We're looking into it, please be patient".
Grinding: Grinding is very real in this game. Finding materials or items for quests or crafting can take hours. Training some skills can also be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
AP: Skills are more important than levels and all skills have their own rank and use AP to get those ranks. I listed this in the Cons because it shouldn't be spent wildly, even though it is technically unlimited, because it can take a while to get. If you do have excess AP, you can spend it to train skills, but that AP is forever lost.
Quests: A number of the quests are the generic, lackluster fetch or hunting quests. You'll do most of these when trying to learn (or train) some skills. For some, get ready for a lot of dungeon runs (see below).
--Pros--
Events: Nexon always has some sort of event running and 9/10 are at least decent (there is one where I had to fight two dragons (with other players) and all I got was a crappy MP potion. That event was cut short and replaced). Some events will give cash shop consumables, unique outfits, pets, exp, or just other unique items.
Customization: There are several free options for physical appearance and your armor and weapons can be dyed. Finding a player with the exact appearance and outfit and colors would be difficult unless you coordinate it.
Classless: Something I like in games. Rather than choosing a class, you choose a talent that helps with training associated skills. You can change your talent and it doesn't restrict any equipment or skills. You could be a Mage with heavy armor bashing things in the face with an umbrella.
Story: There is an extensive story, but all of it is optional. There are some exceptional rewards for parts of the story (transformations, a free pet) but with the open world you never have to touch it. It's also possible to start later parts of the story. Best of all, the quests are generally unique.
--Neutral--
Dungeons: Dungeons are randomly generated and are have some unique rewards. Searching for a specific reward, however, goes back to the grinding note. It's especially annoying to have a multiple floor dungeon and not get the drop you need.
Races: There are three playable races in game, each with their own pros and cons. This and your name are the only things locked about your character, but I listed it in Neutral because I'm not especially for or against it.
Tutorial: They added a new tutorial a while back that allows you to learn the controls and even allow you to sample the talents before you pick your first one. Sampling the talent includes the higher tier abilities for that talent so you have an idea of what to look forward to. If I recall, parts of it are skipable (good if you have another character), but other parts are not. You'll also always start at that tutorial when creating a character.
Skill Resets: All players can reset their skill ranks (in exchange for some gold) and get back all of the AP used in ranking those skills. If you spent AP on training, that's lost, but you don't have to retrain skills. Resets like this are mostly for extra challenge or training other skills.
Overall, I'd rank Mabinogi a 8/10. There's an extensive wiki available online, and you can find some helpful cash shop items in player shops (can be a little expensive though). There's also a few minor glitches, but all games have that.
The real question is: how do you want to play today?

A Druid's Duel delivers what it promises: turn-based strategy. If you're looking for a simple game with some strategy elements to play while taking a break from other tasks this is a good choice, but don't expect overwhelming difficulty from it, as it won't be there in most stages.
The campaign mode consists of several levels where you fight normal enemy druids(1-3 AI parties) and a couple boss fights where among the enemy units there will be one that has abilities of 2 different druid types and two extra lives. Overall the interaction between different units is good and for the most part balanced.
The difficulty of the game, however, is strongly lacking. While I can not comment on the online play due to not having tried it yet, the AI often makes sub optimal moves even at the highest difficulty setting.
I still find myself turning the game on often enough to just pass time, but the appeal started lessening about halfway through the campaign as there is very little difference between the stages in any of the "seasons".
That said I still enjoy the game and think it's worth getting if you're the type of person that enjoys quick games to pass time every now and then.
Suggested fixes to the game would include:
- a max amount of summons per turn (AI often leaves heaps of mana unspent - this would be less of an issue if 4 units per turn were maximum)
- levels with limitations on what unit types can be used or alteration of unit capabilities

The Avernum series is a remastering of the Exile series. Avernum: Escape from the Pit itself is actually a remastering of Avernum I. The Exile series originally had 3 games, not counting Blades of Exile. My first experience with Exile was actually Exile III: Ruined World. I found a demo of the game on a Mac Addict CD. I immediately fell in love with the game. I had, up to that point, never really liked turn based RPGs. Exile III changed all of that for me. The amount of thought and effort that Jeff Vogel put into the stories of these games is incredible. After completing Exile III numerous times, I had to have the rest of the series. The 3 orginals, Exile: Escape from the Pit, Exile II: Crystal souls, and Exile III: Ruined world, have in my opinion stood up to the test of time. I really must say that I prefer the originals. But these latest remasters have brought new life to the games that may have otherwise have faded into oblivion. Prepare for countless hours of adventuring, and see how your choices can affect the outcome of the game. I cannot recommend this game enough, and hope you enjoy it as much as I have.

My negative rating is based purely on my own opinion, so will differ from that of others.
I think conceptually, the game has a lot going for it; the levels are nice, it is graphically pleasing, the characters (despite the very VERY poor voice acting) are unique and interesting, and the pirate setting is fun - but that's all.

The story is so diffuse I struggled to know what was going on, and i'm very much a narrative junkie. Where to to go, why you're going there, and what to do next were questions that for me were left unanswered. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy running about 'just because', but after the story is done.
I struggled through these ~4 hours of gameplay, and, unfortunately, didn't enjoy much of it. I have Risen 2 and 1, so I will give those a go. The game holds promise, but falls flat. For those looking for a fun RPG, look elsewhere. For those who have exhausted all possible RPG's, go play a FPS.

What to say about this game.  This is my first review, so I'm gonna be rambly as hell and probably lose track of what I was saying.
The gameplay is this title is just about as amazing as one could get, for the kind of action involved.  Swinging and jumping and everything makes you feel like a big ol' badass.  Shooting is sub-par though.
Otherwise the game is merely okay.  The writing ranges from mediocre to laughable.  The tone is incredibly confused.  There are funny moment and Spencer rattles off one-liners as fast as Duke Nukem, but the lines are cliche and boring.
The themes explored in the game are about as shallow as a kiddie pool, dealing with trust of one's government, loss of loved ones, and betrayal.  So much more could have been done with this game.  I just can't even.
Overall, it's good for one or two playthroughs.  If Capcom could get around to adding some kind of mod support, that'd be great, but the game was a commercial and critical flop, so I doubt that would happen.  This is the game that sunk developer Grin, so there ya go.

This was my second favourite game of 2013 and that was a list with Assassins Creed Black Flag, GTA V and a lot of other great games.
The game mechanics are just amazing (using electrics to cleverly make your way through a building).  There are parts of this where you can go into a mission any way you want; go in all guns blazing but remember that there are one shot kills, stealthy or go in with an idea of electrocuting a guard next to a plug hole.
There are also points in this game where there can be multipul story lines going on at once!
One more thing to think about is game progression in not just the character you're controlling but also the game.  The game gets better and a lot more puzzelling as you get further on.  However, if you don't want it to be harder, go to the in game shop and buy a new gun, or wiring systems with in game currency (you get money for completing missions)!
Also, if you like choices in games, there are calls that at the end, you get a mission.  In them calls, you can very slightly change the direction of the call by answering how you want (by using the two or three options)!
Overall, this game is awesome and I think all indie lovers should have it!

WARNING! THIS GAME IS ADDICTIVE!
Out of all the MMO's i have played over the years, EVE tops them all, i have played WOW, PWI, DCUO,RS, D&D:NW, FFXIV:ARR etc etc
EVE is not a game that holds your hand, nor is it a game where evything is handed to you on a silver plate.
EVE is an MMO sandbox where you can be involved with battles of up to thousands of players
Example:
B-R5RB BY THE NUMBERS
·         Around 21 hours of total fighting
·         7,548 unique characters belonging to those two coalitions participated in the overall battle (i.e. landed on at least one killmail).  6,058 participated directly in the B-R5RB system with 2,670 in system at max
·         717 unique player Corporations
·         55 unique player Alliances
Just from that battle.
To survive in EVE you need income, to buy upgrades, ships, modules, anything really, so you need a proffession. Now as i write this, Mosiac expansion was released not two days ago, introducing the Opportunites system (revamped tutorials) so whe you start EVE they will show you the basics of the basics, nothing hardcore. After this you can choose a path to proceed on, be it:-
- Exploration , wandering the EVE universe scanning down abandoned relic or data sites, or protected sleeper sites, and even wormholes, and making money off what you find in these sites.
- Industrial , from mining to building ships and components, to manipulating the markets for yoru benefits, you make money ehre by being patient and clever.
- PvE , in EVE there are still missions to do that go up in levels, if you would prefer not to PvP, and there is also Pirate (Ratting) sites where with the right friends and in the right areas, you can make a LOT of ISK.
- PvP , obvious, blow the enemy up and loot their wreck, but on the side there is also bounty hunting, while not the most productive way of making money, and usually over-looked by players, by finding the right people and putting them down you can roll in some nice amount of cash.
EVE is unlike any other MMO, as you are not told what to do or where to go, it's open, you do what you want, and one thing EVE has been applauded for is that, what you are punished for in most games, youa ren't here, it is encouraged.
You want to manipulate a CEO for months, become "best friends" fight side-by-side, only then. once they open up a weak spot, you take everything from them, everything from the Corporation and run with it. That is fine.
You want to get a few friends, and set up a camp on a stargate, killing anyone that comes through, it's fine.
Want to manipulate the prices of items in certain regions for your benefit, yup, it's fine.
Obviously the specific rules still apply, like any exploits, hacks or RMT is against the rules (With some exceptions with RMT, like with selling characters, so long as it is done through the right proccess.)
But, honestly, this game is fantastic, you will make many friends and enemies, some of these may even come into your Real life. One of the best things about this game is it is a mostly mature adult community, no annoying 10 year olds or whining emo-teens. (some exceptions, but they never last long)
Why take my word for it anyway, play the game now! But don't play alone, join a corp, get contacts, make allies/enemies, play the game to it's true potential, and you will never love another game more.
TL;DR:  Addictive, demanding, socialising...download now. You won't regret it.

Oh man... Where to start... This game. Isn't really a game in a sense. It's more of a hobby of sorts where you spend a couple hours doing wormhole relic sites or ratting in -1.0 sec systems to gather ISK then spend it on PvP ships and go out and blow up other nerds. And to have fun. Joining a corp other than the NPC corps is also a good idea. You can either join a massive null-bloc coalition like Brave, Goons, PL, etc or a smaller one that does say faction warfare, small-gang PvP, etc such as Straya. and Redemption Road.
My one word of advise to anyone who is just starting with a 2+ week trial; go join a corporation that has a well made and reputable newbro program, such as Brave Newbies, Pandemic Horde, Eve Uni, etc. They will most certainly and 100 percently get you started at Eve and get you into the good fights as soon as they can even though your character is new. Sure, you'll likely die a lot but that's all part of the learninig experience. And if you did decide to join one of these newbro friendly alliances/corps, they have a thing called Ship Replacement Program (SRP) so it doesn't really matter if you lose your little tackle or EWAR frigate, they'll just give you a new one. When you're first starting up, that little 1 million ISK frigate of yours is the most expensive thing you've ever owned in the game. But for some of us, that's a single module on one of our ships. And so many people are happy to throw money at newbros simply because they can.
EVE doesn't necessarily need a huge commitment to play it, but the more you're involved with it, the more fun you can have. And most importantly of all, we should all remember three things:
1) The best ship in the game is the Friend Ship
2) Never fly what you can't afford to lose.
3) F*** CODE.

DISCLOSURE:  I checked product received for free because I received this game through a giveaway.
When I first started to play Aaero I was slightly disappointed initially due to my own misconceptions.  I didn't know much about it beforehand and had expected it to be a rhythm game.  I even went back and read the Steam store description for the game, and in fact nowhere does it suggest Aaero is a rhythm game.  Although the music plays a major role in Aaero, it's first and foremost a twin-stick rail shooter.
There is no apparent story at all.  It's all about the action here.  You pilot a small ship through through fifteen stages.  Along the way you fight an assortment of enemies and huge bosses while trying to trace an illuminated ribbon of light as accurately as possible.  There isn't much more to it than that, the basic idea is fairly simple.
Motion is restricted within a circular space.  One stick controls the ship and the other stick controls the aiming reticle.  Enemies are attacked by moving the reticle over them to lock on and them by pressing a button to fire homing shots at them.  There is a rhythm based shot timing that determines how fast your missiles fly but I didn't see any discernible visual cue for it.  If you can pull it off, it's a great way to increase your damage output as well as your score.  As far as I could tell, it was the only mechanic of the game that directly involved timing with the music.  I suspect someone more musically inclined would do a better job than I did, but I was able to make it through the normal and advanced difficulties without being particularly skilled at the shot timing.  The majority of enemy attacks are avoided by shooting down their missiles rather than dodging out of the way.  In other words you can't manually dodge them, once a shot is fired it must be countered with your own fire.  This was a little strange for me at first because I desperately wanted to fly out of the way but was unable.
The stages have a variety of environments and themes, but most notably each one is accompanied by a licensed music track. Mad Fellows managed to curate an outstanding soundtrack.  Although it isn't the type of rhythm game where you spend each song constantly tapping buttons to the beat, everything in Aaero is designed around the music.  The shape and flow of the light ribbons and even individual enemy placement meshes well with each song.  Unfortunately, there was one thing that didn't seem as well thought out. In some stages the enemies, their shots, your own lock on notifications, and the enemy proximity warning are all colored red.  It all can blend together and sometimes I failed to shoot down one enemy missiles in a volley that I thought I had a complete lock on.  Perhaps it was just my eyesight or inexperience, but it did leave me wondering why they couldn't have used a few extra colors.
Once I became relatively proficient at the game it felt great to fly to hug the ribbon while simultaneously battling foes.  And I really do mean that it felt great, Aaero makes awesome use of controller rumble.  The rumble intensity is even adjustable for those that don't like their gamepad shaking.  It took me a little under two hours to clear normal mode for the first time, which some people will no doubt consider to be a short playtime.  Individuals only playing to finish the tracks once on normal may end up disappointed by the low playtime.  Aaero is clearly a game that's intended to be played multiple times and eventually on higher difficulty levels to attain mastery and compete on the leaderboards.  I enjoyed Aaero and would recommend it to fans of Rez and to people looking for a rail shooter rather than a more traditional rhythm game.

I've only played 2 spiderman games before (both demos) Spiderman The movie and Spiderman, the one where smoke is at the bottom. Both were kind of boring to me. This wasn't. It was awesome.
Story
You play as Nathan Spencer a guy who is on death row. He is released and given a chance to earn his freedom and the location of his wife by taking down the enemies in a town that was nuked. You fight against Bio Reign a pro bionic terrorist group. In the time between the NES game and this one bionics are outlawed because of a rumor that it causes agression (and other reasons). Yes it sounds like a Hollywood remake of something simple (like half the shows on TV) but it works out fine. The story is very cool and is told through conversations between Super Joe and Spencer and messages on relays. Half of the time Spencer is serious but the other half he is not. When killing enemies he sometimes gives one liners like "Sucks to be you!" and "Go long son!". When he tries to put a password in and it isn't right he says "Well that sucks". Also the big gunmen are cocky and call you names that a 7th grader would make.
Gameplay
You use your bionic arm to attach to objects and swing. Use W to swing forward and S to swing back. You can also "reel in" to objects (attach to it and ram yourself towards it). It's very fun and you can go far with it. Lots of people say it's hard but it's not really hard to me. In midair even if you are not close enough to your latch target yet you can hold the cursor there and when your body gets close enough it will latch on. The harder thing to do is to reel in to attack bionics in the back (if you dont aim right you will latch to the ground). There are two kinds of enemies, regular gunmen and bionics. Gunmen can be killed by your guns and grenades or your bionic arm. You can throw objects in the world at them, fling an enemy up and throw one at the other. The bionics are the real fun enemies to fight. You swing around looking for objects to throw while dodging their attacks and then wait till they get close enough to attack while worrying that they will get you before you can throw the object. It's very fun and intense.
Music
The music is really good. It is very epic and sounds patriotic for some reason. Most of the tracks are remixes of the original theme (which are still good) but some of them are ambient and it has a very cool action theme. There is a fight in a library that will give your goosebumps because of how epic the music is making it.
You will feel so free when you play this game and swing. You can go great heights in distance and combat with just your arm. And it's pretty easy despite what others say. Checkpoints are available right before big fights so I don't understand why some reviewers like GT said they weren't. The only problem is that if you want to get all of the collectables the checkpoints are unforgiving because you could get the item (after risking your life for 5 min trying to get it) and then miss a swing or die from the enemies before you get another one. Then you have to get it again

You can't change your choice afterwards. I like to get the most out of my games, so I chose COMMANDO immediately. And on COMMANDO... things get very very very very messy, and still other things which would make the game challenging now make it cheap.
And that's what BC is: C-H-E-A-P. And I don't mean price-wise.
BC's challenging (or frustrating) difficulty comes from its checkpoint system, where they're pretty far apart. And basically your character Spencer is not a badass; he's a wimp that can get killed by each and any single enemy you encounter. You're armed with a pea-shooter, and occasionally you're given special secondary weapons with very limited ammo. But the pea-shooter's your main thing. Piu-piu-piu-piu, goes Spencer as he has to fire 5-10 bullets into one soldier. Bam, bam, bam, goes the soldier as he kills you in three. Oh, and they can shoot you from literally miles away, even if you don't see them. Reload checkpoint.
Oh, your extendable grappling arm - aka your bionic part that the game's all about? Yes, you can grab enemies with it, toss them around. But about 0.5 seconds after you hook onto them, they whip out a sort of taser and send a jolt across the arm. If you're not at full health then - you're dead. Reload checkpoint.
You can go melee with the foes. And yes, they will again whip out their taser and bash you with it. Health scenario from above? Reload checkpoint.
Snipers? One hit takes you out, with your default health. There's always at least 3-4 of them aiming at you from different directions. They can shoot you across the whole map. Ka-bam! Reload checkpoint.
There's robots - flying nimble crafts, or heavy earth-bound behemoths that will pump you full of led and rockets. You can't just shoot them, there's a technique to beat each. And yes, they will soon start coming out in pairs and trios. Reload checkpoint.
Scenario: you take out a pair of flying polycrafts in a crazy battle, and while you take a second to congratulate yourself, some 5-6 soldiers parachute from the sky and shoot you dead. Checkpoint? Oh, it was placed BEFORE the fight with the polycrafts. Enjoy! And the game's full of it, so full of this damn cheapness that about a third of the way in I just thought of giving up... and I rarely, rarely, rarely give up on a game, at least for difficulty reasons.
You die in 5 seconds if you fall into water, because Spencer can't swim since his arms weighs a ton. If your stray a little from a seemingly open-world levels, you die of "radiation" in an equally quick amount of time.
Despite it all - BC is a GOOD GAME... as much as that's hard to believe. The Spiderman-like mechanics of your bionic arm are pretty neat, if a little buggy at times. They do take time getting used to. You get to dispatch of your enemies in plenty of awesome ways. The challenge system is awesome: the game offers you to perform challenges (kill 5 guards with one grenade, etc.) and rewards you with character ability and/or weaponry upgrades. There's also collectibles for your hoarding needs. The catch? Well, completed challenges and collected collectibles get saved AFTER the checkpoint. So you may find yourself pulling off extremely difficult challenges or getting that inaccessible collectible, only for a random guy to shoot you - and then you have to repeat the WHOLE section again, and do everything from the start.
My playtime's 12 hours at the time of this writing, and I'm only at about 55-60% completion of a single-player playthrough. That's pretty long for a very linear 3rd person shooter/platformer.
Bottom line: If you can get past its quirks and cheapness, BC can be very fun.

I purchased this game the day it was released on PS3, and completed the game, so don't mind the low play time on the steam version.
The gameplay itself can actually be an enjoyable experience. The combat is quick just like the game itself, and the graphics themselves are pretty good. Unfortunately, that's all the game really has going for it. It used a couple of big names to try to draw in appeal (Mike Patton as Spencer and Steve Blum as Super Joe) and garner favor among buyers, but those few things are really the only good points about it.
The story in the game is simply atrocious, and will leave you feeling cheated if you actually make it all the way through. The game itself is designed swinging around, and the first level you are permitted to, you are given a vast view that you jump in to, only to find out it's just a big linear corridor with very VERY little room for exploration. Whether you are moving through a building, a "city" or a minefield, you just keep moving along the same path occasionaly looking for, what brings me to the next couple of issues: the collectibles and checkpoints.
Collectibles are an addition to any game, and while I'm not complaining about them being in the game, in and of themselves, the checkpoints are spread VERY far apart, and dying in this game can become a common occurence, especially in certain parts. ANY and ALL progress you made is erased when you die, back to the previous check point which can be rather far back in the game, as they are so spread out. Another incredibly annoying factor for the game which ties into the checkpoint and collectible point is, there is NO replaying of levels for progress. Certain weapon or game "Challenges" can only be completed at certain points of the game, and collectibles MUST be collected in full. Why? Replaying a level is permissible, however, doing so is merely so you can "locate" everything. It does not save when you use the "Level jump" feature. The fact is, if you missed something, your only option to get it again is to RESTART the entire game.
All in all, if it's a game you can get on sale like I did for $2.00, you really can't go wrong, but if you are a completionist for a game like myself, this game is your worst enemy. For anything more than what I paid for it, I can't reccomend it.

Since you're here, I assume you already have an opinion about LD: Season 1.
In summary, I liked it a lot better than the first season. The episodes are longer and very generously fleshed out. The main character is now Dr. Wakefield, which, in my view, helped a lot with the story pacing, which is now much more straightforward and less cryptic (for the fans of ambiguity, fear not, there's still a whole lot of it). The first three episodes of S2 are extremely well done, adding map travel and a micronarrative element to the already very atmospheric environments of the first game. The last episode follows the classic format, tying the story together nicely.
While the pixelated look remains, the mechanics were improved and both movement and text skipping feels less sluggish. Most puzzles are more straightforward while still being fun to solve (except one or two occasions where you're just expected to stumble upon some seemingly random location before proceeding).
If you enjoyed Last Door: Season One, even if you don't praise it as highly as other reviews, definitely don't forget about Season Two: it's more than a worthy sequel.

[Review as of Update 17]
What's good:
It's a fun coop experience, it feels really unique and it requires you to think before you act whenever possible. It seems pretty realistic too (as far as that's doable in a SciFi setting), but without being annoying about it. It's great to wander around in pitch-black darkness and the adrenaline rush when something pops up right next to or behind you is something you don't find in many games these days. I didn't try much "PvP" yet, but it also seems fun I guess... it really feels like the game is focused on coop though, but I don't mind that. It's better to focus on polishing one thing first rather than trying to do everything at once and ending up with mediocre results.
What's bad:
There's some bugs and the engine could offer better performance (as in, graphics look decent, but not good enough to warrant the fps drops that happen sometimes), and it definitely feels like there should be more content... but hey, it's still early access, and it's probably the most polished early access game I've come across in a long time. Also, the devs try to keep the community up to speed on their plans and what's planned next. They also seem to talk to people on the forums, so that really seems promising. It's sad when a game has an interesting concept but the devs make you feel like they don't care anymore and abandoned the project without notice - this is not the case for Interstellar Marines, in my opinion. I really appreciate that.
There isn't much left to say. It probably won't become my competitive game of choice, but after Warframe, Payday 2 and Insurgency, this is something new to waste my time on with friends, and I'm really looking forward to the new content even though I still have to try more of what's already there.

left analog follows the musical ribbons (blue lines), right stick + right trigger is to aim and fire against the scurge of enemies. Every single thing in this game, is on time with the beat. and i mean EVERYTHING. scenery, enemies, ribbons, doors, pistons, walls, debris. EV-ER-Y-THING. This meticulous design from Mad Fellows is top notch. and puts this game on one of my all time favourite Rhythm games, nay all time favourites PERIOD.

This game was on my wishlist since forever, but the price never went down and I've been burned by a lot of early access games. Finally, my son bought me a copy as a gift. I started it up after work on day... and the next thing I knew it was 3 am. I started in a beta, but didn't encounter any bugs, so switched to the most recent alpha. I have countless hours in the game and haven't had a problem.
Ordinarily I loathe games when I put a lot of time and energy into characters only to have them die. With this game, if a colony dies I'm sad, but excited to try again. There are so many biomes to explore and so many things to do, the game has near-infinite replay value. Plus, there are different storytellers, so you can set the difficulty level.
There is a goal to the game. You want to either build a space ship or else get to a ship to leave the world. One of my colonies has the technology to leave, but I'm having too much fun to go anywhere. I may never win this game (and I don't mind). It's one of my favorite games of all time already.
Now, this game isn't for everyone. You can set up some truly gruesome scenarios. Your friend dies. Bury him, feed him to your warg, or eat him? It's all up to you. Appalled? Look elsewhere. Intrigued? Get this game right now!

"A good game for what it is, which is sort of spin off on chess where the board can be changed as you go along. Although it looks like it was primarily made for ipad, which it probably was."
A game that is "easy to learn - difficult to master", where you control your own circle of druids. These druids can transform, depending on their skills, into 4 different animals - a wolf, an eagle, a bear and a tortoise. Each of these druids have a different amount of moves and way of attacking, which also change with their form. The game is played out on a board that can be altered during the game by destroying tiles (sending the unwary occupant into the abyss) or creating new tiles or bridges. Not all of these thing can be done immediately though. The land creation and destruction is not available unless you have a tortoise druid (this is his way of attacking). You can transform your druids or summon new ones to any of the tiles you own by the use of mana. Mana is gained at the start of each round, based on the amount of tiles you got. The goal of the game is to take all the tiles from your opponent(s) (since this will leave them without mana, unable to do anything).
I have yet to encounter problems with it, apart from the mouse optimization where the point and click system is not a 100% accurate, leading you to clicking the wrong tile.
It's a very simple, but highly strategical game that makes you think extra carefully about every move. If you like chess then you will most certainly enjoy this.

Very cool entry into the turn-based strategy genre. All the combat is one-hit kills so it's all strategy- no luck involved. Your task is to secure every enemy-held tile on the board. Each tile acquisition increases your mana which is used to spawn more units or use special abilities to increase movement/attack range and create or destroy tiles and obstacles. There are only 4 different classes so the options are limited to that but there is enough there to have very fun and tactical games.
There are a few things to be aware of, though. First, there is only campaign and multiplayer at this point. The devs have mentioned an interest in adding a versus AI mode but it isn't there yet. The multiplayer could also be improved. As of now, unless you are playing with a friend, you will likely be playing games 1 turn per day at a time, similar to the old PBeM games. This is great to have as a feature, but as of now it is the only option. There is no chat or lobby to see if anyone is active. There IS local hotseat multiplayer though, up to 4 players, so that's nice.
All in all, I do recommend especially if you are a fan of the genre. The devs are very friendly and seem sincere in wanting to improve the game if they have the resources to do it. As it stands the campaign is very engaging and I look forward to playing multiplayer with friends.   9/10

Difficult to recommend/not recommend. I'd say more like 50/50. It's not an easy title to review. I appreciate the fact it's a small team game, but it seriously ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your progress sometimes. The setting is good. In fact, a lot of the tripple A titles can only wish for a world setting that is as interesting as Avernum's. Writing is ok; again, it's a lot of text for a small team and it shows. While you can follow the CLEAR directions given to you and still explore with abandon, oftentimes the writing falls just a centimeter short of a tropey throw-away. The saving grace here being that it is when you're dealing with the side quests. There is an interesting and challanging monster variety. Character progression is good. My tank feels like a tank, my mage is not terribly squishy. Things USUALLY agro the first character that charges at them(that helps you immensely when you play). Combat is not too repetitive and sometimes requires unique approach for bosses. There are some solid consumables to play with.
It's lacking some quality of life elements that can make the game a lot better--UI organization, interaction with the environment. Ease of accesss stuff, so to speak. More shortcut spaces. Easier periphery organisation for the player. A plethora of small stuff, that was perhaps overlooked. Combat balance and difficulty spikes are all over the place. But I guess people would form their own opinion about that. A good deal of misses, even for characters who have invested in dexterity and skills. Mobs can have too much resistances and too high of an evasion, or too high damage and easy spammable abilities that do too many things at once. It can get downright frustrating at times. Consumables can massively alter the direction of combat(can be good/bad). Bullet sponges also make an appearance. Sometimes that is alright. Sometimes it feels inapropiate (a shaman that is ridiculously overpowered). Sometimes it feels boring (especially when it happens with every boss mob that is also showering you with poison in a tight nephelim fortress, which leads you to overconsume potions). Sometimes it feel great and done right, for instance, fighting a giant for which you get a specific side quest and he is a real challange with a really good reward. It's a lot of hit and miss with this game. There is a lot of content to go through and I just get the feeling that in the making of this game there wasn't enough thought about which is going to be good/bad. There are things like pacing between conversation and combat, exploration, main story, side quests. Avernum somehow manages to strike a balance in that regard. But it doesn't feel like it was because somebody wanted it.
The game as a whole is not bad. I suppose you should play it on it's easiest/normal setting. But who wants to do that? It needs polish; balance polish. 50/50. I am truly in the middle, despite the tag. And I will play through the whole of it, because I am an RPG nerd. For my kind Avernum is a must. And for you, too, if you're one.

This is a great turn-based strategy game! The energy / land grab mechanic is a very interesting take on resource management. The goal of the game is not to defeat your opponent's units, (although you will have to do that too!), it's to control the land. You basically have to balance your turns between grabbing and controlling the land, or attacking your opponent(s), using the energy you gain from controlling the land to do so. The more land you control, the more energy you have at the start of your next turn.
In my opinion, this is a very nice "born digital" board game. (And this is a good thing!) But far from feeling like a static game you play over and over again, there are so many options for play that it will feel very different every time. Playing through the single-player campaign, you would probably not even realize this. For instance every level has a different starting setup, and there are a ton of those to choose from when you start a multiplayer game.
Don't let the beautiful graphics / presentation fool you, there is a very tactical strategy game here, and LOTS of single-player content to get you ramped up before you play against other folks.

People will call this a bad game. It really isn't. (Depends on your computer though.) It's a rather short game, only lasting about 5 hours if you get good at it. But those five hours have a lot going for them.
The combat is excellent, always pushing you to do your best against the multides of enemies. But it reaches a point where it keeps throwing the giant mech robots at you (Which is conviently after you learn how to use and instant kill grapple.) The combat manages to flow smoothly into the swinging mechanic, and you can zip around the area, using that as your advantage against the many enemies the game hurls at you.
There is seriously nothing more fun than tossing your enemies around like little dolls.
But, the game has an challenge mod, where you get in-game abilities and perks for completeing them. The problem? This only works in story mode. If you level jump to an earlier area, you can can't collect any missed collectables or try to complete any challenges. So, if you like to speed through the game and keep the momentum going, you'll miss out on a lot.
The boss fights are hit or miss. Some, like the fight against a giant robot worm, manage to be exciting. Others, like the last boss, are annoying. None of them really take advantage of the swingings, so you'll be fighting bosses on a lot of flat areas. (It would have been really fun to fight the last boss by swinging off his flying drones and shooting him from above.)
The story though, and by extension the big plot twist, is bare bones and stupid. Your goal is to fight off some terrorists while trying to find out what happened to your wife. New characters come in and pop away forever in the same cutscenes they're introduced in, and very little feels resolved. The game even ends on a cliff hanger, and you just feel cheated by the end.
Do I recommend this game? Yes. But get it on sale. Like for 2 dollars. Because it won't last long enough (Since the multiplayer servers are down forever) to justify a big price. (There is a reason it's only 1$ to buy it for a console.)

I've been a longtime player before this game was made available to steam, so here's some of my thoughts for you all:
- If you're looking for a different mmo to settle down in  with good social AND combat aspects, consider playing this one. It's a great mmo to return to; especially if you're into long term commitment. There is a reason why this game's catchphrase is something akin to 'live your own life.' Every single skill you upgrade contributes towards the growth of your character.
- There is no class system. There's specific skills filed under skillsets. Your role in combat is loosely determined by what skills you prioritize in ranking up. It's purely up to you how you want to play the game.
- You can literally be every class if you wanted to.
- Combat can take getting used to, but flows together well. You're allowed to be creative in your playstyle.

Season 1 of The Last Door proved to be one of the best horror games I've played in a long time. It stuck with me long after I finished it, the many surprises and revelations rolling around in my head during dark hours. I was anxious to see if Season 2 lived up to expectations, since it was continuing the story along a different path. I've just finished it, and I can barely contain my adoration for what the developers have accomplished with this series.
You take on the role of Dr. John Wakefield, on the trail of his vanished patient Jeremiah Devitt who also happened to be the protagonist of Season 1. Knowing what you know about the events of the first game, the second wastes no time delving into the secrets of the world by sending you on a chase across a nightmare version of Victorian England. Your search will take you to a decaying asylum, a forlorn manor, a distant island, and beyond. In each locale you will uncover clues, puzzle through riddles, and peer into the darkness underpinning the world.
There are no major diversions in the core gameplay from Season 1, really. You navigate interconnected scenes, collect items to use in puzzles, and converse with any useful individuals present. Each episode now has a map you can use to travel between different areas, but all this means is a little more variety in the locales within the episode. It also makes the game feel a little sparser, since you'll be spending less time in a given place as you zip around in search of secrets.
What is different is the pace of the game. Season 2 is a bit longer than Season 1, around 45 minutes to an hour per episode, and that time is a little more guided than before. Whereas Season 1 left you to mostly wander and puzzle out the details of each location yourself, Season 2 has more cutscenes and incidental events to stumble across. There's more going on in each area, and that sometimes means the spooks and the puzzles are more spaced out than before. The connections between episodes are also noticeably rougher, with a few of the jumps coming up in the closing cutscene with not much context.
By episode 2 I wasn't sure if I was liking where it was going or how it was getting there. But by the end of that episode I was hooked, and the game improved to previously unseen heights as it rolled on. For one thing, the puzzles become more intricate and clever further in, especially once you pass the sprawling riddle in episode 2. Season 2 also dispenses with most of the jump scares and stingers of Season 1 in favor of some incredible atmosphere and creeping dread. The stakes of the story are much higher here, and you see that play out in the events that unfold.
I really can't stress enough how good the atmosphere and storytelling are here. Honestly, The Game Kitchen really
Lovecraft better than anyone else I've seen in the gaming world. Season 2 takes place in a world where ancient, eldritch forces simply
, where they are clearly a foundation of reality and the little people you meet have simply learned to live with them in their own twisted ways. From start to finish you feel that great and terrible weight, moreso than in Season 1, and the story does not shy away from the ultimate confrontation in the end. The final episode is a triumph of eldritch terror, diving head-first into true cosmic horror and giving life to everything hinted at up to the point in a way that does not disappoint.
Fans of cosmic horror need to have this series at the top of their list. The Last Door captures that feeling of hopelessness in the face of the vast unknowable, while at the same time telling a very human story about temptation and hubris. Don't let the chunky pixel art put you off, for it very effectively leaves just enough to the imagination to make the terrors you face that much more terrible. And the the fantastic sound design more than makes up for any graphical gripes, featuring rich, detailed effects and an orchestral soundtrack that soars when it needs to and unsettles when it can. Rare are the games that can engage your fears and imagination so effectively, and The Last Door should be lauded for standing so tall among them.

:
--------------------
:
-Your "unique", "original" character is central to playing the story and unlocking moves and other features. However, when you create him/her/it, your custom character can only be Human, Saiyan, Majin (eg. Buu), "Namek" (Namekian), or "Frieza clan" (Icer). Sorry to fans of Androids, Bio-Androids, Half-Saiyans, Truffles, Konatsus, Mutants, Arlians, Demons, Zombies, and all the other unique races from the shows. You'll have to use your imagination (I'm not kidding -- because I couldn't be an Android, I made a Human character, gave him Android moves, and named him Android 67, which worked pretty well, especially considering that I had to improvise on such a stupid thing).
-You can only have one character at first. Other slots are locked until the main story is fully finished. This will surely be frustrating for multiple people sharing one system and one copy of the game (spouses, siblings, roommates, etc.).
-All custom characters share the same clothing and accessories, and if one character's many outfits uses a piece that you only have 1 of, you must get another for another character. Also, all characters access the same pool of owned items (eg. senzu beans) and money, and have access to the same unlocked moves. This is both great and not so great, depending on how you look at it.
-If you are working with a Trainer (Goku, Captain Ginyu, Gotenks, etc.), all other custom characters of yours will also have the same trainer. If one of your secondary character switches trainers, the same goes for all your other characters. Once again, it's as if the game was designed for one player, even though there are perhaps 9 available character slots.
-The appearance categories (eyes, mouth, hair, etc.) are too limited and entirely unoriginal. The few you have to choose from were taken from the DBZ characters. The whole process feels very lacking and bland for a modern game, especially with how great the rest of the game is. I'm not saying character creation should be as extensive as Skyrim, but still, a little creativity would have been great.
-Likewise, there are MANY moves and super moves, but none of them are original.
-Out of the five races, only a Saiyan player can learn a genuine transformation (no, devs, Kaioken
really count. :-P), but Oozaru (Great Ape) isn't one of them. Though under very rare, very specific circumstances an NPC will go Oozaru. In fact, your Saiyan character doesn't even have a tail. But I suppose if they made a tail, they'd have to add the ability to go Oozaru.
-I was really disappointed that you can't edit your custom character's stance, aura/ki color, basic melee and throwing style, etc. As with several other features of the game, you simply get what you get, and if you don't like it, recreate and pick a different race. All of the unlockable characters have their own stances, throws, ki colors, etc. But your character will simply be very generic in too many ways. This again reveals a sad lack of creativity.
-Perhaps the ultimate Dragonball signature is missing: you cannot have "power struggles" with another character (like in the show and other games, where two ki beams collide and compete).
-I have mixed feelings about the grinding system. Playing the same side quest 50-60 times to get one move or piece of clothing you really want is both awesome, and annoying. Some of it is skill, but largely it's sheer luck.
-Help/Tutorials are very vague. Some gameplay elements were confusing my first couple weeks, until I finally figured them out on my own through trial and error. Other elements of the game aren't explained at all.
-When buying new clothes and accessories, you cannot preview before buying. You can only see the stats.
-If you really like the looks of one piece of clothing, but you really want the stat boosts from another piece of clothing, well, that sucks. You
choose between stats OR appearance, which is a disappointing feature that could have been easily worked around. Want your character to specialize in Ki blasts, but you love the look of clothes that specialize melee? Too bad. Pick one or the other. There are some games out there where you can pick the clothing accessories you are *technically* wearing, and also pick the appearance of clothing accessories you've already unlocked. This game isn't one of them.
-All the clothing I've seen is from series characters. Combine that with the already limited customization, and you will almost inevitably look like you have no imagination, and are copying characters from the show.
-There's a tournament arena which supposedly hosts competitions, but I have never once seen it open. There are also special events bulletin boards, but I have never seen anything on them, either.
-Wish it had Workshop so the community could fix the things that the devs couldn't or didn't want to.
--------------------
More and more, it seems that the devs were just trying to release a game that would be "good enough" to get people to pay a hefty price. That is honestly why the video game industry as a whole is so underwhelming these days. Where's the passion and creativity?

I don't often review anything, mostly because I don't think I'm qualified to. This game, however, is an exception.
Please note that I have not and do not plan to play any PVP, so that will not be factored in here.
A little backstory:
Growing up, DBZ was one of my biggest influences and loves. I fell in love with the characters, the story, and the outrageous combat elements that made up what is today one of my most favorite anime series of all time. Naturally, when I first played a DBZ game (Budokai 1) I was very excited to see the universe I'd grown to love and be able to play it. Flash forward to now, with the release of THIS game (Xenoverse) and I couldn't be happier.
Pros:
Story- VERY much like the anime, but of course with that cool, time-warped twist. I found myself on the edge of my seat a LOT.
Characters- Not much to say here other than they're the ones you came to love (or hate in case of villains). Customization could stand to be a bit better, but overall I'm happy with what I can create in the games' system.
Gameplay- Plays much like the Tenkaichi series of games. Fly around, auto-combos, teleports, ki-blasts, ultimate attacks... you name it, it's pretty much there. A blast (buh-dum-tss) to play, and I never get bored of it. Can be a bit wonky, but overall is very well polished.
Graphics- GORGEOUS. Damn this universe looks amaaaaazing in this game. Couldn't be happier with it.
Cons:
Story- None that I have problems with.
Characters- Villains (Toma, Mira, Demigra) can be a bit too predictable or cliche, but that doesn't necessarily detract from the overall experience.
Gameplay- AI is sort of barebones, but once you get further along into the story and PQs (which are good, varied, and challenging at higher levels) the ai becomes a real challenge to deal with. Up until about the android saga and PQs 17+, the AI isn't very good. Some attacks whiff when they shouldn't, but no other gripes with attacks.
Graphics- N/A.
Do I recommend this game?
HELL YES (if you're a fan of the series).
Yes! (if you're a fan of rpg/fighter hybrids).
No. (if you don't like SOME (partly unnecessary unless you want to GIT GUD) grinds). (Diablo-esque, but a bit better in my opinion).
Yes again! (If you like gorgeous games with a wealth of content that won't leave you bored).
Overall score: As a fan of the series- 9.5/10. Very great game, well-polished and satisfying.
Objectively- 8.5/10. Good, if a bit irritating, in terms of gameplay and adaptability (at first).

This game has a lot of potential, and overall, I have to say that I like it. The visuals are stunning, if a little monotonous, the controls handle just fine; it acts like you would expect an FPS to.
I understand that I played it in what seemed to be the early stages. I think it's still in Alpha, which impresses me.
But I do have some not-so-good comments about it. For one thing, the two playable single-player missions are both difficult and...strange, I guess?
In the first one, you have to test the defenses of a research facility by infiltrating it without raising an alarm.
I love love LOVE that there are multiple different ways to enter the facility; I think that is great, and points to great things in the future. But the mission was just too damn difficult. If you don't spend ten to twenty minutes just sitting there observing the security drones, you won't even make it into the facility before the alarm is raised; and they raise it the moment you are spotted.
The other mission is extremely dark, which provides a very creepy atmosphere; it's great, but it isn't at all what I expected from a game called "Interstellar Marines". What I expected was more like an action-packed shooter, like Arma or Call of Duty but in space. What you actually get is closer to FEAR or what Aliens: Colonial Marines tried (and failed) to be. I'm not saying that that is necessarily a bad thing, it just wasn't at all what I was expecting.
Also, I am very confused about why you can lift your facemask up; I understand that maybe it will have a purpose later on, but right now all it really does is it removes your HUD.

Aaero is a beautiful hybrid of a rhythm game and on-rails shooting that shines brightest in its 3 boss battles.
== VISUALS
Heavily inspired from  the early rhythm game days of FreQuency, Amplitude, and REZ, the low-polygon models look stunning in HD, especially when coupled with the particle effects. Color plays a large part in the portrayal of their environments and reinforces the digital playground you navigate through. EDM fans will feel right at home as this visual style is often used in music videos for Drum & Bass, Dubstep, Future Funk, etc.
The levels seem to "breathe" with the music, which is great feedback and a trip to play while high.
== AUDIO
The licensed soundtrack of Noisia, Flux Pavillion, Habstrakt & Megalodon, and more is one of the reasons this game was so successful. While it is still possible to have a great rhythm game without the licensing (a-la FreQuency), it really helps when selling the game to a skeptical audience.
The audio mastering was very well done in this game and is slightly different than the official track releases by the artists, giving each song a fresh feel that worked for each of the game's levels (even if you've heard these songs before).
== MECHANICS
Just like the visuals, the mechanics feel like an homage to early rhythm games with a fresh spin on their execution. The controls are tight but forgiving, so players who aren't accustomed to rhythm games won't be instantly turned off to it. The game can sometimes feel like a brain-teaser, having to move the controller's analog sticks clockwise and counter-clockwise (and at the same time), but in a way that encourages practice and mastery rather than frustration.
All of the games actions are performed on beat to the song, whether or not you perform them on the beat yourself. This all helps the player stay on beat or find the beat if they tend to lose their way while enhancing the player's engagement.
== SCORING
The game's scoring system is a nice blend of intense but non-intrusive, allowing players who don't care about scoring big to complete the levels without worrying about how well they're doing. For those looking to climb the leaderboards, however, the game does a great job of providing depth by rewarding precision movement and timing. If none of this really interests you, there's always "Chillout" mode, which forgoes the scoring altogether. There's definitely something here for everyone.
== BOSS BATTLES
Amazing. Brilliantly crafted. The boss battles are where Aaero really shows how innovative it is. The bosses movements and attacks are all timed with the music, and even the levels themselves fit in perfectly with how the boss is tackled. If Shadow of the Colossus was a music game, this is how it would be done.
My only gripe with the game is that the entirety of the game wasn't just a collection of boss battles past the first boss. The way the music really ties into the feel of the boss designs was also a great feeling, and made defeating the bosses that much more satisfying.
== CRITICISMS
The first criticism I have with the game is that the difficulty progression doesn't always flow nicely, especially when you have to beat the songs in order. The song, "Edge of Tomorrow" was the biggest culprit of this, where the mechanics felt like the song should have been placed down further into the game.
The screen size scaling was also an issue (at least for me). Running on a 21:9 monitor, I scaled the game size to 100% (the default is 80%, and it made some parts of the game almost unplayable at times as the enemies and projectiles I was trying to destroy were often outside of the shooting range. From videos I've seen of other people playing, this didn't seem to be a problem, so I'm assuming it wasn't a "feature" but a bug, though I can't be sure. Either way, it was frustrating.
The music ribbon (the line you have your ship follow to the beat) patterns were also fairly basic. This is fine on normal mode, as the entire Normal playthrough seemed like a tutorial run, but these basic patterns also continued into Advanced mode as well, meaning the difficulty curve didn't stretch too far.
== FINAL THOUGHTS
Some people will criticize this game for not being "strictly" a rhyhtm game and including a shooting aspect, but I feel as though they are ignoring the fact that the combat is directly tied to the music and rhythm as well. As I said before, every detail of this game is tied to rhythm, it just might not be apparent at first. The combination of the shooting and timing your movements might just be the gateway for people to see the draw to rhythm games in the future.
Highly recommended.

Trace ribbons of light with one stick, and shoot enemies with the other - all to the beat of an outstanding soundtrack - Aaero is an intensely exciting experience that is both accessible and has more than a bit of challenge to the dedicated player.
At the time of writing, I'm one of 5 people to have accessed and completed all difficulties in the game, having taken me 8 hours to achieve this.
While the limited amount of people to reach this stage demonstrates the difficulty involved in the game, it also highlights a lack of content; while what is in the game is intensely fun, there isn't a lot of it, and it can be completed in a few sittings.
This is not to say the game is easy at all - Aaero is, indeed, a rhythm game at heart - to beat higher difficulties, a lot of perseverance is required to master the nuances of each song.
However, the difficulty change between the levels - Normal, Advanced, and Master - are minimal, only adding a few more enemies and hazards to the level. I'm not sure if there actually was a difficulty change between Advanced and Master, other than only having 1 life in the latter, but to achieve a competitive score at the Advanced level, it is necessary to stay alive the whole time anyway.
As a rhythm game, one of the most important aspects are the controls, and Aaero really shines in this department. Controls are tight and responsive, and easy to learn. When something goes wrong, you know that it's your fault, and this helps make sure that failing to complete a level or achieve a certain score feels like your own fault, and not one inherent to the game.
The soundtrack chosen for the game is excellent - a fine selection of music in the vein of dubstep, electronic, drum and bass etc. Following the ribbons of light will add layers to the music, and every sound effect in the game - target locking beeps, weapon impacts, enemy spawns and so on - is quantised to the beat of the rhythm, achieving a state where the game is as much a part of the music as the music is the game.
The shooting aspect is simple enough to understand, and has a little more depth to it than first seems. Attacks will always land on the 1st or 3rd beats of every 4/4 bar, and you are rewarded for hitting these exactly on time - in attack efficiency, as well as score. Understanding this mechanic is crucial, but skipped over in the game's tutorial, which can lead to some amount of frustration when your shots seem inconsistent.
When these two main mechanics are combined, Aaero comes to life as a fantastic rhythm rail shooter in the long-empty void of Rez. A lack of content will disappoint the most dedicated and skilled players, but in spite of that, Aaero is not an experience to be missed.

Subtle strategy meets simple rules for a deceptively complex game.
If you're a fan of non-random turn based strategy games (no dice rolling folks!) then this is a game you can't pass up.
Think of it like this: Imagine a game of chess where each unit has a simple set of rules. Then add in the ability to conquer tiles on the board, create new tiles and paths, and destroy others (sometimes with enemies on them!). Then add in the ability to collect resources (mana) and buy new units. You now have an idea of A Druid's Duel.
It features Async multiplayer for those of us who can't always dedicate large amounts of time at once and a pretty huge and EXTREMELY challenging campaign.
While on the easiest difficulty it can easy be a gateway for a newcomer to strategy games, on the higher difficulty this game will challenge the very best strategy players among us.
Well worth the price of admission!

Avernum is an epic fantasy role-playing adventurer set in an enormous, subterranean nation. Avernum is a land underground, a subterranean nation full of rogues, misfits, and brigands, struggling for survival and wealth in the monster-infested darkness.
You have been banished to the underworld, never to see the light of day again.
The surface is ruled by the cruel Emperor Hawthorne, master of the Empire. All of the known lands are subject to his brutal command. Everyone who speaks out, misbehaves or doesn’t fit in is cast into the dark, volcanic pits of Avernum, far below the surface. There, you are expected to die, a victim of starvation, horrible monsters, or simple despair.
But not all of the Avernites have surrendered. With magic and steel, they are forging a new nation deep underground. You can join them and fight for safety. Or freedom. Or, if you dare, revenge on the surface-worlders who tried to destroy you. Join your new countrymen, explore a huge game world, hunt for hundreds of magical artifacts, choose from hundreds of quests, and become the hero of the underworld!
This is not a mindless RPG. Don't go into this game desiring mindless fun, for you will have to read quite a bit, manuever Avernum's cave systems via map systems, and retain information about quests, as the game doesn't hold your hand with doing so. The game does have a journal system that is VERY nice for its time; when you're speaking to an NPC who says something worth noting, you can "record" their speech with the click of a button, so you can pull this up at any time. This comes to be very useful, as quest notes don't update as you progress through a quest, so it's up to you to pay attention and know what the next step is. Despite all this, Avernum stays very much so to the right side of the line when it comes to tedium. I encountered no game-breaking quests during my playthrough like I have with other RPGs of the time (Divine Divinity, I'm looking at you, though I love you so). It IS possible to kill NPCs that you'll need for certain questlines, though the other questlines are still available, and there is also a cheat system to help you through this as a last resort (just look up your problem online).
All in All
is a good RPG Game!

An ancient milestone in RPG adventures, so monolithic it still stands tall today.
When I was the tiniest of children, I was introduced to a series of party-based adventure stories - rich in character and consequence - called Exile. These games instilled in me a great appreciation for video games that try to create and simulate an actual world, alive with a beating populace for whom one could feel genuinely acquainted.
Twenty years later, after decades of wondering where those games went and why there are so many series that use the word 'Exile', I discovered that Spiderweb Software are alive and well, still developing and still destributing the Exile series.
Sadly, that series cannot be run on modern operating systems. I should restate... it would be sad - if Spiderweb hadn't taken the time to update said games and make them available once more.
Full and oddyssean, not just for the time but even compared to some modern games, Avernum is a highly enjoyable and suprisingly replayable Fantasy classic dealing with the ever-poignant themes of loss, fear, struggle, unity and the determination of the living to do just that.
I cannot describe my elation, at the continued existence of this universe. I strongly recommend this and any other Spiderweb RPGs to anyone who misses the simple complexity of the classic RPG format, or of pure, analogical storytelling.

First off let me say, you do not want to play this alone. It's a much better time if you play it with at least one other person. Getting past that, this game is an odd gem. Released around 2009, this is a first person shooter/open world/rpg game with quite a bit of weapon variety across the 4 classes you can play as. You have (as I just mentioned) 4 choices, Lilith the support character, Roland the most black support gunner in gaming, Mordacai, the sniper with a cool bird that kills things, and my personal favorite, Brick, a bulky hamfisted guy with a bad temper. Each of these classes have "action skills" which are unlocked at level 5. Brick being able to go beserk and punch things, doing very heavy damage and recovering health. Mordacai being able to use bloodwing, a bird that homes in on enemies and does damage
. Lilith, being able to phasewalk (don't ask me how that works, I don't play much of the siren). And Roland has his turret, which is very useful if you do decide to play alone. Moving on, the game itself is quite large, but the locations are level locked with the foes. So if you're level 20, going back to the start you will still fight the level 1 enemies there. Grinding is also a debatable issue, but it's not terrible in this case as there are plenty of side and main quests that will fetch you decent XP. The gunplay is what you would find in any other fps, exept this has more of a Halo feel to it due to the slight moon jumping and grenade physics. Another big part of this game is the driving, which feels amazing once you get used to the mouse sensitivity on the steering
Again, the driving goes to the Halo style of control, floaty yet tight turns where the camera controls the car. Now on to the gun variety. I think that the marketing strategy they pulled for this game (and the ones after it) of having billions of guns, is a lie. You may have quite a few guns, by quite a number of in-game gunsmiths, but they are mostly the same gun with slighty different stats and maybe a longer name or a model change. Guns also have elemental effects, as do your action skills, going from explosive to corrosion, they make fighting some enemies go from hard to easy, or the other way around. Moving away from that, the controls are tight and the keybinds are set just fine. Maybe it was just my game or my pc, but voice chat is a little iffy on my reciving end. All in all, is this a good game and worth the $20? Maybe. If you're looking to have a good time with a couple of your friends, then yes, by all means get this. In my opinion, this is the best game out of the current three. I also advise getting the DLC along with it, at least the one that increases your level cap.

The grappling swinging controls are not as awesome as a lot of user reviews would lead you to believe, but they are competent. The problem being that swing points are usually too close together making consistent swinging very awkward to do. It is also very hard to gauge when to release to swing outward correctly even though it shows you a blue icon letting you know when. You still have to pinpoint release to swing even remotely how you want to, which leads to a lot of swinging straight up or at a upward angle, or too low, as opposed to straight forward or at a much desired but very hard to do forward upward angle to propel you forward correctly. The third person shooting aspect is forgettable especially since the only weapon you have in the game is a pistol, although you can find secondary weapons sometimes like a minigun which blows, or a grenade launcher which rocks. You can also punch objects into the air then jump up and punch them at your enemy, or you can latch your grapple onto an object and whip it into them, or you can grapple onto an enemy and jump kick them twice to kill them. I don't often review anything, mostly because I don't think I'm qualified to. This game, however, is an exception.
Please note that I have not and do not plan to play any PVP, so that will not be factored in here.
A little backstory:
Growing up, DBZ was one of my biggest influences and loves. I fell in love with the characters, the story, and the outrageous combat elements that made up what is today one of my most favorite anime series of all time. Naturally, when I first played a DBZ game (Budokai 1) I was very excited to see the universe I'd grown to love and be able to play it. Flash forward to now, with the release of THIS game (Xenoverse) and I couldn't be happier.
Pros:
Story- VERY much like the anime, but of course with that cool, time-warped twist. I found myself on the edge of my seat a LOT.
Characters- Not much to say here other than they're the ones you came to love (or hate in case of villains). Customization could stand to be a bit better, but overall I'm happy with what I can create in the games' system.
Gameplay- Plays much like the Tenkaichi series of games. Fly around, auto-combos, teleports, ki-blasts, ultimate attacks... you name it, it's pretty much there. A blast (buh-dum-tss) to play, and I never get bored of it. Can be a bit wonky, but overall is very well polished.
Graphics- GORGEOUS. Damn this universe looks amaaaaazing in this game. Couldn't be happier with it.
Cons:
Story- None that I have problems with.
Characters- Villains (Toma, Mira, Demigra) can be a bit too predictable or cliche, but that doesn't necessarily detract from the overall experience.
Gameplay- AI is sort of barebones, but once you get further along into the story and PQs (which are good, varied, and challenging at higher levels) the ai becomes a real challenge to deal with. Up until about the android saga and PQs 17+, the AI isn't very good. Some attacks whiff when they shouldn't, but no other gripes with attacks.
Graphics- N/A.
Do I recommend this game?
HELL YES (if you're a fan of the series).
Yes! (if you're a fan of rpg/fighter hybrids).
No. (if you don't like SOME (partly unnecessary unless you want to GIT GUD) grinds). (Diablo-esque, but a bit better in my opinion).
Yes again! (If you like gorgeous games with a wealth of content that won't leave you bored).
Overall score: As a fan of the series- 9.5/10. Very great game, well-polished and satisfying.
Objectively- 8.5/10. Good, if a bit irritating, in terms of gameplay and adaptability (at first).
Any fan of the show should not miss this.
