Slightly weaker than Season 1, but still an amazing story-driven horror adventure game. If you're looking for Lovecraft, Edgar Poe or Kafka-type unease, madness and horror, look no further than The Last Door. And play both seasons chronologically.
Season 2 seems to be a definite finale to the storyline that began in Season 1 (of course, with possible new games set in the same universe) and answers all the questions that needed answers, without ruining the unspeakbleness of horrors you encounter, leaving them still beyond your understanding. The story feels trailing off guidelessly at times, unlike Season 1, where it always felt like it was more bits of the same story. But it's still interesting, told in a great way that mixes story and puzzle bits without breaking the pace all that much. There are few moments where I felt that I was starting to wonder aimlessly not noticing a necessary item/dialogue trigger to move the game forward, but those moments were rare and didn't ruin the experience in any way. There were also several simple non-game-breaking bugs that will probably get fixed soon. With only big complaint remaining from the previous Season - that you can't really skip scenes if you're replaying the episode and want to find something you might've missed or just to re-experience specific moments. Still, amazing atmospheric horror story game.

Purchasing this game was one of the easiest and most satisfying decisions of last year.  The gameplay is easy to understand, the story and dialogue are both engaging and hilarious and the overall artistic value of the game is unique yet very welcoming.  There are parts of 'Elevator Action' and 'Spy vs Spy' going on in the visual aesthetic which I really like.
I really appreciate the fact that I can easily pick this game up, play for an hour, put it down and then come back and not lose a beat from when I played last.  Gunpoint does this trick exceptionally well.  The controls are very intuitive so the only task presented to you when you come back is to figure out the next mission.
Missions are challenging but not punishing.  There are some head-scratchers in here but they won't force anyone to look for an outside guide or anything of that sort.  Also, the game rewards and encourages creative solutioning so there's good chance a puzzle could (and should) be solved in various ways.  Even though I'm only on my first playthrough, I have full intention to playing it more times to see how else I could have solved previous missions.
Now that community made missions are in the future roadmap for Gunpoint, the money spent on the game seems even more well-spent.

I have never actually just uninstalled a game, to never play it again, even if I haven't finished it...but I am seriously considering it with this one. I paid $5 for this and still have trouble finding any redeeming value in it. It's hard to even figure out where to start when it comes to the issues, but I think my first one would have to be the sheer difficulty of the game. Anything and *everything* can kill you...and exceedingly quickly. Walk to close to fire(not even touching it), and you're dead in less than a second. Enemy hits you with some sort of electrified stick, you're dead. Flying mech-thing shoots a missle that just kind of grazes you, you're dead. Add to it that you have only have a *pistol* 99.9% of the time with unbelievably limited ammo and you're left trying to punch these enemies to death. No joke, you're sitting there *punching* mechs. The swing mechanic, as you'll read in a lot of other reviews, is also hard to get used to. Why they couldn't just simply make it as easy as it was in the original NES(or remake) game, I have no idea. They took the single most important thing about Bionic Commando and turned it in to a frustrating guessing game of "when do I release?"...and, of course, when you miss it, you're dead most of the time. Add to it these weird "Radiation Zone" areas(basically invisible walls that cut you off from going too far off the pre-determined path) that sap your life away if you happen to go swinging in to one(most times dying before you can get back out) and you've got a game that basically punishes you in every conceivable gameplay area. I'll give it another hour or so...maybe something will change, but I doubt it...

Heavily underrated game. Story is sort of cliched but it just adds to the fun. It's got the dopest swinging mechanic, comparable to the Arkham games, graphics aren't the worst in the world. In short: I don't really get what all the hype is for. (I also don't really understand why I've been playing this game for almost 100 hours, both co-op and solo. Probably achievements.)
Borderlands is a decent mix of influences and game elements - Mad Max meets Idiocracy, Diablo meets Call of Duty.
It probably would have had a whole lot less success if it did not drop the more serious tone it was going for early in development in favor of tongue-in-cheek humor and cartoonish cell shaded graphics. DLCs also abandoned all pretense of subtlety subsequently and went all out - zombies, psycho claptraps, the works.
GOOD
+ melds RPG mechanics with FPS gameplay (and one of the few to do so)
+ 4 different characters (theoretically) support 4 different gameplay archetypes and these were designed for co op play from the start
+ anesthetics are quite nice - Unreal engine 3 good looks + cell shaded style
+ great diversity in weapons - procedurally generated (different colors, scopes and barrels all viewable in-game) and with multiple rarity tiers distilled into 7 or so major weapon types and a couple dozen unique weapon effects
+ good production values - animation, sound design, character design and voice-overs are all pretty great
+ some of the writing and dialogue is genuinely funny if you've got the patience to go through it
+ ultimately, it's a decent time filler - run around, shoot things, loot, cash-in, rinse, repeat
BAD
- the story is about as shallow as your ex-girlfriend and all characters have as much depth as a bath tub
- core gameplay kind of sucks - enemies are brain-dead bullet sponges, the bazillion of different weapons all feel like pea-shooters, quests become absurd chores after a while. All player characters (including bad♥♥♥♥♥Brick) feel like weak sissies that go down after a few enemy shots if you don't use cover
- crappy ARPG implementation and FPS don't mix very well - it doesn't really matter how "good" you are within the game, what really matters is the arbitrary number that describes your level. That in turn determines what arbitrary damage numbers your weapons inflict upon your enemies... It's a "Woah did you see how high that number went?" type of game, from an FPS perspective. Not exactly ideal.
- the game is artificially prolonged because of this as well - killing enemies a good couple of levels above yours is almost impossible (unless you're willing to literally chip at them from a safe position for something like an hour). Progress a bit through the game however, and surprise, an hour and couple of XP levels later you'll be able to run them over in a couple of shots.
- co-op play isn't that much fun either  - you tend to fast forward through the game (enjoying it less along the way) and race to open all the chests to get all the loot before your mates do
- you have vehicles, in-game maps and objective markers - but somehow Borderlands manages to be one of the worst games out there when it comes to spatial awareness. Identical environments + horrible in-game map + claustrophobic FOV = "Dude where's my car?"
- oh, the FOV is locked for some reason at a vomit-inducing value under 90, and requires editing game files (or installing a separate program) to bind a key to be able to change it at a desired value. Squad is a game that creates a new level of excitement when working with teammates towards a common goal. This game has taken its design thesis of being a worthy predecessor of the Project Reality mod for Battlefield and crafted some of the greatest experiences I’ve had in games since the days of milsim groups in ArmA 2.
When joining a server, you step into a new atmosphere filled with 80 all working towards team collective, group collective, or individual collective goals. These goals can all be achieved or failed through the use of various tools such as squad-to-squad radios, transport vehicles to quickly move squads around, setting up fire, and many other tools.
One of the greatest aspects of Squads tools is its class system. You are put into a squad with 8 other people and the option to specialize in specific roles within your squad. Depending on how full your squad is, you can opt to be a rifleman with a long-range optic, a machine gunner, designated Anti-Tank rocketeer, combat medic, and various other roles. These roles are vital to helping be part of a high-functioning squad on the battlefield.
While it’s great being part of the team and falling in line, the aspect that truly makes this game shine for me are the leadership roles. I almost solely play as a Squad Leader when playing this game. The feeling of mapping out a plan and working with my squad mates to figure out what we are capable and willing to do, then tackling that challenge is a rush like no other.
There are a few issues with squad however. This game can be a slug to run, especially on lower end systems. It also has some glairing issues with the meta-gameplay. One of the current tactics is that whichever team rushes the enemies first capture point, almost always win. While this is being fixed in the next patch, there will still be meta-gaming for many other aspects of the game.
I’ve now realized that squad has become a game that in years I will be looking back at as those golden times. However, the great thing is those golden times are now and it’s only been getting better with every other update.

If I haven’t convinced you yet that you need this game, let me describe one of the best experiences I had while playing this game.
Starting on a remote part of a battle-ridden landscape, our goal was to place down a forward operating base within the enemy controlled side of the map. This was to ensure that we could effectively attack their capture points incase the rest of the team couldn’t break through the enemies controlled territory. Before we spawned in my squad and I planned out the route would all be taking, what vehicles we would use, and established our rules of engagement.
Spawning in, all 9 of us make our mad dash for two vehicles, a logistics truck to help place the FOB, and a troop transport to move the rest of our team. I get into the driver seat of the logistics truck with 3 other teammates while my designated troop transport driver takes on the other 5. We roll out and begin our trip along the backroads to our placement spot for the FOB.
While traveling, we crossed the river into the enemy controlled side of the map. At this point, the enemy forces had already moved out of their main base and were closing in close to our positions. After driving further past the river crossing, we spotter a convoy of multiple BTR’s and troop transports to our left, heading towards the same Y intersection we were heading too.
Immediately I prepared for losing both vehicles, but rather than diverting or stopping, I decided to keep pursing towards our mission objective. I got on the radio and announced our plan “Hold fire and comms, keep driving, merge into the convoy, and don’t look back.” Right after saying that, my buddy in the squad chimed up “You jackass, your going to get us killed!”
With ourselves and the convoy approaching, we saw an opening between the BTR and transport truck. I took my opportunity and quickly slid into line as my driver in the transport did the same a few vehicles down. We were all stunned, but knew we weren’t out of the clear yet. We were surrounded by at least 20-30 enemies and still needed to divert to our objective. We didn’t know if they would realize their mistake and shoot us or not realize what was happening.
After a few moments of driving and the BTR’s curiously staring at the uniform of my squad mate in the back of the truck, we found our turning point and quickly pulled into where we needed to lay down our FOB while the rest of the enemies convoy headed further East to assault the rest of our team.
Once we were in the clear I immediately jumped on our squad-to-squad radio and began announcing what armament, number of enemies, and direction of travel to my other Squad Leaders while my friend driving the transport helped coordinate to our squad members where we needed to go.
Once we placed our FOB we had a spawn point for everyone else on the team and would later go on to having a massive multi-squad fight over a grape farm in a desperate push to keep the enemies from pushing us too far back into our own territory. We would later go on an win that match due in large part to my squads work in getting that spawn point down.

You will get a good amount playtime for your money, and the game becomes alot of fun as soon you figured out the combat system. As the gothic series and the previous risen games, one of the biggest appeals of the game is the exploration. You will always find some hidden treasure and secrets, if you just look for them
This game gets a bad rap for being not as streamlined and polished as some other AAA rpg's, quite undeserved if you ask me. And i'm not a blinded fanboy of the franchise who desperately wants to defend it. I started playing this game after Witcher 3, and the transition was more than rough, since Witcher 3 was  doing everything right that matters in a good RPG.  Going over to risen was very difficult, since the clunky animations, odd combat system, and campy dialogue made it very appaling after Witcher 3. I even stopped playing entirely until i got back into it much later. But if you're willing to put some effort in the game you can get alot of entertainment out of it. Especially if you love exploring, this game will be for you. While the seperate Islands that you will visit throughout the game are not as huge as for example Skyrim, there are still tons of areas to discover that are completely optional, but will always reward you for exploring them.
In conclusion, i'd recommend this game to every rpg fan, although if you only want to play perfectly balanced and polished games, this one might not be for you as it comes with a series of issues coming from the sometimes faulty game design. If you played and like the previous Gothic and Risen games, you can't do anything wrong with this one.

The Combat is sadly still like Risen 2's and not as good as the first Risen's, wich had the best combat of PB's games, Gothic series included.
Though it seems that PB doesn't even WANT you to use melee combat since every class gets the option to use powerful magic that is superior to melee in every conceivable way.
Like Risen 2, I ended up not hating this game simply through picking the most fun class/playstyle there was (back then it was the gunslinger, this time its the mage.) Though as I said, every class can do everything, which sadly means your decision of who to join in the first half of the game is just fluff, especially when you take into consideration that even the few spells that only a certain faction teaches are still abundantly available as scrolls. This also means that the game doesn't lend itself well to multiple playthroughs.
Now, all that sounds pretty negative, but everything else here is at least solid. I liked most of the quests and NPCs, the dialogue and interactions are fun, the magic is satisfying to use (though that is partially by virtue of being overpowered) and the presentation, while not amazing, still works in creating distinct and cool looking environments.
All in all, while I still cant wholeheartedly recommend this game to people that are - understandably- still sour about Risen 2, its a step in the right direction and I want to see where PB takes the series.

proper review:
This game is hilarious! The main character has the most overly manly voice ever and the people you can interact with have epic lines, which are adapted beautifully to what you are doing. Take for example the moment after you kill a rammer or a golem, if you have edward with you he will say 'looks like size did not matter after all'. Yes, generally the game is full of sexual innuendos, which makes for an epic time! But besides being hilarious the game also has some very thoughtful lines of dialogue, sometimes coming from the most unexpected characters. In this regard I can only recommend to everyone to explore the pirate island together with jaffar the gnome!
A lot of love did obviously also go into the design of the world. The game is really beautiful and at times you feel like completely turning the mission marker off and just exploring what the developers hid all over the place. This ties in nicely with a design choice I, as someone playing a lot of RPGs, really cherish. Namely, the focus on exploration combined with a world that is not so big that you have the feeling of getting lost simply by wandering around for a minute, but also not tieing you down at any moment. Those familiar with Gothic or other Risen games know that the enemies in pyranha games are never scaled, which is just brilliant! Instead of having the feeling that hm basically I can go into any dark cave without consequence though I carry nothing but a rusty dagger, you are being challenged by the stronger monsters and quickly run over the tiny enemies like giant rats. I also really love the possibility to commit early to fighting an enemy that is intended for a latter stage and just grinding him down and then receiving powerful loot and glory in return. This is definitely a big part of this franchise! They truly achieved a world which never feels empty or repetitive (looking at you dragon age II).
At this point I feel the need to address the whole balancing issue, which has been largely criticized by everyone and their grandma. The basic gist of most reviews is that you can beat the game relatively easily. Now in my point of view it is absolutely up to you how difficult it is for you. it is true you can begin by putting your early skill points (glory in risen 3) into toughness and mellee fighting, play the game on normal mode and always take 'bones' (an ally) with you. In that case the game will be fairly easy and you'll hardly ever die, allowing you to focus on the story. However, if you play the game on hard and dont always take an ally with you, while also skilling for the more innovative skill trees, such as cunning and dexterity you will die a whole lot and better save often. This I would describe as my preferred experience with the game, because it allows you to make use of some interesting dialogue choices and gets you access to all the fancy loot and seriously, if you do that, the game is definitely not easy!
A central part of the game are yet three new factions one of which the player can join. Here a design choice was made which I only partly support. Basically there are three fighting styles, pure mage, melee and mage support, melee and voodoo support. Of course you don't ever have to use magic if you don't want to, but really there is no reason why you shouldn't use the magic boosts available. Both the shadow hunters and the guardians allow for a pure magic built, with the guardian built being incredibly OP if you commit all your early game glory (I'll probably write a guide for that). My problem with the fighting system is that the 'put some glory into everything'-built is basically very similar in each of the factions. I personally dont really like this similarity. For example, in my point of view it was not necessary to make the guardians so viable for melee combat.
Additionally to the choice of a faction, the caracter development in Risen 3 is based on an a very simple morality system. Here the choice is mostly between a hillarious line of dialogue in which the protagonist disses whoever he is talking to (resulting in minus 1 of 100 'Soul') or a generally very empathetic playstyle. Both of these are fun choices and have minor, but interesting effects, particularly on your own crew. However, don't expect a morality system that completely changes the game or your fighting style, like in dishonored (great game btw).
As a long time Gothic 1/2 fan (have been playing those games for over 10 years) I am super thrilled to find all those easter eggs that the developers hid. Everyone that played gothic 1 knows the guy that talks to you in the old camp, if you walk through his two doored hut and complains about everyone using his hut as a gateaway. I also think most will remember Moe the tavern guard from G2? Well all I want to say is explore calador a bit!
So finally, the one thing I really did not like (though I also heard a lot of people loving this) were the battles against sea monsters. The problem is these battles are unavoidable and basically super repetitive, centering around a cannon in the front that is blocked by the ship.
In conclusion, this is a fantastic and heavily underrated game. Its a great ride and shouldn't be missing in any RPG fans game library.

The concept is solid and the old school feel is right.  If you get this at a discount and want to try it for a few dollars, sure.  But as a game that isn't just fan made and shared amongst friends, but is sold commercially, with all due respect: (1) the game mechanics are too simplistic for its release date; (2) the plot and quests lack depth and there are glaring issues that detract from a player's ability to immerse himself in the game; (3) the interface is incredibly clumsy, and there is a lot of trial and error necessary to understand how certain items operate, which in the heat of battle is not great; (4) the writing is not as good as people say it is-it's not bad for English as a second language, but it doesn't stack up against its peers; and (5) the dialogue trees are terribly frustrating: you will find yourself having the same circular conversation for ages before you can actually hand in your quests or trigger new ones, and sometimes it's just a matter of mashing the text options at random until you can finally finish the dialogue and advance the plot.

Okay, so maybe you don't much care for the Borderlands games by 2K/Gearbox. I can respect that. I don't have strong feelings about them one way or the other; I've tried one of them, and it didn't compel me to keep playing, but neither did I dislike it. But I liked the concept of "Vault Hunters" on the planet Pandora, and other mythos from the games, and that is what this game runs with.
And maybe you've gotten tired of the TellTale formula... maybe you've played The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, perhaps even Game of Thrones, and feel that your choices don't amount to anything. Well, this game... still has an element of that, BUT! If you liked ANY of those games at all, then I think you will like this one, because your choices matter much more than usual! Or at least, they seem to matter, and ultimately that's the important thing.
I will admit, I have not replayed the game making different choices (yet), so I don't know if the illusion is shattered upon doing so. But there are plenty of RPG's out there that give you choices that still lead to more or less the same storyline, so surely an adventure game can be cut a little bit of slack in that regard, right? Yes? No? Well, anyway. It felt much more like I was in control than in other TellTale Games of recent memory.
But even if it didn't, Tales From The Borderlands has a great storyline anyway (in my opinion). Told from the perspective of two fairly different characters who, through various circumstances/fate, were thrown into each other's lives and [judging from the fact that they're retelling the story] lived to tell about it. There's more to it than that, but it's best to discover in the process of playing the game.
Most games like this, I play over the span of several days, maybe an episode a day; sometimes taking as long as a week. But this game was so engaging, so amusing, and so action-packed that I played it from start to finish in less than 48 hours. And I enjoyed (almost) every minute of it. (There are a few tedious moments, and the "hit this button rapidly" moments do get annoying at times, but they're a small price to pay to get to the other portions.
The TellTale engine isn't getting any younger, but the Borderlands graphic style works with this really well. (Or badly, if you strongly dislike the Borderlands visual style.) There are some plot elements that benefit from knowledge of some of the basics of Borderlands [the existence of megacorp Heilos, and its murderous founder Handsome Jack], but it's not strictly necessary and the game does a fairly decent job bringing people up to speed. There are some Easter eggs that only Borderlands players would get, but everything works without having to pick up on those.
I always felt that tongue-in-cheek humor was TellTale's forte, and this episodic series reconfirms my opinion. There are dramatic moments, even some vaguely "emotional" moments, but for the most part it's witty, goofy, sarcastic, and clever. I don't want to oversell it, but it's the only game I've actually laughed out loud at in I don't know how long.
Also, Patrick Warburton voices an antagonist, which is just awesome. Even if it did feel weird to hear Brock Samson's voice coming out of someone who isn't Brock Samson.
Anyway... it was a fun little game, and if you can get it on sale or as part of a bundle or some sort, so much the better.
Enjoy! And try not to get killed too much.

That being said, the impression I get is that people seem to consider this game a "diamond in the rough", a game with poor publicity but surprisingly good gameplay given how unknown it is. As for me... well, all I can say is that I understand why this game is as obscure as it is.
Let's start with the atmosphere... the immersion, the feeling, the factor that makes any good RPG its salt. Avernum uses a very similar plot premise to a game I love, Gothic (a game that came out later than Exile, apparently - so Avernum did technically beat Gothic to the punch). An oppressive monarchy throws its criminals - as well as political opponents and anyone it just doesn't want around - into a sealed prison colony where they have to fend for themselves and struggle against each other as well as the wilderness down below. The difference is - where Gothic pulled this off flawlessly (and seriously - if you like Avernum's premise, and haven't played the Gothic games yet, try those out first), Avernum just fails to impress. It becomes obvious immediately as soon as you descend that the prison colony is actually an IMPROVEMENT over the Empire - prosperous, free, and the Empire's rule does not actually have any influence down there. That is a big no-no. It makes it hard to get into the shoes of your characters, who seem to be motivated by revenge or a desire to escape (depending on what conversation options you take as them), because one can't help but think... "okay, what's the conflict here? What's the big deal? Why don't I just settle down, become a mushroom farmer and have a happy life now that the Empire does not rule me?"
Because that's a very valid question. Unlike in Gothic (where the prisoners are dependent upon the surface for luxury goods, weapons and other advanced items, and have to excavate ore in return), Avernum (the prison colony and the game's namesake) is utterly self-sufficient and does not have to give anything back to the Empire. Unlike in Gothic (where there are several camps all ruled by tyrants, the insane and other questionable figures, and there is danger both inside the camps and on the roads, where bandits lie in wait), most of the Avernum world is ruled by a rather unified monarchy with a just king at its helm and with the rule of law largely upheld. (Or so it still seems anyway, well into the midgame. If there is any shocking twist by the end, I know as little of it as you do. Wouldn't matter either way as far as the enjoyment of the story is concerned.) Avernum actually has its sub-prison colony, the Abyss, where the criminals of Avernum are thrown. Not exactly a very inspiring world, is it? Far from the gritty world of Gothic's penal colony, here you stroll almost freely between established towns, the only  enemies being the occasional cat people (sorry - they aren't bikini-clad babes, don't reflex-click the Buy button), snake people (same deal), and generic RPG monsters. Oh, and where Gothic had exciting, living, breathing characters, Avernum's characters are so incredibly dull and lacking any fantasy, it is almost an insult to the genre of Role-Playing Game.
Seriously - I haven't completed the game, but I have played through a good chunk of it, I think. There is not a single interesting character that I met. Not even the King, nor any of his Mayors - all of them interact with your character in the same way. "Hello adventurer! Glad/not glad to see you. I love/hate mercenaries. We are fighting the cat/snake people here. I have a quest for you that involves either killing a lot of cat/snake people or retrieving a trinket guarded by cat/snake people. Or occasionally something else like a jelly or a drake, woo hoo!" Far from being an adventure, the gameplay feels like you are King Micah's head marshal, taking care of his endlessly boring errands throughout the realm, one after the other, never given a break or even an amusing distraction. (And let me just say: this doesn't just apply to the sidequests! Even the main quests themselves are just more of the same.)
Oh, of course, the game mechanics aren't stellar either. The combat system and the skill tree are nothing extraordinary, but at least they are serviceable... except for the horrible pathfinding system. There is no way to see whether your mage/archer is able to strike at the enemy from any given point. You have to click and hope for the best, then one of two things will happen: 1. your character attacks the target (woo hoo!) or 2. your character starts running around like a headless chicken, doing all kinds of crazy stuff, taking non-obvious paths, even attempting (and failing) to run all the way around the map to get at an enemy standing down a corridor
. Nor are the line-of-sight mechanics intuitive - often you can attack when you shouldn't be able to, even more often you can't attack when you should be able to.
The interface isn't exactly great either. Aside from simply being old and dated, it isn't that informative either - there are a lot of weird things that can happen: for example, there is a mechanic that your mages cannot cast spells if they are too "encumbered", but either the game just doesn't mention this or it is way too easy to miss, same difference: being "encumbered" means not that your gear is too heavy, but that your to-hit chance is too low (...I know right, WTF?). This means, for example, that a +1 strength blade and no shield may leave your character unable to cast spells, but a heavier blade with no strength bonus (but a +5% to hit bonus) and a wooden shield (which doesn't have a to-hit malus) will let you do so. Beyond that, there are - of course - bugs. The game isn't riddled with them, but there are some - some traits don't work at all, for example.
While the big Spiderweb Software bundle may well be worth the price on sale (I don't know, haven't really tried much else from it yet), I can safely say I do not recommend Avernum: Escape from the Pit. If you get the bundle, try something else from it. Give this one a miss. It really isn't worth the hype. I'm sorry I couldn't finish it, but it was simply too much of a brutally boring slog - nonetheless, I hope that even my incomplete experience is enough to cast a convincing judgment... Avernum fails in the worst way an RPG can fail - it prioritizes quantity over quality and does not deliver much of the latter, it showcases how an RPG can go utterly wrong even before you take gameplay mechanics into account.

As someone who has played games since the age of 8 (that's 18 years on the trott now), I can safely say this is one of the most addictive games I've ever played.
The amount of things you can do in the game is staggering. You choose how want to progress through the missions, either you stick to the plot ones to the storyline, or you can choose to do all the other missions and side missions first and come back to the main ones.
There are 4 playable characters, each with their own special skill and focus regarding weaponry. The game uses a experience based progression system helping the player level up. After each level the player gains a skill point that they can choose to apply in 3 different branches for their character, thereby choosing the attributes they want.
In terms of the graphics, the game uses a almost cartoon like style. Some of the maps really are huge with a generous amount of detail within.
There are a couple of glitches and bugs, but not enough to detract from the wonderful game experience. If you haven't played any of the games in the Borderlands series, do yourself a favour and pick this first one up. It is the most streamlined of all the games, but in no way lacking in quality.

Overall, this is a VERY fun game and I can't put it down, but it has a few issues. My review will be a simple list of pros and cons:
PROS:
1. The combat is really fun and has a high skill cap. The game rewards you for improving your fighting skills.
2. The art is AMAZING and gets Dragon Ball Z's art style perfectly.
3. The load times are really fast.
4. There are a ton of skills and equipment in the game so you can really specialize your character. You really feel unique in this game.
5. You can play online with your friends.
6. The game's story is pretty cool actually.
CONS:
1. Online matchmaking really sucks. If you want to do a 2v2 with a friend on your team, you may NEVER get a match. We waited for like 10-15 minutes searching for a match and never got one. In addition, sometimes if you search for quest partners, you will not find a room, and if you try to create a room, no one may join it. This game would be WAY better if they just fixed the online multiplayer problems.
2. The user interface they came up with for this game, "Toki Toki", is terrible. You have to run around the town to do simple stuff like buying items and starting matches that could be done 100x faster from a PC-like user interface.
3. The controls are a little bit stupid at times and you will end up accidentally locking onto the wrong target, or opening up the teammate communication list instead of items, or stuff like that. The controls for flying up and down are a little annoying too and not easy to use.

Okay, so maybe you don't much care for the Borderlands games by 2K/Gearbox. I can respect that. I don't have strong feelings about them one way or the other; I've tried one of them, and it didn't compel me to keep playing, but neither did I dislike it. But I liked the concept of "Vault Hunters" on the planet Pandora, and other mythos from the games, and that is what this game runs with.
And maybe you've gotten tired of the TellTale formula... maybe you've played The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, perhaps even Game of Thrones, and feel that your choices don't amount to anything. Well, this game... still has an element of that, BUT! If you liked ANY of those games at all, then I think you will like this one, because your choices matter much more than usual! Or at least, they seem to matter, and ultimately that's the important thing.
I will admit, I have not replayed the game making different choices (yet), so I don't know if the illusion is shattered upon doing so. But there are plenty of RPG's out there that give you choices that still lead to more or less the same storyline, so surely an adventure game can be cut a little bit of slack in that regard, right? Yes? No? Well, anyway. It felt much more like I was in control than in other TellTale Games of recent memory.
But even if it didn't, Tales From The Borderlands has a great storyline anyway (in my opinion). Told from the perspective of two fairly different characters who, through various circumstances/fate, were thrown into each other's lives and [judging from the fact that they're retelling the story] lived to tell about it. There's more to it than that, but it's best to discover in the process of playing the game.
Most games like this, I play over the span of several days, maybe an episode a day; sometimes taking as long as a week. But this game was so engaging, so amusing, and so action-packed that I played it from start to finish in less than 48 hours. And I enjoyed (almost) every minute of it. (There are a few tedious moments, and the "hit this button rapidly" moments do get annoying at times, but they're a small price to pay to get to the other portions.
The TellTale engine isn't getting any younger, but the Borderlands graphic style works with this really well. (Or badly, if you strongly dislike the Borderlands visual style.) There are some plot elements that benefit from knowledge of some of the basics of Borderlands [the existence of megacorp Heilos, and its murderous founder Handsome Jack], but it's not strictly necessary and the game does a fairly decent job bringing people up to speed. There are some Easter eggs that only Borderlands players would get, but everything works without having to pick up on those.
I always felt that tongue-in-cheek humor was TellTale's forte, and this episodic series reconfirms my opinion. There are dramatic moments, even some vaguely "emotional" moments, but for the most part it's witty, goofy, sarcastic, and clever. I don't want to oversell it, but it's the only game I've actually laughed out loud at in I don't know how long.
Also, Patrick Warburton voices an antagonist, which is just awesome. Even if it did feel weird to hear Brock Samson's voice coming out of someone who isn't Brock Samson.
Anyway... it was a fun little game, and if you can get it on sale or as part of a bundle or some sort, so much the better.
Enjoy! And try not to get killed too much.

I shouldn't be surprised. Any time I hear that Telltale is tackling a new franchise, I inevitably think "wait...that one? No way it will be good! What are they thinking?!" And then its inevitably really good, amazing even. This is not the case here. No, Tales from the Borderlands is not good nor amazing. Those words are not strong enough to describe what Tales from the Borderlands is. This game is nothing short of some of the best fiction out there period.
What they managed to do here was nothing short of a miracle. Borderlands is a series known for its shooting and its guns, because it proudly advertises it has eleventy squillion guns. Tales from the Borderlands is another of Telltale Games' signature blend of point and click adventure game/choose your own adventure/visual novel. Inbetween all of those choices and point and click adventuring you get hit with a lot of quick time events, and due to Telltale Games' sorcery, these are
Exciting? Yes while Telltale has had their signature blend for a good while, they keep improving on it and that formula is at its absolute best here. For the rest of time they could make no further improvements to the formula and they would be good. Its not particularly challenging, but it is really fun.
But how does it feel as a Borderlands game? Well its...almost better than the actual games? For the first game and the Pre-sequel, that's not a very high bar, but for modern classic Borderlands 2? If its not better, its certainly on equal standing. That's because while it retains the proper feel of a Borderlands game, Telltale games' influence can also be felt in the most natural way possible. Gone is the reliance on dank memes, replaced with grade AAA+++ writing that had me dying of laughter on more than one occasion. Alternatively things would take a turn for the dramatic as I start crying like a little girl. All of this possible thanks to some of the best character writing I have witnessed in any medium. I cared what happened to these characters more than I care what happens to actual people. Seeing the ones I loved be happy and have good things happen to them filled me with joy, seeing the ones I hate die horribly filled me with grim satisfaction.

After completing the outstanding 'Bionic Commando: Rearmed', I was eager to see if Grin, the developer, could transfer the swing mechanic into the third-dimension. 8 hours later to beat the game on Hard difficulty, I can confirm they did. No other game does it better, not even the Spider-Man games. There is a learning curve due to the free-form nature of the swing mechanic. But once you master it - once you grasp where to attach your grapple, know what point in your swing trajectory to detach your grapple, understand which direction to shift your weight to, and think far ahead to identify your next two or three grapple points - once you master all that will you truly feel like a "rad" Bionic Commando.
The swing mechanic also integrates with the combat fluidly. You swing around to avoid bullets, lasers, missiles and other projectiles all while getting into angles that will allow you to strike the enemy at their most vulnerable side. The enemies are usually a mix of airborne and ground units which presents a plethora of challenging scenarios and opportunities for badass maneuvers. Your arsenal is primarily the usual shooter-game affair except for this one move where you latch on an enemy with your grapple, zip towards them at high speeds and kick their face in. Swing, zip-kick, swing, shoot, swing, zip-kick, shoot, swing, shoot, and so on and so forth at different enemies without ever touching the ground. When you have a chain going, it's beautiful.
Unfortunately, there are a good number of areas where the fight is too focused on the ground. You can still swing, but since most of the enemies in those areas are infantry units and sometimes there isn't much room to swing or there are too few surfaces to grapple onto, the game feels less like Bionic Commando and more like an average third-person shooter. Also, the fact that you can't zoom your gun while swinging despite being able to do so on foot means half of your bullets are likely going to miss when going for fancy shoot/swing combos. It encourages the separation of combat and swinging when the game is at its best when the two are merged seamlessly together. Thankfully the game is at its best majority of the time.
Now moving on to the artistic aspects. Before the game was released, a graphic novel was made available called 'Bionic Commando: Chain of Command' (which I was still able to find via Google search). It sets up the game's plot and promised an exploration of the theme of human enhancement - using bionics beyond a "cure" for physical disabilities. Well, the game's story squandered that opportunity (although the story is still passable by gaming standards). The score, however, is an amazing modern interpretation of the 8-bit original.
Finally, the multiplayer. There is nothing much to say. I've never tried it since the population is virtually nil. I would imagine Capture The Flag would be awesome with the game's unique traversal system. If you're reading this and know others that are interested, we should get a game going (though we have to use Hamachi or Tunngle since Capcom dropped their servers).

This game reviewed badly.
The press hated it, and the community didn't get it.
The story was gaped at and lambasted as being one of the worst in gaming.
It caused the death of its development studio, Grin.
And yet, it's still one of my favourite games.
Originally, I bought this when it came out on PS3, having thoroughly enjoyed Bionic Commando: Re-Armed.
I didn't read any reviews, and trusted in Grin to deliver a cracking bionic experience, and they delivered in spades.
It's all about the arm you see; you CAN play it as a straight-up third-person shooter with occasional swingy bits, but to do so is to miss the point entirely.
You should be swinging, punching and throwing at every opportunity. You should be concentrating on evading the enemy through being a target that's impossible to hit.
You should be damn good if you're to get the most out of this game.
And that's what people didn't get; they were fooled by how it looked and were expecting a more open experience. So they played it as such and moaned when they didn't get much out of it in return.
Bionic Commando is a linear game, and it makes no bones about it. It's not trying to be an open-world roamer; it's giving you a series of tightly packed scenarios to let loose upon as you see fit, encouraging you to experiment as much as possible with the sublime tool it's giving you.
And boy, does it reward good play; it has the best use of an achievement system I've come across, even better than Dead Rising (although it definitely took a few queues from there).
Under all other circumstances, I hate achievement systems; they're poorly implemented checklists of things you're likely to do anyway most of the time.
Yet here, the achievement system rewards you in game as well as with achievement points (less noticeable on the PC where they're simply challenges and the subsequent rewards without the Steam achievements).
Manage to kill 3 grunts with one grenade? Congrats, have an upgrade to the amount of nades you can carry!
Taken out 3 grunts with one grenade launcher shot? Aces, your grenade launcher radius is improved!
And each completed challenge may lead to another, more difficult one, meaning you'll scout out opportunities while playing the levels that'll let you complete those challenges. It's rewarding you for excellent play in the best way possible, and never completely overpowered.
On top of this, you have an incredibly well realised vision of a city hit with a recent disaster of apocalyptic scale and some of the best music in gaming. The first encounter with Polycraft, BC's flying mech suits, is a particular early game highlight, with a dramatic, pulse-quickening tune driving your emotions higher as you swing between buildings kicking robot suits out of the air.
It's exhilirating, and makes you realise that BC is one of the best "Super-hero" games out there.
Many games that claim to be about more traditional super-heroes end up feeling flat and distinctly non-super, but BC at its best outclasses them all.
It's about larger-than-life caricatures, ridiculous technologies, moustache-twiddling conspiracies and ♥♥♥♥ing sweet bionic♥♥♥♥♥♥
Oh, and swinging like a loon through a post-apocalyptic city while Mike Patton hollers like a howler-monkey on cocaine.
It's not without its flaws, and could really have done with a little longer in development. Being able to revisit earlier levels with some of the sweet unlocks from later in the game would have been nice; a New Game + a la Demon's / Dark Souls would have been fantastic.
But ♥♥♥♥ it. This is a near-perfect slice of third-person arcade action, bombastically delivered by people who had an obvious love for the source material.
Age and SSDs has also given it that wonderful Meatboy instant restart feel, positively encouraging you to fail, so that one time in 100 you'll pull off something so incredibly sweet you'll punch the air then sadly realise you don't have an awesome bionic arm like Spencer in real life.
Well, you can't have a bionic arm.
But you CAN have Bionic Commando.
Buy it.

You can actually see the casualization of the series: the most deep one is Exile escape from the pit where you had food management (you could die of starvation), a 6 members party, more weapon variation and a lot of spells.
Avernum 1 is more streamlined and simplified version in a good way: you have a simplified conversation mechanic (no need to guess the right word to type anymore like in Ultima or king's quest), most of the useful skills are still there but it lacks the 6 party people which gave you the option of specialization to each character (a swordsman,a spearman,a blunt weapon user, a rogue that uses ranged weapons, a mage and a priest) and tou had less spells.
Avernum escape from the pit is bad.....the story is still there (and it’s a good story!!....because it’s the same story for the 3rd time) but it dropped the skill system for a skill tree (why??), the food management aspect which gives more depth is gone (in Avernum 1 you had to be careful where you rest and in the second game where you took the journey to the Vahnatai lands you had to make stops in order to scavenge for food because you always lose some in the waterfalls), some of the useful skills like poisoning are gone, less weapon variation (no one handed spear, no rock throwing, no arrows, no clubs), even less spells, you cannot bash doors and alchemy? Forget it because you need to find alchemist in a town to do this for you and there are no recruitable NPCs...and death has no consequences because youer dead party members revive when entering a friendly town for free unlike in avernum 1 and exile where you had to pay a priest to revive them for a huge sum.
Exile is still my all-time favorite because of the RPG elements (but sadly I need to emulate win 3.1x to play this or get a windows XP machine), Avernum 1 is a very good remake and escape from the pit......no just no, it's bad compared to the originals - a real casualized version for phones and iPads.
If it would have kept the skill system and spells from Avernum 1 at least then I would have given it a good review but as it is…. it's too dumbed down compare to the other versions.
Play Avernum 1, you can still buy it on GOG (AVERNUM: THE COMPLETE SAGA)

This game isn't per se bad, but it is very obvious that it's been made by one guy with a vision and no knowledge on game design.(do note that the developer states that the game is finished except for some bugs)
There are multiple flaws in how the game works, a few examples would be:
- There is a rebirth system, but the rewards are very minimal and extremly expensive. With an idle game you expect each run to go twice as far.... rebirthing here feels useless.
- The scaling of costs is insane while there is no scaling in generation of recourses. And like mentioned before the rebirth won't really solve this enough.
- There is a lot of important info missing that you really need, for example. Before you choose your regligion and be stuck with that for the run it would be nice to actually see the benefits.
- At one point your gold recourse literally generates a milion times more then your other recources. So you'll be ignoring leveling these recourses completly and resort to the trading market to convert your gold to these recources.
I can go on but I think you get the gist. (I might discover some stuff that debunks some of my statements, but that will only go back to the point of missing information)
The game is a bit fun if you are really into idle games (which I am). But I would never recommend it to others as it simple holds too many flaws over the slight increased depth it holds. Also this depth becomes nothing more then an automated system you a couple of times a day before you close it again. You don't have to think if you know where to click.

This is an enjoyable game and I do recommend it.
Pro:
1: It sticks to what made the anime enjouable and lets you share in the epic fights of the series.
2: Character creator. Deviant Art online
3: Huge number of abilities in the game
4: Play as your favorite characters in your favorite forms
5: The gameplay is just fun

1: The DLC are all uninspired and uninteresting. The only positive thing really to come from them is the retcon removing GT as a continuation of Dragon Ball Z. Even Res of F gives a very small amount of content.

The games main characters voice annoyed me in every dialog.  Titan Lords is an easy game to play.  The combat felt over simplified. One of the best Dragon Ball Z games in recent memory, Xenoverse expands on the best feature of Ultimate Tenkaichi (and the only good feature, depending on who you talk to) by providing a character customization function and an original story to play through. As much as people who grew up watching the series may love it, you can only do the story so many times before it gets old. Xenoverse manages to spice up the experience by altering key events and giving you a new focal villain to deal with.
Those who are fans of the previous Dimps DBZ games such as the Budokai series will sadly feel a bit let down. While the gameplay is fun and can get very frantic, it embraces the 3D flying aspects of more recent games than the traditional 2D pure fighting game style that their games were praised for. If you are looking for a strict fighting game, Xenoverse is not that. It is a fun experience, but it is not what some people were looking for.
Now that the server issues cleared up from launch, the game runs solidly, though I have experienced server hiccups still. Sometimes in-game connections can get spotty, and I have had a few missions end up with everyone swinging at an invincible Krillin as the server struggles to realign everyone. Despite this, I still recommend it to anyone who enjoys the series and wants a fun time making their notebook OCs into a reality.

As my first foray into Telltale Games' "interactive storybook" style games, my expectations certainly weren't high. Having received it as a birthday present, I had in fact procrastinated for 4 months before finally deciding to play it in a bout of boredom.
I was hooked instantly, jumping from episode to episode right to the much awaited conclusion.
Incredible storytelling with characters that grow and change as the story progresses (or "development", as some might call it), consistently pleasant (and at times stunning) visuals, top-notch voice acting and an authentic Borderlands soundtrack to wrap it all together.
At times thrilling and exciting, at some hilariously witty and at others tragic and bleak, the story was masterfully crafted and engaging throughout. While there were a few weak segments in the story and pacing that felt either slightly draggy or rushed at times, they were few and far between.
All in all, this title gets the highest of recommendations from me. Even to those who have their qualms about getting something that could hardly pass as a "game", just think of it as an well-written interactive storybook where you get to make some dialogue and key story decisions.

A memorable, explorable piece of dreamlike atmosphere, Proteus articulates an essence of each of the four seasons with joy, loss and sadness.
★★★★☆
Immediately defined on the surface with its' soft, comforting colour palette and a distinctively blocky impression of an inhabited island, Proteus quickly captures the attention and brings to life a lush, fertile playground. Trees sway periodically in an autumn breeze. Snow gently falls to the ground as overbearing grey clouds loom overhead. Bunnies hop away to a brief tune as you approach - and soon chase - them. All of this accompanied by an indulgent and evocative soundtrack that perfectly accompanies you on your meandering voyage across this landscape. There's the faint sound of bagpipes, perhaps, as you close in on what appears to be abandoned castle. An almost military-like instrumentation joins you when you find yourself in what seem to be clusters of gravestones, positing the idea that maybe, in a day past, this island now inhabited by wildlife was also home to a human community.
What someone will actually get out of Proteus is ultimately down to the player - and whether this is a strength of the experience or to its' detriment, I'm not sure. There will be countless players who either don't care for the idea of a piece like this that all but completely strips back mechanical interference, or who just don't enjoy what Proteus has to offer. However, in the right frame of mind, at the right time of day, in the right mood, Proteus hits a nerve and relaxes it, eases it, and offers an experience unlike much else. One that is almost inherently and necessarily short, but utterly memorable and worth the attention of those seeking a very pure form of escaping to another place and, indeed, other times.

If you fancy playing a decent 2D platformer, consider putting Trial By Vikings somewhere near the top of your shopping list!
This review is also available, incl video, on :
Style
With both visual style and gameplay mechanics reminiscent of The Bitmap Brothers’ 1991 game GODS (Into The Wonderful), Last Life Games’s developers may have been inspired by the old classic, but have clearly modernised both aspects to stay more up-to-date with development in gaming.


Where GODS put you in the leathery footwear of Hercules, with a Greek pantheon to address, Trial By Vikings heads north and into Norse and Germanic mythology. You play as a viking who looks like a cousin to Erik the Swift from The Lost Vikings (1992), taking on the jotun Loki and his minions across a set of nine realms, created by Loki and seeming quite unlike the original ones.


Story
Loki has, we learn, destroyed the sunstone, and scattered it across his new realms, and our fearless viking is chosen by the Alföðr (aka Odin) to collect these and restore order.
Oddly enough, you can use these sun-stones to trade for upgraded equipment; You were meant to get them for Odin, but end up bartering them away for faster shoes, better axes, and grappling hooks. Whether this is in trade with Odin, or if you’re handing them off to a 3rd party despite your initial deal with the Allfather, is left unsaid.


The game does manage several nods towards various elements of Norse Mythology, though with a few liberties, that may or may not irk some people. An early example in the game has Níðhöggr the dragon portrayed as a winged, fire-spewing lizard, when dragons in the Eddas are closer to ground-based, or subterranean, serpents with poison or acid, though one reference does state that Níðhöggr can fly.
The wolf Fenrir is naturally also included in the game, being it is a son of Loki, but visually it seems closer to later revisions of the Greek hell-hound of Cerberus with its 3 heads.
Of course deviations from old mythology is nothing to get too worked up about, or I’d be busy writing about Marvel’s “interpretations”.


Controls
Controls are separated into their own section here as they can be make or break in a game like this and in this one they feel a bit slippery and awkward.
The first thing you’ll notice is it uses a slightly odd combination of WASD and arrow-keys, but you can remap these easily to e.g. a controller. Yes, I recommend you find an old controller and use that instead of keyboard, even if you’re used to the latter.
The initial introduction level seems simple enough, and controlling the main character seems easy, but soon it feels as if some ice has been added to the floors, and you skid a little bit after jumps, making landing on ledges slightly very frustrating.
There is also a spirit-rolling-maneuver, which is initiated by pushing forward twice – this is an ingenious setup, as it means you’ll drop off edges if you try inching forward step-by-step.
Puzzles
The game presents all the usual puzzles and mechanics (rotating big gears and stacking boxes), and a few novel ones (Polar bear!), and while they are usually trivial enough, there are cases where the controls seemingly freak out and the box you were pushing starts flying through the air.
Some of the puzzles seem designed to be revisited once you have bought the required gear, while others are very in-your-face about how to solve them immediately.


There are 130 levels in the game, across 13 areas and with 27 boss battles, so some repetition should be expected, but the game still manages keep things varied through most of this. Level design is generally good, but there are places bound to frustrate you simply because the ways it can be failed.


Overall
Trail By Viking is definitely a little gem, with a decent amount of playtime and value for money at the usual 15 Euro, especially if you’re into single-player 2D platformers and puzzle games. The save-game mechanics let you stop and restart on any level already visited, so even taking a longer break is not a problem; just go back a few levels to get into the groove again.
The graphics are clear, though music is a bit underdeveloped. Sound effects are simple and to the point, but the game could perhaps do with some Voice Over for the story-parts.

Let me tell you my tale...
I was given a key to review this game, but I only take keys for games I am at least 80% sure I will enjoy.
As someone who is not a huge fan of platformers(at least not since the "console golden age") I am pleased to still be able to recommend this game. It has a unique premise and interesting level designs. There's a LOT of content (over 130 individual levels in 9 worlds) and I've barely scratched the surface.
The levels I played are certainly challenging but not unfair like other platformers I have played.The controls are not exactly intuitive; there is a chance to change them before you start the game at the "Input" screen but it would be great if there was an in-game option with a screen showing a controller or keyboard and being able to change each key individually. I often ended up using the keyboard to jump and the controller to control the direction but with practice it is achievable. There's no mistake that it is worth the practice, either.Your viking will likely slide around a bit as well.
The graphics harken back to an era when games like Castlevania Dracula X and Super Metroid were all the rage, for good reason. I cannot speak for the developers intent but I like to imagine he was writing a bit of a love letter to those classics.
Before you start a level you're able to choose from a variety of main and sub-weapons as well as passive bonus items. You will be able to upgrade these with Sun-stones collected during each level. There are health potions, "mini-viking" potions, invulnerability potions and more, typical fare for a platformer of this type.
The story is obviously influenced by Norse mythology although very loosely. I say this as someone who owns academic copies of the Heimskringla, The Icelandic Sagas, and the Younger and Elder Eddas, among other books about the subject.The monsters are stalwarts of fantasy games(kobolds, orcs, and wyverns for instance) and there are dragons, kraken, and other legendary boss monsters.
Overall I give this 3.5  axes out of 5.I will definitely be playing this game to the end.
Oh also...vikings did not wear horned helmets.

After 25+ hours of playing this on normal, I'd say this is a very good, almost great game. My attention span for games seems to be around 15-20 hours but this kept me interested the whole time, up through about level 103 out of 130. And I'd still be playing it if it weren't for the dark holes.
They are not fun. At all. They are like gravity holes that suck you in and spin you around them. They are highly annoying and hard to escape without falling to your death. It was a ton of fun for the first 100 levels but I lost interest after fighting dark holes for 30 minutes.
Honestly, I almost think the game is *too* long. 100 levels and a bit faster upgrades would be better, imo. The upgrades are nice and for the most part keep you motivated, but I fell behind in the "passive" upgrades. I then came to a level that you apparently need one of the passives to get all the gems. I will have to complete 10+ levels and not upgrade anything else before I can go back and finish that one. So...don't do that.
The levels also get progressively more elaborate and a few of them in the 90's got a bit tedious, but the level design overall is very good.
Movement is defintely not perfect, but it's workable once you get the hang of it. It can be a bit frustrating at times, like when you need to jump through a one-character high hole.
The boss fights are mostly on the easy side. A couple of them took 4-5 tries but most were 1 or 2 tries.
Overall, it is a very fun game that is worth the price even if you end up wimping out at the dark holes as I have. I will probably go back and finish it at some point but even if I don't it was money well spent.

As a fan of retro RPGs, I can think of few that take place in a world as expansive as Avernum.  I originally played it back when it was called Exile, before the revamp that gave it a tutorial level, made sure you couldn't leave the first town without knowing about the free supplies, updated the graphics (including work by Phil Foglio!), and dropped the party from six members down to four (the part I am saddest about; having a six-person custom party was sweeeeet).
The number of hours I spent exploring just the first portion of the game would be enough to fill a regular game by themselves.  Maybe it's just my play style, but I doubt you could get to the original's Shareware Demon if you weren't by that time ready to play through the rest of the game -- I still consider that the best form of shareware I've ever seen.
And the world-building within that area was astounding.  The idea of living in a giant cave, and how it would affect the citizens, was richly explored, down to the type of farming (mushrooms) and livestock (giant lizards).  The political in-fighting was interesting without being overbearing; it comments here and there on modern issues through the types of people who got tossed in the pit.  The monsters had some variety to them (not, perhaps, as much as more modern games) and the way the combat flows from the environment is really appealing (there's Fight and Peace states, but the fights happen within the place you're at, not in a separate screen).  There's a lot of loot, including bits of trash and such to make the world more immersive; there's little bits of story everywhere.  And although the character-customization options seem to have been streamlined (reduced), there's still plenty of ways to make a unique team.
If you're up for an old-school RPG with a very large world to explore, do give this one a try.

Amazing game. I'm sure many of you here already own this on a console and pretty much know what the game is all about. So I won't waste my breath here regurgitating all the much-deserved praise this game has already received for being a beautiful and fantastic story and its masterful art. You already know that you want this game, and you already know that you will love it. All you want to know now is really: Should I go invest in a controller? Will my computer run this?
The answer is yes and no. Yes you MUST invest in a controller for this game, there is no way around it. Get yourself something you'll be comfortable, I use my 360 controllers, because this isn't the only game you'll ever need one for. And the 2nd answer is no, because this game is a port it's uber poorly optimized. I have a 1200p monitor and I was extremely confident in my PC running the game full resolution with 2x anti-aliasing. Quickly my PC told me to go ♥♥♥♥ myself because YES - THIS IS APPARANTLY HARDER TO RUN THAN BATTLEFIELD 4! So - this being a fighting game and all - you are shooting for 60 solid fps, so you will need to turn your resolution down to 720p and don't even bother with that anti-aliasing crap.
Still on the same topic - the game looks fantastic no matter what, just do everything in your power to keep it ~60fps because if you don't then the animations will all slow down accordingly (30 fps will slow the game down to 1/2 the speed). Just trust me - this will look much sharper on your PC than your console even in 720p with no anti aliasing and that actually made it a more enjoyable experience and worth picking it up a 2nd time!

What could be a fun game ruined by a really bad port.
I'm not really a fan of the Naruto Manga/Anime but I always enjoyed the games, for some reason Naruto (as well as DBZ) games always seemed to range from decent to top notch. So I saw this game on sale, and I decided to pick it up.
I can tell it's not a bad game, but holy hell it's a very bad port. Let us make a list on important features it's missing
-No Graphic Options other than Screen Size (made the game nearly unplayable for me).
-Game has no PC controls, you have to make them yourself.
-Even if you put them in, the game still shows the Xbox control promps.
I heard it was a bad port, but...not this bad.

Edit: A more serious review of this game is that it is a fantastically bland looking generic game that has a wealth of depth in what you can pull off and put your time into for the game.
I've never experienced a game that made me feel like I could do as much as I could playing this and nowadays despite the age of the game getting to itself if you can look past the janky buggy movement and gameplay you'll see the charm it holds.
A more serious note on progression of this game is that it is surprisingly not that Pay2Win formula other reviews tend to give you a whole plethora of new player friendly content is out to ease the transition and the most you would ever feel encouraged to spend on is a mount or a pet for extra storage. The one argument that can made is that all the tools to make oneself into a stronger and steamrolling character exist but to feasibly pull this off would require hundreds if not more of real life money to pull off.
If you ever plan on making it far in this game please be aware that the game treats skills and advancing as a slow more methodical approach with being consistent about your intentions to raise and level which can turn some people off if they're too used to MMO's since progression is more usually linked to gear/level progression.

TL;DR at the bottom
This game follows the DBZ storyline, but with a twist. A distortion in time has occured, and you must be the one to stop it. You will be summoned by Trunks, and the story revolves around your custom-made character. I have seen many comments on the combat, and how it seems shallow. I don't really agree with this, though, as I found the combat to be rather fun. You can choose to button-smash, but if you have skills and timing, you can get a long way. A controller is highly advised though, as it makes everything easier.
PROS:
- Interesting story
- Lots of skills and clothes
- RPG-elements
- You don't have to purchase the DLC, but it's a nice addition.
- Custom characters (!!)
- Parallel quests
- Masters you can train under (Frieza, #18, Cell and many more!)
- Multiplayer is fairly stable now
- Collecting Dragon Balls can be grindy, but summoning Shenron and wishing, definitely makes it worthwhile ;)
CONS:
- I highly recommend a controller. I had a hard time playing with keyboard & mouse.
- Tokitoki city is pretty big, and you have to walk around to each seperate booth to get things going.
- Lacks some characters (Zarbon, Dodoria, #16 and the likes)
- The DLC doesn't add a whole lot, yet is expensive (25 euros for season pass)
- I found the Great Apes to be a bit clunky, but I suppose it is understandable with those huge models.
- You have to grind levels quite a lot
- Combat is pretty simple, and I understand why passionate fighting-genre fans would find it shallow. I enjoy it, nonetheless.
TL;DR:
If you are a fan of Dragon Ball, you will most likely enjoy this game (get a controller, though!)
If you are a fan of the fighting genre, and want in-depth combat, you should probably look elsewhere.

This game hasn't updated in so long, and honestly, it needs to do so.
What you have here is a much different clicker experience. It's really like Adventure communist (which this came before btw) in that you have multiple different resources, but unlike that, each building costs a specific resource, but each one you can alsi immdeiately gather manually. Only, one resource you cannot gather, is population, which also must be allocated between each resource in order to idly gather it. Population requires food, and room, whihc is increased via houses.
After building enough structures, you gain the ability to start building an army, which is used for exploration (random bonuses and resources can be gained from these, depending on how many troops or people you send exploring), and raiding NPC villages and towns of varying and scaling difficulty and strength, (for a special resource which you can use to build monuments).
You can prestige by creating a new colony, after doing so, you have Civilization Points which you can use to spend on perks. Standard fare for the most part.
The game itself is pretty good, it's a nice breath of fresh air from the somewhat monotony that clicker games essentially are suffering from (what with the clones of clicker heroes which barely have any difference and all).
Things it could help to have added:
- Multiplayer Raids
- Some kind of Guild system where you launch joint-attacks on massive fortresses for special artifacts with help from other players.
- Tougher NPC towns for when you have literally thousands of Templars
- NPC Towns that scle based on the number of Colonies you've built.
- NPC Raids upon your town, Walls are basically useless. Or more tougher raids.
- Leaderboards.
Right now, I can't recommend the game as I just have no interest in it right now. Sadly, it doesn't have much in the way of end-game content and is a bit incomplete for hte time being. With any hope, it'll get updated more with more content, features, but right now, just don't bother.
If I gave a rating, I'd give it a 5/10 honestly. It's intersting, but has very little here as far as clicker games go.

I didn't think Tales from the Borderlands would work as a Telltale game.  I played The Walking Dead and I thought that was the best way to present a story-based game -- life or death situations.  Not that TFTB doesn't give you tough decisions, but I thought the humor of Borderlands would return it to a too simplistic game without impact.
First though, I'd like to say that if you feel that these aren't real games and just Quicktime events, I'm not going to persuade you to buy this game.  But if you like Borderlands and if you've enjoyed games like The Walking Dead from Telltale, then this game is a good fit for you.
I really enjoyed this game.  There are so many entertaining characters, whether they are the main characters, supporting cast, or villians.  I was unsure about controlling two different main characters before playing, but this really worked welll in Tales.   It was entertaining to play as either main character (though the control usually changes as a part of the story and not by choice).  I never thought that either main character was a weaker part of the story.
I didn't get some of the Borderlands references since I had only finished the first game before playing Tales (I finished Borderlands 2 after this game), but it didn't really take away from the game. The story and characters are good enough that it won't matter if you don't get references to past Borderlands games.
If you like Telltale games and haven't played this one, then you're missing out on what I think is the best Telltale game yet.
