NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Trial by Viking is a two-dimensional platform game with puzzle elements set in the worlds of Viking mythology.
You play a bearded Viking, referred to mostly as "Me", who looks a lot like a Lord-of-the-Rings-style Dwarf. At the beginning of the game you are shown a brief cut scene in which you hack down a dragon and are visited by Odin, who requires your help in tracking down and defeating Loki. Never shying from such a heroic task, you accept and Odin teleports you off to the first world.
So begins what looks like a rather long platform game of 13 realms, each with a number of 'constructs' (levels), through which you must progress and reclaim as many pieces of the stolen and shattered Sunstone as you can.
You wield your large battle axes (of which you have an unlimited supply) with great strength as you leap a little awkwardly around from platform to platform, slaying enemies, flicking switches, drinking potions, teleporting, and performing various other platforming feats, all while collecting Sunstone shards.
Graphics - The in-game graphics are good, with an appealing and consistent style that is easy on the eye and doesn't detract from your tasks. I do find some breakable objects tend to blend in to the background a little, but that's only a minor inconvenience, quickly overcome once I worked out what they were.
The common Unity pre-game graphics option and control settings launcher is displayed when you first run the game, with the usual resolution and full screen / windowed options, as well as the typical detail settings from Fastest through to Beautiful and Fantastic. I'm not sure what the settings actually change, however, as the game ran perfectly smoothly on my gaming laptop in full HD and the highest detail.
Sound - Music is 'large' and theatrical, building up to crescendos at appropriate times and fading away into the background at others. It's well done, if a little loud in its default configuration, tending to drown out the sound effects. Sound effects are good, doing their job without showing off.
There is some voice work for the main character, which is actually pretty well done, but it's only used in very few situations. This actually makes it seem a bit out of place; I think it would have been better to be removed completely, or expanded and used everywhere -- or at least in all of the cut scenes.
Gameplay - The heart of a platform game, in my opinion, is in the gameplay, and Trial by Viking doesn't let the player down. The many levels all have the same goal: to collect as many Sunstone pieces as possible and make it to the exit. But the platforming skills, combat reflexes, and mild puzzle-solving required in each level add up quickly to make even some of the levels in the first world quite tricky to finish perfectly. The addition of occasional 'boss levels' is appreciated, if somewhat expected, and the bosses themselves add a welcome distraction to the pure platforming levels.
You control your Viking using WASD with the left hand to control left and right movement, crouching, and zooming the camera out for a better look at the level around you; and the arrow keys with the right hand to control weapon attacks (melee, ranged, and sub-weapon), as well as jumping. It takes a bit to get used to, and even after an hour of play I found myself occasionally missing a jump and falling to my doom due to pressing the wrong key. The Steam page says the game has partial controller support, which may be preferable. Alternatively, remapping the keys to something a bit more intuitive is probably worthwhile.
The game also has various upgrades available to you for Sunstone shards, and you can also find some new abilities while playing. There are five difficulty levels, but no explanation given as to the differences between them, which seems to be a bit of an oversight.
There are a couple of little niggles, like two-handed keyboard control being required while playing, but having to use the mouse to advance the story dialogs, and I think that the main character is a little too 'slippery', reminding me a little of Superfrog at speed, which doesn't seem quite appropriate for a bearded Dwarf-like Viking. And the story itself, while mostly well, but fairly simply written, does have some grammatical errors and rather too many ellipses... .
Pros:
+ Interesting setting and story, which is mostly well presented
+ Appealing graphics and atmospheric music
+ Achievements and trading cards
Cons:
- The main character has a little too much inertia, and not enough friction, making some platforming more frustrating than it should be
- Minor inconvenience with the default keyboard controls and mouse being required for story progression
- Some errors in the writing
- Voice acting is minimal, standing out at odd times
Don't take the fact that I've listed more cons than pros above as an indication that this game is bad. The cons are really very minor, with the exception of the frustration due to the character's inertia and slipperiness, coupled with the unintuitive control scheme, which have caused me to replay some levels far more times than I care to remember.
No, Trial by Viking is a solid platform game that shouldn't disappoint anyone who enjoys the genre. It's well presented and mostly fun, with plenty of content and no bugs to speak of. I'm very happy to recommend it. Just be prepared to take some deep breaths.

Summary: Gunpoint is a highly engaging 2D spy puzzle game with some very unique gameplay mechanisms, rewarding players for thinking through and innovative, but without constricting the player to a set path. The game focuses mainly on two major mechanics: the ability to jump (and land safely) at extreme heights and the ability to crosswire switches throughout the game. There are additional upgrades that can be purchased throughout the story, but they can easily be passed over but they can add some extra flavor to how you approach a level. Overall, I would highly recommend the game and put it at a 4/5.
For me an engaging storyline is essential for a great game, there needs to be something pushing you to the next level, to find the next laptop or computer, and connect you with the characters involved. Gunpoint isn't going to change your life, but the storyline is easily identifiable, namely you play a freelance spy that is contracted to investigate a high-profile murder that you witness and have to work with a cast of employers to find out who was responsible. The script was well done and the ability to choose from a pre-set list of dialogue options gives the perception that you have the ability to affect the plot. There is a point where you can choose from two employers and it may seem like it makes a big difference, but honestly all paths will lead to the same conclusion, level, boss fight, etc. But honestly, it doesn't bother me and everything was well-done and fits perfectly with the noir-esque atmosphere that the game projects.
The gameplay mechanics really boil down to two concepts, which involves jumping and crosswiring circuits. The player is equipped from the very beginning with "Bullfrog Pants," which allows you to jump at incredible heights, crash through windows, and pounce on guards with relative ease. You don't have to worry about dying from a long fall and in many ways you can crash through a level that was designed to use finesse by just timing your jumps well and disabling guards before they become an issue. The second element, the crosswiring of circuits is introduced about 1/4 into the game. This will allow you to change the function of a circuit and allow you to progress further into a level. Is there an Enforcer blocking your path?  Well you can crosswire that power outlet next to him to shock him and knock him out. This element was clearly designed for the player to exercise finesse, to carefully consider what the secondary effects are of opening that door with a lightswitch, or will the guard open a door when walking through a body sensor and get you killed? With an autosave feature that can trace back the last 1-15 seconds before a death or using a manual save, it gives you a lot of flexibility, is pretty forgiving (which makes the game more accessible for casual players), and allows for experimentation.
Now my biggest complaint about the game is length, it is remarkably short and just on my first playthrough it took me roughly 2.5 hours. This includes a couple replays of a few early missions, carefully reading the dialogue, and even playing through all the training missions. On my first playthrough I received about 1/2 of the achievements and I thought, hell, might as well see if I can get more. So including the second playthrough it took me a total of 4.5 hours and I was able to get all 42 achievements without any real strain. For a game to take 4.5 hours to play through twice and achieve everything set out makes it obvious to me (at least) that the content is limited. There is a level editor and I'm sure there is a community that is churning out maps to fans, but the developer content should have had more levels, missions, and clientele. There is some limited replayability for the game, midway and until the final level, there are probably dozens of ways to tackle it. But it's the same level, same enemies, same mission, same locations for all items. This is also worth mentioning, but puzzle games usually don't do well with replayability, because once you've solved it, then every subsequent playthrough will be very similar to the last.
The final section I'll discuss is the music and sound effects, which for me I thought was well-done but nothing too noticeable. Granted, the music was probably composed to add a dark, noir feel to the world rather than detracting from it with rock ballads and an electric orchestra churning out pop hits. So my feelings about it are probably in line with the intent, it's there and barely noticeable. It really won't affect your gaming experience, both in a positive and negative way.
So in conclusion, pick up the game if it's on sale or if you're looking for something fun and easy to get into. The replayability is low, almost atrociously for a game that retails for $10, but there is potential to elongate your playtime with a robust level editor and the diversity in your methods to tackle each level. I think if the campaign was doubled, had a few more gameplay functions thrown in, it would easily be a masterpiece, but considering how limited the main game is I'm reviewing it as a 4/5.

Avernum: Escape from the pit is a remake of the first game in the Avernum series. It is a grid, turn based CRPG with sandbox elements.
The plot is straight forward. On the surface there is the empire, ruled by the mad king hawthorn, a cruel dictator who rules with an iron fist. Those who go against the empire, or simply earn the ire of anyone in government, are tossed through a portal and left to die on the other side. The portal transports anyone who goes through it down to the depths of the planet, to a massive cave system with no hope of escape. So many people have been sent down there that they have begun to form their own nations as well, but, just because they are able to band together doesn't mean they are safe from the horrors that live down there with them. Your task as the newest exiles? Survive. Survive and do what you can for yourself, and for the underground nations.
Gameplay is easy to understand. Everything is done on a square grid, from exploring the overworld to navigating in combat. Each character has four core stats, followed by talents, then perks. Each core stat effects an aspect of your characters growth. Strength determines how hard you hit with melee weapons and your characters carrying capacity, dexterity determines how likely you are to dodge attacks and how accurate you are with weapons as well as how much damage you deal with ranged weapons, endurance determines how resistant you are to certain status effects and how much health you have, and finally, intelligence determines how much mana you have, how powerful your spells are, and how resistant you are to magic.
Every character has access to the exact same talent tree, allowing them to mix and match what skills they have to create whatever kind of character you want. Most of these talents are passive, but others grant active abilities which are worth investing into. You can put ten points into most talents, at which point you can't dump any more in, which is probably for the best considering at ten points in any skill, the bonuses are astounding. This really gives you the ability to build your own character however you want, from a long range crit machine, to a tank who casts spells.
Then there are the perks, which give minor buffs to certain things, but can also have a pretty big impact on your character depending on which ones you pick. If you use summons alot, you can get a perk that makes them stronger, or if you want to cast more elemental spells, get the perk which makes them work as if they were a level higher.
Combat works in terms of inititive, with the unit with the highest moving first, then the second highest going second and so on. Every unit has a set amount of time units to use during their turn, some actions costing more points than others. It might take one unit to move a single space, but ten to take an attack. You need to carefully position your characters and plan out what abilites your going to use on the many enemies you will encounter throughout your quests.
Speaking of quests, you will encounter many on your travels, most of which are very fun. Granted, they can be as simple as "clear out the fort" or "bring me five bear asses", but few of the quests are exactly the same, and alot of them are actual, lengthy detours from the main quest lines. This really does help make the world feel that much more alive, which brings me to my next point.
Avernum is a rather bland game visually. There are a few interesting things to look at here and there, but for the most part, you are inside a huge cave, with fungus growing around you. Thankfully, you start the game off with a world map, and they went out of their way to design the terrain so that its destinctive enough to be able to navigate based on land marks, like a river or an odd rock formation. While every dungeon uses alot of the same textures (in fact, most of the game does), each one is very different, This is because they designed them in very different layouts, with a wide enough variety of enemies to keep things interesting. The game has no music though, or voice acting, so bring your own music.
With all this said, Avernum was an enjoyable experience for me, the only frustration i got was when i entered areas clearly too high a level for me or i missed that one hidden switch in the wall. The game does a great job of emulating the feeling of a Pen and Paper RPG, even allowing for player choice and, suprisingly, stupidity. It lets you ask really stupid questions, and the answers you'll normally get back can be equally as funny. I suppose thats what this game has, charm. While it isn't unique in terms of setting or has an overly deep, introspective, thought provoking plot. It does have alot of charm, a very well built combat system, a depressing, but hopeful and great plot, and a world that really inspires the desire to explore. The only limits are the walls of the cave.
I would recommend this rpg to anyone who is a fan of old school rpgs, as well as people who enjoy newer things as well, as it has lots of familiar elements, while casting off some of the shackles older games have. If you are a fan of dungeons and dragons, or pathfinder, this is definitely an rpg you will enjoy, and possibly get some new ideas from.

Trial by Viking
2D Puzzle Platformer
Last Life Games
Last Life Games
is a 2D action puzzle platformer developed and published by Last Life Games.
Set in a world with Norse mythology, you play as a viking who has to help Odin fight the evil god Loki. During the story, you will be able to make some choices that will alter the ending of the game.
The story itself is nothing to write home about, it's pretty standard stuff. But I did like that, for once, we got to play around with Norse gods, even though many monsters are not inspired from Norse mythology and they feel kinda generic.
Made with the Unity engine, the game doesn't look half-bad. The backgrounds and level design are easily the best aspects of the game: there is good variety between each level, and they all feel different. However, the character models look a bit off, like not all of them belong in this game: some are a bit too cartoonish, others are a tad too "realistic". But for the most part it's polished.
Let's just say that this game is not for everyone. It is an hardcore platformer: some levels are more focused on fighting, others more on jumping around, and others on finding keys and beating puzzles. The controls are a bit floaty, meaning that you will slide a little bit when moving the viking, but I got used to it. Your main objective is not only to get to the end of each level, but also to find every sunstone (in-game currency) hidden in the level to buy upgrades for your axe, as well as seconday weapons (bombs, knives) and tools that will help you finish some levels.
The fighting is very weak, and you will mostly rely on ranged combat since it's very hard to avoid getting hit by enemies. Also, I found the game to lack any type of excitment: playing every level felt more like a chore, and after a while I was getting more and more bored. And while many are comparing this to metroidvania games, I (as a huge fan of Symphony of the Night, Guacamelee and Metroid Fusion) don't think this belongs in that genre at all.
The game has a very good difficulty curve, even though it gets very frustrating in the later stages of the game especially in platforming levels due to its controls.
The soundtrack is pretty good and the voice acting (which is kept to a minimum) is pretty good. But the sound effects are very weak, and I am not a fan of the "PUFF" sound when an enemy dies.
Over 100 levels, lots of upgrades, and different choices to make will make you replay this game at least once.
Overall, this is an average platformer that gets more frustrating and less enjoyable as time goes on due to its poor controls and high difficulty. Worth buying to fans of platformers and of Norse mythology; the others should wait for a sale.

You are the viking, a hero who probably wouldn't look out of place in
's Dwarven Kingdom. I mean, just look at that magnificent beard. Anyway, you've been summoned by Odin to rid Asgard of Loki's minions. The story is a standard Norse tale, but the final boss being determined by choices made at pivotal moments in the plot is a nice touch. Oh what am I saying? Not even one paragraph into the review and I'm already talking about the end. So let's step back for just a minute.
Your progress in
is determined not just by being able to reach the end of the 100+ levels. You also have to find sun-crystals. These shiny gems are used to purchase abilities, tools, and weapon-upgrades. This is one of the interesting aspects of this game. Eventually you'll need certain items in order to progress, but there's nothing stopping you from getting them early, in order to make certain levels easier. However, you also have to be considerate of the fact that there are only so many crystals in each level. You can't expect to repeat levels in order to farm them.
Before I start discussing the controls, I want to briefly touch on Super Metroid. As fantastic as this game is, its controls could be considered "floaty" by some people. The jump physics, while extremely flexible, might even frustrate a handful of gamers. I think that this is a unique quality, and the identity it helps create is part of the reason why Super Metroid is so revered.
has controls that are quite different as well, which also gives it an identity of its own. Now if you're thinking that I might be giving this game a little too much credit, by comparing it to a genre-stalwart, then you're probably right.
The Viking in this game moves in a very loose manner. Moving around will take time to get used to, and for some players, the pure-platforming levels are going to be especially difficult. However, this can work to your advantage. If you get some momentum going, you can quickly move past a lot of danger. Also, unlike some other games, taking damage typically won't knock you into the nearest pit. You'll get pushed around, but you have ample time to recover. You might even purposely get hurt just to give yourself a little boost. Oh and even though there are a wealth of spikes in most levels, they don't cause instant-death.
All that said, if you're playing with an Xbox 360 controller, I highly recommend that you change the dead-zone settings.
For the most part, the level-design in this game is great. Each area is well-paced, and offers a good mixture of puzzles, traps, and monsters to contend with. The tools are all very effective, and it's not too much trouble to switch between mid-level. You can expect to use bombs to destroy walls, daggers to hit far-away switches, and so on. The one trap I don't like is the dark hole. These appear very late in the game, and you're liable to struggle for awhile until you figure it out. It's odd to learn a new mechanic far into the game, especially since it only makes a few appearances. Aside from those annoying holes, I don't have any complaints about the level-design.
Unfortunately, the melee combat isn't particularly good. There are numerous ranged options, including throwing your axe, that help mitigate the problem. Until you get used to how the game operates, you'll clumsily bump into the monsters. Basically, there's not a lot of finesse to fighting. For most of the bosses, you'll learn patterns and figure out strategies. Still, that doesn't mean you won't run into a few bruisers that fall to relentless attack-button mashing. Anothing thing to keep in mind is that your survival rate is liable to go up, if you ignore certain monsters. A key aspect to keep in mind is that there aren't any ambushes. Monsters won't appear out of thin air nor will they respawn, unless they're summoned by others. It might be worth clearing the area of danger, so you can explore at your leisure.
Altogether,
is not only a pretty good game; it also offers a fresh spin on the "Metroidvania" genre. Instead of one large world, there are many small levels, and you have to purchase your upgrades. The controls aren't perfect, but they have their own appeal. Most gamers shouldn't have too much trouble adjusting.
In short: I'm impressed.

This is one of my favorite indie platformers. It starts off relatively easy and then becomes gruesomely difficult over the course of 130 hand-crafted levels. You run around collecting Sunstones which can be used to purchase better stuff - magic axes, a grappling hook, double jump, etc - which you'll need to take down tougher challenges. Levels can be repeated to collect Sunstones or bonuses you may have missed, or just to get a better time (the game is speedrun-friendly). There's a lot of level variety: bosses/minibosses every 5 levels, mobility challenges, puzzles, lots of new mechanics being introduced throughout the game, hidden areas, etc. Impressively, the whole thing was put together by pretty much one guy.
I Kickstarted this a while back and I've logged over 60 hours as I write this; I can easily see myself logging 60 more as I try to beat it again on the highest difficulty setting and chase those last few achievements.

In the very beginning, this game had a a cube ranking system tied to the amount of time you played (start at tier 1 which in time gave you access to tier 2 by placing enough tiered blocks on your bot and so on) which in turn was tied to experience of players. Since then, the devs decided to wipe that system from the game. Instead, they implemented the same blocks for everyone, same weapons for everyone.
As a result, no one cares anymore. What happens is: frequent disconnects from players, no teamplay, players scattered across the ingame map, no more player's style combined with the experience they have with the game. The worst is for new players, when you can hardly access good blocks and then try multiplayer, you'd get instakilled by a player who has paid for the weapon he kills you with. In that line of thinking, this game is pay to win.
In my opinion, this type of gaming system invites people to spend more (real life) cash to feel some positively inclined gaming experience. A sad realization. A game must be based upon the fun you can gain, not the depth of your wallet.
And the loading time, ugh. The game itself allows you to see the average waiting time of the sort of game type you have applied to. It usually says under one minute. I can honestly say I've waited three to four times longer that amount of time to get into a game. And then even more variables that can screw up the connection, such as player timeout in the loading screen. This will return you to the garage of the bot you've built with the message that entry hasn't been properly transmitted.
I have reinstalled the game three times over to see whether things have changed, but to no avail. I think I keep it uninstalled. So much potential, yet none of the devs realize it. In my opinion, the devs only care about the company's revenue instead of a combination of it and gaming experience tied to fun and teamplay. Such a shame.

Avernum: Escape From the Pit is the reboot of the Avernum series and it does a great job at that.
While the game isn't anything heavy on graphics, it still brings updated looks in comparison to the original Avernum games, along with other updates, while at the same time maintaining the core mechanics from the original, which work just as great as they did before.
People who enjoy oldschool RPG games and/or games that rely heavily on story and tactical combat will most probably enjoy these games. And even people who like RPG games but aren't too used to these oldschool ones can still pick it up and enjoy it, as the mechanics aren't anything overly complex to learn.
You build your party the way you want (or skip it altogether and use the default party). When making your party, you can either use pre-set character archetypes (Soldier, Sorcerer, etc) or just customize each character the way you want, picking their stats and skills.
The game has an interesting story, even if it's not anything mindblowing, and there's a lot of exploration and side-quests involved, including finding secrets. It's easy to accumulate many hours within the game (I should say, considering I have 91 hours in the game and I only finished it once).
I think my only actual complaint with the game is the limit on summons - each character can only have one summon active, regardless of whether you use magic or items to summon a creature and summoned creatures themselves aren't too strong, save for the very best summon which can be decently useful. So if you want to make a character focused on summoning, he/she probably won't be very effective. It would have been a lot more interesting to be able to summon multiple creatures, maybe one strong summon along with a few weaker ones. (and I know it's possible - this has been done in other Spiderweb Software games)
Nonetheless, a great oldschool RPG.

TL:DR;
Development seems to stop, game has no endgame content, there are bugs like achievements not unlocking.
Only for fans of idle games, otherwise gets boring really fast.
Review:
Idle Civilisation has nothing to put it apart from other idle games, with maybe one exception. However there is no real sense of progression as some basic expected functions are hidden behind a very expensive buildings.
Graphics 4/10:
Despite retro looks the game is actually quite ugly. There is something both in the colony map and in the world map, that puts me off - lack of colour, area design perhaps?
Interface is clunky and cramped, research matrix is barely readable, tavern screen has popup covering some of your heroes making navigation difficult, etc etc.
Audio 4/10:
Apparently music was supposed to be next large update to the game. Right now it's just few annoying loops and whooshing sounds. Monotonous, boring, but there are  option settings for volume and muting!
Gameplay 6/10:
It's difficult sometimes to understand why incremental games are so popular.
This one clearly has little to it, as the massive increase in amounts is not really offset by skills/techs or other things like that. I am not sure how on earth I would ever get 100 000 000 people without leaving game running with CE speedhack for weeks.
One thing that is good however are somewhat nice Hero Quests and Rare Sightings. These are creative and fun to read, but their number is limited.
Conclusion:
Buy only on sale or if real fan of idle games. There is maybe like two dozen hours of action before you get bored to death like me.

This is easily one of the best clickers I've ever played, and that's due largely to the fact that it adequately disguises the clicker elements in a deep set of strategic rules that always empower the player.
I've played over a thousand hours of Clicker Heroes, which I still play to this day, and I've found I'm a pretty big fan of clicker games, as I enjoy the playstyle of making small changes to effect big developments.
This game doesn't let me down on that front. It was a bit overwhelming at first, as I wasn't completely clear on how things related to each other. A couple of hours later, I was playing like a pro and already dreaming up strategies to get further and further.
One of the nicest things about Idle Civilizations is that it doesn't leave you idling for hours, waiting for things to do. If you want to setup a good idle build, you can do that, but you can also sit at the computer and do quests, raids, exploration, or just plain development, while you wait for resources to build.
This is perhaps one of the best things about the game, is that it can feel completely like a strategy game if you want it to, or a clicker idle game if that's what you'd prefer.
Either way, this game is definitely worth the very generously low asking price.

What is Idle Civilization?
Idle Civilization is an idle game that - ironically - can keep you busy.
Whereas in most idle games you have only one resource you mainly spend, and then one reset resource, here you have five main resources, one complementary resource and one reset resource. The game simulates a colony, a settlement in the middle of rich grasslands, with forests and mines abundant. You use food mainly to receive more population (more on this later). Wood and Stone are used to build basic buildings, Metal and Gold are used for more advanced buildings. Sadly each building uses only up to two different resources - more depth would have been good here, even if it wouldn't change the gameplay much. The sixth resource is faith which has no real use beyond a certain income and can't be traded. More on faith later.
I feel like the game is explained best by the order it unlocks its things, so let me try to give an overview here.
At the beginning you have a settlement with two people - I assume they are one male and one female, and please don't make the incest jokes then as I will also assume that the population mainly comes from people immigrating, not from them having thousands of genrations of children.
Starting out:
So you have those two people, but no resources and no research. Thankfully the tutorial tells you what to do: You click ten times to gather food (if you go for all ingame achievements you will need to click on each of the three collectible items 10,000 times in total, while in reality you would need less than 200 clicks in total there for the entire game). After you got the ten food, you can do your first research, after which your people can be freely assigned to any resource you know - food, wood and stone at the beginning. So you should assign them to wood, build a hut, assign them to food to get more population. Now with six population, you distribute them equally, so you have an income of all resources. After about one minute you can build a building that generates food, wood or stone. Of course, you choose wood. After another minute or so, you build the first stone building. You keep on building more then, and when you have three or four you go for the next higher tier which takes like ten times the resources but generates a lot more as well. So you get more income, can build more huts and population.
Exploration:
So far, so standard. Now you can research writing, which enables you to do pretty much everything. It is a prerequisite to metal working, but also enables a random event system with only few bad events. I am not sure if exploration is unlocked now or was already from the start. On exploration you send up to half of your current population to explore the neighborhood. They are either sent on a 20 second exploration with no risk, or later on a 40 second exploration with some risk of dying (you will need drafted but not specialized soldiers for that, more on this later). Each exploration gives you the chance to see a strange event. NEVER click on no here - the strange events always have a positive outcome, and one of the first gives you even a permanent bonus that includes higher birth rates (which further down the road translates into a higher max population but for now only saves some food and time), a 50 percent production bonus, and much more.
Metal and Coins, Reset:
You unlock metal now which unlocks coins. This for now allows you to do further research. At some point you will have 10 colony points (125 civilization points) and you will want to reset the game, but not before having gotten religion. More info below. Invest the few points so you always start with writing, have higher income, By now you will think you never get to 100 colony points, but this is not true - things will soon explode.
After the reset, things go a bit faster, you get back to the point where you were before, including unlocking religion. Things go slightly faster now, and eventually you can unlock wages which don't really do much now - the first few colonies take a while to set up.
Wages will increase your income. Simple as that. You pay a percentage of coins produced, but the gain is so high that  you make more money up to a high extent, essentially multiplying all income. When you have enough resources to build the highest coin production building, you are in for that treat, if not before.
Other activities:
You will have access to religion which allows you to choose one of six deitys, each with five spells that charge over time and need faith to do so - the production will soon be enough to fill all up constantly. Depending on your playstyle each deity has its advantages, but the war deity is especially helpful when you set out to conquer the entire world for the first time. After that, you will have enough colony points to invest into a 100 colony points perk that reduces food costs for new population extremely, so you can always keep on drafting. For that reason, you will also invest some into the perk that drafts more people at once and the one that increases birthrates. At the end, I think Chrysantema is good to choose as she provides a bonus to colony points and free research etc. for the next colony. In fact, if you choose her for your very first colony and use all her abilities ten times (at least the three that stack), the second colony will get you greatly further in the game. But combined with the 100 colony points thing she is even better. The thing is just, you need all six gods for all ingame achievements, so you will want to do them in the early colonies to choose those later that you want to use.
Anyway, eventualy you also unlock a tavern - possibly by choosing the perk - and can have a free hero thanks to the permanent bonus from the strange sighting. The hero is sent on adventures which makes him gain experience - needed to unlock more adventures - and find valuable items, at least in the sense that they grant extra bonuses. Selling them for a small glory price is not recommended, unless you already have one of the item or you are about to reset. The hero can't die, but he can fail the mission - resulting in him just wasting time. In roughly 2 of 3 cases he will succeed and grant a small bonus to your colony then.
You unlock the keep later where you can get Covinari. Those are freelancers like the hero, but give a permanent bonus and malus to the colony. I prefer the 10 percent more production but 10 percent higher food costs for population. They level up over time and can unlock extra bonuses for your colony, including their main bonus - but not malus - being multiplied.
Culture increases your happiness by using - but not spending - part of your civilization score to host festivals, which in turn raises production and later birth rates.
The military finally lets you draft soldiers and specialize them. Unspecialized soldiers are gained by drafting or by losing specialized soldiers - a very beneficial system that makes sure you only lost resources but not population. You can conquer other cities - at the beginning you want to conquer the tier 1 cities, but after a few colonies you can have a military big enough to start with the best cities already and conquer everything. Specialized soldiers come in melee and ranged, where usually ranged deals the damage and melee tanks. You will want to only recruit the highest available tier, as the others just do less but cost less resources.

For all Gothic or Risen fans, I can highly recommend this game, especially for the German speaking gamers, 8.5/10. You get the RPG which are you are expecting from Risen 3, I actually really liked the story, the setting with the 3 main islands (and smaller islands) which had a distinct setting, the huge open World to explore, fight monsters, gain XP, increase your talents with trainers, hunt for treasure chests, win in Mini games, recruit companions... a lot to do.  What really makes this a typical Risen/Gothic game is the athmosphere, and the "dirty rough" dialogs, which work really well in German (likely not as good in English). So why not an even higher grade? Well first, the story is almost completely dissociated from the Risen 1+2, which is particularly wierd as you start with the "Girlfriend" from Risen2 as companion, but in Risen 3 she is your sister... the 2nd reason is the difficulty... its a bit too easy... and the monsters are not so different in strength anymore... in previous games, stronger monsters like Snappers can kill you in 2 attacks, and you have no chance to kill them... here, you can kill them from the start... which does not make you feel so much that you get stronger with time... and from ca. half-2/3 of the game, you kill everything without much fear of death...
In conclusion, Risen 3 is well suited for both veterans who want more of the same formula, but is also good for newcomers, as you dont need knowledge of previous games to enjoy this one.

Risen 3: Titan Lords is an RPG game developed by Piranha Bytes and published by Deep Silver. It’s the third game in the Risen series. The game was released in August 2014 on PC, Xbox360 and PS3, but the PS4 got a remastered version of the game is August 2015.
The game plays almost the same as the first two games in the series. An easy to use combat system which makes you counter and parry enemy sword swings whilst you weave in your own attacks. I found the combat system to be very clunky and not very responsive to your input.  Whilst in combat you are able to use your range weapon too; I found this to be a rather pointless addition as it misses the majority of the time even on much bigger targets.  You are able to freely explore the world and take on plenty of side quests. Each of the quests has different ways to solve them, which is a nice element, depending on how you resolve the quest; you may even get a different outcome.  I liked the fact you can play the game in almost any order you choose, meaning you can mould your character exactly how you want it to be.
Graphically, I wasn’t too impressed, for me it looks worse than the previous games. I was playing on 4k and it looked really poor. Texture quality was mediocre at best. The lush scenery when exploring islands does redeem itself a bit, but what’s inside that lushness is some really bad looking modelling. The animation and sound effects are so bad, they are sometimes laughable. I believe all modern games should have voice acting in, and sadly Risen 3 has some absolutely awful voice actors. Every single word that is spoken just feels out of place and does not match up with the game play at all. It almost made the cut scenes unbearable sometimes. During the first fifteen minutes of gameplay, there is almost silence. All you hear is the gun fire, no shouting, sound effects of fights, nothing. It just seems to have very poor production values.
The game is pretty easy even when playing on the hard settings. The combat system, when you get a hang of it, is easy to use, meaning you can be taking on larger groups of enemies before too long. A lot of the time throughout the game you will be accompanied by a companion which also makes the combat scenes more easily handled too. I only died a handful of times so there isn’t any major challenge to be found here.
Risen 3 does have a very good amount of content to play through. Each chapter of the game has at least 20+ side quests for you to tackle. Whilst the side quests don’t distract you too much from the main plot, they are a good addition to the game, that rewards you with money and much needed experience for completing them. I didn’t find myself wanting to complete a lot of them though; they are all very samey after you complete half a dozen; the side quests in this game are nothing when you compare it to the likes of Witcher.
The game took me almost twenty five hours to complete, with a fair few of the side missions completed. For me, since I was struggling to get through the abundance of cut scenes and dialogue, I feel that was almost a bit too much, even now I have plenty of side quests I could complete but I honestly don’t think I can put myself through any more of it. You can probably get about 40 hours of content out of this game, and you may even want to consider a second play through given the amount of choice some of the quests offer.
I didn’t have any technical problems whilst playing thankfully. I was able to play at 1440p with all of the graphical settings turned up to max and still have a steady 60 fps. I played the game with keyboard and mouse, as I found that to be best for the previous games in the series, but the game will work perfectly well with a controller since it is in the third person perspective.
To sum up, I believe Risen 3 to be the worst of the series so far. The first two games had better animation and voice acting in than this one, and to some extent, they even looked better graphically.  The game is currently retailing for £24, 99, and sadly I don’t think it’s even worth half of that. If you are a fan of RPG games and the Risen series, I would suggest you wait till it drops to the £10 mark, just so you don’t feel too let down by the poor production values on show here. Whilst the game does have a vast open world exploration feel to it, it just didn’t live up to my expectations for the third game in a really good pirate series.

PLUS:
Music.  Spot on. Genre leading in most instances.
Graphics:  I played the Enhanced Edition.  Graphics were well done with the various environments.
Quest / fetch:  If you like that sort of game, it’s done really well here.
World is detailed and intricate and rewards the player for exploring

MINUS:
Horribad dialog.  Not voice acting, dialog.  Unfortunately, this can impede your immersion in the game.  Seems like such an easy area they could have addressed.
Quest / fetch:  If you don’t like that sort of game, then Risen isn’t for you.
Graphics.  Shouldn’t be possible to run up a tree then fall off and die.  Minor glitches.
AVERAGE:
Voice Acting.  I didn’t find the actual voices an issue, but as mentioned the script was painful at times.
Acquiring items/loot:  First third of the game I didn’t like it, but as I played I appreciated the fact I had to actually “look” for items, instead of the usual acquiring by merely walking over them.  However, the drawback is I found myself constantly clicking for fear of missing something.  I liked that they didn’t dumb down exploring and finding items, but at the same time Important items can be easily overlooked.  As such, expect to find things occasionally in areas you’ve already combed over.
Combat.  I hated it a first… until I figured it out, then it was okay.  Yes, I had moments of aggravation and/or camera issues, but it was the exception not the norm.  There are those that hate Risen combat but I’m not among them.
CONCLUSION:
If you’re the type of gamer who appreciates well-designed areas to explore--and likes getting rewarded for exploring with additional quests and loot, then Risen 3 is most likely right for you.  The Risen series seems to be a love it or hate if affair.  For me, I think Risen does just enough keep me playing each new installment, and number 3 is no exception.   It wouldn’t be RPG GOTY but it would garner a nomination and maybe even make runner up.  Piranha Bytes knows how to build beautiful worlds and design quests, now if only they were just as good when it came to creating stories and English dialog translation.
This review is from playing the PC version Enhanced Edition with the 3 DLC.  I recommend this game @ 75% off and get all the DLC.  It’s cheap now, and makes the game more complete.

Now here is where the game get's a bit rocky. When trying to join a server I normally try and connect to one with a low ping. It loads halfway then my game crashes. I'm not sure if it's my computers fault or the server I'm trying to join. The servers I try to join have ridiculously low ping, like 90-120 maybe. That's not all though. When you die your respawn timer is anywhere from 100-120 second. Not joking. Sometime this is okay but other times it's not. If your team is doing well and capturing zones every 30 seconds then you're probably going to respawn instantly. You respawn early if your team captures a zone. If your team is doing bad though and isn't capturing zones/point, well your screwed. You will have to wait until the entire timer is gone before you can respawn. Other than that though the multiplayer is absolutely amazing! It's very intense. You feel so rewarded when you get a 3 killstreak.
I highly recommened getting this game. It's and intense FPS that feels good. It emphasises teamwork and coordination.
9/10.

A lot of people have gone through the mechanics of the game better than I would. Everything in the game is mechanically sound and allows for ample strategy. You should absolutely buy it and support a great indie developer.
The only thing I would comment on is the writing. A lot of people have gushed over the writing saying it's wonderful. Well, it
good, but have the right expectations: the writing is less the next Lord of the Rings in video game form and more having the best DM you could possibly imagine creating adventures for you.
Definitely should get this game!
EDIT: So I wanted to just add a final thought to my review. after putting almost 30 hours into the game, I've pretty much abandoned it. After thinking about it, I've realized the game lacks player agency. This means that there are no real choices in the game - there are dozens of quests to partake in, but there is no consequence if you don't do them. They are also almost all linear. The greatest choice present in most of them is whether you
give a discovered quest item to the patron the commissioned the quest. Again, if you don't, the only consequence is not receiving the quest reward (which may or may not be better than the legendary item you're handing over).
Games can overcome this if they have an immersive narrative or compelling aethetics and atmosphere. Unfortunately, this game lacks both. The narrative is ok and the world is unique, but it isn't enough to keep me going after 2 dozen hours.
Now, some of Spiderweb's other offerings do give the player more agency. So again, I recommend the game, it's fun, but I just thought some may want to know.

The Short: Awesome fighting game (even if you aren't a Naruto junkie!), but make sure you have a controller and the patience to sit through the annoying matchmaking
The Long: I can't compare this game to earlier entries in the Ninja Storm series because I haven't played any; I picked this game up while it was on sale a while ago because I liked similar style fighting games (DBZ Budokai Tenkaichi) and was very pleasantly surprised.
Unlike the aforementioned Tenkaichi, all of the characters feel like they have a different playstyle and most of them have at least one unique trait that makes them viable. At first the game seems like it is all button mashing because there are no arcade-style button combos to put in, but it is not! Timing and managing your substitutions is critical otherwise you will be crushed by a more skilled player.
The storymode is great in this game. All of the critical scenes in Shippuden are re-enacted for the most part, and the cinematic battles are great.
Most people probably care about Online Mode the most though, so I'll put a good bit of my thoughts in here too:
The fun you will have Online depends on who you play with. The netcode can be spotty with this game, as I've had it drop inputs playing with someone who lives in the same town. The community can also be very frustrating, as you will see a lot of TenTen/Temari/Deidara spammers who are looking for stat-padding and spend the whole match throwing projectiles, or people who turn off assists to do infinite combos with Neji/Rock Lee.
Eventually you will find people who aren't trying to cheese out the game though, and when you do, you will have lots of fun. I recommend building a list of friends who play this game and doing tournaments, as this game can be insanely fun when your opponent isn't spamming jutsus or using cookie-cutter teams.
I haven't tried to play this game on the keyboard, I imagine it is dreadful, so make sure you bring your wired 360 controller before you buy. Cheers.

Online can be very laggy, combos can stop just because the enemy floated away somehow, or you weren't even actually hitting them as the hit detection can also be terrible when playing online, then there's the RNG of getting items/gear/skills, which can be ontop of other RNG known as "ultimate finishes" which even if you can trigger correctly may not even happen!

All in all, if you're a DBZ fan this is a very fun game, or you can get it on sale, but I just really hope the next game takes the issues the community has with DBXV and fixes them in time for the inevitible Dragonball Super era game they will release next.

Mabinogi one of the longer lasting MMO titles, dating even WoW by one year. Started in korea before making its way over to America. While Nexon America has made some bad marketing decisions from time to time, they're usually spot on when it comes to Mabinogi. If you're under a total of 1000 levels you're considered a beginner and despite its homely appearence the game is quite brutal. Not vindictus brutal or god of war but you feel pain after taking 60 damage. they're still using Polygons for their character models but that holds its old school charm when combined with its cell shaded graphics. The game has an easy to follow storyline and gets pretty immersive but I'm going to keep this as neutral as possible. First I'm going to look at the cons.
If you made it this far good. Here's the con list:
-Most customizations cost actual money. before you gripe I'm talking cosmetics.
-While free to play some things you have to buy if you want to look nifty. If you're cool with getting your own look through hard work then play free. I do reccomend saving up for at least one Karma koin at some point as a just in case you hit over level 1000.
-Rebirth's do cost money but for the first 1000 levels its free.
-Tough combat. This game doesn't have auto attack you have to click each time you want to hit your enemy. It follows a very rock-paper-sissors combat formula. While rewarding, mess up and you end up hurting.
- Prices. In game armor and weapons are expensive and repairs can get pricey. While the numbers may not look all that impressive they do stack up.
- Death and Ressurection. Is both a positive and negative. Its highly inconvienient to die in a dungeon but at the same time if the boss killed you its because of a reason. when you're out of nao stones is when dying is bad but normally its a drop in the pan.
- camping field penalties. Killing field enemies is rough in that stay in one area too long and you'll get penalized. Getting less and less each kill.
- Cel shaded graphics. This is for those of you who are very nitpicky. Its cel shaded so if you don't like those I put this here and in the positives.
-Hard work. If you're like me and have a blacksmith, or a similar profession in game you know that its not easy being that. You need materials which sometimes means going after dangerous enemies. It can suck but the reward is in the product. See positives.
- Solo play. This is very hard to do as there is power in numbers.
- time consuming.
Positives:
+ Use any gear. You can use any gear avaliable to you as long as its in your inventory. Want to be a ninja gunslinger? Go ahead. You just need a shuriken, dual pistols, ninja skills and gunslinger skills. Want to be an explorer? Then grab some gear and go do some dungeons for that loot.
+ Rewarding combat. When you're doing well in combat it feels very rewarding especially if it means maximising your loot by the boss of a dungeon.
+ soundtrack. Great soundtrack that is very catchy and nostalgic. After 8 years of playing this I'm still going back to this classic.
+ dungeoning with friends. While chaotic this is still very fun. At times a necessity as the later dungeons become longer and harder to complete.
+ many ways to level. whether its leveling up from gathering eggs from chicken, defeating wolves or mining ore there are plenty of ways to earn money and level up.
+ the options. As long as you know the skill you can use it. There are even some secret skills that used to be harder to learn like the Fire Arrow skill.
+ getting to higher levels of combat. This in and of itself is rewarding to see enemies that previously murdered you deal only one damage.
+ generally a very supportive community. I myself have on several occasions handed out armor and weapons I crafted by hand to people without gear. If you're not an archer and you see an archer, give them some arrows.
Neutral:
+/- Time consuming. Don't let it rule your life. Remember, its a virtual world, its not going anywhere.
+/- traveling can take time but good things happen to those who wait.
+/- rebirthing after a cetain point costs money for character cards.
ultimately I think if you like games similar to mabinogi then give it a shot. This game isn't for everyone but you'll never know until you try it. I reccomend it to those who like being creative and getting into a world. I'm someone who first went to Mabinogi as an escape and now go back to it as a fan.

I love it; the plot is a fun twist on believable science fiction in the near future, the weapons present thus far feel very solid, the controls are simple and work very well...
all around this game even in an unfinished state does so much right that I wonder what the hell the developers of more mainstream games are doing that their finished products are so underwhelming in comparison. I would love to see the addition of a few item, weapon, and ability hotkeys (grenades, quickknife/melee, deployables, night vision anybody?) but considering the game currently only has two guns and killer robots for npc's I understand it may be a while before it is that far.

TL;DR EVE is a phenomenal game. There are many reviews out there that will give you a sense of what you can expect of the game, so I will spend my time detailing some useful pointers to those who are considering playing the game for the first time.
One thing I have to get out of the way:
______________________________
Do NOT buy any of the 'add ons' you see advertised on Steam. Anyone with experience in the game can tell you that the items they give you in the add ons are not in any way special, and even a newbie can afford these items fairly easily with money you earn in game.
Also: know that if you create an account through steam you will not be able to take advantage of buying and selling characters on that account. This is not an issue for newer players but once you are wealthy enough to be buying characters you may find it an annoyance.
______________________________
So some advice if you do decide to pull the trigger and join EVE:
- Do not consider mining as a career. It is an acceptable and easy way to make small sums of money as a new pilot, but does not lead to the type of glorious and engaging gameplay that makes EVE so incredible. Too many newbies pidgeon hole themselves into mining, this either ends in extreme boredom or unsubbing the game.

- Sure when you begin the game you will have to spend some time training skills and it may be a bit boring in that initial month. Do a bit of research, join a decent looking corp that does something other than mining, and have fun. This game pays off immensely for those who are patient and persistent.
- Do not look at the capital ships and be discouraged it will take you 120 days to fly them. This is not a game where bigger is always better. The biggest ships in the game are very limited in their practical use, there is tons of fun to be had in all sizes of ships.
- Try to avoid the temptation to spend money on PLEX to buy ships you can't afford, this just makes it hurt that much more when you lose them. You will lose ships, you will feel bad when your pride and joy is destroyed. The fact that you can lose almost anything you have is a big part of what makes the game so compelling.
- If you find yourself unhappy with what you are doing or the corporation you are flying with: do something different! Join a new corp! There are TONS of different things you can do in this game, and there are groups of people out there who specialize in all of these various activities. Joining the right group can make the difference between playing for a month and unsubbing, or being happy to play the game for years.
- If something sounds too good to be true, it is. There are many scammers in the game, anyone offering to double your money is one of them.
- Do not think you are perfectly safe if you are in high security space. People willing to sacrifice their ship can still attack you. They will be dealt with by the NPC Police, but they will still be able to destroy you before that happens. Always be on your guard.
- Do not try to play this game solo. As an individual you can have an impact on the game, but you will probably not have much success trying to do it alone. Again, the social aspect of this game is a big part of its draw and having a great group of people around you to share in your successes and failures is really what makes the game so fun.
I could go on, but in short: if you like spaceships and the idea of joining a game where your ability to succeed and make your mark in the universe is only limited by your ambition then EVE is definitely for you. You will experience crushing defeats, and glorious triumphs. All of it in a universe completely run by players in a way that will amaze you more and more as you play the game.

I have loved the Borderlands series for years, and it all started with the first one on Xbox (I own Borderlands, Borderlands 2, and Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel for Xbox 360) and I have to say, getting 1 and 2 on PC was an amazing idea!  It runs really well on my laptop, and can even go between the keyboard/mouse combo and an xbox controller.  I haven't had any frames drop yet, and it controls fairly smoothly with the controller.  Plus, I can play online with friends for free, instead of buying an xbox subscription and never getting a chance to play.  I've also enjoyed the semi-realistic but still cartoony art style, and the humor is always great, there's even some pop culture references if you listen hard enough.  I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes to play single player games or co-op, because even when you beat the main storyline in the game once, there's quite a bit of replay value in achievements and a second phase where you replay from the beginning but everything is at a higher level.  The DCL for the first Borderlands has been my favorite bunch so far, and the bosses are actually pretty difficult.  Seriously, a great series all around.  10/10.

SUMMARY: A relaxing game where you wander around a procedurally generated island, and your travels create the soundtrack.  With some interesting visuals and a focus on playing around, the game is for people who want something experimental and playful and/or want to back an innovative game.  Not for something where you're looking for scores, skilltrees, and so on.
Proteus is wandering through a child's drawing while listening to a freeform prog rock soundtrack.  If that appeals to you, then it's probably a game to get.  Be warned - it's not for everyone.
Every time you start Proteus, you end up in the ocean near a procedurally generated island.  As you explore, the sound reflects the surroundings.  You wander into the soundtrack, as it were.
Exploring the island allows you to experience various sites, find interesting things, or just hang out.  There's various landmarks in each game that provide certain features, as well as plenty of randomness.  There's some discoveries to be made that will let you experience the game in depth, and there is an "end" to get to if you want (and lets you experience assorted visual and auditory experiences).
Then?  You can start again.
It's really a game of wandering, playing on that urge that often drives us to see "just what's around here", combined with the freeform soundtrack.  It's compelling and relaxing, like you're experiencing a dream.
If you want a game with skilltrees, combat, construction, etc. it isn't for you.  You don't do anything except choose where you go and what you experience.  I find myself playing it when I need to take a short break, and it's surprisingly soothing.
Is it for you?  Like many games it depends on you - if the description has you interested, it probably is.

I felt like reliving games I liked in the early 90s. Games like The Magic Candle and old SSI and Ultima games.
Spider Web games taps into this nostalgia. They've released over a dozen isometric rpgs that offer hundreds if not thousands of hours of gameplay.
I've put in 30+ hours into this title alone, one of 7 full titles in Avernum (I think), and that's not counting the Abadon games that take place in the same world. I'm estimating I'm about 25-30% into the game, though there are 3 completely different ways to win, so I really have no idea. The map is truly massive.
A couple huge issues: The clumsy pathfinding will drive you nuts. Characters often take the long way around to a place with a misclick, ruining a battle and forcing you to restart.  The boat pathfinding is ridiculously awful. If you are patient enough to get accustomed to these old school mechanics, you'll be fine. Save. A. Lot.
The world is dangerous. Don't expect clearcut level caps between regions, though the game is designed for widening challenges the further you venture. Money is hard to earn, and you get a real sense of accomplishment when you get a nice weapon or learn a new spell. While the starting area around Formello is relatively safe, the rest of the world is not. If it's a rich, nostalgic, challenging world you're looking for, get these. Can't be beat for the price either.

Before I bought Squad, I watched multiple videos of gameplay and of people spectating matches. I only now realize that the videos I watched were completly different from any normal game you will get into.
All of the videos I watched were videos of organized and/or competitive events. Everybody on both teams had mics and were constantly communicating and exchanging information. Both teams in all of the videos had a chain of command, with the head commander, the squad leaders, then the infantry men in each squad. The commanders would assess the situations they found themselves in and then develop a plan according to said situation, they would then relay their plan to the squad leads, then the squad leads would work together and give orders to their infantry men that would best carry out the commanders plan. The infantry men would execute the orders they were given and relay back to the squad leads how the execution of their orders went, then the squad lead would relay that back to the commanders. Then commanders would re evaluate their circumstances and tweak their plan, then the cycle of relaying information down the chain of command, then back up, would begin agan.
Now, I know that was a mouthful, but the point of all of that was to show how ♥♥♥♥ing organized this game needs to be in order for it to actually be fun, and succeed as a game. Public matches are nothing, and I mean NOTHING like described above. They are complete cluster♥♥♥♥s. There is no organization at all. Hell, there are barely even people using mics. This game NEEDS to have organization and teamwork for it to be fun, and public matches dont have either, so obviously they arent fun at all.
However, when we talk about competative/organized matches, the game is absolutely amazing. Despite the questionable quality of its graphics, Squad really comes together to make for an awesome experience. I mean, I've only seen videos of organized/competitive games, and they all had me squirming in my seat and holding my breath because of how captivating they were. You can tell just by watching that its a whole lot of fun to take part games like that.
There is just one problem, you're never going to participate in competative/organized game unless you go a third party sight and do the whole spiel of creating an account, then registering your account, then signing up for games, then hope that you get picked. Personally, i'm not willing to do that. So for me, the game is a bust. But for anybody who is willing to jump through all of those hoops to get into a competative/organized game, you're probably going to have a great time.
I downvoted this game because of how situational it is regarding on whether or not you're gonna have fun. Most of the time, you're gonna be in a cluster♥♥♥♥ of a game thats not fun at all, but on the rare occation in which you find yourself in a pub game with actual organization and teamwork, or if you get into a competative/organized game, you're in for an amazing experience.

I absolutely love this game. Tallowmeres' combat is very punishing for mistakes, like if you aren't paying attention to what enemies are in the room, or you attack at the wrong moments. But that makes the game even more fun for me. If you dislike difficult games then don't get this, but if you like a good challenging game, I definately can't recommend this enough. The price of $3.99 is more than worth it.
Almost every weapon in Tallowmere has a different, unique ability. If you watched the video for it already then you've probly seen them. For example, my favorite weapon, the Emerald Dagger, allows you to turn invisible after a few seconds. Allowing you to sneak up behind enemies and backstab them for massive damage. The Katana, probably the most risky weapon to use, allows you to automatically teleport to nearby enemies and damage them. While risky to use, it is one hell of a joyride. But unfortunately, Tallowmere doesn't have many items, so the game can get repetetive in terms of items.
Finally, we're going to be talking about the enemies of Tallowmere. Tallowmere doesn't have too many enemies So I should be able to get through all of them, this is more of a guide, so you can skip to the end if you want. FIrst of all is the leaper or jumper or whatever they're called lol. So the leapers are grey with weird masks. They have a very short line of sight but are very dangerous if not approached right. I'd recommend using an emerald dagger and sneak up behind them and backstab them for an instant kill. If you don't have an emerald dagger, approach the leaper with your shield up, and let them attack your shield, then attack them once and repeat.
The next enemy we're talking about is the zaeries. Zairies are small flying things that can get annoying. They are pretty easy to take care of so just block one or two attacks, then try to attack them 3 times to kill them.
The next enemy we're talking about is the ogre. These guys are either the most annoying or second most annoying enemy in basically everyones opinion. These guys throw purple potions that will track you down no matter where you what. If one of these potions hits you, you will be stunned for a short time. This can be very troublesome if you're in a cluster of enemies or there are multiple ogres in a crammed area. The strategy I use for killing these guys is that I will slowly walk up to them with my shield raised and when I get right up in their faces, I'll wait for them to raise their arm up to throw a potion, I'll jump up with my shield still in hand because if you don't jump, the potion will go over your head and behind you. After I block the potion, I'll just spam them to death.
The next enemy are the feelers. After a second or two of noticing you, they will shoot a little harpoon like object that will pull you towards them, this can be blocked with your shield, but if you don't block it this can be very deadly, especially if there's an ogre or a group of enemies next to them. The easiest way of taking these guys out is using the rocket launcher due to it locking onto nearby enemies. But if you don't have a rocket launcher, here's my method. So I'll charge them, with my shield up, and when I reach them, I'll make them do their attack, block it, and then hit it 2 times and repeat.
Next up are the lightning mages. These guys are pretty easy to kill so let's just get this out of the way. You can make them kill themselves by bating their attack, running up to them point blank, putting your shield down and waiting for the white aura around them to appear, then raising your shield. This will damage them. To kill them with weapons, follow the same method as earlier but attack them in between attacks.
Next up are the fire mages. These guys are easy to kill just like the lightning guys. Use the same method as you would for the lightning guys to take them out, but they can't take any damage from their own fireballs.

Next up are the flail knight. These guys can get pretty annoying. So alert them, wait for the ball to spin around 2 times and then rush them, they should die before the ball can get back to them.
Next up are the archers. These guys are different than most enemies. So just hold your shield up and run at them, then hit them as much as you can while blocking as many arrows as you can.
And finally we have the bloats I'm pretty sure they're called. These guys are pretty easy to take care of lure them towards you, then when they start doing their suicide animation, run away. If you do manage to get caught in the explosion radius, you will be stunned, this can be blocked by your shield though. You can use these guys as a weapon, as they can stun other enemies for you, including the feelers, which makes them fall to the ground, making them much easier to kill.
Well that just about does it, all around I love this game, I only have 4 hours and I'm already hooked on the addicting gameplay, you should definately give it a try, I hope I helped you decide on if you should buy it or not. Thanks for taking the time to read through my review, have an awesome day.

On a serious note, I've been playing Idle Games for a long time. The thing I like about Idle Civilization is the lack of excessive clicking.
At the start you will need to click for about 20 times to get a few starter resources, From then on workers do the rest of the work.
It's got a great Event system and an interesting research tree for progression.
Still, I feel that the world map and hero system could be improved a little.
At the time of writing this review I have roughly 15 hours spent active ingame, Sending my hero on adventures and soldiers out to collect books or concur cities.
The map seems to be limit to the point that once you've taken all the cities then all you can do is upgrade a few things and collect resources from them.
Id like to see some sort of system where the AI tries to reclaim the cities, And you need to station units to protect them.
Your main village also has walls that you can build, Only thing that really does any damage is Wolves that take down 1-2 walls every attack. These attacks are rare so if you build 100 walls then you can go 15 hours and only lose 3 walls.

Other than that it's a great Idle game, Good for a few days of gameplay.
Id rate this game 8/10 and recommend it to any Idle gamers.

Interesting Game with many Aspects for Tactical Coop and MP.
Right now (Early Alpha) it was a bit of confusion finding a coop match, cause you cant host yourself. You had to join a free or empty lobby to "host" it. If you're the first one to join, its you decision to make the lobby public or privat.
Anyway the amount of free lobbys was huge, but i doubt, that after early acces you find fast a empty one. The own hosting mode is atm missing.
I cant say much about the MP, cause i played it just once. A bit hectic and not that much tactical like the game demands. Easy TDM mode with long respawn timers.
About the Game itself:
Graphics were okay, but a bit plain. On the contrary the shadow and lightning were pretty impressing, especially if the maps turn nearly complete dark in some mode/maps. Makes it really intense and gave a bit of a horrorgame like Amnesia or Slenderman. No nightvison guys, only a Flashlight which attracts the enemys. Your call what to do^^
Gameplay:
It was fun, really fun. Even with randoms it wasnt that hard to win a map by killing all robots. Ok...if you get killed your teammates have to resurrect you in time or you're out. thats not really happening with randoms.
And please!! THIS IS NOT CoD or BF OR UT! you cant rush a map and spray'n'pray for the win.
The enemys are quite good, organized and deadly aiming. Afterall it is a Tactical Shooter which requires Teamwork and strategic thinking.
Malus: I found it a bit confusing that step sounds you make, are coming from behind yourself. It makes you always look behind you unnessesary^^
Conclusion:
Interstellar Marines has huge potential. Not for Esports, but for a serious Tactial Coop Shooter. Tweaking the difficulty a bit, maybe give the enemy a "face" or make them more threating like being human/alien. And punish none-tactical playing like spraying, rushing, running etc harder. :)

"God's Work" is a speculative fiction story of a future after the repeal of Roe v. Wade (legalized abortion in america), and the reaction of pro-life forces in a specific rural area. The ending was less than this viewer expected, but overall the film was acceptable, and one I'll likely watch again.

Bionic Commando is a game that is hampered by a case of consolitis, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ save system, horrible swaths of deadly blue fog that kill you if you so much as even LOOK at it funny, and a twist climax that's such a horrendous slap in the face you'd swear the writers accidentally swapped scripts with someone's anime fanfiction.
But if you can manage to stomach that, you'll find a game with a tricky-but-surprisingly-fluid and intuitive swinging mechanic, lovingly-rendered maps, and the best game music ever composed . Evading streams of tracer-fire with frantic rappelling before launching yourself off of a bridge with a perfect swing that allows you to zip-kick a gunship set to the tune of "The Gauntlet" was one of the most exhilarating experiences I've had from a piece of software in a long time.
If you ever find yourself with a few extra bucks and some time to kill, give this underdog a try, then lament at how its commercial failure will ensure that a sequel will never happen.
