There's a lot to be said for fan service and its role in entertainment. Providing material that speaks directly to an audience with a specific love and appreciation of a given source provides a palpable sense of private-club-like inclusion, allowing fans to feel connected through their shared interest whether they're in the same room or on the other side of the world. Rather than feel isolated and frustrated by an undying love for a given movie, character, comic, or novel, the existence of indulgence-orientated products makes us feel part of something bigger--there are people out there who like this stuff as much as I do. The Ultimate Ninja series has always taken this idea to heart, concentrating its focus to a laser point that other franchises would never dare to attempt for fear of alienating all but the most dedicated of followers. If you're part of the club, then such single-mindedness is great. If you're not, then don't let the door hit you on the way out.
Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 Full Burst is perhaps the most extreme example yet of Namco Bandai's attempt to appeal to the converted and only to the converted. Here's a game not simply for any old Naruto fan, but for Naruto fans who are completely up to date with the story and characters as they currently exist in the anime/manga episodes and are seeking a new way of experiencing previously explored plotlines. If you're not up to date, then not only are you going to struggle enormously with the story as depicted in the game's early stages, but you're going to ruin what you've not yet seen of the TV series. Unfortunately, due to gameplay that is as unwieldy and bloated as its title, Full Burst is not an acceptable way to get yourself up to date with this franchise.
This may be a beat-'em-up, but the primary Ultimate Adventure mode features so little gameplay in comparison to cutscenes and dialogue-heavy exposition that you'd be forgiven for thinking you're sitting through a barely interactive (albeit combat-heavy) soap opera. It feels as though developer CyberConnect2's plan was to create a condensed edition of the anime in which fight scenes are playable, rather than create a game in its own right. This leads to an experience that features such haphazard and irregular pacing that your principal cause for intrigue rests in trying to work out just how long it's going to be before the game asks you to pick up the controller again--and even when you do, the core combat is a shallow, button mashing affair that requires little in the way of skill. While there's definite and worthwhile value in repackaging the events of a beloved series in a new format, there's also value in a game giving you something to do.
There may be a lack of interaction in story mode, but that doesn't hold true for the package as a whole. Including all of the downloadable content released for the original Naruto Shippuden Ultimate Ninja 3 release, the volume of content on offer is gargantuan. Chief among the additions is the extra Ultimate Adventure chapter, which sees Sasuke and Itachi Uchiha take on the nefarious Sage Kabuto, a segment that is so phenomenally difficult in comparison to the rest of the game that all previously learned tactics become essentially redundant. The same Sage Kabuto is unlockable as a playable character if you have the patience to jump through the numerous hoops to unlock him, and there are also some new costumes to swoon over.
The biggest, but certainly not most interesting, piece of extra content comes in the form of supplementary challenge missions. One hundred of these have you beating an opponent in a fight while handicapped in some way--removing your ability to jump, for example, or setting a limit on the number of attacks at your disposal. While these missions do add some welcome variety to the combat, they primarily serve to highlight just how shallow the core mechanics are. Without these externally shoehorned twists on battle, fighting suffers from an overwhelming shallowness that sees you engage autopilot once the basics become second nature. Only during set-piece boss battles are you asked to do something out of the ordinary.
To compound matters, the most members of the enormous character roster plays in the same way. You swap between characters regularly during Ultimate Adventure, but this is done predominantly to facilitate the narrative rather than to spice up gameplay through variety and diversity. Granted, significant and impressive visual flair is achieved by switching often between characters with attacks that are literally out of this world, but that aesthetic quality doesn't remain interesting long enough for the combat inadequacies to be forgiven. Clearly, this is not a game with the remotest desire to cement its place in the bastion of hardcore fighting game legacy, but that doesn't excuse the fact that there's so little meat to the gameplay that you're essentially feasting on elaborately painted bones.
Similar problems exist with Ultimate Adventure's role-playing-game-lite elements, which allow you to roam around a number of different environments with a view to collecting and buying items to use in combat (health potions, strength buffs, and so on) and optionally talking to loitering non-player characters. At times, these moments provide a welcome break from the cutscene/fight/cutscene pattern, but more often than not, they feel designed to artificially lengthen the game and trick you into thinking you're playing something with genuine genre-blending aspirations.
The closest comparison to this format is Asura's Wrath, another of CyberConnect2's offerings. However, where Asura's Wrath succeeds in this style of storytelling thanks to its short length and ferocious pace, Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 suffers from attempting to cover far too much ground for the core mechanics to handle. If you do classify yourself as a Naruto aficionado, then simply having another medium through which to consume the narrative is potentially going to be enough to satisfy you. Without a doubt, everyone else should look elsewhere.

This game has changed very much in the history of its development. Often to the dislike of its verteran player base.
I myself tend to play it less often by far. I have put in a lot of hours in this game, more than any game before.
It is totally recommanded, its free to play and fair enough, although in the past the f2p model was better.
The cubes and other hardware you need to build a bot now comes from loot crates you get by either daily log in, fights, special rewards or by buying them. The crates com in different qualities which increses the rarity of the lloot inside. Higher quality crates comes with better placement of scores in battle.
Means even when you are the best player in a match, your reward is still by chance.
You can craft blocks and other parts by using robits which are also partially found in crates or by selling the blocks you found there, although at a pretty bad rate.
You can double the loot by getting premium which also unlocks better exchange rates for selling parts and new building colours as well as an EXP boost.
EXP was once a system of progression alongside techpoints before lootcrates. Now you get a free crate per lvl and techpoints for unlocking parts is gone in favour of the crates.
The game is NOT P2W since rarer items are not ultimately stronger but rather how you design the bot and play the meta. It does not take too long to aquire rarer parts if needed too.
It must be said although that in the past the game had a better system of matching similar strong players/bots against each other with the use of tiers and other mechanics.
The reduced player base alone was reason enough to change the tier system to a more open everything goes one where smaller and bigger bots and pros and contras. There is a noob bubble withing the beginning where matchmaking tries to get new players into the same match but other than that new players will face the meta and veteran players rather quickly. Seeking the meta and getting bots from players via the ingame shop I would recommend. The bot shop is a placeto share your builds. This and the simplification of many build aspects of the game took away some of the edge against other players for expert builders.
But yeah I can go on for some time, just try it.

Interesting little arcadey roguelike. I find it to be what many call 'cozy' similar to the old Win3.1 game Castle of the Winds. Although this game isn't nearly as complex as that game, despite being much more advanced graphically.
I saw everything it has to offer hours ago and am just trying to go as deep into Lady Tallowmere's dungeons as possible, but I find myself coming back to it when I'm between other games or just momentarily bored with my current PC game. Success is kind of contingent upon the gear you can find, but that's usually the case with games in this bloated genre.
Unlike many other games in its genre, weapons all have different handling dynamics and some impart special powers, like the valuable daggers which allow you to move unseen unless you attack or are touched/damaged and are vital in setting up your approach to taking out groups of monsters. Most of the time I've died I've unintentionally killed myself, and once you know how to handle all the things your game can throw your way, it's really only about optimizing your equipment and keeping strategies in mind. The mechanics are extremely simple but it's easy to understand how they work and if something happens, it's because you messed up. You will blow yourself up with grenades. Be forewarned.
The one mark against it is that the procedural generation occasionally screws you royally, particularly with placement of buzzsaws, but this is the nature of procedural generation.
You may want to wait for a sale, but $3.99 isn't all that much for what you get, especially since the game has a sense of humor about itself which I enjoy.

My new favorite hardcore tactical shooter, probably the most authentic miltary game out. Screw clunky Arma.
I have yet to find a game like this where people work so well as a team together. People take this game seriously and it's awesome. It feels so real. The maps are incredible. You think Battlefield has big maps? Pshh. The maps in Squad feel like actual places, not arenas. Expect huge, wide open spaces with little cover. You really have to plan your every move, or you will be killed. 1-2 bullets kill so you will die alot. There are no stupid enemy name tags and you can actually hide in bushes. If you are in a city, there could be an enemy on any floor, in any building. This makes traversing moutaintops, citys or large fields with your team a very tense experience.
The graphics aren't the best out, but the game still looks stunning at times. It takes a more photorealistic approach to it's art style and it can look pretty real.
The sound design is top notch. Explosions will make you jump. Guns sound very meaty. The way the weapons work and handle is perfect. Every gun functions like it would in real life.
I hope they add MBTs and maybe a couple of helicopters in the future. A dedicated long range sniper role would be great too. I found the marksman class to be not quite long range enough sometimes. It could be a 2 person role where the sniper needs to have a spotter or you won't be allowed to spawn.  Atleast having some longer range optics would be appreciated.
Overall amazing. Not for the casuals. 9/10

Steak & Ale Pie
Heat the oil in the pan with the onion and garlic for 1 minute.
Add the steak. Cook until the meat is seared all over and there is no pink left.
Pour in half the Ale and allow to simmer for a minute, then pour in the rest with the thyme, chilli powder salt and pepper.
Crumble in the oxo cubes- both the beef and the vegetables. Add in the chopped vegetables.
Simmer for 10 mintues and then transfer to a large casserole pot. If the gravy doesnt cover the meat then add some water and mix in.
Pop the dish into the oven at gas mark 3 or 4 and leave for at least 1 hour 30 mins.
20 minutes before you want to serve, roll out the pastry and cut appropriate size tops for your pie dishes.
Take the dish out of the oven and ladel the meat into the individual dishes.
Pop on the tops on the dishes and put back in the oven for 20 mins (gas 4). You could make one large pie using the casserole disk if desiered.
Enjoy!

With 60+ hours on record, I can give a full review of the game.
Story:
Storyline is great! I love that there's a new story with new characters. Cool ideas and well executed. However, it would be great if they recorded some lines for the character for the cutscenes. I mean, trunks and the others talk to you and you just stare at them like a re-tard. I really missed that. The main villain was good, wasn't as memorable or original as the original dbz villains but I liked his concept, design and the story mode in general.
Created Characters:
This is what I always wanted to have and it's awesome! I was expecting that with one of the DLCs or updates we would get more customization options for our characters but apparently that's not happening. What also really sucks is that you can't recolor 95% of the clothes so often your character looks...weird. But I understand it's a work in progress and hopefully the character creator in future games or updates will be upgraded with more races and options. Speaking of which, why has no DLC attended that area? I mean, the game is freaking focused around your created fighter but none of the 3 DLCs attended character creation or customization AT ALL. WHY? It was said they wanted to add ssj3 for the characters but couldnt since nah time...
Battle system:
Combos? Forget about them. Either you spam throws or supers. No use trying to combo in this game, which I hate. the opponent will either teleport, spam evasive skill or other things that will break your combos, unlike let's say BT3 (I may use the example of BT3 a lot since it's in my opinion the only game better than xenoverse). In BT3 you had more complex combos and more options to connect them, you had a far better guard or dodge system and....what's with the recent update that you can knock someone out of the ultimate? Were 12yr old noobs crying about being hit by ultimates? What re-tarded idiot gets hit by a spirit bomb? I can understand super galick gun or symphonic destruction but all other moves are easily avoidable if you aren't a complete skillless dumba**. That goes for supers too. Most of them are easily avoidable and the updates that happened because of whiny 12yr olds rendered some moves so useless that they dont even do what they're supposed to anymore. That addition was unneccessary. Kudos however, to the supers, charging and stamina system. It brings hell of a lot balance. I love that charging has to be a special move not given to all characters and that transformations are temporary and with drawbacks. I also love the in-depth fighting. Every character fights uniquely which is, honestly really amazing to me. You put such time and effort into making each character fight differently, yet in some areas it seems like you just made them in 5 minutes. The supers system is also great, no problems there and the gameplay, despite the criticism above can be really fun (if your opponent isn't an idiot who uses the most broken moves and z souls to kill you in 20 seconds). If you play games to have fun, not to win, this game is definitely for you.
Game Modes:
Wait there are game modes? There's Parallel quests, normal 1v1 or up to 3v3, endless battle is pretty much 1v1 for when you have a 3rd wheel among your friends and the team of time patrollers thingy that literally noone uses.... Where's training? Or any kind of practice? Or a battle like tenkaichi 3 where you have a team of 3 people but they switch out once one fighter dies...Where's time limit settings?  This game has literally dozens of options for awesome game modes and variations but there is....none, practically. The team battle is great, PQs are mostly well thought out and designed, and that's it. Really expected more in this area from the developers.
Servers:
I have to dedicate a special section to this. Xenoverse server is among the sh**tiest, if not the worst game server I've been on. Constantly laggs, it's nigh impossible to complete a parallel quest online with a friend. It laggs more than a stuttering championship. And im sure it's not my fault, my internet speed goes over 15MB/s. Ran BF3, gta V and everything on high graphics nicely but Xenoverse.... It glitches, disconnects on perfectly fine wifi connection, laggs every minute, someone grabs me from the other side of the map....seriously, I almost dont play online anymore, 9/10 cases I dont have a well-running matchup with somebody. Please...urgently fix. Biggest issue of the game. Maybe use an onion instead of a potato, maybe that'll work.
DLC:
First off, I am a huge enemy of DLCs. We can wait. Finish the game until it's perfect to you and then release it. A well rounded, finished game will sell a lot better than a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥game with 10 DLCs. Let's see, shall we? Remove DLC bullsh**. Now,
unlock Vegeta ssj4: Goku is unlocked by completing all PQs. Why not unlock vegeta ssj4 by completing the story?
GT packs 1-2: Story mode has NO replayability. My suggestion would be to hide black star dragonballs in story missions after you beat it so you'd have to reaply story missions to collect 7 black star balls. once you do, take them to trunks and he unlocks the story quests. Beat them, and unlock pan, trunks and goku, along with the GT PQs, where you unlock Eis shenron. Unlock Nova shenron by completing the training with Pan (you'd have motivation to train with masters who dont teach you useful moves)
ssgss goku, vegeta and golden frieza: Complete all parallel quests with at least rank A to get Golden frieza, complete with at least rank S for ssgss Vegeta and rank Z on all PQs for ssgss Goku. Imagine the challenge and gameplay for gamers. Unlock Jaco by completing his training since he also doesnt teach too useful things. Unlock the 3rd DLC PQs by unlocking ssgss Goku. (these 3 characters are the most powerful in the game, it would make sense that they would be hard to unlock)
Towa and mira: same as for PQs. All story missions with rank A unlocks Towa, all missions rank S unlocks Mira and that leaves room for Demigra for rank Z. You'll be replaying the story anyway in order to find the 7 blackstar balls.
BAM, you have a more in-depth unlock system that requires gameplay, is interesting, you can do it with friends anyway and you skip the DLC idiocy. Just letting you know. WE CAN WAIT. we dont care if the game is realeased in 2040, as long as it's really good and awesome. Work on it until it's finished. DBZ fans fap to these games and everyone will buy it even if you put the end price as 200$. Finish the game properly and get great reputation that this game deserves. My friend is a modder. There were files for the gt characters in the game before the DLC was even released. It's more than obvious you could go into an unlock system rather than DLCs.
Character Roster:
Honestly, nice roster, medium-sized, but missing a few characters. Android 16? Uub? Janemba? Cooler? you have clothes for androids 19 and 20 but you dont have them as characters? Buu's forms? Cell's forms? SSJ gogeta?  Then again, yamcha, Krillin and raditz are useless so at least that's staying 100% true to the source material :D
Overall:
Pros: Great story, fun battles, awesome customization, in depth fighting, enjoyable missions, new masters system is a great idea....really fun game
Cons: THE WORST SERVER EVER, DLCs should not be a thing. Please be more creative than that in the future. There's no game modes and customization has a bit too many drawbacks at some areas.

**If you are a Naruto fan** who always wanted a good Naruto game on pc go for it, its totally worth it :D Story mode is really done nicely tho ending is sort of an alternative ending which is not canon, can't blame them for that since the time this was finished cannon story was still going without any sorts of ending. Some cut scenes are very long but animated and voiced superbly so its not a torture to watch 'em. Also in story mode its not just fight after a fight after the cut scene, instead you can explore,so some side missions,send letters(sms equivalent I guess lolz) to your friends & lot more. Even after finishing the main story mode there are so much to do if you are a perfectionist. Fighting mechanism is not complicated at all but its done really well considering this is an anime based game. To finish the story mode you don't need a controller, but its not easy with the keyboard until you get used to it. This edition have all the costume(apart from Goku costume for Naruto & hello kitty costume for Sakura,Goku costume is already ported by the community) & one story dlc included,complete edition.
About the multiplayer mode, this is where things went to hell,at least at the release. At the release netcode was so bad that was impossible to finish a single match without game getting disconnected. But I guess CC2 patched most stuff out & it is more than playable now. But you will need a good connection with good ping to get everything working pretty well. Also beware in matches there will be guys who will spam long range technique characters like no tomorrow to increase their win rank, believe me I played this when it was first out on ps3 thanks to my cousin and it was much worst, most characters CC2 patched out to reduce the unfair advantages I guess so that's a plus.
As a pc port its not a superb port but for me its an okay port considering this was CC2 first PC release. This is more like a direct emulation on pc type of port. It don't have any advanced graphics settings(you can only set resolution,supersampling & vsync) to play with. Game will need at least a good pc to run it on 1080p I guess since game is not greatly optimized to the pc platform. Also there is a 30fps cap that is hard coded to the game engine but it is not that noticeable but might change your decision. Game keys use the xbox style X,Y,A,B method and before starting the game you can map the controls of the keyboard, inside the game it shows X,Y,A,B keys.
As final thoughts this is the best Naruto game out there right now and a year ago nobody even thought there will be a pc port and the best thing is next Naruto game will be released to ps3,xbox 360 & pc simultaneously. Its not a perfect port but its a very enjoyable game, I have 100+ hours on this & this is the only game I've ever pre-ordered. Also this title is not going on sale very much so if you want it now go for it dattebayo :D
Hope my two cents helped someone with their decision =)

Having put a lot of time and effort into the first two titles (and the Gothic trilogy, of course), I figured I'd review this final title.
The ability to sprint is a welcome improvement from the sluggish movement in the first two titles, with the second game's fast-travel making it more bearable than the first game.
I don't think the music keeps in line very well with the themes of the earlier games (risen 2 all the way back to the first Gothic title), though it has its moments. I found the interface clunkier than the second game's, which is very unfortunate.
The main character's (English) voice is terrible; I really wish this horrible voice was allotted to a minor character that dies off very early in the game rather than the one person you have to endure through its entirety. While the voices on the other characters are nice enough, with some, like Bones', improving a bit in my opinion, I find the characters less interesting than in the earlier games.
I thought the combat in Risen was too plain, I thought the combat in Risen 2 was *excellent*, and I think the combat in Risen 3 is...not very good, though not necessarily a step backward. I was hesitant to try Risen 2 after my pleasant experiences with the Gothic titles and the first Risen, but after getting it on sale I was extremely impressed and thought it kept the spirit of the earlier games alive. As a consequence, I approached Risen 3 with very high expectations, none of which were really met. I don't think anyone stands to *lose* from trying it, but I can't recommend it.

I prefer single player games, so this is what I've tested during the free week on Steam. At that time game was in Early Access, so one could expect a lot more stuff to be added in the final release.
However I can assure you that what is already present is quite solid.
The look and feel of the game kind of reminded me of Alien vs Predator game. Dark setting, enemies die quickly, but so do you. There were just 2 functional weapons, and both were on fully automatic mode, where you can easy waste all your ammo. There are some stealth elements, and while the game is not DeusEx or Thief, it certainly helps to shoot the light out. That also reminded me of AvP. I like that game.
There was no campaign, the available levels were mostly designated as training. Even the levels that looked like story mission ended up as training. It is kind of frustrating that there wes no savegame/checkpoint since some of the levels are quite huge and repeating same entry again and again might not be as fun. Maybe respawning without resetting the level when in SinglePlayer should be an option. Trying to avoid been shot in the back, kind of forces you to avoid exploration (there are journals that try to tell you a story in one of the levels).  All the enemies on the available levels were humanoid robots, that kind of reminded me of Terminators. Because of the dark settings you are most likely to rely on the sound they make in order to ... locate and neutralize them,
I should praise one of the enemies. They are robots that are kind of crazy. They run around the room aimlessly, hiding behind obstacles, staying out of your sight, walking when you walk, stopping when you stop and then, suddenly they sprint at you (usually behind your back) in order to beat you. To be honest, despite their low danger level, they were one of the most creepiest enemies I've seen so far. For a moment I felt like I'm playing Amnesia (Dark Descent). I'm kind of terrified from the though of such enemy with a ranged weapon - a real nightmare.
I didn't test Coop or Deadmatch, and I do expect these to be the strongest sides of this game. However I liked what I saw. The game is promising and I hope that it stays on the right course.

Ive never been a very big fan of MMO's. Ive tried WoW, Guild Wars, LoTR online and others and just never felt the call that would make me stay with it. Ive also never written a Steam review before. But this game is an absolute masterpiece of science fiction and online sandbox gaming that I feel deserves my recommendation.
It needs to be said immediatly that this is a game that you MUST have innitiative to play. This game will not grab you by the hand and take you on a magical adventure. If you expect this, you will sit in station, spinning your ship, get bored, maybe mine a bit and quit claiming eve to be boring and for masochists. Dont do this. If you are not willing or able to put the time and effort in to learn a bit and do things without being told to explicitly, Eve may not be for you.
If you do dive into the universe of New Eden though, after completing the tutorials I have some advice. Grab your cheapest, fastest, frigate and set destination to the deepest corner of player controlled Null Security space you can and try to get there. You wont. You will explode at some point. But along the way you will learn a lot, have fun, meet people who will most likley help you in learning the game, and begin to see this world for what it is and forget about the stupid "spread sheet simulator" and "i dont have a PhD so i cant play eve" non sense.  This sort of "lets get out there and do stuff" attitude will lead to you creating your own stories and fun and that is what eve is about.
The new devolpment cycle is another reason to recommend this game. Previously Eve had a bi yearly expansion cycle. All expansions free. Now CCP has moved to a 6 week release cycle (still free) that has given the game an incredible sense of momentum and constant refinement that it didnt have before. They have also doubled down on listening to community feed back and iterating on the games strengths, along with playing up the story and lore of the universe.
No other MMO has the ability for new players to become invovled in end game level content so fast. Titans (the biggest most powerful ships in the game) have been killed with the help of trial account new players. My wormhole based corp has recruited players in their first two weeks and they have thrived. A tech 1 frigate with basic skills can wreak havoc with electronic warfare modules, or tackle ships that cost literally thousands of times as it with a pilot who has been playing for years, holding them down for fleet members to blast away at them. What other MMO allows a new player to get in the face of and actually threaten a veteran player in PvP?
One last note is, for the love of god dont try to make enough money to buy your subsription with in game money in the first few months. It will suck the fun out of this incredible experience and will burn you out. Buy ships. Explode them. Learn. Laugh. Find a good group of players to play with and do what excites you. There is literally no other game on the market like eve and you wont regret trying it.

Proteus, while not really a game, definitely comes close to being one.
Placing you in a randomly generated world, you walk around exploring an island as the seasons change. The design of the island and the art style, and what I presume to be dynamic sounds, go far in giving the game a very calm and relaxing atmosphere.
Things seem very upbeat and alive in summer, with lots of wildlife that reacts to your movements dynamically, and when winter comes around things start to feel extremely bleak and lonely. Despite the fact that everything is pixelated, it is still very immersive.
Controlled with either a gamepad or the keyboard (mouse optional), the game plays very well with the sole exception of you not being able to jump.
I wouldn't bother buying this game if you want a story or some aim, but if you want to spend an small while just exploring a randomly generated artistic representation of an island you should buy it.

I am ghoultrooper of Alexina lvl 11k. I've been with Mabinogi for a long time playing on and off since 2008. i wanted to input my views of the game so here we go:
The Pros~
+ Unique Rock paper Scissor style of combat *
+ Infinity customization in coloring anything from the soles of your shoes and outfits to the hilts of your weapons
+ Newbie Friendly Beginner System ( helps you somewhat catchup to the current players )
+ Unique Rebirth Leveling up System which has no LvL Cap ( main reason i haven't ever permanently quit )
+ Events come by frequently and so do content updates every few months
+ Many Crafting Skills
+ Abundant amounts of daily minigames/quests that you can do
+ Nice Story
+ Playerbase is Mostly Friendly.
The Cons...
- Nexon.
- Has a somewhat steep learning curve.
- Reforges are from cash shop only but are obtainable from other players via in game gold.
-* The unique combat system slowly dies off as you gain High Dmg. you will end up using just the efficient clearing methods ( although that can be said for most of any game )
-~ Inventory can become an Issue if you're a hoarder like i am. Pets are almost a must buy utility BUT you are able to buy pets from other players with gold also so...
-in my honest opinion, at least half of the NA server is lazy af. so many  people just afk and don't run anything ( missions, dungeons, etc. )
- 7  channels but everyone clogs up on channel 1 and channel 2 through 7 are almost like ghost towns zzzz....
- Durability.
Neutral
**- Despite what many people say, Nothing in Mabinogi is actually Pay2Win. Everything is obtainable through grind or luck. things in the Cash Shop are more of Convenience/ Fashion Items.
Conclusion.
I find the game fun to play every now and then but once you've got your gear and many of the skills done there isn't much left to do. the Dye customizations are great!
I Recomend any new players to find a nice guild or just a nice veteran player in general to help guide you through. guilds are generally very nice in Mabi overall and will help you often.

So, I got this game a while back but put it to the side for a while because I had other flashier games that were calling for my attention.
After a while I wound up bored while doing work study at my local college and finding out it was more workSTUDY with a severe lack of enough study to keep me busy, so I was compiling a list of all the titles my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Toshiba laptop could run and this one came up.
Today I killed the leader of the lizardfolk that were threatening the lives of the humans of Avernum, explored the Abyss, discovered the return of a demonic overlord, plunged into a crypt, reforged the legendary sword 'Demonsbane' and after all that paused finally to say "wait, what ♥♥♥♥ing time is it?".
As Ben 'Yahtzee' Croshaw once said there are two types of games. Games I've stopped playing because I'm approaching a state of boredom akin to rigor mortis and games I've stopped playing because I just realized I should have had dinner two hours ago. This one is officially the latter.
Don't let the 'this thing was cutting edge when the SNES was still big news' appearance scare you off. If you let yourself get drawn into it you'll find a surprisingly deep game with some really well-written dialogue, funny characters, some genuine excitement, and loads of exploration. I honestly laughed out loud when I found the Spider village, where all the sentient spiders live who are very friendly, talk like small children, and are all named Spider. It was both cute and pretty damn weird.
So yes, if you an old RPG fan like me this game is definitely worth a look, as are Spiderweb's other titles. Sadly Geneforge seems to♥♥♥♥♥♥up on my computer, probably Windows 10, but the Avernum games are top notch for those who want something that feels more like a classic game or whose computers can't handle big stodgy titles like Fallout 4.

This game used to be a charming experience where magic, fighting bows and fantasy came together in a unique way. The game is far butchered now compared to it's older version.
Before: Up to three levels of spells in both priest and mage classes so that you can indulge in a magic fantasy playing the game. With secrets at every turn for your wizard to decode and dangerous territory where they have to show their wit in using their magic to upgrade their arsenal and using it creatively to beat the lords of magic themselves, the slitheraki or however you spell that...
Now: Even with three levels of spells you are limited to 5 spells either mage or priest. Mages might as well be replaced with archers until you find a spell that can hit more than one target. Priests are nice for minor heal but cannot bless the party for a long time.
Now:
Speaking of buying, selling and upgrades... nothing you get from battles is worth anything... There are times that have values that shops will not take anywhere. Items worth 240 suddenly worth 6 in a shop...
Before:
Things costed alot but you could sell items during battle, find money and not [5 coins] per 3 mobs or even find loot that is an upgrade to what you had without going into their preset dungeons.
Before:
A game about survival where your party had to eat in order to sustain themselves so sleeping outdoors while sometimes bad was a way of hunting AND healing your party. If you didn't play this well, you'd end up with having to remake characters you put time into because they died. [Unless you found/decoded a high level revive spell]
Now:
The revive spell is in the game but... what's the point!? You can walk into town and get free heals. "Survival" You don't need to eat anything. The food items aren't even worth picking up, they heal you for garbage amounts. Speaking of which rather than enriching their item pool and allowing you to diversify how you play, they've just created more garbage for you to pick up.
Before:
The game was hard but you could select information out of conversations you had with people in order to find interesting things to do and tidbits of information. The quests that you took up on your own accord were the experience to level up your party and when you came back to claim the gold reward after barely surviving that was the icing on the cake.
Now:
THe quests give experience because the mobs sure don't give enough. You are forced into conversations where you have pre-established answers which sound nothing like what you'd even ask about in a conversation to the point where it makes you seem really naive or stupid. Hell half of the information you can ignore and walk into who needs conversations anyway. Also they'll mark it on the map for ya, no need to explore or be a cartographer.
Before:
Having useful skills in and out of combat was possible and while not needed sometimes made the return to civilization what little you got pretty fun.
Now:
Some things are taken out because during a level up you really don't get all that much to train yourself. It's probably due to the fact that the items and money drops from mobs are garbage because in the old Exile you had to not only have leveled up to train and allot points, you also had to pay for the training. Now you somehow train yourself cuz you know everything you just don't have "EXP" and only casters suffer the need of learning from someone else.
Before:
Armor reduced damage, better armor reduced it better. These were flat amounts. You still needed hp, magic doesn't care about your armor and the strongest foes can use magic that you like to use all the time!
Now:
Enemies don't need to use magic to overwhelm you because armor only increases the damage you reduce by a percentage. So rather than buying something nice to actually protect yourself it's more like you will always take damage from a foe but can lower it somewhat. Mind you that healing in battle either cost money [which you won't have] via potions or mana [which cannot be healed outdoors or in dungeons even by waiting in safe areas that you've explored and mapped like a smart survivor.]
Exile used to be a brutal game where you felt like you were thrown down the pit and each battle brought you closer to your goal of getting out. This version either you play at a low difficulty and give yourself a yawn fest or you play at a high difficulty and wonder why you play. This isn't one of those "Strategizing rpgs" at that point, it becomes a luck and trial game because the game cannot sustain itself. I did play it on the strongest difficulty but that's because I played it before expecting the same fun gameplay with a tough twist. Instead the gameplay is boring and now feels like a rip off of newer games. [Questing for exp, dumbed down,  does not self sustain, barely on topic, pompous pretending to make something hard with modes when it's just a percentage modifier to things that are there already... Give me back Exile. I am glad I only bought Avernum for 3 bucks but it really wasn't worth that either!]

It's very... Early access.
The overall athmosphere of the game is great, the graphics and the ambience play very well together. As for now, I will not comment on the RPG aspects of the game, which are as of now nonexistent. If you've ever played the classic "Chaser", you know what the gameplay is like at the moment. Run around, find objectives, shoot stuff.
Let's dissect this.
Running around feels nice and fluid, the view bobbing is nice and I really appreciate the way stamina in this is done.
It effects your aim and you can tell by how heavy your character is breathing how exhausted you are.
Also walking around reduces your accuracy and increases recoil.
The jumping gets a bit tacky when you access areas you're not supposed to be in, but I guess I really can't complain about that.
Find objectives.
This one is more on the negative side.
There are only waypoints, nothing else to help you navigate.
Also, there doesn't seem to be a way to review mission objectives, but I'm not sure.
How the campaign missions play out has already been mentioned: Run around, Find objectives, Shoot stuff. At the moment, the "Story" is not very rewarding.
Shoot stuff.
It took me quite some fiddling to get the camera sensitivities to acceptable levels. It's either agonizingly slow, or 5px further on the slider it's ridiculously fast. Plus points for independantly adjustable sliders.
You do well to fire single shots or bursts in this, as going full auto scatters your aim all over the place. Currently, there are only 2 weapons available but more have been promised, so I can't give you any reviewing on that. The weapons that are implemented work, one for close quarters combat and one for medium range combat (SMG and Assult Rifle).
Overall I like the game. The state it's in right now makes it kind of fiddly and hard to keep paying attention to, but the developers very well showed what they can do and I would say they have the potential to make something of this. Although when I first started it, I was hoping to see a lot more story done, a campaign mode (instead of this mission based stuff like WarFace and all these other games), that jig so I'm hoping I won't be disappointed in the later stages of this game's development. I would also like to see world physics - The ragdolls already work.
TL:DR
+ Very nice athmosphere
+ Good stamina implementation
+ Neat graphics and style
+ Starts right at the tutorial
~ Gameplay is solid but repetitive. No RPG elements yet
~ The aim sensitivity is very fiddly
~ The moving physics get fiddly when you try to balance in areas
- Some bugs naturally, sometimes the screen goes dark as if the light turned off when you look at your own shadow in a corner
A perfect pick-up-and-play title. Hope to see more from this developer.

Oh man, what a god-awful console port. I can't believe I bought this at full price.
Menu? It doesn't exist, there's only a hub world so going to the shop is a major hassle, as is doing anything, really. Also, you have to be online the whole time, even for story mode.
Oh, and I didn't like having to use a third party script to make use of my 2560*1080 monitor. It's dumb because there's even an option for 2560*1080 in the settings but all that does is put black bars on the side.
The levelling system sucks, I finished the story at level 40-something and you really need to grind to be able to keep up with the levelling pace of the story.

First of all, let me emphasize that this is a Piranha Game in all aspects. Which is good for me, but apparently does not fit well with some people.
I started playing Piranha Games with Gothic 1 and played every game since, so I knew what to expect and am happy to report that the NPCs talk at length about trivial things and have to be forced to get to the point, you only get a fixed set of useful Armor that is restricted to your Group etc.
A lot of people apparently don't like this, but for me that's a Piranha Game. If you liked the first two Gothics, this game is for you.
As a long-time fan, here's what I think about Risen 3 compared to the Gothic series and the other two Risens:
I loved it. It reminded my why I fell in love with Gothic and I am going to play it again to see the way the game goes if you choose to be something else then a Voodoo-Pirate.
In comparison to Risen 2 I think it's much better. Which is great, as I thought Risen 2 was way better then Risen 1, so this seems to be a trend.
Even the usually sucking Piranha Final Boss Battle was bearable. As a reminder, in Risen 1 the final Boss Battle neglected all your "life choices" and stuck you into magic Armor and Weaponry that made you a great fighter, even if you had gone the Mage way and put you into some kind of Arcade-Battle against a Big-Boss. Ugh.
Risen 2 had Mara, but I only remember from that fight that I didn't like it.
This time, it had sucking moments, sure. But I could play to my strengths I acquired during the game and at one point Bones jumped in to save the day, which I assume was a bug, but I liked it.
Compared to the Gothic Series I dare say this is the game I was hoping for when Gothic 3 came out. It had all the charm, wits and anecdotes that made the first two Gothic Parts great and none of the empty world and hastily crafted Quests. Playing Risen 3 I couldn't but think of how great a game Gothic 3 could have been if it came out a year later. Even half a year.
So all good? Of cause not. There are a lot of things they can do better and I hope they will for Risen 4. But none of the following "bad stuff" really impacted my great experience, so read them as "minor issues".
- I love the Kila, but hate the Post-Imperialistic, "noble savage", "half naked exotic beauty that speaks in Umpa-Lumpa" stile. You can do better than just throwing together all the cliche to mix up a "tribe".
- Whatever happened to Patty? Why does she look like some Pirate-Porn Star? Honestly, this kind of "Fan Service" makes me feel treated like a 14 year old with a puberty issue. I see what you thought I would like and feel dirty.
- Where's my Marvin Mode? One of the really cool things about Piranha Games was the "and now I will change everything to how I like it" Marvin Mode. Missed it greatly. Reduces replay-value. Basically, give me back my Marvin Mode.
- If I have to hear Bones say "Aus deiner Haut mache ich mir eine Mütze!" one more time...
- I would have liked a way to solve the Noise behind Paula's house without killing the armadillo.
- Light. I know this does not happen to everyone, but every time I entered a cave darkness took me like a black flood that even torches could not dispense. Looting caves without telekinesis was basically impossible as I could not see anything smaller then a sword.
- Story-restriction to Voodoo body-snatching. I get that this could be a story breaker, but there have to be better ways to restrict this then simply allowing it only if it fits the narrative.
These things I could go without
* Astral View. Never used it. No idea why I would or should have.
+ The World. I liked to just hang out with the Pirates on Kila or the Kila on Kila (Reaaallly smooth...) or...
+ The Characters. There are no Diegos, but a lot of likeable NPCs and taking some of them along was great fun.
+ The Story. It was easy to follow without being too predictable. Yeah, there was obviously some arch-nemesis going to be there for the surprisingly minor-sucking End Battle, but other then that I liked it. Quests were mostly fun too.
+ Easy mode that means "easy fights" for people like me who take fighting as a "have to do that" in RPGs
+ Mud. Yeah, really. Loved it. Even took him along after he left on his own free will. That's how it goes with old “friends”...
++ Parrot-Flight. You'll know it when you get it. I've spend hours flying around.

A fine RPG styled like the games back in the DOS days. Not much handholding here, which takes some getting used to if you've grown accustomed to that. It has a sizeable world that's depressive, but still full of flavor. The game's not easy, it requires patience and cunning to get through its dungeons, castles and ruins. There are even hidden bosses that you might not want to trigger until you've grown a bit stronger. And there's often more than one way to approach a problem, or enter an area. In short, the game demands patience and tactical thinking, and offers a great experience in return.

I would rate this game a solid "Good".  The storyline is interesting.  But the NPC interactions do get extremely long and boring.  The fight mechanics (left mouse - attack, right mouse - parry) is okay but isn't and hasn't been perfected.  The fights end up being a cross betwen easy (at times) to extremely annoying.  The game allows you to play in it as (almost) open world.  But by doing so you end up completing most every quest on an island by the time you actually head to town.  The user interface is adequate and all the controls do take a bit to get used to especially if you have played more modern games as of late and then decided to play an older one like this.
Is this worth the purchase?  I would say, "Yes".  It isn't a game that I feel I would replay.  But it is enjoyable enough for me to immediately consider purchasing Risen 4 if and when it comes out.  All in all, this isn't a game you will love but it is a game you will like.

There's no way I could not give this game a "Recommended" rating, but it comes with some significant qualifications:
Avernum: Escape from the Pit is better than the original Avernum 1 in some ways, and worse in others.  I was disappointed that it wasn't much of an upgrade.  The engine is practically identical, so it just felt like I was replaying Avernum 1 with a couple of usability mods tacked on.  Fortunately, Avernum 1 was an amazing game, so I had almost as much fun replaying it as I did playing it for the first time.  I loved the story, I loved the length, and I loved the challenging turn-based tactical combat which rewards good planning and equipment choice as well as good combat decisions.
Long-time fans of the series will know that there are three versions of this game.  The first, Exile 1, is a non-isometric overhead 2D tactical RPG.  Very fun, but the Avernum remake blew it out of the water.  This remake of Avernum just adds a few "enhancements," some of them desirable and some not.
BETTER THAN THE ORIGINAL AVERNUM:
Notable locations in towns and dungeons (shops, important NPCs, spellbooks you may want to return to a second time, etc.) are now marked on your map, which helps decrease the copious note-taking this game requires.  Note that you will still have to have some paper beside you (or a text file ready to alt-tab to), to record many places you will want to return to later, or quest details that aren't automatically added to your quest journal.
There are some additional areas to flesh out the game world, and some additional fun dungeons.
Hidden areas now have a visual cue, obviating the need to tediously bump your character against the sides of the maps to find them.
WORSE THAN THE ORIGINAL AVERNUM:
The skill and perk system has been overhauled to make it less likely you will unintentionally create a weak character.  I consider this undesirable both because the players who actually need such a feature aren't a good match for a game like this and because much of the fun, flexibility, and personality of the original system has been lost.  Furthermore, I believe that the "problem" being addressed is already covered by the fact that the difficulty can be changed at any time.
Some of the content additions to this version of the game kill the mystery and thrill of the original game.  I can't be more specific without spoiling it for you, but things you really aren't meant to see until you are well into the game, in my opinion, are now accessible to you early on.
The World Map now autoscrolls instead of letting you explore it one screen at a time, making it both easier to miss things and more annoying to track what you have already explored and what you have left to explore.
Also, I can't remember if this was in the original version or not, but there is a "soft" level cap at 30, after which you only get a chance to allocate level-up points every five levels (which means level 35, really, since you will probably finish the game before level 40).  Worse, there is NO warning about this!  This can really screw up some of your planning, as many skills require a certain level before the ability you want is available to you.  Of course, this downside won't apply to you, because I just warned you. ;)
THE VERDICT:
Both versions of this game are amazing, so there's no question about my recommending it or not.  So which version should you play?
If you are a more casual player, worried about making mistakes with your character creation and upon leveling up, get this version.  And if you are not interested in challenging combat, you can also put the difficulty on "Normal" or "Casual," and just enjoy the story.  If you have trouble finding the original and/or getting it to run on your modern computer, you can settle for this version as well--it's not significantly worse.
If you are a player who cut your teeth on old CRPGs in the 80s and 90s, or if you don't mind dealing with retro conventions, go for the original.  Much of the content you are giving up is not necessarily an improvement to the overall package, and character creation and growth is a LOT more fun.  Just be prepared to take lots of additional notes on the locations of shops and important NPCs in towns.

It's a simple roguelike with an okay first five (30 second) levels and then it gets... pissy.
You have to get in front of every enemy's face with your melee weapon and shield the entire time.  Your enemies have nothing but homing projectiles that go around you, stun effects, fire effects, frustrating positioning, and all-around pain in the A to kill.
The spikes and gas faces are just there to top it off.  You can't stand in the same place for more than 1 second.  You can't hug the wall while you're being cornered.  You can't try to skip enemies.
The game definitely gives you your challenges, but no real solutions to handle them.

Even though it's in EA and not f2p, this is still pretty good for how it is. It's slow at first, but it starts to stack up over time. It's not like the other ones, i.e. Tap Heroes, Clicker Heroes, or Sakura Clicker, it's more like Adventure Capitalist where you sit and gradually upgrade your mineral per second. Edit 2: With the update that fixed minor things, it seemed to have gotten a bit better. I, honestly, enjoy the new wage system. Just be careful, if you type in "100", it'll get rid of all your coins per second.
Edit 3: After playing over a hundred hours, I can honestly say this is the best clicker/idle game I've played, it's really quite enjoyable. It's not too clicky or too grindy, you can even restart every 30 minutes if you gain enough culture points (One Civilization Point per 125 Culture) in a short amount of time.

A sandbox community/colony simulator that, thanks to years of development and an abundance of mods, is really starting to stand shoulder to shoulder with famous greats in the genre such as dwarf fortress. although the depth of minute detail is not equal here, it makes up for it with much simpler to use clickable graphical interfaces. the ingame scenario editor and development mode make customizing challenges or world conditions to suit your whims a breeze.
still, the game needs many more improvements to meet its full potential. especially interactions with other factions and settlements is very basic, and certain features and creatures mentioned in the "background lore" writeup file the game do not appear at all, yet.
the greatest downside i can think of is the fact that my 8 years old laptop struggles with it, which is why i tend to play it with steam shut off, because steam hogs resources too these days. also, some of the stats and damage values on some of the weapons are a bit iffy, like a short bow doing more damage per shot than an assault rifle, but that's what mods and complaining on the suggestion forums is for.
what i'm going to say next may not make sense without the qualifier of the fact that i sometimes suffer extremely bad buyer's remorse and guilt and etc. but i would like you to know that i have not regretted this purchase one bit, and that says a lot, in my mind. if youre waiting on a sale, youre probably going to be waiting a few more years, or maybe even more than just a few.

Rarely do I feel obligated to write a 100% glowing review for a game, yet I can't help but to do so with Tales from the Borderlands. The characters are all smartly written and compelling, the dialogue is hilarious (though it may be a hit or miss case if you aren't normally a fan of typical Borderlands style humor), and the animation is done very well, especially considering Telltale's less than stunning engine. If you want a story driven Borderlands game with shooting elements and a lack of QTEs, you shouldn't be looking here. Yes, the 'game', in true Telltale fashion, simply boils down to an interactive movie, but the choices in this game are interesting enough that I really felt like I was a part of the experience. Finally, I have to give credit to Telltale for their phenomenal music choices in Tales from the Borderlands. Each episode features a different opening track, and each one is equally awesome and memorable.

To make it short, just read this review as it's basically how I feel about this game:
I don't know what this game wants to be, nor I care to follow its history and the current discussions as I don't care much about early-access stuff, but I can give you some short details about my own, short, experience with it.
To descript it visually, just take the first F.E.A.R., worsen visual quality by reducing models polygon count, quantity and quality of textures, and take out most of its special effects except shadowing. Now reduce framerate by at least 75% and you pretty much have a good idea of how this game looks like.
I'm not kidding. I don't know what engine this game uses and how, but even reducing graphics quality to the minimum gives me only like 5fps more than max settings, and I can play any game here, usually at max detail with 16xAF and 4x AA.
It's not unplayable but the performance/detail ratio is just terrible right now, so consider that if your system is not very powerful.
(EDIT: ok I just checked the game's directory and the game is using Unity. That explains the terrible performance and will also give you a good insight of what you can expect from this game in the future: a lot of troubles.)
The game starts with a tutorial. It all goes well though it's pretty tedious, but I've seen worse. The real problem starts with the campaign. I'm not really into tactical shooters and I don't even see anything that tactical in this game, I just know that there's no save button that I can find and the enemy can take you down in just 2 shots, and that happens more often than just taking 1 single shot. With that I mean that you often die by what seem to be just a single bullet but I learned that it's actually 2 shots in rapid succession: the first takes out your armor completely (it will auto regenerate after a lot of seconds) and the second will kill you.
Ok I'm probably too much into Rambo-style games, where you just rush into packs of enemies at once, but that's just silly. I would have enjoyed it a bit more if it weren't for that, but after dying a couple times I decided it was time to move on and try the coop.
I don't like versus games, so I just wanted to test the coop mode. Despite of me choosing coop from the menu, I was presented by a big server list of on-going games, which keeps updating making it hard to pick the one you need (at least if you sort them by ping, as I usually do). It becomes a FPS game into a FPS game to aim and shoot the join button of the right server you want to join in less than a second, but I'm sure that situation will get better after the free week.
The real problem is that this list also had versus games, which I accidentally joined. I then realized my mistake (I was attracted by the high player count), got killed in the usual 2-shots-that-looked-like-1 and then left it.
I then joined a real coop game and the situation didn't get better, but actually worse.
People kept joining and then leaving after 10 minutes of going around pointlessly, looking for whatever the game wanted us to look for, with no sight of enemies, unpickable cards (they were maybe audiologs but I don't know, they just looked like keycards to me), closed doors and out-of-map fun, but yeah, that gets old soon.
I tried a couple more games but one ended seconds after I joined, with the usual mass player leave after it, and the other had a mass leave before it ended, so I was left alone with not much to do.
It all looks very early, very simple, already seen, bland.
I'm not sure for how long the developers has been working on this, but considering what I saw, the road ahead is very long still. So long that it looks almost endless considering how much work this game seem to need before becoming interesting, at least for me.
From my very little experience, it seem that the only thing this game has to offer right now is a versus mode that seem to work, though I didn't really look so much into it because of the reasons above.
Not my kind of game right now, but I hope one day it'll get finished, and then I'll happily take another look at it.

Having not even 10 hours into ann MMO game, so my point of view is only really of the first impressions I got of the game.  10 hours is still a hefty amount of time spent on one thing, though, and do I have a wall of text of an opinion on it.
VISUAL:  Nothing noteworthy graphics-wise, if not even decent.  It’s a shame you can’t see more of what’s happening since the draw distance is abysmal, even with highest settings.  The camera will go out of control in certain areas (such as Bangor with their tight cliff walls), and one of my first game experiences had me stuck in the first quest giver’s building as the camera glitched out and could not zoom or focus enough to see the exit door and leave.
The minimap is only useful for seeing where you are, as by default it shows no other players and party members are represented by delayed or outright wrong last seen locations.  The HUD is your standard MMO fare, but beware when you increase the resolution; it shows its age and the thing becomes so small it is near unreadable.
SOUND:  Really not much to say here, it will probably be too loud by default when you first start it up.
GAMEPLAY:  Skill system seems like a good idea on paper, being able to strengthen which skills you want by using them more often and in certain ways, but quickly shows its flaws.  “Windmill” move in particular, unless you use this move exclusively early game I don’t know how one can max this skill out.  I got to the point where it will only gain experience if I use it on “powerful” enemies, but even using it on enemies classified so soon became impossible; progression on the move completely stalled simply because I leveled up too much before the exponential growth of the enemies overtook me.  Even using it on a dungeon boss did not qualify as being “powerful” despite being able to destroy our entire group with one swing.  Which brings me to the next issue, the rampant spikes in enemy strength.  The particular dungeon was filled with goblins and imps that we could all easily defeat without a scratch on us, if they even get a chance to hit us before we systematically genocide the entire ruin.   Then comes out the bosses (plural), each one we can barely put a dent in before severely or outright killing a member of the party.  Practically no prior warning to the sudden player abuse that was waiting for us.  Similar experiences from friends who were grinding in the underpowered monster areas that for some odd reason had something incredibly more powerful mixed in.
The combat system does not help fight them either.  While, once again, the pseudo RPS and timing oriented turn based combat sounds at least a step above an average click-based combat, connection issues plagued half the battles I was involved in.  Animations skipped and enemies warped, my computer and internet was more than enough to handle this game, yet I easily kept getting stunlocked due to me sometimes not being able to make a move from the input lag (unless this is normal, then which case being stunlocked by PvE is ♥♥♥♥ing annoying).
When not in combat, the inventory is a mess.  Items had no pattern that I could see whether it could be stacked or not, a single sheet of paper can take up the same amount of space as a pair of shoes, if items can be stacked most of the times they cannot be stacked high, if you were to accidentally use a stack of items for a cooking ingredient the entire stack was used instead of the single item, etc. etc.  The worst was how much space gold takes up the inventory, especially considering how ridiculously expensive everything is, even more so considering how as a beginner player most of it was practically inaccessible.
TL;DR:  Everything feels clunky, and a common thought while playing the game was: “This could be done better.” 3/10

If you're a fan of the Risen games, this iteration won't dissappoint.  The character levelling/RPG elements are unique and as entertaining as always.  The writing and voice acting are extremely rough.  If you're a fan of exploration, there are hundreds of secret nooks and crannies if you're willing to spend the time to look around.  Unlike the previous games, the melee combat in this one is actually enjoyable.
The game does one particularly interesting thing - it opens up pretty much the entire world to you immediately, and the enemies do not scale with your level.  This has advantages and disadvantages. Oh, boy. Where do I start? I probably wasn't even 5 when Spiderweb Software came out with games but somehow they managed to reach our old Mac. Needless to say the original game was unplayable with the skill and attention span a child might have between the ages of 5 to 10 but something about the original Exile games managed to stick with my older brother who's 4 years older than me. He's followed Spiderweb's releases and remakes of Exile religiously ever since, so naturally he was ecstatic to see me checking out this remake on Steam. Having never touched the games aside from making a party, getting lost at the starting point and giving up, what did I think of this incarnation of a classic?
The first thing that's clear is how streamlined the interface has become, I believe Jeff has been working on making all the Avernum games run on the same engine to get them all consistant. It was a lot easier to maneuver through making a party and looking at all the spells/abilities... which used to have a lot more of to the point of insanity. Luckily, the spells that have been removed were either combined with other spells or removed because they really weren't necessary.
Questing and leveling is also pretty straightforward. Conversing with NPCs used to require you entering actually words yourself to get answers and information, now it's more standard with a choice of questions or answers to get what you want. The world itself feels large and lively with a map that you will be using a lot. There's a lot of choice in how your party gets shaped and your actions in questlines affect what happens at the end of the game for at least 3 types of endings.
There's no music in this game but the ambience and sound effects make up for that. If it gets too quiet for your liking you can run some of your own music to fit the mood, classical music was my choice and it fit surprisingly well. :) The graphics are also pretty simple but detailed enough to tell what's going on. Spell effects are different for each spell so you know what you just fired is indeed a fireball and blizzards are made of ice.
Combat is done in turns and has each character in the battle using action points. Using all your action points ends that character's turn while saving action points smartly allows you to attack or move multiple times. There's various skills and spell effects, defending, mana conservation and looting to take into account in every battle so there's some pretty large amounts of strategy to this game. Running in blind is a very bad idea and you should save often however...even on easy you can get ambushed and overwhelmed whether it's a fort, dungeon or out in the open-world... some of the enemies run faster than you also btw. :P
The most unique thing about Avernum (and most of Spiderweb's other games) is the writing and sometimes bizarre humor. It's charming and sometimes unnecessarily descriptive about some items or people in the world of Avernum... it's also a legacy to Jeff's imagination all those years ago, he's admitted while updating these games that even he thinks he was crazy when writing them and he'll never be able to create something like them ever again.
While admitting I am influenced a bit by the nostalgia, I think there's plenty for a new player to enjoy in Avernum if RPGs are their favorite pastime. There's a plethora of guides covering all sorts of playthroughs and party builds. This game was also a decent challenge on the lowest difficulty setting and it goes up to nightmare. The community on Steam and the official Spiderweb website is friendly, helpful and pretty enthusiastic about new people getting into the games AND in case you still aren't sure about the games, Spiderweb offers a free demo which you can upgrade to the full game without having to start a new game. :)
P.S.: There are 574 rocks in the game... I may have missed a couple.

The sluggish movement and bad camera design make this game tedious and frustrating.
Touring a procedurally generated island would usually be a fun thing to do, but I wouldn't exactly call this exploring. The constant wrestling with the restrictive camera angle and the stifling walking speed makes this an exercise in patience. Instead of feeling free to explore, I feel claustrophobic.
The camera cannot look up or down past a certain angle from the horizon. Looking down from a precipice or up at the tree isn't possible. Climbing up or descending steep slopes means the player can't watch where they're going, which feels very unnatural.
The environment is nice enough from a distance, but the 2D sprites can be really immersion breaking. Tree branches rotate to constantly face the camera in that eerie fashion.
The music is not good.
The day-night cycles are much too quick, and the stars in the sky look very artificial.
Some creatures just ignore collision detection.
The default mouse settings has smoothing enabled, and only 10% sensitivity.

Pros:
-Easy to learn combat that still manages to heavily rely on tactical gameplay
-Enough of a story line to keep you interested
-Many many many hours of gameplay if you search out side content (I'm guessing I'm not even half way through the game yet at 41 hours)
-Noticeable area difficulty - stray too far too soon and you're sure to get burned to a crisp
-Skill customization - you can level whatever skills you like, as long as you've unlocked the prerequesite
-Working control scheme that hasn't been brutalized in favor of controller support (as is the fad nowadays)
Meh:
-Character customization is pretty simplistic.  Choose from a handful of stock avatars.  Doesn't detract from the game, but doesn't stand out either.
-Graphics - Same as the character customization, the graphics work, but feel rather dated.  At times, the art gives me the distinct feel of a late 90's PC RPG.
Cons:
-At times, it can be easy to get lost when looking for new locations, even with the help of a questline.  While this can sometimes lead to good things, like finding secret areas, more often than not it has caused me to wander into areas above my level, causing me to die or run away screaming.  This is subjective of course, as I may also have poor sense of direction lol.
-When learning to play the game, you really need to pay attention to what strategies work in combat, or you'll find yourself in frustrating situations.  In the beginning, almost any strategy works, misleading you into thinking your current strategies are good enough.  In reality, I found myself being forced to reroll a new game a couple times just to try some different approaches to combat.  New starting skills to aid in my survivability and varying methods of damage output, to fight tough enemies like mages that like to disable half (or more) of your team in a single shot.
(Honestly, I'm not sure if this is a Con or a Pro, as it really makes you think and adds to the strategy any RPG.  But it can be frustrating all the same, having to restart because your current builds can't counter something.  Casual gamers and those new to this type of game, may have trouble with this.)
Summary:
Awesome game.  Plays a lot like older and newer turn based RPGs, like Divinity:OS or perhaps Fallout Tactics:BoS.  Sure to be enjoyed by anyone that's a fan of turnbased isometric RPGs.

* Please note my Hero Siege experience includes owning additional three DLCs: The Karp of Doom, The Depths of Hell and Wrath of Melvius.
Every now and then I get an urge to participate in senseless acts of violence. And it can't get more senseless than hack'n'slash games. Please, don't even try to defy my logic here - RPG take on action genre is mostly ridicolous, yet I admit - it is also strangely satisfying.
I've decided to pick Hero Siege and three available 'rift' DLCs while on discount - I got the whole package for less than four Euros, which is only a fragment of price of, let's say, Diablo 3 or Torchlight 2 full price. Of course, you can get good games for free if you want. See Path of Exile for more details.
However, Hero Siege is not strictly an ARPG game, but a combination of genres. Part RPG, part twin-stick shooter, part bullet hell arcade, Hero Siege allows you to waste a lot of your time fighting various creatures in different arenas. Truth be told, Hero Siege doesn't even try to tell a story. There's none of it, unless you count some gibberish on Steam's store page which was probably written in around five minutes. After you create your character, you appear in typical RPG village. NPCs here don't tell anything interesting nor they give you any clues why you are there and what's your mission. Base game allows you to choose between one of seven available classes and DLC content unlocks several more. You can even unlock more classes with character DLCs which are unreasonably overpriced (spare me 'support the dev' stories unless you're part of MuHa Games team).
Base game consists of four acts. These acts are being unlocked as you play, aside for DLC content which is unlocked as you're buying it. Each act is a rift consisting of five stages; four stages are ending with mini boss fight, while the fifth lets you fight the act boss. Levels are randomly generated arenas, mostly rectangle shaped, although some wild shapes appear in game later. Various dungeons and crypts appear in the game with interesting Sokoban-styled puzzles providing a refreshing variety to usual slaughter. Enemies are being dispersed in waves. Between the waves you can organize your inventory or search for healing orbs.
Basically, fighting the hordes seems satisfying. Twin stick shooter mechanics are forcing you to always move and circle the enemies, trying to evade being caught in the middle. Beside enemies, you need to watch out for different environmental hazards such as flying spikes, acid rain, bullet spitting skulls etc. Every character can upgrade his skill tree which allows him/her to use different skills and fight more efficiently. Two of game currencies, crystals and gold, can be used for different purchases. Crystals are good enough for stats resetting, name changing, new hero skins and AI minion unlocking, while gold can be used to pay for items and Wormhole access which is nothing more but Diablo 3 Rift style dungeon where you fight the same fight for much better loot.
However, there are few crippling problems with Hero Siege. First of all, after trudging through five and half acts and two of them in multiplayer mode, I don't find Hero Siege interesting enough to continue playing. Yes, you can turn up the heat and raise the difficulty level; you can grind all night long to finally unlock all the rifts and all the difficulties; yes, you can collect that gold, unlock those achievements and fight your way through various wormholes, but it is being boring the same way that D3 grinding is boring. There are games out there that disguise grinding as activity vital to the game, yet Hero Siege openly confesses you've seen it all and variations of the same ol', same ol' are all that's left. As I've stated previously, this game relies solely on its players will to waste time and kill senselessly, without the need to ask any kind of questions about anything. Yes, that might work in Binding of Isaac, but that's the thing with Binding of Isaac - it IS Binding of Isaac.
Various bugs are also a serious problem for Hero Siege. Your enemies are getting stuck beyond your reach and unable to come back. Same goes with the items exploding out of arena walls and disappearing forever. An invisible walls will block your movement at the crucial moments. You will die and die again, while the frustration levels keep on rising. Inventory categorizing, equiping, dropping and selling is programmed with controller in mind and it's excruciatingly painful to interact with it using keyboard and mouse. Actually, using only keybord, since you can't use mouse to navigate the inventory. Did I mention severe lag in certain arenas that makes you move in slow motion? There you go.
The main problem with ARPG aspect of Hero Siege is its lack of progress. There's no actual progress if you're able to get epic or legendary item early in the game. And that's what happened to me and, appearantly, several other players who reviewed this game. Overpowered items gained early in the game make players lose their interest early.
Last, but not the least, I have to rate graphics as cute and sounds as damn repetitive.
So, another one of those 'how the ♥♥♥♥ to rate this one' games. Truth be told, in nine hours that I've played, I had some fun because that's what I was aiming for - a senseless, turn off your brain and click game. If you're not a demanding player, lookin' for quick and cheap fix, get Hero Siege, but wait for sale - its lack of content (story, lore, original ideas), replayability and progress scale are actually ruining the fun aspects such as interesting controlling options and bullethell mechanics.
If you're an ARPG veteran or roguelike champion and you're lookin' for a new addiction, you will not find one here. Hero Siege will probably leave you hungry, thirsty and frustrated.
***
